summary: A crash course on the data structures and algorithm patterns behind coding-interview problems: arrays, hashing, lists, stacks, trees, graphs, heaps, greedy, binary search, backtracking and dynamic programming.

unitSummaries.Section 1: Big O complexity analysis and recursion, the two foundations used to judge and build every later algorithm.
unitSummaries.Section 2: Core array and string techniques: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums and other common patterns, with their costs.
unitSummaries.Section 3: Hash maps and sets for fast lookup, existence checks and counting, with worked problems.
unitSummaries.Section 4: Linked list structure, fast and slow pointers, and in-place reversal.
unitSummaries.Section 5: Stacks, queues and monotonic stacks, including string and next-greater-element problems.
unitSummaries.Section 6: Binary trees, BST, graphs, DFS and BFS traversals, and implicit graphs.
unitSummaries.Section 7: Heaps as priority queues and their use in top-K and similar problems.
unitSummaries.Section 8: The greedy approach: when locally best choices give the global optimum, with examples.
unitSummaries.Section 9: Binary search on arrays and on solution spaces.
unitSummaries.Section 10: Backtracking for generation and constrained search problems.
unitSummaries.Section 11: Dynamic programming: the framework, one-dimensional, multi-dimensional and matrix problems.
unitSummaries.Section 12: Code templates, the stages of a coding interview and complexity and technique cheat sheets.
unitSummaries.Section 13: Difference arrays, tries, bit manipulation, intervals, modular arithmetic and Dijkstra's algorithm.
unitSummaries.Whole course: Choosing the right data structure or algorithm pattern for a described problem across the whole course.

concepts.title: What an algorithm must guarantee
concepts.question: What must an algorithm guarantee on LeetCode, and what happens when an input breaks the stated rules?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Answer a question about an input, such as the largest number in a non-empty array of positive integers, with a recipe of steps a computer can follow.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: An algorithm takes an input and produces an output that answers the question. On LeetCode it must be deterministic: the same input always gives the same output, with no randomness. It must also be correct for every valid input the problem allows.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: This recipe reads each element once. Its cost is the subject of the next ideas.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Start the running maximum at 0. Every positive integer beats 0, so after the loop the value is the largest element. The argument only covers the stated inputs: an all-negative array would leave the maximum at 0, which is not in the array.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The recipe in Python.

card.rule: A LeetCode algorithm is deterministic and correct for every input the problem statement allows.
card.limits: Its guarantees stop at the edge of the stated input. Outside the valid inputs, such as negatives where the problem promised positives, the recipe may return a wrong answer.

concepts.title: Big O: time and space complexity
concepts.question: What does big O describe about an algorithm, and which two parts does that description have?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Compare algorithms by how their cost grows as the input gets bigger, instead of by a single run.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Big O is a notation for computational complexity, which has two parts. Time complexity asks how much longer the algorithm takes as the input size grows. Space complexity asks how much more memory it uses as the input size grows.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each part is written as a function of the input size, for example O(n). The next ideas show how to build and simplify that function.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Both parts are taken relative to input size, so they describe how an algorithm behaves as problems get larger, not how it did on one example.

card.rule: Big O describes how an algorithm's running time and memory use grow relative to the input size.
card.limits: Big O says how cost grows with the input, not how long one particular run takes.

concepts.title: Choosing the variables of a complexity
concepts.question: What should the variables in a complexity function stand for, and who decides what they mean?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Write an algorithm's cost as a function, which needs variables that stand for something about the input.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: You define the variables. Each should be a value that changes between inputs and affects the algorithm, such as n for the length of an array. The letter itself is arbitrary; n is only the common convention.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The function is wrapped in a capital O. Examples are O(n), O(n²), O(log n) and O(n ⋅ m). You would say, "The time complexity of my algorithm is O(n)."

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A variable earns its place only if changing it changes the work. The longer nums is, the more elements the loop visits, so its length belongs in the function.

card.rule: Choose variables for input values that change between runs and change the work, and name them yourself.
card.limits: A quantity that stays the same between inputs, or that does not affect the work, has no place in the function. The letter you pick never matters.

concepts.title: Complexity counts growth, not exact steps
concepts.question: Why is the largest-number loop O(n) even though it also has setup and output steps?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Describe how the work changes as the input changes, without counting every single operation.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Count the steps that depend on the input. The largest-number loop runs once per element, so with n as the length of nums it takes about n steps: about 10 for 10 elements and about 10,000,000,000 for 10,000,000,000.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time O(n): the number of loop iterations grows in step with the length of nums.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Setting maxNum and outputting it cost the same few steps whatever nums is. They add a fixed amount to the count and leave the growth unchanged, so the point is how operations change as the input changes.

card.rule: Time complexity states how the number of operations grows with the input, not an exact operation count.
card.limits: An exact count can matter in practice, but it is not what time complexity reports. Steps that do not depend on the input never change the growth.

concepts.title: Ignore constant factors
concepts.question: Why do O(8n) and O(n) describe the same growth?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two algorithms differ by a constant multiplier, for example about n operations versus about 5n. Do they have different complexities?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Constants are ignored: O(9999999n) = O(8n) = O(n). What matters is how the number of operations changes as the input changes, and a constant multiplier does not change that.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Algorithm A uses about n operations and B about 5n. At n = 100 they use 100 and 500; at n = 200 they use 200 and 1000.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Doubling n doubles the operations of both, and making n ten times bigger makes both ten times bigger. Both grow linearly, so both are O(n).

card.rule: Drop constant multipliers: O(5n) is O(n).
card.limits: Dropping constants hides real differences: B really is about five times slower than A, yet both are O(n). Complexity ranks growth, not speed on one input.

concepts.title: Keep only the dominant term
concepts.question: Why does an algorithm needing n + 500 operations still count as O(n)?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A cost has several terms, such as n + 500 or n² + n. Which of them decide the complexity?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Treat the variable as tending to infinity. When terms of the same variable are added or subtracted, keep only the most powerful term and drop the rest.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: n + 500 operations is O(n). At n = 5 the total is 505 steps and the 500 supplies about 99% of them, yet the complexity is still O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: As n grows without bound, the most powerful term becomes so large that the others are effectively zero beside it. At n = 1,000,000 the 500 is about 0.05% of the 1,000,500 steps.

card.rule: With several terms in one variable, keep only the fastest-growing one.
card.limits: The result describes large inputs. For a small n the dropped terms can be most of the real cost, so a good big O does not guarantee speed on small inputs.

concepts.title: Constant time, O(1)
concepts.question: What does O(1) promise, and does it mean the algorithm is fast?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Name the best possible complexity and say exactly what it promises.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: O(1) is called constant time, or constant space when it describes memory. The algorithm always uses the same amount of resources, regardless of the input.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: It is the best complexity possible, because the cost does not grow at all with the input.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Dropping constants turns any fixed amount of work into 1, so O(5000000) = O(1). The label records only that the cost does not depend on input size.

card.rule: O(1) means the cost does not depend on the input size, not that the cost is small.
card.limits: Constant time can still be slow: five million fixed steps is O(1). The label says nothing about how large the constant is.

concepts.title: Best, average and worst case
concepts.question: Which of the three cases should represent an algorithm's complexity if you can only name one?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An algorithm can cost different amounts depending on which input of a given size it receives.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Complexity is normally discussed in three cases: the best case, the average case and the worst case.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: If you must choose one case to represent the algorithm, never choose the best case. According to the book, the worst case is the most correct choice.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: the best case describes the luckiest input, so it says the least about what the algorithm can cost. The worst case is a limit that no input exceeds.

card.rule: When one case must stand for the algorithm, use the worst case, and be ready to discuss all three.
card.limits: The choice is a reporting convention. The book also says you should be able to talk about the difference between the cases.

concepts.title: Nested loops multiply costs
concepts.question: How do you find the time complexity of a loop nested inside another loop?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the time complexity of code with loops, given the cost of what happens inside them.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A loop costs its number of iterations times the cost of one iteration. A single loop over n items with an O(1) body is O(n). When one loop sits inside another, the costs multiply.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Two nested loops over the same n items, with an O(1) body, are O(n ⋅ n) = O(n²).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each inner loop run costs O(n), because it does n steps of O(1). The outer loop starts that inner run n times, so the total is n runs of O(n) each.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: A print of a product costs O(1).

card.rule: A loop costs iterations times the cost per iteration, so nested loops multiply.
card.limits: Multiplying works when the inner count does not change with the outer iteration. If the inner count depends on the outer index, add the counts up instead.

concepts.title: Loops in a row add their costs
concepts.question: How do you combine the costs of loops that run one after another over different inputs?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the complexity of code with several loops in a row, where the loops run over different inputs.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Loops that run one after another add their costs; only nesting multiplies. With arr of length n and arr2 of length m, a pass over arr costs O(n) and a pass over arr2 costs O(m).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A pass over arr followed by a pass over arr2 is O(n + m).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: n and m are separate variables, so neither term can swallow the other and both stay in the answer.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Two loops in a row, each body O(1).

card.rule: Add the costs of loops that run in sequence, and keep a separate variable for each independent input.
card.limits: Our reading: terms in different variables cannot be merged, so O(n + m) does not shrink to O(n) unless the problem says m is never larger than n.

concepts.title: An inner loop that depends on the outer index
concepts.question: What is the time complexity when the inner loop starts at the outer loop's index, and why?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An inner loop starts from the outer loop's index, so it does less work as the outer loop advances. How many steps in total?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Add up the inner counts instead of multiplying. The inner loop runs n times at first, then n − 1, then n − 2, and so on down to 1, so the total is 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: That partial sum equals n(n + 1)/2, which is O(n²).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Count the steps directly for a small case: for n = 10 the loop body runs 10 + 9 + ... + 1 = 55 times, which matches 10 · 11 / 2.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The inner loop starts at i.

card.rule: When the inner count depends on the outer index, add the counts: 1 + 2 + ... + n is n(n + 1)/2, which is O(n²).
card.limits: A dependent loop does not always give n². The answer comes from the actual sum of the counts, which here is the series 1 + 2 + ... + n.

concepts.title: Logarithmic time and halving
concepts.question: What does O(log n) say about how an algorithm treats its remaining input at each step?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Search a large input in far fewer steps than looking at every item.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: O(log n) is logarithmic time. Somewhere in the algorithm, the input is reduced by a percentage at every step. Binary search considers n elements, then n / 2, then n / 4, cutting the search space by 50% each step.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(log n) is extremely fast. The base of the logarithm is usually 2: an input of size n takes x steps, where 2^x = n.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A logarithm is the inverse of an exponent. If the size halves each step, then after x steps about n / 2^x remain, and one item is left when 2^x = n.

card.rule: If each step cuts the remaining input by a fixed percentage, the cost is O(log n).
card.limits: The shrinking must be a percentage of what remains, repeated every step. Removing a fixed handful of items per step leaves a cost that still grows with n.

concepts.title: What counts toward space complexity
concepts.question: Which memory counts toward space complexity, and which memory is usually left out?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide which memory to count when stating the space complexity of an algorithm.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Count the memory the algorithm allocates, such as arrays and strings it creates. Do not count the space used by the input, since modifying the input is bad practice. Usually do not count the output, the answer, unless an interviewer asks you to.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A loop that only prints each element of arr uses O(1) space. The only allocation is the integer variable num, which is constant relative to n.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: space complexity asks how much more memory the algorithm uses as the input grows. The input exists whatever the algorithm does, so only what the algorithm adds is counted.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: O(1) space: only num is allocated.
blocks.code:
for num in arr:
    print(num)

card.rule: Count what the algorithm allocates; leave out the input and, usually, the output.
card.limits: An interviewer may ask you to count the output as well, and then it is included. Allocated memory that stays a fixed size is O(1), however many variables there are.

concepts.title: Space from arrays and grids
concepts.question: How do you read space complexity from the size of the arrays and grids an algorithm allocates?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the space complexity of code that creates arrays or grids.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Space grows with how much the algorithm stores. One stored value for each element of arr gives O(n). Storing a fixed fraction of the elements, such as the first 1%, gives O(n / 100) = O(n). A grid with n rows and m columns stores n ⋅ m cells.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Doubled-values array: O(n). First-1% array: O(n). Grid of n rows and m columns: O(n ⋅ m).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Space follows the same simplification rules as time, so a constant such as 1/100 is dropped. A grid has a cell for every pair of one row and one column, so its two sizes multiply.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: One new value per element.

card.rule: Space complexity is the size of what you allocate, simplified like time: drop constants and keep independent sizes.
card.limits: A structure whose size does not grow with the input stays O(1). Space complexity is about growth, so a fixed-size table is constant however big it is.

concepts.title: Recursion and the base case
concepts.question: What makes a recursive function stop, and what happens when it has nothing to stop it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Repeat a piece of logic using function calls instead of loops, and make sure the repetition ends.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Recursion is a problem-solving method in which a function calls itself. Its opposite is an iterative algorithm, which uses for and while loops. A base case is a condition at the start of a recursive function that ends the calls.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Printing 1 to 10 recursively takes 11 calls: ten that print and fn(11), which meets the base case and returns.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Without a base case, fn(i) prints i and calls fn(i + 1) forever, because the return after the call is never reached. With the check i > 10, fn(11) returns, and each earlier call returns in turn.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Print 1 to 10 recursively.

card.rule: Every recursive function needs a base case at the start that ends the calls.
card.limits: Our reading: a base case helps only if every call moves toward it. Here i grows by one each call until it passes 10.

concepts.title: Call order and local scope
concepts.question: In what order do recursive calls finish, and does each call share its variables?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Predict the output of a recursive function that acts both before and after its recursive call.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Every call exists until it returns. When a call starts another, the old one waits until the new one returns and then continues from the next line. Lines after the recursive call therefore run in the reverse order of the calls.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: each call does constant work besides its recursive call, so the work grows with the number of calls, here 4 (i = 1 to 4). All the waiting calls are alive at once at the deepest point, so the space they use also grows with the depth.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each call has its own local scope, so each has its own i. The waiting calls remember the order in which they started, and each resumes on the line after its recursive call.

blocks.label: Trace
blocks.text: With the base case i > 3, fn(1) prints 1, 2 and 3, then fn(4) returns at once. The End lines then print for i = 3, then 2, then 1.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The End line comes after the recursive call.

card.rule: A call waits for the calls it starts, so code after the recursive call runs in reverse order.
card.limits: Only lines after the recursive call run in reverse. Lines before it run in the order the calls start, as the numbers 1, 2, 3 show.

concepts.title: Breaking a problem into subproblems
concepts.question: How do base cases and a recurrence relation let a recursive function solve a problem from smaller ones?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the nth Fibonacci number (0-indexed): the sequence starts 0, 1 and each later number is the sum of the previous two.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A recurrence relation connects an answer to answers for smaller inputs, called subproblems: F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2). The base cases F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1 stop the recursion. Combine the subproblem answers to solve the original.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: calling F(3) leads to 5 calls in all, counting F(3) itself: F(2) and F(1) from F(3), then F(1) and F(0) from F(2).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: By definition the nth number is the sum of the two before it, so correct answers from the calls give a correct sum. The base cases cover the smallest inputs, where there are not two earlier numbers.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Recursive Fibonacci.

card.rule: Pair base cases with a recurrence that reduces a problem to smaller subproblems of the same kind.
card.limits: Each subproblem must be smaller and must lead to a base case. In the F(3) trace, F(1) is computed twice, so the same subproblem can repeat.

concepts.section: 2. Arrays and strings | 2.1 Arrays and strings
concepts.title: Arrays, dynamic arrays and lists
concepts.question: Which kind of array does the course mean when it says array without a qualifier?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Fix what the word array means in this course, since a strict array and a dynamic array differ.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Strictly, an array cannot be resized and a dynamic array (a list) can. The course uses the one word array for dynamic arrays and lists, as people usually do in algorithm problems.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: there is no running cost to state here. What matters is language detail: Python lists need no declared size or type, C++ asks for both and offers std::vector, and arrays and strings are implemented differently in every language.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: People who say array in an algorithm problem usually mean a dynamic array, so following that habit reads problems the way they are meant. Learn the details for the language you will use in interviews.

card.rule: In this course, array means dynamic array (list), even though a strict array cannot be resized.
card.limits: Language details differ, so learn how arrays and strings behave in the language you will use.

concepts.section: 2. Arrays and strings | 2.1 Arrays and strings
concepts.title: Mutable and immutable data
concepts.question: Why can changing one character of a string cost far more than changing one list element?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find out why changing one character of a string can cost far more than changing one list element.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Mutable data can be changed in place; immutable data cannot, so changing it means recreating the whole value. In Python and Java, strings are immutable.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Rebuilding a string of n characters to change one of them costs O(n). That is harmless for a tiny string and expensive for one of 100,000 characters.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: An immutable string cannot be edited in place, so getting 'abd' from 'abc' means building a new string and copying all n characters. Algorithms that edit a string character by character pay this each time.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With the list arr = ['a', 'b', 'c'] you can write arr[2] = 'd'. With the immutable string s = 'abc' you cannot write s[2] = 'd'; to get 'abd' you must create the new string from scratch.

card.rule: On an immutable type, one small change means rebuilding the whole value, which costs O(n) for a string of n characters.
card.limits: The cost depends on the language; Python and Java strings are immutable, so check how yours behaves.

media.alt: Table comparing time costs of seven operations on an array or list versus an immutable string. Appending to the end: amortized constant for the list, linear for the string. Popping from the end: constant versus linear. Inserting or deleting away from the end: linear for both. Modifying an element: constant for the list, linear for the string. Random access by index: constant for both. Checking whether an element exists: linear for both.

concepts.section: 2. Arrays and strings | 2.1 Arrays and strings
concepts.title: Appending to a list is amortized O(1)
concepts.question: What does amortized O(1) mean for adding an element to the end of a list?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Add elements one by one to the end of a growing list without paying a large price each time.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Append to the end of the list. The course states that appending to the end of a list is amortized O(1).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Amortized O(1) per append, so n appends cost O(n) in total.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Amortized means averaged over the whole run: the odd append may cost more, but across all appends the average per append is constant.

card.rule: Appending to the end of a list costs amortized O(1), so n appends cost O(n) in total.
card.limits: The rule is for lists. Adding a character to the end of an immutable string is a different, costlier operation.

concepts.title: Two pointers: two indexes moving along an iterable
concepts.question: What are the two pointers in the two pointers technique?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Array and string problems where one index is not enough, such as comparing items at two places while scanning.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep two integer variables, usually named i and j or left and right. Each holds an index of the array or string, and both move along the input.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Often linear: when each pointer moves in one direction only and each step is cheap, the scan stays near O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Which pointer moves, and when, is decided by the problem, so correctness comes from the rule used for those moves.

card.rule: Two pointers means two integer indexes that move along an iterable, with the moves chosen to suit the problem.
card.limits: The technique alone proves nothing: the rule for moving the pointers must fit the problem.

concepts.title: Pointers that start at the edges and move inward
concepts.question: How does the method that starts both pointers at the edges and moves them inward work?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Compare or combine elements at the two ends of one array or string, working toward the middle.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Set left = 0 and right = last index. Loop while left < right. Each pass uses the two values, then moves left forward, right backward, or both, as the problem requires.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: At most n - 1 passes for an input of length n, because the gap between the pointers shrinks every pass.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each pass moves at least one pointer closer, so the gap reaches zero and the test left < right fails.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.code:
def pairs_seen(arr):
    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
    seen = []
    while left < right:
        seen.append((arr[left], arr[right]))
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return seen

card.rule: Start left and right at the two ends, loop while left < right, and move one or both pointers each pass.
card.limits: It fits problems about the two ends; the pointers could also start elsewhere, and the moves depend on the problem.

concepts.title: Why an inward pointer loop is linear
concepts.question: Why can an inward two-pointer loop never run for more than about n passes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Justify the running time of a loop whose pointers move inward, without tracing every input.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Track the gap right - left. It starts at n - 1, and each pass moves at least one pointer one step closer, so the gap falls by at least one.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: At most n - 1 passes, so O(n) time when the work in each pass is O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The loop stops when the gap reaches zero, and the gap cannot fall more slowly than one per pass.

card.rule: Count passes by the gap: it starts at n - 1 and falls by at least one per pass, so passes are at most n - 1.
card.limits: The argument needs every pass to move a pointer; if a pass can leave both pointers in place, the loop may never end.

concepts.title: Checking a palindrome with two pointers
concepts.question: How can two pointers check whether a string reads the same forward and backward?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Return true if a string is a palindrome, meaning it reads the same forward and backward.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Compare the first and last characters with left and right. If they differ, return false. If they match, move both pointers inward and repeat until the pointers meet.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time, since each pass costs O(1) and there are at most n passes, and O(1) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Reversing swaps the first and last characters, the second and second-last, and so on, so the string equals its reverse exactly when each such pair matches.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: A string is a palindrome when each pair of characters taken from both ends matches, so compare pairs while moving both pointers inward.
card.limits: It checks a plain palindrome; a different definition, such as one that ignores some characters, needs extra logic.

concepts.title: Finding a pair that sums to a target in sorted data
concepts.question: How do two pointers find two numbers with a given sum in a sorted array?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a sorted array of unique integers and a target, return true if some pair sums to the target.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Put left at the start and right at the end. If the sum equals the target, return true. If it is too large, move right; if too small, move left. If the pointers meet, return false.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(1) space, versus O(n squared) for trying every pair.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Sorted order means moving left only raises the left value and moving right only lowers the right value, so a move never throws away a possible solution.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: In a sorted array, move right when the sum is too large and left when it is too small until the sum matches or the pointers meet.
card.limits: It relies on sorted order; on unsorted input the same moves can discard a valid pair.

concepts.title: Why discarding a pointer's value is safe
concepts.question: Why can one end value be ruled out after a single too-large sum?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Show that moving a pointer in the sorted pair-sum search never loses a solution.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Suppose the left value x and the right value y give x + y > target. Every other left value is at least x, so no partner makes y work, and y can be ruled out.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each move rules out one value for good, so there are at most n - 1 moves.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Sorted order guarantees the left value only rises as left moves, so a pair that failed at its smallest partner fails for every partner.

card.rule: If the smallest remaining partner already makes the sum too large, the larger value cannot be part of any solution, so it can be dropped.
card.limits: The argument needs sorted order and a fixed target; unsorted input gives no smallest partner.

concepts.section: Another way to use two pointers
concepts.title: Two pointers on two inputs
concepts.question: How do two pointers work when the problem gives two arrays or strings?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Process two arrays or strings together, such as combining them or checking one against the other.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Give each input its own pointer, both starting at index 0. Loop while both pointers are inside their inputs. Each pass moves one pointer or both, as the problem requires.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n + m) time when the work in each pass is O(1), with n and m the two lengths.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Which pointer moves is chosen from what the two current items show, so each input is scanned once, front to back.

card.rule: With two inputs, start one pointer per input at index 0, loop while both are in range, and move one or both each pass.
card.limits: The loop ends as soon as one input runs out, so any extra work for the other input must be handled separately.

concepts.section: Another way to use two pointers
concepts.title: Finishing the input that is left over
concepts.question: What must be done after the loop when one input still has unvisited elements?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The two-input loop stopped because one input ran out, but the other still has elements the answer needs.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: After the main loop, run up to two clean-up loops: one finishing the first input and one finishing the second. At most one of them has any work to do.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Still O(n + m): each element is visited once, either in the main loop or in a clean-up loop.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The main loop exits only when a pointer reaches its end, so the clean-up loop of the other input picks up exactly the unvisited elements.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: After the two-input loop, add a clean-up loop for each input; only one will run.
card.limits: Skip the clean-up only when the problem never needs the unvisited elements.

concepts.section: Another way to use two pointers
concepts.title: Why the two-input loop is O(n + m)
concepts.question: Why does a loop over two inputs take at most about n + m passes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Explain the running time of a two-pointer loop over two inputs of lengths n and m.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each pass moves at least one pointer forward, and pointers never move back. Together the pointers can move at most n + m times before the inputs are used up.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n + m) when the work in each pass is O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The pass count is bounded by the total number of forward moves, and the total number of forward moves is bounded by the two lengths.

card.rule: Each pass moves a pointer forward and the pointers can move at most n + m times in all, so the loop costs O(n + m).
card.limits: The bound needs each pass to move a pointer and the work per pass to be O(1).

concepts.section: Another way to use two pointers
concepts.title: Merging two sorted arrays
concepts.question: How do two pointers combine two sorted arrays into one sorted array in linear time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Combine two sorted arrays into one new sorted array.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Start a pointer at the front of each array. Compare the two front values, add the smaller to the answer and move its pointer. When one array is used up, append the rest of the other.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) with n the combined length, instead of O(n log n) for concatenating and sorting.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The smaller of the two front values must come first, because everything behind each front value is at least as large. Leftover values are larger than the exhausted array's largest.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: To merge two sorted arrays, repeatedly take the smaller front value, then append whatever remains.
card.limits: It needs both inputs to be sorted already.

concepts.section: Another way to use two pointers
concepts.title: Choosing what n and m stand for
concepts.question: Does it matter whether n names the total length or the length of one array alone?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the cost of merging two sorted arrays into one sorted array without confusion over what n means.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In big O you may define the variables as you see fit. Either keep two lengths, n and m, or let n be the combined length. Say which you chose and use it throughout.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: With n and m separate: sorting the combined array is O((n + m) log(m + n)) and the pointer merge is O(n + m). With n as the combined length: O(n log n) and O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Both definitions describe the same algorithms. The pointer merge moves a pointer every step and cannot move more than n + m times, and sorting costs the combined size times its log. Only the naming differs.

card.rule: In big O you may define the variables as you like, as long as you use one definition consistently.
card.limits: The definition must be stated and used consistently, or the result is ambiguous.

concepts.section: Another way to use two pointers
concepts.title: Testing a subsequence with two pointers
concepts.question: How can two pointers test whether one string appears in another with gaps allowed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Return true if string s is a subsequence of string t: its characters appear in t in the same order, with gaps allowed. For example, ace is a subsequence of abcde and aec is not.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep i on s and j on t. If s[i] equals t[j], move i. Move j on every pass. Return true if i reaches the end of s.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Linear in the lengths of s and t.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every character of s must be found in order, and i advances only when the next needed character is found, so i reaches len(s) exactly when all are found.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Scan t once, advance the pointer on s only on a match, and s is a subsequence if its pointer reaches the end.
card.limits: It tests order with gaps allowed, not a contiguous substring.

concepts.section: Another way to use two pointers
concepts.title: Why one pointer always moves and the other waits
concepts.question: Why does the pointer on t move every pass while the pointer on s moves only on a match?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Explain the pointer rules of the subsequence check.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The pointer j moves forward on every pass, and the pointer i moves forward only when s[i] equals t[j]. So i waits at a letter of s until that letter is found in t.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: j moves on every pass, so there are at most len(t) passes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every letter of s must be found in order, so i may move on only after its letter is found. Because j moves on every pass, no character of t is looked at twice.

card.rule: Move j on every pass and move i only when its letter is found.
card.limits: The rules fit matches that keep order; a different matching rule needs different pointer rules.

concepts.title: The two recipes are guidelines, not rules
concepts.question: Are the two pointer recipes the only ways to use two pointers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether the two common pointer recipes, edge-inward and one pointer per input, cover every two pointers problem.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Two pointers means using two integer variables to move along iterables. The two recipes are the most common patterns, but pointers can start at other indexes, and with a single input both can start at the first index and move forward.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the cost follows from how far the pointers can move, not from where they start. Pointers that only move forward over n elements, with O(1) work per move, take O(n) time.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The technique is defined by its idea, integer indexes moving along an iterable, so any start and movement that fit that idea count. The recipes are guidelines: look at what the problem needs.

card.rule: Treat the two recipes as guidelines: two pointers means integer variables moving along iterables, however they start and move.
card.limits: The recipes cover the most common cases, so check a new problem against them before inventing a variant.

concepts.title: What a subarray is
concepts.question: What makes a selection of elements a subarray rather than an arbitrary selection of elements?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Tell contiguous sections of an array apart from other selections of elements.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A subarray is a contiguous section: its elements are adjacent in the original array and keep their order. Two indexes define it, the left bound and the right bound. In [1, 2, 3, 4], [2, 3] has left bound 1 and right bound 2.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Looking at every subarray of an array of length n is at least O(n2), which is usually too slow; this is why window methods avoid it. A subarray from left to right has length right - left + 1.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Adjacent and ordered elements are fixed completely by their two bounds. Elements that skip over others, or come in a different order, break contiguity, so they are not a subarray.

card.rule: A subarray is a contiguous section of an array, fixed by its left and right bounds.
card.limits: Elements that skip over others, or come in a different order, are not a subarray.

media.alt: A row of eight boxes holding 3, 6, 2, 8, 1, 4, 1, 5. The four middle boxes (2, 8, 1, 4) are highlighted as a subarray, a contiguous section, described by a left bound at index 2 and a right bound at index 5.

concepts.title: Valid subarrays: a metric and a restriction
concepts.question: What two parts make a subarray valid in a window problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Say exactly when a subarray counts as valid in a window problem.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Validity has two parts: a constraint metric, which is an attribute of a subarray, and a numeric restriction on it. If valid means sum at most 10, the metric is the sum and the restriction is <= 10.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The metric is what you update as the window moves. If each update is O(1), a sliding window runs in O(n) for an array of length n, as the book says.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A subarray is valid exactly when its metric obeys the restriction. Naming the metric tells you what to keep track of, and the restriction tells you when the window is broken.

card.rule: A valid subarray has a constraint metric (such as its sum) that obeys a numeric restriction (such as at most 10).
card.limits: The metric and restriction must be read from the problem; the length being maximised is not the metric.

concepts.title: The sliding window: grow right, shrink left
concepts.question: How does a window find valid subarrays by moving only two bounds?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find valid subarrays of an array, where validity depends on a constraint metric and a numeric restriction.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep two bounds, left and right, starting at 0. Add an element by moving right forward. If the window becomes invalid, remove elements by moving left forward until it is valid again.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each bound moves forward only, so the window sweeps the array once instead of trying every subarray.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Moving left forward is the same as removing the leftmost element, so the window always stays a real subarray and only slides along.

card.rule: Grow the window by moving right and shrink it by moving left whenever it becomes invalid.
card.limits: The window slides right and never back, so a problem whose valid windows depend on elements that were already dropped is not a fit.
card.example: Longest subarray with sum at most 5 in [3, 2, 1, 3, 1, 1]: the window grows to [3, 2, 1], sum 6, which is too large. Removing the 3 leaves [2, 1], sum 3, valid again.

media.alt: Three stacked rows, each showing the numbers 3, 6, 2, 8, 1, 4, 1, 5 with a highlighted window. First the two leftmost boxes, then the three boxes 2, 8, 1, then the four boxes 8, 1, 4, 1. The window gains elements on its right and drops them on its left as it slides along.

concepts.title: Why the left element can be forgotten
concepts.question: Why is it safe to drop the leftmost element once the window is too large?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Justify removing the leftmost element when the window breaks its limit, for an array of positive integers.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: With positive integers, a longer subarray has a larger sum. A window that is already too large cannot be repaired by adding elements on the right.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each element leaves the window at most once, so no element is ever reconsidered.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Keeping the leftmost element would only keep the window too large, so that element can be forgotten for the rest of the algorithm.

card.rule: With positive integers, a window that is too large only gets larger on the right, so its leftmost element can be dropped for good.
card.limits: The argument needs positive integers; with negative numbers a longer subarray can have a smaller sum.

concepts.title: Spotting a sliding window problem
concepts.question: Which cues in a problem statement point to a sliding window?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether an array or string problem should be solved with a sliding window.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Look for two cues together: the problem describes valid subarrays through a constraint metric and a restriction, and it asks you to find the best valid subarray, such as the longest.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A correct window solution is typically linear, because each bound moves forward only.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A valid window can be grown and shrunk while staying valid, so the search can slide along the input in one pass.

card.rule: When a problem defines valid subarrays and asks for the best one, such as the longest, think of a sliding window.
card.limits: The cues are only a guide: some problems with them need another technique, and some window problems lack them.
card.example: Longest subarray with sum at most k: the metric is the sum. Longest substring with at most one 0: the metric is the number of zeros.

concepts.title: Tracking the metric in a single variable
concepts.question: How can a window keep its sum up to date without storing the window?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know the window's constraint metric at every step without recomputing it from scratch.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Do not keep the window in a separate array. Keep a variable curr. When right brings in an element, update curr with it. When left removes one, undo that update. The window exists only as the bounds left and right.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(1) per update. Storing the window in an array makes removing and summing O(n) operations.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: curr always equals the metric of the window because every element entering or leaving is mirrored by an update.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Keep the window's metric in one variable, updated in O(1) whenever an element enters or leaves.
card.limits: Not every metric can be kept in one integer updated in O(1); the update rule must fit the metric.

concepts.title: The sliding window loop template
concepts.question: What is the loop that implements a sliding window?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the length of the longest valid subarray, such as the longest with sum at most k.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Loop right over the input. Add the new element to the window. While the window is invalid, remove the element at left and move left forward. Then update the answer.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One for loop over right, with the shrinking handled by a while loop inside it.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: After the while loop the window is valid, so the answer is only updated from valid windows, and the window length is right - left + 1.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Add at right, shrink from left while invalid, then update the answer with right - left + 1.
card.limits: Update the answer only after the shrink step; before it the window may be invalid.

concepts.title: How many subarrays there are
concepts.question: How many subarrays does an array of n elements have, and why does that matter?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Explain why examining every subarray is too slow.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: An array of n elements has n subarrays of length 1, n - 1 of length 2, n - 2 of length 3, and so on down to 1 of length n. The total is \(\frac{n(n + 1)}{2}\).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Any algorithm that looks at every subarray takes at least O(n squared), which is usually too slow.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A length-k subarray is fixed by its starting index, and only the first n - k + 1 indexes leave room for it.

card.rule: An array of n elements has n(n + 1)/2 subarrays, so looking at all of them costs at least O(n squared).
card.limits: The count is for contiguous subarrays; subsequences and subsets are far more numerous.

concepts.title: Why a while loop inside a for loop is still O(n)
concepts.question: How can a sliding window with a while loop inside a for loop still run in O(n)?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Show that the sliding window loop is O(n) even though a while loop sits inside a for loop.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: left starts at 0, only ever increases and never passes n. So over the whole run the while loop can iterate at most n times in total, not n times per for iteration.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: right moves n times and left moves at most n times, so there are at most 2n steps: O(n) when the work per step is O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every while iteration is paid for by a move of left, and left has only n moves to spend in the entire run.

card.rule: The inner while loop shares one budget of at most n moves of left across the whole run, so the window is O(n).
card.limits: The budget argument needs left to move forward only; a loop that restarts left would lose it.

concepts.title: Worked example: the longest subarray with sum at most k
concepts.question: How does the window template solve the longest subarray with sum at most k?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given positive integers nums and an integer k, find the length of the longest subarray whose sum is at most k.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Track the window sum in curr. Add nums[right], and while curr > k subtract nums[left] and move left forward. Then update the answer with the window length.

blocks.label: Trace
blocks.text: nums = [5, 1, 3, 2, 2, 4, 1], k = 7. The window after each step is [5], [5, 1], [1, 3], [1, 3, 2], [3, 2, 2], [2, 4], [2, 4, 1]. The longest has 3 elements.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The answer is updated only after the window is valid, and every shrink drops a left element that can never be part of a valid window again.

card.rule: Add at right, shrink from the left while the sum is above k, and keep the longest valid window length.
card.limits: It needs positive integers; with negative numbers the shrinking step can throw away windows that are valid.

concepts.title: Worked example: flipping one zero in a binary string
concepts.question: How can a flip-one-zero problem be turned into a window problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a binary string, you may flip up to one 0 to a 1. Find the longest substring of 1s you can get.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Restate it as: find the longest substring with at most one 0. The constraint metric is the number of zeros and the restriction is at most one. Keep that count in curr.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A window with at most one 0 becomes all 1s after flipping that 0, so the longest such window is the answer.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Restate a flip-at-most-one problem as the longest window with at most one 0, and count zeros in curr.
card.limits: The restatement relies on the string holding only 0 and 1.

concepts.title: Counting valid windows that end at right
concepts.question: How many valid subarrays end at the current right index?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Count the valid subarrays instead of finding only the longest.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: After the shrink step the window from left to right is valid. Fix right and choose any left bound from left to right inclusive: each choice is a valid window ending at right.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Adding right - left + 1 to a running total costs O(1) per step.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: In the book's positive-number examples, a window that starts later is smaller, so it is also valid. Every valid window ends at some index right, so no valid window is counted twice.

card.rule: The number of valid windows ending at right equals the window size, right - left + 1.
card.limits: The count assumes every shorter window inside a valid window is also valid, as with positive numbers and a sum or product limit.

concepts.title: Worked example: subarrays with product below k
concepts.question: How does a window count the subarrays whose product is below k?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given positive integers nums and k, count the subarrays whose product is strictly less than k.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep the product in curr, starting at 1. Multiply by nums[right] on entry and divide by nums[left] on exit. The window is invalid while curr >= k. After shrinking, add right - left + 1 to the answer.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(1) space, since the work in each iteration is amortized constant.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every valid subarray is counted at its right end, and the window size after shrinking is the number of valid subarrays ending there.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Keep the product, shrink while it is at least k, and add the window size after each step.
card.limits: The test must be curr >= k, since the product has to be strictly less than k.

concepts.title: Fixed-size windows: add one, remove one
concepts.question: How do you slide a window whose length k is given?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A problem fixes the window length at k, for example the largest sum among all subarrays of length k.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Build the first window from indexes 0 to k - 1. Then for each i from k onward, add the element at i and remove the element at i - k, and update the answer.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each slide adds one element on the right and removes one on the left, so the window keeps exactly k elements.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.code:
def max_window_sum(nums, k):
    curr = sum(nums[:k])
    ans = curr
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        curr += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
        ans = max(ans, curr)
    return ans

card.rule: For a fixed length k, build the first window, then add index i and remove index i - k at each step.
card.limits: It applies when the length is stated; if the window must grow and shrink with a constraint, use the dynamic window.

concepts.title: Fixed windows versus dynamic windows
concepts.question: How do fixed-size and dynamic sliding windows differ in the loop?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choose the loop for a window problem: does the window keep a stated length or change size?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A dynamic window grows by moving right and shrinks from the left when the constraint breaks, so it needs a while loop. A fixed window has a stated length k and every step adds one element and removes one.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: With O(1) work per step both are O(n). A dynamic window moves each pointer at most n times, so at most 2n iterations; a fixed window makes one add and one remove per step.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A dynamic window must shrink until it is valid again, which takes a loop of unknown length. A fixed window changes by exactly one element in and one out, so no loop is needed. The statement tells you which.

card.rule: If the length is given, slide a fixed window; if validity is defined, grow and shrink a dynamic one.
card.limits: Some problems mix both ideas, so check which part of the statement fixes the window.

concepts.title: What the window needs next: hash maps
concepts.question: Can every window metric be tracked with a single integer?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know when one integer is enough to track a window's metric and when it is not.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A single integer such as a sum, a product or a count of zeros can track simple metrics. Many window problems need more and also use a hash map, which the hashing chapter introduces.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A single-integer metric costs constant extra space and an O(1) update per step, so the window stays O(n) time; the book's window example uses only three integer variables.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: a sum, a product or a count of zeros changes by one element's contribution when the window moves, so one integer suffices. Metrics about several different elements need more state, which is why a map comes in later.

card.rule: A single integer tracks simple metrics, and many other window problems also need a hash map, covered later.
card.limits: These notes cover only the integer-metric window problems.

concepts.title: What a prefix sum array holds
concepts.question: What does each entry of a prefix sum array contain?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Answer sums of subarrays quickly by recording running totals of an array.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The prefix sum array of nums has prefix[i] equal to the sum of nums from index 0 up to index i, inclusive. For [5, 2, 1, 6, 3, 8] it is [5, 7, 8, 14, 17, 25].

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Building it costs O(n) time and O(n) space. Afterwards the sum of any subarray from i to j is O(1): prefix[j] - prefix[i - 1].

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A subarray starting at index 0 is a prefix, and each entry is the sum of one such prefix. Subtracting two entries removes the shared start and leaves exactly the elements between them.

card.rule: prefix[i] is the sum of nums[0] through nums[i], inclusive.
card.limits: The definition includes nums[i] itself; an off-by-one in either direction changes every later result.

concepts.title: Subarray sums by subtraction
concepts.question: How can a prefix sum array give the sum of any subarray quickly?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the sum of the subarray from index i to index j, inclusive, quickly.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Take the sum of everything up to j and remove the sum of everything before i: prefix[j] - prefix[i - 1].

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(1) per query once the prefix array exists.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: prefix[i - 1] is the sum of all elements before index i, so subtracting it from prefix[j] leaves exactly the elements from i through j.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: The sum of nums[i..j] is prefix[j] minus the sum of everything before i, prefix[i - 1].
card.limits: At i = 0 there is no prefix[i - 1]; the answer is prefix[j] alone.

media.alt: Top: a row of eight numbers 3, 6, 2, 8, 1, 4, 1, 5 with the boxes 8, 1, 4, 1 highlighted, sum 14. Bottom: the prefix sums 3, 9, 11, 19, 20, 24, 25, 30. A long green line reaches the prefix value 25 and a short red line the value 11; 25 minus 11 gives 14, found in constant time.

concepts.title: Building a prefix sum array
concepts.question: How is a prefix sum array built in one pass?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Build the prefix sum array of nums.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Start with prefix = [nums[0]]. For each i from 1, append nums[i] plus the last value of prefix.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(n) space for the new array.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The last value of prefix is the sum of everything before index i, so adding nums[i] extends the total by one element.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Start with the first element, then append each element plus the previous prefix value.
card.limits: The loop starts at index 1; starting at 0 would add the first element twice.

concepts.title: Why prefix sums pay off
concepts.question: When does building a prefix sum array save time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Answer m subarray-sum queries on an array of length n.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Build the prefix sum once in O(n), then answer each query with one subtraction in O(1).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n + m) time and O(n) space, against O(n x m) when each query adds up its own subarray.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A query that would loop over up to n elements becomes two lookups, so the O(n) build is paid once and shared by all queries.

card.rule: Build the prefix sum once in O(n), then each of m queries costs O(1), giving O(n + m) instead of O(n x m).
card.limits: With a single query, the O(n) build costs as much as adding up the subarray.

concepts.title: Worked example: range queries against a limit
concepts.question: How does a prefix sum answer many queries that compare a range sum with a limit?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given nums, queries [x, y] and a limit, return for each query whether the sum from x to y is less than limit.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Build the prefix sum. For each query, compute prefix[y] - prefix[x] + nums[x] and compare it with limit.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n + m) time, where m is the number of queries, and O(n) space for the prefix sum.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each subtraction gives the exact range sum, so the comparison with limit decides the query.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Build the prefix sum, then answer each query with one subtraction and one comparison.
card.limits: Strictly less than the limit means equal sums are false; use < not <=.

concepts.title: Worked example: counting valid splits
concepts.question: How does a prefix sum count the ways to split an array into two parts?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Count the ways to split nums into a first part and a non-empty second part so that the first part's sum is at least the second part's sum.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Build a prefix sum. For each split index i from 0 to n - 2, the first part sums to prefix[i] and the second to prefix[n - 1] - prefix[i]. Count the splits where the first is at least the second.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(n) space with the prefix array.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each split gives two adjacent subarrays, and a prefix sum gives the sum of each in O(1).

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: For each split, the first part is prefix[i] and the second part is the total minus prefix[i].
card.limits: The second part cannot be empty, so there are only n - 1 splits to try.

concepts.title: Replacing the prefix array with a running sum
concepts.question: Can the prefix sum array be dropped to save space?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Cut the space of the split-counting solution below O(n).

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Do not store the prefix array. Compute the total once. Then keep a running left_section, adding nums[i] each step, and take the right section as total minus left_section.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(1) space, down from O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The running left_section equals prefix[i] at every step, and the right section is everything not in the left section.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Replace the stored prefix array with a running left sum and a precomputed total.
card.limits: This works only when the prefix values are needed one after another in order of index.

concepts.title: Why building a string by concatenation is slow
concepts.question: Why does adding one character at a time to a string cost O(n squared) overall?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Build a string of final length n one character at a time using simple concatenation, in a language where strings are immutable.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each concatenation creates a new string and copies the old one into it. The k-th step therefore costs about k, and the steps add up to 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: That sum is the partial sum of the series, which is O(n squared).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The step costs grow with the current length, and there are n steps, so the total is about n squared over 2.

card.rule: Concatenating one character at a time onto an immutable string costs 1 + 2 + ... + n, which is O(n squared).
card.limits: It applies only where strings are immutable; in a language with mutable strings, appending does not copy the whole string.

concepts.title: Building a string in O(n)
concepts.question: How can a string be built one character at a time in linear time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Build a returned string of length n from characters produced one at a time, in O(n) time.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In Python or JavaScript, append the characters to a list and join them once at the end. In Java, use a StringBuilder, append to it and call toString at the end.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each append is O(1), so n appends cost O(n). The final join or toString is O(n). Together O(n + n) = O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Appending to a list or builder does not copy what is already there, and only the final step copies the pieces once.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Collect characters in a list or builder, then convert once at the end: O(n) in total.
card.limits: Learn the right tool for your language; the usual list or builder is not the same in every language.

concepts.title: Subarray, subsequence and subset
concepts.question: How do a subarray, a subsequence and a subset differ?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Tell apart three words that problems use for selections of elements.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A subarray or substring is contiguous. A subsequence keeps the original relative order but its elements need not be adjacent. A subset is any selection, in any order.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: what grows is the number of candidates. An array of length n has O(n2) subarrays, since two bounds fix one, but up to 2^n subsequences or subsets, since each element is in or out.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every subarray keeps order, so it is also a subsequence, but a subsequence may skip elements, so the reverse fails. A subset also drops the order requirement. [3, 2] is not a subsequence of [1, 2, 3, 4] because it reverses the order.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For [1, 2, 3, 4]: [2, 3] is a subarray. [1, 3], [4], [2, 3] and the empty selection [] are subsequences. [3, 2] is not a subsequence because it reverses the order.

card.rule: A subarray is contiguous, a subsequence keeps order but may skip elements, and a subset ignores order.
card.limits: Every subarray is also a subsequence, but not the other way around.

concepts.title: When order matters: subsequence versus subset
concepts.question: How does the order requirement make a subsequence harder to find than a subset?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether a problem needs elements in a particular order or only needs them to exist.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In a subset the elements need only exist, and subsets with the same elements are the same subset, so [1, 2, 4] equals [4, 1, 2]. In a subsequence they must also appear in the right relative order.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: both choose from the same n elements, up to 2^n selections each. Order changes which selections are valid, not how many selections there are to consider.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A subsequence must meet everything a subset meets, plus the order, so order is the extra constraint. In [3, 2, 1] the numbers 1, 2, 3 form a subset but not a subsequence.

card.rule: A subset needs its elements to exist; a subsequence also needs them in the right order.
card.limits: If a subsequence problem's answer does not depend on order, such as a sum, treat it as a subset.

concepts.title: Choosing between the patterns from the wording
concepts.question: Which clues in a problem point to a sliding window, a prefix sum or two pointers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Pick between a sliding window, a prefix sum and two pointers from the wording of a problem.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Consider a sliding window for a subarray or substring problem with an explicit constraint, such as a sum limit or at most k unique elements, that asks for a best length, a count or a best sum. Consider a prefix sum for many subarray sums on an integer array.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A window is O(n) when its per-step work is O(1), at most 2n iterations. A prefix sum costs O(n) to build and then O(1) per subarray sum.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each clue matches what the technique saves: a window avoids examining all subarrays, at least O(n2), and a prefix sum turns each subarray sum into a subtraction. The clues are guidelines only.

blocks.label: Size of a subarray
blocks.text: The size of the subarray from i to j inclusive is j - i + 1, which is also the number of subarrays that end at j and start at i or later.

card.rule: Read the constraint and the question: limited subarrays with a best length or count suggest a window; many subarray sums suggest a prefix sum.
card.limits: The clues are only a general guideline; not every problem with them needs a window, and not every window problem has them.

concepts.title: Interface versus implementation
concepts.question: What is the difference between a data structure's interface and its implementation, and which one do you need?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide what you need to know about a data structure: the contract for using it, or the code that carries it out.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The interface is the contract: which operations you may perform, what inputs they expect and what they return. The implementation is the code that stores the data and carries those operations out. Learn the interface well enough to use the built-in version.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the cost here is study and interview time, not running time. Knowing the interface lets you use a built-in structure at once, while writing the implementation yourself would spend time the book says an interview does not ask for.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every major language ships built-in versions of the major data structures, and the book says an interview expects you to use them well, not to build them. So the interface is what matters most.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For a dynamic array the interface lists appending, inserting, removing and updating. The implementation allocates memory, tracks the size and shifts elements when something is removed.

card.rule: Learn a data structure's interface well enough to use the built-in version; treat the implementation as background.
card.limits: Implementation details still help when you discuss trade-offs, so know them in outline even though you rarely have to code them.

concepts.title: What a hash function does
concepts.question: What does a hash function take in, what does it give back, and what stays the same every time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Arrays need integer indices, but keys can be strings or other types. We need a repeatable way to turn any key into an integer below a fixed size.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A hash function takes a key and deterministically converts it to an integer below a fixed size set by the programmer. Deterministic means the same key always gives the same integer; the output always lies from 0 up to size minus 1.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Computing the integer means reading the key, so the work depends on the key: hashing a string of length m takes O(m), as the book notes later. The output never exceeds the chosen size, however many entries exist.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Determinism is what makes lookup work: a key stored under some index is found at that same index later, because the same key gives the same integer. The fixed bound keeps every index inside the array.

card.rule: A hash function maps each key to the same integer every time, and that integer is below a size the programmer chose.
card.limits: Not every integer-producing recipe is a good hash function. The book offers a letter-weighting recipe only as an illustration of turning strings into integers.

concepts.title: Hashing a string with a modulo
concepts.question: How can a string of letters become an integer inside a fixed range?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Turn a string of English letters into an integer that fits a fixed limit x.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Give each letter its place in the alphabet (a is 1, c is 3, z is 26), multiply it by its place in the string (index plus 1) and add the results. Take that total modulo x.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One pass over the characters of the string.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Taking the total modulo x leaves a value from 0 to x - 1, so the result always fits the limit. The same string always gives the same total, so the conversion is deterministic, as a hash function must be.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For abc: a gives 1 x 1 = 1, b gives 2 x 2 = 4, c gives 3 x 3 = 9, so the total is 14. With x = 10 the converted value is 14 % 10 = 4.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version of the recipe:

card.rule: Weight each letter by its place, add them up, then take the total modulo the limit.
card.limits: This is the book's teaching example, not a good hash function; real tables use better-designed ones.

concepts.section: What is the point of a hash function?
concepts.title: A hash function plus an array makes a hash map
concepts.question: How does adding a hash function to an array free us from integer-only indices?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An array reads and updates any position in constant time, but its indices must be integers and its size is fixed.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A hash function converts any input into an integer, so the converted integer can serve as the index. An array combined with a hash function is a hash map, also called a hash table or dictionary.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Reading, adding and updating by key stay constant time, like indexing into an array.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Arrays map indices to values. Hash maps map keys to values, and a key can be almost anything.

card.rule: A hash function plus an array gives key-to-value lookup in which the key can be almost anything.
card.limits: Keys can be almost anything, not anything: they usually need to be immutable, and the array behind the map still has a fixed size.

concepts.section: What is the point of a hash function?
concepts.title: Keys are immutable, values can be anything
concepts.question: What restriction usually applies to hash map keys, and what restriction applies to values?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide what may be used as a hash map key and what may be stored as a value.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Typically the only constraint on a key is that it is immutable, meaning it cannot be changed after it is created. Values can be anything. Integers, strings and tuples are safe keys; a mutable array is not.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the rule adds no running cost to add, remove or look up, which stay O(1). The price is that a mutable collection must first be converted into an immutable key, which takes work in its length.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: the key is hashed to an integer that decides where its entry sits. If a key could change after it was stored, its integer could change and the entry would no longer be found, so keys must stay fixed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A map from a pupil name (a string) to a list of that pupil's marks is fine: the key is immutable and the value can be any type.

card.rule: Keys are immutable; values can be anything.
card.limits: Immutability is a rule of thumb for keys, not a law of every language, and it says nothing against changing the value stored under a key.

concepts.section: What is the point of a hash function?
concepts.title: What a hash map offers
concepts.question: Which operations does a hash map do in constant time, and what order does iteration follow?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know what a hash map stores and which operations are cheap, so you can tell when it fits a problem.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A hash map is an unordered data structure that stores key-value pairs. You can iterate over both the keys and the values, but the iteration need not follow any order.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Adding an element, removing one, updating the value of a key and checking whether a key exists are each O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The hash function turns each key into an array position, so every operation goes straight to its entry instead of searching. That is why the cost does not depend on the number of entries, and why constant-time lookup by key makes hash maps so useful.

card.rule: A hash map does add, remove, update and exists in O(1); iteration order is not guaranteed.
card.limits: O(1) describes single operations, not a loop over all entries, and iteration order must not be relied on.

concepts.section: What is the point of a hash function?
concepts.title: Why the hash map is worth mastering
concepts.question: How large an improvement can a hash map bring, and what should you take from this chapter?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Judge how much a hash map can improve an algorithm, and what to take from the chapter.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Replace slow searching or counting with hash map lookups. Every major language has a built-in implementation, such as the dictionary in Python, so you learn its interface rather than build the structure.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The book says that for a huge number of problems a hash map reduces time complexity by a factor of O(n): a presence check that costs O(n) in an array costs O(1) in a map.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
