blocks.text: Our reading: if a loop does an O(n) search on each of n steps, replacing the search by an O(1) lookup removes one factor of n. The book states this as emphasis, not as a proof for every algorithm.

card.rule: Many problems get a factor of n faster with a hash map, so master your language's hash map interface.
card.limits: The factor of n applies to problems where the slow part is searching or counting; it is the book's emphasis, not a promise for every algorithm.

concepts.title: Hash map operations versus an array
concepts.question: Which operations cost O(1) in a hash map, and which array property does the map keep?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Arrays need O(n) to find out whether a value is present. Lookup is the weak spot hash maps fix.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In a hash map these are all O(1): add an element and associate it with a value, delete an element if it exists, and check if an element exists.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A hash map also keeps the array's useful properties at the same time cost: finding the number of elements, updating values and iterating over elements.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A hash map turns the key into an array position, so add, delete and exists go straight to the slot instead of scanning as an array search must. The book sums it up: in time complexity hash maps blow arrays out of the water.

card.rule: Hash maps make add, delete and exists O(1), where an array needs O(n) to check presence.
card.limits: Constant factors and extra space can cost more than they save on small inputs; the next ideas cover that.

concepts.title: Keys with no known maximum
concepts.question: Why can a hash map handle integer keys when we do not know how large they get?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Even when keys are integers, an array indexed by key must be at least as large as the biggest key, and you may not know that maximum in advance.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A hash map converts each key into a new integer within its own size limit, so the size of the structure does not depend on how large the key is.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The hash function's output is always below the fixed size, whatever the key's value.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Constant time per operation, and no sizing guesswork.

card.rule: A hash map does not need to know the largest key in advance.
card.limits: If the keys are small and the range is known, an array can still be leaner and faster, because a hash map carries overhead.

concepts.title: Overhead on small inputs
concepts.question: When can a hash map be slower than an array despite O(1) operations?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Big O ignores constants, so O(1) can hide real work.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Every key must pass through the hash function. For small input sizes that overhead can make a hash map slower than an array.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each operation is constant relative to the map's size, but the constant is bigger than a single array read.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The map pays a fixed hashing overhead on every operation, while the array scan pays per element. A fixed price beats a per-element price only once there are enough elements, so scanning can win on small inputs.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a toy model where a hash lookup costs 10 steps and an array scan costs 1 step per element, scanning wins when there are fewer than 10 elements.

card.rule: Hash maps carry a constant overhead, so on small inputs they can lose to an array.
card.limits: The overhead is a fixed cost; as the input grows, the O(1) versus O(n) difference outweighs it.

concepts.title: Resizing and wasted space
concepts.question: Why can resizing a hash table cost more than resizing a dynamic array, and when is space wasted?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A dynamic array is a fixed-size array that resizes itself past capacity. A hash table also sits on a fixed-size array whose size the programmer sets.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Resizing a hash table is much more expensive, because every existing key must be re-hashed into the new array.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Space can be wasted: the array may be much larger than the number of elements stored.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each key's position comes from the hash function and the array's size, so a new array means every existing key must be hashed again to find its place. A dynamic array has no such step, which is why a hash table resize is much more expensive.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Choose a limit of 10,000 but store only 10 items, and almost all slots are empty. Choose a smaller limit and a test with 100,000 items forces a costly resize.

card.rule: A hash table's fixed size forces a guess: too big wastes space, too small forces costly re-hashing.
card.limits: These costs matter when the number of elements is unknown; they do not change the O(1) cost of ordinary operations.

concepts.title: O(1) is relative to the map size
concepts.question: How does the length of a string key affect the cost of a hash map operation?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find out what the O(1) of a hash map operation is measured against, and what a long key adds.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: O(1) means constant relative to the number of entries n only. The key itself must still be hashed, and hashing a string of length m takes O(m) time.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Inserting n strings of length m each costs O(n x m) in hashing work.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Hashing reads the whole key, so its work grows with the key's length however many entries the map holds. A long key costs more than a short one even in a small map. For short, bounded keys the length is a constant and O(1) holds.

card.rule: Hash map operations are constant in the map size n, but hashing a key costs time in the key's own size.
card.limits: For short, bounded keys such as small integers, the hashing cost is a constant and can be ignored.

concepts.title: Sets for existence checks
concepts.question: When is a set a better fit than a hash map?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choose a structure when a problem only asks whether something is present.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A set uses the same mechanism as a hash table to turn keys into integers, but it does not map its keys to anything. Use it when you only care whether an element exists.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Add, remove and check-exists are each O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A set shares the hash table's mechanism, so add, remove and check-exists stay O(1). With no value stored per key, it holds exactly what an existence question needs.

card.rule: When you only need to know whether something is present, use a set.
card.limits: A set stores no value per key, so it cannot answer how many times or where.

concepts.title: Sets do not count
concepts.question: What happens when the same element is added to a set many times?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know what a set remembers when the same element is added many times, and whether it can count.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A set remembers only whether an element is present, not how many times it was added. Adding an element that is already present changes nothing.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: adding a duplicate costs the same O(1) as any add, and the set never holds a second copy, so its space grows with the number of distinct elements, not with the number of additions.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A set stores no count per element, so a repeat has nowhere to be recorded. Duplicates vanish for free, but occurrences cannot be counted; for counts, use a hash map from element to integer.

card.rule: A set records presence, not how many times an element was added.
card.limits: If counts matter, store them in a hash map from element to integer.

concepts.title: Choosing a set or a map
concepts.question: How do you decide between a set and a hash map for a problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether a problem needs a set or a hash map.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Ask what you need to remember about each key. If only that it exists, use a set. If you need something attached, such as a count or an index, use a hash map.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Both do add, remove and check in O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A set holds presence only and a map holds a value per key, so what you must remember about each key picks the structure. Both have O(1) operations, so cost does not decide between them.

card.rule: Use a set for presence; use a hash map when each key carries a value.
card.limits: If a problem seems to need only presence but later needs a count or position, the set must be replaced by a map.

concepts.title: Turning an array into a key
concepts.question: How can an ordered collection of elements serve as a hash map key when arrays are mutable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Keys should be immutable and arrays are mutable, so an array cannot be used directly as a key.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Convert the array into a unique immutable key. In Python a tuple does it: tuple(arr). In any language, join the elements into a string with a delimiter, such as commas: [1, 51, 163] becomes the string 1,51,163.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: building the key reads every element, so it costs O(length of the array) time and space for the new tuple or string. After that, adding or looking up the key is an ordinary hash map operation.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The delimiter must be a character that cannot appear in any element, otherwise different arrays could produce the same string.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Two ways to build a key in Python:
blocks.code:
arr = [1, 51, 163]
key1 = tuple(arr)
key2 = ','.join(str(x) for x in arr)
print(key2)

card.rule: Convert a mutable array to a tuple or a delimited string, then use that as the key.
card.limits: A delimiter that can occur inside an element, or no delimiter at all, can make different arrays collide.

concepts.title: The hash map interface
concepts.question: Which calls declare, read, update, delete and iterate a hash map?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know which calls check, read, write, delete, count and iterate a hash map in your language.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Java: containsKey checks, get reads, put adds or updates, remove deletes, size counts, keySet and values iterate. Python: k in d checks, d[k] reads, d[k] = v adds or updates, del d[k] deletes, len(d) counts, and loops go over d and d.values().

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: each single call is O(1), as the book says for add, remove, update and exists; a loop over all n entries visits each once, so it costs O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Both languages expose the same hash map interface, so the O(1) operations carry over between them. Reading an absent key behaves differently between languages, so check with containsKey or k in d first.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Add, update and delete in Python:

card.rule: Know how your language checks, reads, writes, deletes, counts and iterates a hash map.
card.limits: Iteration order is not guaranteed, and reading a key that is absent behaves differently between languages.

concepts.title: Speeding up repeated existence checks
concepts.question: What does it mean when an algorithm keeps asking whether an element is in a collection?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An algorithm asks again and again whether an element exists in a collection. In an array each check is O(n), so a loop around the check costs O(n squared).

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Put the elements in a hash map or set. Each existence check then costs O(1).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The loop drops from O(n squared) to O(n), usually.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The questions asked are the same; only the structure that answers them changes. A hash lookup answers exists exactly as a scan would.

blocks.label: Signal
blocks.text: Anytime your algorithm runs the check if x is in the collection inside a loop, consider a hash map or set.

card.rule: Store the elements in a set or hash map so that each repeated existence check takes O(1).
card.limits: The set takes extra space and a pass to build, so the gain is real only when the check repeats many times.

concepts.title: Two Sum with a hash map
concepts.question: How does a hash map find two numbers that add up to a target in one pass?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to the target. The same index may not be used twice.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Walk along the array. For each num, look for target minus num among the numbers already seen. Record every num with its index in a hash map after checking.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Brute force checks every pair, O(n squared). With the map each lookup is O(1), so one pass takes O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: num plus (target minus num) equals the target. If a valid pair exists, the later of the two numbers finds the earlier one already in the map.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: At each element, look up target minus the element in a map of the values seen so far.
card.limits: The check must come before the insert, otherwise an element can pair with itself.

concepts.title: Why Two Sum needs a map and not a set
concepts.question: What does the answer format tell you about whether a set or a hash map is needed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Pick the right structure for a Two Sum variant.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: If the task asks only whether a pair exists, a set of seen numbers is enough. If it asks for the indices, a hash map from value to index is needed to remember where each number was.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One pass over the numbers with O(1) set or map operations per number gives O(n) time. The set or map can grow to hold up to n numbers, so space is O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A set remembers presence but not position, so it cannot tell you the index of the match.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Boolean version with a set:

card.rule: Ask what the answer must report: presence needs a set; positions need a map.
card.limits: Anything beyond presence, such as a position, a count or a stored value, takes a map.

concepts.title: First letter to appear twice
concepts.question: How do you find the first character that appears a second time in a string?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a string guaranteed to contain a duplicate, return the first character to appear twice.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Scan left to right with a set of characters seen so far. If the current character is already in the set, return it; otherwise add it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Brute force compares each character with all earlier ones, O(n squared). With a set each check is O(1), so the scan is O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The first time a character is found in the set, every earlier character was new, so this is the earliest second appearance.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: Check the set first, then add: the first hit is the first second appearance.
card.limits: The answer is the first character to complete a repeat, which may differ from the first character that has a repeat somewhere later.

concepts.title: Space with a bounded alphabet
concepts.question: Is the space used by a set of lowercase letters O(1) or O(n)?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the space complexity of the set in the first-repeat solution.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The set holds distinct characters only, and the input uses only the 26 English letters. A constant bound means many people argue the space is O(1), and that is technically correct.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(n): one pass over the string with O(1) set operations. Space is O(1) because the set never holds more than 26 letters, or O(m) for m allowable characters.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: However long the string gets, the set cannot hold more than 26 distinct letters.

blocks.label: Interview note
blocks.text: The book says O(1) is probably a safe answer in an interview.

card.rule: A set limited to a fixed alphabet takes O(1) space.
card.limits: O(1) rests on the alphabet being bounded; with an unbounded character set the bound is the number of distinct characters.

concepts.title: Pre-processing into a set
concepts.question: How do you find values with no neighbouring value one above or one below?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: From an integer array, return every x for which x + 1 and x - 1 are both absent. A repeated valid value is reported once.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Build a set of the numbers first. Then for each value in the set, test whether x + 1 or x - 1 is in the set.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Building the set is O(n); each of the checks is O(1), so the whole algorithm is O(n) time and O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Looping over the set visits each distinct value once, so a repeated value is reported once. Building the set first makes each test for x + 1 and x - 1 a constant-time lookup instead of a scan of the array.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: Build a set first, then answer each neighbour question in O(1).
card.limits: The set costs O(n) space. Looping over the set rather than the array reports each value once.

concepts.title: Counting with a hash map
concepts.question: What structure should you reach for whenever a problem asks you to count things?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Track how many times each thing appears, whenever a problem asks you to count.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Counting means tracking frequency. Map each key to an integer, the number of times it has been seen, and add one to the key's count each time the key appears.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each update is O(1), so counting n items takes O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each key's entry holds its running total, so every occurrence updates only its own count, in O(1). After one pass each count equals that key's frequency in the input.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Count letters in Python:

card.rule: To count anything, map each key to its frequency in a hash map.
card.limits: A map is more than a single integer needs: if only one kind of element is counted, one integer variable is enough.

concepts.title: Sliding window with a counts map
concepts.question: How can a hash map check a distinct-character limit on a sliding window in constant time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the length of the longest substring with at most k distinct characters. For eceba and k = 2 the answer is 3, the substring ece.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Slide a window to the right and keep a hash map counts of the characters inside it. When counts has more than k keys the window is invalid, so shrink it from the left until it is valid again.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Checking the constraint is O(1) with the map, instead of O(n) by rescanning the window.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: counts always describes exactly the characters in the window, so its number of keys is the number of distinct characters.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: Keep a counts map for the window; shrink from the left whenever it has more than k keys.
card.limits: Without the map the constraint check would cost O(n) per step. The window grows and shrinks, so the pointers never move backwards.

concepts.title: Delete a key when its count hits zero
concepts.question: Why must a count of zero be deleted rather than left in the map?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When the window shrinks, a character may drop out of it entirely. If its key stays in counts with value 0, the map still lists a character that is no longer there.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Decrement the frequency when a character leaves the window. If it becomes 0, delete the key.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: After deleting, the number of keys is the number of distinct characters in the window, so the validity test stays accurate.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One extra O(1) delete per removal.

card.rule: Delete a key when its frequency reaches zero so that the number of keys stays honest.
card.limits: This matters when the key count is used as the measure, as with distinct characters. A plain count lookup does not suffer from a leftover zero.

concepts.title: Cost of the counts-map window
concepts.question: Why does the window with a counts map run in O(n) time and O(k) space?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the time and space cost of a sliding window that keeps a map of counts for its contents.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Move the right edge forward, adding each element to the counts map. When the window breaks its constraint or the map grows beyond k keys, remove elements from the left, deleting keys whose count reaches zero.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(n) and space is O(k). The map is trimmed whenever it grows beyond k keys, so it holds about k keys at a time, not n.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each element is added to the window once and removed at most once. Because every hash map operation is O(1), the work per step averages out to constant.

blocks.label: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: A sliding window is linear when the work inside each iteration is constant on average.

card.rule: With O(1) map operations the sliding window is O(n) time and O(k) space.
card.limits: The O(k) bound depends on deleting zero-count keys; if keys were kept, the map could grow with the number of distinct characters seen.

concepts.title: Intersection of multiple arrays by counting
concepts.question: How can counting tell which numbers appear in every one of n arrays?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given n arrays of distinct integers, return a sorted array of the numbers that appear in all of them.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Count every element across all the arrays in one hash map. Each inner array has distinct integers, so a number's count equals n exactly when it appears in all arrays. Collect those numbers and sort them.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Counting visits every element once: O(n x m) for n arrays of average length m, plus the sort of the answer.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: since each array holds distinct integers, each array adds at most 1 to a number's count. A count equal to the number of arrays therefore means every array contributed, so the number appears in all of them.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: Count all elements; the ones whose count equals the number of arrays are in every array.
card.limits: The count test needs the elements inside each array to be distinct; a repeated value inside one array would inflate its count.

concepts.title: Counting sparse keys
concepts.question: Why can a counting map beat a counting array when the keys are spread far apart?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Count how often each integer appears. An array indexed by value must be at least as large as the biggest value.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A hash map keeps one entry per distinct key that actually occurs, so its size follows the number of distinct keys, not their magnitude.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Space grows with the number of distinct keys; a counting array grows with the largest key.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A key never seen has no entry and needs no slot.

card.rule: A counting map costs space for the keys present; a counting array costs space for the largest key.
card.limits: When keys are small and densely packed, an array has less overhead and can be the better choice.

concepts.title: Equal frequencies with a set of counts
concepts.question: How can a set of frequencies show whether every character occurs equally often?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a string, decide whether all its characters have the same frequency.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Count each character with a hash map. Then put the map's values (the frequencies) into a set. All frequencies are equal when that set has exactly one element.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Counting and converting the values to a set are each O(n) for a string of length n, so time is O(n). Space equals the number of unique characters: O(1) for a 26-letter alphabet, or O(k) in general.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A set ignores duplicates, so it keeps one entry per different frequency. One entry means one frequency.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: Count with a map, then check that the set of counts has size one.
card.limits: The set of frequencies says how many distinct frequencies exist, not which characters have them.

concepts.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
concepts.title: When sliding window stops working
concepts.question: Why does a constraint like sum exactly k break the usual sliding window?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Count the subarrays that satisfy a constraint. For a constraint such as sum less than k with only positive numbers, a valid window stays valid when you drop elements from its left.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: An exact constraint, such as sum equal to k, does not have that property. A valid window can become invalid when shrunk, so the shrink-and-count logic of sliding window no longer works.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The prefix sum and hash map approach still runs in O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: With positive numbers and sum less than k, dropping an element from the left only lowers the sum, so a valid window stays valid. With sum equal to k, dropping an element can push the sum below k, so shrinking no longer preserves validity.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: These problems call for another tool: prefix sums with a hash map, covered in the next ideas.

card.rule: Sliding window needs a constraint that stays true when a valid window shrinks; exact constraints do not.
card.limits: Sliding window still works for inequality constraints on positive numbers, such as sum less than k.

concepts.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
concepts.title: Prefix sums plus a counts map
concepts.question: How do prefix sums and a counts map find subarrays with sum exactly k?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Count the subarrays whose sum equals k exactly.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums. Keep curr, the sum of everything so far, and a hash map counts of earlier prefix sums. At each index add counts[curr - k] to the answer, then record curr in counts.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: If a subarray ending here has sum k, the prefix before it was curr minus k. Each earlier occurrence of that prefix gives one such subarray.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One pass with O(1) work per element: O(n) time and O(n) space.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: At each index, the number of earlier prefix sums equal to curr - k is the number of subarrays with sum k ending here.
card.limits: Record curr after adding counts[curr - k], and start counts with the empty prefix; the next ideas explain both.

media.alt: An array 6, 5, -3, 2, -4, 8, 10 with k = 3. Marker j sits on -3 and marker i on 8. The first two numbers form a red prefix with sum 11, the stretch from -3 to 8 is green with sum 3, and everything up to the 8 is blue with sum 14. It shows that curr minus k equals the prefix sum before j.

concepts.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
concepts.title: Starting the map with the empty prefix
concepts.question: Why must the map start with counts[0] = 1?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some subarrays start at index 0. Their sum equals the whole prefix up to their end, so the matching earlier prefix is curr minus k = 0, which was never recorded.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Initialise counts with 0 mapped to 1. This stands for the prefix before the first element.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the initial entry is one map entry, so it adds O(1) time and space. The prefix-sum and counts-map algorithm still runs in O(n) over n numbers.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Without it, any subarray that starts at the first element and sums to k is missed.

card.rule: Start the counts map with 0: 1 so that subarrays beginning at index 0 are found.
card.limits: It does nothing special when every valid subarray starts after index 0, but leaving it out is still an error in general.

concepts.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
concepts.title: Why the prefix map counts frequency
concepts.question: Why can the algorithm not use a set of prefix sums instead of a counts map?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With negative numbers or zeros the same prefix sum can occur several times. For [1, -1, 1] the prefix sums are [1, 0, 1], where 1 appears twice.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each earlier occurrence of curr - k is a different starting point, so each makes its own subarray. The map must store how many times each prefix occurred.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the map holds one entry per distinct prefix sum, up to n entries, so space is O(n). Each update and lookup is O(1), so the pass over the array stays O(n) time.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A set would count each prefix sum once, however many starting points share it.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: If all numbers are positive, prefix sums strictly increase, so no sum repeats and a set would be enough.

card.rule: Repeated prefix sums create several subarrays, so store frequencies, not mere presence.
card.limits: For all-positive input a set of prefix sums works, but the constraints must allow it: check for negatives and zeros.

concepts.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
concepts.title: Same pattern, different metric
concepts.question: How can the prefix-sum pattern count subarrays with exactly k odd numbers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given positive integers nums and k, count the subarrays with exactly k odd numbers.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Let curr track the number of odd numbers seen so far instead of the sum. Add num % 2 for each element, since odd numbers give 1 and even numbers give 0. Then use the same lookup of curr - k.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The difference of two prefix odd-counts is the number of odd numbers in the subarray between them.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(n) space, identical to the sum version.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: Change what curr measures; the counts-map lookup stays the same.
card.limits: Only constraints that behave like a running total over the prefix, such as sums or counts, fit this pattern directly.

concepts.title: Grouping with an identifier key
concepts.question: How can one key identify every string in a group of anagrams?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Group the strings that are anagrams of each other. For eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat the groups are eat, tea, ate; tan, nat; and bat.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sort the letters of each string and use the sorted string as the key of a hash map whose values are lists of the original strings. The answer is the map's values.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Sorting each string costs O(m log m) for average length m, so n strings cost O(n x m log m) time and O(n x m) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Two strings are anagrams exactly when they are equal after sorting, so every member of a group shares one sorted form.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: Use a canonical form shared by the whole group, such as the sorted string, as the hash map key.
card.limits: The key must be identical for every member of a group and different across groups; a weaker key merges groups that should stay apart.

concepts.title: A count tuple as the group key
concepts.question: What trade-off does using a tuple of 26 letter counts as the key bring?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Group strings that are anagrams of each other without sorting every string.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Instead of sorting, build a tuple of 26 numbers: how often each letter occurs in the string. Anagrams have identical count tuples.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Building a key is O(m) for a string of length m, so the total is O(n x m); the 26 is a constant fixed by the problem.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Two strings are anagrams exactly when each letter occurs equally often in both, so equal tuples of 26 counts mean anagrams. A tuple is immutable, so it can serve as the hash map key.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: For short strings it can be slower than sorting, because Big O hides the constant factor of building the 26 counts.

card.rule: A 26-count tuple key gives O(n x m) but with a larger constant and a 26-letter assumption.
card.limits: It assumes only 26 possible characters, which makes it less general and less resistant to follow-up questions.

concepts.title: Shortest distance between equal elements
concepts.question: How do you find the shortest subarray that contains a repeated value?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given an array, find the length of the shortest subarray containing at least one duplicate, or -1 if none exists.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Such a subarray starts and ends with the equal pair, otherwise edge elements could be trimmed. So find the shortest distance between two equal elements. Record the indices of each value in a hash map, then compare neighbouring indices.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Indices for a value are stored in ascending order, so the closest pair is always a neighbouring pair.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time even with a nested loop, since the inner loop visits each index once overall; O(n) space.

card.rule: The shortest repeating subarray is the shortest gap between two equal elements, found with a map from value to index.
card.limits: Subarray length is gap plus one: distance between indices is one less than the number of elements covered.

concepts.title: Grouping numbers by digit sum
concepts.question: How can a map find the largest sum of two numbers that share a digit sum?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the maximum value of nums[i] + nums[j] where the two numbers have the same digit sum. Return -1 if no such pair exists.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Use the digit sum as the group identifier. Group the numbers by digit sum in a hash map, then in each group with at least two numbers take the two largest and add them.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Sorting each group may cost O(n log n) in the worst case, when all numbers share one digit sum, and the map stores every number.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Within one digit sum, the best pair is the two largest numbers of that group.

card.rule: Group by an identifier that numbers in a group share, then pick the best pair per group.
card.limits: The group identifier must be computed for every number, and the result is -1 when no group has two members.

concepts.title: Counting equal row and column pairs
concepts.question: How do two counting maps count the row and column pairs that are equal?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In an n by n grid, count the pairs (R, C) where row R and column C are equal as 1D arrays.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Convert each row and each column into a hashable key, such as a tuple or a delimited string. Count how often each key occurs among the rows and among the columns. For each key in both maps, add rows-count times columns-count.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: If x rows equal y columns, each of the x rows pairs with each of the y columns, giving x times y pairs.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each element is read twice, once as part of a row and once as part of a column: O(n squared) time and space.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: Count rows by key, count columns by key, and add the product of the two counts for every shared key.
card.limits: Arrays are mutable, so rows and columns must be converted to tuples or strings before they can be keys.

concepts.title: Hash maps keep coming back
concepts.question: Which hashing patterns from this chapter should you recognise in a new problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Recognise which hashing pattern fits a new problem.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Existence checks with a set; counting with a map from key to integer; exact-sum subarrays with prefix sums and a counts map; grouping with a derived identifier as the key.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: each pattern makes one pass with O(1) set or map operations per element, giving O(n) time and up to O(n) space; keys such as strings add the cost of hashing them.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: each pattern replaces a repeated search, count or match over earlier elements by a lookup in O(1). That is the saving the chapter describes, and it helps most where the slow step is searching, counting or matching.

card.rule: Recognise the pattern (exists, count, exact prefix, group by identifier) and reach for a set or map.
card.limits: A hash map is a tool for some problems, not all; it helps most where the slow step is searching, counting or matching.

concepts.title: Nodes joined by next pointers
concepts.question: How does a linked list keep values in order when its elements are not side by side in memory?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Keep values in a fixed order without needing the elements to sit at neighbouring memory addresses, as array elements do.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each value lives in a node object with a val field and a next pointer to the node holding the following value. The last node's next is null. The chain of pointers, not an index, carries the order.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Building a list of n values makes n nodes, so O(n) time and O(n) space. Getting from one node to its successor is one step.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Starting at the first node and following next visits every value in order, once, and stops at the node whose next is null. The pointers rebuild the sequence that adjacent addresses give an array.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Three nodes holding 1, 2, 3 linked in that order.
blocks.code:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.next = None

one = ListNode(1)
two = ListNode(2)
three = ListNode(3)
one.next = two
two.next = three
head = one
print(head.val, head.next.val, head.next.next.val)

card.rule: A linked list is nodes joined by next pointers, with null marking the end.
card.limits: A node knows only its successor, so a singly linked list cannot be walked backward, and there is no jump straight to position k.

media.alt: Three round nodes in a row holding 0, 1 and 2, with an arrow from the first node to the second and another from the second to the third: a singly linked list where each node points to its successor.

concepts.title: Keeping a reference to the head
concepts.question: Why should a program hold on to the head of a singly linked list?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Be able to reach every element of a singly linked list later, although next pointers only run forward.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep a variable pointing at the head, the node where the list starts. It is the only node from which all elements can be reached.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One variable, so O(1) extra space. Getting from the head to the k-th element takes k - 1 steps.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Links run forward only, so no later node leads back to an earlier one. If nothing refers to the head any more, the nodes after it can no longer be found.

card.rule: Keep a reference to the head so that no element of the list is lost.
card.limits: A head reference does not let you move backward, and a reference to a middle node gives no access to the nodes before it.

concepts.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
concepts.title: Linked list versus array costs
concepts.question: When is a linked list cheaper than an array for changing a position, and when is it costlier for reading one?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Pick between a linked list and a dynamic array for adding, removing and reading at an arbitrary position.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A linked list adds or removes at any position in O(1) when you already hold a reference to a node at that position. It has no random access: reaching position k means walking from the head.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Linked list: O(1) change with the reference in hand, O(n) to find the position from the head. Dynamic array: O(1) indexing, O(n) to add or remove at an arbitrary position.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Rewiring pointers touches a fixed number of nodes, so no element moves. An array keeps elements side by side, so a change in the middle shifts the rest, but the same layout gives direct indexing.

card.rule: A linked list wins at changing a position you already hold and loses at reaching a position by number.
card.limits: The O(1) change needs a reference to a node at the position. Without one you walk from the head, O(n), the same class as an array's shift.

concepts.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
concepts.title: Flexible size, pointer overhead and choice
concepts.question: Besides indexing, what do linked lists gain and cost compared with arrays, and how often does a problem let you choose?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Weigh the other trade-offs between a linked list and an array that come up in interview discussion.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A linked list has no fixed size. A dynamic array is allocated a fixed size and is resized, at some expense, once that size is exceeded. The list pays with an extra pointer stored in every node.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: both use O(n) space, but each list node adds pointer storage. For small items such as booleans or characters, a list can more than double the space an array needs.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Growing a list adds one node and moves nothing else. Every node must hold a reference besides its data, and that reference is the overhead.

card.rule: Lists grow without resizing but spend extra storage on a pointer per element.
card.limits: In most algorithm problems the list is part of the input, so you are forced to use it and make no choice. The overhead matters most for small items.

concepts.title: Assignment moves variables, not nodes
concepts.question: After ptr = head and then head = head.next, which node does each variable refer to?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Predict where each variable points after several pointer assignments, without mixing up variables and nodes.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A variable holds a reference to a node. Writing ptr = head makes ptr refer to the same node. Changing head later does not move ptr. A variable stays at its node unless that variable itself is assigned.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each assignment takes O(1) and creates no new node.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Only an assignment to a variable changes what that variable refers to. head = head.next changes head alone, so ptr keeps its node.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Start with head at the first node of 1 -> 2 -> 3.
blocks.code:
ptr = head          # ptr and head both refer to node 1
head = head.next    # head now refers to node 2
head = None         # head refers to nothing
print(ptr.val)      # 1: ptr still refers to node 1

card.rule: A variable stays at its node until that same variable is assigned.
card.limits: Changing a node's own field, such as node.next = other, is seen by every variable that refers to that node.

concepts.title: Chaining .next along the list
concepts.question: In head.next.next, which part names a node and which part is the field being read or written?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Read or change a node a few steps ahead of a pointer without extra variables.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In a chain such as head.next.next, everything before the last .next names a single node, and the last .next is a field of that node. On 1 -> 2 -> 3 with head at 1, head.next is the node 2, so head.next.next is 2's next field and refers to node 3.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each .next is one step, so a chain of two costs two steps, O(1) for a fixed chain length.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: head.next is itself a node, so any field can be taken from it. Repeating .next walks one node per use.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Cutting a 1 -> 2 -> 3 list after node 2.
blocks.code:
print(head.next.val)         # 2
print(head.next.next.val)    # 3
head.next.next = None        # node 2 is now the last

card.rule: In a chain of .next, all but the last name a node, and the last is the field you read or write.
card.limits: If any link before the last one is null, the chain fails with an error, so check for null first.

concepts.title: Traversing a list until null
concepts.question: How do you visit every node of a singly linked list in order, and what ends the loop?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Visit each node once, from the first to the last, for example to add up all the values.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Loop while the current pointer is not null: use the node, then move to its next. At the last node, next is null, so the pointer becomes null and the loop ends. A recursive version returns 0 at null and otherwise val plus the sum of the rest.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time, as each node is handled once. The loop needs O(1) extra space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each pass moves one node forward, so after n passes the pointer has stepped past the last node and is null. Every node is added once.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Iterative and recursive sums.

card.rule: Walk until the pointer is null, using each node once.
card.limits: The loop moves the pointer it is given; if that is your only reference to the head, the start is lost unless another variable holds it.

concepts.title: Inserting and deleting in a singly linked list
concepts.question: Which node must you hold to insert or delete at position i, and in what order do the pointers change?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Insert a new node so that it becomes the element at position i, or delete the element at position i, in a singly linked list.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Hold prev, the node at position i - 1. To insert, first set new.next = prev.next, then prev.next = new. To delete, set prev.next = prev.next.next, which skips the doomed node.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(1) when prev is already held. Finding prev from the head costs O(n) for an arbitrary position.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Setting prev.next first would overwrite the only link to the old successor. A deleted node could be reached only from prev, so once prev skips it, it is no longer part of the list.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Both edits.

card.rule: Hold the node before the position; when inserting, point the new node at the old successor before relinking prev.
card.limits: Everything hinges on holding the node at i - 1. Our reading: position 0 has no node before it, so this recipe does not cover it as written.

concepts.title: Doubly linked lists
concepts.question: What does a prev pointer add to a node, and what extra work does it create?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Move both ways through a list, and edit at a node when you hold only that node.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each node also stores prev, the node before it. Walking works in both directions. To add or remove at node i you need only node i, because node.prev gives the node at i - 1.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: An edit at a held node is O(1), with no search for the predecessor. Each node stores one more pointer, and every edit must update prev as well as next.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Following prev from node i reaches node i - 1, which the singly linked edit needed. Updating both directions keeps the forward and backward links in agreement.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Insert before a node and delete a node.
blocks.code:
def add_node(node, node_to_add):
    prev_node = node.prev
    node_to_add.next = node
    node_to_add.prev = prev_node
    prev_node.next = node_to_add
    node.prev = node_to_add

def delete_node(node):
    prev_node = node.prev
    next_node = node.next
    prev_node.next = next_node
    next_node.prev = prev_node

card.rule: A prev pointer lets you edit from the node itself, at the price of updating links in both directions.
card.limits: These versions fail at the ends: deleting the last node leaves next_node null, and next_node.prev then raises an error.

concepts.title: Sentinel nodes at both ends
concepts.question: How do sentinel head and tail nodes remove the special cases at the ends of a doubly linked list?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Add or remove at the front or back of a list in O(1), without null checks at the ends.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep two dummy nodes, head and tail, even when the list is empty. The real first node is head.next and the real last is tail.prev. The sentinels are not part of the list's data.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(1) to add or remove at either end, because the sentinels are always held. The price is two extra nodes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every real node has a node on each side: the last real node's next is the tail sentinel, never null. So one set of pointer updates works for first, middle and last nodes alike.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Setup, add at the end, remove from the end.
blocks.code:
head = DNode(-1)
tail = DNode(-1)
head.next = tail
tail.prev = head

def add_to_end(node_to_add):
    node_to_add.next = tail
    node_to_add.prev = tail.prev
    tail.prev.next = node_to_add
    tail.prev = node_to_add

def remove_from_end():
    if head.next is tail:
        return
    node = tail.prev
    node.prev.next = tail
    tail.prev = node.prev

card.rule: Sentinel nodes make every real node an interior node, so the ends need no special case.
card.limits: Sentinels hold no data and are not part of the list, so code that reads or counts the list must skip them, and removal must check for an empty list.

concepts.title: A dummy pointer for walking
concepts.question: How can you walk a list and still have the head afterwards?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Traverse the whole list while keeping a reference to the first node.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Set a second variable, a dummy pointer, to head and move only that variable. The head variable stays on the first node.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One extra variable, so O(1) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Assignment moves only the variable assigned. Advancing the dummy leaves head where it was, so the first node is never lost.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Walk with dummy.
blocks.code:
dummy = head
while dummy is not None:
    # use dummy.val here
    dummy = dummy.next
# head still refers to the first node

card.rule: Walk with a spare pointer and keep head where it is.
card.limits: A dummy pointer is only a variable. It does not change the list, unlike a sentinel node, which is real storage linked into it.

concepts.title: Pointer solutions beat copying into an array
concepts.question: Why does copying a list into an array miss the point of most linked list problems?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Solve a linked list problem the way an interviewer expects, instead of taking an easy route.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: You could copy all values into an array and solve there. According to the author this defeats the point and will almost guarantee failing the interview. The aim is usually to manipulate pointers cleanly in O(1) space.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The array copy uses O(n) extra space. The pointer solutions in this chapter use O(1) extra space and O(n) time.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The problems are set to test pointer rewiring and node tracking, which an array copy avoids. A pointer solution shows that skill and saves the space.

card.rule: Aim for clean pointer manipulation in O(1) space; copying the list into an array is the shortcut to avoid.
card.limits: This is the author's view of what interviews expect. The array route still gives correct answers, but with O(n) extra space and without the skill being tested.

concepts.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
concepts.title: Fast and slow pointers
concepts.question: How do two pointers moving at different speeds work through a list, and why must the loop test fast.next too?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Learn something about a list in one pass without knowing its length in advance.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Two pointers start at the head and move at different speeds: fast two nodes per iteration, slow one node. The loop runs while fast and fast.next both exist.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One pass, O(n) time, with two variables, O(1) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each iteration reads fast.next.next, so fast.next must not be null, or the code would read a field of null. Testing fast and fast.next keeps every step safe.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The skeleton.
blocks.code:
slow = head
fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    # do something here
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next

card.rule: Move fast two nodes and slow one, and loop while both fast and fast.next exist.
card.limits: The pointers can also start in different places or differ in some other way, so the speed gap is one form of a wider technique.

concepts.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
concepts.title: Finding the middle in one pass
concepts.question: How do fast and slow pointers find the middle of a list without first counting its nodes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Return the value of the middle node of a list with an odd number of nodes: for 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, return 3.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Run fast two steps and slow one step per iteration. When fast cannot move on, slow stands at the middle, since it travelled at half fast's speed.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(1) space: two pointers and one pass.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Fast needs about n / 2 iterations to reach the end. Slow takes one step per iteration, so it has taken about n / 2 steps and stands at the middle.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Middle value.
blocks.code:
def get_middle(head):
    slow = head
    fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    return slow.val

card.rule: When fast reaches the end, slow stands at the middle.
card.limits: The book states the task for an odd number of nodes. Our reading: with an even count, this loop leaves slow on the second of the two middle nodes.

concepts.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
concepts.title: Why an iteration cutoff cannot detect a cycle
concepts.question: Why does following next for a huge number of steps fail as a test for a cycle?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether a list has a cycle: some node can be reached again by following next.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: One tempting plan is to iterate a very large number of times and, if the end was never reached, decide there is probably a cycle. It is not a general solution.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The cutoff loop takes as many steps as the cutoff, and its answer can still be wrong.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: It is not correct, and the argument shows why. For any cutoff, an acyclic list with more nodes than the cutoff is wrongly judged cyclic. Raising the cutoff only invites a longer list, and a cutoff that is too large becomes impractical.

card.rule: A fixed iteration cutoff cannot prove that a list has a cycle.
card.limits: Our reading: if the list size were known to be bounded, a cutoff above the bound would be sound; the general problem gives no such bound.

concepts.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
concepts.title: Cycle detection with fast and slow pointers
concepts.question: How can a fast and a slow pointer tell whether a list has a cycle?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether a list has a cycle, whatever its length.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Move fast two nodes and slow one per iteration. If they ever meet after the start, there is a cycle. If fast reaches the end, there is none.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(1) space for n nodes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: On a straight track, the faster runner finishes the track. On a circle it laps the slower one. Once both are inside the cycle, fast gains on slow every iteration, so it is bound to catch it.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Cycle test.

card.rule: Fast and slow pointers meet if the list has a cycle, and fast reaches null if it does not.
card.limits: The pointers are equal at the start, so the check is made after moving. They meet only once both are inside the cycle.

media.alt: Two small linked-list drawings. Left, labelled as having no cycle: nodes 0, 1, 2 in a row with arrows pointing right. Right, labelled as having a cycle: four nodes 0, 1, 2, 3 in a square, with arrows 0 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 3 and 3 back to 0, so following next never ends.

concepts.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
concepts.title: Cycle detection with a set
concepts.question: How does a set of seen nodes detect a cycle, and what does it cost compared with fast and slow pointers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Detect a cycle by remembering which nodes have already been visited.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Walk with next and add each node to a set. Reaching null means no cycle. Meeting a node that is already in the set means a cycle.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(n) space, since every node may end up in the set.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A straight list never returns to a node, so a repeat can only come from a loop in the pointers. The set records each visit, so it can spot the repeat.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Set-based cycle test.

card.rule: A set finds a cycle by spotting a repeated node, at the price of O(n) space.
card.limits: Our reading: store the nodes themselves, not their values, since two different nodes can hold equal values without any cycle.

concepts.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
concepts.title: The k-th node from the end
concepts.question: How do two pointers separated by a gap of k find the k-th node from the end in one pass?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Return the k-th node from the end: for 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 and k = 2, return the node 4.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Start both pointers at the head. Move fast ahead by k nodes. Then move both one node per iteration until fast is null. Slow then stands on the k-th node from the end.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(1) space, for the same reasons as finding the middle.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The gap of k nodes does not change while both move at the same speed. When fast steps off the end, slow is k nodes behind that point, which is the k-th node from the end.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: k-th from the end.

card.rule: Open a gap of k, then move both pointers together until fast falls off the end.
card.limits: Our reading: if k is larger than the list, fast hits null during the head start and the next step fails.

concepts.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
concepts.title: Reversing a list in place
concepts.question: How do prev, curr and a saved next node reverse a singly linked list in one pass?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Turn 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 into 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 without building a new list.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Walk with curr and keep prev behind it. At each node, save nextNode = curr.next, set curr.next = prev, move prev to curr, then move curr to nextNode. When curr is null, prev is the new head.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time, since the loop runs n times with O(1) work each. O(1) space for the few pointers.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each pass flips exactly one arrow while holding on to the rest of the list. After a pass, the nodes already visited form a reversed list that ends at prev, and the nodes from curr on are untouched.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Reversal.
blocks.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        next_node = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = next_node
    return prev

card.rule: Save the next node, flip the arrow, then advance prev and curr.
card.limits: It destroys the original order: afterwards the old head is the last node, and a variable still holding the old head sees only that one node.

concepts.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
concepts.title: Why each reversal line sits where it does
concepts.question: Why must the next node be saved before the arrow is flipped, and prev moved after?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Explain why each line of the reversal loop is placed where it is.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The loop is built from needs. The arrow at curr must point to the node visited before, so prev must be tracked and moved on every pass, after the flip. Changing curr.next loses the old successor, so nextNode must be saved first.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Three pointers and O(1) work per node: O(1) space overall.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Saving nextNode keeps the rest of the list reachable. The flip reads the old prev. Only after that is prev overwritten with curr, so no line reads a value that an earlier line destroyed.

blocks.label: Trace
blocks.text: On 1 -> 2 -> 3: save 2, 1.next = null, prev = 1, curr = 2. Save 3, 2.next = 1, prev = 2, curr = 3. Save null, 3.next = 2, prev = 3, curr = null. Return 3, giving 3 -> 2 -> 1.

card.rule: Each line depends on the one before it: save, flip, then advance.
card.limits: The order is forced by what each line reads. Moving the prev update ahead of the flip makes a node point at itself.

concepts.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
concepts.title: Swapping nodes in pairs
concepts.question: Which pointers must be saved and relinked to swap each pair of nodes, and what does the function return?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Swap every pair of nodes: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 becomes 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3 -> 6 -> 5.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: For a pair A -> B: save nextNode, the node after the pair; point B back at A; remember A as prev; move head to nextNode; link the previous pair's A to the new pair's second node. Save B up front as the answer, and set A.next = nextNode so an odd leftover node stays linked.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time, with O(1) work per pair. O(1) space for the few pointers.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each pair is flipped in place while saved links keep the rest reachable, and each finished pair is reconnected to the next. The loop needs head and head.next, so a lone last node ends the loop untouched.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Swap pairs.
blocks.code:
def swap_pairs(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head
    dummy = head.next
    prev = None
    while head and head.next:
        if prev:
            prev.next = head.next
        prev = head
        next_node = head.next.next
        head.next.next = head
        head.next = next_node
        head = next_node
    return dummy

card.rule: Save what follows the pair, flip the pair, and reconnect the previous pair to it.
card.limits: The answer's head is the original second node, so the original head cannot be returned. An odd node count leaves the last node unswapped.

concepts.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
concepts.title: Planning a pointer problem from what you need
concepts.question: How should you approach a new linked list problem so that no pointer step is missed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find a correct pointer solution to a linked list problem you have not seen before.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Break the problem down: list what you need to accomplish and what each need requires. The order in which the steps occur to you need not be the order in which they run. Work from a small example such as 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4, on paper if you can.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A few minutes of planning. The chapter's solutions this way come out as O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each need becomes a pointer or an assignment, so nothing is forgotten, and a worked example exposes missed cases such as the last node. A wrong answer on LeetCode will also point at a missed step.

card.rule: List your needs, turn each into a pointer step, order the steps by what they depend on, and test on a small example.
card.limits: The order of listing is not the order of execution, so sequence the steps only after listing them.

concepts.section: Reversal as only part of an algorithm
concepts.title: Reversal as one step: maximum twin sum
concepts.question: How can finding the middle, reversing the second half and one more pointer give the maximum twin sum?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Twins are the first and last node, the second and second-last, and so on. Find the largest sum of a twin pair (LeetCode 2130).

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Find the middle with fast and slow pointers. Reverse only the second half, keeping it attached to the first. Now each node's twin is exactly n / 2 nodes ahead, so a second pointer set n / 2 ahead gives every pair sum in n / 2 steps.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time: one pass for the middle, one for the reversal, one for the sums. O(1) extra space. An array copy is simpler but uses O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Twins mirror each other around the centre. Reversing the second half turns that mirror into a fixed offset of n / 2, so one pointer can sit n / 2 ahead of the other and visit every twin pair in step.

blocks.label: Trace
blocks.text: 5 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1 becomes 5 -> 4 -> 1 -> 2 after the second half is reversed. Two nodes ahead of 5 is 1, and of 4 is 2. The sums are 6 and 6.

card.rule: Reversal can be one step: find the middle, reverse the second half, then read mirror pairs at a fixed offset.
card.limits: Reversal is a tool here, not the goal. Our reading: it changes the list, so reverse the second half back if the original order must be kept.

concepts.title: A stack adds and removes at one end
concepts.question: Which element leaves a stack first, and why?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Keep a collection in which the most recent item is the next one handled, such as the pages in a browser tab's back history.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A stack is an ordered collection where items are added and removed only at the same end, the top. Adding is pushing, removing is popping, and peek reads the top without removing it. The rule is last in, first out, written LIFO.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Every operation touches only the top, so push, pop and peek each take one step on a typical array-backed stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Because all changes happen at one end, items leave in the reverse of the order they arrived: the newest is on top and goes first.

card.rule: A stack adds and removes at one end only, so the newest item always leaves first.
card.limits: A stack gives no cheap way to reach the oldest item or the middle. If the oldest item must leave first, a stack is the wrong tool.
card.example: A tab visits A, then B, then C, so the history is [A, B, C]. One press of back removes C and leaves [A, B]; a second press leaves [A].

concepts.title: What stack operations cost
concepts.question: How fast are push, pop and search on a stack held in a dynamic array?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Judge how fast a stack is before choosing how to store it.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The cost of stack operations depends on the implementation. The most common and easiest base is a dynamic array: push adds at the array's end and pop removes from it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: On a dynamic array, push, pop and random access are each O(1), and searching for a value is O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Push and pop touch only the last slot, so no other element moves. A search has no shortcut and may have to look at every element.

card.rule: On a dynamic array, push and pop cost O(1) and searching costs O(n).
card.limits: These costs belong to the implementation, not to the stack interface itself. A stack gives no fast way to search for a value.

concepts.title: Recursion runs on a stack
concepts.question: Which stack is hidden inside every recursive program?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: See why recursion and stacks behave alike, so you can reason about the order in which calls finish.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Function calls are pushed on a stack. The call on top at any moment is the active call. When a function reaches a return statement or the end of its body, its call is popped off.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each call is one push and each return one pop, both O(1) on an array-backed stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A function that was called later must finish first, so the call pushed last is popped first. That is LIFO.

card.rule: Function calls are pushed on a stack, and the call on top is the active one.
card.limits: This explains the order in which calls finish. It does not tell you whether to prefer recursion or an explicit stack in a given problem.
card.example: main calls f, and f calls g. The stack is [main, f, g] with g active. When g returns, it is popped and f is active again.

concepts.title: Recognising a problem that needs a stack
concepts.question: What feature of a problem tells you a stack will help?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choose a stack for an algorithm problem rather than only knowing what one is.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Look for the LIFO pattern. Usually some part of the problem has input elements interacting with each other, for example matching elements together or comparing them. The most recent unresolved element is then the one to deal with first.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Spotting the pattern costs nothing at run time. The payoff is that a stack lets each element be pushed and popped about once.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A stack holds exactly the elements still waiting, with the newest on top, so the next element to resolve is always the one you can reach.

card.rule: Reach for a stack when the most recent unresolved element must be handled first.
card.limits: The LIFO pattern is sometimes hard to see. If the oldest element must be handled first, the pattern points away from a stack.

concepts.title: A stack keeps the history of earlier characters
concepts.question: What does a stack hold while you scan a string, and what is compared at each step?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Solve a string problem in which later characters must match, cancel or close earlier ones.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Scan the string from left to right, putting characters on the stack. At each step compare the top of the stack with the current character. The stack works because it saves a history of the previous characters.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One pass with O(1) stack operations per character gives O(n) time.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The top is the most recent character that is still unresolved, so comparing with it covers every case where recent history matters.

card.rule: Scan the string, push characters, and compare each new character with the top of the stack.
card.limits: This helps when the match depends on the most recent unresolved character. A problem that compares each character with an old or distant one does not fit.

concepts.title: Valid parentheses with a stack
concepts.question: How does a stack decide whether every bracket is closed by the right type in the right order?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a string of the brackets ( ) [ ] { }, decide whether every opener is closed by the same type in the correct order.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Push each opening bracket. When a closing bracket arrives, pop the most recent opener and check that it is the matching type. A mismatch means the string is invalid.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One pass with O(1) work per character, so O(n) time.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The correct order is LIFO: the last opener seen must be closed first, and the top of the stack is exactly the latest opener that is still open.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: A compact version:

card.rule: Push openers; on each closer pop the top and check that it matches.
card.limits: The scan must also handle a closer that meets an empty stack and openers left over at the end. A check on pops alone is not enough.

concepts.title: Why the bracket scan is correct and what it costs
concepts.question: In which three situations does the bracket scan reject a string, and why is it O(n)?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know exactly when the bracket scan says invalid, and bound its cost.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A string is invalid if a closer meets a different type on top, if a closer arrives when the stack is empty, or if openers remain on the stack at the end.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(n): each character is pushed at most once and popped at most once. Space is O(n) because the stack can grow with the input.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: At any moment the stack holds the openers seen so far that are not yet closed. If it is empty at the end, every opener found a matching closer.

card.rule: Reject on a mismatch, on a closer with an empty stack, or on leftover openers; the scan is O(n).
card.limits: The O(n) bound counts pushes and pops, not nested loops; a version that rescans the string for each bracket would be slower.

concepts.title: Deleting adjacent duplicates in the right order
concepts.question: Why can a deletion be impossible at first, and how does a stack handle that?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Repeatedly delete two equal characters that sit side by side until none remain, and return what is left.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Scan the string and compare the current character with the top of the stack. If they are equal they are adjacent at this moment, so pop; otherwise push. Characters between a pair are in the way and must be deleted first.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The stack holds the characters still waiting. When the top is deleted, the one beneath it becomes adjacent to the next character, so the newest is deleted first: LIFO.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: A compact version:

card.rule: Pop when the top equals the current character; otherwise push.
card.limits: The method removes equal neighbours. A rule that needs three equal in a row, or a distant pair, needs a different test.
card.example: In abbaca, bb is deleted to give aaca, and only then are the two a's adjacent. The result is ca.

concepts.title: Any structure with one working end can be the stack
concepts.question: Does a stack have to be a special stack type?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Return the final string from a stack-based scan without an extra conversion step.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Stacks are defined by their interface: add and remove at the same end. Any structure that offers that can serve, such as a list of characters or a mutable string, and the finished stack is then the answer.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Adding and removing at the last position is O(1), so the time and space stay O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Only the end where items are added and removed matters to the algorithm; the container behind it does not change the result.

card.rule: Any structure with adding and removing at one end can serve as the stack.
card.limits: A container that adds at one end and removes at the other is a queue, not a stack, even if it is used inside the same scan.

concepts.title: Typing with backspaces
concepts.question: How do you compare two typed strings in which a hash sign deletes the previous character?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two strings are typed into empty editors, where the hash sign is a backspace. Decide whether the editors show the same text.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Simulate typing with a stack: push every ordinary character, and pop on a hash sign. Build the result for each string, then compare them.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each string is read once, so time and space are linear in the input sizes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A backspace removes the most recently typed character still present, which is the top of the stack. A backspace on empty text changes nothing, so guard against popping an empty stack.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: A compact version:

card.rule: Push characters, pop on a backspace, then compare the two built strings.
card.limits: The pop must be guarded. If backspace could also delete characters typed in the other string, one stack per string would not be enough.

concepts.title: A queue adds at one end and removes at the other
concepts.question: How does a queue differ from a stack in where it adds and removes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Handle items in the order they arrive, such as people in a line at a counter.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A queue follows FIFO, first in first out. Elements are added at the back and removed from the opposite end, the front. Adding is called enqueue and removing is called dequeue.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Only the two ends are touched, so each operation can be O(1) with a suitable implementation.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The first element to enter is at the front, so it is the first to leave: arrival order is service order.

card.rule: A queue adds at the back and removes at the front, so the oldest item leaves first.
card.limits: A queue cannot give the newest item first. Problems that resolve the most recent element first need a stack instead.
