card.example: At a fast-food counter people join at the back and leave from the front after ordering. The first person to join is the first to leave.

concepts.title: Making a queue fast
concepts.question: Why does a queue on a plain array get slow, and what implementation fixes it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Make both enqueue and dequeue run in O(1) time.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: On a dynamic array, adding or removing at the front takes O(n), where n is the array size, so one end of a queue is slow. A doubly linked list that keeps pointers to its head and tail can serve as an efficient queue.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Plain array: O(n) at the front. Doubly linked list with head and tail pointers: O(1) for enqueue and dequeue.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: In a doubly linked list, with a pointer to a node you can add or delete at that location in O(1). Pointers to both ends reach both ends directly.

card.rule: A plain array queue pays O(n) at the front; a doubly linked list with head and tail pointers makes both ends O(1).
card.limits: The O(n) cost shows up on the front of an array. For a stack on an array nothing like that happens, and a small queue may not feel the cost.

concepts.title: A deque opens both ends
concepts.question: What can a deque do that an ordinary queue cannot?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Add or remove items at either end of a collection.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A deque, short for double-ended queue, lets you add and delete elements at both ends. A normal queue designates one end for adding and the other for deleting.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: With a good implementation, such as a doubly linked list, each end operation is O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Both ends are open, so one structure can serve the front and the back; a queue and a stack are both special uses of the same two ends.

card.rule: A deque allows adding and deleting at both ends.
card.limits: Opening both ends does not give cheap access to the middle. If one end is used only for adding and the other only for removal, a plain queue is enough.

concepts.title: Where queues appear in problems
concepts.question: When does a queue earn its place in algorithm problems?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know where to expect queues, so you recognise them when they appear.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In algorithm problems queues are less common than stacks. The most common use is to implement breadth-first search (BFS), an algorithm taught in a later chapter. Outside BFS, few problems have a queue as their main focus.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: As for any queue: O(1) per enqueue and dequeue with an efficient implementation.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The book gives this as a guide to frequency, not as a proof: expect a queue most of all when BFS is the plan.

card.rule: A queue is mostly used to implement BFS; few problems have a queue as their main topic.
card.limits: This describes how often queues turn up, not when they are allowed. A first come, first served job that appears in a problem still calls for a queue.

concepts.title: Counting recent calls with a queue
concepts.question: How can a queue count the calls of the last 3000 time units without rescanning old ones?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: ping(t) records a call at time t and returns how many calls happened in the range from t - 3000 to t. Times increase.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Store timestamps in a queue. On each ping, remove from the front every timestamp that is older than t - 3000, add t at the back, and return the length of the queue.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each timestamp is added once and removed once, and each queue operation is O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Because t increases, the queue is sorted with the oldest at the front. Once a timestamp is outdated it can never be counted again, so it is safe to drop.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: A compact version:

card.rule: Drop outdated timestamps from the front, add the new one at the back, and the queue length is the answer.
card.limits: The front holds the oldest timestamp only because times increase. If times could arrive out of order, checking the front would not be enough.

concepts.title: The stack interface in code
concepts.question: Which operations does the stack interface offer, and what are their names in Java and Python?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Use a stack in code, whichever language it is written in.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Java's Stack offers push, pop (removes and returns the top), peek (reads the top without removing it), empty and size. In Python a list does the same job: append, pop, stack[-1] and len.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each operation touches only the top, so each is O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Pop changes the stack and peek does not. That is the only difference between taking the top and looking at it.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version of the stack demo:
blocks.code:
stack = []
stack.append(1)
stack.append(2)
stack.append(3)
print(stack.pop())
print(stack.pop())
print(stack.pop())
stack.append(5)
print(stack[-1])

card.rule: Push and pop change the top; peek only reads it.
card.limits: Popping or peeking an empty stack is an error in most languages. Check that the stack is not empty first.

concepts.title: The queue interface in code
concepts.question: Which operations does the queue interface offer, and which end does each use?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Use a queue in code, whichever language it is written in.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In Java the Queue interface is used with a LinkedList: offer adds at the back, poll removes and returns the front, peek reads the front, and isEmpty and size report its state. In Python, collections.deque gives append at the back and popleft at the front.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each of these operations is O(1) on a linked list or a deque.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Offer and poll work at opposite ends. In Python, deque's pop() works at the back, so using it to dequeue would behave like a stack.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version:
blocks.code:
from collections import deque

queue = deque([1, 2, 3])
queue.append(4)
queue.append(5)
queue.popleft()
queue.popleft()
print(queue[0], len(queue))

card.rule: Add at the back with offer or append; remove from the front with poll or popleft.
card.limits: The names belong to the language and class. The rule that decides which end each operation uses holds in every language.

concepts.title: A monotonic stack keeps itself sorted
concepts.question: How does a monotonic stack stay sorted while new elements arrive?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Keep a stack or queue sorted as elements arrive one at a time.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A monotonic stack or queue is one whose elements are always sorted, ascending or descending depending on the algorithm. To keep the order, pop every element that would break it before pushing the new one.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each push and each pop is O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: After the violating elements are removed, the new element fits at the top, so the sorted order holds after every push.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Template for an increasing stack:

card.rule: Before pushing, pop every element that would break the sorted order.
card.limits: Popped elements are lost. The method suits problems where a popped element can no longer matter.
card.example: An increasing stack holds [1, 5, 8, 15, 23] and 14 arrives. Pop 23 and 15, then push 14 to get [1, 5, 8, 14].

concepts.title: Why the nested loop is still O(n)
concepts.question: Why does a while loop inside a for loop still give O(n) for a monotonic stack?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Bound the cost of a loop that pops elements and then pushes.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The inner while loop pops elements, but across the whole run each element can be popped at most once, because each was pushed once.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) total time for n elements. Each iteration of the for loop is amortized O(1), meaning O(1) on average over the whole run.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Total pops cannot exceed total pushes, which is n. So the inner loop body runs at most n times in total, whatever the input.

card.rule: Each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole run is O(n).
card.limits: The argument needs every element to be pushed once. A loop that pushes the same element again can break the count.

concepts.title: When a monotonic stack or queue helps
concepts.question: Which kinds of problem call for a monotonic stack or queue?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Recognise the problems where a monotonic stack or queue is the right tool.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Use one when, for each element, you must find the next element that meets a criterion, such as the next greater element. Use it also when a dynamic window of elements changes and you need to know its maximum or minimum at each step.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Typically O(n) for the whole input, because of the amortized argument.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Elements that can never be the answer are removed as soon as a better one arrives, so what remains is exactly what future steps may need.

card.rule: Look for a next-greater-style query or a window maximum or minimum.
card.limits: In harder problems the monotonic structure is only one part of the algorithm. It is not a general replacement for sorting.

concepts.title: Daily temperatures with a decreasing stack
concepts.question: How does a decreasing stack of indices find the wait for a warmer day in one pass?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: For each day, report how many days to wait for a warmer temperature, or 0 if there is none.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep a stack of the indices of days still waiting for a warmer day. For each new day i, while it is warmer than the day at the top, pop that index j and set the answer for j to i - j. Then push i.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time, since each index is pushed once and popped at most once, and O(n) space for the stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The stack's temperatures never increase from bottom to top, so the top is the coldest waiting day. The first day that beats it is its answer.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: A compact version:

card.rule: Pop waiting days that today beats, record the distance, then push today's index.
card.limits: The stack holds indices because the answer is a distance between days. Storing only temperatures would lose that.
card.example: For [40, 35, 32, 37, 50]: at 37 the days with 32 and 35 are popped, and at 50 the days with 37 and 40 are popped.

concepts.title: Why only the top of the stack needs checking
concepts.question: Why can earlier days wait while a day is compared only with the top of the stack?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Show why comparing the new day with the top of the stack is enough.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: If 32 is not warmer than 33, and 33 is not warmer than 34, then 32 is not warmer than 34: the relation is transitive. Days therefore wait on the stack, and are resolved in reverse order once a warmer day arrives.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each index is pushed once and popped once, so the whole scan is O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The stack's temperatures never increase from bottom to top. A day that fails to beat the top therefore fails to beat any day beneath it.

card.rule: A day that is not warmer than the top is not warmer than anything below it.
card.limits: This relies on the comparison being transitive. A rule that compares each element only with a fixed target needs another approach.

concepts.title: Non-increasing or strictly decreasing
concepts.question: Does the stack for daily temperatures allow equal temperatures, and what is the exact term?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Name the stack's order precisely and decide whether equal values may stay together.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Strictly speaking the stack is monotonically non-increasing, because equal temperatures can sit side by side, as in [5, 3, 3, 2]. Monotonically decreasing would mean always falling, which excludes 3, 3. The book says decreasing for short, since what matters is that the stack is sorted.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: No extra cost: only one comparison changes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: An equal day is not warmer, so it must not pop its equal neighbour. Equal values therefore stay on the stack.

card.rule: Non-increasing allows equal neighbours; strictly decreasing does not.
card.limits: A different problem may need equal values to pop each other. Check whether an equal element should remove the top.

concepts.title: Sliding window maximum with a deque
concepts.question: Which structure keeps a window's maximum available when the maximum leaves the window?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: For every window of size k sliding from left to right over an array, report its maximum.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep a deque of indices whose values decrease from front to back. For each new element, pop from the back every index with a smaller value, push the new index at the back, and pop the front if it has left the window. From the k-th element on, the front index names the window maximum.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time, because each index enters and leaves the deque once.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A smaller element that arrived earlier leaves the window before the new, larger element, so it can never be a maximum. The deque keeps only the candidates, with the best at the front.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: A compact version:

card.rule: Keep a decreasing deque of indices: smaller values leave the back, expired indices leave the front.
card.limits: The deque stores indices so that expiry can be checked. It gives maxima only; a window sum or an average needs other tools.

concepts.title: Two deques inside a sliding window
concepts.question: How do two monotonic deques let a sliding window check the largest gap in the window?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the longest subarray in which any two elements differ by at most limit.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The largest difference in a window is its maximum minus its minimum. Slide a window: add elements on the right and, while maximum minus minimum exceeds limit, shrink from the left. A decreasing deque gives the maximum at its front and an increasing deque gives the minimum.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time, since each iteration is amortized O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The two fronts are always the window's extremes, so the constraint is checked in O(1) after each change, and the window only ever grows or shrinks by one element.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: A compact version:

card.rule: Keep the window's maximum and minimum with two monotonic deques, and shrink the window while their gap is too large.
card.limits: A deque only keeps extremes. A constraint that depends on other facts about the window, such as its sum, needs a different structure.

concepts.title: Why trees and graphs get a whole chapter
concepts.question: Why does this course give trees and graphs the longest chapter, and which earlier skill does it rely on?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A learner must decide where to spend study time. Many interview problems hand over a tree or graph as the input, and the whole problem is about it.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The course ranks trees and graphs as probably the most common type of interview question and gives them its longest chapter. The chapter uses recursion heavily, so a reader unsure of it is sent back to the recursion article in chapter 1.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: No algorithm is costed here. What grows with what: the study time worth spending grows with how often these structures appear, and skipping recursion makes the chapter's code hard to follow.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: the ranking is the course's own judgement, not a measured count. It is backed by the book's observation that a huge number of problems give a tree or graph as input and are entirely about it.

card.rule: Trees and graphs are probably the most common interview topic, and the chapter assumes you can read recursion.
card.limits: The ranking is the course's own judgement about interviews, not a measured count. Treat it as advice on where to spend study time.

concepts.title: A node holds data and pointers
concepts.question: What two things does every node store, and what can the data be?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Trees and graphs need a common building block. Linked lists used nodes with one pointer, and this chapter needs the same piece for shapes with other pointer patterns.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A node is an abstract data type with two parts. It stores data, which can be an integer, a boolean, a hash map, a custom object or all of these, and it stores pointers to other nodes. The pointers fix the shape; the data is free-form.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: a node takes a fixed amount of space for its data plus one reference per pointer, so a structure's space grows with its number of nodes and pointers.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Following a pointer reaches another node, so pointers turn separate values into a structure. Linked lists already work this way with one pointer; trees and graphs reuse the idea with different pointer patterns.

card.rule: A node is data plus pointers to other nodes.
card.limits: The data is free-form, but the pointers fix the shape. A node with no pointers is an isolated value.

concepts.title: A graph is any set of nodes and pointers
concepts.question: What counts as a graph, and where do linked lists and trees fit?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Name the general structure that covers lists, trees and everything else built from nodes and pointers, so that one vocabulary serves all of them.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A graph is any collection of nodes together with their pointers to other nodes. Linked lists and trees are graphs with restrictions on how the pointers may be arranged. The field that studies graphs is called graph theory.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the size of a graph is counted by its nodes and its pointers, and the cost of any graph algorithm is later stated in those two counts.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The definition asks only for nodes and pointers, which every list and tree has, so they qualify. Extra rules such as one parent or two children only narrow it, which is why a general graph can look nothing like a list.

card.rule: A graph is any collection of nodes and the pointers between them; lists and trees are graphs.
card.limits: The definition is very loose, so a general graph can look nothing like a list or a tree. Special cases carry extra rules.

concepts.title: Vertices and edges are nodes and pointers
concepts.question: What are the other names for the nodes and pointers of a graph, and how are they drawn?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Graph writing uses two sets of words for the same parts, which can look like two separate ideas. The reader needs to map one pair onto the other.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The nodes of a graph are also called vertices, and the pointers that connect them are called edges. In drawings, vertices are usually circles and edges are lines or arrows between the circles.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Renaming costs nothing. Later costs are written with n for the number of nodes (vertices) and e for the number of edges.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The names are synonyms for the same parts, so a statement about vertices is a statement about nodes. The words say nothing about whether edges point one way or both.

card.rule: Nodes are vertices, pointers are edges.
card.limits: The words are interchangeable, so a statement about vertices is a statement about nodes. They say nothing about whether edges point one way or both.

concepts.title: Trees come first although they are graphs
concepts.question: Why does the course study trees before graphs even though a tree is a graph?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A tree is a graph, yet algorithm problems treat trees and graphs as different topics. The course has to choose which to teach first.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Start with trees. The book gives the reason that graphs are the more advanced and difficult topic, so the course teaches trees first and graphs afterwards.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the cost is study effort. Tree skills are paid for once and reused when graphs arrive, so the later topic needs less new work.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Trees need only two child pointers per node, so recursion on children can be learned before meeting nodes with any number of neighbours. Being a special case does not make the topics identical; graph problems need extra care.

card.rule: Trees are graphs, but they are taught first and treated as their own topic.
card.limits: Being a special case does not make the topics identical. A graph problem usually needs extra care that a tree problem does not.

concepts.title: The root is where a tree starts
concepts.question: What is the start of a binary tree called, and which linked list idea does it mirror?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A tree needs an entry point, as a linked list has its head. Without one there is no way to start working with it.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The start of a binary tree is called the root. The head leads along a next pointer; the root leads along pointers to its children instead.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Getting the root costs nothing, because tree problems hand it over as the input. Our reading: reaching a deeper node takes one pointer step per level below the root.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every node can be reached starting from the root, so one entry point is enough, as with the head of a list. The word names the starting node, not a position on the page.

card.rule: The root is the first node of a tree, the counterpart of a list's head.
card.limits: A tree in a drawing has its root at the top, but the word describes the starting node, not a position on the page.

concepts.title: Pointers lead from parent to child
concepts.question: What are the parent and child of a pointer, and how does a tree differ from a list in the pointer used?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Say how two nodes relate along a pointer, and how a tree pointer differs from a list pointer.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A list node's pointer leads to the next node. A tree node has pointers to its children. If node A points to node B, then B is a child of A and A is the parent of B. A tree node may have several onward pointers.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: a node's space grows with its number of child pointers. A list node has one, and a binary tree node has up to two.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The two words name the two ends of one edge, and the pointer's direction decides which end is which. They describe direction, not age or size, so a node can be a parent and a child at once.

card.rule: If A points to B, then A is B's parent and B is A's child.
card.limits: The words describe a pointer's direction, not age or size. A node can be a parent and a child at once.

concepts.title: Binary means at most two children
concepts.question: What does 'binary' limit about a node, and what are the children called?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Keep tree nodes simple enough that code can name each child directly rather than loop over an unknown number of them.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In a binary tree every node has at most two children, called the left child and the right child. At most two includes zero and one. The book notes that left and right is only a convention that suits drawings.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: each node needs room for two child references, so space per node is constant, and reaching a child is one field access.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: With the bound fixed at two, code can write node.left and node.right instead of looping over a list. The rule limits children, not parents or depth.

card.rule: A binary tree allows each node at most two children: a left child and a right child.
card.limits: The rule limits children, not parents or depth. Trees that allow more children per node exist but are not binary.

concepts.title: Zero to two children, one parent
concepts.question: What two conditions together define a binary tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether a given structure is a binary tree.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A binary tree is a collection of nodes in which every node has between 0 and 2 children and every node except the root has exactly one parent. Count the children of each node, then count the parents of each non-root node.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the test inspects each node a constant number of times, so it grows with the number of nodes n, in O(n) time.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The two conditions are the definition, so a structure that breaks either one is not a binary tree. The test covers shape only and says nothing about values, order or balance.

card.rule: Every node has 0 to 2 children, and every node except the root has exactly one parent.
card.limits: The test covers shape only. It does not say anything about values, order or balance.

media.alt: A binary tree drawn top-down with arrows from parent to child. Root 3 has children 5 (left) and 1 (right). Node 5 has children 6 and 2, node 1 has children 0 and 8, and node 2 has children 7 and 4. Nodes 6, 0, 8, 7 and 4 have no children.

concepts.title: Trees all around us
concepts.question: Which everyday structures are trees, and what are their roots and children?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Recognise trees outside code, so that a real situation can be mapped onto a tree.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: File systems, comment threads and company org charts are trees. In a comment thread the root is the original post with comments and replies below it; in an org chart the root is the CEO with direct reports below. Real trees often have more than two children per node.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: No algorithm is costed. Our reading: such a tree grows by one node for each new file, comment or employee, and its depth grows with the levels of folders, replies or management.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The book lists each example as a tree with a root and children. The company case shows why: each person has one manager and everything is connected. A real-life tree is not automatically binary.

card.rule: File systems, comment threads and org charts are trees, each with a root and children.
card.limits: A real-life tree is not automatically binary. Look at how many children each node can have.

concepts.title: Modelling a company as a tree
concepts.question: In a tree of a company, what is a node, what is an edge, and why is the CEO the root?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Model a company as a tree, to see how roots, parents and children arise from a real structure.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Make each person a node, with an edge from A to B when A manages B. The CEO, managed by nobody, is the root. Direct reports are children, and VPs, directors and so on continue below.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the tree has one node per employee and one edge per reporting line, so a company of n people has n - 1 edges.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The CEO has no manager, so has no parent, which is the root's definition. The model holds only because each person has one manager; someone with two managers would have two parents and the structure would stop being a tree.

card.rule: In an org chart tree, edges run from a manager to each direct report, and the unmanaged CEO is the root.
card.limits: If someone had two managers, that person would have two parents and the structure would stop being a tree.

concepts.title: A tree that is not binary
concepts.question: When is a tree not a binary tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Tell a tree apart from a binary tree.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A tree is not binary when some node has more than two children. A company whose CEO has six direct reports is such a tree: six children on one node, with a limit of two for binary.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: a node with k children needs a way to hold k of them, such as a list, so its space grows with k and code loops where a binary tree uses node.left and node.right.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Binary limits only the number of children per node, so six breaks it. Parents and connection are separate checks and still hold, so the structure remains a tree, but binary tree code does not apply to it unchanged.

card.rule: More than two children at any node means a tree is not binary.
card.limits: A tree that is not binary is still a tree, and none of the course's binary tree code applies to it unchanged.

concepts.title: What makes the company a tree
concepts.question: Which two properties make the company structure a tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide what makes the company, or any structure, a tree rather than a general graph.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Two properties: each person has only one manager, who is their parent, and the whole structure is connected. If you start at anyone and keep tracing managers, you always end up at the CEO.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: tracing managers up to the CEO takes one step per level, so the cost grows with the depth of the starting person.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: One parent per node gives a clean top-down shape, and connectedness puts everyone under the single top node. If either property fails, as with two managers or a team cut off from the rest, the structure is not a tree.

card.rule: A tree needs one parent per node and one connected structure.
card.limits: A structure with two managers for one person, or with a team cut off from the rest, is not a tree.

concepts.title: Everything is reachable from the root
concepts.question: Which nodes can you reach from the root, and what does a tree problem usually give you?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Reach any node of a tree when the input is a single reference.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The root is the node at the top, and every node in the tree is accessible starting from it. In most tree questions the root is the input, as the head was for linked lists. Reaching nodes means moving down child pointers.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: reaching a node takes one step per level, so the cost grows with its depth. The book later puts a full traversal of all n nodes at O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Since every node is reachable from the root, one reference gives access to all of them. Reachability runs downward only, so a reference to a deeper node does not reach nodes above or beside it.

card.rule: Every node of a tree is reachable from the root, so the root is usually all you are given.
card.limits: Reachability runs downward. A reference to some deeper node does not reach the rest.

concepts.title: Leaves are nodes without children
concepts.question: What is a leaf in a tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find where branches end, so that walks down the tree know where to stop.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A node with no children is called a leaf, and the leaf nodes are the leaves of the tree. To test a node, check its children: if it has none, it is a leaf.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the test is constant work, because it only inspects the node's own child fields.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A branch cannot continue past a node with no children, so leaves are the natural stopping place. A leaf still has a parent unless it is the only node, and a node with one child is not a leaf.

card.rule: A leaf is a node with no children.
card.limits: A leaf has no children but still has a parent unless it is the only node in the tree. A node with one child is not a leaf.

concepts.title: Depth is the distance from the root
concepts.question: How is the depth of a node measured, and what is the depth of the root?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Measure how far a node sits from the root, to order nodes by distance and later separate a tree into levels.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The depth of a node is how far it is from the root. The root has depth 0, and every child has its parent's depth plus 1, so the root's children have depth 1, their children depth 2, and so on.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: finding a node's depth means counting one per step down from the root, so the cost grows with the number of steps.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each pointer followed downward adds exactly one step of distance, so depth equals parent's depth plus 1, starting from 0. Some problems count nodes on a path and start the root at 1, so read the problem's definition first.

card.rule: A node's depth is its parent's depth plus 1, with the root at 0.
card.limits: Some problems count nodes on a path instead and so start the root at 1. Read the problem's definition before using the usual one.

concepts.title: A subtree is a node and its descendants
concepts.question: What is a subtree, and which part of a tree does a node's subtree cover?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Name a part of a tree that is itself a tree, so that problems can be split into smaller copies.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A subtree of a tree is a node together with all of its descendants. Every node starts a subtree: a leaf's subtree is the leaf alone, and the root's subtree is the whole tree.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: a subtree's size is its node plus all its descendants. Visiting the root's subtree costs all n nodes, and visiting a leaf's costs one.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Everything below a chosen node hangs from it, so the node plus all descendants is a closed piece. In a company, the engineering SVP and everyone under that person form a subtree. Nodes beside or above are outside it.

card.rule: A node's subtree is that node plus everything beneath it.
card.limits: A subtree includes all descendants, not only the children. Nodes beside or above the chosen node are outside it.

media.alt: A binary tree: root 3 with children 5 and 1; 5 has children 6 and 2; 2 has children 7 and 4; 1 has children 0 and 8. A green box encloses node 1 together with its children 0 and 8, marking the subtree rooted at 1, the right subtree of the root.

concepts.title: Any node can be treated as its own tree
concepts.question: Why can a subtree be treated as a tree of its own, and what does that make possible?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Solve a problem on a large tree by working on smaller trees of the same kind.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Detach a node from its parent and what remains below it is still a valid tree, with that node as the root.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: treating a node as its own tree needs no extra work, since the subtree is already there. The cost comes only from visiting the subtree's own nodes, one visit each.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A subtree has one top node, and each node in it has one parent and at most two children. The tree conditions hold after the cut.

card.rule: Cut a node from its parent and its subtree is a smaller, valid tree.
card.limits: This works for the subtree below a node. The nodes outside the subtree are not part of that smaller tree.

concepts.title: A tree node is an object with val, left and right
concepts.question: What fields does the TreeNode class give each node?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Represent a binary tree in code the way algorithm problems provide it.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each node is an object of a custom class. It has a val for its data, a left field for the left child and a right field for the right child.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: each node stores one value and two child fields, so space is constant per node and O(n) for n nodes. Reading val, left or right is a constant-time field access.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The two child fields match the at-most-two-children rule, and a field holds either a node or nothing.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The typical class, written here in Python.

card.rule: A TreeNode holds val, left and right.
card.limits: The class shown is the one problems typically provide. Other designs, such as a list of children, give non-binary trees.

concepts.title: You get the root and walk down with .left and .right
concepts.question: How do you reach the subtrees of the root, and what does each node carry?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A tree problem hands you a single reference, the root. Reach any part of the tree from it.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: root.left is the root's left subtree and root.right its right subtree. Chain the dots to go deeper, and read val on any node for its data.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: each .left or .right moves down one level, so reaching a node at depth d takes d steps. Reading val is constant work.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each child field holds the child node, so the chain follows the edges. The data sits in val on every node.

card.rule: Start at the root and use .left and .right to move down, reading val at each node.
card.limits: A chain breaks if a link is empty. Reading a field of an empty child fails, so check before going deeper.

concepts.title: A missing child is null
concepts.question: How does code show that a node has no left or right child, and how does it recognise a leaf?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Recognise in code when a node has no left or right child, and spot leaves.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: If a node has no left child, node.left is null; the same holds for the right child. This mirrors a list tail, whose next pointer is null. A leaf is a node whose left and right are both null.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: each check is a constant-time comparison of a field with null.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Null in a child field is how the class says nothing is attached there, so both null means no children, which is the definition of a leaf. One null child is not enough: a node with only a left child still has a child.

card.rule: A missing child is null, and a leaf has two null children.
card.limits: One null child does not make a leaf. A node with a left child but no right child still has a child.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Traversal means moving through every node
concepts.question: What is a tree traversal, and how does it differ from traversing a linked list?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Access the elements of a tree. Traversal is how we do that, so it is mandatory for solving tree problems.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A list traversal starts at the head and moves with .next. A tree traversal starts at the root and moves with .left and .right. Lists are usually traversed iteratively; trees are usually traversed recursively.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A traversal visits each node once, and with constant work per node the book puts the time at O(n) for n nodes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The idea carries over from lists: at each node there is a moment when a variable references it, and we move on by following pointers. A tree has two ways forward from a node, so one loop cannot follow it; recursion handles both branches.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The list version, in Python, sums all values.

card.rule: To traverse a tree, start at the root and follow .left and .right, usually with recursion.
card.limits: A tree has two ways forward from a node, so a single loop cannot follow it the way it follows a list.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Two kinds of traversal, three flavours of DFS
concepts.question: What are the two main kinds of tree traversal, and how many ways can a binary tree be traversed depth first?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choose how to reach every node of a tree, which needs knowing the available kinds of traversal.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: There are two main types of tree traversal: depth-first search (DFS) and breadth-first search (BFS). For binary trees, DFS has 3 forms: preorder, inorder and postorder. The book covers DFS first and BFS afterwards.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Every form visits each node once, so with constant work per node the time is O(n). Space differs by form and is covered with each one.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The three DFS forms visit the same nodes and differ only in the order of visits, so the choice among them is about ordering, not coverage. Knowing the families lets you pick the right tool.

card.rule: Traversals are DFS or BFS, and DFS on a binary tree comes in preorder, inorder and postorder forms.
card.limits: The three DFS forms visit the same nodes. They differ in the order of visits.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: DFS goes deep before wide
concepts.question: What does depth-first search prioritise, and what happens once it has chosen a direction?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Visit every node of a tree so that one branch is finished before another is started.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Depth-first search prioritises depth. It travels as far down the tree as possible in one direction, until a leaf, before considering the other direction. With left as the priority, move with node.left until the left subtree is fully explored, then explore the right.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited once with O(1) work, so time is O(n). The call stack can reach O(n) deep on a straight-line tree.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A branch is explored completely before the next one starts, which gives DFS visits a recognisable order. Left first is a choice, not a law: preferring right would mirror the order.

card.rule: DFS follows one direction to the bottom before trying the other direction.
card.limits: Left-first is a choice, not a law. You could prefer right, and the order of visits would mirror.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: DFS backtracks along branches
concepts.question: What does DFS do when it reaches the end of a branch, and what keeps track of the way back?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After DFS reaches the end of a branch, it has to get back up to the branches it has not yet explored.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The paths of a binary tree are like branches growing from the root. DFS chooses a branch and goes as far down as possible. Once it has fully explored the branch, it backtracks until it finds another unexplored branch.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(n). Space is the deepest the stack gets: O(n) for a straight-line tree, and O(log n) in the best case of a complete tree.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Because it must go back up after each dead end, DFS is typically implemented with recursion, whose call stack remembers the way up. It can also be done iteratively using a stack.

card.rule: DFS dives down a branch, then backtracks to the nearest unexplored branch, remembered by a stack.
card.limits: The stack, explicit or from recursion, is what makes backtracking possible. Without it a node cannot go back up.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: The recursive DFS function
concepts.question: What does the smallest recursive DFS function look like, and what ends the recursion?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Visit every node of a binary tree.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Return at once when the node is empty. Otherwise call the function on the left child, then on the right child. Each call to dfs(node) is a visit to that node.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Left is visited before right.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited by one call, so the work grows with the number of nodes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The empty-node check stops the recursion, and every real node makes calls on both children, so no node is left out.

card.rule: A recursive DFS stops at an empty node and calls itself on the left and right child.
card.limits: This skeleton only visits nodes. Real problems add logic around the calls.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: The four-step DFS template
concepts.question: What four steps does almost every recursive tree solution follow?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Write a tree algorithm in a form that fits many problems.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: 1. Handle the base cases, usually the empty tree. 2. Do some logic for the current node. 3. Recursively call on the current node's children. 4. Return the answer.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is handled once, so the work per node is whatever step 2 costs.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The structure is similar across problems, so only the logic at step 2 and the return value change. Steps 2 and 3 may swap order.

card.rule: Base case, logic, recursion on children, return: the shape of nearly every tree DFS.
card.limits: The template fixes the order of the work, not its content. The logic and the returned value come from the problem.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Each call answers the question for its subtree
concepts.question: What question does every call of a recursive tree function answer?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Design a recursive tree function without tracing every call by hand.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each function call solves the original problem, and returns its answer, as if the subtree rooted at the current node were the whole input.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node's call runs once, so with O(1) work per node the time is O(n). If O(k) work is done at each node, the time is O(n times k).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every subtree is a tree, so the same function works on it. The call on a child may be trusted to return the correct answer for that child's subtree.

card.rule: A call on a node returns the answer for the subtree rooted at that node.
card.limits: This trust holds only if the function really solves the full problem on any subtree, including the empty tree.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Many calls at once, each with its own node
concepts.question: While a DFS runs, how many calls exist at once, and what does each call have of its own?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Understand how DFS holds a separate state for many nodes at once without the states overwriting each other.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: During DFS many calls to the function exist at the same time. The ones waiting on the call stack each have their own version of node.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(n). The pending calls sit on the call stack, which counts as extra space, and the most that wait at once is the height of the tree: O(n) for a straight line.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every call stores its own variables, so the call for a node does not disturb the call for its parent.

card.rule: Each pending call has its own node and variables, which is why recursion on a tree works.
card.limits: The variables are separate per call, but a variable defined outside the function is shared by all calls.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Preorder: the node first
concepts.question: In preorder, when is the current node handled relative to its children?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Do the work on a node before its children, for example printing each value starting from the root.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In preorder traversal the logic for the current node is done before moving to the children. To print values, print the node, then call on the left child, then on the right child. Function calls and handling happen in the same order.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(n) for n nodes, with constant work at each visit. The call stack adds up to O(n) space in the worst case.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The logic sits at the start of each call, so the root is handled first and every node before anything beneath it. On the book's example tree the printed order is 0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 2, 5.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Preorder printing in Python.

card.rule: Preorder handles the node, then the left subtree, then the right subtree.
card.limits: Preorder is one order among three. It suits work that needs to happen at a node before its subtrees.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Inorder: left, node, right
concepts.question: In inorder, where does the current node's logic sit between the two child calls?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Do the work on a node between its left subtree and its right subtree.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In inorder traversal, first call on the left child, then do the logic on the current node, then call on the right child. No logic runs until the recursion reaches a node without a left child.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(n) for n nodes with constant work per visit. The call stack adds up to O(n) space in the worst case.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A node's value is not handled until everything in its left subtree has been, and the right subtree comes only after that. On the book's example tree the order is 3, 1, 4, 6, 0, 2, 5.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Inorder printing in Python.

card.rule: Inorder handles the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.
card.limits: The sorted-order property of inorder holds only for binary search trees, which come later in the chapter.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Postorder: children first
concepts.question: In postorder, when is a node handled relative to its children?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Do the work on a node only after both of its subtrees are finished.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In postorder traversal, call on the children first, then do the logic on the current node. No logic runs until the recursion reaches a leaf, and the root is the last node handled.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(n) for n nodes with constant work per visit. The call stack adds up to O(n) space in the worst case.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A node is handled only after its whole left subtree and then its whole right subtree, so its own work can use what they produced. On the book's example tree the order is 3, 6, 4, 1, 5, 2, 0.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Postorder printing in Python.

card.rule: Postorder handles the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the node.
card.limits: Postorder is the order to reach for when a node needs its children's results before it can do its own work.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: What pre, in and post name
concepts.question: What do the names preorder, inorder and postorder describe, and what is the only difference between them?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Tell the three DFS orders apart, and read which one a piece of code uses.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The name of each traversal describes when the current node's logic is performed. Pre: before the children. In: in the middle of the children. Post: after the children.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Moving the node's line does not change the work: every form visits each node once, so time is O(n) with constant work per node.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The three types differ only in the order in which they carry out steps 2 and 3 of the template: the logic for the node and the calls on the children.

card.rule: Pre, in and post say whether the node's work comes before, between or after its child calls.
card.limits: The left call still precedes the right call in all three. Only the position of the node's own work changes.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Tracing all three orders on one tree
concepts.question: How can you produce the preorder, inorder and postorder sequences of a given tree reliably?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a small tree, list its nodes in preorder, inorder and postorder.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Apply one rule at every node. Preorder: node, left subtree, right subtree. Inorder: left subtree, node, right subtree. Postorder: left subtree, right subtree, node.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node appears once per list, so every list has as many entries as the tree has nodes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: At each node the rule fixes where the node falls relative to the two subtree lists, so the lists are built by concatenation.

card.rule: Write the node in front of, between or behind its left and right subtree lists.
card.limits: Do the rule at every node, not only at the root. Applying it once at the top gives a wrong list.

media.alt: A binary tree with arrows from parent to child. Root 0 has children 1 (left) and 2 (right). Node 1 has children 3 (left) and 4 (right). Node 4 has only a right child, 6. Node 2 has only a right child, 5. Nodes 3, 6 and 5 are leaves.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: The DFS type rarely matters
concepts.question: When does the choice among preorder, inorder and postorder matter in practice?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide which DFS form to write when given a tree problem.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: With recursion, switching between the three forms is trivial, because only the position of the logic changes. In many problems the type does not matter as long as every node is visited. A problem that needs the children first, such as maximum depth, uses the postorder shape.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The choice costs nothing: all three forms visit each node once, so time is O(n) whichever you pick.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: For visit-everything problems every visit stores enough information whatever the order, so any form gives the same result. Order matters only when the logic needs information from earlier or later nodes. The book calls knowing the differences mostly trivia.

card.rule: Pick any DFS order that fits the logic; for visit-everything problems the order does not matter.
card.limits: Order does matter when the logic depends on information from earlier or later nodes. Then choose the form that supplies it.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Maximum depth by recursion
concepts.question: How does a node compute the maximum depth of its subtree from its children's answers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given the root of a binary tree, find the length of the longest path from the root to a leaf, counted in nodes.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: An empty tree has depth 0. Otherwise take the larger of the left and right depths and add 1 for the current node.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Recursive maximum depth in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited once with constant work, so time is O(n). The call stack can reach O(n) on a long chain.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A call on a child returns the longest path from that child down to a leaf. The best path from this node goes through whichever child is deeper, plus the node itself.

card.rule: maxDepth(node) = 1 + max(maxDepth(left), maxDepth(right)), and 0 for an empty tree.
card.limits: The shape gives the longest path only. A problem that wants the shortest path or the total of values needs a different combination.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: How a leaf answers and the +1 climbs
concepts.question: What does a leaf return in the maximum depth recursion, and how does the count grow on the way up?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the length of the longest path from the root to a leaf, counting nodes, so the root has depth 1 in this problem.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A leaf's two calls hit the base case and return 0. The leaf therefore returns 1 + max(0, 0) = 1.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited once with constant work, so time is O(n). The recursion stack can reach O(n) deep on a straight-line tree.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A leaf treated as a tree of its own has depth 1, since the only node on the path is the leaf. Each ancestor adds its own node to the best path below it.

card.rule: A leaf returns 1, and each ancestor returns one more than its deeper child.
card.limits: The values are depths counted in nodes. Counting edges instead would make the leaf return 0.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Maximum depth is a postorder walk
concepts.question: Which DFS form does the recursive maximum depth solution use, and why?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Compute the maximum depth when each node's answer depends on the answers of its children.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The recursive solution does its logic for the current node, the return statement, after the calls on the children. That makes it a postorder traversal.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited once with constant work, so time is O(n). Space is O(n) in the worst case for a straight-line tree, from the call stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A node cannot compute its depth until it knows the depths of both children, so its own work has to wait for the calls to return.

card.rule: When a node needs its children's answers first, its logic runs after the child calls: postorder.
card.limits: Not every tree problem needs this. If the logic needs no child results, any DFS form works.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Iterative DFS with a stack
concepts.question: How does an iterative DFS replace recursion, and how does it remember each node's depth?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Do a DFS without recursion, for example to find the maximum depth.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Use a stack. Push the root with its depth, then loop while the stack is not empty: pop a node, handle it, and push its children with depth + 1.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Iterative maximum depth in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is pushed and popped once, so time is O(n). The stack can hold O(n) entries in the worst case.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Recursion returns no values to hold the depths, so each stack entry carries its own depth. Every node is pushed once from its parent, so each is handled once.

card.rule: Iterative DFS: push (node, depth), pop one, update the answer, push its children.
card.limits: The pairing method depends on the language. Python stores tuples, while other languages need a pair class or two stacks.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: One loop pass is one function call
concepts.question: What does one pass of the iterative DFS loop correspond to in the recursive version?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Write DFS without recursion, for example when an interviewer asks for it.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each iteration of the while loop handles a single node, which is equivalent to one function call in the recursive version.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is pushed and popped once with constant work, so time is O(n). The stack can reach O(n) entries, the same bound as the recursive call stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: All the logic done inside the function goes into the loop body, and handling the children is done by pushing them onto the stack.

card.rule: In iterative DFS, popping a node is the same as entering a call, and pushing children is the same as calling on them.
card.limits: The loop body has no return values from children, so state that recursion would return must be carried on the stack.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: The stack reverses the push order
concepts.question: In which order does an iterative DFS visit the children of a node, relative to the order they were pushed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know which child an iterative DFS visits first, since it differs from the recursive version.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A stack removes the most recently added entry. If the code pushes node.left before node.right, the right child is popped first.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The reversal costs nothing extra: each node is still pushed and popped once, so time stays O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A stack removes the most recently added element, so pushing left before right pops right first. The visit order is opposite the insertion order, and the recursive version visits left first. The difference is irrelevant when only visiting every node matters; to visit left first, push right before left.

card.rule: A stack pops the last pushed child first, so push left then right to visit the right subtree first.
card.limits: If a problem depends on visiting the left subtree first, push the right child before the left child.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Iterative DFS: preorder is easy, recursion is the default
concepts.question: Which DFS forms are easy to write iteratively, and when should you prefer recursion?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Pick between recursive and iterative DFS when writing a solution.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: All three types of DFS can be written iteratively with a stack. Preorder is very easy; inorder and postorder are more complicated. The book says to prefer recursion and use the iterative form only if an interviewer asks for it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Both forms cost the same: O(n) time, and in the worst case O(n) space for the stack or the call stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The iterative form needs extra bookkeeping, such as pairing each node with its depth, and keeping inorder or postorder correct with a stack is harder. Recursion is shorter and more common. The iterative code can feel more intuitive if recursion is unfamiliar, and being asked for both is possible.

card.rule: Prefer recursive DFS; use the iterative form for preorder or when asked.
card.limits: Being asked for both forms in an interview is possible, so the iterative method is worth keeping in mind.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Tree DFS takes time proportional to the nodes
concepts.question: What time does a tree DFS usually take, and when does the cost per node change it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the running time of a DFS over a binary tree with n nodes.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The time complexity is almost always O(n), where n is the number of nodes.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) in total: each node is visited once, and the work done at that visit is O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A node is reached only from its parent, so no node is visited twice. Constant work at each of n visits adds up to n times a constant.

card.rule: Visiting each of n nodes once with constant work costs O(n).
card.limits: The O(n) claim needs constant work per node. Heavier work at each node multiplies the cost.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Tree DFS space follows the height
concepts.question: What space does a tree DFS use, and when is it O(n) or O(log n)?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the extra space of a tree DFS, recursive or iterative.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The largest the stack grows depends on the shape of the tree. It is linear in the height of the tree.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) in the worst case, a tree that is a straight line. O(log n) for a complete tree, which is a best case.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: At any moment the pending calls are the nodes on one path from the root. The longest such path is the height, n for a line and about log n for a full-level tree.

card.rule: DFS space is the height of the tree, so O(n) is the safe answer and O(log n) is the best case.
card.limits: Quoting O(log n) assumes a near-full tree. Without that guarantee, give O(n).

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Carry the running sum down as an argument
concepts.question: In the path sum problem, what extra information must each call know, and why add the node's value before recursing?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a root and an integer targetSum, decide whether some path from the root to a leaf has node values adding to the target.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Give the helper a second argument curr, the sum of the values from the root down to the current node. The helper dfs(node, curr) answers whether a path from this node to a leaf completes the target.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited once with constant work, so time is O(n). In the worst case, a straight line, the recursion stack grows to the number of nodes, so space is O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every path from the root into a child's subtree passes through the current node. Adding node.val to curr before calling the children keeps curr accurate at every node, and each call holds its own copy.

card.rule: Pass the sum so far into each call and add the current value before recursing.
card.limits: The extra argument works because it flows downward. It cannot describe nodes below the current one.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Path sum: empty tree and leaf checks
concepts.question: What are the two base cases of the path sum recursion, and what does each return?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide where the path sum recursion stops and what it answers there.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: An empty tree has no path, so it returns false. At a leaf, where both children are null, return whether curr plus the leaf's value equals the target.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Recursive path sum in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time, because each node is visited once with constant work. The call stack can reach O(n) space on a line-shaped tree.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A path must end at a leaf, so the sum is only tested there. A node with one child must not be treated as a leaf, since its empty side has no path.

card.rule: Empty returns false; a leaf returns whether its path sum equals the target.
card.limits: Checking the sum at a non-leaf would accept paths that stop short of a leaf.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Path sum: any path is enough
concepts.question: How are the answers from the two child calls combined, and why?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Combine the answers of the two child calls into one answer for the path-sum question.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The problem asks whether any path exists, so at a non-leaf node we return true if either the left call or the right call returns true.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited at most once with constant work, so time is O(n). The call stack adds up to O(n) space on a straight-line tree.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A true from a leaf is carried upward by the or at each ancestor. One successful path is enough to make the call on the root return true.

card.rule: For an any-path question, combine the child answers with or.
card.limits: Swapping or for and would ask a different question: whether every route works.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Good nodes: pass the maximum so far
concepts.question: What does a node need to know to decide whether it is good, and how is that passed down?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Count the good nodes of a binary tree, where a node is good if no node on the path from the root to it has a greater value.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A node is good if its value is at least the largest value on the path above it. Pass maxSoFar into each call, and update it with the current node's value before calling the children.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited once with constant work, so time is O(n). Space is O(n) for the recursion stack in the worst case.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every path from the root to a node in a subtree passes through the current node, so folding node.val into maxSoFar before the calls keeps it accurate at every node.

card.rule: Carry the largest value seen on the path and compare each node against it.
card.limits: maxSoFar summarises only the path above. It says nothing about other branches.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Good nodes: left plus right plus one
concepts.question: How does a node combine its children's counts to count the good nodes in its own subtree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Return the number of good nodes in the subtree rooted at node, given the maximum seen so far.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The count for a subtree is the count from the left subtree, plus the count from the right subtree, plus 1 if the current node is itself good.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Recursive good node count in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(n) space, as for the other DFS examples: each node is visited once with constant work.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every node in the subtree lies in the left subtree, the right subtree or is the current node, so the three parts cover it with no overlap.

card.rule: good(subtree) = good(left) + good(right) + 1 if the current node is good, with 0 for an empty tree.
card.limits: The recurrence counts nodes, so it adds the sides. A question asking for a maximum or a boolean needs another combination.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Same tree: the recursive definition
concepts.question: When are two binary trees the same, and why is that definition recursive?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given the roots p and q of two binary trees, check whether they are the same: structurally identical with equal values at matching nodes.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Two trees are the same when three things hold. The two roots have equal values, the two left subtrees are the same, and the two right subtrees are the same.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each pair of matching nodes is compared once with constant work, so time is O(n). The recursion stack adds O(n) space in the worst case.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: If two trees are the same, their matching subtrees must also be the same, so the definition refers to itself on smaller trees.

card.rule: Trees p and q are the same when p.val equals q.val and both pairs of subtrees are the same.
card.limits: The check compares matching positions only. The same values in different positions do not make the trees the same.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Same tree: base cases
concepts.question: What should the comparison return when one or both nodes are empty?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide where the same-tree recursion stops.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: If both nodes are null, they are the same empty tree: return true. If exactly one is null, the trees differ: return false.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The base cases end the recursion in constant time. Overall, each pair of nodes is visited once, so time is O(n) and space is O(n) for the call stack at worst.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Test the recursion on two one-node trees with equal values. The value check passes, and both pairs of children are null, so both child calls return true.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Recursive same-tree check in Python.

card.rule: Both null is true; one null is false; otherwise compare values and recurse.
card.limits: Check both-null before either-null, or an empty pair would be called different.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Same tree: combine with and
concepts.question: How are the checks combined, and how does the iterative version express the same logic?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether two trees match at every position, not only at the roots.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: All three conditions must hold at once: equal values, same left subtrees and same right subtrees. The recursive solution combines the two child answers with and.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each pair is checked once with constant work, so time is O(n). The stack, recursive or explicit, adds up to O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A single mismatch anywhere makes the trees different, so every pair has to match. Using and carries a false from any depth up to the root.

card.rule: Same trees need every pair to match, so combine the results with and.
card.limits: And suits every-pair questions. For any-path questions the combination is or.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Lowest common ancestor: three cases at a node
concepts.question: At a node, which three situations decide where the lowest common ancestor of p and q is?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a binary tree and two nodes p and q in it, find their lowest common ancestor: the lowest node that has both as descendants, where a node counts as its own descendant.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Look at the current node. Case 1: the node is p or q, so the answer is this node. Case 2: p is in one subtree and q in the other, so the node is the answer. Case 3: both are in the same subtree, so the answer is somewhere inside it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited at most once with constant work, so time is O(n). The recursion call stack can use up to O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: In case 1 no lower node can include the node that is p or q. In case 2 the node is the connection point of the two subtrees. In case 3 a lower node already has both.

card.rule: The LCA is the first node where p and q split, or a node that is p or q itself.
card.limits: The three cases assume both p and q are in the tree.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: LCA: return non-null to say 'found one'
concepts.question: What does a call on a subtree return, and how does a node use its two children's results?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Turn the three LCA cases into a recursive function.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Return null for an empty tree. Return the node at once if it is p or q. Otherwise a call on a subtree returns non-null only if p or q is in that subtree, so if both children's results are non-null, return this node; if only one is, return it.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Recursive LCA in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time, since each node is visited once with constant work, and up to O(n) space for the call stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A non-null result means at least one target is in that subtree. Two non-null results mean the targets are on different sides of this node, and one non-null result carries a found node upward.

card.rule: Each call returns null if p and q are absent from its subtree; two non-null child results make this node the LCA.
card.limits: The method relies on both p and q being in the tree. If one is missing, the returned node may not be an ancestor of both.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: LCA: both sides can be null
concepts.question: What happens in the LCA code when both child calls return null?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In the lowest common ancestor code, understand what happens in a region of the tree that contains neither p nor q.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: There, both child calls return null, and the function returns null. The video says that if the left call is null the right call must be non-null. That is not necessarily true, but the code works anyway.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The same as the whole LCA solution: each node is visited at most once with constant work, so time is O(n), with up to O(n) call stack space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A call returns non-null only if p or q is in that subtree, and null for a subtree with neither. Returning null when both sides are null matches that meaning exactly, so the small slip in the video does not break the code.

card.rule: If both child results are null, the node returns null, meaning neither target lies below.
card.limits: The reasoning that the right call must be non-null whenever the left is null holds only when the node is above both targets.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
concepts.title: Information goes down as arguments and up as return values
concepts.question: For a tree problem, how do you decide what to pass as arguments and what to return?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choose the right state for a recursive tree function.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Arguments carry what the node must know from above, such as the path sum so far or the maximum so far. The return value carries what the subtree reports upward, such as a depth, a count or a boolean.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Passing an argument or returning a value is constant work per call, so the examples stay at O(n) time. If more than O(1) work is done at each node, say O(k), the time is O(n times k).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each call has its own arguments, so state passed down is correct for that node. Each call returns the answer for its own subtree, so the parent can combine what its children report.

blocks.label: Use
blocks.text: Ask two questions. What does a node need to know from its ancestors? What does a parent need back from each child?

card.rule: Pass context down in arguments and report results up in return values.
