card.limits: Some problems need nothing from above, and some need nothing reported back. Add only what the problem demands.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
concepts.title: BFS goes level by level
concepts.question: What does breadth-first search prioritise, and in what order does it visit depths?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Visit tree nodes one level at a time, all nodes of depth d before any node of depth d + 1.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Breadth-first search prioritises breadth. Think of each depth as a level, like floors of a building with the root on the top floor. BFS traverses all nodes at a given depth before moving on to the next, so depths come out as 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, ... on a complete tree.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: With an efficient queue each node is visited once, so time is O(n) with constant work per node. Space grows with the level that has the most nodes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Visiting nodes in order of distance from the root means every node of depth d is handled before depth d + 1. The order inside a level follows the order children are added, and left to right is the code's choice.

card.rule: BFS visits every node at depth d before any node at depth d + 1.
card.limits: Order within a level follows the order children are added, so left-to-right is a choice that the code makes.

media.alt: A binary tree split into four horizontal bands labelled Depth 0 to Depth 3. Depth 0 holds node 0; depth 1 holds 1 and 2; depth 2 holds 3 and 4 (children of 1) and 5 (right child of 2); depth 3 holds 6 under 3, and 7 and 8 under 4.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
concepts.title: BFS uses a queue
concepts.question: Which structure drives BFS, and why is a recursive BFS not worth writing?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choose the structure that makes a tree traversal level by level.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: DFS uses a stack, which recursion supplies under the hood. BFS is implemented iteratively with a queue.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: With an efficient queue, adding and removing are O(1), so BFS has the same time as DFS: O(n times k) for k work per node, usually O(n). Space is the level with the most nodes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A queue serves nodes in the order they arrive, so every node of one level is served before the children that were added behind them. A recursive BFS is possible but much harder, with no benefit.

card.rule: BFS is iterative and uses a queue; DFS is recursive or uses a stack.
card.limits: A queue only helps if both ends are cheap. A queue implemented with expensive removals from the front loses the speed.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
concepts.title: The BFS template with a level loop
concepts.question: What does the standard BFS loop look like, and where do level logic and node logic go?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Traverse a binary tree level by level and run logic per level and per node.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Put the root in a queue. While the queue is not empty, record how many nodes it holds, run the level logic, then take that many nodes off the front, run the node logic, and add each node's children to the back.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: BFS in Python, printing every value.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time with constant work per node, because each node is added and removed once. The queue holds up to a level of the tree.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The size is recorded before the for loop, so the loop touches only the current level and the children added during it wait for the next pass.

card.rule: Snapshot the queue size, process exactly that many nodes, and queue their children.
card.limits: The for loop is only needed when levels matter. A plain traversal can drop it and loop on the queue alone.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
concepts.title: Why the queue holds one level at a time
concepts.question: Why does the queue hold exactly one level at the start of each while iteration?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Process one level at a time in BFS code, for example to find a value per level.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: At the start, the queue holds only the root, which is level 0. Each pass removes exactly the nodes of the current level and adds their children.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node enters and leaves the queue once, so time is O(n). The queue holds one level at a time, so space grows with the widest level, up to O(n) for a perfect binary tree.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Nodes are removed from the left and added on the right, opposite ends. Once the for loop finishes, everything left in the queue is a child of the level that was processed last, so the queue holds the next level.

card.rule: Each pass leaves the queue holding exactly the next level.
card.limits: The invariant needs the size to be recorded before the loop and children to be added only at the back.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
concepts.title: Choosing between BFS and DFS on a tree
concepts.question: On a binary tree, when does the choice between BFS and DFS matter?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choose between BFS and DFS for a binary tree problem.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: If a problem only needs every node visited, BFS works as well as any DFS. It is very rare for DFS to be better than BFS in binary tree problems.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Both visit each node once, so time is O(n times k) either way. Space differs: DFS uses space linear in the height, BFS linear in the widest level.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: When the problem only needs every node visited, each visit stores enough information whatever the order, so either works, and DFS is usually quicker to write with less code. When nodes are handled by level, such as the rightmost node of each level, BFS makes more sense.

card.rule: Use DFS for plain visits because it is shorter; use BFS when the problem is about levels.
card.limits: The choice never changes what is visited, only the order. It matters when the answer depends on that order.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
concepts.title: The drawback of each traversal
concepts.question: What is the main disadvantage of DFS, and of BFS, when searching for a value?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Answer the interview trivia question on the drawbacks of DFS and BFS when searching a tree for a value.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: DFS can waste a lot of time: searching left before right may cover a huge left subtree for a value one step away on the right. BFS has the opposite problem: if the value is near the bottom, it goes through all the levels above first.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Space also differs. DFS uses space linear in the height, and BFS linear in the widest level. In a perfect binary tree that is O(log n) against O(n); in a straight line it is O(n) against O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each strategy fixes its exploration order before it knows where the target is. DFS commits to depth and BFS to breadth, so each is slow in the case the other handles well. Neither wins in general.

card.rule: DFS can waste time exploring a deep wrong branch; BFS can waste time on shallow levels when the target is deep.
card.limits: Neither wins in general. Which is faster depends on where the target sits.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
concepts.title: Space: height for DFS, widest level for BFS
concepts.question: How does the space used by BFS and DFS depend on the shape of the tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Compare the extra space of DFS and BFS.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: DFS space is linear in the height of the tree, the maximum depth. BFS space is linear in the number of nodes on the widest level.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: For a perfect binary tree DFS uses O(log n) and BFS uses O(n), because the last level holds about n over 2 nodes. For a lopsided tree such as a straight line, BFS uses O(1) and DFS O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: DFS keeps one root-to-node path of pending calls. BFS keeps one whole level in its queue.

card.rule: DFS space follows the height; BFS space follows the widest level, so either can win.
card.limits: A lopsided tree is an edge case. Fuller trees are the usual expectation, where DFS tends to use less space.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
concepts.title: BFS has the same time as DFS
concepts.question: What is the time complexity of BFS on a tree, and what does it need from the queue?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the running time of BFS on a tree with n nodes.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: With an efficient queue, adding and removing are O(1), so the time complexity is the same as DFS: O(n times k), where k is the work done at each node, usually O(1).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(n times k) for n nodes and k work per node, usually O(n). Each node is added once and removed once. The queue may hold up to O(n) nodes at a time.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each node is added to the queue once and removed once, and each visit costs the node's constant work.

card.rule: With an O(1) queue, BFS visits each node once for O(n) total, like DFS.
card.limits: An implementation that removes from the front in O(n) would raise the cost. The efficiency of the queue matters.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
concepts.title: Right side view: the last node of each level
concepts.question: How do you find the nodes visible from the right side of a tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Standing on the right of a binary tree, return the values of the nodes you can see from top to bottom.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: You see the rightmost node of each level. Run BFS, adding left children before right children, and record the last node taken from the queue in each pass.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Right side view in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and up to O(n) space, since each node is visited once and the queue may hold a wide level.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Children are added left then right, so each level sits in the queue in left-to-right order. The final node of the level is its rightmost one.

card.rule: Rightmost per level is the last node dequeued in that level's pass.
card.limits: The answer takes one node per level. A level hidden behind a taller right branch is still seen if its node is the rightmost at that depth.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
concepts.title: Largest value in each row
concepts.question: How does BFS keep a separate running maximum for each level?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Return the largest value in each row of a binary tree. Row and level mean the same.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each while iteration handles one level, so create currMax at the top of the iteration, update it for each node in the for loop, and append it after the loop.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Largest value per row in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(n) space: each node is handled once with constant work.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Creating currMax inside the while loop resets it for every level, so levels never share a maximum. Updating it while handling nodes avoids a second pass.

card.rule: Reset the level's running maximum at the top of each while pass and fold in every node of that pass.
card.limits: A maximum declared outside the while loop would carry over between levels and report the wrong value.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: The binary search tree property
concepts.question: What must be true at every node of a binary search tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Arrange the values of a binary tree so that a search can discard a whole side at each step.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree where, for each node, all values in the left subtree are less than the node's value and all values in the right subtree are greater.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Searching, adding and removing take O(log n) on average, but O(n) in the worst case, such as a tree that is a straight line.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The property covers the whole subtree, not only the children. Looking for 20 at a root of 23, everything on the right is greater than 23, so that side is ignored. Checking parent against child only is not enough.

card.rule: In a BST every left-subtree value is smaller and every right-subtree value is larger than the node.
card.limits: Checking only parent against child is not enough. A value deep in a subtree can still break an ancestor's bound.

media.alt: A binary search tree: root 23 with left child 8 and right child 37. Node 8 has children 6 and 17; node 17 has children 9 and 20. Node 37 has children 29 and 50. Every node's left subtree holds smaller values and its right subtree larger ones.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: Distinct values in a BST
concepts.question: What does the BST property imply about repeated values?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know whether a binary search tree may contain repeated values.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The property says left values are less and right values are greater. There is no allowance for equality.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: this is a property, not an algorithm, so there is no running time to state. Keeping it costs nothing, since an equal value is not allowed in.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A value equal to a node has to go left or right, and neither side permits it. So the values in a BST must be unique.

card.rule: Strict less-than and greater-than mean a BST holds no duplicates.
card.limits: Some other definitions let equal values go to one side. This course's property does not.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: Searching a BST by discarding half
concepts.question: How does the BST property let a search skip a whole subtree at each step?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Check whether a value exists in a BST.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Start at the root. If the target is smaller than the node, ignore the right subtree and go left. If it is larger, ignore the left subtree and go right. Stop on a match or on an empty child.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Search in a BST, in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(log n) on average.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every value in the discarded subtree is on the wrong side of the target by the BST property, so the target cannot be there.

card.rule: At each node, compare the target and go left if it is smaller, right if it is larger.
card.limits: The speed depends on the shape. On a tree that is a straight line, the search can visit every node.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: BST operations: average and worst case
concepts.question: How fast are searching, adding and removing in a BST, and when do they slow down?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the time of searching, adding and removing in a BST with n nodes.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: These operations take O(log n) time on average, because each step discards one side of the tree.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The worst case is O(n): a tree with no right children, a straight line like a linked list.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The number of steps is the height of the tree. A balanced shape has height about log n, while a line has height n.

card.rule: BST operations cost the tree's height: O(log n) on average and O(n) for a lopsided line.
card.limits: The O(log n) figure is an average, not a guarantee. It needs a reasonably balanced tree.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: Inorder on a BST is sorted
concepts.question: In what order does an inorder traversal of a BST handle the nodes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Get the values of a BST in sorted order.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: An inorder DFS that prioritises left before right handles the nodes of a BST in sorted order.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Inorder visits each node once, so the time is O(n), with no O(n log n) sort needed.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: At each node the left subtree, which holds smaller values, is finished first. Then the node is handled, and the right subtree, with larger values, comes last.

card.rule: Inorder on a BST visits the values from smallest to largest.
card.limits: The sorted order holds for a BST only. Inorder on a general binary tree is not sorted.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: Range sum: skip subtrees outside the range
concepts.question: How does the BST property let a range sum skip whole subtrees?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a BST and a range [low, high], sum the values of all nodes inside the range.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A plain traversal that checks every node works. The BST property allows pruning: if the current value is below low, nothing in the left subtree can be in range; if it is above high, nothing in the right subtree can be.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The worst case is still O(n), when all nodes lie in the range, but on average pruning does better. The stack or recursion uses O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node, so a node that is already too small has only too-small values on its left. The same argument holds on the right.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Range sum with pruning, in Python.

card.rule: Visit the left side only if low is less than the node, and the right side only if the node is less than high.
card.limits: Pruning needs the BST property. In a general binary tree every node must be checked.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: What pruning saves
concepts.question: What are the time and space of the pruned range sum, and how much can pruning save?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the cost of the pruned range sum and say what the pruning gains.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The time is still O(n) in the worst case, when all nodes lie in the range. On average it does better than searching every node.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Space is O(n) for the stack or recursion. Example: in a full tree with a million nodes whose root exceeds high, the whole right subtree of about 500,000 nodes is skipped at once.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Pruning removes work only where subtrees lie outside the range. If nothing lies outside, every node is visited.

card.rule: Pruning cuts work on average, but the worst case stays O(n).
card.limits: The saving depends on how much of the tree lies outside the range.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: Minimum difference: from pairs to sorting
concepts.question: How do the naive and sorted approaches to the minimum absolute difference compare, and why does adjacency matter?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a BST, find the minimum absolute difference between the values of any two different nodes.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Collect all values and compare every pair, which costs O(n squared). Sorting the values and comparing only neighbours costs O(n log n).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Comparing all pairs costs O(n squared). Sorting and then scanning neighbours costs O(n log n), dominated by the sort.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: In a sorted list, the closest pair is always adjacent: another value between two members would only make the gap between its own neighbours smaller.

card.rule: The closest pair of values is always adjacent in sorted order.
card.limits: Sorting costs O(n log n). A BST can supply sorted order without a sort, which the next idea uses.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: Minimum difference with an inorder walk
concepts.question: How does an inorder walk remove the sorting cost from the minimum difference?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the minimum absolute difference between any two nodes of a BST in linear time.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Do an inorder DFS that appends each value to a list, which comes out sorted. Then scan the list and keep the smallest difference between neighbours.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Minimum difference via inorder, in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(n) space. The sorted order comes free from the traversal.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The traversal produces sorted values, and the closest pair is adjacent in a sorted list.

card.rule: Inorder gives the values sorted for free, so only the neighbour gaps need scanning.
card.limits: The method depends on the BST property. For an unordered tree the sort cannot be skipped.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: Iterative inorder is harder
concepts.question: How does an iterative inorder walk work, and why does the book prefer recursion?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Produce the inorder sequence without recursion.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep a stack and a pointer curr. While curr is not empty, push it and move left. When curr is empty, pop a node, record its value, and move to its right child. Stop when the stack is empty and curr is empty.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The book gives O(n) time and space for the solution built on it. Our reading: each node is pushed and popped once, and the stack can hold up to O(n) nodes on a straight-line tree.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Pushing down the left side postpones each node until its left subtree is finished. Popping records the node, and moving right then handles the right subtree.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Iterative inorder in Python.

blocks.label: Use
blocks.text: Inorder is a lot more complicated to write iteratively. If given the option, stay with recursion; the iterative form is uncommon but may be asked.

card.rule: Iterative inorder pushes the left spine, then pops, records and moves right.
card.limits: It is easy to get wrong. Prefer the recursive form unless an interviewer asks for the stack version.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: Validating a BST with bounds
concepts.question: What range must a node's value fall in, and how do the bounds change going left and right?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether a binary tree is a valid BST.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Pass an open interval (small, large) down with each node and require small < node.val < large. Going left, set large to node.val. Going right, set small to node.val. The root starts with minus infinity and infinity.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Validate BST with bounds, in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(n) space, as in other DFS examples.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every node in the left subtree must be less than the node and every node in the right subtree greater. Tightening one bound at each step keeps all ancestors' limits in force.

card.rule: Each node must lie strictly between the lower and upper bounds inherited from its ancestors.
card.limits: Bounds are exclusive. A value equal to a bound breaks the strict BST property.

concepts.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
concepts.title: Validating a BST: base case and combination
concepts.question: What does an empty tree return in the BST check, and how are the two subtree answers combined?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide the base case and the combination rule for checking whether a tree is a valid BST.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: An empty tree is technically a BST, so a null node returns true. The answers for the two subtrees are combined with and.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited once with constant work, so time is O(n), and space is O(n) for the stack or call stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: At any node all subtrees must also be BSTs, so both subtree checks must be true along with the node's own bound check. A single node is a BST by definition, so its two empty children must return true.

card.rule: Empty is a valid BST; a tree is valid only if the node, left subtree and right subtree are all valid.
card.limits: Returning false for an empty child would reject every tree that has a leaf.

concepts.title: A binary tree is a graph with restrictions
concepts.question: Which restrictions make a binary tree a special graph, and what happens when they are lifted?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: See how binary tree knowledge connects to general graphs, and what changes when the tree restrictions go away.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A graph is any collection of nodes (vertices) and connections (edges). A binary tree is a graph with many restrictions, most prominently at most one parent and at most two children. Lift the restrictions and graphs take many more forms.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: a tree with n nodes has n - 1 edges, while a general graph can have up to about n squared. So graph costs are written in both n and e.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A tree meets the definition of a graph and adds extra rules. Our reading: so whatever works on a graph also works on a tree, but not the other way round. A graph problem may break assumptions tree code relied on, such as a unique parent.

card.rule: A binary tree is a graph limited to one parent and two children per node.
card.limits: A graph problem may break an assumption that tree code relied on, such as a unique parent or a single top node.

concepts.title: Graphs are everywhere
concepts.question: Which real situations are modelled as graphs?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Spot a graph in an everyday system, so a real situation can be modelled.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Treat the things as nodes and their relationships as edges. The book's examples are social networks such as Facebook and TikTok, the roads in cities, circuit boards, internet network traffic, blockchains and models in biology.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: No algorithm is costed. Our reading: the model's size is its number of nodes n and relationships e, and later graph costs are stated in those terms.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Any collection of things with connections between them already fits the definition of a graph, so the model applies. Not every relationship needs one; it helps when the connections are the point of the problem.

card.rule: Model things as nodes and their relationships as edges to see a graph in everyday systems.
card.limits: Not every relationship needs a graph. The model helps when connections between items are the point of the problem.

concepts.title: Directed and undirected edges
concepts.question: What is the difference between a directed and an undirected edge?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know in which directions a traversal may move along an edge.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A directed edge can be traversed one way only: with an edge from A to B you can move from A to B but not back. It is drawn as an arrow. An undirected edge can be traversed both ways and is drawn as a plain line. Binary trees are directed graphs.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: an undirected edge is stored as two directed entries, so it takes twice the neighbour-list space of a directed one. The book adds y to x's list, and x to y's list when undirected.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The kind of edge decides where a traversal can go from each node. In a tree the edges are directed, so you can reach a node's children but never its parent. Problems state which kind applies.

card.rule: Directed edges go one way; undirected edges go both ways.
card.limits: A problem states whether its edges are directed or undirected. Reading that decision carefully matters more than the picture.

concepts.title: Connected components
concepts.question: What is a connected component, and how many does a tree have?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Describe the separate pieces of a graph, and count them.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A connected component of a graph is a group of nodes connected by edges. A graph can have several components that do not touch; the book's second example graph has three. A binary tree has exactly one, since every node is reachable from the root.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Counting components with a DFS costs O(n + e), as the graph DFS ideas show later.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Nodes in one component can reach each other through edges, and no edge links two components, so each node belongs to exactly one group. With directed edges, reachability in one direction is a weaker link, so definitions need care.

card.rule: A connected component is a group of nodes linked by edges, and a tree has exactly one.
card.limits: If edges are directed, being reachable in one direction is a weaker link than being connected both ways, so definitions need care.

concepts.title: Indegree, outdegree and neighbours
concepts.question: What do the indegree and outdegree of a node count, and who are its neighbours?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Count and name the connections around a node.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In a directed graph a node can have any number of edges entering and leaving it. Indegree is the number of edges that reach the node, and outdegree is the number that leave it. Nodes joined by an edge are neighbours: in A, B, C chained both ways, B has neighbours A and C.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: all indegrees come from one pass over the e edges plus an array of n counters, so O(n + e).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Entering and leaving edges are counted separately because directions differ. In a binary tree every node except the root has indegree 1, and outdegree 0, 1 or 2, where 0 means a leaf. In an undirected graph both counts coincide as the degree.

card.rule: Indegree counts edges coming in, outdegree counts edges going out, and neighbours share an edge.
card.limits: In an undirected graph an edge works both ways, so the in and out counts coincide and are called the degree.

concepts.title: Cycles and acyclic graphs
concepts.question: What is a cycle, and which graphs are cyclic or acyclic?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Tell whether following edges can lead back to a node already visited.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A graph is cyclic if it has a cycle, a path along the edges that leads to visiting the same nodes over and over, and acyclic if it has none. Binary trees by definition cannot have a cycle.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A traversal on a cyclic graph needs a seen set, with O(1) add and check, so that each node is visited once and the walk ends.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A cycle can be walked forever, like a linked list cycle, unless the traversal remembers where it has been. In trees the edges only move down, so there is no way back. One cycle anywhere makes the whole graph cyclic.

card.rule: A cycle is a loop of edges; a graph without any is acyclic.
card.limits: A graph can contain a cycle in one part and be tree-like elsewhere. One cycle anywhere makes the whole graph cyclic.

concepts.title: A binary tree in graph terms
concepts.question: Which graph terms describe a binary tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Describe a binary tree using the general graph vocabulary.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A binary tree is a directed graph, with edges from parent to child, so you cannot access a node's parent. It has one connected component and no cycle. Every node except the root has indegree 1, and every outdegree is 0, 1 or 2, where 0 means a leaf.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the n - 1 non-root nodes each have one incoming edge, so a tree has n - 1 edges, and a graph traversal cost of O(n + e) becomes O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The facts follow from the definition. Edges point down, so there is no way back to a parent. Every node is reachable from the root, giving one component. One parent per node gives indegree 1. Parent and child replace neighbour in tree talk.

card.rule: A binary tree is a directed, connected, acyclic graph in which only the root has indegree 0 and every outdegree is at most 2.
card.limits: These facts describe trees only. A general graph can break each of them.

concepts.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
concepts.title: A graph problem gives only information about the graph
concepts.question: What does a graph problem give you, compared with a list or a tree problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Read a graph problem, which gives information about a graph rather than node objects.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Linked list problems give the head and tree problems give the root, but a graph does not literally exist in memory; only the idea of it does. The input describes it, often with nodes labelled 0 to n - 1, perhaps as a story such as n cities. You choose how to represent and traverse it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the representation you choose decides the cost. Scanning the whole input to find neighbours at every node is very slow, while a prepared structure gives them quickly.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: No node objects or pointers exist, so there is nothing to follow until you build a representation. Each labelled item is a node, and the statement or story supplies the edges. Every graph solution begins with that decision.

card.rule: A graph problem gives data about a graph, not node objects; you choose how to represent it.
card.limits: Nothing is given as ready-made node objects with pointers. Every graph solution begins with a decision about representation.

concepts.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
concepts.title: Why neighbours need fast access
concepts.question: Why can't you start a graph traversal straight from an array of edges?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the neighbours of a node when the input is only an array of edges.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A node can have any number of neighbours, unlike a binary tree node with left and right. With an edge array, finding a node's neighbours means scanning the whole input.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: That scan is repeated at every node during the traversal, which is very slow.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Before traversing, preprocess the input into a structure that returns all neighbours of a node at once, ideally a hash map from node to its list of neighbours.

card.rule: Build a neighbour lookup first so each node's neighbours are one access away.
card.limits: Preprocessing costs time and memory, so it pays off only when the traversal would otherwise rescan the input many times.

concepts.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
concepts.title: Input as an array of edges
concepts.question: What does an array of edges look like, and what does the problem still have to tell you?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Read a graph given as a 2D array of pairs [x, y].

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each element [x, y] means there is an edge between x and y, and the problem says whether edges are directed. Before traversing, build a hash map from each node to its list of neighbours: put y in graph[x], and also x in graph[y] if the edges are undirected.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Without preprocessing, finding the neighbours of each node means scanning the whole input, which is very slow. Our reading: building the map is one pass over the e edges, and then each neighbour lookup is direct.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A hash map lookup returns a node's neighbours at once, so the traversal never re-scans the input. The array [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 0], [2, 3]] describes four directed edges; the graph exists only as an idea derived from it.

card.rule: An edge array lists pairs [x, y]; the statement says whether they are directed.
card.limits: The array alone does not say if [x, y] also means [y, x]. Reading the statement decides it.

media.alt: A directed graph of four numbered nodes. Arrows run from 0 to 1, from 1 to 2, from 2 back to 0, and from 2 to 3. Nodes 0, 1 and 2 form a cycle, and node 3 has one arrow arriving and none leaving.

concepts.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
concepts.title: Building a neighbour map from edges
concepts.question: How do you turn an edge array into a map from each node to its neighbours?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Preprocess an edge array so that graph[node] gives that node's neighbours.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Make a hash map from integers to lists of integers. For each pair [x, y], append y to the list of x. If the edges are undirected, also append x to the list of y.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Build the map in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n + e) time to build, where n is the nodes and e is the edges, since each edge is processed once.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each edge adds its entry once for a directed graph and twice for an undirected one, so every edge is listed from each end it can be used from.

card.rule: For each pair [x, y] add y to graph[x], and x to graph[y] too if edges are undirected.
card.limits: A node that appears in no edge still needs an empty list if the traversal will look it up.

concepts.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
concepts.title: Input as an adjacency list
concepts.question: What is an adjacency list, and why is it the most convenient input?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Read a graph given as an adjacency list.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The nodes are numbered from 0 to n - 1, and the input is a 2D integer array graph where graph[i] lists all outgoing edges from node i. The graph with edges 0 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 0 and 2 to 3 is [[1], [2], [0, 3], []].

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: No preprocessing is needed, so finding the neighbours of any node is a single access, such as graph[6].

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: graph[i] already is the neighbour list of node i, the shape a traversal wants, which is why this is the most convenient format. The list does not say if edges are undirected; the statement decides that.

card.rule: In an adjacency list, graph[i] holds the neighbours of node i directly.
card.limits: The list does not say whether the edges are meant as undirected. The statement decides that.

concepts.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
concepts.title: Input as an adjacency matrix
concepts.question: What does an adjacency matrix look like, and what are the two ways to use it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Read a graph given as an n by n matrix, where 1 marks an edge, and choose how to find neighbours.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Option one: at each node, loop over graph[node] and treat every i with graph[node][i] equal to 1 as a neighbour. Option two: convert the matrix to a hash map of neighbours first.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Both approaches cost O(n squared).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Converting costs a full pass over the matrix once, but then each node's neighbours are quick to read, which helps when nodes have few neighbours and n is large.

card.rule: graph[i][j] == 1 means an edge from i to j; either scan the row or convert to neighbour lists.
card.limits: A matrix always takes n squared cells, even when there are few edges.

media.alt: A directed graph with arrows 0 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 0 and 2 to 3, drawn beside its four-by-four adjacency matrix of 0s and 1s. Row 0 has a 1 only in column 1, row 1 only in column 2, row 2 in columns 0 and 3, and row 3 is all zeros.

concepts.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
concepts.title: A grid as an implicit graph
concepts.question: How is a matrix of squares treated as a graph, and where do the edges come from?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Read a graph hidden in a 2D matrix plus a story.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each square (row, col) is a node, and the problem description, not the input, defines the edges. If villages trade with those directly above, below, left and right, the neighbours are (row - 1, col), (row, col - 1), (row + 1, col) and (row, col + 1), when in bounds. Nodes are not numbered 0 to n - 1.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: With a fixed number of neighbours per square, the work at each node is constant, so a traversal over an m by n grid costs O(m times n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The edges come from the statement, so careful reading gives the neighbours. Border squares have fewer neighbours, so bounds must be checked before using a neighbour.

card.rule: In a grid problem every cell is a node and the statement defines its neighbours.
card.limits: Squares at the border have fewer neighbours, so bounds must be checked.

concepts.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
concepts.title: How graph code differs from tree code
concepts.question: What changes when you move from tree traversal code to graph traversal code?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Adapt tree traversal code to graph problems.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A tree gives a root and objects with left and right. A graph has no obvious start and may first need converting into a hash map. Loop over all neighbours instead of two children. DFS keeps its shape: base case, recurse on neighbours, compute, return. Add a set seen so no node is visited twice.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited once, thanks to seen with O(1) checks, but the neighbour loop is not constant. The time is usually O(n + e) rather than the tree's O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Trees need no seen set because edges only move down. In an undirected graph, or a directed graph with cycles, an edge pair like A and B would let the walk go on forever, so seen is needed. The start node depends on the problem.

card.rule: Loop over neighbours instead of two children, convert the input if needed, and choose the start yourself.
card.limits: The overall DFS shape stays the same. The extra concerns are the start, the neighbour access and repeated visits.

concepts.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
concepts.title: A seen set stops endless walks
concepts.question: Why do graph traversals need a seen set, and why did trees not?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In an undirected graph, or a directed graph with cycles, a tree-style DFS walks in a circle forever.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep a set seen. Before visiting a node, check whether it is in seen. If not, add it and then visit it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Adding to and checking a set takes constant time, so each node is visited once at O(1) cost.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Trees did not need it because edges only move down. Once you leave a node there is no way back. With a relationship such as A <-> B you could move between the two nodes forever.

card.rule: Mark a node as seen before visiting it, so each node is visited once and cycles end.
card.limits: The set can be an array when labels are 0 to n - 1. This changes speed in some languages but not the algorithm.

concepts.title: DFS from one node covers its component
concepts.question: Which nodes does a DFS from one node of an undirected graph reach?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Cover a whole connected component, or count components, with traversals.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In an undirected graph, a traversal from any given node visits every node in the connected component that node belongs to.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A DFS from one node visits each node of its component once. Over the whole graph the time is O(n + e), since every edge is iterated once.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Undirected edges can be followed both ways, so any node in the component can be reached by a path from the start. A tree is the same: a traversal from the root visits every node.

card.rule: A traversal from any node of an undirected graph visits exactly its whole connected component.
card.limits: With directed edges a traversal reaches only what the arrows lead to, which may be less than a whole component.

concepts.title: Counting components with DFS
concepts.question: How do you count connected components with a loop over the nodes and a DFS?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Count the provinces: groups of cities that are directly or indirectly connected, given an n by n adjacency matrix isConnected.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Build a neighbour map, then loop over the nodes from 0 to n - 1. Whenever a node is not in seen, count one more province and run a DFS that marks its whole component as seen.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Number of provinces in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n squared) here, because the matrix has to be read to build the map.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each DFS marks a whole component, so no component is counted twice. A node that is still unseen must belong to a new component.

card.rule: Loop over the nodes; each time you find an unseen one, add 1 and DFS its component.
card.limits: The answer counts components only if edges are undirected, so that a DFS covers the entire component.

concepts.title: Graph DFS passes labels, not node objects
concepts.question: What does the graph DFS function take as its argument, and how does the iterative version differ?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Write DFS when graph nodes are integer labels 0 to n - 1, not objects.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: dfs(node) takes the integer label instead of a node object, because the graph only exists as an idea and you represent it. For the iterative version, modify only dfs: use a stack, and each loop pass pops a node and acts like a call with that node as the argument.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: As for other graph DFS: each node is visited once and each node's edges are iterated once, so time is O(n + e). The stack or call stack adds up to O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Neighbours are looked up by label in the map, so a label identifies a node as well as an object would. Most problems number nodes 0 to n - 1, so the logic is reusable. Without a numbering you need another way to identify nodes.

card.rule: A graph DFS takes the node's integer label; the iterative form replaces recursion with a stack inside dfs.
card.limits: Labels work because nodes are numbered. Without a numbering you need another way to identify nodes.

concepts.title: Graph DFS takes O(n + e)
concepts.question: What is the time complexity of DFS on a graph, and why does it include the edges?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the running time of a graph DFS.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In a binary tree each visit cost O(1) since a node has at most two children. In a graph a node can have any number of neighbours, so each visit loops over them. The time is usually O(n + e), where n is the nodes and e the edges.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node is visited once, and a node's edges are looped over only when that node is visited. So every edge is looked at once overall, for O(e).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The argument resembles the sliding window one: a nested loop does not mean n times n if the inner loop runs only e times in total across the whole algorithm.

card.rule: Graph DFS visits each node once and each edge once, so it costs O(n + e).
card.limits: In the worst case every node touches every other and e is about n squared.

concepts.title: Graph DFS space: n + e
concepts.question: What space does a graph DFS use, and why is it not O(n squared)?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the extra space of a graph DFS with a built neighbour map.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The map stores all the edges in lists, the recursion call stack is O(n) at worst, and seen holds up to n nodes. The space is O(n + e).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Extra space is O(n + e): the neighbour map holds the e edges, the call stack is up to O(n) deep, and seen holds up to n nodes. Time for the same DFS is O(n + e).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The map grows only with edges that actually exist. In the worst case e is about n squared, but e is still a quantity of its own and not always that large.

card.rule: Space is the neighbour map plus the stack plus seen: O(n + e).
card.limits: Reading a matrix costs n squared time, but the map built from it still only grows with existing edges.

concepts.title: Directions and a valid check for grids
concepts.question: Which two helpers make DFS on a grid clean?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Write the neighbour logic of a grid DFS once and keep the code tidy.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Declare a directions array of coordinate changes, such as (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0). Add a helper valid(row, col) that checks the cell is in bounds and is the kind of cell you want, such as land.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each cell has a fixed four directions to try and valid does constant work, so each cell costs O(1). A grid DFS then costs O(m times n) for m rows and n columns.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Looping over directions gives all four neighbours in one place, and valid guards the bounds so no out-of-range access occurs. Neither is necessary, but they make the code cleaner and more modular.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The two helpers in Python.
blocks.code:
directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]

def valid(row, col, grid):
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    return 0 <= row < m and 0 <= col < n and grid[row][col] == '1'

card.rule: Loop over a directions list and test each neighbour with a valid helper.
card.limits: valid must test bounds before it looks at the cell. Reversing the checks risks reading outside the grid.

concepts.title: Number of islands is components on a grid
concepts.question: How does counting islands reuse the counting of provinces?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a grid of 1 (land) and 0 (water), count the islands, where an island is land cells connected horizontally or vertically.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: It is the same problem as provinces: count connected components in an undirected graph. Each land cell is a node, with edges to adjacent land cells. Only the format of the graph differs.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(m times n): each cell is visited once, and each has at most 4 edges, so the work per cell is constant. Our reading: seen adds O(m times n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Scanning every cell, an unseen land cell begins a new island, and the DFS marks all land connected to it as seen. Water is never a node.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Number of islands in Python.

card.rule: Islands are connected components of land cells; scan the grid and DFS from each unseen land cell.
card.limits: Diagonal land does not join islands here, because edges are horizontal and vertical only.

concepts.title: Islands: cost and the modify-the-input trick
concepts.question: What is the time of the islands DFS, and how can the seen set be avoided?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State the cost of counting islands and discuss the seen set.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The graph time was O(nodes + edges) because a node's edge count was unknown. Here a cell has at most 4 edges, so the work per cell is O(1) and the time is O(m times n) for an m by n grid.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Space is O(m times n) for seen and the recursion stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each cell is visited once with constant work. As an alternative, set a visited land cell to 0 to avoid the set, though an interviewer may not want the input changed.

card.rule: Islands cost O(m x n) because each cell has at most four neighbours.
card.limits: Modifying the input is faster to write but destroys the grid. Ask before doing it.

concepts.title: Reorder routes: DFS away from the root city
concepts.question: How do you count the roads that must be turned around so every city can reach city 0?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: There are n cities and n - 1 directed roads with exactly one way between any two cities. Count the fewest roads to reverse so every city can reach city 0.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Treat the roads as undirected only to run a DFS from city 0. Every step the DFS takes goes away from 0. If the original input has the road from the current node to the neighbour, it points away from 0 and must be reversed, so add 1.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Reorder routes in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n): each city is visited once, and there are n - 1 roads. The graph, the roads set and seen are O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: With one route between cities, every road must point towards 0. A road met while moving away from 0 points the wrong way exactly when it is in the original set.

card.rule: DFS from 0 over undirected roads; each road crossed that exists as given, pointing away from 0, is flipped.
card.limits: The method relies on the one-route guarantee. With several routes between cities, reversing a road could be unnecessary.

media.alt: A directed graph of six cities numbered 0 to 5 with one route between any two. Arrows run from 0 to 1, from 3 to 1, from 2 to 3, from 4 to 0 and from 5 to 4. City 0 is at the left, and the other cities hang off it like a tree.

concepts.title: Why only edges pointing away from 0 are flipped
concepts.question: Why does every road have to point toward city 0, and what does that say about which roads to flip?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Flip the fewest roads so that every city can reach city 0.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The cities and roads form a tree rooted at city 0, so each city has exactly one way to reach 0. For a city to reach 0, every road on that single way must point toward 0.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each city is visited once and there are n - 1 roads, so time and space are both O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Take any road. If it points away from 0, the cities beyond it cannot get back to 0 along it, and no other route exists, so it must be flipped. A road that already points toward 0 can stay. The fewest flips is therefore the count of roads that point away.

card.rule: With one route per city, a road must be flipped exactly when it points away from city 0.
card.limits: A graph with extra routes between cities breaks the argument, because a road could be unneeded.

concepts.title: Keys and rooms: reach every room from room 0
concepts.question: How do you tell whether DFS from room 0 can open every room?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: There are n rooms, all locked except room 0. rooms[i] lists the keys found in room i, each key opening one room. Return True if every room can be visited.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Rooms are nodes and keys are edges. The input is already an adjacency list, so the neighbours of room i are rooms[i]. Run a DFS from room 0 and compare the size of seen with the number of rooms.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Keys and rooms in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n + e) time: each room is visited once and the key loops add up to e in total. Space is O(n) for seen and the stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every visited room is added to seen, and the DFS reaches every room that is reachable from room 0. If seen holds all n rooms, all can be opened.

card.rule: DFS from room 0 and check that the number of seen rooms equals the number of rooms.
card.limits: The test only decides yes or no; it does not give an order or a count of keys used.

concepts.title: Smallest set of vertices: indegree zero
concepts.question: Which nodes must be in the smallest set that reaches every node of a directed acyclic graph?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a directed acyclic graph with n nodes and an array of edges, find the smallest set of nodes from which every node can be reached.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A node that can be reached from another node is not needed in the set, since its parent can stand in for it. So the set is the nodes that no other node can reach: those with indegree 0, meaning no edge enters them.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Minimum vertices to reach all nodes in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n + e) time, since the edges are counted once and then the nodes are scanned.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A node with indegree 0 cannot be reached from anywhere else, so it has to be a starting node. Every other node has an incoming edge, and following edges backward in an acyclic graph ends at an indegree 0 node, so the set reaches all.

card.rule: Count how many edges enter each node; the nodes with count 0 are the answer.
card.limits: A cycle breaks the argument: a graph that is a single cycle has no node with indegree 0.

concepts.title: Graph BFS visits nodes by distance from the start
concepts.question: What does a graph BFS guarantee about the first visit to each node?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the fewest steps from a start node to other nodes of a graph that may have many paths between two nodes.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Imagine the start node as a root. Its neighbours are the next level, their neighbours the level after. BFS on a graph visits nodes in order of their distance from the start, so each first visit uses the minimum steps from the start.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: With an efficient queue BFS costs the same as DFS: O(n + e) for a graph, and O(n squared) for an n by n grid.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every node at distance d is processed before any node at distance d + 1, so shorter paths are explored before longer ones. On trees even DFS used the only path. The guarantee counts steps, so with different weights it does not hold.

card.rule: The first time BFS visits a node, it has used the minimum number of steps from the start.
card.limits: The guarantee counts steps. When edges have different weights, fewer steps need not mean a smaller total.

concepts.title: Why DFS can give a wrong shortest path
concepts.question: Why can a DFS report a path longer than the shortest one on a graph?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide which traversal to trust for a shortest path on a graph.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A DFS follows one path as far as it can before trying another. On a graph, the first path it finds to the target may be long, while a shorter one exists elsewhere.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: BFS finds the shortest path at the book's usual graph cost, O(n + e) with an efficient queue. Our reading: a DFS made to try every path to be sure would cost far more.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: BFS explores by distance, so when it first meets the target, no shorter path can exist. DFS gives no such ordering. Example: in a square 0-1-2-3 where 0 is also joined to 3, a DFS that tries node 1 first reaches 3 in 3 steps, but BFS finds it in 1.

card.rule: Use BFS for shortest paths on graphs; a DFS may find a longer path first.
card.limits: DFS would need to try every path to be sure of the shortest, which is far more work than BFS.

concepts.title: Shortest clear path in a binary matrix
concepts.question: How does BFS find the shortest clear path in a grid?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In an n by n grid of 0s and 1s, find the length of the shortest path from the top left to the bottom right that uses only 0 cells. Moves may go in 8 directions. Return -1 if none exists.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Cells with value 0 are the nodes, and edges join cells that touch in any of 8 directions. Run BFS from the top left, storing the step count with each cell in the queue. The first time the bottom right comes off the queue, return its steps.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Shortest clear path in Python. The length counts cells, so steps starts at 1.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n squared) time and space, because each of the n squared cells is queued at most once and has 8 neighbours.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: BFS reaches each cell by the fewest steps. A DFS could reach the bottom right by a longer path first.

card.rule: BFS from the top left with a (cell, steps) queue; return the steps when the bottom right is reached.
card.limits: If the start cell is blocked, no path exists, so the answer is -1 straight away.

media.alt: A six-by-six grid of 0s and 1s for a shortest path from the top-left to the bottom-right cell. Red cells mark a long route down the left column, along the fourth row and down the right side, eleven cells. A green arrow shows a shorter seven-cell route: right once, diagonally down-right four times, then down.

concepts.title: Store steps or loop over levels
concepts.question: When can a BFS skip the inner level loop?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Report the number of steps a BFS takes to reach a target in a graph.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Two ways. Store a steps value in each queue entry and return it on arrival, with no inner for loop. Or keep the tree-style while and for loops and raise a level counter once per while pass. Tree BFS used the for loop because each level was analysed as a whole.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: both styles cost the same O(n + e), since each node is queued once. Storing steps adds one integer per queue entry.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: BFS reaches each node first in the fewest steps, so returning the stored steps, or the level counter, on reaching the target gives the answer. If the problem needs to look at a whole level together, use the for loop over the queue size.

card.rule: Store steps per node when only the target matters; loop by level when levels are analysed together.
card.limits: Either style is correct for shortest paths. Choose the one that reads cleaner for the problem.

concepts.title: Parent pointers turn a tree into an undirected graph
concepts.question: How can BFS reach nodes outside the target's subtree in a binary tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a binary tree, a target node and an integer k, return the values of all nodes at distance k from the target.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A tree node only points down to its children, so the nodes outside the target's subtree cannot be reached. First run a DFS from the root and record each node's parent. Now a node has up to three neighbours: left, right and parent, which makes the tree an undirected graph.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: All nodes at distance k in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and space: the DFS visits each node once, and so does the BFS. The parent map and seen hold up to n nodes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: BFS from the target visits nodes by distance. After k levels, the queue holds exactly the nodes at distance k. A seen set stops the search from stepping back to a parent it came from.

card.rule: Record each node's parent with a DFS, then BFS from the target for k levels; the queue holds the answer.
card.limits: The parent record can be a hash map or an attribute added to each node, and some interviewers frown on changing node objects.

concepts.title: Multi-source BFS: level 0 can hold many nodes
concepts.question: Can a BFS start from more than one node at once?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find, for every node, the distance to the nearest of many source nodes, such as the nearest 0 in a matrix.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Start the queue with all the source nodes at level 0 instead of one, mark them in seen, and run the usual BFS. Starting from the zeros rather than from each 1 works because the distance from x to y equals the distance from y to x.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time and space are O(m times n), since each square is visited once. Running a BFS from every 1 would cost O(m squared times n squared).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The first-visit guarantee still holds: each node is reached in the fewest steps from the nearest source. Marking the sources in seen first keeps them from being queued again, and seen keeps later visits from overriding the distances already found.

card.rule: Put every starting node in the queue at level 0; each node is then reached from its nearest source.
card.limits: A multi-source BFS gives the nearest source for each node, not the distance to one chosen source.

concepts.title: 01 Matrix: BFS from all the zeros
concepts.question: How do you find the nearest 0 for every cell with one BFS?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: For each cell of an m by n matrix of 0s and 1s, find the distance to the nearest 0. Moves go up, down, left or right.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Start the BFS from every 0 at once, each with 0 steps. When BFS first reaches a 1, the current step count is its answer, and seen stops it from being overwritten.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: 01 Matrix in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(m times n) time and space: each cell is queued once with constant work.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The distance from a 1 to its nearest 0 is the same walked in either direction. Starting from all zeros, the first arrival at a cell comes from its nearest zero.

card.rule: Queue every 0 at level 0; the first time BFS reaches a 1, its steps value is the answer.
card.limits: A BFS from each 1 separately would work but repeats a search for every 1 cell.

concepts.title: Extra state: (node, remain)
concepts.question: When does a BFS node need more information than its position?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Search a graph when the position alone does not decide what moves are allowed, for example when at most k obstacles may be removed.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A state is everything that decides what you can do next. Often the node alone is the state; here it is the pair (node, remain). From (cell, remain), a 0 neighbour keeps remain, and a 1 neighbour costs one removal and is allowed only if remain is above 0. Store whole states in seen.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There are m times n values for the node and k values for remain, so m times n times k states. With constant work per state, time and space are O(m times n times k).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Reaching the same cell with 2 removals left and with 0 left are different situations, so each must be allowed once. Storing only the node in seen would wrongly block the better one. Adding a variable multiplies the number of states.

card.rule: If the node does not fully describe your options, extend the state and store the whole state in seen.
card.limits: Adding a variable multiplies the number of states, so only add what the rules need.

concepts.title: Cost counts states, not nodes
concepts.question: How does adding a state variable change the BFS cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Work out the BFS cost when the state is more than the node.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Count states, not nodes. Seen prevents any state from being visited twice, so the cost O(nodes + edges) really counts states. Until now each node was one state. With (node, remain) there are m times n times k states.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Constant work per state gives time and space of O(m times n times k). A variable with a fixed range of 2, like a colour, only doubles the cost, so the order is unchanged.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each state is queued at most once because seen records it, so the cost is the number of states times the work per state. If the work per state is not constant, multiply that in too.

card.rule: The cost is the number of states times the work per state.
card.limits: If the work at each state is not constant, multiply it in as well.

concepts.title: Alternating colours: state (node, colour)
concepts.question: How does BFS find shortest paths that alternate edge colours?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In a directed graph with red and blue edges, find the shortest path from node 0 to every node using edges that alternate in colour. Return -1 for unreachable nodes.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Make the state (node, colour), where colour is the colour of the next edge to use. Store the edges as graph[node][colour], and start with both (0, 0, 0) and (0, 1, 0) in the queue. Crossing an edge flips the colour with 1 - colour.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Alternating colour paths in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n + e) time and space. Colour has only 2 values, so the states number 2n.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: BFS reaches each state in the fewest steps. For each node, the answer is the smaller of its values over the two colours, and -1 if it is never reached.

card.rule: Use (node, colour, steps) states, flip the colour on each move, and keep the minimum steps per node.
card.limits: The colour flip trick 1 - colour only works with colours coded as 0 and 1.

concepts.title: Four questions for any BFS problem
concepts.question: What four questions help you set up a BFS problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Set up an unfamiliar BFS problem quickly.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Ask four questions: what are the nodes, what are the edges, is a state variable needed besides the node, and where does the BFS start? For a binary matrix path, cells are nodes, 8-direction touches are edges, and the start is the top left. For alternating colours, colour is extra state and the start is node 0 in both colours.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The cost follows from the answers: the number of states times the work per state, which is O(n + e) when the node alone is the state.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every BFS problem here uses the same queue loop with seen, steps and a neighbours step. The four answers fix what goes in the queue, how neighbours are found, what seen stores and what level 0 is. Several readings can be valid if they agree on what a step means.

card.rule: Before coding a BFS, say what the nodes, edges, extra state and start are.
card.limits: A problem may have several valid readings, such as different node definitions, but they must agree on what a step means.

concepts.title: Implicit graphs: states as nodes
concepts.question: How can you spot a graph problem whose input does not look like a graph?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Recognise a graph problem whose input does not look like a graph.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A graph is any abstract set of elements joined by an abstract relationship. If a problem moves between states, try states as nodes and the allowed transitions as edges. If it asks for the fewest operations or the shortest path, BFS is a strong candidate. Examples: the lock readings, and the division equations.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The traversal costs the number of states plus transitions, and the state count can grow fast: a lock with n wheels has 10 to the power n states.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The graph model needs only elements and a relationship, not a given input format, so states and transitions qualify. Fewest moves is a shortest path, where BFS's first-visit guarantee gives the minimum. Check that the transitions are well defined.

card.rule: If a problem moves between states, model the states as nodes and the transitions as edges.
card.limits: Not every state-change problem needs a graph search. Check that the transitions are well defined and a traversal fits the question.

concepts.title: Open the lock: BFS over lock readings
concepts.question: What are the nodes and edges in the lock problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A lock has 4 wheels, each with digits 0 to 9, wrapping around. It starts at 0000. One move turns one wheel one slot. Some readings in deadends are blocked. Return the fewest moves to reach target, or -1.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each reading from 0000 to 9999 is a node. Two readings are neighbours if they differ in one wheel by 1. Run BFS from 0000 with a (reading, steps) queue, and return the steps when the target comes off the queue.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Open the lock in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Constant apart from turning deadends into a set: O(d) for d deadends.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: BFS reaches each reading in the fewest moves, and deadends are never visited because they are already in seen.

card.rule: BFS from 0000 over single-wheel turns, with deadends already in seen.
card.limits: If 0000 itself is a deadend, the lock cannot move at all.

concepts.title: Modulo neighbours and deadends in seen
concepts.question: How do you generate lock neighbours with wrap-around, and handle deadends cleanly?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Generate the neighbours of a lock reading with wrap-around, and respect the deadends.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: For each of the 4 wheels, turn it up and down by 1, using modulo 10 for the wrap-around. The book's code writes (num + change + 10) % 10 so negative results cannot occur. Put all deadends into seen before the BFS starts.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each reading has 8 neighbours, 2 per wheel. With n wheels each neighbour is built by string slicing, giving O(n squared) work per state; for the fixed 4 wheels that is constant.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Modulo makes 0 and 9 neighbours: turning 0 down gives 9 and turning 9 up gives 0. Deadends in seen are never queued, because seen is checked before a neighbour is added, so no extra if is needed.

card.rule: Each reading has 8 neighbours from 4 wheels turned up or down with modulo 10; put deadends in seen first.
card.limits: Putting deadends in seen only works because seen is checked before queuing a neighbour.

concepts.title: Lock cost with n wheels
concepts.question: What is the lock BFS cost when the lock has n wheels?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Work out the BFS cost for a lock with n wheels.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each wheel has 10 values, so there are 10 to the power n states. At each state the code loops over the n wheels and builds strings. For the fixed 4-wheel lock the search is constant apart from O(d) to build the deadend set.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(10 to the n times n squared + d), where d is the number of deadends. With mutable strings it drops to O(10 to the n times n + d).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Seen lets each state be handled once. Per state, looping over n wheels with O(n) string copying gives n squared work, times 10 to the n states, plus O(d) for the deadend set. The extra factor of n comes from immutable strings.

card.rule: Time is the number of states times the work per state: 10^n states, O(n^2) each.
card.limits: Treat the lock as constant only when the number of wheels is fixed.

concepts.title: Evaluate division: variables as nodes
concepts.question: How do division equations become a graph?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given equations [x, y] with x / y = values[i], answer each query [a, b] with the value of a / b, or -1 if it cannot be determined.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each variable is a node. An equation x / y = val is an edge from x to y with weight val, and also an edge from y to x with weight 1 / val, so the edges are undirected. For each query, search from the numerator for the denominator, multiplying the weights along the way.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Evaluate division in Python.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(q times (n + e)) for q queries on a graph of n variables and e edges.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A path from a to b multiplies ratios that chain together: a / c = (a / b) times (b / c). If no path exists, the value cannot be derived, so return -1.

card.rule: Variables are nodes; each equation adds a weighted edge and its reciprocal; each query is a traversal.
card.limits: A query with a variable missing from the equations cannot be answered, even a / a.

concepts.title: Why multiplying along a path gives the quotient
concepts.question: Why does the product of weights along a path give the answer to a query?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Answer a query a / b from a set of equations by traversing a graph.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: If a / b = 5, then a is 5 times bigger than b, so moving along the edge a to b gives a multiplier of 5. If b / c = 2, the edge b to c gives 2. Moving from a to c passes both edges and gives 5 times 2 = 10.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each query is one traversal of the equation graph, costing O(n + e) for n variables and e edges. With q queries the total is O(q times (n + e)).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Chaining equations cancels the middle variable: (a / b) times (b / c) = a / c. Any path from the numerator to the denominator gives the same product in a consistent set of equations, so the first path found is enough.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Start the traversal with a ratio of 1 for the numerator. Each time you cross an edge, multiply the current ratio by that edge's weight, and return the ratio on reaching the denominator.

card.rule: Carry a running product from the numerator; the product on reaching the denominator is the answer.
card.limits: The argument assumes the equations agree with each other. Contradictory inputs would give different products on different paths.

concepts.title: Weighted graphs and what a weight is
concepts.question: What is a weight on an edge, and why are weighted graphs rare in interviews?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know what a weight is, and when a plain traversal is enough.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A weight is a value associated with an edge. Earlier graphs were unweighted. In the division problem, variables are nodes, equations give the edges and the ratios are the weights: if a / b = 5, the edge from a to b has weight 5 and the edge from b to a has weight 1 / 5.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A plain traversal still costs O(n + e). Weighted shortest paths need more advanced algorithms, which the book treats as out of scope for most interviews. In the division graph, applying a weight is one multiplication per edge.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A traversal only follows edges, and here the weights multiply along the path, so plain BFS or DFS works. The reverse edge has weight 1 / val because x / y = val implies y / x = 1 / val.
