card.rule: A weight is a value on an edge; plain BFS and DFS treat every edge alike.
card.limits: Do not use BFS for shortest paths when edge weights differ, since fewer edges need not mean a smaller total.

concepts.title: Evaluate division: time and space
concepts.question: What is the cost of answering q queries on the equation graph?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Estimate the running time for q queries on the equation graph.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Let n be the number of variables, e the number of edges and q the number of queries. Build the graph once, with each equation in both directions. Each query then starts a fresh traversal from its numerator with a new seen set.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time is O(q times (n + e)). Space is O(n + e) for the graph, seen and the call stack, if the output is not counted as extra space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each query's traversal visits each node at most once and iterates the edges once, which is O(n + e), and q independent traversals multiply that by q. n is linear in the number of equations in the worst case.

card.rule: Time is O(q(n + e)) because every query runs its own traversal.
card.limits: n is linear in the number of equations in the worst case, so the cost can also be written with the equation count.

concepts.title: What a heap is and what it costs
concepts.question: What does a heap do for you, and what does each operation cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Keep a collection that keeps changing, and still be able to reach its smallest (or largest) item quickly.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A heap is a container that supports three operations: add an element, remove the minimum, and find the minimum. It implements the abstract priority queue. People use the two terms interchangeably, and the course says heap.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Add is O(log n), remove the minimum is O(log n), and find the minimum is O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The minimum is kept ready at the top at all times, so reading it is free. The logarithmic work on each add or removal is the price of keeping it ready.

card.rule: A heap finds its minimum in O(1) and adds or removes in O(log n).
card.limits: Our reading: the O(1) promise covers the extreme element only. The three listed operations include no fast lookup of other values.

concepts.title: A binary heap in an array
concepts.question: How can a plain array hold a tree with the smallest element on top?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Store a heap, a tree whose smallest element sits on top, without a Node object per element.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A binary heap holds a binary tree in a single array: each array element stands for one tree node, and the root is the smallest element. The tree must be complete. At every node the rule holds that a parent's value does not exceed its children's.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Reading the minimum is reading the root, so O(1). Changes need a number of operations that scales logarithmically with the element count.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every other node reaches the root through a chain of parents, each no larger than its child. So no node can be smaller than the root, and the root is the minimum.

card.rule: A binary heap is a complete binary tree in an array where every parent is no larger than its children, so the root is the minimum.
card.limits: Our reading: the rule compares a parent only with its children, so the array is not sorted and siblings may come in either order.

media.alt: A small min heap drawn as a binary tree, with arrows pointing from each parent down to its children. The root holds 3 and has two children, 5 and 24. The node 5 has two children of its own, 99 and 62, while 24 is a leaf. Every parent is smaller than the children below it.

concepts.title: Finding children with index arithmetic
concepts.question: How does the array find a node's children without any pointers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the children of a heap node when the heap is only an array.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The root is at index 0. The node at index i has its children at indices 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. So indices 1 and 2 are the root's children, 3 and 4 belong to index 1, and 5 and 6 belong to index 2.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A child's position comes from one calculation on the index, with no search.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The complete tree is numbered level by level from left to right, and the formula follows that numbering.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: In an array heap, the node at index i has its children at indices 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
card.limits: Our reading: a child exists only if its index is below the heap's size, so a node near the end may have one child or none.

concepts.title: Repairing the heap and building one
concepts.question: What keeps the heap rule true after adds and removals, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Keep the parent-no-larger-than-child rule true after an element is added or removed.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: After each add or removal, the heap runs repair operations that restore the rule; the course calls the process bubbling up. An existing array can also be converted into a heap in one go.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each add or removal needs a number of operations that scales logarithmically with the element count: O(log n). Converting an existing array of n elements takes linear time: O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: the repair only has to follow one path of the tree, so its length follows the tree's height, which grows logarithmically.

card.rule: Adds and removals repair the heap in O(log n), and an existing array becomes a heap in O(n).
card.limits: Our reading: n separate adds, each O(log n), cost O(n log n) in all, so converting an existing array in one go is the cheaper way to build.

concepts.title: When a heap speeds up an algorithm
concepts.question: When does a heap turn a quadratic algorithm into an O(n log n) one?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An algorithm needs the maximum or minimum of a changing collection, again and again.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Scanning for the extreme costs a pass over the data each time. With a heap, each lookup is O(1) and each change is O(log n). The course says a heap is a great option whenever you need the maximum or minimum of something repeatedly.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: n scans of O(n) each give O(n^2). n rounds of heap work at O(log n) give O(n log n). For n = 1,000,000 that is about 50,000 times fewer steps.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The heap keeps the extreme at the top as items come and go, so the repeated question never needs a fresh scan.

card.rule: If a problem needs the max or min of a changing collection again and again, a heap turns O(n^2) into O(n log n).
card.limits: Our reading: the gain is for repeated extremes. A single minimum of a fixed list needs one pass.

concepts.title: Using a built-in heap: min or max
concepts.question: Which kind of heap does my language give me, and how do I get the other kind?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Use the language's own heap in a solution. Some languages give a min heap by default and some a max heap.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Learn four calls: add, peek at the top, pop the top, get the size. Python's heap is a min heap only. For numbers, the easy way to get the opposite kind is to multiply every number by -1 on the way in and again on the way out.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The same as any heap: add and pop are O(log n), and peek is O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The smallest of the negated numbers belongs to the largest original number, so the min heap's top is the original maximum.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.code:
import heapq
heap = []
for x in [4, 9, 2]:
    heapq.heappush(heap, -x)       # store negatives
largest = -heap[0]                 # peek: 9
popped = -heapq.heappop(heap)      # pop: 9
size = len(heap)                   # 2

card.rule: Check which heap your language gives; for the opposite kind of numbers, store them multiplied by -1 and negate again when reading.
card.limits: Negating works for numbers only. Other keys need another ordering rule.

concepts.title: Last Stone Weight: smash with a max heap
concepts.question: How does a max heap simulate repeatedly smashing the two heaviest stones?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones together, and report the weight of the last stone.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Put all stones in a max heap. While at least two stones remain, pop the two heaviest. If their weights differ, push their difference back onto the heap; if they are equal, both vanish.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each round does two pops and at most one push, each O(log n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The two heaviest stones are always at the top of the max heap, even after leftovers are pushed back, so each round smashes exactly the stones the rules ask for.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Simulate the smashing with a max heap: pop two, and push back the difference when it is not zero.
card.limits: Python only has a min heap, so the code negates every weight on the way in and out.

concepts.title: Why the stone simulation is O(n log n)
concepts.question: Why does the stone-smashing loop take at most O(n log n) time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Bound the running time of the stone-smashing loop.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Every smash destroys at least one stone, so the number of stones drops by at least one per round and there are at most n rounds. Each round does a fixed number of heap operations.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: At most n rounds of O(log n) work gives O(n log n) time, with O(n) space for the heap.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The round count is bounded by the number of stones, not by their weights, so heavy stones add no rounds.

blocks.label: Trace
blocks.text: Stones 8, 6, 5, 2: round 1 smashes 8 and 6 and returns 2 (3 stones left). Round 2 smashes 5 and 2 and returns 3 (2 left). Round 3 smashes 3 and 2 and returns 1 (1 left). That is 3 rounds for n = 4.

card.rule: Each smash destroys at least one stone, so there are at most n rounds of O(log n) work: O(n log n).
card.limits: Our reading: the n-round bound relies on every smash destroying a stone. A rule that could leave both stones alive would need a new argument.

concepts.title: Minimum operations to halve an array sum
concepts.question: Why is a max heap the right tool for picking which number to halve next?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Halve numbers one at a time, a number may be chosen again, and find the fewest operations that cut the total by at least half.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Always halve the current largest number, because that cuts the sum by the most. Put the numbers in a max heap and set a target of half the sum. Repeat: pop the largest x, subtract x / 2 from the target, push x / 2 back, and count one operation, until the target is zero or below.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each pass costs O(log n) in heap work, and the whole loop is O(n log n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Halving x removes x / 2 from the sum, so the largest number removes the most. No other choice at that step reaches the target in fewer steps.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.code:
import heapq
def halve_array(nums):
    heap = [-n for n in nums]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    target, ops = sum(nums) / 2, 0
    while target > 0:
        x = -heapq.heappop(heap)
        target -= x / 2
        heapq.heappush(heap, -(x / 2))
        ops += 1
    return ops

card.rule: To cut the sum in the fewest halvings, always halve the current largest number, using a max heap.
card.limits: Our reading: the halves are fractions, so use real division. Whole-number division would change the answer.

concepts.title: Two heaps and the middle value
concepts.question: How can two heaps expose the middle value of a growing dataset?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Report the median of numbers that keep arriving, quickly, at any moment.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep the smaller half of the numbers in a max heap and the larger half in a min heap, so the top of each heap faces the middle. The sizes stay equal, or the max heap holds one extra when the count is odd. Every element of the min heap is at least as large as every element of the max heap.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Finding the median reads one or two tops, so it is O(1). The two heaps together use O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The max heap's top is the largest of the lower half and the min heap's top is the smallest of the upper half, so the two tops are the middle of the sorted data. With an even count the median is their average; with an odd count it is the extra top.

card.rule: Keep a max heap of the lower half and a min heap of the upper half in balance, and the median sits at the tops.
card.limits: The method needs the sizes balanced and the halves ordered after every add. If either breaks, the tops are no longer the middle.

media.alt: A row of eleven boxes split into two groups. Six green boxes under the label max heap end with the value 26 beside the middle; five blue boxes under min heap begin with 32. Other boxes show question marks for hidden values. An arrow under 26 marks the median. A note says hidden min heap values are at least 32 and hidden max heap values at most 26.

concepts.title: Adding a number to the two heaps
concepts.question: How does addNum keep the two heaps balanced and ordered?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Add a number to the two heaps without breaking the size balance or the order between the halves.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Three steps. Push the number onto the max heap. Pop the max heap's top and push it onto the min heap. If the min heap is now larger than the max heap, pop its top and push it onto the max heap.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: addNum is a fixed number of heap operations, so O(log n). findMedian stays O(1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Step 2 moves the largest of the lower half to the upper half, so no min-heap element is below a max-heap element. Step 3 restores the rule that the max heap takes the extra element.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.code:
import heapq
def add_num(small, large, num):    # small: max heap (negated), large: min heap
    heapq.heappush(small, -num)
    heapq.heappush(large, -heapq.heappop(small))
    if len(large) > len(small):
        heapq.heappush(small, -heapq.heappop(large))

card.rule: Push to the max heap, move its top to the min heap, then move one back if the min heap is larger.
card.limits: The steps assume the max heap takes the extra element. If the roles were swapped, every step would need mirroring.

concepts.title: Top k with a bounded min heap
concepts.question: How can a heap pick the k best of n items faster than sorting?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Return the k best elements of n, with 'best' defined by the problem.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sorting and taking the first k costs O(n log n). Instead, keep a min heap ordered by the problem's criterion. Push every element, and pop whenever the size exceeds k. Each pop removes the worst element held, so the k best remain.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The heap never grows beyond k plus one element, so each operation is O(log k). Over n elements that is O(n log k).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A min heap pops the lowest-valued element, which is the worst by the criterion. After every pop the heap holds the k best seen so far.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: To get the k best in O(n log k), keep a min heap of at most k elements and pop whenever it grows past k.
card.limits: Our reading: the heap holds the k best but not in sorted order, so sort them at the end if the order matters.

concepts.title: Top K Frequent Elements
concepts.question: Why does a size-k min heap of (frequency, element) pairs return the k most frequent elements?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Return the k most frequent elements of an integer array; the answer is guaranteed to be unique.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Count each element's frequency with a hash map. Push each (frequency, element) pair onto a min heap, with the frequency first so the heap orders by it. When the size exceeds k, pop, which drops the least frequent pair.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n log k) time. The space is O(n + k) for the hash map and the heap.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Suppose x is among the k most frequent. If x were popped, k other elements in the heap would be at least as frequent as x, which contradicts x being among the top k. So x is never popped.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Count with a hash map, then keep the k most frequent in a min heap of at most k pairs keyed by frequency.
card.limits: Our reading: the argument leans on the answer being unique. Ties for the last place would make the set ambiguous.

concepts.title: Find K Closest Elements with a heap
concepts.question: How does a max heap on distance, with a tie rule, keep the k closest elements?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: From a sorted array, return the k elements closest to x in ascending order; on a tie in distance, take the smaller element.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep a max heap ordered by distance from x, so the farthest element is on top. Push every element and pop whenever the size exceeds k. On equal distances the larger value must be popped first. At the end, sort the k survivors.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O((n + k) log k): n pushes and pops of O(log k) each, plus O(k log k) to sort the answer.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: As in top k, each pop removes the worst candidate, here the farthest, and the tie rule makes the larger value count as worse. The k best remain.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: For the k smallest distances, use a max heap on distance, break ties by value, and sort the survivors.
card.limits: The method treats the array as unsorted, so approaches that use its order can beat it.

concepts.title: What a greedy algorithm is
concepts.question: What makes a decision in a greedy algorithm both optimal and local?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Many problems ask for the maximum or minimum of something, one choice at a time. How can a procedure decide at every step without planning the whole answer in advance?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal decision at every step. Optimal is set by the problem: for a largest sum, the larger of two numbers wins. Local means the choice uses only the options at the current step and ignores later consequences.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Greedy is usually very efficient, since each step looks only at the current options; many solutions sort the input first so the max or min is easy to pick. The book's example: greedy for the travelling salesman problem takes O(n^2) time.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Being locally best does not by itself make the final answer best. The book calls the proof that a greedy strategy works the hard part; a greedy answer can be close to correct and still wrong, as with its travelling salesman example, so correctness is argued per problem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A shopper who wants as many items as possible within a budget keeps taking the cheapest item left on the shelf. Each pick compares prices now and does not plan the rest of the basket.

card.rule: A greedy algorithm takes the best option visible at this step, as the problem defines best, without looking ahead.
card.limits: The definition says what greedy is, not that it works. A locally best choice can still lead to a worse final answer, so whether a problem rewards the greedy choice has to be argued separately.

concepts.title: When the locally best choice misses the best answer
concepts.question: Can a greedy choice at every step still end with a wrong final answer?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A courier must deliver pizzas to five houses and wants the least total travel time. The order of the visits decides the total.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Plan nothing: always drive to the nearest unvisited house. Each choice is local, since it looks only at the next house and ignores every later decision.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The nearest-house rule is cheap. The book's figure for the travelling salesman problem: greedy runs in O(n^2) and is usually about 25 percent off, while no classical exact algorithm faster than O(2^n) is known.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: It need not be correct. A bridge between two houses would have cut the trip with a different order, although every step was locally best. A local choice ignores what it does to later options, so a run of best steps may not give the best whole.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Largest coin first, as a Python function:

card.rule: A strategy that picks the best option step by step is trustworthy only once you have a reason that it reaches the best whole.
card.limits: Nothing here says greedy usually fails: many problems are solved exactly by a greedy rule, as later ideas show. The point is that correctness is not automatic.

concepts.title: Recognising greedy problems: extremes, steps and sorting
concepts.question: Which clues in a problem suggest trying a greedy approach?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether a new problem should be attacked by repeatedly taking a best or smallest option.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Look for a maximum or minimum being asked and for a result built step by step. A greedy step picks an extreme, so the first move is often to sort the input, which puts the largest or smallest elements where they are easy to take.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Greedy solutions are short loops, usually after one sort, so the sort tends to set the cost: O(n log n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Sorting is preparation only. Why the greedy rule is right has to come from reasoning about the specific problem.

card.rule: When a problem wants a maximum or minimum from step-by-step choices, sort the input and test a rule that takes the extreme option each time.
card.limits: These are only clues. A problem can show all of them and still defeat the greedy rule, so the rule still needs a reason to be trusted.

concepts.title: Easy to code, hard to justify
concepts.question: Where does the real effort in a greedy solution go: writing the code or trusting the strategy?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You have a greedy rule that looks sensible and must decide whether to rely on it.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Writing a greedy rule is typically easy. The hard part is realising that the strategy works and being able to say why.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The code is usually a short loop, often after a sort.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The check is an argument that no other choice at a step can do better. Passing a few examples does not supply one.

card.rule: Writing a greedy loop is the easy part; the work is showing that the greedy choice is safe.
card.limits: Easy to code does not mean easy to find: spotting the rule can be the hard thing. A rule that fails on some inputs is wrong however tidy the code is.

concepts.title: Destroying asteroids: smallest first
concepts.question: Which asteroid should the planet meet next, and how is it found cheaply?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A planet of a given mass meets asteroids one at a time, in any order you choose. An asteroid heavier than the planet destroys it; otherwise the planet absorbs the asteroid's mass. Decide whether every asteroid can be destroyed.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sort the masses ascending and meet them in that order. If the next asteroid is heavier than the current mass, the answer is no; if the loop finishes, the answer is yes.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n log n) for the sort over n asteroids, plus one pass.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The smallest remaining asteroid is the easiest to take, and absorbing it only helps. The next idea gives the full argument.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version:

card.rule: Sort ascending and absorb asteroids in that order; answer no at the first one heavier than the current mass.
card.limits: Our reading: the method relies on being free to choose the order. If the asteroids had to be met in a fixed order, sorting would change the problem.

concepts.title: Why smallest-first is safe: the mass only grows
concepts.question: Why does the order among asteroids the planet can already destroy not matter?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Show that the order among asteroids the planet can already destroy is irrelevant, so taking the smallest first is safe.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The planet's mass can only increase. An asteroid it can destroy now can still be destroyed after absorbing any other asteroid, so between two destroyable asteroids the choice does not matter.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The argument adds no work: the algorithm stays O(n log n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every destroyable asteroid stays destroyable, so any order of them ends with the same absorbed set. Choosing the smallest each time is a convenient way to keep track of which are destroyable.

card.rule: Mass only increases, so an asteroid that can be destroyed now can be destroyed later, and the order among destroyable ones does not matter.
card.limits: Our reading: the argument needs the mass to never shrink. If a collision could reduce the mass, a destroyable asteroid might stop being destroyable and the order could matter.

concepts.title: Grouping values within a gap of k
concepts.question: How can sorting and one pass count the fewest groups whose largest and smallest differ by at most k?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Split an array into the fewest subsequences so that, in each, the largest and smallest values differ by at most k.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sort. Let x be the smallest value not yet grouped and put into its group every value up to x plus k. The first value beyond x plus k starts a new group and becomes the new x.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n log n) for n values.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Starting at the smallest value and taking everything within k packs the largest possible group. The next idea gives the argument.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version:

card.rule: Sort, start a group at the smallest unused value x, absorb everything up to x plus k, then start again at the first value beyond.
card.limits: Our reading: the method works because only each group's maximum and minimum matter. If a group had to be a run of neighbours in the original order, sorting would change the problem.

concepts.title: Why sorting is safe and taking all within k is best
concepts.question: Why can we sort the array and take every value within k of the smallest?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Justify two moves in the partition solution: sorting an array when the groups are subsequences, and taking every value within k of the smallest.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A group is judged only by its maximum and minimum, so the order of the values inside it is irrelevant and sorting cannot spoil a grouping.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: None: this is an argument, and the algorithm stays O(n log n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Take the smallest value x. Leaving out a value in the range x to x plus k cannot help: the next group would have to start at a smaller value, which narrows the range it can cover.

card.rule: Order inside a group is irrelevant, and leaving out a value within k of the group's smallest only makes later groups worse.
card.limits: The argument needs both facts: only the maximum and minimum matter, and the groups need no particular positions. If either changes, sorting may no longer be safe.

concepts.title: Choosing projects: the most profitable one you can afford
concepts.question: Which project should be done at each step to finish with the most capital?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You start with capital w and may complete up to k projects. Project i needs at least capital[i] to start and adds profits[i] to your capital when finished. End with as much capital as possible.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: At each step, among the projects you can afford with your current capital, do the one with the highest profit. Finishing it raises the capital, which can make further projects affordable.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Set by sorting and a heap, covered in the next idea.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A project with more profit is at least as good for the next step as one with less. A later idea gives the argument.

card.rule: Among the projects you can afford, take the one with the most profit, and repeat up to k times.
card.limits: The choice is only among projects affordable now, and the pool grows as capital grows, so it must be recomputed after every project.

concepts.title: Sorting by capital and a max heap for the best affordable project
concepts.question: How can the most profitable affordable project be found quickly at every step?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Run the project rule efficiently: know which projects are affordable now, and take the highest profit among them.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sort projects by required capital. A pointer moves forward over those now affordable, pushing their profits into a max heap. Each step pops the largest profit and adds it to the capital.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O((k + n) log n): n pushes and k pops on a heap of up to n items, plus the sort. Space is O(n) for the heap.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The heap holds the profit of every project affordable so far, so its top is the best choice.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version; heapq is a min heap, so profits are stored negated:

card.rule: Sort by capital, move a pointer to add newly affordable profits to a max heap, and pop the largest each step.
card.limits: The k pops are a ceiling: the loop stops early when the heap is empty. Python's heapq is a min heap, so a max heap needs negated profits.

concepts.title: Why the highest profit is a safe pick
concepts.question: Is there ever a reason to pick a project with less profit when a more profitable one is affordable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Show that, among affordable projects, no choice does better than the most profitable one.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Compare two affordable projects with profits x and y, where x is less than y. Whatever new projects finishing x makes affordable, finishing y makes affordable too, because y adds more capital.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: None: this is an argument, not extra computation.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: No state exists where the lower profit unlocks something the higher profit misses, and the higher profit also gains more. So picking the smaller profit has no advantage.

card.rule: A bigger profit unlocks at least the projects a smaller one would, so the most profitable affordable project is a safe pick.
card.limits: Our reading: the argument relies on profits only adding to capital and on each project having a fixed requirement. If finishing a project could cost capital, a bigger profit might not be a safe pick.

concepts.title: Fewest distinct values after k removals
concepts.question: Which values should be removed to leave the fewest distinct values after exactly k removals?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Remove exactly k elements from an array so that as few distinct values as possible remain.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Count how often each value occurs. Removing some copies of a value does not lower the distinct count; only removing all of them does. So remove whole values starting from the least frequent while removals remain.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n log n) time for n elements, and O(n) space for the counts.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A removal helps only when it finishes off a value. Values with few copies cost the fewest removals to finish, so taking them first finishes the most values with k removals.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version:

card.rule: Count frequencies, then remove whole values from the least frequent upward until the removals run out.
card.limits: Our reading: exactly k removals must be made, but partial removals never lower the count, so leftover removals are spent on copies of values that stay.

concepts.title: Rescue boats: the heaviest rides, the lightest joins if possible
concepts.question: How should the heaviest person be paired to use as few two-person boats as possible?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: People have weights. A boat holds at most two people whose combined weight is within the limit, and nobody weighs more than the limit. Use the fewest boats.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sort the weights. Keep a pointer i on the lightest and j on the heaviest remaining person. The heaviest boards; the lightest boards too if the pair fits.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n log n) for the sort, then an O(n) two-pointer pass. Extra space is only what the sort uses.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A boat carrying two saves one boat, and the heaviest person is the hardest to pair. The next idea gives the argument.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version:

card.rule: Sort, then let the heaviest remaining person board each boat and add the lightest remaining person when the pair fits.
card.limits: Our reading: the method relies on the two-person cap and on nobody exceeding the limit. If a boat took three people, pairing the two ends would not be enough.

concepts.title: Why pairing the heaviest with the lightest is safe
concepts.question: Why does the heaviest person either ride alone or ride with the lightest?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Argue that pairing the heaviest remaining person with the lightest remaining person never costs an extra boat.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Let x be the heaviest and y the lightest. If x plus y is over the limit, x can fit with nobody, so x rides alone. If it is within the limit, y could pair with anyone, so y may as well pair with x.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: None: this is an argument, and the algorithm stays O(n log n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every pairing saves one boat, whoever is paired, so y gains nothing by choosing a lighter partner. Pairing with x is at least as good.

card.rule: If the lightest can ride with anyone, give them the heaviest; if even the lightest cannot ride with the heaviest, the heaviest rides alone.
card.limits: Our reading: the case split uses the two-person cap. If boats took three people, the same split would not cover the choices, and the rule would need a new argument.

concepts.title: What binary search finds and what it needs
concepts.question: What must be true of the search space, and what can binary search return from it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a sorted array and a value x, find the index of x if it is present. Or find the first or the last index where x could be inserted while keeping the array sorted.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Compare x with the element in the middle, throw away the half that cannot hold x, and repeat on the half that is left. The search space usually needs to be sorted for this to work.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(log n) time in the worst case, where n is the size of the search space, and O(1) extra space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Sorted order lets one comparison speak for a whole half of the array. That is why a single look can remove many elements at once.

card.rule: Binary search needs a sorted search space, and then answers in O(log n) time with O(1) extra space.
card.limits: The authors say the space usually needs to be sorted, and later sections search a range of answers that is not an array at all. On an unsorted array a single comparison tells you nothing about the rest.

concepts.title: Why dropping half is safe
concepts.question: Why can binary search discard half of the array after looking at one element?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find where x sits in a sorted array when you know x is present but not its index.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Look at the middle element. If it is too small, every element to its left is too small as well. If it is too large, every element to its right is too large as well. Drop that half and repeat on the other.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each look removes half of what remains, so the number of looks grows with the logarithm of n and not with n.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Because the array is sorted, the middle element bounds a whole side. The dropped half cannot contain x, so x, if present, stays inside the part you keep.

card.rule: After comparing with the middle, discard the half that cannot contain x, because sorted order bounds everything on that side.
card.limits: The argument uses the order of the array. In an unsorted array a too-small middle element would say nothing about the elements on its left, so no half could be dropped safely.

concepts.title: The inclusive-bounds template
concepts.question: How do left, right and mid work together in the standard binary search loop?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find a target in a sorted array that has no repeated values, or learn where it would have to be inserted.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep left and right as inclusive bounds of the current search space, starting at 0 and the last index. While left <= right, check the middle: equal means done, too large means right = mid - 1, too small means left = mid + 1.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Every pass halves the space, so the loop takes O(log n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The two bounds always enclose every index that could still hold the target. A failed middle is removed by stepping past it with mid - 1 or mid + 1, so the space shrinks on every pass.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The loop in Python:

card.rule: With inclusive bounds, loop while left <= right and step past a failed middle with mid - 1 or mid + 1.
card.limits: Our reading: the choices in this template go together. Mixing them with another template, for example right = mid with left <= right, can break the loop. It is also meant for arrays without repeated values.

concepts.title: Why the cost is logarithmic
concepts.question: How many halvings does it take to empty n elements, and why does that mean O(log n)?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Say how the work of binary search grows as the sorted array gets larger.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each pass looks at one element and keeps at most half of the rest, so the number of passes is the number of times n can be halved.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(log n) comparisons in the worst case, and O(1) extra space, since only left, right and mid are stored.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Because the search space is halved at every iteration, the worst case is about log base 2 of n passes. Doubling the array adds a single pass.

blocks.label: Trace
blocks.text: With the inclusive template, 1,000 elements need at most 10 passes, 2,000 need at most 11, and 1,000,000 need at most 20.

card.rule: Halving each pass makes the worst case O(log n), so doubling the input adds one pass.
card.limits: Logarithmic time describes the search itself. If the array has to be sorted first, the sort costs more than the search, as the pairs example later shows.

concepts.title: Computing the middle without overflow
concepts.question: Why do Java and C++ write the middle as left + (right - left) / 2?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In Java and C++, the sum left + right can overflow a fixed-size integer when both bounds are large, and the middle then comes out wrong.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Write mid = left + (right - left) / 2. It names the same middle element, but it never adds the two bounds together.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The same O(1) arithmetic in every pass, so the O(log n) time of the search is unchanged.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The two expressions are equivalent as arithmetic. They differ only in which intermediate values get stored along the way.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python imitating a 32-bit signed integer shows the wrap-around of the sum and the safe middle:

card.rule: In languages with fixed-size integers, compute the middle as left + (right - left) / 2 so the two bounds are never added.
card.limits: This guards against overflow only. In Python and JavaScript numbers do not overflow, or the limit is ridiculously huge, so (left + right) // 2 is fine there.

concepts.title: Where left ends when the target is absent
concepts.question: If the target is not found, what does left tell you when the loop ends?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Search for a value that may be missing, and still learn something useful from a failed search.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: If the loop ends without arr[mid] == x, then left sits at the index where x would have to be inserted to keep the array sorted.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: It is the same loop, so O(log n) time and O(1) space; the insertion index comes free.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every index below left was shown to hold a smaller value, and every index above right a larger one. When the bounds cross, right = left - 1, so left is the first position of a larger value.

blocks.label: Trace
blocks.text: Searching for 20 in [3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31] ends with left = 5 and right = 4: 19 is at index 4 and 23 at index 5.

card.rule: When a failed search ends, left is the index where the target would be inserted to keep order.
card.limits: This holds for the no-duplicates template. With repeated values the left-most and right-most templates decide which insertion index you get, as the next ideas show.

concepts.title: The left-most template for repeated values
concepts.question: How do you find the first index of a value that appears several times in a sorted array?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The sorted array has repeated values. Find the left-most index of the target, or its insertion index if it is missing.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Start with right = len(arr) and loop while left < right. If arr[mid] >= target, set right = mid, which keeps mid as a candidate. Otherwise set left = mid + 1. Return left.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(log n) time and O(1) space, the same as the basic template.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A middle element that is at least the target might itself be the first match, so it stays in the space. Only elements below the target are dropped, and when left meets right they stand on the first element at least as large as the target.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: For the first copy, start right at the length, loop while left < right, and set right = mid whenever arr[mid] >= target.
card.limits: This is a different template from the basic one: right starts at the length, not length - 1, and the loop test is left < right. Mixing the two sets of choices breaks the search.

concepts.title: The right-most insertion point
concepts.question: Which single change turns the first-match search into a search for the spot after the last copy?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The sorted array has repeated values. Find the right-most insertion index, which is the index of the right-most copy plus one.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Use the left-most template, but test arr[mid] > target instead of arr[mid] >= target. Equal elements are now passed over to the left, so the search keeps moving right across them.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(log n) time and O(1) space again.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Only elements strictly larger than the target stay as candidates. Equal elements are dropped, so left ends on the first element that is larger than the target.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: To land one past the last copy, use the first-match template with arr[mid] > target.
card.limits: If the target is missing, left - 1 is not a copy of it, so check arr[left - 1] == target before treating it as found. Our reading, from how the template ends.

concepts.title: Replacing a linear scan with binary search
concepts.question: When is binary search a better tool than checking every index, and what does it save?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given an integer array sorted in ascending order and a target, return the index of the target, or -1 if it is absent. This is the authors' first array example, LeetCode problem 704.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The brute-force answer checks every index. Because the array is sorted, binary search can halve the range on each pass instead, using the inclusive-bounds template and returning -1 after the loop.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The scan is O(n). Binary search is O(log n) time and uses only a few integer variables as extra space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The target, if present, always lies between left and right, and each pass removes the half where it cannot be.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: On a sorted array, replace an O(n) scan with a binary search that costs O(log n).
card.limits: The saving needs order. On an unsorted array the halving argument fails, and sorting first adds its own cost.

concepts.title: The authors' advice: copy a template
concepts.question: According to the authors, how should you handle the many small choices in writing binary search?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Many people get confused implementing binary search: how to initialise right, whether to loop while left < right or left <= right, whether to update with mid + 1 or mid, and whether with mid - 1 or mid.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: According to the authors, do not ponder these details while solving problems. Copy the templates they provide, either by committing them to memory or by keeping them open on paper or in another tab during an interview.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Copying a template costs nothing at run time. Each template is binary search, which the book states takes O(log n) time in the worst case and O(1) space, because the search space is halved every iteration.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each template is a fixed set of choices that fit together: the start of right, the loop test and the updates. Copying one whole avoids mixing parts of different templates. Our reading, not the authors' wording.

card.rule: According to the authors, pick the matching template and copy it whole instead of re-deriving the bounds each time.
card.limits: This is the authors' advice for interviews, an opinion about practice and not a proof. A template still has to fit the job: one exact target, the left-most copy, or the right-most spot.

concepts.title: Searching a sorted matrix as one array
concepts.question: How can a sorted matrix be searched as a single array, and how do you turn an index into a cell?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An m by n matrix has each row sorted left to right, and the first number of each row is larger than the last number of the row above. Does a target appear in it?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Treat the grid as one array of length m * n and search the indexes 0 to m * n - 1. To read the value at index mid, convert it with row = mid // n and col = mid % n.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The search space has m * n cells, so the time is O(log(m * n)), and the extra space is a few integer variables.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each row is sorted and lies entirely below the next, so reading the rows one after another gives a fully sorted sequence.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: Binary search the indexes 0 to m * n - 1 and read each middle from row = mid // n, col = mid % n.
card.limits: It needs both matrix conditions. If a row could start below the end of the previous one, the flattened sequence would not be sorted. Our reading.

media.alt: A grid of three rows and four columns, each cell holding one number. The numbers run from 0 to 11, filling the first row left to right, then continuing along the second row and the third. It shows a matrix read as one long numbered line, row after row.

concepts.title: Why row = i // n and col = i % n
concepts.question: Why does dividing an index by the row length give the row, and the remainder the column?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Explain why a flat index i maps to row i // n and column i % n in a grid with n columns.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Lay the rows end to end. Row 0 uses indexes 0 to n - 1, row 1 uses n to 2n - 1, and so on, with n cells in each row.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The conversion is a division and a remainder, which is O(1) per pass, so the search stays O(log(m * n)).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The row number goes up by one every n indexes, which is floor division by n. The column starts again at 0 every n indexes, which is the remainder after dividing by n.

card.rule: Floor division by the row length gives the row, and the remainder gives the column.
card.limits: It needs every row to hold the same number of cells n. With rows of different lengths, one divisor does not fit all rows. Our reading.

concepts.title: Counting with an insertion point
concepts.question: How does the insertion point of a threshold in a sorted array tell you how many elements reach it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given spell strengths, potion strengths and a number success, count for each spell how many potions give a product of at least success with it. All strengths are positive.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sort the potions. A spell of strength x needs a potion of at least success / x. Binary search that value for its insertion index i with the left-most template; every potion from index i on qualifies.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each lookup is O(log m), where m is the number of potions, and it uses a few integer variables as extra space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Sorted order puts every potion at or above the threshold from index i to the end. With m potions that range holds (m - 1) - i + 1 = m - i of them.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The count for one spell, in Python:

card.rule: The count for a spell is the number of potions minus the insertion index of success / spell in the sorted potions.
card.limits: The threshold success / x assumes positive strengths, as the problem states, and the potions must be sorted first. Sorting is part of the cost.

concepts.title: Sort once, then search many times
concepts.question: Why does sorting once and searching for each spell beat comparing every spell with every potion?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Compare the cost of checking all spell and potion pairs with sorting the potions and searching for each spell.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The brute-force version checks every pair. The faster version sorts the potions once, then binary searches once for each of the n spells.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Brute force is O(n * m). Sorting costs O(m log m) and the n searches cost O(n log m), so the total is O((m + n) log m).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The sort is paid once and every search costs only a logarithm. Because log m is small, (m + n) log m is much smaller than n * m.

card.rule: Pay for one sort, and then each query costs only a logarithm.
card.limits: The saving comes from many queries on the same sorted data. With a single spell, sorting first would cost more than scanning once. Our reading.

concepts.title: When you can binary search the answers
concepts.question: What conditions let you binary search over possible answers rather than over an array?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some problems ask for the largest or smallest value with which something can be done, and no sorted array is given. The candidate answers themselves form the solution space.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Binary search the range of candidate answers. For each mid, a check function says whether the task is possible for that value, and the result tells which half of the range to keep.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: It is valid when: a value can be checked in O(n) or better; for a maximum, a working value means every smaller one works and a failing value means every larger one fails; for a minimum, the same holds with larger and smaller swapped.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: With a check of O(n), the search takes O(n log k), where k is the size of the range of the solution space.

card.rule: Binary search the answers when a quick check exists and the results change only once along the range.
card.limits: If a value can fail and a larger one work again, then fail again, one check at mid does not say which half to keep. Our reading.

concepts.title: Two zones and a threshold
concepts.question: What do the possible and impossible answers look like along the range, and what does the problem ask for?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Say how the possible and impossible candidate answers are arranged along the range, and what a min or max question asks for.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The candidates split into two zones: one where the task is possible and one where it is impossible. The zones have no breaks and no overlap, and they meet at a threshold. A min or max question asks for the value at that threshold.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Finding the threshold takes O(log k) checks over a range of k candidate values.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Inside a zone, every check gives the same answer. So one check at mid says which side of the threshold mid is on, and half of the range can be dropped.

blocks.label: Trace
blocks.text: Suppose a speed fails for 1 to 5 and works for 6 and above. The threshold sits between 5 and 6, and the minimum answer is 6.

card.rule: Possible and impossible answers form two gap-free zones, and a minimum or maximum is the value at the point where they meet.
card.limits: A threshold exists only if the zones really have no breaks. If results alternate along the range, a check at mid does not say which side holds the answer. Our reading.

media.alt: Under the heading 'Problem is asking for a maximum', a number line is marked 0, 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, 100,000, 1,000,000 and on toward infinity. A teal block labelled possible covers the left part and a red block labelled impossible covers the right part, meeting just to the right of 1,000. An upward arrow at that boundary carries the caption 'The threshold is the answer and can be binary searched for'.

concepts.title: Choosing the bounds and counting the cost
concepts.question: Where do the bounds of the search start, and what does the whole search cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Set the start and end of the range to search, and state the cost of the whole procedure.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Left is the smallest possible answer and right is the largest possible answer. At each mid, run check and keep the half of the range that can hold the threshold.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: If check takes O(n), the total time is O(n log k), where k is the size of the range of the solution space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The range always contains the threshold, and every pass halves it, so about log k passes are needed, each with one O(n) check.

card.rule: Start at the smallest and largest possible answers; the total cost is log k checks, each costing as much as one check.
card.limits: The range must really contain the answer. If a bound is too tight, the threshold is never inside the search and the result is wrong. The total is only as fast as the check.

concepts.title: Minimum eating speed: the check and the bounds
concepts.question: How is the time for an eating speed counted, and where does the search start and end?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: There are n piles of bananas and h hours. Each hour Koko eats from one pile, k bananas at most. Find the smallest whole-number speed k that finishes every pile within h hours.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A speed k works when the sum over the piles of ceil(pile / k) is at most h. Search the speeds from 1 to max(piles) for the smallest one that works.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: check is O(n) over the piles, and the search over speeds adds log k passes, so the total is O(n log k) with k = max(piles). Extra space is a few integers.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A faster speed never needs more hours, so working speeds form one block. One pile per hour means a leftover banana costs a full extra hour, so each pile is rounded up on its own.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python:

card.rule: Count ceil(pile / k) hours for each pile, and search speeds 1 to max(piles) for the smallest speed within h.
card.limits: Round each pile up on its own, then add. Adding the piles first and rounding afterwards undercounts, because a leftover part of an hour cannot be shared between piles.

concepts.title: Path with minimum effort: a graph search as the check
concepts.question: How can a reachability search act as the check for the smallest allowed height difference?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A grid holds heights. You move up, down, left or right, and a path's effort is its largest absolute height difference between consecutive cells. Find the least effort of any path from the top left to the bottom right.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Binary search the effort. check(effort) runs a depth-first search from the top left, stepping to a neighbour only if the height difference is at most effort, and reports whether it reaches the bottom right.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The search is O(m * n) and runs O(log k) times, with k the largest height: O(m * n * log k) time. The stack and the seen set take O(m * n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A path that works for some effort works for any larger effort, and if no path exists for an effort, none exists for a smaller one. So the results form two zones.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The check in Python:

card.rule: Make the check a reachability search that crosses only steps within the allowed effort, and binary search for the smallest effort that reaches the goal.
card.limits: The binary search is only a wrapper: its log k factor multiplies whatever the check costs, and a depth-first search costs far more than a counting loop.

concepts.title: Minimum speed to arrive on time
concepts.question: How does the train problem change the check, and when is it impossible?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You take n trains in order, and each departs only at a whole hour. Given the distances and a time limit, find the smallest whole-number speed that arrives on time, or -1 if no speed can.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: It is like Koko: search the speeds and check each one. In check, the elapsed time is rounded up to a whole hour before each ride, but not after the last ride. Return -1 if there are more trains than ceil(hour).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The check is O(n) and the search adds log k passes, so the time is O(n log k) with k the largest possible speed. Extra space is a few integers.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A faster speed never arrives later, so the speeds form two zones. Every ride except the last takes at least one whole hour because of the wait, which is why too many trains make the task impossible.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The check in Python:
blocks.code:
import math

def on_time(dist, k, hour):
    t = 0
    for d in dist:
        t = math.ceil(t)    # wait for the next whole hour
        t += d / k
    return t <= hour

card.rule: Round the elapsed time up before each ride but not after the last, and return -1 when there are more trains than the rounded-up limit.
card.limits: The whole-hour departure rule is specific to this problem. A different timing rule needs a different check, though the wrapper search stays the same.

concepts.title: Why left holds a minimum and right holds a maximum
concepts.question: Why does left hold the answer for a minimum but right hold it for a maximum?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After the loop ends, decide which pointer to return for a minimum question and which for a maximum question.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: For a minimum, return left. For a maximum, return right.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: It is the same loop as before, so O(log k) passes, each with one check.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Take a minimum x. After check(x) passes, right becomes x - 1, which leaves x outside the search space. Every later check fails, so left climbs until it tries x - 1, fails, and sets left = x. Then left > right and the loop ends with left at x. A maximum mirrors this.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Both templates in Python:
blocks.code:
def smallest(lo, hi, ok):     # ok is true from the answer upward
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid): hi = mid - 1
        else: lo = mid + 1
    return lo

def largest(lo, hi, ok):      # ok is true up to the answer
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid): lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return hi

card.rule: Return left for a minimum and right for a maximum, because the pointer that moved past the answer ends right beside it.
card.limits: This holds for the loop that moves by mid plus or minus one and runs while left <= right. A template that keeps mid inside the range ends differently. Our reading.

concepts.title: Exhaustive search
concepts.question: What does exhaustive search do, and why is it so slow when the answers must meet a constraint?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You need every item of some kind that meets a constraint, and you know no shortcut to the answers. Example: all strings of length n over the letters a to z that satisfy a rule.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Exhaustive search is the most brute force way to solve such a problem: generate all possibilities first, then check each one for a solution.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Strings of length n over 26 letters give \(26^n\) candidates. If one check costs k, the total is \(O(k \cdot 26^n)\). The book calls this ridiculously slow.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Nothing is skipped, so every solution is found. The price is that the many candidates that fail are generated and checked too.

card.rule: Exhaustive search generates every candidate and checks each one afterwards, so its cost is the number of candidates times the cost of one check.
card.limits: It is correct but wasteful. A tight constraint leaves few answers, yet the generating and checking work is the same, because the checking happens only after generation.

concepts.title: Possibilities as a tree
concepts.question: How can all the possibilities of a build-it-piece-by-piece problem be drawn as one tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Many tasks build a candidate piece by piece, such as a string of n letters, and want all candidates or those meeting a constraint. How can all the possibilities be seen at once?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Draw the possibilities as a tree. The root is the empty candidate, such as the empty string. Each node has one child for every choice for the next piece. The path from the root to a node is the candidate built so far.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The tree is a picture, so it has no cost of its own, but it shows the size of the search. With 26 choices per piece and depth n there are 26^n candidates, so exhaustive search grows exponentially with n.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every choice picks exactly one child, so each candidate is one path from the root and no two candidates share a path. The tree therefore holds every candidate once and none twice. Our reading.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For strings over a to z, every node has 26 children. Going from the root to the child g, then to its child p, spells the string gp. The depth of the tree is n, the length of the strings wanted.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: A tree lets you count and compare work: more candidates means more nodes, and a whole group of candidates is a single subtree.

card.rule: Picture the possibilities as a tree whose root is the empty candidate and whose paths from the root spell the candidates being built.
card.limits: The tree is a picture of the search space. Our reading: the program does not store it, it only walks it, so the tree can be far larger than anything held in memory.

media.alt: A tree for strings built from the letters a to z. The root is the empty string and has 26 children, one arrow to each letter, laid out in a row with a bracket beneath them. A caption says the level below holds 676 nodes and that every node has 26 children.

concepts.title: Pruning a path
concepts.question: When may a search abandon a path, and what does abandoning it save?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Exhaustive search wastes effort on candidates that were doomed from the start, such as strings with a forbidden letter in the first place.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Abandon a path as soon as you know it cannot lead to a solution. Abandoning a path is called pruning, and it discards the entire subtree below the path, so none of those candidates is built.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Exhaustive search generates all 26^n strings and then checks each, O(k * 26^n) with k the cost of one check. Pruning every subtree that holds a non-vowel reduces the candidates from O(26^n) to O(5^n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A path that already breaks the constraint cannot be repaired by extending it, so no real solution is thrown away.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Building strings that may contain only vowels: after choosing the letter b, drop every string that begins with b at once.

card.rule: Prune a path the moment it cannot lead to a solution, which skips every candidate below it.
card.limits: Prune only on certainty. A path that only looks unpromising must still be explored, because abandoning it could throw away a real answer.

media.alt: A tree for strings built only from the five vowels. The root is the empty string with five children, one per vowel, and each of those has five children, again one per vowel, so the leaves spell every two-letter vowel string. A caption says the path from the root to any node is a string.

concepts.title: Backtracking versus exhaustive search
concepts.question: How do backtracking and exhaustive search differ, and how many candidates does each generate on the vowel example?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Both methods run through all possibilities of a problem. The question is how many candidates each one builds before it is done.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Exhaustive search generates all possibilities, then checks them for solutions. Backtracking prunes paths that cannot lead to a solution, so it generates far fewer possibilities.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Take vowel-only strings of length n. Exhaustive search generates \(26^n\) candidates and checks each. Backtracking discards every subtree that holds a non-vowel, so it generates \(5^n\).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Backtracking only skips paths that cannot lead to a solution, so it finds the same answers as exhaustive search.

card.rule: Backtracking finds the same answers as exhaustive search while generating only the paths that can still succeed.
card.limits: The saving depends on pruning early. If a constraint can be checked only on a complete candidate, there is nothing to prune sooner, and the work stays close to exhaustive search.

concepts.title: When to reach for backtracking
concepts.question: Which features of a problem point to backtracking?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Backtracking is a good tool when a problem wants you to find all of something, or when there is no clear way to reach a solution without checking all the logical possibilities.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Look at the wording first: does the task ask for all of something, or is there no clear route to an answer short of checking the logical possibilities? Then look at the limits: n of about 15 or less is a strong hint on LeetCode.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Backtracking usually has exponential time, such as 2^n or n!. That is why only small inputs fit it, and why small input limits are the hint to look for.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: a search for all answers cannot do better than the number of answers, which grows exponentially with the input. Small limits are therefore consistent with the method. Interviews rarely give limits, so the skill is to judge from the shape of the problem.

card.rule: Reach for backtracking when the task is to find all of something and the input is small enough for exponential work.
card.limits: Small limits are a hint, not a proof. A problem that asks for one best value from a huge input is a poor fit, however many choices each step offers.

concepts.title: The backtracking template
concepts.question: What are the parts of the general backtracking function, and in what order do they run?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You are building something piece by piece, such as an array or a set of state variables, and need every complete version of it.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Write a function backtrack(curr) where curr is the thing being built. If the base case holds, record the answer and return. Otherwise loop over the choices: modify curr, call backtrack(curr), then undo the modification.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the skeleton has no fixed bound. The time is the number of nodes in the tree of choices times the work in each call, and the book notes that backtracking time complexities are typically hard to calculate exactly.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The undo restores curr to the state before the choice, so each choice in the loop starts from the same partial candidate.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The skeleton in Python, with the problem-specific parts as placeholders:

card.rule: Backtracking checks the base case, then for each choice modifies curr, recurses, and undoes the change.
card.limits: This is only a skeleton. What curr is, when the base case holds, and which choices are allowed differ by problem, and a missing undo breaks every later iteration.

concepts.title: The code as a tree
concepts.question: How does each part of the backtracking function correspond to a part of the tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The tree is a way to think about the code. Which part of the backtrack function is a node, which a child, and which the move back up?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each call to backtrack is a node of the tree. Each iteration of the for loop is a child of the current node, and calling backtrack inside the loop is the move to that child.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One call is one node, so the work of the search is the number of nodes visited times the work inside each call. The book treats subsets this way: a DFS on a tree with 2^n nodes.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The undo line is the move from a child back up to its parent, so after each child the path is the parent's again. The next child then starts from the same partial candidate, and every branch is explored.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: At any node, the path from the root down to it is the candidate being built. The leaf nodes are complete solutions, where the base case is reached.

card.rule: A call is a node, a loop iteration is a child, the recursive call goes down, and the undo goes back up.
card.limits: The tree is a way to think, not an extra structure. Some leaves are dead ends rather than solutions, so a leaf and a base case do not always coincide.

concepts.title: Generating permutations
concepts.question: How does the template build every ordering of an array of distinct numbers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return every permutation: every ordering that uses all the numbers once. For [1, 2, 3] there are six.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Build each permutation in curr. The base case is reached when curr is as long as nums, and then curr is added to the answer. Every call loops over the whole input and skips numbers already in curr.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The book expects about O(n!) calls. Each call loops over n numbers and the 'num not in curr' test costs O(n), so about O(n^2) per call: O(n^2 * n!), or O(n * n!) with a hash set. The exact bound is more complicated.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each position tries every number still unused, so every ordering is reached once, and the skip rule keeps a number from appearing twice.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version of the book solution:

card.rule: To build permutations, loop over the whole input at every call and add only numbers that are not yet in curr.
card.limits: The in-curr check works because the numbers are distinct. It would also drop a legitimate repeat if values could repeat, so it does not carry over to such input.

media.alt: A tree of orderings of the numbers 1, 2 and 3. The root is empty and has three children, one per number. Under each child hang the two numbers not yet used, and under each of those the one number left, so every path has three steps. The six leaves are labelled with the six orderings.

concepts.title: Copy curr before recording it
concepts.question: Why must the code add a copy of curr to the answer instead of curr itself?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The code keeps changing one list, curr, as it adds and undoes choices. If the answer list stores curr itself, it stores a reference to that one list.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: When recording a result, add a copy of curr, such as curr[:] in Python. The copy is a separate list that later edits to curr cannot reach.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A copy costs time proportional to the length of curr. The book charges it per recorded answer: O(n) for each subset, giving O(n * 2^n) overall, and O(k) for each combination of size k.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The undo steps shrink curr back to the empty list by the end, so references would all show that final state, not the answers.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The reference changes with curr; the copy keeps its contents:
blocks.code:
curr = [1, 2]
by_ref = [curr]
by_copy = [curr[:]]
curr.pop()
print(by_ref, by_copy)  # [[1]] [[1, 2]]

card.rule: Record a copy of curr, because curr is only a reference to one list that keeps changing.
card.limits: A copy is needed only when you store curr. If the function only counts solutions, nothing is stored and no copy is made.

concepts.title: Cost of permutations
concepts.question: How many calls does the permutations code make, and what does each call cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Estimate the running time of the permutations code for n distinct numbers.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Count calls level by level. The root call makes n calls, each of those makes n - 1, each of those n - 2, and so on, so the tree has about n! calls.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each call loops over n numbers, and each loop step asks whether the number is already in curr, which costs \(O(n)\). One call therefore costs about \(O(n^2)\), and the total is about \(O(n^2 \cdot n!)\).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The number of choices falls by one with each number used, and the products of those choices give the number of calls; multiplying by the cost per call gives the time.

card.rule: The permutations code makes about n! calls of about \(n^2\) work each, which is an estimate and not an exact count.
card.limits: The book calls the true complexity extremely complicated and says an explained estimate is enough in an interview. The estimate is an upper-bound style argument, not an exact count of steps.

concepts.title: Subsets versus permutations
concepts.question: How do subsets differ from permutations, and how does that change where answers are recorded?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given an array nums of unique elements, return all subsets without duplicates. For [1, 2, 3] the answer holds eight subsets, from the empty one to the whole array.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Subsets differ from permutations in two ways. A subset can have any length, while a permutation has the fixed length n. And order does not matter: [1, 2, 3] and [3, 2, 1] are the same subset but different permutations.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There are 2^n subsets, since each element is taken or not. The search is a DFS on a tree with 2^n nodes and each node copies curr, so time is O(n * 2^n). Space is O(n) for curr and the recursion stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every subset is the curr of some node and is recorded as soon as that node is reached, so none is missed. Only a start index, in the next idea, stops one set appearing in several orders.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Because lengths vary, answers are not found only at leaves: the curr of a node at any depth is already a valid subset and is recorded as the call begins.

card.rule: A subset has any length and ignores order, so every node holds an answer and each set must be built in only one order.
card.limits: The same code cannot serve both problems unchanged. Recording only at leaves would miss the shorter subsets, and looping over everything would build each set in several orders.

concepts.title: A start index avoids duplicates
concepts.question: How does passing an index keep the same subset from being built in two orders?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Subsets ignore order, so [1, 2] and [2, 1] must come out once, not twice, while every subset still appears.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Pass an index i meaning where to start looping. Loop j from i to the end, add nums[j], and recurse with j + 1. After a number, only later numbers can follow, so every result is built in sorted order.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The tree has 2^n nodes, one per subset, and each node copies curr, so time is O(n * 2^n). Space is O(n) for curr and the call stack, not counting the stored answers.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A set can be built in exactly one way: take its numbers by increasing index. Skipping earlier indexes removes the other orders and loses no set.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version of the subsets solution:

card.rule: Loop from a start index and recurse with the next index, so each set is built only in increasing order.
