card.limits: A start index suits problems where order does not matter. For permutations, where [1, 2] and [2, 1] are different answers, the loop must cover the whole input in every call.

concepts.title: Cost of subsets
concepts.question: How many subsets are there, and what do time and space cost for the subsets code?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Estimate the time and space cost of generating all subsets of an array of n unique elements.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: For each element there are two choices: take it or leave it. So there are \(2^n\) subsets, and the search is a depth-first walk over a tree of \(2^n\) nodes.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Every node copies curr, which costs up to \(O(n)\). The time is \(O(n \cdot 2^n)\).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The tree has one node per subset because every subset is built in exactly one order, so the node count is the subset count and no work is repeated.

card.rule: Subsets of n elements number \(2^n\), and with a copy at each node the time is \(O(n \cdot 2^n)\).
card.limits: These figures count nodes and copies. The estimate does not change if the elements are numbers or names, but it does assume unique elements, since repeats would change how many distinct subsets exist.

concepts.title: Generating combinations
concepts.question: How does the subsets code change to return only the subsets of size k from the numbers 1 to n?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given integers n and k, return every combination of k numbers out of 1 to n. For n = 4 and k = 2 there are six, such as [1, 2] and [3, 4].

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A combination ignores order, so this is the subsets problem restricted to size k. Reuse the subsets code, but record curr only when it has k numbers and then return, since longer lists are not wanted.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The book gives an upper bound of about O(k * n! / (n-k)!): the n * (n-1) * ... factors stop after depth k, and each copy costs O(k). The exact figure is harder to derive. Space is O(k) for curr and the stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The start index builds each set in one order, and stopping at k numbers keeps exactly the sets of the right size.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version, starting the index at 1:

card.rule: Combinations are subsets of size k: record at length k only, and stop extending there.
card.limits: This reuses the start-index loop, so it assumes order is irrelevant. If [1, 2] and [2, 1] had to be separate answers, the loop would have to cover all numbers again.

concepts.title: Bounding the cost of combinations
concepts.question: How can you bound the running time of the combinations code when the exact count is hard to derive?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The exact running time of the combinations code is hard to derive. The goal is a sound upper bound that you can explain.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Reason as for permutations: the first call loops n times, the next n - 1, then n - 2. The tree is only k levels deep, so the product stops after k factors, at n - k + 1, instead of going down to 1.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Stopping early divides the factorial by \((n-k)!\), giving about \(n!/(n-k)!\) calls. Each combination is copied at cost \(O(k)\), so the time is about \(O(k \cdot n!/(n-k)!)\). Space is \(O(k)\).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: It is an upper bound: it counts every path of length k as if numbers could come in any order, so it can only overcount the real work.

card.rule: Bound the combinations code by \(O(k \cdot n!/(n-k)!)\) time and \(O(k)\) space: depth k cuts the factorial at \((n-k)!\).
card.limits: An upper bound is not the exact count. The bound ignores that each combination is built in only one order, so it overestimates, and the gap grows with k.

concepts.title: One pattern for generation problems
concepts.question: For generation problems, which two questions about the tree decide the shape of the code?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Permutations, subsets and combinations all ask for every object of some kind. Can one way of thinking produce all three solutions?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Model the problem as a tree, then work out what children each node should have and which nodes hold answers. Those two choices are the only difference between permutations, subsets and combinations.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Cost is the number of nodes in the chosen tree times the work per node: about n! calls for permutations, 2^n nodes for subsets, and fewer than n!/(n-k)! for combinations because depth stops at k. All grow exponentially or faster.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each wanted object must be exactly one path to an answer node. Permutations allow any unused number, so each ordering is one path; subsets and combinations allow only later numbers, so each set is one path. Right children and answer nodes give each object once.

blocks.label: Per problem
blocks.text: Permutations: children are numbers not yet in curr; answers are the leaves with n numbers. Subsets: children are numbers after the last one chosen; answers are every node. Combinations: children as for subsets; answers only where curr has k numbers, and the search stops there.

card.rule: For a generation problem, decide the children of each node and which nodes are answers; the rest is the template.
card.limits: The pattern fits problems that ask for all of something. It does not say how to represent a more complex state, such as a chessboard, which later problems need.

concepts.title: Reusing a number in a combination
concepts.question: When a number may be chosen again, which index does the recursive call receive?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Combination Sum: given distinct positive integers and a target, return all unique combinations that add up to the target. The same number may be chosen any number of times.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep the start index to avoid order duplicates such as [2, 2, 3] and [2, 3, 2]. But where subsets passed j + 1 because each element was used once, here the recursive call passes the same index i, since the number just added may be added again.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The book's approximation is O(n^(T/M)), with n candidates, target T and smallest candidate M. The tree is at most T/M deep, since the smallest number can repeat that often, and each node has up to n children. Space is O(T/M).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The start index never moves backwards, so each combination is built in one order, and keeping the same index still allows repeated use of a number.

card.rule: Pass the same index to allow reuse and the next index to forbid it, and never go back to an earlier index.
card.limits: If reuse is forbidden, pass the next index as in subsets. If the loop restarts at the beginning in every call, the same combination appears in several orders.

concepts.title: Tracking the sum and pruning
concepts.question: How does Combination Sum stop extending a path, and when is a path recorded?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Combination Sum needs only the combinations whose numbers add up to the target, so most paths in the tree of all combinations are not answers.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Pass the running sum curr along with path and start. Add a number only if curr + num stays within the target, and record path when curr equals the target.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the worst-case bound stays the book's O(n^(T/M)), since the check only trims branches. Passing the running sum curr along makes the check O(1) per number, and the path and stack use O(T/M) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: All numbers are positive, so a sum above the target can only grow and no extension can reach the target. Pruning such a path loses no answer.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version of the book solution:

card.rule: Prune a path whose sum would exceed the target, and record the path when its sum equals the target.
card.limits: The prune is safe only because every candidate is positive. A leaf is not always an answer: a path can stop with a sum below the target when no candidate fits.

concepts.title: Cost of Combination Sum
concepts.question: What bounds the depth and the time of Combination Sum?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Bound the time of Combination Sum for n candidates, a target T and a smallest candidate M.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The deepest path uses the smallest candidate over and over until the sum would exceed the target, so the tree is at most T / M levels deep. Each node has at most n children.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A tree at most T / M deep with at most n children per node has about \(n^{T/M}\) nodes, so the time is about \(O(n^{T/M})\).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each level adds at least M to the sum, so after T / M levels the sum exceeds the target. This depth limit and the branching limit bound the node count.

card.rule: Combination Sum takes about \(O(n^{T/M})\) time, since the tree is at most T / M deep with n children per node.
card.limits: This is a loose upper bound. The start index and the prune remove many children, so the real count can be far smaller; the bound tells the shape of the growth, not the exact work.

concepts.title: N-Queens: only the state you need
concepts.question: What is the smallest state needed to place queens row by row without attacks?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: N-Queens II: place n queens on an n by n board so that no two attack each other, and return the number of distinct solutions.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Place one queen per row, so each call handles one row and row is an argument. Keep three sets: the occupied columns, the occupied diagonals and the occupied anti-diagonals. A square is allowed only if none of its three is occupied.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The book says the true time is not known but approximately O(n!): the first row has n options, the next about n - 2, then n - 4, and so on. Space is O(n) for the three sets and the recursion stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A queen attacks only along its row, column and two diagonals, so these sets are all the information needed to test a new square. Reaching row n means n queens are placed safely.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Python version; the diagonal numbers row - col and row + col are explained in the next idea:

card.rule: Represent the board by the row and three sets of attacked lines, add them when placing a queen and remove them when backtracking.
card.limits: The sets suit queens, whose attacks are all along lines. A puzzle whose rules depend on exact pieces on the board may need more state, but only as much as the rules require.

concepts.title: Naming a diagonal with one number
concepts.question: Why can a single number identify the diagonal or anti-diagonal that a square lies on?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To test whether a new queen shares a diagonal with an earlier one, comparing it with every placed queen would be slow. A set of occupied diagonals gives the answer in one lookup, if each diagonal has a single name.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A diagonal runs from top left to bottom right, an anti-diagonal from top right to bottom left. All squares on a diagonal share the value row - col. All squares on an anti-diagonal share row + col.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Computing the two numbers and looking them up in a set takes constant time per square.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Moving down and right along a diagonal adds 1 to both row and col, so their difference never changes. A different diagonal has a different difference.

card.rule: Use row - col to name a diagonal and row + col to name an anti-diagonal, and keep one set for each.
card.limits: The trick needs squares numbered by row and column. It names lines on the board; it does not by itself say which squares are free, since that depends on the queens already placed.

media.alt: An eight by eight board whose squares hold the row index minus the column index. Zeros run down the main diagonal from top left to bottom right, positive values fill the area below it and negative values the area above it. Every line parallel to the main diagonal repeats one value, as the caption says.

An eight by eight board whose squares hold the row index plus the column index, from 0 at the top left toward 14 at the bottom right. Values stay equal along each line running from top right to bottom left and grow when moving down or right. A caption says squares on one anti-diagonal share the same value.

concepts.title: Cost of N-Queens
concepts.question: How does the N-Queens search shrink its choices row by row, and what does that give?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Estimate the time and space cost of the N-Queens code.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The first row offers n squares. The next row has fewer: a queen takes away its column and at least one diagonal square, leaving about n - 2. The next has about n - 4, and so on.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The product of these shrinking choices is approximated by \(O(n!)\) time. The space is \(O(n)\), for the three sets and the recursion call stack.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each placed queen blocks squares in every later row, so the number of choices only falls with depth. That is why the count of nodes resembles a factorial.

card.rule: N-Queens costs approximately \(O(n!)\) time and \(O(n)\) space, because each queen blocks squares in the rows below.
card.limits: The factorial is an approximation of the choices, not a proof. Pruning by attacked squares keeps the real count well below n!.

concepts.title: Word Search: why it is not plain DFS
concepts.question: Why does Word Search need backtracking and not just depth-first search?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a grid of letters and a word, decide whether the word can be spelled by moving between horizontally or vertically adjacent cells. No cell may be used twice in one word.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Walk the grid like a depth-first search, with a set seen of the cells on the current path. When a path fails, remove the cell you are leaving from seen, so other paths may use it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: seen holds only the cells on the current path, so with a set the space is O(L), where L is the word length, the same as the recursion stack. A boolean array over the grid would use O(m * n) instead. The time bound is on the next card.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: One cell can belong to many different candidate paths in the same search: going right then down reaches a cell that going down then right also reaches. A mark that stayed would wrongly block the second path.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: In plain DFS a visited cell stays visited. Here the marks describe only the current path, so backtracking must clear them.

card.rule: Mark cells while they are on the current path and unmark them when the path backs out, so other paths can use them.
card.limits: The unmarking is needed only because different paths may share cells. If each cell had to be visited once for the whole search, as in a plain DFS, the marks would stay.

media.alt: A letter grid of three rows and four columns. Green cells trace a path spelling the target word ABCCED: along the top row across the first three cells, down through the second C and the E beneath it, then left to the D. Remaining cells are grey. Each step moves to a horizontal or vertical neighbour.

concepts.title: Word Search: guided moves and cost
concepts.question: How does Word Search limit its moves, and what does the search cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether a word is in an m by n grid, using the Word Search rules, and bound the time of the search.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Pass an index i meaning the search is looking for word[i]. Move into a neighbour only if it is unseen and holds that letter. Because the word may begin anywhere, start the search from every cell that holds word[0].

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The tree has depth L, the word length, and each node has at most 3 children, since one neighbour is where the path came from. With \(m \cdot n\) starting cells the time is \(O(m \cdot n \cdot 3^L)\). Space is \(O(L)\) with a set.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A move needs an unseen cell holding word[i], so every extended path spells a prefix of the word and failing paths are cut without losing a match. Starting from every cell with word[0] covers every start, and reaching i equal to the word length means the whole word was spelled.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The recursive helper in Python; the outer loops call it from every cell holding the first letter:

card.rule: Word Search moves only to unseen cells with the next letter, starting from every cell with word[0], in \(O(m \cdot n \cdot 3^L)\) time.
card.limits: The bound is a worst case. A word whose letters rarely match the grid is pruned almost at once, so the real work is usually far below the bound.

concepts.title: Why DP has a reputation
concepts.question: What two things does the book give as the reasons dynamic programming is feared?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Many programmers avoid dynamic programming (DP), a problem-solving technique. What lies behind that fear?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The book names two causes. A learner who has not met DP finds even an easy DP problem almost impossible. And DP is less common in interviews, which gives people less reason to learn it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There is no algorithm here to cost. What the book offers against the cost of learning is that DP complexity is easy to analyse: with N states and work F per state, time is O(N * F).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The two causes feed each other: the topic is hard to stumble on, so it is skipped, so it stays unfamiliar. The rest of the chapter answers this with a systematic framework.

card.rule: DP is feared because it is nearly impossible to solve without having learned it, and interviews ask it less often.
card.limits: These are the book's remarks on reputation, not a measure of the method. A learner who has the framework can build DP solutions step by step.

concepts.title: DP is optimized recursion
concepts.question: What must a DP function return for the arguments it receives?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You want the answer to a whole problem. How can a recursive function help, and what makes it dynamic programming?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Dynamic programming is optimized recursion. Define a recursive function, usually called dp, that returns the answer to the original problem as if its arguments were the whole input. In trees the same role was played by dfs(node), which answered for the subtree at node.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Defining dp costs nothing extra. With a cache each state is computed once, so time is O(N * F) for N states and F work per state, and space is O(N). Without a cache, calls repeat and time can be exponential.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Because dp(args) is defined to answer the original question for that input, a larger answer can be built from the answers of smaller calls, the same argument used for trees.

blocks.label: Breaks when
blocks.text: If dp's meaning does not depend on its arguments, calls cannot be combined into an answer.

card.rule: A DP function returns the answer to the original problem as if its arguments were the whole input.
card.limits: Recursion with this meaning is a start, not yet DP: without a cache the same calls can repeat and the running time can blow up.

concepts.title: Repeated states make plain recursion explode
concepts.question: Why does a plain recursive Fibonacci take exponential time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A tree DFS visits each node once, so a state does not repeat. What changes in a DP recursion?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In DP, states can repeat, usually an exponential number of times. Fibonacci shows it: fib(n) calls fib(n - 1) and fib(n - 2), so every call creates two more calls. In the call tree of fib(6), f(4) is computed twice, f(3) three times and f(2) five times.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Because each call makes two calls, the time is O(2^n). Counting every call, fib(6) makes 25 calls and fib(7) makes 41.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Nothing is remembered, so every call spawns two fresh calls and the number of calls roughly doubles per level. The repeats in fib(6) are the same sub-answer recomputed. Storing each result once, the next idea, removes the repeats.

blocks.text: Plain recursion in Python:

card.rule: In DP the same state is reached again and again, so plain recursion repeats work at an exponential rate.
card.limits: Repetition is the problem only when states repeat. In a tree DFS every node is reached once, so there is nothing to save.

media.alt: The call tree of a recursive Fibonacci function started with 6. Each node shows the argument of one call and has two children, the argument minus one on the left and minus two on the right, down to leaves labelled 1 or 0. Identical subtrees recur in several places, so the same calls are repeated.

concepts.title: Memoization caches each state once
concepts.question: How does saving results turn exponential recursion into a linear algorithm?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Plain recursion repeats the same states. How can each state be solved only once?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Memoization: when you find the answer for a state, cache it, usually in a hash map. Before recursing, check the cache; if the state is there, return the saved value. Plain recursion plus memoization is dynamic programming.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each state is computed once, so memoized Fibonacci takes O(n) instead of O(2^n). For fib(6) the function is entered 11 times and 5 results are stored.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A state's answer depends only on the state, so the saved value equals what recomputing would give.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Memoized Fibonacci in Python:

card.rule: Cache the answer to each state the first time, and look the cache up before recursing.
card.limits: A cache pays off only when states repeat, and it costs memory for every state it stores.

concepts.title: The recurrence relation
concepts.question: What do we call the equation that gets one state's answer from other states?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A DP function must compute the answer for a state from other states. What is the rule for that called?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A recurrence relation is an equation used to calculate states. For Fibonacci it is F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2), and the values F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1 are the base cases where the recursion stops.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Evaluating the relation at one state is the work done at that state; for Fibonacci it is one addition.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: It states exactly how a state's answer follows from smaller states, so computing states in the right order gives the answer.

card.rule: A recurrence relation is the equation that gets a state's answer from the answers of other states.
card.limits: The relation alone does not finish a computation: it needs base cases, and it only fits a problem if it lists every way a state can be reached.

concepts.title: Top-down: from the problem to the base cases
concepts.question: In top-down DP, where does the computation start and which way does it move?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Recursion with memoization is one way to run a DP algorithm. Why is it called top-down?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Top-down starts at the top, the original problem, and moves down by recursion toward the base cases. To find the nth Fibonacci number you call fibonacci(n) first and recurse until you reach F(0) and F(1).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: With memoization each state is computed once, so Fibonacci is O(n) time. The recursion also holds up to n calls on the stack at once.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each call waits for smaller calls that are defined by the same meaning, so base cases return first and answers flow back up to the original call.

card.rule: Top-down DP starts from the original problem and recurses down to the base cases, caching as it returns.
card.limits: Top-down needs the memo to be DP: without it, the same recursion is only basic recursion.

concepts.title: Bottom-up: from the base cases to the answer
concepts.question: How does bottom-up DP get the answer without recursion?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Top-down uses recursion and a cache. Is there a way to compute the same answers with a loop?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Bottom-up starts at the bottom, the base cases, and works up to larger problems iteratively. It is also called tabulation. For Fibonacci, set arr[1] = 1 and fill arr[i] = arr[i - 1] + arr[i - 2] for i from 2 up to n.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The loop makes n - 1 steps and the table has n + 1 cells, so O(n) time and O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The loop goes from smaller to larger states, so when a cell is filled the two cells it reads are already final.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Bottom-up Fibonacci in Python:

card.rule: Bottom-up fills a table from the base cases upward, so every cell is final before it is read.
card.limits: The loop must run from the base cases outward. If it runs the other way it reads cells that are still empty.

concepts.title: Two styles, one algorithm
concepts.question: Are top-down and bottom-up different algorithms, and what defines a DP algorithm?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The same problem can be solved top-down or bottom-up. Is that two algorithms, and what makes a solution DP at all?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Top-down and bottom-up refer only to how the algorithm is implemented. There is nothing fundamentally different: every top-down implementation can be written bottom-up and the reverse. The base cases and the recurrence relation are what define a DP algorithm.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Both visit each state once, so the number of states times the work per state sets the time for either.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Both compute the same recurrence from the same base cases, so they give the same answers; only the order of evaluation and the cache type differ.

card.rule: Top-down and bottom-up differ only in implementation; the base cases and the recurrence relation define the DP algorithm.
card.limits: Same algorithm does not mean same cost in practice: iteration has less overhead than recursion, and only bottom-up can drop the stored states.

concepts.title: Choosing between top-down and bottom-up
concepts.question: Which style is usually faster, and which is usually easier to write?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Both styles solve the same DP problem. How do you choose between them?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Bottom-up is usually faster, because iteration has less overhead than recursion. Top-down is usually easier to write, because with recursion the order in which states are visited does not matter.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Both visit the same states. The speed gap is only in per-call overhead, not in the number of states.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: In a loop you must visit each state after the states it needs, while recursion finds that order for you through its calls.

card.rule: Bottom-up usually runs faster; top-down is usually easier to write.
card.limits: Both are usual tendencies, not rules. In a language that implements tail recursion the speed gap shrinks.

concepts.section: When should I consider using DP?
concepts.title: First sign of a DP problem: an optimum or a count
concepts.question: Which wording of a problem is the first hint that DP may fit?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given a new problem, how do you decide whether DP is worth trying? The first check is the wording of the question.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Problems that suit DP usually ask for the optimal value, the maximum or minimum, of something, or for the number of ways to do something. Typical openings: what is the minimum cost of doing, what is the maximum profit of, how many ways are there to, what is the longest possible.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Reading the wording costs nothing to run. Once DP fits, the book's cost is O(N * F): the number of states times the work per state.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: a maximum, minimum or count over many ways compares combinations of choices, which DP does by combining the best answers of smaller states. The wording is only the first of two signs; the second concerns decisions.

blocks.label: Breaks when
blocks.text: Many problems in these formats are not meant for DP, and some DP problems are not in these formats. Treat it as a guideline.

card.rule: A question that asks for an optimum or a number of ways is a first hint of DP, to be confirmed by the second sign.
card.limits: The book calls this a general guideline that holds up very well, not a test: a maximum can be found by one scan, and a DP problem can be worded differently.

concepts.section: When should I consider using DP?
concepts.title: Second sign: decisions that affect future decisions
concepts.question: What does it mean for one decision in a problem to affect future decisions?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The wording hints at DP. What property of the choices confirms it?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: At each step you make a decision, and decisions affect future decisions. For example, if you take element x, you cannot take element y later.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Spotting this sign costs no running time. The cost comes after DP is chosen: O(N * F), the number of states times the work per state.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: When a choice shuts out later choices, you cannot judge it from the current step alone; you need the best results of the states it leads to.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: House Robber: house i holds nums[i] money, and robbing two houses beside each other triggers the alarm. Choose the most money without alerting the police. Taking one house takes its neighbours out of play.

card.rule: If taking one option changes which options remain later, the decisions interact and DP is likely to fit.
card.limits: Decisions that are independent do not need DP. This sign is a guideline, as the first one is.

concepts.section: When should I consider using DP?
concepts.title: Telling DP apart from greedy
concepts.question: What usually tells a DP problem apart from a greedy one?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Greedy and DP both pick options step by step, so how do you tell them apart on a new problem?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The second sign usually separates DP from greedy. In House Robber the first choice for nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] is between the 2 and the 7. A greedy robber takes the 7, and that blocks the 9, so the total ends below the best.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A greedy scan is O(n), and the DP for this problem is O(n) as well, so greedy is not a cheaper win when it is wrong.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A choice that blocks later options may cost more than it gains. Greedy does not see that cost; DP compares the results of both branches.

card.rule: When decisions affect each other, a locally best choice can lose, so use DP instead of greedy.
card.limits: If decisions are independent, greedy is fine and DP is not needed. The two signs are guidelines, not proof.

concepts.title: A state describes a scenario
concepts.question: What information does a DP state have to carry?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A DP function takes arguments. Which variables belong in them, and what must the function return for them?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A state is a set of variables that can fully describe a scenario. A call to dp(state) should return the answer to the original problem as if state were the input.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each distinct combination of state values is one state, so the choice of variables sets how many states there are and how much work the algorithm does.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: If the variables describe the scenario fully, two calls with the same values are the same scenario and must give the same answer, which is what makes caching valid.

card.rule: Choose state variables that fully describe a scenario, and let dp(state) answer the original problem for it.
card.limits: Too few variables merge scenarios that differ, and the cached answer is wrong. Too many split equal scenarios apart and the cache saves little.

concepts.title: The most common state variable: an index
concepts.question: What does an index in a DP state say about the input?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Which state variable shows up most often, and what does its value mean for an array or a string?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: An index along the input string, array or number is the most common state variable. In Fibonacci the index is which Fibonacci number you are on. For an array, the state i stands for the input up to and including index i: with nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] and i = 2, it is as if nums were [0, 1, 2].

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One index that runs over an input of length n gives n states.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The prefix up to i is itself a smaller input of the same kind, so dp(i) can use the answers for shorter prefixes.

card.rule: An index state i means: treat the input as if it ended at position i.
card.limits: One index is not enough in some problems: some problems add a second index, a numerical limit or a status flag.

concepts.title: A second index along the input
concepts.question: When does a DP state need two indices instead of one?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: One index marks where the input ends. What if the input needs a second bound?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sometimes you need a second index to represent the right bound of the array. With nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4], i = 1 and j = 3, it is as if nums were [1, 2, 3]: only the input from i through j inclusive is considered.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Two indices over an input of length n give up to n times n states, and the work at each state multiplies that.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The pair (i, j) names a contiguous piece of the input, which is itself a smaller input, so dp(i, j) can be defined for it.

card.rule: Two indices mark both ends of the piece of input a state stands for.
card.limits: A second index need not be a right bound: it can also walk a second input, as in two-string problems.

concepts.title: State from a limit or a status
concepts.question: Which other kinds of variable can a DP state need besides indices?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Indices describe where you are in the input. What else can change what you are allowed to do next?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Two more common kinds of state variable. An explicit numerical constraint from the problem, usually called k, for example: you may remove k obstacles; the variable counts how many more you can remove. And a boolean for a status, for example true if you are holding a package and false if not.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: A boolean doubles the number of states. A constraint k multiplies the number of states by about k.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Both change which moves are allowed later, so they belong in the description of the scenario.

card.rule: Add a variable for a limit that shrinks or a status that flips whenever it changes what you can do later.
card.limits: Add only what changes future options; extra variables multiply the states without helping.

concepts.title: Dimensionality: counting state variables
concepts.question: What does it mean to call a DP algorithm one-dimensional or multi-dimensional?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: DP problems differ in how many variables their states have. What name describes that?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The number of state variables used is the dimensionality of the algorithm. One variable such as i means a one-dimensional algorithm. Several variables mean a multi-dimensional one.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each added dimension multiplies the number of states by that variable's range.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each variable ranges independently, so the states are all combinations of values and their number is the product of the ranges. That is why the dimension count gives the table shape and the nesting of loops in a bottom-up version.

card.rule: Dimensionality is the count of state variables.
card.limits: A boolean counts as a dimension even though it only has two values; the number of dimensions is not the number of states.

concepts.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
concepts.title: Time: states times work per state
concepts.question: How do you work out the running time of a DP algorithm?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A memoized DP solution has been written. How long does it take?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each state is calculated once, the same argument used for tree and graph problems. If there are N possible states and the work done at each state is F, the time complexity is O(N * F).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Fibonacci has n states with O(1) work each, so O(n). A state whose work scans n earlier items makes the time O(n * n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: After the first calculation, a state's repeat visits only read the stored value, so the real work of each state is done once.

card.rule: DP time is the number of states times the work done at one state.
card.limits: F counts the work at one state excluding the recursive calls it makes, which are counted as their own states. The formula assumes each state is calculated once.

concepts.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
concepts.title: Space: one stored value per state
concepts.question: How much memory does a plain DP solution use?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A DP solution caches answers. How much memory do the cached answers need?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The space complexity is O(N), where N is the number of states. In top-down the hash map holds every state by the end. In bottom-up the array for tabulation is as large as the number of states.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One stored value per state, so for Fibonacci with n + 1 values the space is O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each state has exactly one answer, and both styles keep every state's answer until the end.

card.rule: A plain DP stores one value per state, so its space is O(N).
card.limits: O(N) is the figure for the plain table or map. It is a ceiling that later ideas lower in some problems.

concepts.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
concepts.title: Counting the states
concepts.question: How do you get the number of states from the state variables?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The time and space formulas need N, the number of states. How is N found?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: N is the product of the ranges of the state variables. For each variable, find the range of values it can take, then multiply the ranges. With variables i, k and holding, where i runs over nums, k is given and holding is a boolean, N = nums.length * k * 2.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: If the work at each state is O(1), time and space are both O(n * k), where n = nums.length. The boolean contributes only a constant factor of 2.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every combination of values is a distinct scenario, so the number of combinations is the product of the numbers of choices.

card.rule: Multiply the ranges of the state variables to get the number of states.
card.limits: The product counts all value combinations, even ones that do not occur. A constant factor such as 2 for a boolean drops out of the big-O.

concepts.title: The three parts of a DP algorithm
concepts.question: Which three components make up any DP algorithm in the book's framework?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Min Cost Climbing Stairs: cost[i] is the price of step i; after paying it you climb one or two steps; you may start at step 0 or 1; return the least cost to reach the top, which lies beyond the last index. How do you build the DP systematically?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Every DP algorithm needs three components. First, a function or data structure that holds the answer to the problem for any given state. Second, a recurrence relation that moves between states. Third, base cases that give actual values to stop the recursion.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The function fixes what each state means, the recurrence builds a state's answer from smaller ones, and the base cases anchor the smallest ones, so every answer is built from known pieces.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Memoizing turns the exponential recursion into O(N * F), where N is the number of states and F the work at one state.

card.rule: Write three things for any DP: what the function returns for a state, how states connect, and where it stops.
card.limits: The three parts give a correct algorithm but a slow one until the function is memoized.

concepts.title: First part: what dp returns and takes
concepts.question: How do you decide what dp(state) returns and which state variables it needs?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: For Min Cost Climbing Stairs, what should dp return, and what should it take as arguments?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Return what the problem asks for: here the minimum cost to climb the stairs. For the arguments, ask what information fully describes the situation. Here only the step you are on matters, an index i. So dp(i) returns the minimum cost to climb the stairs up to step i, as if the input were the part of the array from index 0 up to i.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One index means about n states, so the later time and space are small.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The answer for step i depends only on i and the costs, so no other variable is needed to separate one scenario from another.

card.rule: Make dp return the quantity the problem asks for, and give it only the variables that change that answer.
card.limits: Extra variables are not wrong, but they split equal scenarios apart and multiply the states for no gain.

concepts.title: Second part: the recurrence relation
concepts.question: How do you write the recurrence relation for minimum-cost stair climbing?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With dp(i) defined, how is dp(i) computed from smaller states?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Moves are one or two steps, so you reach step i from step i - 1 or step i - 2. Reaching step i - 1 cost dp(i - 1) and leaving it costs cost[i - 1]. The same holds for i - 2. So dp(i) = min(dp(i - 1) + cost[i - 1], dp(i - 2) + cost[i - 2]).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Two lookups and a minimum, so O(1) work per state.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every way to arrive at step i ends with a move from i - 1 or i - 2, and dp already holds the best cost of reaching each of those, so the smaller sum is the best total.

card.rule: List every way a state can be reached, price each as the smaller state's answer plus its move cost, and take the best.
card.limits: The recurrence is simple here because each state has two predecessors. Other problems can need many more cases.

concepts.title: Third part: base cases
concepts.question: Why does a recurrence need base cases, and where do they come from?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The recurrence for stair climbing is written. Why can it not run on its own, and what values should stop it?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: On its own the recurrence is useless: dp(100) needs dp(99) and dp(98), those need dp(97) and dp(96), and the chain runs on without end. Base cases are known values that stop it. The problem lets you start on step 0 or step 1, so dp(0) = dp(1) = 0. Then dp(2), dp(3) and on up to dp(100) can be found.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Base cases are fixed values, so they cost O(1) work.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A base case must be the true answer for its state, read from the rules of the problem: starting free on steps 0 and 1 means reaching them costs nothing.

card.rule: Base cases are the states whose answers are known from the problem statement; they anchor the recursion.
card.limits: Base cases are usually easy but need a careful reading of the problem. A wrong base value spreads to every state built on it.

concepts.title: Putting the three parts into code
concepts.question: How do the function, recurrence and base cases fit together in memoized code?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You have the three parts for Min Cost Climbing Stairs. How do they become a working memoized solution?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Wrap them in a function dp(i) with a cache. The order inside it: return the base case for i of 1 or less, return the cached value if there is one, otherwise compute the recurrence, store it and return it. The answer is dp of the array length, because the top is one past the last index.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Memoizing brings the time from O(2^n) to O(n), where n is the length of the cost array. The memo holds O(n) states.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Base cases stop the recursion, the cache means each i is computed once, and the recurrence builds dp(i) from smaller states that are already correct. Asking for dp(len(cost)) gives the top, one past the last step.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Memoized solution in Python:

card.rule: Check the base cases, then the cache, then compute and store the recurrence, and ask for dp(len(cost)).
card.limits: Without the cache the same code is still correct but takes exponential time. The answer index is len(cost), not len(cost) - 1.

concepts.section: Converting a top-down solution to a bottom-up one
concepts.title: Converting top-down to bottom-up, step by step
concepts.question: What are the steps for turning a top-down solution into a bottom-up one?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You have a working top-down solution and want the iterative form. What are the steps?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Start from the top-down solution. Make an array dp sized by the state variables. Set the base cases as in the top-down code. Write for-loops over the state variables, from the base cases to the answer state. Copy the function body into the innermost loop, changing dp(...) to dp[...]. Return the dp[...] entry for the answer.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The work stays O(N * F); the table has N cells, and sometimes it can later be shrunk.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each pass of the inner loop does the same work as one call of dp in top-down, and the loop order puts every state after the states it reads.

card.rule: Build the table from the base cases outward, replacing each dp(...) call by a table read.
card.limits: This is a general method, not a guarantee of a simple loop. Choosing the order of several nested loops can be hard.

concepts.section: Converting a top-down solution to a bottom-up one
concepts.title: Details of the conversion
concepts.question: How do base cases and loop order work in a bottom-up conversion?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The steps are known. How are the base cases set, and how do the loops line up with the function?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Initialising the dp array with 0 sets the base case implicitly when the base value is 0, as in the stairs problem where dp(0) = dp(1) = 0. Loops start at the base cases and end at the answer state. With several state variables, nest one loop per variable. Each pass of the innermost loop equals a call to that state in top-down.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Looping over every state once costs what memoized top-down costs: the number of states times the work per state. The table holds one value per state, so space is O(N).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The loops move from base cases to the answer, so a state is computed only after the states it depends on.

blocks.label: Breaks when
blocks.text: Other problems have more complicated base cases, which have to be written out in the array explicitly.

card.rule: Zeros in a new array can stand in for zero-valued base cases; every other base case must be written in.
card.limits: The implicit zero is a shortcut for the stairs problem only. Check each base value before relying on it.

concepts.title: House Robber: the state and the recurrence
concepts.question: At each house, which two choices does the House Robber recurrence compare?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: House i holds nums[i] money, and robbing two neighbouring houses sets off the alarm. What is the most that can be robbed? Choose the function, the state and the recurrence.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Let dp(i) be the most money that can be robbed using houses up to and including i. At house i there are two choices. Rob it: gain nums[i], but skip house i - 1, so the total is dp(i - 2) + nums[i]. Skip it: the total is dp(i - 1).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There are n states, one per house, and each takes O(1) work to compare two values, so time is O(n). Storing a value for every state uses O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The rule on neighbours is built into the choice. Robbing i moves back two houses, so the alarm cannot trigger, and skipping i keeps the best total so far. Taking the larger covers every case.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: The recurrence as a bottom-up step in Python:

card.rule: dp(i) = max(dp(i - 1), dp(i - 2) + nums[i]): skip the house or rob it and jump back two.
card.limits: The recurrence relies on the alarm rule for neighbours only. A different rule, such as a gap of two houses, changes the jump.

concepts.title: House Robber: two base cases
concepts.question: Why does House Robber need two base cases instead of one?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The recurrence reads dp(i - 1) and dp(i - 2). Which starting values does it need?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: With one house, rob it, so dp(0) = nums[0]. With two houses only one can be robbed, so take the richer: dp(1) = max(nums[0], nums[1]). Two base cases are needed because the recurrence on dp(1) would need dp(-1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each base value is the true best total for its prefix, read from the rules: one house gives nothing to compare, and two neighbours exclude each other.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Both base cases are O(1) values. The recurrence runs from i = 2.

card.rule: The recurrence looks back two houses, so houses 0 and 1 get their answers directly.
card.limits: Setting dp[1] needs a second house. A one-house input must be handled before that line.

concepts.title: Cutting space to O(1) with two variables
concepts.question: When can a bottom-up table be replaced by a few variables?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The bottom-up House Robber table holds n values, but dp(i) reads only two earlier ones. Can the space shrink?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Yes. Keep only the previous two states in two variables and update them as the loop moves on. The older cells are obsolete once the loop passes them.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time stays O(n) with one pass, while space drops from O(n) to O(1). The book says this works only in bottom-up: a recursion stack still uses O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: dp(i) depends only on dp(i - 1) and dp(i - 2), so no value older than those affects a later state and can be dropped.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Two-variable House Robber in Python:

card.rule: If each state reads a fixed number of recent states, keep only those in variables and drop the rest.
card.limits: It needs a recurrence that stays the same and reads a fixed number of earlier states. It does not apply to top-down, where the recursion stack still uses O(n) space.

concepts.title: Flipping the direction of dp
concepts.question: What changes if dp(i) means the answer from index i to the end?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: So far dp(i) covered the elements from index 0 up to i. Can dp(i) be defined from index i to the end instead?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Yes. Let dp(i) be the answer considering the elements starting from index i. Then the original answer is dp(0), the base cases sit at dp(n - 1) and dp(n - 2), and the recurrence looks at i + 1 and i + 2 instead of i - 1 and i - 2.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Unchanged. Flipping the direction gives the same n states with O(1) work each, so time and space match the prefix version. Only where the recursion starts and stops changes. Our reading.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The new meaning is again a smaller input of the same kind, so a recurrence and base cases written for it give the right answer.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: House Robber with the flipped definition, in Python:

card.rule: Flip the meaning of dp(i) and you must flip the base cases and the recurrence with it.
card.limits: The flip changes where you start and stop, not the cost. The book calls it valid but not recommended for House Robber.

concepts.title: You choose what dp means
concepts.question: Who decides what dp represents, and what must follow from the choice?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two correct solutions can define dp differently. How strict is the definition of dp?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The programmer is in full control of what dp represents. Any definition works as long as the base cases and the recurrence relation are changed to fit it. Defining dp(i) as the answer for the prefix up to and including i is extremely common, and worth getting used to.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: the definition itself adds no cost. Time is the number of states times the work per state, so two definitions with the same states and the same work per state cost the same.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The three parts only need to agree with each other and with the meaning of dp, so more than one choice can lead to a correct algorithm.

blocks.label: Breaks when
blocks.text: If the meaning, the base cases and the recurrence do not match each other, the answers are wrong.

card.rule: The definition of dp is yours to pick, but the base cases and the recurrence must fit it.
card.limits: Freedom is not a reason to pick an awkward direction. The prefix definition is the common and more intuitive choice.

concepts.title: Longest increasing subsequence: why it is a DP problem
concepts.question: What two signs make the longest increasing subsequence problem a DP problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given an integer array nums, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. Which method fits?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Both signs of a DP problem are present. The question asks for a maximum length. And whenever you take an element into the subsequence, it changes which numbers you can take later: after a large element, smaller ones are shut out.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Recognising the problem runs nothing. The book's solution, next idea, has n states with O(n) work each: O(n^2) time and O(n) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A rule that grabs every rising number can lose, so the choices have to be compared. That is the job of DP.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For nums = [2, 3, 8, 4, 5, 6], taking the 8 gives a subsequence of length 3, but it shuts out the 4, 5 and 6. Skipping the 8 gives 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, which has length 5.

card.rule: The longest increasing subsequence asks for a maximum, and each element taken limits what can follow it.
card.limits: Both signs are guidelines. They point to DP here, but the method still needs a state, a recurrence and base cases.

concepts.title: Longest increasing subsequence: state and recurrence
concepts.question: What does dp(i) mean for the longest increasing subsequence, and how is it computed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With an index state, what should dp(i) return, and how does it use earlier states?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: dp(i) is the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends with the element at index i. It can extend any earlier j with nums[j] < nums[i]: dp(i) = max(dp(j) + 1) over those j. Every element alone is a subsequence of length 1, so the base value is 1.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There are n states and each loops over up to n earlier indexes, so time is O(n^2). The space equals the number of states, O(n), and the book says it cannot be improved in bottom-up.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A subsequence ending at j with nums[j] < nums[i] can take nums[i] as its next element, giving dp(j) + 1. The answer is the largest dp(i) over all i, since the best subsequence can end anywhere.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Bottom-up version in Python:

card.rule: dp(i) = 1 + the best dp(j) among earlier j with a smaller value, and the answer is the maximum of all dp(i).
card.limits: dp(i) ends at i by definition. The answer is not dp(n - 1), because the best subsequence may end before the last element.

concepts.title: Longest increasing subsequence: cost
concepts.question: What are the time and space of the longest increasing subsequence DP, and why?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The LIS table has one entry per element, and each entry looks back at earlier ones. What does that cost?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: There are n states, and the work at each state is a loop over the earlier indices, which is linear in n. So the time is O(n^2). The space equals the number of states, so it is O(n).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The product rule applies: n states times O(n) work per state. Each pair (j, i) with j less than i is compared once.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: For n = 10 the comparison nums[i] > nums[j] runs 45 times; for n = 20 it runs 190 times.

card.rule: Longest increasing subsequence takes O(n^2) time and O(n) space.
card.limits: This is the plain DP cost. It is not the best known running time for the problem.

concepts.title: Solving questions with brainpower: take or skip
concepts.question: What does the recurrence for the questions-with-brainpower problem compare?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Each entry questions[i] = [points, brainpower]. Questions are processed in order. Solving i earns its points but you cannot solve the next brainpower questions. Skipping lets you decide on the next one. What is the most points?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Define dp(i) as the most points from questions i onward. Solve question i: points plus dp(j), where j = i + brainpower + 1 is the next question you may solve. Skip it: dp(i + 1). Then dp(i) = max of the two. No extra variable is needed to count questions still blocked.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There are n states, one per question, and each does O(1) work, so time and space are both O(n). The next card covers the base case and why space cannot shrink.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Solving jumps straight to the first question that is free again, so the blocked ones are skipped by the index alone. Skipping moves one step. The larger of the two is the best from i.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Memoized solution in Python:

card.rule: dp(i) = max(points[i] + dp(i + brainpower[i] + 1), dp(i + 1)): solve and jump, or skip one.
card.limits: The recurrence moves forward, so its base case is at the end of the array, not at the start.

concepts.title: Brainpower: base case, bottom-up and cost
concepts.question: Where is the base case of the brainpower DP, and how does bottom-up avoid going out of range?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The recurrence moves forward and the jump i + brainpower + 1 can pass the end of the array. How are the end and the cost handled?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The base case is dp(i) = 0 for i at or beyond n, since the exam is over. Bottom-up uses an array of n + 1 cells, loops i from n - 1 down to 0, and clamps the jump with min(j, n) so it stays inside the array.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There are n states with O(1) work each, so the time and the space are O(n). The recurrence is not static, since the jump depends on questions[i][1], so the space cannot be improved in bottom-up.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Questions past the end earn nothing, so dp equal to 0 there is exact. Clamping a jump with min(j, n) maps any overshoot to that same value. Looping i downward fills every cell the recurrence reads, since j is larger than i.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Bottom-up in Python:
blocks.code:
def most_points(questions):
    n = len(questions)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        j = i + questions[i][1] + 1
        dp[i] = max(questions[i][0] + dp[min(j, n)], dp[i + 1])
    return dp[0]

card.rule: Base case at and past the end, an extra cell at index n, and a clamp on the jump.
card.limits: The clamp and the extra cell are needed only because jumps can overshoot. Remove them and a long brainpower reads out of range.

concepts.title: Longest common subsequence: two indices
concepts.question: How do two index variables and a match-or-mismatch rule give the longest common subsequence?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence. For abcde and ace the answer is 3, because ace appears in both. The question asks for a longest value, and using or skipping a letter changes which letters come next.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Use one index per string. dp(i, j) is the longest common subsequence length when starting at the ith character of text1 and the jth of text2. If the two characters match, dp(i, j) = 1 + dp(i + 1, j + 1). If they differ, try both ways: dp(i, j) = max(dp(i + 1, j), dp(i, j + 1)).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There are n * m states, one per pair of positions, and each takes O(1) work, so time and space are O(n * m), where n and m are the two string lengths.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: On a match one letter is gained and both strings move on. On a mismatch at least one of the two letters cannot be part of any common subsequence from here, so dropping either one and taking the better result covers every case.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Memoized solution in Python:

card.rule: Match: add 1 and move both indices. Mismatch: take the better of moving either index.
card.limits: Moving both indices on a mismatch is wrong, as it can skip a letter that would have matched. The base case is covered in the next idea.

concepts.title: Why take every match, and the base case
concepts.question: Why does LCS take every match, and what ends the recursion?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The recurrence has a match case and a mismatch case. Why does the match case not also try skipping, and when does the recursion stop?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: When two characters match, take the match; trying to skip it cannot give a longer subsequence. The base case is i equal to the length of text1 or j equal to the length of text2: one string has no characters left, so no more common characters exist and dp returns 0.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: A match is gained at once and keeps both strings moving, so an option that skips it cannot beat it. An empty string has no common subsequence with anything, so 0 is the true answer there.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each state tries at most two follow-up calls, so the work per state is O(1).

card.rule: Take every match, and return 0 once either string is used up.
card.limits: The match shortcut holds for this problem only. Where taking an option can block better ones, as in House Robber, both branches must be tried.

concepts.title: Longest common subsequence: bottom-up and cost
concepts.question: How is the LCS table filled bottom-up, and what are its time and space?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Convert the LCS recurrence to a table, and work out its cost.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Make a table with (n + 1) rows and (m + 1) columns, where n and m are the string lengths. The extra last row and column hold the zero base cases. Loop i from n - 1 down to 0 and j from m - 1 down to 0, so each cell is filled after the cells it reads.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each state costs O(1), so time and space are both O(n * m).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Loops run from the end, so dp[i + 1][j + 1], dp[i + 1][j] and dp[i][j + 1] are filled before dp[i][j]. The extra zero row and column are the base case where a string is used up, so the table matches the recursion.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Bottom-up in Python:

card.rule: Fill the (n + 1) by (m + 1) table from the last row and column back to dp[0][0].
card.limits: Both tables and loops follow the forward-moving definition. The reverse definition moves the base case and the loop direction.

concepts.title: Stock trading with k transactions: the state
concepts.question: Which three state variables does the buy-and-sell-stock problem with k transactions need?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given daily prices and an integer k, you may hold one unit of stock at a time and make at most k transactions. What is the maximum profit? Buying today bars buying again until you sell, and every transaction uses up the limited k.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Many decisions interact, so DP fits. Let dp return the maximum profit. The state needs the day i, a boolean holding that says whether stock is held, and an integer remain, the number of transactions left. dp(i, holding, remain) is the best profit from day i on with those settings.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The day says how many prices are left, holding says whether the next move may be a buy or a sell, and remain says how many more trades are allowed. Nothing else changes what can happen next.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The ranges are n days, 2 values of holding and k values of remain, so about n * 2 * k states.

card.rule: The state is the day, whether you hold stock, and how many transactions remain.
card.limits: Each variable earns its place by changing the allowed moves. Drop one, and two different situations look the same.

concepts.title: Stock trading: skip, buy or sell
concepts.question: On a given day, which moves can the stock recurrence choose from, and how does each change the state?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With state (i, holding, remain), what are the choices on day i and what does each lead to?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Skip: move to the next day with nothing changed, dp(i + 1, holding, remain). Buy, allowed only when not holding: pay prices[i] and move to dp(i + 1, true, remain). Sell, allowed only when holding: receive prices[i] and move to dp(i + 1, false, remain - 1). The answer for the state is the maximum of the moves that are allowed.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The states are i, holding and remain: about n * 2 * k of them, each with O(1) work, so time and space are O(n * k). Holding has two values, so it only adds a constant factor.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: These are the only moves, so the maximum covers every strategy. Buying does not change remain, and selling lowers it by one.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Memoized solution in Python:

card.rule: dp(i, holding, remain) = max(skip, buy if not holding, sell if holding), and only a sale lowers remain.
card.limits: The maximum includes only the moves allowed by holding. A buy is not a candidate while holding, and a sale is not a candidate when not holding.

concepts.title: Stock trading: base cases and cost
concepts.question: What are the stock base cases, how does bottom-up loop, and why is the cost O(n * k)?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The recurrence needs stopping points, a bottom-up table, and a cost.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Two base cases return 0: the end of the prices (i = n) and no transactions left (remain = 0). Bottom-up uses an array of n + 1 by 2 by k + 1 and loops i downward from n - 1 and remain upward from 1, since remain = 0 is already the base case. The loop over holding is innermost.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There are about n * 2 * k states with O(1) work each. The factor 2 from holding is a constant, so time and space are O(n * k).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: With no days or no transactions left no more profit can be made, so 0 is right. i runs downward and remain upward from 1, so the cells read, at i + 1 and at remain - 1 (the base case at 0), are filled first.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Bottom-up in Python:

card.rule: Base cases: no days or no transactions left. Cost: O(n * k), because holding contributes a constant.
card.limits: Getting the three nested loops right is the hard part. Start from the base cases, or a cell is read before it is filled.

concepts.title: Coins from piles: choose how many to take
concepts.question: How does the piles-of-coins recurrence handle taking several coins from one pile?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: There are n piles of coins, each listed from top to bottom. A move takes the top coin of any pile. Choose exactly k coins to get the largest total value.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The state is the pile index i and the number remain of coins still allowed. dp(i, remain) is the best total from pile i on. At pile i, skip it: dp(i + 1, remain). Or take its first j + 1 coins: their sum plus dp(i + 1, remain - j - 1), trying each j up to min(remain, pile length). Take the maximum.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There are O(n * k) states for n piles and k coins. Each state loops over up to x choices, where x is the average pile size, so time is O(n * k * x) and space is O(n * k).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Coins come off the top, so taking j + 1 coins from a pile means exactly its first j + 1. Trying every j covers every count. The base cases are i = n and remain = 0, both returning 0.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Memoized solution in Python:

card.rule: At each pile, skip it or try every number of top coins, then recurse with fewer coins allowed.
card.limits: The loop over j makes the work per state larger than O(1). The min with remain keeps the count within the allowance.

concepts.title: Coins from piles: time and space
concepts.question: Why is the piles-of-coins time O(n * k * x) while its space is only O(n * k)?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The coins DP has a loop inside each state. How does this change the cost compared with stock trading?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: There are n * k states, where n is the number of piles. At each state a loop runs about x times, where x is the average pile length. So the time is O(n * k * x). The table or memo holds one value per state, so the space is O(n * k).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Time is the number of states times the work per state, and that work is now x steps rather than O(1). Space depends only on the states, as the loop stores nothing.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: For n = 20 piles, k = 10 and x = 5 the work is about 20 * 10 * 5 = 1000 steps.

card.rule: Time is O(n * k * x) and space is O(n * k).
card.limits: The bound uses the average pile length x. A few very long piles make the real cost depend on their sizes.

concepts.title: A matrix is a graph of squares
concepts.question: How does DP on a matrix reuse the graph ideas and what is the state?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Matrix problems are common in DP. How do you think about a grid, and what is the state?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A matrix can be modelled as a graph, exactly as in the trees and graphs chapter: each square is a node, and edges join adjacent squares. A position on the grid is described by its row and column, so the state is (row, col).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Moving from one square to another is moving from one state to another, so the recurrence for a square is written in terms of the squares next to it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: An m by n grid has m * n squares, so m * n states. Two state variables make the algorithm two-dimensional.

card.rule: Treat each square as a state (row, col), and write each square's answer from its neighbours.
card.limits: Not every grid problem has states that depend only on the position. Extra rules, such as a limit on moves, add variables.

concepts.title: Unique paths on a grid
concepts.question: How many ways reach a square when you can only move down or right?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A robot on an m by n grid starts at the top left and may move only down or right. How many different paths lead to the bottom right?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Let dp(row, col) be the number of paths from (0, 0) to (row, col). A square can be entered only from the square above or the square to its left, so dp(row, col) = dp(row - 1, col) + dp(row, col - 1), staying inside the grid. The base case is dp(0, 0) = 1. The answer is dp(m - 1, n - 1).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: There are m * n squares, each costing O(1) to compute, so time and space are both O(m * n) with a full table. The next idea shows how the space can shrink.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every path to a square ends with a move down from above or a move right from the left, and these two groups do not overlap, so their counts add.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Bottom-up in Python:

card.rule: Paths to a square = paths to the square above + paths to the square on the left, with dp(0, 0) = 1.
card.limits: The addition needs moves limited to down and right. With more allowed moves, more neighbours enter the sum.

concepts.title: Minimum path sum
concepts.question: How does the unique-paths recurrence change when the goal is the smallest sum?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A grid holds non-negative numbers. Find a path from the top left to the bottom right, moving only down or right, with the smallest sum of the numbers along it.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Let dp(row, col) be the smallest path sum from (0, 0) to (row, col). A path comes from above or from the left, so dp(row, col) = grid[row][col] + min(dp(row - 1, col), dp(row, col - 1)), staying in bounds. The base case is the start: dp(0, 0) = grid[0][0]. The answer is dp(m - 1, n - 1).

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The cheapest path to a square must arrive from one of two squares, and the cheapest way to reach each of those is already known, so adding the square's own number to the smaller of the two is the best total.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: m * n states with O(1) work, so O(m * n) time and space.

card.rule: dp(row, col) = grid[row][col] + min(above, left), with the start square's own value as the base case.
card.limits: The recurrence relies on moves being only down and right. The base case must include the start square's value.

concepts.title: Matrix DP in O(n) space
concepts.question: How can a bottom-up matrix DP shrink its space from O(m * n) to O(n)?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Unique paths and minimum path sum use a table with m * n cells. Can the space be smaller?

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Yes, with bottom-up. The recurrence is static and reads only the row above and the previous square in the same row. So iterate one row at a time, keep the previous row, and build the next one.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time stays O(m * n) since every square is still computed. Space drops from O(m * n) to O(n), one stored row. The book says this works only for bottom-up with a static recurrence.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Rows older than the previous one are not read again, so they can be dropped.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text: Unique paths with one stored row, in Python:

card.rule: Keep only the previous row: O(n) space, same time, for a static recurrence that reads the row above.
card.limits: It works for bottom-up only. A top-down memo must still hold its states and the recursion stack.

concepts.title: Two-pointer templates
concepts.question: Which loop shape scans one input from both ends, and which walks two inputs together to the end?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: You scan one sequence from both ends, or you walk two sequences together, for example to merge two sorted lists.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: One input: put left at 0 and right at the last index, loop while left < right, do the logic, then move exactly one pointer according to the condition. Two inputs: start i and j at 0 and loop while both are in range, moving one pointer per pass. Then run one more loop per input to handle what is left.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: Every pass moves a pointer, so the loop ends. Merging [1, 4, 9] with [2, 3, 10, 11, 12] gives [1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 12]; after the main loop the first input is used up and the second input's leftover loop handles its last 3 items.

blocks.label: Code (Python)
blocks.text: Concrete versions of the book's two templates, with a real condition filled in.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: In the two-input version the main loop stops when either input is used up. Leaving out the follow-up loops silently drops the rest of the other input.

card.rule: Move one pointer per pass, and with two inputs finish the leftovers after the main loop.
card.limits: The skeleton leaves the condition and the per-pass logic blank. It does not say which pointer to move or whether the input must be sorted; the problem decides that.

concepts.title: Window, prefix and exact-count templates
concepts.question: How do the sliding window, prefix sum and exact-count templates each handle a subarray problem?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: A problem asks about contiguous stretches of an array: the longest stretch that stays valid (window), many range sums (prefix sum), or how many stretches add up to exactly k (exact count).

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Window: for each new right element, add it to the running value; while the window condition is broken, remove the left element and move left; then update the answer. Prefix: the first entry is arr[0]; each later entry is the previous entry plus arr[i]. Exact count: start a map with total 0 seen once; per element update the running total, add the map's count for total minus k, then record the total.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: Prefix of [2, 1, 3] is [2, 3, 6]. For sales [3, 1, 2, 7, 4, 2, 1, 1, 5] and a limit of 8 the longest window has 4 days. For [1, 2, 3, 3, 0, 3] and k = 6 the exact count is 4.

blocks.label: Code (Python)
blocks.text: Concrete versions of three of the book's templates.
blocks.code:
def longest_window(arr, limit):     # non-negative numbers
    left = curr = ans = 0
    for right in range(len(arr)):
