        curr += arr[right]
        while curr > limit:         # window condition broken
            curr -= arr[left]
            left += 1
        ans = max(ans, right - left + 1)
    return ans

def build_prefix(arr):
    prefix = [arr[0]]
    for i in range(1, len(arr)):
        prefix.append(prefix[-1] + arr[i])
    return prefix

def count_exact(arr, k):            # subarrays with sum exactly k
    counts = {0: 1}
    ans = curr = 0
    for num in arr:
        curr += num
        ans += counts.get(curr - k, 0)
        counts[curr] = counts.get(curr, 0) + 1
    return ans

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: In the exact-count template, look up the map before you record the new total. Recording first lets a total match itself.

card.rule: The window shrinks only while its condition is broken, and the exact count asks the map before it records.
card.limits: These are skeletons: the lines that change the running value or test the window condition depend on the problem. The window version shown also assumes that removing from the left can repair a broken window.

concepts.title: Fast-slow and reversal templates
concepts.question: What loop test and pointer moves do the fast-slow and reversal templates use on a linked list?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: You must find the middle of a linked list in one pass, or turn the list around so the tail becomes the head.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Fast-slow: slow and fast both start at the head; loop while fast and the node after fast both exist; slow moves one node and fast moves two. Reversal: keep prev (starting empty) and curr (starting at the head); per node save curr's next, point curr's next at prev, move prev to curr, move curr to the saved node; return prev.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: On the list 1 to 5, slow stops at 3; on 1 to 6 it stops at 4. Reversing 1, 2, 3 returns the list 3, 2, 1.

blocks.label: Code (Python)
blocks.text: Concrete versions of the book's two templates.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: In the reversal, rewiring a node's next pointer before saving the old one loses the rest of the list.

card.rule: Test both fast and its next node before moving, and save the next node before you rewire.
card.limits: Both skeletons work on singly linked nodes and leave the per-node logic blank. Which of two middle nodes you get on an even-length list depends on this exact loop test.

concepts.title: Monotonic stack, top-k heap and string builder
concepts.question: What does each of the monotonic stack, top-k heap and string-building templates rely on?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: You must compare each item with those before it (monotonic stack), keep only the k best items from many (heap), or assemble a long string from pieces.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Monotonic increasing stack: for each number, while the stack is not empty and its top is greater than the number, do the logic and pop; then push the number. For a decreasing stack, flip the comparison. Top k: add each number to the heap and remove the head whenever the size exceeds k; then remove the k survivors one by one. Strings: append pieces to a builder and convert once at the end.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: The stack after 5, 3, 8, 1, 4 holds [1, 4], and it popped [5, 8, 3] along the way. The top 3 of 4, 1, 7, 3, 8, 5 come out as [5, 7, 8].

blocks.label: Code (Python)
blocks.text: Concrete versions of three of the book's templates.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: The heap's ordering decides which item leaves. With the smallest at the head, the template keeps the largest k.

card.rule: Pop while the top breaks the order; cap the heap at k and drop its head.
card.limits: The template shows only the pops; what you do while popping is problem logic. Because the test is strictly greater than, equal numbers stay on the stack.

concepts.title: Tree and graph traversal templates
concepts.question: What structure drives each traversal template, and what extra does a graph need that a tree does not?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: You must visit every node of a tree or graph: either going deep first (DFS) or level by level (BFS).

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Tree DFS: stop on an empty node, do the logic, then recurse left and right; the iterative form pushes the root, then pops a node and pushes its children. Tree BFS: use a queue; each outer pass fixes the level size first, then processes exactly that many nodes. Graph (adjacency list, nodes 0 to n - 1): same loops plus a seen set, and a neighbour joins the set when it is added to the stack or queue.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: The sample tree has level sizes [1, 2, 3]. On the graph [[1, 2], [0, 3], [0, 3, 4], [1, 2], [2]] from node 0, DFS visits [0, 2, 4, 3, 1] and BFS visits [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]; each node once.

blocks.label: Code (Python)
blocks.text: Concrete versions of the book's tree BFS and graph DFS and BFS templates.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: A graph traversal without a seen set can circle a cycle forever.

card.rule: A stack gives DFS, a queue gives BFS, and a graph also needs a seen set filled when a node is added.
card.limits: The graph templates assume nodes numbered 0 to n - 1 and an adjacency list, so other inputs must be converted first. A tree has no cycles, so the tree templates have no seen set.

concepts.title: Binary search templates
concepts.question: Which binary search template fits a plain lookup, the first or last of several copies, or the smallest or largest answer?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: You search sorted data, may have repeated values and want the first or last position, or you search a range of possible answers whose check switches once.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Plain: left 0, right last index, loop while left <= right, compare the middle, shrink one side; leaving the loop, left is the insertion point. Duplicates: right starts at the array length, loop while left < right; if the middle is at least the target (greater than it, for the right-most) set right to mid, else left to mid + 1; return left. Search space: left and right are the smallest and largest possible answers; for a minimum, a passing mid sets right = mid - 1 and you return left; for a maximum, it sets left = mid + 1 and you return right.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: On [1, 2, 2, 2, 3] with target 2: plain returns 2 (a copy of 2), left-most 1, right-most 4. For target 4 the plain template returns 5, the insertion point.

blocks.label: Code (Python)
blocks.text: Concrete versions of three of the book's templates.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: With repeated values the plain template returns whichever copy the middle lands on first.

card.rule: Pick the template by what you need back: any match, the first or last copy, or the best passing answer.
card.limits: Every template needs sorted data, or a check that changes its answer only once. The skeletons leave the check and the answer range to the problem.

concepts.title: Backtracking and DP templates
concepts.question: Which steps does the backtracking template repeat, and how does the DP template turn into a bottom-up loop?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: A problem asks you to try choices and undo them (backtracking), or to reuse answers for repeated states (dynamic programming), top-down or bottom-up.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Backtracking: at the base case record the answer and return; otherwise loop over the choices, modify the state, recurse, undo the modification. Top-down DP: return at the base case, return a stored answer if the state is in the memo, otherwise compute with the recurrence and store it. Bottom-up: make an array sized by the state variables, set the base cases, loop over the states from the base cases toward the answer, replace dp(...) calls with dp[...] reads, and return the answer's entry.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: Subsets of [1, 2, 3] come out as 8 lists, and of four items 16. Climbing 10 stairs by 1 or 2 steps gives 89 ways in both the top-down and bottom-up versions.

blocks.label: Code (Python)
blocks.text: Concrete versions of the backtracking, top-down and bottom-up templates.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: If the undo step is left out, the changed state leaks into the next choice.

card.rule: Backtracking changes, recurses and undoes; DP stores answers by state, and bottom-up fills them from the base cases.
card.limits: The skeletons leave the state, the base cases and the recurrence to the problem. A bottom-up array must follow an order in which every state's inputs are filled before it.

concepts.title: Introductions
concepts.question: What should you prepare for the opening of an interview, and what should you do while the interviewer speaks?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: The interview opens: the interviewer briefly introduces themselves and their role, then asks you to introduce yourself.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Before the interview, prepare and rehearse a brief introduction that summarizes your education, work experience and interests in 30 to 60 seconds. In the room, smile and speak with a confident voice. While the interviewer describes their work, pay attention. If they mention something you are also interested in, say so.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: Your introduction fits in 30 to 60 seconds and covers education, work experience and interests. You also took in what the interviewer said about their own work.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: Waiting for your turn without listening wastes what the interviewer tells you about their work.

card.rule: Rehearse a 30 to 60 second introduction, and listen closely to the interviewer's own.
card.limits: These are habits for the opening minutes and earn no technical credit. The shared-interest step is conditional: mention an interest only when the interviewer actually mentioned one you share.

concepts.title: Problem statement
concepts.question: What should you do after the problem is read to you, before you start designing a solution?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: The interviewer gives you the problem, often pasted with a test case into a shared editor and read aloud.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: First, paraphrase the problem back to the interviewer. Then ask clarifying questions about the input: its types, whether it is sorted, whether it can be empty, and what to do with invalid input. Ask about the expected input size. Finally, walk through one of the given examples quickly to confirm you understand.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: You and the interviewer agree on what is asked, you know what the input may look like, and one example has been traced.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: Skipping this stage risks solving a different problem from the one asked.

card.rule: Paraphrase the problem, question the input and its size, and trace one example before you design.
card.limits: Interviewers can be vague about size. When they do give a range, treat it as a clue, not a rule: the book's pairings of size and technique are tendencies.

concepts.title: Brainstorming data structures and algorithms
concepts.question: How should you choose and present a data structure or algorithm before you write any code?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: You understand the problem and must choose a data structure or algorithm before you write code.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Break the problem down and look for patterns you have learned. Work out what the problem needs and which structure or algorithm does it with a good time complexity. Think out loud while you do. Once you have chosen, outline the rough steps and explain them to the interviewer. Stay receptive to hints.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: The interviewer understands your outline and agrees that it is a reasonable approach before you begin to code.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: Being stubborn about a hint. The interviewer knows the optimal solution, so a hint is there to help you succeed.

card.rule: Think out loud, and get the interviewer to agree to your rough steps before coding.
card.limits: Thinking aloud does not replace knowing the patterns; the book says practicing LeetCode problems is the best way to train that skill. A hint steers you but does not write the solution.

concepts.title: Implementation
concepts.question: How should you write code during the interview, and what should you do when you get stuck?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: You have an algorithm and the interviewer is on board: it is time to write code.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Check with the interviewer before importing a library or module. Explain your decisions as you write. Keep the code clean, following your language's conventions, without duplicated code, and use helper functions. If you are stuck, say so. One strategy is to write a brute force solution, acknowledge it is suboptimal, then find its slow steps and speed them up with the interviewer.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: The code follows the language's conventions, repeats no logic, and the interviewer has heard the reason for each major decision.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: Struggling in silence makes the interviewer's job harder.

card.rule: Explain as you code, keep it clean, and say so when you are stuck.
card.limits: The brute force start is one strategy the book offers, not a requirement, and it must be labelled as suboptimal when you present it.

concepts.title: Testing and debugging
concepts.question: How do you test your code in each of the three interview environments, and how do you find a bug?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: Your code is written and the interviewer wants it tested. The environment decides how.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Built-in tests with code run: the platform supplies the tests. Your own tests with code run: call your function from the outermost scope with tests you write (edge cases, ordinary inputs, invalid inputs if wanted) and print the results. Code not run: walk each test through by hand, writing the variables in the editor and updating them. To debug, add prints where code runs or walk a small test case, and compare expected with actual values aloud.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: Each test gives the result you expected, or the first variable that differs from your expectation shows where the bug is.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: Do not trace trivial loops step by step; say what the result will look like after the loop.

card.rule: Match the testing method to the environment, and compare expected with actual values aloud.
card.limits: The three environments are the book's list; a real interview may mix them. Condensing a trivial loop works only where its result is easy to state.

concepts.title: Explanations and follow-ups
concepts.question: Which questions should you expect after your solution works, and how do you answer them?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: Your algorithm is coded and tested, and the interviewer starts asking about it or adds new work.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Be ready for three questions: the time and space complexity (answer for the worst case, and mention the average case too if the worst is rare and the average is significantly faster); why you chose your data structure, algorithm or loop layout; and whether it could be improved in time or space. If time remains you may get a new question, which restarts at the problem statement, or follow-ups with new constraints.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: Your complexity answer names the worst case, your choices come with reasons, and you claim no more than you can back up.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: Memorizing solutions: follow-ups with new constraints need real understanding.

card.rule: Expect questions on complexity, choices and improvements, and answer from understanding.
card.limits: A new unrelated question starts again at the problem statement, so earlier answers do not carry over. Follow-ups test understanding that a memorized solution does not give.

concepts.title: Outro
concepts.question: How should you use the closing minutes of an interview, and what can go wrong?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: The interviewer has reserved the last few minutes for your questions about them or the company.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Prepare questions before the interview, for example what an average day looks like, why the interviewer chose this company, what they like and dislike most about the job, and what work you could expect. Read posts on the company's tech blog and note questions about its decisions. Listen to the answers, keep smiling and ask follow-ups.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: You asked questions that were prepared and followed up on the answers, and the interviewer saw you were interested.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: You rarely improve the outcome now, but you can make it worse by having no good questions or looking bored.

card.rule: Bring prepared questions and show real interest; the outro can hurt more than it can help.
card.limits: The question list is a set of prompts, not a script. The book also asks you to listen and follow up on the answers instead of reading questions out in turn.

concepts.title: Operation costs by data structure
concepts.question: Which operations are cheap and which cost a full scan across the common data structures, and why?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: You are choosing a data structure for the operations a loop will repeat, and need the cost of each operation.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Name the operation, then read its cost for that structure. Reaching an index is O(1) in arrays, strings and stacks but O(n) in linked lists and queues. Checking membership is O(1) in a hash map's keys or a set, but O(n) in arrays, lists, stacks, queues, heaps and a hash map's values. Heap add and remove-min are O(log n), with find-min O(1). Then apply the caveats on strings, hashing and trees.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: You can state each operation's cost and multiply by the number of passes. Looking up 1,000 names in a set costs about 1,000 steps, and in a list of 1,000 names about 1,000,000.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: Strings are immutable, so adding or removing a character costs O(n); building a string with n such additions therefore adds up to O(n squared).

card.rule: Direct access is cheap, and search is a full scan unless the structure hashes or keeps order.
card.limits: The sheet's stack and queue costs assume particular implementations, and real queues can differ. A hash map's O(1) is constant relative to its size, not to the length of its keys.

media.alt: A line chart titled as a Big-O complexity chart, with elements on the horizontal axis and operations on the vertical axis, shaded from red at the top to green at the bottom. Factorial, exponential and quadratic curves shoot upward almost at once, in that order of steepness. The n log n curve rises moderately, the linear line is a gentle slope, and log n and constant lines hug the bottom.

concepts.title: Estimating the cost of a whole algorithm
concepts.question: How do you estimate the time of a pointer scan, a tree or graph traversal, a DP table or a binary search?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: You must state or compare the cost of a whole algorithm, not only one operation.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Count what the algorithm visits and multiply by the work at each visit. Two pointers, sliding window and tree DFS or BFS: n times k, where k is the work per step and is usually O(1) for trees. Graph DFS or BFS: n times k plus e, the number of edges. DP: the number of states times the work per state. Binary search: log of the search space. Sorting: n log n.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: Your answer names n, k and e. A graph of 10,000 nodes, constant work and 30,000 edges costs about 10,000 + 30,000 = 40,000 steps.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: Treating k as 1 when each visit runs its own loop.

card.rule: Cost is visits times work per visit, plus the edges for a graph.
card.limits: These are general rules, not always exact. The tree rule assumes BFS uses an efficient queue, and k is not always constant.

concepts.title: Small input limits
concepts.question: What complexity and technique do input limits of up to about 1,000 suggest?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: A problem states a limit on n, or you ask for one, and you want to guess the intended complexity.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Read the limit as an upper bound on cost. Up to 10: factorial or exponential with a base above 2, so backtracking or brute-force recursion. 11 to 20: about O(2 to the n), the take-or-skip choice over subsets, so backtracking. 21 to 100: about O(n cubed), so nested-loop brute force. 101 to 1,000: O(n squared), so nested loops.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: The counts match the bounds: 10! = 3,628,800; 2^20 = 1,048,576; 100^3 = 1,000,000; 1,000^2 = 1,000,000. Each is within reach of a computer.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: At n = 20 a base of 3 is too slow: 3^20 is 3,486,784,401, about 3.5 billion.

card.rule: Small limits allow brute force: exponential at 20, cubic at 100, quadratic at 1,000.
card.limits: A limit suggests the intended solution but does not prove it. In the top range O(n squared) is usually expected, as long as the constant factor is not too large.

concepts.title: Large input limits
concepts.question: What complexity do limits above 1,000 call for, and which techniques replace a nested loop?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: The limit on n is above 1,000, so a nested loop is probably too slow and you need a faster approach.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: 1,000 to 100,000: the slowest acceptable common cost is O(n log n), and O(n) is the usual goal. Ask whether sorting or a heap helps; if not, aim for O(n) by replacing the inner loop with a hash map, two pointers or sliding window, a monotonic stack, binary search, a heap, or a combination. Up to 1,000,000: likely O(n), probably with a hash map. Above that, around 10^9: O(log n) or O(1), by binary search or math.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: At n = 100,000, a nested loop costs 10,000,000,000 steps, while n log n is about 1,660,964.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: Nested loops that run in O(n squared) are unacceptable for n up to 100,000.

card.rule: Above about 1,000 items the nested loop is probably too slow: aim for O(n log n) or better with a technique that replaces the inner loop.
card.limits: Interviews often state no limits, so ask. The ranges are tendencies, not guarantees, and rare costs such as O(square root of n) also exist.

concepts.title: Sorting cost and the flowchart
concepts.question: What cost should you assume for sorting, and what does the book's flowchart leave out?

blocks.label: When you need it
blocks.text: Your solution sorts its input, or you want a quick pointer to a data structure or algorithm to try.

blocks.label: Procedure
blocks.text: Use the language's built-in sort and state its cost as O(n log n), with n the number of elements. A stable sort keeps records with equal keys in their original relative order. For a pointer to the structure or algorithm to try, use the general flowchart, and treat its advice as general.

blocks.label: Check it worked
blocks.text: Your sorting step is stated as O(n log n) and included in your total. If equal keys matter, you know whether your language's sort is stable.

blocks.label: Pitfall
blocks.text: Do not assume every language uses the same algorithm. Python uses Timsort, but C++ does not mandate a specific one.

card.rule: Assume built-in sorting costs O(n log n), and use the flowchart as a general guide only.
card.limits: The flowchart only covers methods taught in the book's course, so more advanced algorithms such as Dijkstra's are excluded. It is very general because every scenario cannot be covered.

media.alt: A table of sorting algorithms with best, average and worst time, worst-case extra space and a stability column, cells colored from green to red by cost. Merge sort and Timsort are stable; quicksort, heapsort and shellsort are not. Quicksort's worst case is quadratic, while merge sort and heapsort stay at n log n. Counting, radix and bucket sorts depend on a range or key length.

A flowchart headed by the kind of input, with three starting boxes. For a graph, a question about the shortest path or fewest steps leads to breadth-first search, otherwise depth-first search. For a tree, a question about specific depths or levels leads to breadth-first search, otherwise depth-first search. For a linked list, finding a position or detecting cycles leads to fast and slow pointers, reversing to a prev pointer, and returning the original head to a dummy pointer.

A flowchart titled 'Input is an array or string', starting at a Start box. First it asks whether the input is sorted: yes leads to binary search and two pointers. If not, it asks what the question is asking for. All of something leads to backtracking. The number of ways, a max or min possible, or whether something is possible leads to a test of whether decisions are affected by other decisions: yes leads to dynamic programming; no leads to greedy, and a note says that a problem whose possible and impossible answers are two zones separated by a threshold goes back to binary search. String building or distance between elements leads to a stack or monotonic stack; prefix matching leads to a trie; finding a specific element leads to a hash map or set, which a green box says to think about for any problem. Not necessarily greedy: continuously finding a max or min element leads to a monotonic queue when elements are added and removed in sliding-window fashion, or to a heap when the max or min is continuously removed; subarrays or substrings lead to a sliding window or counting hash map.

concepts.title: Spotting events on a number line
concepts.question: What does a problem look like when a difference array can solve it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Recognise problems where stretches of a line, either time or position, each carry some value, and the question is about a point on that line.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Picture the events along a number line, each with a starting and an ending point. The input is usually a 2D array whose inner arrays read [left, right, value], or an equivalent form. The story says that between left and right there is value of something. Car pooling, with trips along a road, is the course's first example.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Recognising the pattern costs nothing. The approach it leads to, a difference array, runs in O(n + m) with n events and m the farthest right end.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: the amount at any point is the sum of the values of the events whose stretch covers that point, so a question about a point is a question about the overlapping events.

card.rule: If a story says that between left and right there is value of something, think of events on a number line and reach for a difference array.
card.limits: The pattern needs stretches that carry values along a line. A plain array of numbers, or a problem with no start and end points, gives it nothing to work on.

concepts.title: Build the change array, then walk it
concepts.question: How do you find the busiest point without adding each event to every point it covers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Decide whether the load on a line ever exceeds a limit, as in car pooling, where trips [people, from, to] must stay at or under capacity passengers at every point.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Find the farthest right end and make an array arr of length farthest + 1. For each event add its value at left and subtract it at right. Then take a running total (prefix sum) along arr: each total is the load at that point, ready to compare with the limit.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n + m) time and space, where n is the number of events and m is the farthest right end.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: arr stores the change at each position, and a running total of changes is the amount present. An event raises the total at left and lowers it again at right, so it counts only between those points.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Add the value at left, subtract it at right, and a prefix sum over the array gives the amount at every point.
card.limits: The array is as long as the farthest position, so memory and time grow with that position and not only with the number of events.

concepts.title: When the line is too long to build
concepts.question: What do you do when positions reach 10^18 and an array of positions is impossible?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the point where the most events overlap when the line is far too long to build as an array. The course's example is street lights with positions up to 10^18.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Skip the long array. Turn every event into two change records [position, value]: add the value where it starts and subtract it right after it ends. Sort the records by position, then walk them with a running total and remember where it was highest.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n log n) for sorting the 2n records. Memory grows with the number of events, not with the length of the line.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: the total can change only at a record, so its highest value is reached at some record's position. Sorting puts the records in line order, so each running total equals the lights shining there.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: When positions are too large to build, sort change records and walk them with a running total; the constraints decide which version to use.
card.limits: Sorting adds a log factor. When the line is short enough to build, the array version is cheaper and simpler.

concepts.title: A trie is a tree of prefixes
concepts.question: How does one tree hold a whole list of words so that shared beginnings are stored once?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Keep track of which words in a huge list begin with the characters typed so far, for example while someone is typing.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A trie, also called a prefix tree, is a tree that usually holds one character per node. Every path from the root down to a node spells a string, so the node stands for a prefix. The root stands for the empty string, and words with the same beginning share the nodes of that beginning.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Building a trie takes O(n * k), where n is the number of words and k is their average length.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: a prefix is the same for every word that starts with it, so storing it once as a path lets one walk from the root stand for all of those words at the same time.

card.rule: A trie is a tree in which each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that start alike share nodes.
card.limits: It answers prefix questions about a list of strings. Our reading: it does not help with questions about the middle of a word, such as anagrams or substrings.

media.alt: A tree with the empty string at the root and one letter per node. The root has two children, a and n. Under a hang x, g and s, with x leading to h and s leading to x; under n hang t and s, with t leading to another t. Beside each node is the string spelled by the path from the root.

concepts.title: Building a trie word by word
concepts.question: How do you insert a list of words into a trie?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Turn an array of words into a trie.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Start with an empty root. For each word start at the root and go through its characters: if the current node has no child for the character, create one, then step into that child. When the last character is reached, the path ends at a node standing for the whole word, and you may attach more information there.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n * k) time for n words of average length k, because each character of each word is handled once.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each character either follows a child that already exists or creates it. So when a word is finished its full path exists, and words with a shared beginning reuse the nodes already made.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: To build a trie, walk each word from the root, creating a child only where one is missing.
card.limits: This is one way to build a trie, not the only one. Our reading: as written it does not mark where a word ends, so that needs extra data at the end node.

concepts.title: Why a trie beats scanning for every prefix
concepts.question: How much faster is a trie than checking every product for every typed prefix?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After each character of a search word is typed, list the products that share the typed prefix. The course's example is Search Suggestions, which suggests at most three products.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The brute force repeats the work for each prefix: it checks every product against it. A trie is built from the products once. Typing then walks down the tree one character at a time, so reading the answer for the whole search word takes O(m) steps, where m is its length.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Trie: O(n * k + m) in total, with n products of average length k. Checking every product again for every prefix is far more expensive.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The expensive matching of prefixes against products is done once, during the build, and every later lookup reuses the tree. Because k is small, the build is cheap.

card.rule: A trie pays O(n * k) once and then answers each prefix in a step, which beats rescanning all products for each prefix.
card.limits: The saving relies on reusing one built trie for many prefixes. For a single prefix on a small list a plain scan is simpler. Our reading: the trie also uses extra memory.

concepts.title: Storing suggestions at trie nodes
concepts.question: How can every prefix of a search word get its three smallest matches in one step?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: For each prefix of a search word, return up to three products that start with it, choosing the lexicographically smallest when more match.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each node stands for a prefix, so give it an attribute, suggestions, holding at most three products. While inserting a product, add it at every node along its path, sort that short list and drop the last entry if it has more than three. To answer, walk the search word: each step down gives that node's list. If a letter has no child, the answer is an empty list.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Building costs O(n * k); sorting is cheap because each list holds at most three or four strings. Reading all the answers costs O(m) for a search word of m letters.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: every product passes through the node of each of its prefixes, so each node sees all products with that prefix. Keeping only the three smallest as they arrive leaves exactly the three smallest.

blocks.label: Trace
blocks.text: Products bag, baggage, banner, box, cat and search word bags give: b -> bag, baggage, banner; ba -> bag, baggage, banner; bag -> bag, baggage; bags -> empty list.

card.rule: Keep a sorted list of at most three products at every trie node, and each prefix is answered by one step down the tree.
card.limits: The cap of three is what keeps the per-node sort cheap. A node that had to keep every match would make the build far more costly.

concepts.title: OR, AND, XOR and shifts
concepts.question: What does each bit operation do to two integers written in binary?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Treat integers as rows of bits so that simple fast operations can replace slower data structures, which can improve an algorithm's complexity.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: OR (|) gives 1 if any combined bit is 1. AND (&) gives 1 only if all combined bits are 1. XOR (^) gives 1 if the number of 1 bits is odd. A left shift (<<) moves every bit one place up, which multiplies by 2. A right shift (>>) moves bits down, which is floor division by 2 and drops the lowest bit.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each operation on an integer takes a single fast step; the course calls integer and bit operations extremely fast.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: binary place values double from right to left, so moving every bit one place up doubles the number and moving it down halves it.

card.rule: OR keeps a 1 if any input is 1, AND needs all inputs to be 1, XOR needs an odd count of 1s, and a shift multiplies or floor-divides by 2.
card.limits: Shifts discard bits pushed off the end, so a right shift floors the result: 7 >> 1 is 3, not 3.5. Priority among bit operators is low, so use parentheses.

concepts.title: A mask picks one bit
concepts.question: How do you test or flip one chosen bit of an integer and leave the others alone?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Look at, or change, a single bit of a number, for example the bit worth 4, without disturbing the others.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Make a bitmask with a single 1 in the wanted place: mask = 1 << i, where bits are numbered from 0 at the right. To test the bit, compute mask & x: it is non-zero if and only if bit i of x is set. To flip the bit, compute mask ^ x.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One shift and one AND or XOR: O(1) per test or flip.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: AND with a mask that is 0 everywhere except bit i clears every other place, so only bit i can make the result non-zero. XOR with the same mask leaves every other place as it was.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Build mask = 1 << i, then x & mask tells whether bit i is set and x ^ mask flips it.
card.limits: The result of the AND is the bit's value (such as 4), not 1, so compare it with zero rather than with one.

concepts.title: Equal numbers cancel under XOR
concepts.question: What happens when you XOR a number with itself, and why does that help?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Collapse a long list of numbers to one result by combining them with XOR, when most of the numbers come in equal pairs.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: XOR has two properties. A number XORed with itself gives 0: x XOR x = 0. And 0 XOR y = y. Together, x XOR x XOR y = y.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One XOR per number: O(n) time for n numbers, and one variable of extra space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each equal pair becomes 0, and 0 XORed with anything leaves it unchanged. So pairs vanish from the result and the leftover number stays.

card.rule: x XOR x is 0 and 0 XOR y is y, so equal numbers cancel out of an XOR.
card.limits: It cancels numbers in pairs. Our reading: a number that occurs three times does not vanish, because two of its copies cancel and one remains.

concepts.title: Single Number with XOR
concepts.question: How do you find the one value that appears once when all the others appear twice?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In a non-empty array every value appears twice except one. Find that single value.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A hash map of counts finds it in O(n) time but O(n) space. Sorting needs less space but O(n log n) time. Better: start a variable mask at 0 and XOR every number into it. The pairs cancel, and the single value is what remains.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Every value that appears twice contributes x XOR x = 0, and the zeros leave the rest unchanged. That leaves 0 XOR y = y, the single value.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: XOR every number together: the pairs cancel and the one unpaired number is left.
card.limits: It relies on every other value appearing exactly twice, or at least an even number of times.

concepts.title: A bitmask as a hashable set of used items
concepts.question: Why is an integer mask a good way to record which items are already used?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Backtracking and DP problems often use each array element at most once, so they need a record of which elements are used, and DP needs that record to be hashable for memoization.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: A boolean array cannot be hashed, so it cannot be a memo key. Use an integer mask instead, where bit i is 1 if element i has been used. XOR flips the bit to mark or unmark an element, and AND tests whether it is marked.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each mark, unmark or test is O(1). One integer replaces an array of n booleans.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: An integer is immutable, so it can be hashed, and one integer names the whole set of used items. The function can then be memoized, which allows many problems to be solved cleanly with DP.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.code:
used = 0
used ^= 1 << 2               # mark item 2
print((used & (1 << 2)) != 0)  # True
used ^= 1 << 2               # unmark item 2
memo = {used: 'seen'}        # a mask can be a key

card.rule: Store used items as bits of an integer: XOR marks and unmarks, AND tests, and the integer can be a memo key.
card.limits: XOR flips, so marking an item that is already marked unmarks it. Check first, or the bit goes back to 0.

concepts.title: N-Queens II with three integers
concepts.question: How do three integers replace the three sets in N-Queens II?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Count the ways to place n queens on an n by n board, as in the backtracking chapter, but store the attacked columns and diagonals more cheaply than with sets.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep three integers: columns, diagonals and anti-diagonals. A queen at (row, col) uses the masks 1 << col, 1 << (row - col + n) and 1 << (row + col). A square is free if all three AND tests give zero. To place the queen XOR the three masks in; XORing them again removes it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The recursion is as before. Space is still O(n) for the call stack, but in practice integers use less than sets, and bit operations are faster than hashing.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: each integer has one bit per column or diagonal, and a set bit means that line already holds a queen. Applying the same XOR twice restores the earlier state, so the board is correct after each trial.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Track columns and both diagonals as bits of three integers, test with AND, and place or remove a queen with XOR.
card.limits: The O(n) space bound does not change: the gain is in constant factors, not in the big-O class.

concepts.title: Sort intervals, then compare neighbours
concepts.question: Why does sorting the intervals make overlaps easy to find?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Answer a question about intervals [start, end], for example whether any two overlap, without comparing every pair.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sort the input by start time, then pass over it once and compare adjacent intervals. If there is a conflict, the conflicting intervals are next to each other in the sorted order, so neighbours are the only pairs to check.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: The sort costs O(n log n) for n intervals, which is much better than the O(n^2) of checking every pair.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: After sorting by start, the intervals are in the order in which they would be attended, so an overlap with any earlier interval shows up as an overlap with the one right before it.

card.rule: Sort intervals by start time and compare neighbours, because any conflict appears between adjacent intervals.
card.limits: Sorting costs O(n log n). The pattern suits problems where overlap with neighbours is what matters. Our reading: it does not apply if the input must keep its original order.

concepts.title: Can one person attend every meeting?
concepts.question: How do you decide, after sorting, whether any meeting clashes with the one before it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given meeting times [start, end], decide whether one person could attend all of them.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sort the meetings by start time. Then from the second meeting onward compare its start with the end of the meeting before it. If a start is earlier than the previous end, the person would have to leave the previous meeting early, so the answer is false. If no pair clashes, the answer is true.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n log n) time, dominated by the sort. The scan itself is one pass of n - 1 comparisons.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The sorted order is the order of attendance, so only a meeting that starts before its predecessor ends can clash, and by the neighbour argument no other pairs need checking.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: After sorting by start, a meeting clashes only if it starts before the previous one ends.
card.limits: The test is a strict less-than on start against previous end. Changing it to less-or-equal changes which touching meetings count as clashes.

concepts.title: Merging overlapping intervals
concepts.question: How do you merge overlapping intervals into a minimal set of non-overlapping ones?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Merge all overlapping intervals [start, end] and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover all of the input.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Sort by start and build the answer one interval at a time. For each interval, if its start is less than or equal to the end of the last interval in the answer, they overlap: raise that last end to the larger of the two ends. Otherwise append the interval as a new one.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n log n) for the sort, then one pass. If the answer is not counted as extra space, the space is whatever the sort uses.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Merging [a, b] and [c, d] gives [min(a, c), max(b, d)]. Sorting by start makes the earlier start a, so the minimum can be ignored and only the larger end needs updating.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Sort by start; extend the last merged interval's end with a max when the next one starts at or before it, else start a new interval.
card.limits: The end must be raised with a maximum, because a later interval can lie entirely inside the last one and have the smaller end.

concepts.title: Why answers come modulo 10^9 + 7
concepts.question: Why do problems ask for an answer modulo a number, and how should you compute it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A problem asks for an integer answer mod x because the true answer could be massive, too large to store in a variable. On LeetCode x is usually 10^9 + 7 = 1,000,000,007.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: You could compute the full huge answer and return ans % MOD at the end. That is correct but slow, because arithmetic on numbers with very many digits cannot be ignored. Instead apply the modulo operator at every step and still get the same answer.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Every intermediate value stays below the modulus, so each operation works on a small number and stays cheap.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: the next idea shows with a worked example that the result is the same however early the modulo is applied.

card.rule: When a problem asks for an answer modulo x, reduce modulo x at every step instead of only at the end.
card.limits: The course says modular arithmetic is unlikely in an interview, but it is simple and matters in competitive programming and some LeetCode problems.

concepts.title: Reducing at every step changes nothing
concepts.question: Why does taking the remainder at every step give the same answer as taking it at the end?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Show that applying the modulo operator after every addition or multiplication gives the same final remainder as computing the huge exact value first.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Take the remainder after each operation and carry only the remainder forward. The final answer is the same, no matter how early you stop reducing or how many more numbers you add.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each step works on numbers smaller than the modulus, so no step costs more than a small multiplication.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: a sum or a product has the same remainder whether its inputs are reduced first or not, so reducing after each step amounts to reducing the inputs of the next step.

card.rule: Applying the modulus after every operation gives the same remainder as applying it once at the end.
card.limits: It works for the operations the course shows: addition and multiplication. Our reading: a comparison such as which number is larger is not preserved by the remainder.
card.example: With modulus 9 and the numbers 14, 23, 35, 41: the exact product is 462,070, which leaves remainder 1; the exact sum is 113, which leaves remainder 5. Reducing after each step gives remainders 5, 7, 2, 1 for the product and 5, 1, 0, 5 for the sum, ending at the same values.

concepts.title: Maximum product after k increments
concepts.question: Which element should each increment go to, and where does the modulus come in?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given non-negative integers and k operations that each add 1 to one element, return the largest possible product modulo 10^9 + 7.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Increment the smallest element every time, found with a min heap. If x > y, incrementing x gives xy + y, but incrementing y gives xy + x, which is larger. After k rounds multiply all elements together, taking the remainder after each multiplication.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Our reading: each increment is one heap removal and one insertion, O(log n), and each multiplication works on numbers below the modulus.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: At every step the smaller element is the better one to raise, because the gain from raising it equals the other, larger factor. The product therefore ends as large as possible.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Raise the smallest element k times using a heap, then multiply with a remainder after every multiplication.
card.limits: The greedy choice relies on all numbers being non-negative so that raising the smaller factor always adds the larger one.

concepts.title: Divisibility of every prefix of a digit string
concepts.question: How can you test every prefix of a long digit string for divisibility without building huge numbers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: For a digit string word and a positive integer m, mark each index i with 1 if the number formed by word[0..i] is divisible by m, otherwise 0.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Do not convert each prefix to an integer. Append digits one at a time with curr = curr * 10 + digit, and since only divisibility matters, keep curr reduced: curr = (curr * 10 + digit) % m. A prefix is divisible exactly when curr is 0.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: O(n) time for a string of length n, and O(1) extra space apart from the output.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: The prefix value reduced mod m is what decides divisibility, and the earlier lesson shows that reducing at every step gives the same remainder as reducing the exact value.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.code:
def divisibility_array(word, m):
    div = []
    curr = 0
    for ch in word:
        curr = (curr * 10 + int(ch)) % m
        div.append(1 if curr == 0 else 0)
    return div

card.rule: Append each digit with curr = (curr * 10 + digit) % m, and report 1 when curr is 0.
card.limits: This reports divisibility only. Our reading: the reduced curr is not the real prefix value, so it cannot answer questions about that value's size.

concepts.title: Shortest means lowest weight
concepts.question: What does the shortest path mean when edges carry weights?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the cheapest route between two nodes when every edge carries a weight, such as a toll between two cities.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: In a weighted graph each edge has a value, its weight. The weight of a path is the sum of the weights of its edges, and the shortest path is the one with the lowest total weight. That path can use more edges than another path to the same node.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Evaluating one path costs one addition per edge. Finding the best of many paths needs an algorithm built for weights, which the next ideas supply.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: fewer edges mean a lower total only when every edge costs the same. With different weights one heavy edge can outweigh several light ones.

card.rule: On a weighted graph the shortest path is the one with the lowest sum of edge weights, not the fewest edges.
card.limits: When every edge weight is the same, the lowest weight and the fewest edges agree. The distinction matters only when weights differ.

media.alt: A directed weighted graph of five numbered nodes. Edges: 0 to 1 weight 2, 1 to 2 weight 1, 2 to 4 weight 3, 0 to 4 weight 10, 0 to 3 weight 4, and 3 to 4 weight 15. Three different routes lead from node 0 to node 4, with different numbers of edges and different total weights.

concepts.title: Dijkstra's algorithm in a nutshell
concepts.question: How does Dijkstra's algorithm find the shortest paths from one source to every node?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Find the shortest distance from one source node to every other node in a weighted graph.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Keep a min-heap of nodes, each stored with the weight of the path that reached it, and an array distances of the best weight found so far, large everywhere except 0 at the source. Pop the node with the smallest path weight. For each neighbour compute dist = curr_dist + weight: if dist is less than distances[nei], record it and push the neighbour; otherwise ignore it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each push or pop on the heap costs a logarithmic amount; the exact bound is in a later idea.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: the heap hands over the closest unprocessed node first, and with non-negative weights no longer route to that node can later become shorter.

card.rule: Dijkstra's repeatedly pops the node with the smallest known distance from a min-heap and improves its neighbours' distances.
card.limits: It is for non-negative weights; negative weight cycles are covered in a later idea. It measures weight, so the nodes it pops first are not those with the fewest edges.

concepts.title: Dijkstra's step by step
concepts.question: What does the loop of Dijkstra's do on each pass?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Turn the idea into a loop that fills distances for every node from a source.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Set distances to infinity except the source at 0, and start the heap with (0, source). While the heap is not empty, pop (curr_dist, node). Skip it if curr_dist is greater than distances[node], because a better path was found since it was pushed. Otherwise, for each neighbour compute dist = curr_dist + weight and, if dist < distances[nei], update distances[nei] and push (dist, nei).

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Each node can be pushed more than once, once per improvement, so the loop pops every pushed entry; the exact bound is in a later idea.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: an improvement pushes a fresh entry and leaves the old one in the heap. When the old one is popped its distance exceeds the recorded best, so it is recognised and skipped.

blocks.label: Code

card.rule: Pop the smallest entry, skip it if stale, and push a neighbour only when the new distance is strictly smaller.
card.limits: The graph is given as lists of (neighbour, weight) pairs. The loop assumes there are no negative weight cycles.

concepts.title: Network Delay Time
concepts.question: How does one Dijkstra run answer how long a signal takes to reach every node?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A signal starts at node k of a directed network whose edges [u, v, w] mean it takes time w to go from u to v. Return the time until every node has the signal, or -1 if some node does not get it.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Run Dijkstra's from k to get the shortest time to every node. The last node to receive the signal decides the answer, so return the largest value in distances. If the largest value is still the large starting value, a node is unreachable, so return -1.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: One run of Dijkstra's plus a pass over the n distances to take the maximum.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Each node receives the signal at its shortest travel time from k, because the signal spreads along every route at once. The whole network is done when the slowest node has it.

blocks.label: Trace
blocks.text: Edges 1 to 2 (3), 1 to 3 (10), 2 to 3 (4), 3 to 4 (2), with k = 1: the times are 0, 3, 7 and 9, so the answer is 9. Remove the edge 3 to 4 and node 4 stays at infinity, so the answer is -1.

card.rule: Run Dijkstra's from the start node and return the maximum distance, or -1 if any distance is still infinite.
card.limits: The answer is a maximum of shortest times, not their sum. It is also not the shortest time to reach any one node.

concepts.title: What Dijkstra's costs
concepts.question: What is the time and space cost of Dijkstra's algorithm?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Predict how the running time of Dijkstra's grows with the number of nodes V and edges E.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Each heap operation costs up to O(log V). The course counts O(V) pops and O(E) pushes. Adding these gives a time of O((V + E) * log V). The heap and the distances array together take O(V) space.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: Time O((V + E) * log V) and space O(V), counting only the run of the algorithm.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: a push happens only when a distance improves, and each heap operation costs a logarithm. The course counts O(V) pops and O(E) pushes, which is where the (V + E) comes from.

card.rule: Dijkstra's runs in O((V + E) * log V) time and O(V) space, with the cost of building the graph not included.
card.limits: The time bound depends on how the heap is implemented. The formula is the general form, and a dense graph with E near V squared makes it much larger.

concepts.title: Negative weight cycles break Dijkstra's
concepts.question: Why must Dijkstra's not be used on a graph with a negative weight cycle?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Know when Dijkstra's cannot be trusted: a graph that contains a cycle whose edge weights add up to a negative number.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Use Dijkstra's only on graphs without negative weight cycles. Each trip around such a cycle lowers the weight of the path, so a better path to the cycle's nodes exists after every lap and the algorithm keeps finding improvements.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.text: On such a graph the cost is unbounded, because the loop does not finish.

blocks.label: Why it is correct
blocks.text: Our reading: the loop stops only when no neighbour can be improved. A negative cycle allows an improvement after every lap, so that moment does not arrive.

card.rule: Do not run Dijkstra's on a graph with a negative weight cycle, since every lap lowers the distances and the loop does not stop.
card.limits: Our reading: a cycle whose total weight is exactly zero never improves a distance, because the update needs a strictly smaller value, so it is not the failure case.

media.alt: A directed weighted graph of four nodes. Edges run from 0 to 1 with weight 3, from 1 to 2 with weight minus 500, from 2 back to 0 with weight 2, and from 2 to 3 with weight 5. Nodes 0, 1 and 2 form a cycle whose weights add up to a negative number; node 3 hangs off it.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Reading a problem for its pattern
concepts.question: Which phrases in a problem statement point to a sliding window, a stack, a heap or a breadth-first search?

paragraphs: A statement shows its pattern in two places: what it asks you to return and what the input looks like. The course's guides work as cues. A limit on a contiguous piece plus a request for its best length or count suggests a sliding window. Many subarray-sum queries suggest a prefix sum. A most recent unresolved element that must be handled first suggests a stack.

More cues: for each element, the next greater one, or the maximum of a moving window, suggests a monotonic stack or deque. A maximum or minimum needed again and again from a changing collection suggests a heap. The fewest steps or operations between states suggests breadth-first search. A request for all of something, on a small input, suggests backtracking.

A cue is a hypothesis, not a proof. Say the cue aloud, sketch the approach it implies and test it on a small example before coding. The course advises thinking out loud and agreeing the rough steps with the interviewer first.
card.example: Statement: given positive daily sales and a budget b, find the longest run of consecutive days totalling at most b. The cues are a constraint on a contiguous piece (total at most b) and a request for its longest length. Hypothesis: a sliding window that grows on the right and shrinks on the left while the total exceeds b.
card.rule: Read what the statement asks for and what the input looks like, name the cue, and test the pattern it suggests on a small example before coding.
card.limits: The course calls its cues guidelines. A statement can show a cue and still need another tool, and a problem can need a window without showing any cue.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Choosing a structure by the operation you repeat
concepts.question: Which operation does my loop repeat most, and which structure makes that operation cheap?

paragraphs: Before choosing a structure, name the operation the loop repeats. Reading by index is cheap in an array. Asking whether a value is present, or fetching a count for it, is O(1) in a hash set or hash map, against O(n) for a scan of an array or list. Use a set when presence is enough and a map when each key carries a value.

Other operations: changing a position you already hold is O(1) in a linked list, but reaching a position by number costs O(n). Taking the newest or the oldest pending item suits a stack or a queue, and both ends suit a deque. A repeated minimum or maximum suits a heap: O(log n) to add or remove, O(1) to peek.

Then multiply by the number of repeats. A membership test against a 20,000-item list can take 20,000 comparisons, so 20,000 tests take up to 400,000,000 steps. The same tests on a set take about 20,000 steps.
card.rule: Name the operation the loop repeats most, then choose the structure where that operation costs O(1) or O(log n).
card.limits: A hash map's O(1) is constant relative to its size only: hashing a long string key still takes time in the key's length. Stack and queue costs depend on how they are implemented.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Choosing by which waiting item comes next
concepts.question: When items wait to be processed, which one comes next, and what structure hands it over?

paragraphs: Many algorithms hold items that are waiting, and the rule for which one comes next picks the structure. The newest unresolved item first is a stack, as in matching brackets. The oldest first is a queue, which the course meets mostly in breadth-first search. Adding and removing at both ends calls for a deque.

The best item by some key first calls for a heap: peeking at the extreme is O(1) and each change is O(log n), while scanning costs O(n) every time. A min heap capped at size k leaves the k best items. A monotonic stack or deque stays sorted by dropping items that cannot be the answer, which suits next-greater and window-maximum questions.
Stack and queue operations are O(1) with a good implementation, heap operations are O(log n), and a monotonic structure costs O(n) in total, because each element enters and leaves once.
card.example: Undo in an editor reverses the latest edit first, so it needs a stack. A printer that serves jobs in the order they were submitted needs a queue.
card.rule: Ask which waiting item must come next: the newest means a stack, the oldest a queue, and the best by a key a heap.
card.limits: The course says the last-in pattern can be hard to see, and that queues mostly appear in breadth-first search. A heap earns its cost for repeated extremes; one minimum of a fixed list needs only one pass.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: What sorted order and thresholds unlock
concepts.question: What does sorted order, or a yes-or-no threshold, let me do that unordered data does not?

paragraphs: Order is information. In a sorted array, one comparison with the middle element speaks for a whole half, so binary search takes O(log n). A sorted array also lets two pointers discard one end after each sum, so a pair search takes O(n).

Order can also be produced or found. An inorder walk of a binary search tree returns its values sorted, and sorting intervals by start time puts every conflict between neighbours. Sorting costs O(n log n), so it pays when it replaces more work: checking every pair of 3,000 meetings is about 4.5 million checks, and sorting then scanning about 35,000 steps.

A threshold gives the same power without an array. If a check function says yes for every answer on one side of a cutoff and no on the other, the candidate answers behave like a sorted list, and binary search over the range finds the cutoff.
card.rule: When order or a threshold lets one comparison rule out many candidates, sort first or define the check, then discard half or one end at each step.
card.limits: Our reading: sorting costs O(n log n) and loses the original order, so it does not help one query on small data or a task that needs positions. A threshold needs results that change only once along the range.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Choosing among the array patterns
concepts.question: For an array or string problem, how do I choose between two pointers, a window, prefix sums and a counts map?

paragraphs: Each sequence pattern needs a property from the problem. Two pointers need order or two inputs to walk: a sorted array and a target pair, or two sorted arrays to merge. A sliding window needs a constraint that stays true when a valid window shrinks, such as a sum at most k over positive numbers. Both run in O(n).

Prefix sums suit many range-sum queries: one O(n) build, then O(1) per query. An exact constraint, such as a sum equal to k, breaks the window, because shrinking can ruin a valid window. Keep a running prefix sum and a hash map counting earlier prefixes, and add counts[curr - k] at each index: O(n) time and space.

A length stated in the problem means a fixed window: add one element and remove one at each step. Start the counts map with the empty prefix, a sum of 0 seen once, so runs that begin at index 0 are counted.
card.rule: Match the property the problem offers: sorted order for pointers, a shrink-safe constraint for a window, many range queries for prefix sums, an exact count for prefix sums with a counts map.
card.limits: These are guidelines, and some problems fit more than one pattern. A window over distinct values also needs a hash map.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Choosing a traversal
concepts.question: For a tree or graph question, when do I use DFS, BFS or Dijkstra's algorithm?

paragraphs: Start by asking what the answer depends on. If it needs every node visited, or a value built from each subtree such as a depth or a path sum, use DFS: it is shorter to write, especially with recursion. Counting connected components is DFS from each node not yet seen. Time is O(n times k) on a tree and O(n times k plus e) on a graph.

If the answer depends on levels or distance, use BFS. Its queue visits nodes in order of distance from the start, so the first time it reaches the target the path is shortest, while a DFS may find a longer path first. It also fits puzzles whose states are nodes and whose moves are edges, when the question asks for the fewest operations.

If edges carry different weights and the question asks for the lowest total weight, BFS counts edges and measures the wrong thing. Use Dijkstra's algorithm, which repeatedly pops the node with the smallest known distance from a min heap. It needs non-negative weights.
card.rule: Use DFS for visits and subtree answers, BFS for levels and fewest steps, and Dijkstra's algorithm for the lowest total weight.
card.limits: The course's flowchart is general and leaves Dijkstra's out. DFS and BFS visit the same nodes, so the choice affects the order of visits, not which nodes are visited.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Choosing among greedy, DP, backtracking and binary search
concepts.question: When a problem asks for a best value or for all solutions, which of the four approaches fits?

paragraphs: Four approaches answer questions about a best value or about all solutions. Backtracking lists all of something, or searches when no shortcut exists, on a small input (n around 15 or less), because the cost is exponential, such as 2 to the n or n factorial.

For one best value, or a count of ways, ask whether choices interact. If taking one option blocks later ones, a locally best choice can lose, so use DP: define a state, a recurrence and base cases, and expect time of states times work per state. If a rule that takes the extreme option, often after an O(n log n) sort, can be shown safe, greedy is enough.

If the question asks for the largest or smallest value for which a task is possible, and one value can be checked in O(n), binary search the answers when possible and impossible values form two zones. Greedy code is short; the hard part is arguing that its rule is safe.
card.example: Coins 1, 5, 6 and 9, amount 11. Taking the largest coin first gives 9 + 1 + 1, three coins. Taking 5 and 6 gives two coins. Taking the 9 blocked the better pair, so the interacting choices point to DP.
card.rule: Backtrack to list everything on a small input, use DP when choices interact, use greedy when a safe extreme can be argued, and binary search the answer when a check splits the answers into two zones.
card.limits: The wording cues are guidelines, and a problem can fit several approaches. Our reading: small limits point to backtracking but do not prove it, and a greedy rule that matches samples can still be wrong.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Reading input limits for the intended cost
concepts.question: How do the limits on input size narrow down which approach a problem intends?

paragraphs: The limits on n are hints about the intended cost, so read them before choosing. Up to about 10 allows factorial or high-base exponential work, and 10 to 20 allows about 2 to the n; both point to backtracking or recursion. Up to 100 allows n cubed, and up to 1,000 allows n squared, so nested loops can be intended.

Above 1,000, up to 100,000, the slowest acceptable common cost is n log n, and O(n) is the usual goal. Nested loops are out, so replace the inner loop with a hash map, two pointers or a window, a monotonic stack, binary search or a heap. Around 10^6, expect O(n), probably with a hash map. At 10^9 and above, expect O(log n) or O(1).

Turn a limit into a step count to test an idea. At n = 20, 2 to the n is 1,048,576 steps but 3 to the n is about 3.5 billion. At n = 100,000, n squared is 10 billion steps and n log n is about 1.7 million.
card.rule: Substitute the stated limit into the cost of each candidate idea and discard the ideas that grow too large at that limit.
card.limits: The ranges are tendencies, and interview problems often state no limits, so ask. Our reading: a limit shows the intended cost class but cannot prove that a particular idea is correct.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Improving a brute-force idea
concepts.question: Given a slow brute-force idea, how do I find the step to speed up and the structure that fixes it?

paragraphs: A brute-force idea is a fine start if you say it is brute force. The course suggests implementing it first, then analysing each part for slow steps and speeding those up, with the interviewer in the discussion. Cost the idea first: a loop over all pairs of n items costs about n squared.

Look for the repeated work inside the slow step and match it to a tool. Re-checking membership by scanning: a hash set or map. Re-adding a range for every query: a prefix sum. Re-finding the largest remaining item: a heap. Re-scanning a sorted list for a value: binary search. Re-solving a recursive case with the same arguments: memoization. Scanning ahead for the next greater item: a monotonic stack.
Then state the new cost and check it against the input limit.
card.example: Two Sum: for each number, an inner loop looks for target minus that number, so the cost is n squared. The repeated work is that membership scan. A hash map answers it in O(1), so the whole pass is O(n).
card.rule: Say the brute force and its cost, find the step that repeats work, and swap in the structure that makes that step cheap.
card.limits: A small limit can make the brute force the intended answer, as with n up to 100. Not every slow step has a ready tool, and some problems need a different algorithm.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Combining two patterns in one solution
concepts.question: When one problem needs two patterns, which job does each pattern do?

paragraphs: Harder problems often pair a pattern that frames the loop with a structure that answers one question inside it. A window over distinct characters pairs the window with a counts map. Subarrays with an exact sum pair a running prefix sum with a counts map. A window maximum pairs the window with a monotonic deque. Top k frequent pairs a counts map with a min heap capped at k.

Searches pair too. The least effort across a height grid binary searches the effort, with a graph search as the check. Picking the best affordable project sorts by capital and keeps a max heap of the profits unlocked so far. A shortest path with limited wall breaks runs BFS over states made of a cell and the breaks left.

To split a problem, ask what the outer loop or search does, and what question it asks at every step. Pick the structure for that inner question. Costs combine: a heap capped at k gives O(n log k), and the log k rounds of a binary search multiply the cost of each check.
card.example: Longest substring with at most k distinct characters: the outer job is sliding a window, and the inner question is how many distinct characters it holds now. A counts map answers that in O(1), so the whole solution is O(n).
card.rule: Name the job of each part, the outer pattern and the structure that answers its inner question, then combine their costs.
card.limits: Our reading: not every problem splits cleanly into two parts, and a combined solution is only as fast as its slowest part. The pairs above are the course's examples, not a complete list.

questions.q: A function finds an array's largest value, starting its running maximum at 0. Which array makes it return a number not in the array?
optionExplain: Every value beats 0 in turn and the function returns 8, a correct answer.
A one-element array of a positive number is handled correctly: 4 beats 0.
Right: no negative value beats 0, so the function returns 0, which the array does not contain.
Equal values do not confuse the comparison: the result is 10, which is in the array.
questions.explain: With a start value of 0, only an array with no value above 0 can leave the result at 0. The card next shows why this matters.
questions.rule: A starting value outside the data can leak into the answer.

questions.q: An algorithm that gives the same output every time it is run on the same input is called ____.
questions.explain: A deterministic algorithm has no randomness: the same input always produces the same output. LeetCode expects this of every solution.
questions.rule: Same input, same output: deterministic.

questions.q: A leaderboard routine ranks players by score but breaks ties by flipping a coin. Which LeetCode requirement does it break?
options: It is not correct, because ties are rare and the coin is usually fair
It is not deterministic: the same scores can give different rankings
It is too slow, because each coin flip takes extra time
It uses invalid input, because a tie is not a legal score list
optionExplain: Correctness is about the output being right for valid inputs; the failure here is that the output changes between runs.
Right: the same input can give different outputs from run to run.
Speed is a separate matter (complexity); the issue here is repeatability.
Ties are allowed inputs; the routine mishandles them by adding randomness.
questions.explain: A coin flip makes two runs on identical scores disagree, so the routine is not deterministic.
questions.rule: Randomness in the steps breaks determinism.

questions.q: With the maximum started at nums[0] instead of 0, the function returns ____ for [-3, -1, -2].
questions.explain: The maximum starts at -3. Then -1 is larger, so it becomes the maximum; -2 is not larger. The result is -1, an element of the array.
questions.rule: Start from an element of the input and the answer always comes from the input.

questions.q: True or false: starting the running maximum at the first element, not at 0, keeps the recipe correct if negative numbers become valid input.
questions.explain: The maximum then always comes from the array itself, so negative-only arrays no longer return a value that is absent from them.
questions.rule: Seed the maximum from the data, not from a guess.
questions.teaches: Starting from the first element makes the answer always come from the array itself, which handles negative numbers.

questions.q: A problem states that nums is a non-empty array of integers from 1 to 100. Which input is outside what a correct solution must handle?
options: An empty array
A single element, 100
An array with repeated values, such as 7, 7, 7
An array holding only 1s
optionExplain: Right: the statement requires at least one element, so an empty array is not a valid input.
One element is allowed; non-empty means at least one.
Repeats are not excluded by the statement, so they are valid.
1 is inside the stated range, so the array is valid.
questions.explain: Correctness is required only for the inputs the problem allows. An input that breaks a stated requirement is invalid, so the algorithm need not handle it.
questions.rule: Correct for valid inputs; invalid inputs are outside the contract.
questions.teaches: An input that breaks a stated requirement, such as negatives where only positives were promised, is invalid, so correctness is judged only over the valid inputs.

questions.q: Which pair of resources does big O notation describe for an algorithm?
