options: Lines of code and number of variables used in the program
Running time and memory use, each relative to input size
Compile time and size of the source file on disk
Best score and worst score on the test cases it passes
optionExplain: These measure how the code is written, not how its cost grows with the input.
Right: these are time complexity and space complexity.
These belong to building the program, not to how the algorithm scales.
Test scores are results of runs, not a growth description.
questions.explain: Complexity has a time part and a space part. The card next defines both.
questions.rule: Time and space, relative to input size.

questions.q: The amount of memory an algorithm uses relative to the input size is its ____ complexity.
questions.explain: Space complexity asks how much more memory the algorithm needs as the input grows; time complexity asks the same about running time.
questions.rule: Space is memory; time is running time.

questions.q: A route planner takes twice as long when given twice as many stops, while its memory use stays the same. Which description fits?
options: Its space complexity grows with the number of stops, but its time complexity does not
Both complexities grow, since time and memory cannot be told apart
Its time complexity grows with the number of stops, but its space complexity does not
Neither complexity grows, since the machine running it stays fixed
optionExplain: This swaps the two: the planner's running time is what doubles.
They are separate measures, and in this case only one grows.
Right: time grows with the input here and memory does not.
Complexity is about the algorithm relative to input size, not the fixed machine.
questions.explain: Time complexity tracks running time against input size and space complexity tracks memory against input size; here only the first one grows.
questions.rule: Check time and memory separately.

questions.q: Sort each question by the complexity it asks about.

items.t: Does the loop take longer when the array holds 10 million items?
Does the result list get larger when the array holds 10 million items?
How many more steps are needed when the input doubles?
How much more memory is needed when the input doubles?
Does a second pass over the data add running time?
Does a second copy of the data add stored memory?

questions.explain: Questions about steps and waiting are time questions; questions about stored data are space questions.
questions.rule: Steps are time; stored data is space.

questions.q: Besides answering an interviewer, what does the book say analysing an algorithm's complexity lets you do?
options: Guarantee that the algorithm is deterministic
Predict the exact seconds a run takes on your machine
Skip testing on valid inputs
Work out which parts of the algorithm can be improved
optionExplain: Determinism is a separate requirement that complexity analysis does not check.
Complexity describes growth, not a precise timing.
Complexity does not replace checking correctness.
Right: the book says analysis also enables you to find parts that can be improved.
questions.explain: The book says interviewers ask for complexity to check you understand your algorithm, and that analysis also shows what could be improved.
questions.rule: Complexity analysis shows where an algorithm can improve.
questions.teaches: Interviewers almost always ask for complexity to check that you understand your algorithm, and analysing it also shows which parts could be improved.

questions.q: A contacts app is slow on large lists but uses little memory. According to the book, which complexity do people typically look at first?
options: Time complexity
Space complexity
Neither, because the two are the same measure
Whichever is smaller, because small costs matter most
optionExplain: Right: the book says people typically care about time complexity more than space complexity.
Memory matters, but the book says it usually gets less attention than time.
They are two parts of computational complexity and are measured separately.
The book gives no such rule; the typical focus is time.
questions.explain: According to the book, people usually care about time complexity more, though knowing both is important.
questions.rule: Time usually first, but know both.
questions.teaches: People typically care more about time complexity than about space complexity, though both are important to know.

questions.q: A program loops over a list of orders. What would you let the variable n stand for in its complexity?
options: The number of seconds one order takes to print
The number of lines in the program
The name of the list variable
The number of orders in the list
optionExplain: That is a cost per step, not a value that describes the input.
The program text does not change between inputs.
A name does not change how much work the loop does.
Right: the length of the list changes between inputs and sets how many loop steps run.
questions.explain: A good variable describes something about the input that changes the work. The card next gives the full rule.
questions.rule: Variables describe the input.

questions.q: True or false: the letter n is required in a complexity function.
questions.explain: The book says the letter is arbitrary and even jokes that a banana emoji would do; n is only the accepted convention.
questions.rule: The programmer decides which variables mean what.

questions.q: An app resizes every photo in an album. Which value is the best choice of variable for its time complexity?
options: The number of characters in the album title
The number of photos in the album
A fixed value such as 100, to keep the function simple
The index of the photo being resized right now
optionExplain: It changes between inputs, but it does not change how much resizing is done.
Right: it changes between albums and sets how many resize steps run.
A variable must change between inputs; a fixed number would hide the growth.
The index changes during the run but is not a property of the input as a whole.
questions.explain: The photo count both varies from input to input and drives the amount of work.
questions.rule: Pick the input quantity that drives the work.

questions.q: A student marks the answer O(k) wrong, where k is the length of nums, because the letter n is mandatory. What is the flaw?
options: There is no flaw, because only n has a defined meaning in big O
The flaw is that k can only stand for constants, never for lengths
Any letter works once its meaning is stated, so O(k) is fine
O(k) is right, but only after renaming k to n in the final answer
optionExplain: No letter has a built-in meaning; each analysis defines its own.
Nothing restricts k; it can stand for any input value you define.
Right: any symbol works once its meaning is stated.
Renaming is never needed; the statement of what k means is what counts.
questions.explain: n is a convention shared by programmers, not a rule of the notation.
questions.rule: Define your letters; the notation does not fix them.

questions.q: In theory larger integers make addition slower. A LeetCode analysis of an integer array ignores this and uses ____ variable in total.
questions.explain: In theory bigger integers take longer to add or print, but the difference is tiny in practice, so LeetCode analyses treat all integers the same and use only n, the length.
questions.rule: For an integer array, the length n alone is the variable.
questions.teaches: LeetCode analyses ignore the extra time larger integers take and treat all integers alike, so an array of integers needs only its length n.

questions.q: A function loops once over n students and once over m courses. How many variables does its complexity involve?
options: One, because a second list can reuse n
Two, one for each list's length
One, the longer of the two lengths
Three, adding one for the total of students and courses
optionExplain: The two lists can differ in length, so one letter would misdescribe the work.
Right: each list has its own size, so n and m both appear.
The work depends on both lengths, not on the longer one alone.
The total is made from n and m, so it needs no variable of its own.
questions.explain: When an input has two independent sizes, each gets its own variable. The book's example is n for the length of one array and m for the other.
questions.rule: Independent sizes get separate variables.
questions.teaches: When the input has two independent sizes, such as two arrays, each size gets its own variable: n for one array's length and m for the other's.

questions.q: A recipe sets one variable, loops over n elements doing one step each, then outputs the variable. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n)
O(2n)
optionExplain: Right: the loop dominates, and the two fixed steps do not change the growth.
It counts the fixed steps, but time complexity reports growth, not an exact count.
The loop runs once per element, so the work grows with n.
Nothing in the recipe runs twice per element.
questions.explain: The work that depends on the input is the loop. The card next explains why the other steps drop out.
questions.rule: Only input-driven work sets the growth.

questions.q: A loop that touches each of n elements once has a time complexity of O(____).
questions.explain: One touch per element means about n steps, so the complexity is O(n).
questions.rule: One pass over n items is O(n).

questions.q: A script runs 3 setup steps, 1 step per item for n = 1,000 items, then 2 output steps. What is the count and complexity?
options: 1,005 steps, which is O(1,005)
1,005 steps, which is O(n)
1,000 steps, which is O(1,000)
5 steps, which is O(1) because setup and output are all that is fixed
optionExplain: The count is correct, but the complexity is stated in terms of n, not the total.
Right: 3 + 1,000 + 2 = 1,005 steps, and the growth is linear in n.
The fixed steps are still operations, and the complexity uses n, not the number 1,000.
The loop is the part that depends on the input and it dominates.
questions.explain: 3 + 1000 + 2 = 1005. Only the 1,000 loop steps depend on n, so the complexity is O(n).
questions.rule: Count exactly if you like; report the growth.

questions.q: True or false: the two fixed steps, setting maxNum and outputting it, make the recipe O(n + 2) rather than O(n).
questions.explain: The fixed steps add the same amount whatever nums is. Time complexity describes how the operations change as the input changes, which leaves O(n).
questions.rule: A fixed addition does not change the growth.

questions.q: An app takes 1 step to load a title, 1 per song for 5,000,000,000 songs, and 1 for a summary: ____ steps in all.
questions.explain: 1 + 5,000,000,000 + 1 = 5,000,000,002. The two fixed steps are still real, which is why the book notes the exact count is 10,000,000,002 for 10,000,000,000 elements, but they do not alter the O(n) growth.
questions.rule: Fixed steps add a constant; the loop sets the growth.
questions.teaches: Even at ten billion elements the fixed steps add only a couple of operations to the count (10,000,000,002 steps), a negligible part that the growth description leaves out.

questions.q: Algorithm B takes 5 times as many steps as algorithm A at every input size. How do their time complexities compare?
options: They are the same, since a factor of 5 does not change the growth
B is a worse complexity class, because 5 is greater than 1
They cannot be compared until both are timed on a real machine
A is a worse class, because it has fewer steps to spread its work over
optionExplain: Right: both grow in step with the input, so they share a complexity.
A bigger multiplier makes B slower, but not a different growth rate.
Complexity compares growth and needs no stopwatch.
Fewer steps is not worse; and the multiplier is not a growth rate.
questions.explain: A constant multiplier scales every input size equally, so growth is unchanged. The card next gives the rule.
questions.rule: A constant factor is not a different growth.

questions.q: Simplified, O(500n) is O(____).
questions.explain: The constant 500 is ignored, leaving O(n).
questions.rule: Drop the constant multiplier.

questions.q: A scan makes 3 passes over n records; another makes 1 pass over n records. How do their big O classes compare?
options: The first is O(3n), which counts as a different class from O(n)
The first is O(n³) because it makes three separate passes
Both are O(n), since 3n and n differ only by a constant factor
The first is O(1) because 3 is a constant number
optionExplain: O(3n) simplifies to O(n), so there is no separate class.
Three passes multiply the work by 3; they do not raise n to the third power.
Right: the factor 3 is dropped.
The 3 multiplies n; the n stays, so the growth is still linear.
questions.explain: Three passes cost about 3n steps and one pass costs about n; both double when n doubles, so both are O(n).
questions.rule: k passes over n items is still O(n) for fixed k.

questions.q: A student says B uses 5n steps and A uses n, so B is O(5n), a worse class than A. Which step is wrong?
options: Counting B's steps as 5n in the first place
Writing the class using the variable n
Comparing two algorithms that solve the same problem
Treating the factor 5 as a new growth rate
optionExplain: B's step count can be 5n; the mistake is in what to report.
Using n is correct; the class is O(n) for both.
Comparing is fine; the error is keeping the constant.
Right: both grow linearly, so the factor is dropped.
questions.explain: Complexity is about growth. Both algorithms scale linearly, so the student should report O(n) for both.
questions.rule: Report growth, not the multiplier.

questions.q: Which of these simplify to O(n)? Select all that apply.
options: 7n
n + n
n · n
n² / 2
optionExplain: Right: the constant 7 is dropped.
Right: this is 2n, which simplifies to O(n).
This is n squared; the second n is a variable, not a constant.
Right: the constant 20 is dropped.
Halving is a constant factor, but it leaves n², so this is O(n²).
questions.explain: A constant multiplier goes away, but a multiplier that is itself a variable stays and changes the growth.
questions.rule: Only constants are dropped, not other variables.

questions.q: A batch job processes one record in every 100 of n records. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n), since n / 100 is n times a constant
O(n / 100), a smaller class than O(n)
O(1), since 100 is a constant
O(100n), since each kept record costs 100 steps
optionExplain: Right: dividing by a constant is dropped in the same way as multiplying by a constant.
The class does not depend on the size of the constant divisor.
Only n / 100 steps happen, and that still grows with n.
There is no factor of 100 in the work, and any such factor would be dropped anyway.
questions.explain: Dividing by a constant is a constant factor too, so O(n / 100) = O(n). The book gives O(n / 500) = O(n) as an example.
questions.rule: Constant divisors vanish too.
questions.teaches: Dividing by a constant is dropped in the same way as multiplying by one: O(n / 500) = O(n).

questions.q: An algorithm takes n² + 3n + 40 operations. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n²)
O(n)
optionExplain: This keeps terms that are tiny beside n² for large n.
Right: n² grows fastest, so the smaller terms drop out.
The n² term outgrows 3n, so n alone understates the growth.
40 is a constant that stays the same while the other terms grow.
questions.explain: The fastest-growing term decides the class. The card next states the rule.
questions.rule: The largest term wins.

questions.q: In n + 500 operations, the term that stops mattering as n tends to infinity is ____.
questions.explain: The 500 stays fixed while n grows, so beside n it becomes negligible.
questions.rule: Fixed amounts vanish next to growth.

questions.q: A leaderboard job costs n² + 20n + 300 steps. What is its time complexity?
options: O(20n), because 20 is the biggest coefficient
O(n² + n), keeping the second-largest term for safety
O(300), because 300 is the largest term at n = 10
O(n²)
optionExplain: The coefficient is not the growth; n² beats 20n once n is large.
Only the most powerful term is kept.
At n = 10 the terms are 100, 200 and 300, but big O looks at n tending to infinity.
Right: the n² term outgrows 20n and 300.
questions.explain: Big O looks at the variable tending to infinity, where n² dwarfs 20n and 300.
questions.rule: Judge at infinity, not at one small n.

questions.q: True or false: n + 500 is O(n) only when n is larger than 500, so for n = 5 the claim is false.
questions.explain: Big O describes behaviour as n tends to infinity. A small n such as 5 does not test the claim, even though the 500 matters a lot there.
questions.rule: Big O is a statement about growth, not about small inputs.

questions.q: An algorithm takes n + 500 steps. At n = 1,000,000, about what share of the steps does the 500 supply?
options: About 50%
About 5%
About 0.05%
About 99%
optionExplain: That would need the 500 to be about as large as n.
5% would need n to be about 10,000, not 1,000,000.
That is the share at n = 5, where the 500 dominates.
questions.explain: 500 / 1,000,500 = 0.05%. At n = 5 the share is 99%, which is why small inputs mislead.
questions.rule: The dropped term fades as n grows.

questions.q: A batch job takes n² − 500n + 90 operations. What does the book's rule give for its time complexity?
options: O(n²), since subtracted terms are dropped too
O(n² − 500n), because a subtracted term cannot be ignored
O(n), since the 500n term is the largest coefficient
O(90), since the constant is all that stays fixed
optionExplain: Right: the rule covers both addition and subtraction.
The rule treats subtraction the same as addition: only the most powerful term stays.
Coefficients do not set the growth; n² eventually exceeds 500n.
The constant stays fixed while n² grows, so it is the term that vanishes.
questions.explain: For large n, n² dominates 500n and 90, so the result is O(n²).
questions.rule: Add or subtract: keep the strongest term.
questions.teaches: The dominant-term rule applies to subtraction as well as addition between terms of the same variable, so O(n² − 500n + 90) = O(n²).

questions.q: An algorithm performs exactly 5,000,000 steps whatever input it gets. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n)
It has no complexity, since it is not tied to the input
optionExplain: A fixed number is a constant, and constants simplify to 1.
There is no input-sized loop, so the work does not grow with n.
Ignoring the input is exactly what constant time means.
Right: the amount of work does not depend on the input.
questions.explain: Work independent of the input is constant time, however large the constant. The card next gives the label.
questions.rule: Fixed work is O(1).

questions.q: True or false: O(1) means the algorithm uses the same amount of resources whatever the input.
questions.explain: That is the definition of constant time (or constant space): the cost is independent of the input.
questions.rule: O(1) is independent of the input.

questions.q: Reading the first item of a list costs one step whether the list holds 10 or 10 million items, so the time is O(____).
questions.explain: The cost does not change with list length, so it is constant time, O(1).
questions.rule: Independent of length: O(1).

questions.q: A reviewer says a routine cannot be O(1) because it takes a slow ten seconds. What is the flaw?
options: Ten seconds is short enough to be allowed as O(1)
O(1) means time independent of input size, however long it is
O(1) refers only to space and not to running time
O(1) is reserved for routines that take exactly one step
optionExplain: Duration is not what the label measures.
Right: O(1) says nothing about the size of the constant.
The label is used for both time and space.
One refers to a constant, not to a single operation.
questions.explain: Constant time means independence of the input. A fixed ten seconds is O(1) even though it is slow.
questions.rule: O(1) is not a speed claim.

questions.q: A routine keeps one running total while scanning n numbers, and stores nothing else. What is its space complexity?
options: O(1), as the memory used does not grow
O(n), because it reads n numbers
O(log n), because totals shrink the search range
It has none, since it allocates nothing at all
optionExplain: Right: a fixed number of variables is constant space.
Reading the input does not count; only the memory the routine allocates does.
Nothing is being halved; one variable is reused.
One variable is still memory, but a constant amount of it.
questions.explain: A few variables of fixed size are constant space, however many numbers are scanned.
questions.rule: Fixed memory is O(1) space.
questions.teaches: Constant space means the memory used stays the same whatever the input size, as with a few variables kept while scanning.

questions.q: A search may find its target at the first position or the last. Which case should represent its complexity if only one is stated?
options: The worst case
The best case, because it shows the algorithm at its fastest
The average case, because it avoids both extremes
The first case tested, because it is easiest to measure
optionExplain: Right: it is the most correct single choice.
That is the one case the book says never to pick.
Averages are worth discussing, but the worst case is the more correct one.
Ease of measuring is not a criterion.
questions.explain: The best case is the one to avoid. The card next gives the book's advice.
questions.rule: Worst case when you must choose.

questions.q: Put the cases in order from least to most work for an algorithm whose cases differ.
questions.explain: The best case is the luckiest input and costs least; the worst case is the unluckiest and costs most; the average lies between.
questions.rule: Best, then average, then worst.

questions.q: A name search scans from the top: 1 check if the target is first, n if last. Which complexity should you state?
options: O(1), taken from the best case, since the first name can match
O(n), taken from the worst case
O(n / 2), taken from the average case and kept exact
O(log n), halfway between best and worst
optionExplain: The book says never to choose the best case.
Right: the worst case needs n checks.
Even the average case is a constant times n, and constants are dropped.
Cases are not averaged on a log scale; this search is linear.
questions.explain: The search takes up to n checks, so O(n) is the worst case and the one to report.
questions.rule: State the worst case.

questions.q: A scan checks names one by one in a book of 8,000. In the worst case it checks ____ names.
questions.explain: The worst case is that the target is last or absent, so every one of the 8,000 names is checked. The best case needs only 1.
questions.rule: Worst case: check everything.

questions.q: True or false: stating only the best case is the most correct way to give an algorithm's complexity.
questions.explain: The book says never to choose the best case when you must pick one; the worst case is the most correct.
questions.rule: Never the best case alone.

questions.q: Finding the largest number loops over all n elements, whatever the values. How do its three cases compare?
options: Best O(1), average O(n), worst O(n)
Best O(1) and worst O(n), since values can be large
All three are O(n), so the choice does not matter
Only the worst case is defined for loops
optionExplain: The loop never stops early, so even the best case visits every element.
Value size does not shorten or lengthen the loop.
Right: every input costs the same loop.
All three cases are defined; here they happen to coincide.
questions.explain: In most algorithms the three cases are equal, as in this loop. The choice matters only for algorithms whose cases differ.
questions.rule: Equal cases make the choice moot.
questions.teaches: In most algorithms the best, average and worst cases are equal, as in the largest-number loop; only some algorithms differ between them.

questions.q: A loop over n items contains a second loop over the same n items that prints a product each time. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n + n)
O(n²)
O(n)
O(log n)
optionExplain: Adding would fit two loops one after the other, not one inside the other.
Right: n inner steps for each of n outer iterations.
A single pass is O(n), but here a full pass is repeated for every item.
Nothing is being halved; every item is visited at every level.
questions.explain: An inner pass over n items repeats n times. The card next gives the multiplication rule.
questions.rule: Nested means multiply.

questions.q: A loop over n items whose body costs O(1) has a time complexity of O(____).
questions.explain: n iterations times a constant cost per iteration is O(n).
questions.rule: Iterations times cost per iteration.

questions.q: Two nested loops compare every student's score with every student's score among 2,000 students. How many comparisons are made?
optionExplain: This adds the loop sizes instead of multiplying them.
That counts one pass, ignoring the repeat for each outer iteration.
That multiplies one extra factor of 2 that nothing in the loops supplies.
questions.explain: The outer loop runs 2,000 times and the inner loop runs 2,000 times for each, so 2,000 · 2,000 = 4,000,000.
questions.rule: Count outer times inner.

questions.q: Two nested loops over the same input run 4,000,000 steps for n = 2,000. For n = 4,000 the steps are multiplied by ____.
questions.explain: Doubling n doubles both loops, so the product of 4,000 · 4,000 = 16,000,000 is 4 times 4,000,000. That is the quadratic growth of O(n²).
questions.rule: Double n, quadruple the steps.

questions.q: True or false: an outer loop over n items containing an inner loop that runs exactly 500,000 times makes the total O(n²).
questions.explain: The inner count is a fixed constant, so each outer iteration costs O(500,000) = O(1) and the total is O(n).
questions.rule: A fixed inner count is a constant factor.

questions.q: Script A prints once for each of n items. Script B prints 500,000 times for each of the n items. Which statement is correct?
options: Both are O(n), but B is far slower in practice
A is O(n) and B is O(500,000n), a different and worse class
B is O(n²) because it contains a loop inside a loop
Both run equally fast, because same complexity means same speed
optionExplain: Right: same class, very different real speed.
The constant 500,000 is dropped, so B is also O(n).
The inner loop runs a fixed number of times, so it multiplies by a constant, not by n.
Same class does not mean same running time; B does far more work.
questions.explain: The book says it is correct that both are O(n), but it is important to be able to discuss practicality as well as theory.
questions.rule: Same class does not mean same speed.
questions.teaches: Two algorithms with the same time complexity can differ greatly in real speed, so be able to discuss both practicality and theory.

questions.q: One loop runs over n items, and then a second loop runs over m items. What is the time complexity?
options: O(n + m)
O(n ⋅ m)
O(n)
O(n²)
optionExplain: Right: costs of loops in a row add.
That would fit one loop inside the other, not one after the other.
The second loop also takes time, and m may be larger than n.
Nothing multiplies n by itself here.
questions.explain: Loops in a row add; loops inside one another multiply. The card next states the rule.
questions.rule: In a row: add.

questions.q: True or false: loops that run one after another multiply their costs.
questions.explain: Sequential loops add their costs. Multiplying is for a loop nested inside another loop.
questions.rule: Add in sequence; multiply when nested.

questions.q: A script prints all n student names, then all m course names. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n + m)
O(n ⋅ m)
O(n² + m)
O(max(n, m)²)
optionExplain: Right: one pass over each list, added.
Printing the lists one after the other is not a pair-by-pair comparison.
Nothing squares n; each student is printed once.
No pairs are formed, so nothing is squared.
questions.explain: A pass over n names and a pass over m courses add up to n + m steps.
questions.rule: Independent passes add.

questions.q: A script loops over 100 items twice and then over 40 other items once, each step printing once. It prints ____ times in total.
questions.explain: 100 + 100 + 40 = 240 prints. Written as a class, this is O(n + m) because the constant 2 is dropped.
questions.rule: Add the passes.

questions.q: Sort each description by how the costs combine.

items.t: A pass over arr, then a pass over arr2
For each student, a loop over every course
Print all names, then print all scores
Inside a loop over rows, a loop over columns
Read the whole file, then write the whole file
For every item, one comparison with every other item

questions.explain: Steps that run one after another add; steps repeated for each iteration of another loop multiply.
questions.rule: After: add. Inside: multiply.

questions.q: A script prints every item in a catalogue of n items twice, then every one of m coupons once. What is its time complexity?
options: O(2n + m), because both passes over the catalogue must be counted
O(n ⋅ m), because the repeated pass makes the loops depend on each other
O(n + m), because the 2n is simplified by dropping the constant
O(n), because the catalogue is passed over twice and that dominates
optionExplain: Constants are dropped, so the 2 does not appear in the class.
Repeating a pass does not nest it inside the coupon loop.
Right: 2n + m simplifies to n + m.
m is an independent variable and may be larger than n.
questions.explain: The two passes over the catalogue cost O(n) each, giving 2n, and the coupon pass costs m. The book writes the total as O(2n + m) = O(n + m).
questions.rule: Drop the constant, keep each variable.
questions.teaches: Repeated passes over the same input add up to a multiple of its variable, such as 2n, and the constant is dropped: O(2n + m) = O(n + m).

questions.q: An outer loop runs n times; its inner loop runs n, n − 1, ... down to 1 times. What is the time complexity?
options: O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(n)
optionExplain: Nothing is halved; the counts fall by one each time.
The total grows with n.
Right: the counts add up to about n squared over two.
The inner counts are all of order n at first, so the total exceeds n.
questions.explain: The counts n + (n − 1) + ... + 1 sum to about n²/2. The card next explains the sum.
questions.rule: Sum the shrinking counts.

questions.q: Inner counts n, n − 1, ... 1 add up to 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1) / ____.
questions.explain: The sum of the first n whole numbers is n(n + 1)/2.

questions.q: For n = 10, how many times does the body of the dependent loop shown run?
optionExplain: That is n · n, the count for an inner loop that always runs n times.
That is n(n − 1)/2, which would be the count if the inner loop started at i + 1.
That is n(n + 1), missing the division by 2.
questions.explain: Running the loops gives 55 = 10 · 11 / 2.
questions.rule: Count by summing, not multiplying.

questions.q: A scheduler checks each of 200 tasks against itself and every later task. It makes ____ checks.
questions.rule: n(n + 1)/2 checks.

questions.q: A student says the inner loop keeps shrinking, so the total averages out to O(n). What is wrong?
options: Adding the counts gives n(n + 1)/2, which grows like n squared
Nothing is wrong, since a shrinking loop cannot cost more than one pass
The student should multiply n by n to get exactly O(n²)
The student should use O(log n), because shrinking means halving
optionExplain: Right: a shrinking inner count still sums to quadratic growth.
A shrinking inner loop still runs for every outer iteration.
The product n · n over-counts, though the class is the same; the sum is the right method.
The counts shrink by one each time, not by half.
questions.explain: Each outer iteration still has an inner loop, and the counts n, n − 1, ... add up to about n²/2.
questions.rule: Shrinking by one is not shrinking by half.

questions.q: A scheduler plays (n² + n) / 2 matches for n teams. Which parts does big O ignore? Select all that apply.
options: The added n in the numerator
The divisor 2
The n² term
The entire expression, because it contains a fraction
optionExplain: Right: the n term is smaller than n² and drops out.
Right: dividing by a constant is dropped.
This is the dominant term, so it is the one that stays.
A fraction of a polynomial still has a growth rate.
questions.explain: The book gets O(n²) because the addition term in the numerator and the constant term in the denominator are both ignored.
questions.rule: Drop the smaller term and the constant divisor.
questions.teaches: In (n² + n) / 2 big O ignores the added n in the numerator and the constant divisor, which leaves O(n²).

questions.q: Binary search discards half of the remaining items at each step. For 1,024 items, about how many halvings leave a single item?
optionExplain: That is the size after one halving, not the number of halvings.
That would be a step per item, as in a plain scan.
That is the square root of 1,024, which is not how halving works.
questions.explain: Each halving is one step, and 1,024 halves down to 1 in 10 steps. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: Halving takes log base 2 of n steps.

questions.q: Each step of binary search reduces the search space by ____ percent.
questions.explain: The search space is cut in half every step, which is a 50% reduction.
questions.rule: Binary search halves the space.

questions.q: Order the search-space sizes of a binary search over 32 items from the first step to the last.
questions.explain: Each step halves the space: 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. That is 5 halvings, and 2^5 = 32.
questions.rule: Halve until one remains.

questions.q: A search over 1,000,000 sorted names takes at most 20 halvings. At most how many halvings does a search over 2,000,000 names take?
optionExplain: That doubles the steps, but doubling the input adds only one step.
That counts only the extra names' doubling, not the existing 20 halvings.
Right: doubling the input adds exactly one more halving.
The extra names need one more halving, since 2^20 is below 2,000,000.
questions.explain: 2^20 = 1,048,576 is below 2,000,000 and 2^21 = 2,097,152 is above it, so 21 halvings suffice.
questions.rule: Double the input, add one step.

questions.q: According to the book, which complexity do efficient sorting algorithms have?
options: O(log n)
O(n ⋅ log n)
O(n²)
optionExplain: That is too fast for sorting, since every item must at least be looked at.
Right: the book calls it reasonably fast for most problems and the cost of efficient sorting.
That is the cost of comparing every pair, which efficient sorts avoid.
No sort can ignore the size of its input.
questions.explain: O(n ⋅ log n) is reasonably fast for most problems and is the time complexity of efficient sorting algorithms.
questions.rule: Efficient sorting is O(n ⋅ log n).
questions.teaches: O(n ⋅ log n) is reasonably fast for most problems and is the time complexity of efficient sorting algorithms.

questions.q: A routine discards two thirds of the remaining items each step, shrinking the size by a factor of 3. What is its time complexity?
options: O(log₃ n) as a separate, faster class from O(log n)
O(n / 3), since a third is kept each step
O(3 ⋅ log n), since the base must be kept as a multiplier
O(log n), since the base only changes a constant factor
optionExplain: The base only changes a constant factor, which big O drops.
That would be a single division; repeated division gives a logarithm.
Constants are dropped, so no multiplier remains.
Right: the base does not change the class.
questions.explain: Dividing by 3 repeatedly gives about log base 3 of n steps. Changing the base multiplies by a constant, which is dropped.
questions.rule: Any base gives O(log n).
questions.teaches: The base of the logarithm does not matter for big O, because all logarithms are related by a constant factor.

questions.q: A function receives an array of n numbers and prints each one. About how much extra memory does it allocate as n grows?
options: A constant amount, one loop variable
n cells to hold the input
n cells to hold the printed output
log n cells for the loop counter
optionExplain: Right: the array already exists, and the loop needs only a variable.
The input is not counted: it exists whatever the algorithm does.
Printing creates no stored result, and outputs are usually not counted anyway.
A counter is a single variable and does not grow with n.
questions.explain: Only memory the algorithm adds counts, and here that is one variable. The card next sets out what is counted.
questions.rule: Count what the algorithm adds.

questions.q: True or false: the space used by the input array counts toward an algorithm's space complexity.
questions.explain: The input is never counted, and modifying the input is bad practice. Only memory the algorithm allocates counts.
questions.rule: The input is not counted.

questions.q: A function reads n log lines and returns how many contain a given word, using a single counter. What is its space complexity?
options: O(n), because the n log lines are in memory
O(1), because only a counter is allocated
O(n), because the answer depends on all n lines
O(n²), because each line is compared with the word
optionExplain: The lines are the input, which is not counted.
Right: one counter does not grow with n.
The answer is one number, and the output is usually not counted anyway.
Comparisons are time, and the space used is still a single counter.
questions.explain: The log lines are input and the returned number is output. The only allocation is the counter, which is constant space.
questions.rule: Counter only: O(1) space.

questions.q: A reviewer says printing every element of arr is O(n) space because it touches n elements. What is the flaw?
options: The reviewer is right, since every element visited must be held in memory
The flaw is that printing counts as output, which makes it O(n)
The flaw is that arrays always count as O(1) space
Visiting the input allocates nothing; only num is allocated, O(1)
optionExplain: The elements are already in the input, which is not counted.
Printing does not allocate memory, and output is usually left out of the count.
Arrays the algorithm creates do count; this algorithm creates none.
Right: reading the input is not allocation.
questions.explain: Space counts what the algorithm allocates. Looping over an existing array allocates only the loop variable.
questions.rule: Visiting is not allocating.

questions.q: An interviewer asks you to include the output. A function returns a new list of the n squares of arr, so its space is O(____).
questions.explain: With the output counted, the new list of n values is stored, so the space is O(n). Without counting the output it would be O(1).
questions.rule: Counted output of size n is O(n).

questions.q: A textbook example only creates a grid and fills it, returning nothing at all. How should the grid be treated when finding the space complexity?
options: Left out, because allocated structures are output
Left out, because it is the input
Counted fully, because there is no answer to leave out
Counted only half, because filling reuses the memory
optionExplain: Nothing is returned, so the grid is not an output.
The grid is created by the code, not supplied to it.
Right: the example only allocates, so everything it allocates counts.
Filling a grid does not split its memory into counted and uncounted halves.
questions.explain: The book says its space examples only allocate memory so they can be analysed, so everything allocated is counted; there is no answer to exclude.
questions.rule: No answer to exclude: count everything allocated.
questions.teaches: In the book's space examples the code only allocates memory and returns no answer, so everything allocated counts toward the space complexity.

questions.q: A function copies every number of arr into a new list, doubling each value. What is its space complexity?
options: O(n²)
O(n)
O(log n)
optionExplain: There is one new value per element, not one per pair of elements.
Right: a list of n new values is stored.
The new list is allocated memory, so it counts, and it grows with the input.
Nothing is halved; every element gets a stored value.
questions.explain: A new list with one value for each of the n elements stores n values. The card next generalises this.
questions.rule: One value per element: O(n).

questions.q: A grid with n rows and m columns has space complexity O(n ⋅ ____).
questions.explain: A grid has n · m cells, so the sizes multiply.
questions.rule: Grid: rows times columns.

questions.q: A program keeps the first 1% of a list of n = 10,000 items. How many items does it store, and what is the class?
options: 100 items, which is O(1) because 100 is a constant
100 items, which is O(n)
100 items, which is O(100)
10,000 items, which is O(n)
optionExplain: 100 is a constant only for this n; as n grows the stored count grows with it.
Right: 1% of 10,000 is 100, and n / 100 simplifies to O(n).
The class is expressed in n, with the constant divisor dropped.
Only 1% is stored, so 10,000 is the input size, not the stored count.
questions.explain: 100 = 10,000 / 100. Dividing by a constant is dropped, so the class is O(n).
questions.rule: A fixed fraction of n is still O(n).

questions.q: A grid with 300 rows and 40 columns holds ____ cells.
questions.explain: 300 · 40 = 12,000 cells, which is the O(n ⋅ m) count with n = 300 and m = 40.
questions.rule: Cells = rows times columns.

questions.q: True or false: storing the first 1% of arr, about n / 100 values, gives space O(n / 100), a smaller class than O(n).
questions.explain: Dividing by 100 is a constant factor and is dropped, so n / 100 is still O(n).
questions.rule: Drop constant divisors in space too.

questions.q: A function appends two copies of each number of arr to a list. How many values does it store, and what is the class?
options: 2n values, which is O(n)
n values, which is O(n)
2n values, which is O(2n) and a larger class than O(n)
n² values, which is O(n²)
optionExplain: Right: the list ends with 2n values and the constant 2 is dropped.
Two copies of each number means 2n values, not n.
Constants are dropped in space as in time.
Appending twice per element doubles the size; it does not square it.
questions.explain: The book reads space from what a structure stores at the end: here 2n values. Dropping the constant gives O(n).
questions.rule: Read space from what is stored at the end.
questions.teaches: The book finds space by asking how many values a structure holds at the end of the algorithm, such as the n integers stored in doubledNums.

questions.q: A function prints i and then calls itself with i + 1, with no condition anywhere. What happens when it runs?
options: It stops on its own when it reaches the largest integer
It prints once and then stops
It keeps printing and never stops by itself
It cannot run, because a function may not call itself
optionExplain: Nothing in the code tells it to stop before running out of resources.
The call to itself happens, so the function does not stop after one print.
Right: with no base case the calls continue indefinitely.
Functions can call themselves; this is recursion.
questions.explain: Without a condition to end the calls, the chain never ends. The card next names that condition.
questions.rule: No base case, no end.

questions.q: A condition at the start of a recursive function that ends the calls is called the ____ case.
questions.explain: The base case terminates the chain of recursive calls.
questions.rule: Base case ends the calls.

questions.q: A countdown function prints n and then calls itself with n − 1. Which line is the right base case?
options: if n == 0: return
print(n)
countdown(n - 1)
n = n - 1
optionExplain: Right: it ends the calls when the countdown is finished.
This is the work done in each call, not a stopping condition.
This is the recursive call, which continues the chain.
This changes a value but never ends the calls.
questions.explain: A base case is a condition that makes the function return before it calls itself again.
questions.rule: The base case is a check that returns.

questions.q: Printing 1 to 10 with base case i > 10 starts fn(1) up to fn(11). The total number of calls is ____.
questions.explain: fn(1) through fn(10) print, and fn(11) is a call that meets the base case: 11 calls in all.
questions.rule: One extra call hits the base case.

questions.q: True or false: placing the base-case check after the recursive call still stops the recursion.
questions.explain: The recursive call comes first, so the check below it is never reached and the calls never end. The book notes the return line is never reached for this reason.
questions.rule: Check the base case before recursing.

questions.q: A codebase bans loops. A colleague needs to add up the numbers 1 to n. According to the book, can it be done?
options: Yes, since any loop-based algorithm can be written recursively
No, because recursion only works for printing numbers
Only if the sum is replaced by a formula, which removes the repetition
Yes, but only by adding a second loop to drive the calls
optionExplain: Right: the book cites a result that every loop-based algorithm has a recursive form.
Recursion is a general problem-solving method, not only a printer.
The claim does not depend on a formula; repetition can be simulated by calls.
The calls themselves provide the repetition; no loop is needed.
questions.explain: While iterative algorithms use loops to repeat, recursive ones use function calls to simulate the same logic.
questions.rule: Loops and recursion can express the same algorithms.
questions.teaches: Any iterative algorithm can be written recursively: loops simulate repetition in one style and function calls simulate the same logic in the other.

questions.q: A function prints i, recurses with i + 1 until i passes 3, then prints an End line. In what order do End lines appear?
options: Only the last call prints an End line
i = 1, then 2, then 3, like the numbers
i = 3, then 2, then 1, the reverse of the calls
They alternate with the number prints
optionExplain: Every call that reaches the line after its recursive call prints one.
The End line sits after the recursive call, so it does not follow the order of the first prints.
Right: the deepest call finishes first.
The End lines wait until the recursive calls below them have returned.
questions.explain: The innermost call returns first and the outer ones resume afterwards. The card next shows the whole trace.
questions.rule: Last in, first finished.

questions.q: True or false: while a function call starts another call, the first call keeps waiting until the new call returns.
questions.explain: Every function call exists until it returns, and the old one waits while the new one runs.
questions.rule: A call waits for the calls it starts.

questions.q: Order the lines printed by fn(1) in the card's code, from first printed to last.
questions.explain: The numbers print on the way in (1, 2, 3). The End lines print on the way back out, from i = 3 down to i = 1.
questions.rule: In: numbers. Out: End lines, reversed.

questions.q: The print(i) line moves after the recursive call and the End line is removed. What does fn(1) print, with base case i > 3?
optionExplain: That would be the output with the print placed before the recursive call.
The calls do not skip around; each resumes after the call it started.
Right: the print waits until the deeper call has returned, so the largest i prints first.
The base case i > 3 returns without printing, so no 0 appears.
questions.explain: Each call waits for fn(i + 1) to return before printing i. The output is 3, 2, 1.
questions.rule: Moving a line after the call reverses its order.

questions.q: A student claims that changing i inside fn(3) also changes i for fn(1) and fn(2), because they are the same function. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, because a function has a single i shared by all of its calls
The change reaches fn(2) but not fn(1)
The change is lost, because a call cannot change its own i
Each call has its own local scope, so only fn(3)'s i changes
optionExplain: Each call gets its own copy of the variable.
Scopes are separate for every call, not only the first.
A call may change its own i; the change stays inside that call.
Right: the calls do not share local variables.
questions.explain: A function's local variables belong to the call, not to the function, so other calls are unaffected.
questions.rule: Local variables belong to the call.

questions.q: A countdown function recurses from n = 5 to n = 1. While the n = 1 call runs, ____ copies of n exist.
questions.explain: The calls for n = 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 are all still waiting or running, and each has its own n.
questions.rule: One copy of the variables per unfinished call.
questions.teaches: All calls that have not yet returned exist at once, each with its own local variables, so fn(3) running means three versions of i (1, 2 and 3).

questions.q: With F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1 and each later number the sum of the previous two, what is F(6)?
optionExplain: F(6) is not 6; the sequence grows more slowly than the index here.
That is F(7); F(6) is one place earlier.
That is F(5), one place before F(6).
questions.explain: The sequence is 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, so F(6) = 8. The card next shows how recursion computes it.
questions.rule: Each number sums the previous two.

questions.q: In F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2), the starting values F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1 are the ____ cases.
questions.explain: They are the base cases: they are defined directly, so the recursion stops there.
questions.rule: Base cases are the directly defined values.

questions.q: How many calls, counting F(5) itself, does the recursive F make when computing F(5)?
optionExplain: Right: each call to F(n) with n above 1 adds its two calls, giving 15 in all.
That counts one call per index, but F(3) alone already makes 5 calls.
That counts too few; the calls branch twice at every level above the base cases.
That squares the index, which is not how the calls branch.
questions.explain: Calls: F(0) and F(1) take 1, F(2) takes 3, F(3) takes 5, F(4) takes 9 and F(5) takes 15, since each call adds itself to its two sub-calls.
questions.rule: Each non-base call spawns two more.

questions.q: A staircase has ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2), with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2. Then ways(5) = ____.
questions.explain: ways(3) = 3, ways(4) = 5 and ways(5) = 8. The base cases are the two given values.
questions.rule: Build from the base cases upward.

questions.q: True or false: if only F(0) = 0 is given as a base case, F(1) is still computed correctly by the recurrence.
questions.explain: F(1) would call F(0) and F(-1), and F(-1) has no base case, so the calls would never reach one. Both base cases are needed.
questions.rule: Cover every smallest input with a base case.

questions.q: To compute the factorial n!, where n! = n · (n − 1)! and 0! = 1, how should the recursive function be designed?
options: It prints each partial product and returns nothing
It loops from 1 to n inside every call
It returns the base case value only
It returns n!, built from the answer for n − 1
optionExplain: Printing does not hand an answer up to the call that needs it.
The loop repeats the work; the recursion should reduce n instead.
That would give 1 for every input.
Right: the function returns the answer for its input and combines the subproblem answer.
questions.explain: The book's most common use of recursion has the function return the answer to the problem for the given input, so each call builds its answer from smaller ones.
questions.rule: Design the function to return the answer.
questions.teaches: The most common use of recursion has the function return the answer to the problem for a given input, so smaller calls hand back answers to subproblems.

questions.section: 2. Arrays and strings | 2.1 Arrays and strings
questions.q: In algorithm-problem talk, which structure does the word array usually mean?
options: A fixed-size block whose length is set once for good
A linked chain of nodes joined by references
A dynamic array, which can be resized
A table that maps each index to a stored value
optionExplain: It is the textbook meaning of array, but algorithm talk usually means something looser.
Linked chains are a different structure, covered much later.
Right: people usually mean the resizable kind, and the card names it.
A table keyed by index is a hash map idea, not what array means.
questions.explain: Most problem statements use array loosely. The card next sets out the exact terms.
questions.rule: In this course, array means dynamic array (list), even though a strict array cannot be resized.

questions.section: 2. Arrays and strings | 2.1 Arrays and strings
questions.q: True or false: Strictly speaking, a plain array cannot be resized, while a dynamic array can.
questions.explain: That is the textbook split, and the course uses the single word array for the resizable kind.
questions.rule: Plain array: fixed size. Dynamic array (list): resizable.

questions.section: 2. Arrays and strings | 2.1 Arrays and strings
questions.q: You need a growable collection in Python and in C++. Which pairing matches the course?
options: Python writes arr = [] with no size or type; C++ uses std::vector
Python needs a declared size and element type; C++ writes arr = []
Both languages need a declared size and an element type first
Python uses std::vector; C++ writes arr = [] with no declaration
optionExplain: Right: Python lists are lenient, and C++ gets its list-like type from std::vector.
This swaps the two languages: it is C++ that wants size and type for a plain array.
True for a plain C++ array, but Python lists need neither and C++ also has std::vector.
std::vector belongs to C++, and C++ has no bare arr = [] form.
questions.explain: Python lists are lenient, so arr = [] works. C++ plain arrays need a size and data type, and std::vector supplies a list.
questions.rule: In this course, array means dynamic array (list), even though a strict array cannot be resized.

questions.q: You append 10,000 numbers one by one to a list. In total, the work grows like:

questions.section: 2. Arrays and strings | 2.1 Arrays and strings
questions.q: Appending to the end of a list costs amortized O(____).

questions.section: 2. Arrays and strings | 2.1 Arrays and strings
questions.q: A loop appends one value to a list in each of n iterations and does nothing else costly. What is the total time?

questions.q: In two pointers, which of these describes a pointer?

A copy of the input that is scanned after the first copy

questions.rule: Two pointers means two integer indexes that move along an iterable, with the moves chosen to suit the problem.

questions.q: In two pointers, each pointer is an integer holding an ____ of the array or string.
questions.explain: A pointer here is an integer used as an index into the array or string.
questions.rule: A pointer is an integer index, nothing more.

questions.q: Which setup counts as the two pointers technique on a string?
options: Variables left and right hold indexes, and each loop pass moves one or both
A counter tracks how many characters have been seen so far, and a result string
A single loop index runs from the first character to the last

Counting uses one number and a result, not two moving indexes.
One index scanning once is a plain loop, not two pointers.
A frequency table is a different tool, with no moving pair of indexes.
questions.explain: Two integer indexes moved by the problem's rule make up the technique.
questions.rule: Two pointers means two integer indexes that move along an iterable, with the moves chosen to suit the problem.

questions.q: Sort each setup into Two pointers or Not two pointers.

i walks through arr1 and j walks through arr2 at the same time
one index loops once and adds each value to a running total

questions.explain: Two moving integer indexes make two pointers. One index scanning alone is not.
questions.rule: Two pointers means two integer indexes that move along an iterable, with the moves chosen to suit the problem.

questions.q: True or false: The technique works only on arrays; strings need a different technique.
questions.explain: It works on anything you can move along by index, so strings and arrays are treated alike.
questions.rule: Arrays and strings are both iterables to move along.

questions.q: A problem supplies two separate sorted arrays. What is the best conclusion about two pointers?
options: It cannot apply, because both pointers must start at the two ends of one array
It applies only after the two arrays are merged into one single array
It still applies, with one pointer per array, since the idea has many forms
It applies only to strings, since arrays need a different kind of technique
optionExplain: Starting at both ends is one implementation, not the definition.
The next ideas show a way to avoid merging first.
Right: the book shows a second implementation for problems with two inputs.
Arrays and strings are treated the same way.
questions.explain: The book describes two pointers as an abstract idea that can be implemented in many ways, including one pointer per input.
questions.rule: Two pointers means two integer indexes that move along an iterable, with the moves chosen to suit the problem.
questions.teaches: Two pointers is an abstract idea with many implementations, such as one pointer per input when a problem gives two iterables.

questions.q: Both pointers start at the ends of a 1,000-element array and at least one moves per pass. At most how many passes?
optionExplain: Ten passes would need the range to halve each pass, which this loop does not do.
Right: the gap starts at 999 and shrinks by at least one each pass.
500 holds only if both pointers move every pass; one pointer may move.
A million would suit all pairs, not a single inward sweep.
questions.explain: At most 999 passes. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Start left and right at the two ends, loop while left < right, and move one or both pointers each pass.

questions.q: The loop keeps running while left is ____ right.
questions.explain: The loop continues while left < right and stops when they meet.
questions.rule: Loop while left < right.

questions.q: Order the value pairs the loop examines for [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42], moving both pointers each pass.

questions.rule: Start left and right at the two ends, loop while left < right, and move one or both pointers each pass.

questions.q: An array has 9 elements and both pointers move on every pass. How many passes does the loop make?
optionExplain: 9 would be one pass per element, but each pass uses two.

Right: the passes use index pairs (0,8), (1,7), (2,6), (3,5); then both pointers are 4 and the test fails.
questions.explain: Pairs (0,8), (1,7), (2,6), (3,5) give 4 passes; the middle index 4 is left alone.
questions.rule: Start left and right at the two ends, loop while left < right, and move one or both pointers each pass.

optionExplain: 4 is the count when both pointers move.
Nine passes would need the gap to start at 9, but it starts at 8.
Right: the gap shrinks from 8 to 0 by one each pass.
One pass would need the gap to fall to zero at once.

questions.rule: Start left and right at the two ends, loop while left < right, and move one or both pointers each pass.

questions.q: Each pass of an inward loop first builds a full copy of the 1,000-element array. What is the total cost, at most?
options: About 1,000 x 1,000, because up to n passes each cost O(n)
About 1,000, because the pointers only need n passes
About 500, because only half the array is copied
About 10, because the range halves each pass
optionExplain: Right: the pass count is O(n), but each pass now costs O(n), giving O(n squared).
The pass count is n, but the work inside each pass must also be counted.
Copying the full array each pass copies all of it, not half.
The pointers do not halve a range; they move in small steps.
questions.explain: The inward loop is linear only when the work inside each pass is O(1); linear is usually the best possible runtime.
questions.rule: Start left and right at the two ends, loop while left < right, and move one or both pointers each pass.
questions.teaches: An inward loop is linear only if the work in each pass is O(1), and linear is usually the best possible runtime.

questions.q: True or false: With pointers at both ends of a 50-element array and one moving each pass, the loop can run over 49 passes.

questions.rule: Gap starts at n - 1 and shrinks every pass.

questions.q: The gap right - left starts at n - ____.
questions.explain: With left = 0 and right = n - 1, the gap is n - 1.
questions.rule: The initial gap is n - 1.

questions.q: True or false: On an array of 100,000 elements where both pointers move every pass, the loop makes 50,000 passes.
questions.explain: The gap falls by 2 each pass, so 100,000 elements need about 50,000 passes, half the one-pointer bound.
questions.rule: Moving both pointers halves the pass count.

questions.q: n = 10. Passes alternate between moving both pointers and moving only right, starting with both. The loop makes ____ passes.
questions.explain: The gap goes 9, 7, 6, 4, 3, 1, 0: six passes, still below the n - 1 = 9 bound.
questions.rule: Follow the gap down to zero.

questions.q: A loop moves right only when the two values match, and moves nothing when they differ. For which array does the loop fail to end?
optionExplain: With one element, left < right is false at once.
The values match, so right moves and the loop ends.
Every pair matches, so right keeps moving until the gap is zero.

questions.explain: The bound needs the gap to fall each pass. Here a mismatch leaves the gap unchanged.
questions.rule: Count passes by the gap: it starts at n - 1 and falls by at least one per pass, so passes are at most n - 1.

questions.q: The inward loop runs on one million elements. How much extra memory does it use beyond the input?
options: About one million entries, one for each element visited
A fixed amount: two integer variables, no matter how big the input is
About 500,000 entries, one for each pair of elements
About 20 entries, one for each halving of the input
optionExplain: Nothing is stored per element visited.
Right: the algorithm only needs left and right, so its extra space is O(1).
Pairs are looked at, not stored.
There is no halving; the pointers only move along.
questions.explain: No matter how big the input is, the loop keeps only two integer variables.
questions.rule: Count passes by the gap: it starts at n - 1 and falls by at least one per pass, so passes are at most n - 1.
questions.teaches: The inward loop uses O(1) extra space, because it keeps only two integer variables regardless of input size.

questions.rule: A string is a palindrome when each pair of characters taken from both ends matches, so compare pairs while moving both pointers inward.

It moves the pointers outward, so the loop ends before any pair is read

left < right is the correct test and skips only the middle.

questions.q: The input arrives as a list of characters instead of a string. What changes in the palindrome algorithm?

The pointers must start at the middle instead of the ends

questions.teaches: The palindrome algorithm is unchanged for a list of characters, because two pointers only needs indexes moving along some abstract iterable.

questions.q: In a sorted array the two end values sum to more than the target. Which pointer should move?
options: The left pointer, moving it toward larger values
Both pointers, moving them toward the middle
Neither; the pair is checked by trying every other pair
The right pointer, moving it toward smaller values
optionExplain: Moving left raises the sum, which is the wrong way.
Moving both can skip a valid pair.
Trying everything is the O(n squared) approach the pointers avoid.

questions.rule: In a sorted array, move right when the sum is too large and left when it is too small until the sum matches or the pointers meet.

questions.q: True or false: In a sorted array, when the sum of the two pointed values is too small, the left pointer moves forward.
questions.explain: Moving left forward replaces the smaller value with a larger one, raising the sum.
questions.rule: Too small: move left. Too large: move right.

questions.q: Order the pairs examined for nums = [1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 14, 15] and target 13.
questions.explain: The sums are 16, 15, 10, 11 and 13: right moves twice, left moves twice, then 4 + 9 = 13.
questions.rule: In a sorted array, move right when the sum is too large and left when it is too small until the sum matches or the pointers meet.

questions.q: nums = [2, 3, 7, 9, 11, 20] and target 18. How many pairs are examined before the search returns true?
optionExplain: Right: 2+20=22 (right moves), 2+11=13 (left moves), 3+11=14 (left moves), 7+11=18 found.
Two pairs stop before the sum can match.
Three pairs stop one step early.
Six would try every element once, but the pointers skip many.
questions.explain: The sums are 22, 13, 14 and 18, so four pairs are examined.
questions.rule: In a sorted array, move right when the sum is too large and left when it is too small until the sum matches or the pointers meet.

questions.q: This code returns false for [1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 14, 15] and target 13, though 4 + 9 works. What is the error?
options: It moves right when the sum is too small, which is correct
It moves left when the sum is too large, which can only make it larger
It uses left < right, which skips the final pair
It returns true too early, before the sum is checked
optionExplain: The code does not do that; it is the too-large case that is swapped.
Right: the moves are swapped, so the pointers run away from the solution.
left < right is the correct loop test.
It returns true only when the sum equals the target.
questions.explain: With the moves swapped, each too-large sum raises the left value, and the pointers never reach 4 and 9.
questions.rule: In a sorted array, move right when the sum is too large and left when it is too small until the sum matches or the pointers meet.

questions.q: nums = [4, 15, 9, 1] is not sorted and the target is 13. What does the pointer method return?
options: True, since the pointers still find 4 + 9
True, since sorted order is not needed for the sum check
False, though 4 + 9 = 13, because it throws away a valid pair
An error, since the pointers cross before the first sum

Sorted order is exactly what makes each move safe.
Right: unsorted input breaks the argument that each move is safe.
The pointers do not cross before the first sum.

questions.rule: In a sorted array, move right when the sum is too large and left when it is too small until the sum matches or the pointers meet.
questions.teaches: On unsorted input the pointer moves are no longer safe and can miss a valid pair, which is why the book treats Two Sum on unsorted data as a different problem.

questions.q: In a sorted array, nums[left] + nums[right] exceeds the target. What does this say about nums[right]?
options: No pairing of it with any remaining value can reach the target
It must pair with the value next to nums[left]

questions.q: True or false: If the smallest remaining value plus the largest is above the target, the largest value can be ruled out.

questions.q: For nums = [2, 5, 8, 12, 30] and target 20, order the events as the pointers run.
items: 8 and 12 are found to sum to 20
questions.explain: 2+30=32 rules out 30; 2+12=14 rules out 2; 5+12=17 rules out 5; 8+12=20 is the answer.
questions.rule: If the smallest remaining partner already makes the sum too large, the larger value cannot be part of any solution, so it can be dropped.

questions.q: nums = [1, 3, 6, 10, 15] and target 14. The search ends with no pair. How many values are ruled out before it ends?
optionExplain: Two drops would leave several values unchecked.
Three drops would leave two values with the pointers apart.

Five would drop every value, but the last remaining one is never paired.
questions.explain: The sums 16, 11, 13 and 16 rule out 15, 1, 3 and 10 in turn; one value is left alone.
questions.rule: If the smallest remaining partner already makes the sum too large, the larger value cannot be part of any solution, so it can be dropped.

questions.q: True or false: A student sees 3 + 25 = 28 > 27 and concludes the 3 cannot be part of any answer.
questions.explain: The sum is too large because of the large value: 25 is the one ruled out, since 3 is already the smallest partner.
questions.rule: A too-large sum rules out the larger value.

questions.q: In sorted data, nums[left] + nums[right] is below the target. Which value can be ruled out, and why?
options: nums[right], because it is the largest value and therefore too large to be useful here
nums[left], because even the largest remaining partner leaves the sum too small
nums[left], because it is the smallest value in the array and so can never matter
Neither, because sorted data does not by itself allow any conclusion about a single value
optionExplain: The right value is the largest partner and cannot be ruled out here.
Right: the same argument works mirrored for the smaller value.
Being smallest is not the reason; the missing partner is.
Sorted order is exactly what permits the conclusion.
questions.explain: The reasoning mirrors the too-large case: the largest possible partner cannot reach the target.
questions.rule: If the smallest remaining partner already makes the sum too large, the larger value cannot be part of any solution, so it can be dropped.
questions.teaches: The same reasoning applies to the left value when the sum is too small, because the right value is already the largest available partner.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Two arrays are scanned side by side with one pointer each. Where do the pointers start?
options: Both at the last index, each in its own array
One at the front of the first array and one at the back of the second
Both at index 0, each in its own array
Both in the middle, each in its own array
optionExplain: Starting at the end is a different recipe for one input.
Mixed ends belong to the edge recipe, which uses one input.
Right: this method starts both at the front.
Nothing about this recipe starts in the middle.
questions.explain: Both start at index 0. The card next explains the loop.
questions.rule: With two inputs, start one pointer per input at index 0, loop while both are in range, and move one or both each pass.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: In the two-input method, both pointers start at index ____.
questions.explain: Each pointer starts at the first index of its own input.
questions.rule: Two inputs: one pointer each, both start at 0.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Order the value pairs compared for [1, 4, 7] and [2, 3, 9, 10] when each pass advances the pointer at the smaller value.
questions.explain: 1<2 moves the first pointer; 4>2 and 4>3 move the second; 4<9 moves the first; 7<9 moves it again, and the first array is used up.
questions.rule: With two inputs, start one pointer per input at index 0, loop while both are in range, and move one or both each pass.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: arr1 has 6 elements and arr2 has 4. Both pointers advance on every pass. How many passes does the loop make?
optionExplain: Right: the loop stops when the shorter input runs out, after 4 passes.
Ten counts every element of both inputs, but each pass moves two.
Six would need the shorter input to last six passes.
Five matches no stopping point: arr2 ends after four.
questions.explain: The loop ends as soon as one pointer reaches its end, so min(6, 4) = 4 passes.
questions.rule: With two inputs, start one pointer per input at index 0, loop while both are in range, and move one or both each pass.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: The loop test i < len(arr1) and j < len(arr2) stops only after both inputs are fully used.
questions.explain: The loop stops as soon as either pointer reaches the end, leaving the other input partly unread.
questions.rule: and means the loop stops when the first input runs out.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Two reading lists are scanned in step. The loop ends when the first list is finished. What does this imply for the second?
options: It is fully read as well, because both pointers always end together
It has been skipped on purpose, so its items are never needed
It must be shorter than the first list, so nothing remains
It may still hold unread items, so extra code is needed if all of them matter
optionExplain: Pointers end together only when the lists have equal length and both move every pass.
Whether the rest matters depends on the problem.
The loop ends on whichever list is exhausted first, not on the longer one.
Right: the loop does not guarantee the other pointer reached its end.
questions.explain: When the loop stops because one pointer reached its end, the other pointer may not be at the end of its input.
questions.rule: With two inputs, start one pointer per input at index 0, loop while both are in range, and move one or both each pass.
questions.teaches: The loop can stop with the other pointer not at its end, so a problem that needs every element needs extra code after the loop.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: When a two-input loop ends because one pointer reached its end, the other input has also been fully processed.
questions.explain: The other pointer is usually still partway through its input. The card next shows how to finish it.
questions.rule: After the two-input loop, add a clean-up loop for each input; only one will run.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: After the main loop, at most ____ of the two clean-up loops has any work to do.
questions.explain: The main loop stops when one input is used up, so only the other can have elements left.
questions.rule: At most one clean-up loop runs.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: arr1 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and arr2 = [9, 8]; both pointers advance each pass. Which values do the clean-up loops handle?
options: 8 and 9
3, 4 and 5
1 and 2
4 and 5
optionExplain: Those belong to arr2, which the main loop has already used up.
Right: after two passes arr2 is used up, leaving indexes 2 to 4 of arr1.
Those are the first two elements of arr1, handled by the main loop.
That misses index 2, which the main loop did not visit.
questions.explain: Two passes use indexes 0 and 1 of both arrays, leaving 3, 4 and 5 for the clean-up loop.
questions.rule: After the two-input loop, add a clean-up loop for each input; only one will run.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: arr1 has 3 elements and arr2 has 7; both pointers advance each pass. ____ elements go through the clean-up loops.
questions.explain: 3 passes use up arr1, leaving 7 - 3 = 4 elements of arr2.
questions.rule: Leftover = difference of the lengths when both pointers advance together.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: Without clean-up loops, this merge returns [1, 2] for arr1 = [1, 2] and arr2 = [3, 4, 5].
questions.explain: arr1 runs out after two passes, and 3, 4 and 5 are never added; the clean-up loops are what add them.
questions.rule: Without clean-up, the other input's remainder is lost.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Merging sorted [2, 5, 8] and [3, 6, 7, 20, 30], the main loop leaves 20 and 30 unread. Where do they go?
options: Compared with 8 again one by one, since 8 may still be larger than a leftover value
Appended unchanged at the end, since each exceeds everything already placed
Inserted by sorting the whole result once more, since the leftovers may be out of order
Dropped, since the shorter array decides the length of the merged result
optionExplain: 8 is already placed, and 20 and 30 exceed it.
Right: they are larger than the largest value of the exhausted array.
Sorting again would work but wastes the sorted order.
Dropping them would lose data the answer needs.
questions.explain: Leftover values are all larger than the largest value in the exhausted input, so they are appended as they are.
questions.rule: After the two-input loop, add a clean-up loop for each input; only one will run.
questions.teaches: In a merge of sorted inputs, the leftover values are all larger than the largest value of the exhausted input, so they can be appended as they are.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Two arrays of 1,000 and 2,000 elements are scanned with one pointer each and O(1) work per pass. The time is on the order of:
options: 1,000 x 2,000, one pass for every pair
log(1,000 x 2,000), halving until done
2,000 x 2,000, the longer length squared
1,000 + 2,000, the total of the two lengths
optionExplain: That would be a nested loop over all pairs, not a single sweep.
Nothing here halves a range; the pointers step one at a time.
The shorter input does not need extra passes.
Right: the pointers only move forward through each input once.
questions.explain: The count is about the sum of the lengths. The card next shows the argument.
questions.rule: Each pass moves a pointer forward and the pointers can move at most n + m times in all, so the loop costs O(n + m).

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: With O(1) work per pass, a loop over inputs of lengths n and m runs in O(n + ____) time.
questions.explain: The pointers move forward at most n + m times in total.
questions.rule: Two inputs: O(n + m).

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Inputs have 5,000 and 15,000 elements. At most how many forward moves can the two pointers make in total?
optionExplain: That is 5,000 x 15,000, the cost of trying every pair.
That is the difference of the lengths.
That counts only the shorter input.
questions.explain: The total number of forward moves is at most the sum of the lengths.
questions.rule: Each pass moves a pointer forward and the pointers can move at most n + m times in all, so the loop costs O(n + m).

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: Because the loop moves pointers over both arrays, its cost is O(n times m).
questions.explain: Each pointer only moves forward, so the cost is O(n + m); n times m would count every pair.
questions.rule: One sweep of each input adds; it does not multiply.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Each pass costs O(log n) instead of O(1), and the pointers still make at most n + m moves. Our reading: the total cost is:
options: O(n + m), since the pointer moves still bound the cost
O(log n), since only the work in one pass matters
O((n + m) log n), since passes times work per pass bounds the total
O(n x m), since each pass now scans the other input
optionExplain: The bound on passes holds, but each pass is no longer constant work.
Every pass costs log n, and there are many passes.
Right: at most n + m passes of O(log n) work each.
Nothing in the change makes a pass scan the other input.
questions.explain: The pass count stays at most n + m; multiplying by the work per pass gives O((n + m) log n).
