questions.rule: Each pass moves a pointer forward and the pointers can move at most n + m times in all, so the loop costs O(n + m).

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: A merge writes an output list of n + m numbers. Not counting the output, what is its extra space?
options: O(n + m), because the output list holds that many numbers
O(n), because the longer list is copied
O(log n), because the pointers halve the range
O(1), because only the two pointer indexes are stored
optionExplain: The output exists in any solution, so it is usually left out of extra space.
No copy of an input is needed.
The pointers do not halve a range.
Right: the output is not usually counted as extra space.
questions.explain: The book does not usually count the output as extra space, so only the two indexes remain.
questions.rule: Each pass moves a pointer forward and the pointers can move at most n + m times in all, so the loop costs O(n + m).
questions.teaches: Extra space is O(1) because the output array is not usually counted as extra space; only the two indexes are extra.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Two sorted arrays are combined by concatenating and sorting, costing O(n log n). Using their sorted order, the combine step can cost:
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n squared)
O(n log n), which cannot be improved
optionExplain: Right: pointers beat the sort by a factor of log n.
Every element still has to be placed, so log n is too small.
Squared is slower than the sort.
Sorted inputs give an improvement the sort ignores.
questions.explain: The sort ignores that both inputs are already sorted. The card next shows the faster merge.
questions.rule: To merge two sorted arrays, repeatedly take the smaller front value, then append whatever remains.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: At each step the smaller of the two front values is added to the answer and its pointer moves forward.
questions.explain: That is the merge step: the smaller front value must come first.
questions.rule: Take the smaller front value.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Merging [1, 4, 9] and [2, 3, 10], order the values as they are added to the answer.
questions.explain: The smaller front value is added each time: 1, 2, 3, 4, then 9, then 10.
questions.rule: To merge two sorted arrays, repeatedly take the smaller front value, then append whatever remains.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Merging [1, 2, 3] with [10, 11, 12, 13], how many value comparisons does the main loop make?
optionExplain: Four counts the pass over the second array, but it has no partner.
Right: three comparisons empty the first array; the remaining four values are appended without comparing.
Six would compare every value of the first array twice.
Seven counts every value of both arrays.
questions.explain: 1, 2 and 3 are each smaller than 10, so three comparisons empty the first array.
questions.rule: To merge two sorted arrays, repeatedly take the smaller front value, then append whatever remains.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: If two front values are equal, taking from the second array first would break the merge.
questions.explain: With equal values it does not matter which is chosen, so either may be taken first.
questions.rule: Ties can go either way.
questions.teaches: When the two front values are equal it does not matter which is taken first.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: A merge is run on unsorted arrays [5, 1] and [2, 3]. What happens?
options: The result is [1, 2, 3, 5], because the merge sorts the values as it compares and copies them
The code fails with an error because the merge requires sorted inputs and checks them first
The result is [2, 3, 5, 1], which is not sorted; combining and sorting would be better
The result is [5, 1, 2, 3], because all of the first array is placed before the second
optionExplain: The merge never reorders within an array.
The code runs and returns an unsorted answer instead.
Right: the merge trusts the sorted order, so it cannot repair unsorted input.
The loop compares 5 with 2 first and takes 2.
questions.explain: The merge relies on sorted inputs. For unsorted inputs, combining and then sorting is a good approach.
questions.rule: To merge two sorted arrays, repeatedly take the smaller front value, then append whatever remains.
questions.teaches: For unsorted input arrays, concatenating and sorting (O(n log n)) is a good approach, because the merge's saving depends on sorted inputs.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: A merge uses n for the first array's length and m for the second's. Its time is:
options: O(n + m)
O(n)
O(n x m)
O(m log n)
optionExplain: Right: every element of both arrays is placed once.
That ignores the second array, which can be much longer.
Multiplying would count every pair.
Nothing here is sorted or searched.
questions.explain: The sum of the lengths. The card next shows how the symbols can be chosen.
questions.rule: In big O you may define the variables as you like, as long as you use one definition consistently.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: You may define n as the combined length of both arrays or keep n and m separate; both are acceptable.
questions.explain: Big O lets you define the variables, and both choices describe the same algorithms.
questions.rule: You choose what n means; state it.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Arrays of 300 and 700 elements are merged. With n defined as the total length, the sort approach is written as:
options: O(n), with n = 1,000
O(n log n), with n = 300
O(n log n), with n = 1,000
O(n squared), with n = 1,000
optionExplain: That is the pointer merge, not the sort.
That uses only one array's length, against the stated definition.
Right: sorting the combined array costs n log n for the combined length.
Sorting does not cost n squared.
questions.explain: Combined length n = 1,000, and sorting it costs O(n log n).
questions.rule: In big O you may define the variables as you like, as long as you use one definition consistently.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Sort each running time into Pointer merge or Concatenate then sort.

items.t: O(n + m), with n and m the two lengths
O(n), with n the combined length
O(n log n), with n the combined length
O((n + m) log(m + n))

questions.explain: Both notations describe the same two algorithms: the merge is linear, the sort has a log factor.
questions.rule: In big O you may define the variables as you like, as long as you use one definition consistently.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: With n and m the two lengths, O(n) bounds the merge even when m is far larger than n.
questions.explain: The merge handles all m elements of the second array too, so O(n) understates the cost when m is large.
questions.rule: Keep both lengths in the bound unless the definition folds them together.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Two sorted lists of 40,000 and 60,000 customers are merged. Which definition best matches the book's reasoning?
options: n = 40,000, the shorter list, since it ends the main loop first
n = 100,000, the combined length, since combining makes the total significant
n = 60,000, the longer list, since it dominates the cost
n = 20,000, the difference, since only the leftover needs work
optionExplain: The shorter list ends the main loop, but the cost covers all elements.
Right: when arrays are combined, the total length is the significant number.
The cost counts both lists, not only the longer one.
The leftover is only part of the work.
questions.explain: The book justifies n as the total length because combining the arrays makes the total significant.
questions.rule: In big O you may define the variables as you like, as long as you use one definition consistently.
questions.teaches: The book's justification for defining n as the combined length is that, since the arrays are being combined, the total length is a significant number.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Which string is a subsequence of abcde?
options: aec
eda
bda
ace
optionExplain: The e comes after the c in abcde, so aec is out of order.
The d comes before the a in this order.
The a comes before b, so bda is out of order.
Right: a, c, e appear in that order, with gaps.
questions.explain: Characters must appear in the same order. The card next shows how to test it.
questions.rule: Scan t once, advance the pointer on s only on a match, and s is a subsequence if its pointer reaches the end.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: In the subsequence check, the pointer on t moves forward on ____ pass, match or not.
questions.explain: Each character of t is looked at once and never reused.
questions.rule: j always advances; i advances only on a match.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: For s = ahc and t = ahbgdc, the final value of i is ____.
questions.explain: a, h and c are found at positions 0, 1 and 5, so i reaches 3 and the answer is true.
questions.rule: Scan t once, advance the pointer on s only on a match, and s is a subsequence if its pointer reaches the end.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: For s = axc and t = ahbgdc, the algorithm ends with i at 1 and returns false.
questions.explain: a matches, but x never appears in t, so i stays at 1 and i never reaches len(s) = 3.
questions.rule: i reaches len(s) only if every letter is found in order.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: This code moves j only on a mismatch. What goes wrong for s = aa and t = a?
options: It returns False because j never reaches the end
It raises an index error when i passes the end of s
One character of t is matched twice, so it wrongly returns True
It returns True only because t is shorter than s
optionExplain: It returns True, not False: i reaches the end of s.
The loop test keeps i in range.
Right: after a match j stays put, so the single a matches both letters of s.
Length is not the reason; the repeated match is.
questions.explain: A character of t can be matched only once, so j must move on a match too.
questions.rule: Scan t once, advance the pointer on s only on a match, and s is a subsequence if its pointer reaches the end.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: A program checks whether a licence code appears in order inside a long string. How much extra space does the pointer method use?
options: O(1): two integer indexes, however long the strings are
O(n): a copy of the long string
O(m): a table of the code's letters
O(log n): a stack of matched positions
optionExplain: Right: the pointers are all it keeps.
No copy of the long string is made.
No table is needed; i and j are enough.
Nothing stacks matched positions.
questions.explain: Like the earlier two-pointer examples, this solution uses O(1) space.
questions.rule: Scan t once, advance the pointer on s only on a match, and s is a subsequence if its pointer reaches the end.
questions.teaches: The subsequence check uses O(1) space, like the other examples, because it keeps only two integer pointers.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: After a mismatch between s[i] and t[j], the pointer i on s should move forward.
questions.explain: The letter s[i] has still not been found, so only j should move. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Move j on every pass and move i only when its letter is found.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: When s[i] differs from t[j], which pointer moves?
options: Only i, since s[i] is wrong
Both, to look at the next pair
Neither, until the characters match
Only j, since t[j] cannot help
optionExplain: Moving i would give up on a letter never found.
Moving both would skip a letter of s.
Waiting would never end the loop.
Right: the current letter of s still needs a partner, so only t moves.
questions.explain: A mismatch discards t[j] but keeps s[i] waiting.
questions.rule: Move j on every pass and move i only when its letter is found.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: For s = bc and t = abcd, how many passes does the loop make?
optionExplain: Two passes would match b and c with no mismatch in front.
Right: pass 1 is a mismatch, pass 2 matches b, pass 3 matches c; then i reaches the end of s.
Four would scan the whole of t, but the loop stops once i is done.
One pass stops after the mismatch on a.
questions.explain: The loop stops when i reaches the end of s, after three passes.
questions.rule: Move j on every pass and move i only when its letter is found.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: For s = abc and t = acb, the final value of i is ____.
questions.explain: a matches, c is skipped, b matches, then t is used up with c unmatched; i is 2, below len(s) = 3, so the answer is false.
questions.rule: Follow i, which moves only on a match.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: True or false: If j stayed in place after a match, one character of t could be used for several letters of s.
questions.explain: Moving j on a match is what stops a single character from being matched twice.
questions.rule: A character of t can be matched only once.
questions.teaches: A character in t can only be matched once, so j moves on after a match, and a mismatched character of t is discarded.

questions.section: Another way to use two pointers
questions.q: Because j moves on every pass, the loop could be written as a for loop over t. Which statement is true?
options: A for loop is wrong, since j must sometimes stay in place
A for loop over t with i updated by hand is equivalent
A for loop is correct only if s and t have equal length
A for loop is correct only if i also moves every pass
optionExplain: j never stays in place in this algorithm.
Right: j advances on every pass, which is what a for loop does.
Lengths need not be equal.
i must stay put on a mismatch.
questions.explain: The book notes that j increases each iteration regardless, so a for loop over t works, with i handled inside.
questions.rule: Move j on every pass and move i only when its letter is found.
questions.teaches: Since j always increments, the algorithm can be written as a for loop over t, with i updated by hand.

questions.q: A problem gives one array. Could both pointers start at index 0 and move forward?
options: No, the pointers must start at the two ends of one array and meet
No, each of the two pointers must start in a different array of its own
Yes, but only if the array is sorted before the pointers start moving
Yes, the technique only needs two integer indexes moving along an iterable
optionExplain: That describes one recipe, not the technique.
That describes the two-input recipe.
Sorting is needed for some problems, not for the idea.
Right: the technique is not tied to one starting position.
questions.explain: Starting positions are up to the problem. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Treat the two recipes as guidelines: two pointers means integer variables moving along iterables, however they start and move.

questions.q: True or false: The two pointer recipes in the course are guidelines, not the only ways to use the technique.
questions.explain: Two pointers is an idea, and the recipes are its most common patterns.
questions.rule: Recipes are guidelines.

questions.q: Which recipe fits each task?

items.t: Check whether a word reads the same backward
Merge two sorted price lists
Find two prices in a sorted list that sum to a budget
Test whether a short code appears in order inside a longer string

questions.explain: Tasks about the two ends of one input take the edge recipe; tasks that combine or compare two inputs take one pointer per input.
questions.rule: Treat the two recipes as guidelines: two pointers means integer variables moving along iterables, however they start and move.

questions.q: Both pointers start at index 0 of the same array and move forward at different times. Which statement is true?
options: It is still two pointers: two integer variables moving along an iterable
It is not two pointers, since the pointers did not start at opposite ends
It is not two pointers, since only one input is given
It is two pointers only if both always move on every pass
optionExplain: Right: the starting positions do not change what the technique is.
Opposite ends are a recipe, not a requirement.
One input is allowed, as in the closing notes.
Each pass may move one or both.
questions.explain: The technique is defined by the two moving indexes, not by where they start.
questions.rule: Treat the two recipes as guidelines: two pointers means integer variables moving along iterables, however they start and move.

questions.q: True or false: A problem where both pointers begin at the first index of the same array cannot be solved with two pointers.
questions.explain: Both pointers can start at the first index of one input and move forward, as the closing notes say.
questions.rule: Same start, same array: still two pointers.

questions.q: A problem needs three positions tracked in an array at once. What does the book say about this?
options: Two pointers cannot be used and a hash table is required
Only two positions can ever be tracked with indexes
Some problems use three pointers, an extension of the same idea
Three positions force the array to be sorted first
optionExplain: A hash table is a different tool, and the book does not say it is required.
Nothing limits indexes to two.
Right: the book mentions problems that make use of three pointers.
Sorting is not tied to the number of pointers.
questions.explain: The closing notes say there are even problems that make use of three pointers.
questions.rule: Treat the two recipes as guidelines: two pointers means integer variables moving along iterables, however they start and move.
questions.teaches: Some problems use three pointers, an extension of the same idea of integer variables moving along an iterable.

questions.q: Which of these is a subarray of [1, 2, 3, 4]?
optionExplain: It picks elements with a gap, so it is not contiguous.
The order is reversed from the original.
Right: 2, 3, 4 are adjacent and in the original order.
The elements are not adjacent and the order is reversed.
questions.explain: A subarray is a block of neighbours. The card next defines it.
questions.rule: A subarray is a contiguous section of an array, fixed by its left and right bounds.

questions.q: A subarray is a ____ section of the array.
questions.explain: Its elements must be adjacent in the original array.
questions.rule: Subarray means contiguous.

questions.q: How many subarrays of length 3 does [4, 5, 6, 7, 8] have?
optionExplain: Five is the array length, but a length-3 block cannot start at the last two elements.
Ten counts selections of three elements with gaps.
Two misses one of the three blocks that fit.
questions.explain: The left bound can be index 0, 1 or 2, giving three blocks.
questions.rule: A subarray is a contiguous section of an array, fixed by its left and right bounds.

questions.q: Sort each selection from [5, 6, 7, 8] into Subarray or Not a subarray.
questions.explain: A subarray is contiguous and in order. The whole array counts as a subarray of full length.
questions.rule: A subarray is a contiguous section of an array, fixed by its left and right bounds.

questions.q: In [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], the subarray [30, 40, 50] has which left and right bounds?
options: Left bound 3 and right bound 5
Left bound 2 and right bound 5
Left bound 30 and right bound 50
Left bound 2 and right bound 4
optionExplain: That counts positions from 1.
The last index is 4, not 5.
The bounds are indexes, not the stored values.
Right: bounds are indexes, counted from 0.
questions.explain: Indexes start at 0, so 30 is at index 2 and 50 is at index 4.
questions.rule: A subarray is a contiguous section of an array, fixed by its left and right bounds.

questions.q: A problem about a window of consecutive days of sales. What is a window in this setting?
options: A set of days chosen freely, whatever their order
Another name for a subarray, set by its left and right bounds
Only the first few days of the array
A subarray that has exactly the same length as the array
optionExplain: Free choice with gaps would be a subset, not a window.
Right: the course uses window as another name for a subarray.
Prefixes are special windows that start at index 0, not all of them.
Windows may be any length, not only the full one.
questions.explain: In this context a window is another name for a subarray.
questions.rule: A subarray is a contiguous section of an array, fixed by its left and right bounds.
questions.teaches: In this context, window is another name for a subarray.

questions.q: A problem calls a subarray valid if its sum is at most 20. What is the constraint metric?
options: The number 20
The sum of the subarray
The length of the subarray
The last element of the subarray
optionExplain: That is the restriction, the limit on the metric.
Right: the metric is the attribute being measured.
Length may be what is asked for, but it is not what is limited.
Nothing limits the last element.
questions.explain: The metric is what you measure. The card next names the second part.
questions.rule: A valid subarray has a constraint metric (such as its sum) that obeys a numeric restriction (such as at most 10).

questions.q: A valid subarray has a constraint metric that obeys a numeric ____.
questions.explain: The restriction is the numeric condition on the metric, such as <= 10.
questions.rule: Valid = metric obeys restriction.

questions.q: Sort each item into Constraint metric or Numeric restriction.

items.t: the sum of the window
at most 10
the number of zeros in the window
at most one
the product of the window
less than k

questions.explain: The metric is the attribute you measure; the restriction is the number it must satisfy.
questions.rule: A valid subarray has a constraint metric (such as its sum) that obeys a numeric restriction (such as at most 10).

questions.q: Find the longest substring with at most 3 different letters. What are the metric and the restriction?
options: Metric: length of the substring; restriction: at most 3
Metric: the letter count of the whole string; restriction: 3
Metric: the position of the last letter; restriction: at most 3
Metric: number of different letters; restriction: at most 3
optionExplain: The length is what is maximised, not what is limited.
The whole string never changes, so it cannot be the metric.
Positions are not limited by the problem.
Right: the metric is the count of different letters, and 3 is its limit.
questions.explain: The limit of 3 applies to the number of different letters in the substring.
questions.rule: A valid subarray has a constraint metric (such as its sum) that obeys a numeric restriction (such as at most 10).
questions.hint: Which attribute does the 3 limit?

questions.q: True or false: For the longest subarray with sum at most k, the constraint metric is the subarray length.
questions.explain: The sum is the constraint metric. The length is what the problem asks to maximise.
questions.rule: The metric is limited; the answer is optimised.

questions.q: A subarray is valid if no value appears more than twice. Which can serve as the metric?
options: The highest count of any single value inside the subarray
Only the sum of the subarray, since metrics must be sums
Only the number of different values in it
The index of the first value inside the subarray
optionExplain: Right: a frequency count is a valid metric, with restriction at most 2.
Sums are one metric, not the only one.
Distinct counts are another metric, but this problem limits a frequency.
An index does not describe what the subarray contains.
questions.explain: Constraint metrics can be sums, the number of unique elements, the frequency of a specific element, and more.
questions.rule: A valid subarray has a constraint metric (such as its sum) that obeys a numeric restriction (such as at most 10).
questions.teaches: A constraint metric can also be the number of unique elements or the frequency of a specific element, not only a sum.

questions.q: After adding a new element on the right, a window becomes invalid. What does a sliding window do?
options: Restarts from index 0 with an empty window
Removes the new element and stops
Removes elements from the left until the window is valid
Removes elements from the right until it is valid
optionExplain: Restarting would repeat work already done.
Stopping would leave the rest of the array unexamined.
Right: the window shrinks from the left.
Right is where the window grows, so it is not where it shrinks.
questions.explain: The card next explains why the left side shrinks.
questions.rule: Grow the window by moving right and shrink it by moving left whenever it becomes invalid.

questions.q: Moving ____ forward by one removes the leftmost element of the window.
questions.explain: left is the window's left bound, so moving it forward drops the element it used to point at.
questions.rule: left++ removes the leftmost element.

questions.q: The sum limit is 8 and the window is [5, 4]. A 3 joins on the right. How many elements leave from the left?
optionExplain: The sum 12 is above 8, so something must go.
Removing two would also be valid but removes more than needed.
Removing three would empty the window.
Right: the sum 12 is too large; removing the 5 gives [4, 3] with sum 7.
questions.explain: The window shrinks only until it is valid again, which takes one removal here.
questions.rule: Grow the window by moving right and shrink it by moving left whenever it becomes invalid.

questions.q: Find the longest subarray with sum at most k. After right reaches index 3 and the window is valid again, what does it hold?
optionExplain: Right: after adding 5 the window is shrunk from the left until its sum is at most 6.
Its sum is 8, which is above 6.
Its sum is 7, so it cannot be a valid window.
Its sum is 7, still above 6.
questions.explain: At index 2 the window shrinks to [1, 2]. Adding 5 gives sum 8, and removing 1 and 2 leaves [5].
questions.rule: Grow the window by moving right and shrink it by moving left whenever it becomes invalid.

questions.q: True or false: To repair an invalid window, a student removes the newest element by moving right backward.
questions.explain: The window slides rightward: repair by moving left forward, so the newest element stays.
questions.rule: Repair by moving left, not right.

questions.q: After a long run of a sliding window, can left ever move backward?
options: Yes, when the window becomes too short to be useful, left steps back to widen it
No: both bounds only move forward, so the window always slides to the right
Yes, when the sum drops far below the limit, left steps back to take in more elements
Yes, once right has reached the end of the array, left can restart from the beginning
optionExplain: Short windows grow again by moving right.
Right: the window grows as far as it can, shrinks until valid, and keeps sliding right.
A small sum means the window can grow, not that left moves back.
At the end of the array the loop stops; left does not restart.
questions.explain: The window's size keeps changing, but it always slides along to the right until it reaches the end of the input.
questions.rule: Grow the window by moving right and shrink it by moving left whenever it becomes invalid.
questions.teaches: The window's size keeps changing, growing until invalid and shrinking until valid, but it always slides to the right until the end of the input.

questions.q: Positive numbers, sum limit 5. The window [3, 2, 1] has sum 6. Why can the 3 be forgotten?
options: The 3 is the largest value in the window, so it is the one that broke the limit
Windows may hold at most two elements, so the 3 must go
More elements on the right only raise the sum, so keeping the 3 cannot make a valid window
The first element of a window is invalid by definition
optionExplain: The size of the value is not the reason; the 2 or the 1 could equally be the problem.
Nothing limits the window to two elements.
Right: with positive values, extending the window can only raise its sum.
The first element is not invalid; the whole window is.
questions.explain: A longer positive-sum window is larger still. The card next lays out the argument.
questions.rule: With positive integers, a window that is too large only gets larger on the right, so its leftmost element can be dropped for good.

questions.q: The argument for dropping the left element needs the array to hold ____ integers.
questions.explain: Positive values make longer subarrays have larger sums.
questions.rule: Dropping is safe because positive sums only grow.

questions.q: Positive numbers, sum limit 6. The window [2, 4, 1] has sum 7. Which window remains after the repair?
optionExplain: Right: removing the 2 leaves [4, 1] with sum 5.
That removes the 1 from the right, but the window shrinks from the left.
That removes more than needed.
That removes the 4 from the middle, which a window cannot do.
questions.explain: The window shrinks from the left only until its sum is at most 6.
questions.rule: With positive integers, a window that is too large only gets larger on the right, so its leftmost element can be dropped for good.

questions.q: True or false: After [3, 2, 1] exceeds the limit, a student removes the middle 2 and keeps [3, 1] as the window.
questions.explain: A window is a subarray, so its elements must be contiguous. Only the left end can be trimmed.
questions.rule: A window is contiguous: only the ends can change.

questions.q: With nums = [5, -4, 2] and k = 3 the window method returns 2. What is the true longest valid length?
options: 2, the same as the window method
1, since 5 is already above the limit
0, since no subarray is valid
3, because [5, -4, 2] itself has sum 3
optionExplain: Two is what the window method reports, not the truth.
The window method drops 5, but a longer window containing it is valid.
Several subarrays are valid, including the whole array.
Right: the window dropped the 5 early, but with a negative number the full array is valid.
questions.explain: With negative numbers a longer subarray can have a smaller sum, so the forgetting argument fails.
questions.rule: With positive integers, a window that is too large only gets larger on the right, so its leftmost element can be dropped for good.

questions.q: Positive numbers, limit 6. The window [4, 2, 1] has sum 7. Could a valid window keep the 4 and end beyond the 1?
options: Yes, by skipping the 2 and keeping the 4 and the new element
No: a window that keeps the 4 and reaches past the 1 also contains the 2 and 1
Yes, because the 4 is smaller than the limit
No, because the limit would have to be raised first
optionExplain: Skipping elements would not be a subarray.
Right: contiguity forces the whole stretch into the window.
Being below the limit alone does not help; the sum of the whole stretch counts.
The limit is fixed by the problem.
questions.explain: A subarray cannot include the 4 without also including the 2 and the 1, so its sum is at least 7.
questions.rule: With positive integers, a window that is too large only gets larger on the right, so its leftmost element can be dropped for good.
questions.teaches: A window cannot include the leftmost element without also including every element between it and the right bound, since that would violate the definition of a subarray.

questions.q: You must find the longest subarray with sum at most k. Which approach should you reach for first?
options: Start pointers at the two ends and move them inward
A sliding window, growing on the right and shrinking on the left
Sort the array and take the smallest elements
Test every subarray one by one and keep the longest valid one
optionExplain: That recipe fits problems about the two ends, not a sum limit.
Right: a defined validity plus a best valid subarray points to a window.
Sorting loses the order that subarrays depend on.
That works but is the slow approach the window avoids.
questions.explain: The card next lists the cues.
questions.rule: When a problem defines valid subarrays and asks for the best one, such as the longest, think of a sliding window.

questions.q: A problem that defines valid subarrays and asks for the ____ one, such as the longest, suggests a sliding window.
questions.explain: The problem asks for the best valid subarray, for example the longest.
questions.rule: Valid subarrays plus a best one: think window.

questions.q: Sort each task into Sliding window or Another technique.

items.t: Longest substring with at most one zero
Longest subarray with sum at most k
Number of subarrays with product below k
Check whether a word reads the same backward
Merge two sorted lists into one
Check whether one string occurs in order inside another

questions.explain: The first three define valid subarrays and ask for the best or the count; the others are two-pointer problems with no validity rule.
questions.rule: When a problem defines valid subarrays and asks for the best one, such as the longest, think of a sliding window.

questions.q: Find the longest run of days with at most 2 rainy days. Which setup fits?
options: Two pointers from both ends; metric is the distance between the pointers
Merge two lists; metric is the date of each day
Sliding window; metric is the length of the run, restriction is at most 2
Sliding window; metric is rainy days in the window, restriction is at most 2
optionExplain: Nothing here is about the two ends of the data.
There are no two lists to merge.
The length is what is maximised, not limited.
Right: the rainy count is the metric and 2 is its limit.
questions.explain: The run is a subarray, its validity depends on a count, and the longest valid one is wanted.
questions.rule: When a problem defines valid subarrays and asks for the best one, such as the longest, think of a sliding window.

questions.q: True or false: Every problem that limits a subarray's sum and asks for its length must be solved with a sliding window.
questions.explain: The cues are a general guideline: not every problem with them needs a window, and not every window problem shows them.
questions.rule: Cues guide; they do not decide.
questions.teaches: The window cues are only a general guideline: not every problem with these characteristics should use a sliding window, and not every sliding window problem has them.

questions.q: Counting the stretches of consecutive days that have at most 2 rainy days is which type of problem?
options: Counting valid subarrays, which a sliding window can also handle
Finding the longest valid subarray, the only type a window handles
A two-input problem, since days and rain are two lists
Not a subarray problem, since it counts rather than measures
optionExplain: Right: the book says problems may ask for the number of valid subarrays.
A window also counts valid subarrays.
Days and rain describe one sequence.
The stretches are subarrays, and counting them is allowed.
questions.explain: Window problems ask for the best valid subarray or for the number of valid subarrays.
questions.rule: When a problem defines valid subarrays and asks for the best one, such as the longest, think of a sliding window.
questions.teaches: Besides the best valid subarray, a window problem may ask for the number of valid subarrays.

questions.q: The sum of the current window is needed after every step. What is the cheapest way to have it?
options: Copy the window into a new array and sum that array each step
Add up all of nums from index 0 again each step
A running variable: add the entering value and subtract the leaving one
Sort the window and read off the largest value
optionExplain: Copying and summing costs O(n) every time.
Re-adding from index 0 repeats all earlier work.
Right: each update costs O(1).
Sorting does not give a sum and costs more.
questions.explain: A single variable tracks the sum. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Keep the window's metric in one variable, updated in O(1) whenever an element enters or leaves.

questions.q: To remove the leftmost element from the sum, the code runs curr -= nums[____].
questions.explain: The leftmost element of the window sits at index left.
questions.rule: Entering: nums[right]. Leaving: nums[left].

questions.q: Calling final_state with nums = [2, 2, 2, 5] and k = 5 leaves curr equal to ____.
questions.explain: The window ends as [5] with sum 5: the 5 forces out all three 2s.
questions.rule: Keep the window's metric in one variable, updated in O(1) whenever an element enters or leaves.

questions.q: True or false: Window [4, 2, 1] has curr = 7; adding 3 on the right and removing 4 on the left makes curr 6.
questions.explain: 7 + 3 - 4 = 6, which matches the sum of [2, 1, 3].
questions.rule: curr += entering; curr -= leaving.

questions.q: This code is correct. What is its weakness?
options: It never moves left, so the window cannot shrink when it is invalid
It adds nums[right] twice, so the sum is larger than the true sum
It gives the wrong answer when the window sum equals exactly k
Re-summing the window at each check costs O(n) in the worst case
optionExplain: It does move left in the loop.
nums[right] is only read in the slice, never added twice.
The test curr > k treats equality as valid, which is correct.
Right: tracking the sum in a variable avoids the repeated summing.
questions.explain: The sum() call walks the whole window every time, so a variable is cheaper.
questions.rule: Keep the window's metric in one variable, updated in O(1) whenever an element enters or leaves.

questions.q: A binary string window tracks the number of zeros in curr. A 1 enters on the right. What happens to curr?
options: Nothing; curr only changes when a 0 enters or leaves
curr goes up by one, since a character entered
curr goes down by one, since a 1 is not a zero
curr doubles, since a 1 adds weight
optionExplain: Right: the update rule follows the metric.
That would count every character, not zeros.
The count of zeros does not fall when a 1 arrives.
Nothing about a 1 changes a zero count.
questions.explain: For a zero count, a 1 entering does nothing; a 0 entering adds one, and a 0 leaving subtracts one.
questions.rule: Keep the window's metric in one variable, updated in O(1) whenever an element enters or leaves.
questions.teaches: How curr is updated depends on the metric: for a count of zeros, only a 0 entering or leaving changes it.

questions.q: Inside the loop over right, when is the best length recorded?
options: Right after adding nums[right], before checking validity
After the while loop, once the window is valid again
Inside the while loop, after each removal
Once at the end, using the last window
optionExplain: The window may be invalid at that moment.
Right: the update must come from a valid window.
After one removal the window may still be invalid.
Earlier longer windows would be forgotten.
questions.explain: Only a valid window may set the answer. The card next shows the loop.
questions.rule: Add at right, shrink from left while invalid, then update the answer with right - left + 1.

questions.q: The length of the window between left and right is right - left + ____.
questions.explain: Both bounds are included, so the count is one more than the difference.
questions.rule: Window length is right - left + 1.

questions.q: Order the steps of one iteration of the sliding window loop.
items: While curr > k, subtract nums[left] and move left forward
questions.explain: Add first, repair while invalid, then record the valid window length.
questions.rule: Add at right, shrink from left while invalid, then update the answer with right - left + 1.

questions.q: What does the template return for the array and limit shown?
optionExplain: Two is shorter than the best valid window.
Length 4 windows such as [1, 3, 2, 1] have sum 7, above 5.
Right: the longest valid window is [2, 1, 1] with sum 4, of length 3.
Every window of length 5 has a sum above 5.
questions.explain: The longest window with sum at most 5 has 3 elements.
questions.rule: Add at right, shrink from left while invalid, then update the answer with right - left + 1.

questions.q: This version returns 2 for nums = [3, 4] and k = 3. What is the error?
options: It records the length before shrinking, so it counts a window that is invalid
It never moves left, so the window cannot shrink and its length keeps growing
It uses right - left as the length, which is one too small for every window
It leaves the loop as soon as the window is invalid, so later windows are never seen
optionExplain: Right: the true answer is 1, because [3, 4] has sum 7.
It does move left in the while loop.
The length formula is right - left + 1, which is used.
The loop continues; the error is where the update sits.
questions.explain: Updating before the while loop lets an invalid window set the answer.
questions.rule: Add at right, shrink from left while invalid, then update the answer with right - left + 1.

questions.q: Longest subarray with at most two zeros, in place of a sum limit. What changes in the template?
options: The for loop must become a nested loop that tries every start and end of a subarray
The answer must be updated inside the while loop, after each removal, instead of after it
Only the add and remove updates and the invalid test; the loop shape stays the same
The window length formula must change to right - left, since the zeros are not counted
optionExplain: The loop shape does not change.
The answer is still updated after shrinking.
Right: the problem-specific parts are the adding, the invalid test and the removing.
The window length stays right - left + 1.
questions.explain: In the book's general template, only the add logic, the invalid test, the remove logic and the answer update are specific to a problem.
questions.rule: Add at right, shrink from left while invalid, then update the answer with right - left + 1.
questions.teaches: In the general template, only the logic for adding an element, testing validity, removing an element and updating the answer is specific to a problem; the loop shape is fixed.

questions.q: An array has 6 elements. How many subarrays does it have in total?
optionExplain: Six counts only the single-element subarrays.
Twelve doubles the length, but there are subarrays of every length.
Thirty-six counts every pair of start and end, including ones where the end is before the start.
questions.explain: There are subarrays of every length. The card next counts them.
questions.rule: An array of n elements has n(n + 1)/2 subarrays, so looking at all of them costs at least O(n squared).

questions.q: There are n subarrays of length 1, n - 1 of length 2, and n - ____ of length 3.
questions.explain: A length-3 subarray can start at any index except the last two.
questions.rule: Length k: n - k + 1 subarrays.

questions.q: An array has 100 elements. How many subarrays does it have?
optionExplain: That counts only the length-1 subarrays.
That is 100 x 100, which counts invalid start-end pairs.
That is 100 x 101 without the division by two.
questions.explain: n(n + 1)/2 with n = 100 gives 5,050.
questions.rule: An array of n elements has n(n + 1)/2 subarrays, so looking at all of them costs at least O(n squared).

questions.q: An algorithm examines every subarray once, spending O(1) on each. Its running time is at least:
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n squared)
O(2n)
optionExplain: That is the cost of one pass over the array.
That would need fewer subarrays than exist.
Right: there are about n squared over 2 subarrays.
That is linear, the same class as O(n).
questions.explain: Visiting n(n + 1)/2 subarrays costs at least O(n squared).
questions.rule: An array of n elements has n(n + 1)/2 subarrays, so looking at all of them costs at least O(n squared).

questions.q: True or false: An array of n elements has n x n subarrays.
questions.explain: For n = 3 the subarrays number 3 + 2 + 1 = 6, not 9: pairs with the end before the start do not count.
questions.rule: Subarrays number n(n + 1)/2, not n squared.

questions.q: For n = 100,000, there are 5,000,050,000 subarrays. How many window steps does a sliding window guarantee, at most?
options: 200,000, since each bound moves at most 100,000 times
5,000,050,000, one step for every single subarray
100,000, since only the right bound ever moves
17, since the window halves its range each step
optionExplain: Right: the two bounds make at most 2n steps in total.
The window is built to avoid visiting every subarray.
The left bound also moves, up to n times.
The window does not halve; it slides step by step.
questions.explain: A sliding window guarantees a maximum of 2n window iterations, so with O(1) work per window it runs in O(n).
questions.rule: An array of n elements has n(n + 1)/2 subarrays, so looking at all of them costs at least O(n squared).
questions.teaches: A sliding window guarantees at most 2n window iterations, since right can move n times and left can move n times.

questions.q: A for loop over n elements contains a while loop that moves left forward. In the sliding window, the total time is:
options: O(n squared), because a loop sits inside a loop
O(n log n), because the while loop halves the window
O(n), because left moves at most n times in the whole run
O(1), because the while loop is not a for loop
optionExplain: Nesting alone does not multiply the work when the inner counter is shared.
Nothing is halved: left moves one step at a time.
Right: the inner loop shares a budget of n moves.
The while loop still does work, at most n steps in total.
questions.explain: The card next shows why the inner loop cannot cost n each time.
questions.rule: The inner while loop shares one budget of at most n moves of left across the whole run, so the window is O(n).

questions.q: Over the whole run, the while loop can iterate at most ____ times in total, where n is the input length.
questions.explain: left starts at 0, only increases, and never exceeds n.
questions.rule: Total while iterations are at most n.

questions.q: For nums = [2, 2, 2, 5] and k = 5, how many times in total does left move?
optionExplain: Right: left moves past the three 2s and ends at index 3.
Left must move, because 2 + 2 + 2 + 5 is far above 5.
Four is the number of right moves.
Seven is right moves plus left moves, not left alone.
questions.explain: Right moves 4 times and left moves 3 times, 7 steps in all, below the 2n = 8 bound.
questions.rule: The inner while loop shares one budget of at most n moves of left across the whole run, so the window is O(n).

questions.q: True or false: Nesting a while loop inside the for loop of a sliding window makes it O(n squared).
questions.explain: The while loop shares one counter, left, which can move at most n times in all, so the total stays O(n).
questions.rule: A shared forward-only counter bounds the inner loop.

questions.q: Our reading: suppose left were reset to 0 at the start of every for iteration. What happens to the O(n) argument?
options: It still holds, because the for loop still runs only n times
It improves, because the window restarts with fewer elements
It still holds, because the while loop only runs when the window is invalid
It breaks, because left could move up to n times in each iteration
optionExplain: The for loop runs n times, but each iteration could now cost n.
A restart would repeat work already done, not reduce it.
Invalid windows could then cost a scan from 0 each time.
Right: the argument needs left to start where it stopped.
questions.explain: Without a shared, forward-only left, there is no total budget of n moves.
questions.rule: The inner while loop shares one budget of at most n moves of left across the whole run, so the window is O(n).

questions.q: n = 1,000 and one iteration moves left 1,000 times. How many left moves can all other iterations make together?
options: 999, because each other iteration may move it once
0, because left cannot pass n
1,000, because each iteration has its own budget
1,000,000, because there are 1,000 iterations of 1,000 steps
optionExplain: That would take left past n.
Right: if it ran n times in one iteration, it does not run in the others.
The budget is shared, not per iteration.
That multiplies a budget that is spent only once.
questions.explain: If the while loop runs n times in one iteration, it cannot run at all in the others.
questions.rule: The inner while loop shares one budget of at most n moves of left across the whole run, so the window is O(n).
questions.teaches: If the inner loop runs n times in one iteration, it runs zero times in all other iterations, because left cannot exceed n.

questions.q: Positive integers and a sum limit k; find the longest subarray with sum at most k. Time and extra space of the window solution?
options: O(n squared) time and O(1) space
O(n) time and O(1) space
O(n) time and O(n) space, to store the window
O(n log n) time and O(1) space
optionExplain: That is the cost of testing every subarray.
Right: the window sweeps once and keeps only a few integers.
The window exists only as bounds and a sum, so no storage is needed.
No sorting or searching is involved.
questions.explain: One sweep and a few integers. The card next shows the details.
questions.rule: Add at right, shrink from the left while the sum is above k, and keep the longest valid window length.

questions.q: True or false: The answer is updated once per for iteration, after the while loop has made the window valid.
questions.explain: Only a valid window may set the answer, so the update follows the shrink step.
questions.rule: Shrink first, then record.

questions.q: For the array and limit shown, what is the length of the longest subarray with sum at most k?
optionExplain: A length-3 window is valid, but there is a longer one.
Every window of five elements has a sum above 5.
Six elements would sum above 5.
Right: the window [1, 2, 1, 1] has sum 5 and 4 elements.
questions.explain: The window [1, 2, 1, 1] has sum 5, and no longer window stays at or below 5.
questions.rule: Add at right, shrink from the left while the sum is above k, and keep the longest valid window length.

questions.q: k is larger than the sum of the whole array [1, 2, 3]. The window method returns ____.
questions.explain: The whole array is a valid window, and the window never has to shrink.
questions.rule: If nothing breaks the limit, the window covers everything.

questions.q: Every number in the array is above k, for example [4, 5, 6] with k = 3. What does the method return?
options: 0, because the window shrinks to empty each time
1, because the first element is always valid
3, because the whole array is the window
An error, because left passes right
optionExplain: Right: each element alone is above k, so the window is emptied and its length is 0.
A single element above k is not valid.
The window cannot be the whole array with a sum above k.
left may pass right, giving an empty window of length 0.
questions.explain: right - left + 1 equals 0 when left has moved one step past right.
questions.rule: Add at right, shrink from the left while the sum is above k, and keep the longest valid window length.

questions.q: A million positive readings are scanned with a sum limit. How many pointer moves does the window make, at most?
options: About a trillion, since every pair of readings is tried as a start and an end
About a million, since only right moves and left stays where it began
About two million, since right and left each move at most a million times
About twenty, since the window halves in size each time the pointers move
optionExplain: That is the cost of checking every subarray.
Left moves too, up to n times.
Right: the work per iteration is amortized constant.
The window does not halve.
questions.explain: The work in each iteration is amortized constant, so the whole run is O(n).
questions.rule: Add at right, shrink from the left while the sum is above k, and keep the longest valid window length.
questions.teaches: The work done in each loop iteration is amortized constant, which is why the whole run is O(n).

questions.q: You may flip at most one 0 in a binary string. Which question is equivalent to finding the longest all-1 substring afterwards?
options: The longest substring that contains no 1
The longest substring that contains exactly two 0s
The longest substring whose length is a power of two
The longest substring that contains at most one 0
optionExplain: That would ignore the 1s completely.
Two zeros cannot both be repaired by one flip.
Power-of-two lengths have nothing to do with a flip.
Right: flipping the lone 0 makes the whole substring 1s.
questions.explain: At most one 0 can be repaired. The card next uses this to set up a window.
questions.rule: Restate a flip-at-most-one problem as the longest window with at most one 0, and count zeros in curr.

questions.q: In the flip problem, the constraint metric is the number of ____ in the window.
questions.explain: The window is valid when it holds at most one 0.
questions.rule: Metric: count of zeros. Restriction: at most one.

questions.q: For s = 1011110010, the longest substring with at most one 0 has length ____.
questions.explain: The substring 101111 has one 0 and six characters; no longer one has at most one 0.
questions.rule: Restate a flip-at-most-one problem as the longest window with at most one 0, and count zeros in curr.

questions.q: For s = 1011110010, up to two zeros may be flipped. Which length does the window method return?
optionExplain: Right: the restriction becomes at most two zeros, and the best window has 7 characters.
Six is the answer for one flip.
No window of eight characters has two zeros or fewer.
The whole string has four zeros.
questions.explain: Only the restriction changes from curr > 1 to curr > 2; the loop is the same.
questions.rule: Restate a flip-at-most-one problem as the longest window with at most one 0, and count zeros in curr.

questions.q: True or false: This version subtracts 1 from curr every time left moves. For s = 1001, where the answer is 2, it returns 3.
questions.explain: A leaving 1 does not change the count of zeros, so lowering curr then lets a window with two zeros pass as valid.
questions.rule: curr falls only when a 0 leaves.

questions.q: A string over the symbols 0, 1, 2 allows flipping one non-1 symbol to 1. Does the at-most-one-0 restatement still work?
options: Yes, because zeros are the only symbols that can be flipped
No: it must count the non-1 symbols, since a symbol that is not 1 may be a 2
Yes, because the window method ignores symbols other than 1
No: the window method cannot work on strings with three symbols
optionExplain: A 2 can also be flipped, so counting only zeros would miss it.
Right: the restatement relies on the string being binary.
Counting is the whole method; symbols matter.
The window method works fine with a different metric.
questions.explain: Because the string holds only 1 and 0, every character other than 1 is a 0, so flipping makes the window all 1s.
questions.rule: Restate a flip-at-most-one problem as the longest window with at most one 0, and count zeros in curr.
questions.teaches: Since a binary string holds only 1 and 0, every character other than 1 is a 0, which is why one flip makes a window with one 0 all 1s.

questions.q: After shrinking, the valid window runs from index 2 to index 5. How many valid subarrays end at index 5?
optionExplain: Only the current window would be counted.
Two counts only the first and last choice.
Right: left bounds 2, 3, 4 and 5 give four windows.
Six counts indexes 0 to 5, but starts before index 2 are invalid.
questions.explain: Any start between left and right works. The card next states the count.
questions.rule: The number of valid windows ending at right equals the window size, right - left + 1.

questions.q: The number of valid windows ending at right is right - left + ____.
questions.explain: Both bounds are included, so there are one more than the difference.
questions.rule: Count = right - left + 1.

questions.q: The valid window after shrinking has left = 7 and right = 12. How many valid subarrays end at index 12?
optionExplain: Five forgets that both bounds are included.
Seven counts the left index itself, not the count.
Twelve is the right index.
questions.explain: right - left + 1 = 12 - 7 + 1 = 6.
questions.rule: The number of valid windows ending at right equals the window size, right - left + 1.

questions.q: True or false: A solution adds 1 to its count at each step, counting only the window from left to right.
questions.explain: Each step has right - left + 1 valid windows ending at right, not only one.
questions.rule: Add the window size, not 1.

questions.q: Sum limit 4, nums = [2, 1, 3, 1]. Counting valid windows by sizes after each step, what is the total?
optionExplain: Four counts one per index.
Six misses a window ending at the last index.
Right: sizes are 1, 2, 2 and 2, total 7.
Ten counts every subarray, but some have sum above 4.
questions.explain: Window sizes after each step: [2], [2, 1], [1, 3], [3, 1], so 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7.
questions.rule: The number of valid windows ending at right equals the window size, right - left + 1.

questions.q: Count subarrays of [1, 1, 1, 1] with sum at most 3. The answer variable should do what each step?
options: Keep the maximum window size, giving 3 at the end
Add the current window size to a running total, giving 9 at the end
Add 1 to a running total, giving 4 at the end
Add the number of elements removed from the left, giving 1 at the end
optionExplain: The maximum answers a longest-window question, not a counting one.
Right: sizes 1, 2, 3 and 3 add up to 9.
That counts one window per step.
Removals do not count windows.
questions.explain: When counting, the answer accumulates window sizes instead of recording a maximum.
questions.rule: The number of valid windows ending at right equals the window size, right - left + 1.
questions.teaches: When a problem asks for the number of valid subarrays, add the current window size to the answer after each shrink, instead of taking a maximum.

questions.q: Count subarrays whose product is strictly less than k. When is the window invalid?
options: When the product is greater than k
When the product is less than k
When the product equals zero
When the product is greater than or equal to k
optionExplain: That would let a product equal to k count as valid.
Those are the valid windows.
With positive integers a product is never zero.
Right: a product equal to k is not strictly less than k.
questions.explain: Strictly less means equal is not allowed. The card next gives the full loop.
questions.rule: Keep the product, shrink while it is at least k, and add the window size after each step.

questions.q: When an element leaves the window, curr is ____ by that element.
questions.explain: A product is undone by division, as a sum is undone by subtraction.
questions.rule: Product: multiply in, divide out.

questions.q: True or false: For nums = [3, 2, 4, 1] and k = 10, exactly 8 subarrays have a product below k.
questions.explain: Window sizes after each step are 1, 2, 2 and 3, so 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8; [3, 2, 4] has product 24 and is excluded.
questions.rule: Total = sum of window sizes after each shrink.

questions.q: With curr > k in place of curr >= k, what does nums = [10, 5, 2, 6] with k = 100 return?
options: It returns 8, since equality never occurs with positive integers
It returns 7, since it removes too many elements
It returns 9 instead of 8, counting [10, 5, 2] whose product is exactly 100
It fails with a division error, since curr becomes zero
optionExplain: Equality occurs here: 10 x 5 x 2 = 100.
The bug removes too few elements, not too many.
Right: strictly less than k requires removing the window when curr equals k.
Division by an element is always exact here.
questions.explain: A product equal to k is not allowed, so the shrink test must be curr >= k.
questions.rule: Keep the product, shrink while it is at least k, and add the window size after each step.

questions.q: For nums = [1, 1, 1] and k = 2, ____ subarrays have a product below k.
questions.explain: Every subarray has product 1, and there are 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 of them; the window never shrinks.
questions.rule: Window sizes 1, 2, 3 add up to 6.

questions.q: nums = [1, 1, 1] and k = 1. What shortcut does the book use here?
options: Return 0 at once, since no product of positive integers can be below 1
Return 3, since each of the three single elements counts as a valid subarray
Return 6, since every one of the six subarrays has a product that counts
Run the loop as usual and return the largest window size that it reaches
optionExplain: Right: every product is at least 1, so none is strictly less than k = 1.
Each element equals 1, which is not below 1.
No subarray qualifies.
Counting needs a total, not a maximum.
questions.explain: If k is at most 1 there can be no valid windows, so the answer is 0 immediately.
questions.rule: Keep the product, shrink while it is at least k, and add the window size after each step.
questions.teaches: If k is at most 1 the answer is 0 at once, because a product of positive integers is at least 1 and so never strictly less than k.

questions.q: The window length is fixed at 3. Index 7 is added on the right. Which index leaves on the left?
optionExplain: Index 3 would leave a window of five elements.
Index 5 would leave a window of only two elements.
Index 6 would leave a window of only one element.
Right: 7 - 3 = 4, leaving indexes 5, 6 and 7.
questions.explain: The leaving index is i - k. The card next shows the loop.
questions.rule: For a fixed length k, build the first window, then add index i and remove index i - k at each step.

questions.q: When adding the element at index i, the code removes the element at index i - ____.
questions.explain: The window length stays k when index i - k leaves.
questions.rule: Add i, remove i - k.

questions.q: What does the fixed-window largest-sum code return for the input shown?
optionExplain: Eighteen is the second window's sum, [4, 2, 10, 2].
Right: the last window [3, 1, 0, 20] sums to 24.
Twenty is the largest single value.
No window of four elements sums to 27.
questions.explain: The window sums are 17, 18, 17, 16, 6 and 24, so the maximum is 24.
questions.rule: For a fixed length k, build the first window, then add index i and remove index i - k at each step.

questions.q: Order these windows from the first one the code builds to the last one it reaches, for the input shown.
questions.explain: The window moves one index right each step, so the sums run 17, 18, 17, 16, 6, 24.
questions.rule: For a fixed length k, build the first window, then add index i and remove index i - k at each step.

questions.q: This version removes nums[i - k + 1] instead of nums[i - k]. What does the final print show?
options: 24, the correct answer, because only the first window matters
22, because the window loses the wrong element and its sum drifts
It raises an index error on the first slide
17, the sum of the first window only
optionExplain: The first window is right, but later sums are wrong.
Right: the removed element is off by one, so each window sum is wrong.
The index is valid on every slide.
The loop still runs and updates the answer.
questions.explain: Removing the wrong element makes the tracked sum differ from the real window sum.
questions.rule: For a fixed length k, build the first window, then add index i and remove index i - k at each step.
questions.code:
def max_window_sum(nums, k):
    curr = sum(nums[:k])
    ans = curr
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        curr += nums[i] - nums[i - k + 1]
        ans = max(ans, curr)
    return ans

print(max_window_sum([1, 4, 2, 10, 2, 3, 1, 0, 20], 4))

questions.q: A fixed window builds its first k elements in one loop and slides over the rest in another. How many iterations in all?
options: n times k, since each slide re-adds k elements
n - k only, since the build is free
k only, since the slide is constant
n, since k builds plus n - k slides each do constant work
optionExplain: The slide adds and removes one element, not k.
The build loop does k iterations.
The slide loop runs n - k times, which is not constant.
Right: constant work per iteration over n iterations is O(n).
questions.explain: Total for-loop iterations equal n and the work in each is constant, so the time is O(n) with O(1) space.
questions.rule: For a fixed length k, build the first window, then add index i and remove index i - k at each step.
questions.teaches: The two loops together make n iterations of constant work, so a fixed window runs in O(n) time with O(1) space.

questions.q: A problem states that the subarray must have length exactly k. Which kind of window fits?
options: A fixed window that adds one element and removes one at each step
A dynamic window that shrinks while the sum is too large
Two pointers that start at the ends
A window whose size is chosen by trying every length
optionExplain: Right: a stated length is the sign of a fixed window.
A dynamic window needs a validity rule, not a stated length.
The ends recipe does not slide a window.
Trying every length is the slow approach.
questions.explain: A stated length means fixed. The card next compares the two kinds.
questions.rule: If the length is given, slide a fixed window; if validity is defined, grow and shrink a dynamic one.

questions.q: True or false: A fixed-size window needs a while loop that shrinks it until it becomes valid.
questions.explain: A fixed window adds one and removes one each step, so no shrinking loop is needed.
questions.rule: Fixed: no while loop.

questions.q: Sort each task into Fixed window or Dynamic window.

items.t: Largest sum among subarrays of length 4
Longest subarray with sum at most k
Longest substring with at most one zero
Average of every run of 7 days
Number of subarrays with product below k

questions.explain: A stated length means fixed; a validity rule means dynamic.
questions.rule: If the length is given, slide a fixed window; if validity is defined, grow and shrink a dynamic one.

questions.q: In which loop does the window size change from step to step?
options: The loop for the largest sum of length-4 subarrays
The loop for the average of every 7 days
The loop for the longest subarray with sum at most k
The loop that builds the first window of size k
optionExplain: A fixed window always has the same size.
Seven-day windows stay seven days.
Right: the dynamic window grows and shrinks.
The build loop only fills the first window.
questions.explain: Only a dynamic window changes its size.
questions.rule: If the length is given, slide a fixed window; if validity is defined, grow and shrink a dynamic one.

questions.q: True or false: A fixed-window loop that adds index i must also remove index i, or the window cannot slide.
questions.explain: It removes index i - k, the element that falls out the left side.
questions.rule: Remove i - k, not i.

questions.q: Why does the book call fixed-size problems easy?
options: They need no variable to track the window at all
Their answers never need updating after the first window
They always come with an input that is already sorted
Only two elements change between adjacent windows
optionExplain: A running sum or count is still needed.
The answer is still updated at each step.
Sorting is not required.
Right: only two elements change between adjacent windows.
questions.explain: The difference between any two adjacent fixed windows is only two elements.
questions.rule: If the length is given, slide a fixed window; if validity is defined, grow and shrink a dynamic one.
questions.teaches: Fixed-size problems are easy because the difference between any two adjacent windows is only two elements: one added on the right and one removed on the left.

questions.q: True or false: Every sliding window problem can track its metric with a single integer.
questions.explain: Many window problems also need a hash map. The card next sets out what comes later.
questions.rule: A single integer tracks simple metrics, and many other window problems also need a hash map, covered later.

questions.q: Which structure do many sliding window problems also use?
options: A hash map
A second sorted copy of the array
A stack of window bounds
A binary tree of window sums
optionExplain: Right: the book says many window problems use a hash map, introduced in the hashing chapter.
Sorting would destroy the order that windows depend on.
The bounds are two plain integers.
A tree is not part of the window method.
questions.explain: The hashing chapter comes before more window problems.
questions.rule: A single integer tracks simple metrics, and many other window problems also need a hash map, covered later.

questions.q: Our reading: sort each metric into One integer is enough or Needs a count per value.

items.t: sum of the window
number of zeros in the window
product of the window
number of different values in the window
how often each letter occurs in the window

questions.explain: Sums, products and zero counts fit in one integer; distinct values and per-letter frequencies need a count for each value.
questions.rule: A single integer tracks simple metrics, and many other window problems also need a hash map, covered later.

questions.q: Our reading: find the longest substring with at most 2 different letters. What extra tool does the window likely need?
options: A second integer holding the product of the letters
A hash map counting each letter in the window
A sorted copy of the string
A separate array holding the window
optionExplain: A product does not say how many different letters exist.
Right: the number of unique letters needs a count per letter.
Sorting would lose the order.
Storing the window is the approach the card warns against.
questions.explain: Counting unique elements needs to know how often each one occurs.
questions.rule: A single integer tracks simple metrics, and many other window problems also need a hash map, covered later.

questions.q: True or false: The integer-tracking patterns in this chapter cover every sliding window problem.
questions.explain: The book says it only scratched the surface because many window problems need a hash map.
questions.rule: One integer is not always enough.

questions.q: A learner asks why this chapter skips many classic window problems. According to the book, why?
options: They are too easy to be worth teaching, so the course leaves them as exercises
They need the array to be sorted first, a tool the course has not covered yet
Many need a hash map, so the course returns to them after the hashing chapter
They are fixed-size problems, which belong to a separate chapter later in the course
optionExplain: The reason is missing tools, not ease.
Sorting is not the missing tool.
Right: the book says it will look at more window problems after hash maps.
They are not fixed-size problems.
questions.explain: After learning hash maps, the course comes back to more sliding window problems.
questions.rule: A single integer tracks simple metrics, and many other window problems also need a hash map, covered later.
questions.teaches: After the hashing chapter, the course returns to more sliding window problems that need a hash map.

questions.q: For nums = [2, 4, 1, 3], which array lists the running totals prefix[0] to prefix[3]?
optionExplain: That repeats the array without adding.
That counts totals from the right end, not from index 0.
Right: 2, then 2+4, then 2+4+1, then 2+4+1+3.
That shifts the totals by one place and drops the last.
questions.explain: Each entry adds one more element to the total. The card next defines it.
questions.rule: prefix[i] is the sum of nums[0] through nums[i], inclusive.

questions.q: prefix[0] equals nums[____].
questions.explain: The prefix that ends at index 0 contains only nums[0].
questions.rule: prefix[0] = nums[0].

questions.q: For nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2], what is prefix[3]?
optionExplain: Eight leaves out nums[3] itself, which is inclusive.
Four is the sum of nums[1] and nums[2] and nums[3] only partly counted.
Fourteen includes nums[4], which is past index 3.
questions.explain: prefix[3] covers indexes 0 to 3 inclusive.
questions.rule: prefix[i] is the sum of nums[0] through nums[i], inclusive.

questions.q: Which of these is a prefix of the array [7, 8, 9]?
optionExplain: It starts at index 1, so it is a subarray but not a prefix.
It skips the 8, so it is not contiguous.
It starts at the last index.
Right: a prefix starts at index 0 and is contiguous.
questions.explain: Prefixes are the subarrays that start at index 0.
questions.rule: prefix[i] is the sum of nums[0] through nums[i], inclusive.

questions.q: True or false: A student says prefix[i] excludes nums[i] and covers only indexes 0 to i - 1.
questions.explain: The book's prefix[i] includes nums[i]; the sum of the elements before index i is prefix[i - 1].
questions.rule: prefix[i] includes nums[i].

questions.q: What does the last entry of a prefix sum array tell you about the whole array?
options: It equals the largest element of the array
It equals the sum of every element of the array
It equals the sum of all elements except the last
It equals the length of the array
optionExplain: Running totals of positive numbers do not give a maximum.
Right: the last prefix runs from index 0 to the final index.
The last prefix includes the last element.
Length is a count, not a sum.
questions.explain: The last prefix covers the whole array, so prefix[n - 1] is the total, as the splitting example uses.
questions.rule: prefix[i] is the sum of nums[0] through nums[i], inclusive.
questions.teaches: The last entry, prefix[n - 1], is the sum of the whole array, which later examples use as the total.

questions.q: prefix = [3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25]. Which calculation gives the sum of the elements at indexes 2 to 5?
options: prefix[5] - prefix[2]
prefix[5] - prefix[1]
prefix[5] + prefix[2]
prefix[2] - prefix[5]
optionExplain: That drops the element at index 2 from the answer.
Adding gives a sum that counts the early part twice.
Subtracting in the wrong order gives a negative number.
questions.explain: Remove everything before index 2. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The sum of nums[i..j] is prefix[j] minus the sum of everything before i, prefix[i - 1].

questions.q: The sum of nums[i..j] is prefix[j] - prefix[____].
questions.explain: prefix[i - 1] is the sum of everything before index i.
questions.rule: Range sum = prefix[j] - prefix[i - 1].

questions.q: prefix = [3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25]. The elements at indexes 1 to 4 sum to what?
optionExplain: Fourteen is prefix[4] alone, including index 0.
Ten uses prefix[4] - prefix[1], dropping index 1.
Nineteen is a different range, indexes 2 to 5.
Right: prefix[4] - prefix[0] = 14 - 3 = 11.
questions.explain: Subtract prefix[0] = 3 from prefix[4] = 14.
questions.rule: The sum of nums[i..j] is prefix[j] minus the sum of everything before i, prefix[i - 1].

questions.q: True or false: For indexes 2 to 5, a student computes prefix[5] - prefix[2] = 15 and calls it the range sum.
questions.explain: The subtraction should use prefix[1] = 4, giving 19; using prefix[2] drops nums[2] from the answer.
questions.rule: Subtract prefix[i - 1], not prefix[i].

questions.q: For i = 0, prefix[i - 1] is out of bounds. Which form of the formula avoids that?
options: prefix[j] - prefix[i] + nums[i]
prefix[j] + prefix[i] - nums[i]
prefix[j] - nums[i]
prefix[i] - prefix[j] + nums[i]
optionExplain: Right: subtracting prefix[i] removes nums[i] too, so nums[i] is added back.
The signs are wrong.
That removes only one element, not everything before i.
The order of subtraction is reversed.
questions.explain: prefix[j] - prefix[i] + nums[i] equals prefix[j] - prefix[i - 1] and never reads index -1.
questions.rule: The sum of nums[i..j] is prefix[j] minus the sum of everything before i, prefix[i - 1].
questions.teaches: prefix[j] - prefix[i] + nums[i] is an equivalent formula that avoids the out-of-bounds read at i = 0.

questions.q: A program must answer thousands of questions of the form: total of the readings from index x to index y. Which tool fits?
options: A sliding window, since the questions are about subarrays
Two pointers from both ends, since each question has two indexes
A prefix sum array, since it suits arrays of numbers and sums of subarrays
A string builder, since the answers must be assembled
optionExplain: A window finds valid subarrays; it does not answer arbitrary range queries.
Having two indexes does not make this the edge recipe.
Right: many subarray-sum queries are what prefix sums are for.
Nothing is being built as a string.
questions.explain: A prefix sum is a great tool whenever a problem involves sums of a subarray and the data are numbers.
questions.rule: The sum of nums[i..j] is prefix[j] minus the sum of everything before i, prefix[i - 1].
questions.teaches: Prefix sums are used on arrays of numbers and are a great tool whenever a problem involves sums of a subarray.

questions.q: Building the prefix sum array of an n-element array in one pass costs:
options: O(1) time
O(log n) time
O(n squared) time
O(n) time
optionExplain: Every element must be visited once.
Nothing here halves the data.
Each entry reuses the previous one, so no nested work is needed.
Right: one addition per element.
questions.explain: One pass is enough. The card next shows the loop.
questions.rule: Start with the first element, then append each element plus the previous prefix value.

questions.q: The prefix array starts as [nums[____]].
questions.explain: The first prefix is the first element on its own.
questions.rule: Start with nums[0].

questions.q: For nums = [4, 0, 3, 2], prefix[3] is ____.
questions.explain: The prefix array is [4, 4, 7, 9].
questions.rule: Start with the first element, then append each element plus the previous prefix value.

questions.q: An array of 1,000,000 numbers gets a prefix sum array. About how much extra memory does that array need?
options: About one million entries, one per element
A fixed handful of entries, whatever the length
About a thousand entries, one per block of a thousand
About twenty entries, one per halving
optionExplain: Right: the prefix array has as many entries as the input.
That is the cost of keeping only a running total.
Nothing is stored per block.
Nothing is halved.
questions.explain: The prefix array is n entries, so O(n) space.
questions.rule: Start with the first element, then append each element plus the previous prefix value.

questions.q: True or false: This build loop starts at index 0 instead of 1. For [4, 0, 3, 2] it returns [4, 8, 8, 11, 13].
questions.explain: nums[0] is added to prefix[0] = nums[0] again, so the first element is counted twice and the array is one entry too long.
questions.rule: Start the loop at index 1.

questions.q: A program first fills a table of running totals, then answers many questions from it. What is this strategy called in the book?
options: Amortization: spreading one slow step over many fast ones
Pre-processing: store computed data before the main logic runs
Brute force: trying every possibility
