Backtracking: undoing choices when they fail
optionExplain: Amortization is a way of counting cost, not a strategy of precomputing.
Right: building a prefix sum is a form of pre-processing.
Brute force would redo the work for every question.
Nothing is being undone.
questions.explain: Pre-processing pays some time up front to save a huge amount of time later.
questions.rule: Start with the first element, then append each element plus the previous prefix value.

questions.code:
def ways_to_split(nums):
    total = 0
    left_section = 0
    ans = 0
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
        left_section += nums[i]
        total += nums[i]
        right_section = total - left_section
        if left_section >= right_section:
            ans += 1
    return ans

Prefix arrays are exactly the tool for queries.
questions.explain: In the split problem prefix values were needed in incremental order, so the array was not needed.
questions.rule: Replace the stored prefix array with a running left sum and a precomputed total.
questions.teaches: The prefix array can be dropped in the split problem because the prefix values are needed in incremental order of index.

questions.explain: Allocation and shifting are implementation details. The interface only says which operations exist, what they take and what they return.
questions.rule: Interface is how you use it; implementation is how it works inside.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it belongs to a hash map's interface or its implementation.
questions.explain: Operations, inputs and outputs are the contract you call. Memory layout, sizing and re-hashing happen behind the contract.

items.t: Adding a key-value pair with an insert call
Checking whether a key exists
Re-hashing every key when the table grows
Choosing how big the underlying array is
What a lookup returns
Where in memory each pair is stored

questions.rule: If you call it or read its result, it is interface.

questions.q: A coder writes: 'calling append adds a value to the end and returns nothing.' Which part of the dynamic array is this?
questions.explain: Describing an operation by input and result is describing the interface.
options: Its implementation: the code that grows the array
Its interface: a defined operation, its input and its result
Its memory layout: the block holding the elements
Its hash function: how elements are indexed
optionExplain: It sounds like how the array works, but nothing here says how memory is handled.
Right: it states what the operation does and returns, which is the contract.
The sentence never mentions where elements live.
A dynamic array has no hash function; this is a mix-up with hash maps.
questions.rule: Learn a data structure's interface well enough to use the built-in version; treat the implementation as background.

questions.q: A candidate spends an interview writing a hash table from raw arrays before reading the problem. According to the book, what is the issue?
questions.explain: The book's advice: understand the interface and use the built-in.
options: Hash tables cannot be built from arrays in an interview setting
The interface cannot be known until the implementation is written
Built-in structures are too unreliable to trust in interviews
Built-ins are expected, so the time is better spent on the problem
optionExplain: They can; the book says tables sit on a fixed-size array. The issue is time, not feasibility.
The interface is documented separately from the code, so it can be learned first.
The book makes no such claim; it says the opposite.
Right: the book says you are expected to use built-ins, not implement them.
questions.rule: Learn a data structure's interface well enough to use the built-in version; treat the implementation as background.

questions.q: A language's list type has a remove(x) operation. Which fact about it belongs to the interface?
questions.explain: The interface also states the specific rules for using an operation and what it returns; the book notes that appending to a dynamic array typically returns nothing.
options: What happens or is returned when x is absent
How the list shifts the remaining elements left
How much extra memory the list reserves
Which sorting method the list uses inside
optionExplain: Right: inputs, outputs and rules for using an operation are the contract.
That is internal; callers need not know how the shifting is done.
Reserve size is an implementation choice.
Not part of the contract of remove.
questions.teaches: An interface covers an operation's inputs and outputs too, for example appending to a dynamic array typically returns nothing, so what a call returns is part of the contract.
questions.rule: Learn a data structure's interface well enough to use the built-in version; treat the implementation as background.

questions.q: A function converts the word cat to a number. What property should it have when called twice on cat?
questions.explain: Repeatability is the guess to make. The card next gives the full definition.
options: It returns the same number both times
It returns a bigger number the second time
It returns a random number each time
It returns the number of times it was called
optionExplain: Right: a hash function is deterministic.
Growth would make stored keys impossible to find again.
Randomness would break repeat lookups of the same key.
That tracks calls, not the key.
questions.rule: A hash function maps each key to the same integer every time, and that integer is below a size the programmer chose.

questions.q: An input handed to a hash function is called a ____.
questions.explain: Inputs to a hash function are keys; the same key always converts to the same integer.
questions.rule: Input = key; output = integer below a fixed size.

questions.q: A table has size 100. A hash function must send any key to a legal position. Which output range is allowed?
questions.explain: With fixed size s the outputs are 0 to s - 1.
options: 0 up to 99
1 up to 100
0 up to 100
Any non-negative integer
optionExplain: Right: the integer must be less than the fixed size, so 0 to size minus 1.
Positions start at 0, so 100 would be one slot beyond the end.
Size 100 allows 0 to 99; 100 would fall outside the fixed size.
The fixed size is the limit on the output.
questions.rule: A hash function maps each key to the same integer every time, and that integer is below a size the programmer chose.

questions.q: True or false: if a hash function sends one key to 7 today, it may send it to 9 tomorrow, as long as both are below the fixed size.
questions.explain: The same input must always produce the same integer. A key that moved would not be found where it was stored.
questions.rule: Same key, same integer.

questions.q: A designer says: 'My hash function adds one to a global counter each call and returns it modulo 50.' What breaks?
questions.explain: Determinism means the output depends only on the key.
options: The output can land beyond the fixed size of the table
It cannot accept keys that are strings, only numbers
The same key gets different integers on different calls
It returns integers that are too small to index an array
optionExplain: The modulo keeps it below 50, so the limit holds.
Nothing in the design limits the input type.
Right: the output depends on call history, not on the key.
Size is not the issue; repeatability is.
questions.rule: A hash function maps each key to the same integer every time, and that integer is below a size the programmer chose.

questions.q: The book shows a letter-weighting recipe for strings. What does the book say about its quality?
questions.explain: Any recipe that gives a repeatable integer in range qualifies, but quality varies; the book calls its own example a poor hash function.
options: It is the recommended recipe that real hash maps use
It converts strings to integers but is not a good hash function
It is incorrect because it can return negative numbers
It works only for numeric keys, not for strings of letters
optionExplain: The book states the opposite.
Right: it is an illustration of converting strings, not a recommended design.
Negative numbers are not the problem it mentions.
It is written for strings of letters.
questions.teaches: The book's own letter-weighting algorithm is described as not actually a good hash function; it only shows how strings can be converted into integers.
questions.rule: A hash function maps each key to the same integer every time, and that integer is below a size the programmer chose.

questions.q: A hash function must keep its result below a fixed size x. Which final step guarantees that for any non-negative total?
questions.explain: Modulo is the operation to guess; the card shows the full recipe.
options: Divide the total by x
Subtract x from the total once
Multiply the total by x
Take the total modulo x
optionExplain: The quotient can still exceed x - 1 when the total is large.
A large total stays too big after one subtraction.
That makes the result larger, not smaller.
Right: total % x always lands from 0 to x - 1.
questions.rule: Weight each letter by its place, add them up, then take the total modulo the limit.

questions.q: True or false: the recipe multiplies each letter's alphabet value by its index counted from 0, so the first letter adds nothing.
questions.explain: The multiplier is the index plus 1, so the first letter counts once. The final modulo then keeps the value in the range 0 to x - 1.
questions.rule: Multiply by index + 1, then take the total modulo x.

questions.q: What does h applied to the string cab with x = 5 return?
questions.explain: Letters c, a, b are worth 3, 1, 2 at places 1, 2, 3: total 11, remainder 1 after dividing by 5.
optionExplain: That is the total before the modulo.
11 divided by 5 leaves 1, not 0.
That would come from 12 % 5; the total is 11.
questions.rule: Weight each letter by its place, add them up, then take the total modulo the limit.

questions.q: Using h from the code with the string zz and x = 7, the result is ____.
questions.hint: Add 26 times 1 and 26 times 2 first.
questions.rule: Weight each letter by its place, add them up, then take the total modulo the limit.

questions.q: Ana hand-computes the total for bad as 2x0 + 1x1 + 4x2 = 9. Which mistake did she make?
questions.explain: The multiplier is the current place in the string, index + 1.
options: She used the wrong alphabet position for b
She used the index starting at 0 instead of index plus 1
She forgot the modulo
She should have multiplied the letters instead of adding
optionExplain: b is 2, which she used correctly.
Right: the recipe multiplies by index + 1, so the total is 2x1 + 1x2 + 4x3 = 16.
No limit was given, so there is nothing to take modulo of yet.
The recipe adds the weighted values.
questions.rule: Weight each letter by its place, add them up, then take the total modulo the limit.

questions.q: A first draft of the string recipe ends with: 'after going through every character, total is the converted value.' What is the verdict?
questions.explain: The book first writes the recipe without a limit, then says it is wrong and repairs it with the modulo.
options: Wrong for a fixed-size table: the total must become total % x
Correct, because an integer total is already a valid converted value
Correct, because 26 letter values keep the total small enough
Wrong, because the converted value should be turned back into a letter
optionExplain: Right: the book says the draft is wrong until the modulo is added.
An integer is not enough; it must also be below the fixed size.
The total grows with string length, so 26 values do not bound it.
The output is an integer, not a letter.
questions.teaches: The book says the draft without the final modulo is wrong, because the total must be limited to a fixed size.
questions.rule: Weight each letter by its place, add them up, then take the total modulo the limit.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: An array reads position 7 instantly. Which change lets the same speed work for the key banana?
questions.explain: Converting the key to an integer is the guess. The card shows how that is done.
options: Sort the keys alphabetically and scan from the top
Store every key as a longer string
Convert the key to an integer position first
Keep two arrays side by side and compare them
optionExplain: Scanning grows with the number of keys, so it is not constant time.
Longer strings do not create positions.
Right: a conversion step turns the key into something that can index the array.
Comparing walks through entries instead of jumping to one.
questions.rule: A hash function plus an array gives key-to-value lookup in which the key can be almost anything.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: With arrays we map indices to values; with hash maps we map ____ to values.
questions.explain: A hash map maps keys to values, and the keys can be almost anything.
questions.rule: Arrays map indices; hash maps map keys.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: A school needs to fetch a pupil record by name in constant time. What combination makes that possible?
questions.explain: The hash function makes a name usable as an index.
options: A sorted array searched by repeatedly halving the range
Two parallel arrays, names and records, scanned together
A dynamic array that grows as each new name is added
An array plus a hash function that maps names to integers
optionExplain: That takes logarithmic time, not constant.
Scanning for the name takes time that grows with the class.
Growth does not turn a name into a position.
Right: the hash result picks the array position for the name.
questions.rule: A hash function plus an array gives key-to-value lookup in which the key can be almost anything.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: Match each part to its job.
questions.explain: The array stores by index, the hash function creates the index from the key, and together they form the hash map.
pairs: converts a key to an integer below a fixed size
maps keys to values using both
questions.rule: Array stores; hash function indexes; hash map combines them.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: A student says: 'A hash map is built on an array, so its keys must be integers.' What is the flaw?
questions.explain: The restriction to integers belongs to the array, and the hash function lifts it.
options: The hash function turns each key into an integer used as the index
Hash maps are not built on arrays at all; they use another structure
Arrays accept any key type directly, so no conversion is needed
Integer keys are slower to hash than string keys, so they are avoided
optionExplain: Right: the integer is made from the key, not the key itself.
They are: the book says a hash function is combined with an array.
Array indices have to be integers.
Speed is not the point; the conversion removes the restriction.
questions.rule: A hash function plus an array gives key-to-value lookup in which the key can be almost anything.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: In Python, which declaration creates an empty hash map?
questions.explain: Applying the idea in Python gives the dictionary.
options: dic = []
dic = {}
dic = ()
dic = hash()
optionExplain: That creates a list, which is indexed by integers.
Right: Python calls its hash map a dictionary, and declaring one is that simple.
That creates an empty tuple, which cannot hold new key-value pairs.
hash() is a function that converts one value, not a container.
questions.teaches: In Python the built-in hash map is called a dictionary, and declaring an empty one is as simple as dic = {}.
questions.rule: A hash function plus an array gives key-to-value lookup in which the key can be almost anything.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: Which of these can usually serve as a hash map key, as a general rule of thumb?
questions.explain: The next card names the rule behind this.
options: A string
A list of numbers you may append to later
A shopping cart object that gains items
A running total that changes every step
optionExplain: Right: strings are immutable and are common keys.
A list can change after creation, so it is usually refused.
An object that changes after creation breaks the key idea.
A changing variable is not a stable key.
questions.rule: Keys are immutable; values can be anything.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: True or false: values stored in a hash map must be immutable, as keys are.
questions.explain: Only keys carry the immutability constraint. Values can be anything.
questions.rule: Keys immutable, values anything.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: Sort by whether the item can serve as a hash map key by the rule of thumb.
questions.explain: Integers, strings and tuples cannot be changed once made. Lists are mutable, so they are not used as keys directly.

items.t: An integer
A string of letters
A tuple of integers
A list of integers
A list of strings
A list of tuples

questions.rule: Immutable in, mutable out.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: A map has string keys and list values. Does it break the stated constraint?
questions.explain: Only the key side is restricted.
options: Yes: values must be immutable in the same way as keys
Yes: values must be integers or other numeric types
No: only keys are restricted; values can be any type
No, but only if every stored list is empty at the start
optionExplain: The constraint is on keys only.
Values can be anything, not only integers.
Right: lists are fine as values.
The contents of a value do not matter.
questions.rule: Keys are immutable; values can be anything.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: A coder converts every value to a tuple before storing it, saying hash map values must be immutable. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Immutability is for keys.
options: Tuples cannot be placed in a hash map as values at all
The constraint is on keys, so converting is unnecessary
Values have to be strings rather than tuples or lists
Tuples are mutable, so they would fail as keys anyway
optionExplain: They can; values can be anything.
Right: the effort protects the wrong side.
No type is demanded of values.
Tuples are immutable, so they work as keys.
questions.rule: Keys are immutable; values can be anything.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: A developer moves to a language they do not know and assumes mutable keys are rejected exactly as in Python. What does the book advise?
questions.explain: Keep the rule of thumb and read the language's documentation.
options: Keep it as a rule of thumb, but check that language's rules
Trust the assumption, because all languages treat keys identically
Ignore immutability, since it does not affect which keys work
Use only integer keys, which every language accepts
optionExplain: Right: the book says it is language dependent but generally a good rule of thumb.
The book says the rule varies by language.
It usually does; ignoring it is risky.
No such restriction is stated.
questions.teaches: The immutability requirement is language dependent, though generally a good rule of thumb.
questions.rule: Keys are immutable; values can be anything.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: How does the time to check whether a key exists in a hash map change as the map grows?
questions.explain: Constant is the guess; the card explains why.
options: It grows in proportion to the number of keys
It grows with the logarithm of the number of keys
It grows with the square of the number of keys
It stays constant
optionExplain: That describes scanning an array.
That is binary search on sorted data.
No lookup works that slowly by design.
Right: an existence check is O(1).
questions.rule: A hash map does add, remove, update and exists in O(1); iteration order is not guaranteed.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: Adding, removing and checking a key in a hash map each take ____ time in Big-O notation.
questions.explain: These operations are O(1): they do not grow with the size of the map.
questions.rule: Add, remove, update and exists are O(1).

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: An app keeps 1,000,000 usernames in a hash map. How many usernames does it scan to check if a given one exists?
questions.explain: O(1) means the cost does not depend on map size.
options: A fixed number of steps, whatever the count
Up to 1,000,000 usernames, one after another
About 1,000, the square root of the count
About 20, the logarithm of the count
optionExplain: Right: the check is O(1), independent of the million.
That is the cost of scanning an array.
A square root scan is not how hash maps work.
That is the cost of a binary search on sorted data.
questions.rule: A hash map does add, remove, update and exists in O(1); iteration order is not guaranteed.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: True or false: by the book's description, looping over the keys of a hash map returns them in the order they were inserted.
questions.explain: A hash map is unordered: iteration over keys and values need not follow any order, and for built-in types it depends on the language.
questions.rule: Do not rely on hash map iteration order.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: A student says: 'Because a hash map is unordered, updating the value of an existing key must be slow.' What is wrong?
questions.explain: Order and speed are separate properties.
options: Updating is slow only when the keys are strings
Unordered refers to iteration order, not speed
Unordered maps cannot update values after insertion
The statement is right, but updates take log n
optionExplain: No key type is singled out.
Right: the lack of order does not slow single-key operations.
They can; update is one of the O(1) operations.
Updates are constant time.
questions.rule: A hash map does add, remove, update and exists in O(1); iteration order is not guaranteed.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: A to-do app must show tasks in the order they were added. How does a hash map fit, going by the book's definitions?
questions.explain: An ordered data structure remembers insertion order; an unordered one treats insertion order as irrelevant.
options: Perfectly, since it stores its pairs in the order they arrive
Perfectly, because loops over it give insertion order
Not by itself: it is unordered, so insertion order is lost
Not at all, since it cannot hold a long list of tasks at once
optionExplain: That is what an ordered structure does.
The book says iteration need not follow any order.
Right: an ordered structure remembers insertion order; an unordered one does not.
It holds many keys.
questions.teaches: The book defines an ordered data structure as one that remembers insertion order, and an unordered one as one where insertion order is not relevant.
questions.rule: A hash map does add, remove, update and exists in O(1); iteration order is not guaranteed.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: A brute-force method with an inner search is O(n squared). Replace the search by a hash map check. What is the likely new complexity?
questions.explain: The card names this effect.
options: O(n squared) still
O(n)
O(n cubed)
optionExplain: A constant-time check removes the inner loop's cost.
Right: the factor of n from the inner search is removed.
The outer loop still visits every element.
A hash map does not make an algorithm slower in this way.
questions.rule: Many problems get a factor of n faster with a hash map, so master your language's hash map interface.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: True or false: the book says only a few languages come with a built-in hash map.
questions.explain: Every major language has a built-in hash map, so you rarely need to write one.
questions.rule: Built-in hash maps are everywhere.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: A pair-finding routine runs an O(n) search inside an outer O(n) loop. With a hash map making the inner check O(1), the total is O(____).
questions.explain: n iterations of constant-time work give O(n). A factor of n disappears when the inner scan becomes a lookup.
questions.rule: Replace an inner scan with a lookup to drop a factor of n.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: If you could study only one thing from the course, which does the book say to choose?
questions.explain: It points to the interface, not the internals.
options: The implementation of a hash table from scratch
The hash map interface in the language you use
Sorting algorithms in every language
The Big-O of every built-in structure
optionExplain: The book treats implementation as background.
Right: the book names this as the single thing to master.
The book does not rank sorting this way.
Complexity matters, but the book names the hash map interface.
questions.rule: Many problems get a factor of n faster with a hash map, so master your language's hash map interface.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: A student concludes: 'The book promises that a hash map speeds up any algorithm by a factor of n.' What is wrong?
questions.explain: Be exact about the claim: a huge amount of problems, not every algorithm.
options: It says a huge number of problems benefit, not all
The book says the speed-up is a constant 10 percent at best
The book says hash maps only help on very tiny inputs
The book says the speed-up is a factor of log n in general
optionExplain: Right: the factor of n applies when the slow step is a search or count.
No such claim appears.
It says the opposite for large inputs.
The factor is n.
questions.rule: Many problems get a factor of n faster with a hash map, so master your language's hash map interface.

questions.section: What is the point of a hash function?
questions.q: You are choosing how to spend a week of practice in a language you recently started. What does the book's advice say to learn first?
questions.explain: Mastering the interface in your own language is the stated priority.
options: How the language's own hash table resizes and re-hashes itself
How to design and write a hash function of your own
Its built-in hash map interface and how to use each operation
Which kinds of keys the language can sort the fastest
optionExplain: Internals are background.
Not needed to use built-ins.
Right: that is the one thing to master.
Sorting is not the book's point here.
questions.teaches: The book says that if you could only take one thing from the course, it should be to master the hash map interface for the programming language you use.
questions.rule: Many problems get a factor of n faster with a hash map, so master your language's hash map interface.

questions.q: In an unsorted array of n items, checking presence takes time proportional to n. In a hash map, the same check takes...
questions.explain: The card compares the two.
options: About half the steps of the array
A constant number of steps
The logarithm of n steps
n squared steps
optionExplain: A halved scan is still linear.
Right: the hash function jumps straight to the slot.
That needs sorted data and binary search.
Hash maps never make this check slower than the scan.
questions.rule: Hash maps make add, delete and exists O(1), where an array needs O(n) to check presence.

questions.q: Select the operations that are O(1) for a hash map.
questions.explain: Single-key operations are constant time. Anything that handles every element grows with n.
options: Print every value in sorted order
Add an element with its value
Delete an element if it exists
Check whether an element exists
Visit every element in a loop
optionExplain: Sorting is a separate cost; the book lists no such O(1) operation.
Right: O(1).
Right: O(1).
Right: O(1).
This touches n elements, so it takes time that grows with n.
questions.rule: Hash maps make add, delete and exists O(1), where an array needs O(n) to check presence.

questions.q: A program makes 1,000 presence checks against 1,000,000 stored items. In an unsorted array each check scans up to all items. What is the worst-case count of item comparisons?
questions.explain: A hash map answers each check in constant time, so the same work is about 1,000 lookups.
options: About 1,000
optionExplain: Right: 1,000 x 1,000,000 = 10 to the power 9 comparisons.
That is one full scan, not 1,000 scans.
That would be one comparison per check.
Adding instead of multiplying the sizes undercounts.
questions.rule: Hash maps make add, delete and exists O(1), where an array needs O(n) to check presence.

questions.q: True or false: updating the value of an existing entry costs more in a hash map than in an array.
questions.explain: The book lists updating values among the properties that match the array's time cost.
questions.rule: Updating values costs the same as in an array.

questions.q: A coder writes in a review: 'Looping through all entries of a map is O(1) because maps are O(1).' What is wrong?
questions.explain: A loop over all n entries cannot cost less than n steps.
options: Maps are O(n) for every operation, including single lookups
Maps cannot be iterated, so no loop over entries is possible
O(1) is per operation; a loop over all entries touches n
O(1) means the loop only ever visits the first element
optionExplain: Single operations are O(1).
The book says you can iterate over elements.
Right: iteration is linear in the number of elements.
O(1) means constant cost, not first element.
questions.rule: Hash maps make add, delete and exists O(1), where an array needs O(n) to check presence.

questions.q: A leaderboard must count players, update a score, loop over players and check a name exists. Which structure matches an array on all four, or beats it?
questions.explain: The hash map keeps the array's useful properties and adds constant-time existence checks.
options: An unsorted array of player records
A hash map keyed by player name
A hash map, but only for the existence check
A sorted array searched by halves
optionExplain: Existence would cost O(n) per check.
Right: it matches the array on count, update and loop, and beats it on exists.
It supports the other three at the same cost as an array.
Not the structure the book compares; lookup there is logarithmic.
questions.teaches: A hash map keeps several of the array's useful properties at the same time cost: finding the number of elements, updating values and iterating over elements.
questions.rule: Hash maps make add, delete and exists O(1), where an array needs O(n) to check presence.

questions.q: You count how often each ID appears in a list. IDs are integers, but the largest one is unknown. What is awkward with a plain array?
questions.explain: The unknown maximum is the problem. The card shows how a hash map avoids it.
options: The array cannot store integer values
The array cannot be updated quickly enough
Deciding how large to make the array
The array cannot be read in a loop
optionExplain: Arrays store integers easily.
Updates are O(1) in an array.
Right: its size must reach the largest ID.
Arrays are easy to loop over.
questions.rule: A hash map does not need to know the largest key in advance.

questions.q: An array used as a counter indexed by key must be at least as large as the ____ key.
questions.explain: Index range has to cover the maximum key, which may be unknown.
questions.rule: An array indexed by key needs room for the biggest key.

questions.q: Counts are kept in an array indexed by ID. Observed IDs are 5, 17 and 1,000,000. What is the smallest array size that works?
questions.explain: A map with only three keys stores three entries; the array needs a million slots.
optionExplain: Right: indices 0 to 1,000,000 need 1,000,001 slots.
Three IDs do not mean three indices; the array is indexed by the ID itself.
ID 1,000,000 would fall outside.
Index 1,000,000 needs a slot, so one more is needed.
questions.rule: A hash map does not need to know the largest key in advance.

questions.q: True or false: adding the key 99999999999 to the input forces a hash map to allocate room in proportion to that value.
questions.explain: The hash function converts the key to an integer within the map's size limit, so a huge key is handled like any other.
questions.rule: Hash maps do not size themselves by the key's value.

questions.q: A solution sizes its counter array at 100 because the sample IDs were small. A hidden test uses ID 100,000. What was the root mistake?
questions.explain: A hash map removes that guesswork.
options: Using integer keys at all instead of strings
Counting the IDs with an array and not with a loop
Choosing an array size that wasted memory on the sample
Sizing the array from the sample, not from the maximum
optionExplain: Integer keys are fine; sizing was the mistake.
A loop is not the issue.
100 was too small for ID 100,000.
Right: the array size depends on the largest key, which was not known.
questions.rule: A hash map does not need to know the largest key in advance.

questions.q: Keys are integers from 0 to 25, so an array would work. What does the book still say in favour of a hash map?
questions.explain: Even when integer keys would let you get away with an array, a hash map is easier and cleaner to work with.
options: It uses less memory than an array holding the same data
It is easier and cleaner, with no array size to choose
It has no overhead even when the input is small
It keeps its keys in sorted order for easy scanning
optionExplain: The book lists extra space as a disadvantage.
Right: convenience is a stated advantage.
The book says small inputs can be slower.
A hash map is unordered.
questions.teaches: Hash maps are easier and cleaner to work with: even when integer keys would let you get away with an array, you avoid deciding how large to make it.
questions.rule: A hash map does not need to know the largest key in advance.

questions.q: For a collection of only 3 items, which membership check is likely cheaper in practice?
questions.explain: The card names the effect.
options: Scanning the 3 items directly, since hashing adds fixed work
A hash lookup, since constant time beats any scan on any input
They cost the same, since both examine only three items
Neither can be compared without running them on real hardware
optionExplain: Right: with so few items the scan can cost less than hashing.
Constant time can still cost several steps per operation.
Fixed overhead differs from a short scan.
They can be compared by counting steps.
questions.rule: Hash maps carry a constant overhead, so on small inputs they can lose to an array.

questions.q: True or false: Big O notation ignores constant factors.
questions.explain: That is why O(1) can be deceiving: the hidden constant can be sizeable.
questions.rule: O(1) hides a constant.

questions.q: In the toy model (hash lookup = 10 steps, scan = 1 step per element), which is cheaper for 4 elements?
questions.explain: Compare actual step counts when n is small.
options: The scan, at 4 steps against 10
The hash lookup, at 10 steps against 40
They tie at 10 steps
The hash lookup, because it is O(1)
optionExplain: Right: 4 is below 10.
The scan costs 4, not 40.
The scan reaches 10 only with 10 elements.
Big O hides the 10-step constant.
questions.rule: Hash maps carry a constant overhead, so on small inputs they can lose to an array.

questions.q: In the toy model, the scan and the hash lookup cost the same at n = ____ elements.
questions.explain: Scan cost n equals hash cost 10 when n = 10; beyond that the hash lookup is cheaper.
questions.rule: Past the break-even point, O(1) wins.

questions.q: A student argues: 'O(1) means a hash lookup takes exactly one step.' What is wrong?
questions.explain: Constants are ignored by Big O, not absent.
options: O(1) means the cost grows with the length of the key
O(1) means the lookup is not allowed on small inputs
O(1) means constant, not one step; the constant can be large
Hash lookups really are one machine step, so nothing is hidden
optionExplain: That is a different matter.
It still works; it may only cost more.
Right: constants are hidden by Big O.
The hash function must run first.
questions.rule: Hash maps carry a constant overhead, so on small inputs they can lose to an array.

questions.q: Interviewers ask about trade-offs of a hash map for a list of 5 items. What does the book suggest saying?
questions.explain: Naming the overhead shows you know Big O hides constants. The book says the constant is more like O(10) than O(1) in practice.
options: It is slower only when the keys are long strings and not numbers
It may be slower than an array here, because of hashing overhead
It cannot be used on 5 items
Trade-offs do not matter when n is as small as 5
optionExplain: The point is overhead, not key type.
Right: the constant matters for small inputs.
It can; it may not pay off.
The book says interviews often discuss tradeoffs.
questions.teaches: The book says O(1) is deceiving; the real cost is usually something more like O(10), because every key goes through the hash function.
questions.rule: Hash maps carry a constant overhead, so on small inputs they can lose to an array.

questions.q: A hash table runs out of room in its array. Compared with a dynamic array, what extra work does growing it involve?
questions.explain: The card shows why.
options: Nothing extra: the elements are copied over in their old order
Removing duplicates from the keys before copying
Sorting all the keys into alphabetical order
Every existing key has to be hashed again for the new array
optionExplain: Positions come from hashing, so a copy is not enough.
Keys are already unique in a map.
Hash maps are not ordered.
Right: positions depend on the array's size.
questions.rule: A hash table's fixed size forces a guess: too big wastes space, too small forces costly re-hashing.

questions.q: When a hash table is resized, every existing key must be ____.
questions.explain: Index positions come from the hash function and the array size, so each key is hashed again after resizing.
questions.rule: Resizing a hash table means re-hashing every key.

questions.q: A table has a limit of 10,000 slots and stores 10 items. What fraction of the slots is in use?
questions.explain: This is the wasted-space example in action.
options: 1 percent
0.1 percent
10 percent
0.01 percent
optionExplain: That would be 100 items.
That would be 1,000 items.
That would be 1 item.
questions.rule: A hash table's fixed size forces a guess: too big wastes space, too small forces costly re-hashing.

questions.q: A table with limit 10,000 is given a test with 100,000 items. What does the table have to do?
questions.explain: More items than slots forces a resize.
options: Keep the array, since hash maps do not fill up
Delete the first 90,000 items
Switch to storing items in sorted order
Grow its array and re-hash every key
optionExplain: A fixed array has a limit.
That would lose data.
Hash maps are not sorted.
Right: it must exceed the old limit.
questions.rule: A hash table's fixed size forces a guess: too big wastes space, too small forces costly re-hashing.

questions.q: True or false: resizing a hash table costs the same as resizing a dynamic array, since both copy elements into a bigger array.
questions.explain: Copying elements is not enough for a hash table: every key must be re-hashed, which makes resizing much more expensive.
questions.rule: Hash table resizing includes re-hashing.

questions.q: You must store values indexed by position 0 to n-1, with n unknown until runtime and growing. Which structure is more flexible?
questions.explain: When you do not know how many elements you need, the book says arrays are more flexible with resizing and avoid wasted space.
options: An array, because it can resize and waste no space
A hash table, since it never wastes any space
A hash table, because resizing is free for it
Neither one can handle an unknown number of items
optionExplain: Right: with unknown size an array is more flexible.
It can waste space when its array is much larger than needed.
Resizing is expensive.
Arrays resize; the book says they are more flexible.
questions.teaches: When you do not know how many elements you need to store, arrays are more flexible with resizing and do not waste space.
questions.rule: A hash table's fixed size forces a guess: too big wastes space, too small forces costly re-hashing.

questions.q: A map holds strings of length m. Hashing one key takes time that depends on...
questions.explain: The card makes this precise.
options: The number of entries in the map
The length of the string, m
Nothing at all
The alphabet size only
optionExplain: That is what the O(1) is measured against.
Right: hashing reads the whole string.
Hashing a string reads its characters.
Length drives the cost.
questions.rule: Hash map operations are constant in the map size n, but hashing a key costs time in the key's own size.

questions.q: In the statement hash map operations are O(1), the variable we hold fixed against is usually ____, the number of entries.
questions.explain: The O(1) is measured against the size n of the map, not against the size of a key.
questions.rule: O(1) is relative to the map size.

questions.q: Two keys go into the same map: one has 10 characters, the other 1,000. Roughly how do the hashing costs compare?
questions.explain: Linear in m means 100 times the characters costs 100 times the work.
options: They cost the same
The long key costs about 10 times more
The long key costs about 100 times more
The short key costs more
optionExplain: That would hold only if hashing ignored the key's length.
That understates the gap; the cost scales with the full length.
Right: hashing a string is O(m), and 1,000 / 10 = 100.
Shorter strings take less time to hash.
questions.rule: Hash map operations are constant in the map size n, but hashing a key costs time in the key's own size.

questions.q: n strings of average length m are inserted one by one. What is the hashing work in total?
questions.explain: Each string is read once, so the cost is n times m.
options: O(n x m)
O(n)
O(m)
optionExplain: Right: n insertions, each O(m).
That ignores the cost of each key's length.
That counts only one key.
Many insertions cannot be constant.
questions.rule: Hash map operations are constant in the map size n, but hashing a key costs time in the key's own size.

questions.q: True or false: a solution that puts n strings into a hash map is O(n) overall, because each insertion is O(1), whatever the string lengths.
questions.explain: The O(1) is relative to the map's size. Hashing each string costs O(m), so the total is O(n x m) in terms of both variables.
questions.rule: Count the key's own size.

questions.q: An interviewer asks the complexity of grouping n words into a map. Which answer follows the book's care with variables?
questions.explain: Complexity functions involve only variables you define, so define m when the cost depends on it.
options: Say O(1), since hash maps are constant time
Define m as the word length and say O(n x m)
Say O(n) and avoid mentioning the word length
Say O(n squared), since words are compared in pairs
optionExplain: That ignores the key's length.
Right: name the variable the cost depends on.
The cost hides in the length.
Words are not compared pairwise.
questions.teaches: Time complexity functions only involve the variables you define, so when key length matters you define a variable such as m for it.
questions.rule: Hash map operations are constant in the map size n, but hashing a key costs time in the key's own size.

questions.q: You only need to know whether a username has been seen before. Which structure is the most convenient?
questions.explain: A structure with no values is the guess. The card names it.
options: A hash map from usernames to their count
A set of usernames
A sorted array of usernames
A two-dimensional array
optionExplain: It works, but the counts are not needed.
Right: it answers presence without storing extra values.
Presence would cost more than O(1).
No second dimension is needed.
questions.rule: When you only need to know whether something is present, use a set.

questions.q: True or false: a set maps each of its keys to a value.
questions.explain: A set holds keys only; it does not map them to anything.
questions.rule: A set is keys without values.

questions.q: Select the tasks best handled by a set.
questions.explain: Presence alone calls for a set; counts and values call for a map.
options: Checking whether a ticket number has been used before
Checking whether a word appeared earlier in a text
Finding how many tickets each customer bought
Looking up the price for a product code
optionExplain: Right: only presence matters.
Right: presence alone.
That needs a count per customer.
That needs a value per key.
questions.rule: Presence alone: use a set.

questions.q: Which statement about a set and a hash map is correct?
questions.explain: Set and map share the mechanism.
options: They share a hashing mechanism; the set has no values
A set uses a different hashing mechanism from a hash map
A set checks existence in O(n) while a map takes O(1)
A set keeps its stored values in sorted order
optionExplain: Right: the difference is in whether keys map to anything.
The mechanism is the same.
Both are O(1).
Sets do not sort.
questions.rule: When you only need to know whether something is present, use a set.

questions.q: True or false: a set is slower than a hash map for existence checks, because it must search through values.
questions.explain: A set has no values to search. It hashes the key, so existence checks are O(1), as in a map.
questions.rule: Sets check existence in O(1).

questions.q: A program stores every key it has seen but does not need any value. How does the book describe the relationship with a hash map?
questions.explain: Keys-only is the whole difference.
options: A set is a hash map whose values are always lists
A set is basically a hash map if you consider only the keys
A set is an array with fixed integer indices
A set is a hash map whose keys are kept sorted
optionExplain: A set has no values.
Right: keys are all it keeps.
A set uses hashing.
Sets are not sorted.
questions.teaches: The book says a set is basically a hash map if you only consider the keys.
questions.rule: When you only need to know whether something is present, use a set.

questions.q: A set starts empty and you add 7 five times. How many elements does it hold?
questions.explain: Only one distinct element remains, because repeats change nothing. The card next shows why.
optionExplain: Right: the first add inserts 7 and later adds change nothing.
That counts additions, which a set does not track.
The first add does insert the element.
7 is the element, not the count.
questions.rule: A set records presence, not how many times an element was added.

questions.q: A set holds at most ____ copy of any element.
questions.explain: Duplicates collapse into one entry.
questions.rule: A set keeps one entry per element.

questions.q: What does the code print?
questions.explain: Count distinct values, not additions.
optionExplain: That is the number of adds.
Right: only 4 and 9 are distinct.
4 appears three times, but that does not mean three entries.
9 is a member, not the size.
questions.code:
s = set()
for x in [4, 4, 9, 4, 9]:
    s.add(x)
print(len(s))
questions.rule: A set records presence, not how many times an element was added.

questions.q: A list of 8 words becomes a set of 5 words. What can you conclude?
questions.explain: Each repeated add leaves the set unchanged.
options: Three words were deleted from the original list
Five words each appear exactly once in the list
The set sorted the words into alphabetical order
Some words repeat: 3 additions were duplicates
optionExplain: Building a set does not delete from the list.
Some of the five may appear many times.
Sets are not sorted.
Right: 8 - 5 = 3 adds changed nothing.
questions.rule: A set records presence, not how many times an element was added.

questions.q: True or false: a coder can build a set of the words in a text and then read the most common word from it.
questions.explain: A set does not track frequency, so it cannot tell which word is most common. Counting needs a hash map.
questions.rule: Frequency requires a count per key.

questions.q: You must remove repeated email addresses from a list, keeping one of each. What does the length of a set built from the list report?
questions.explain: Because a set ignores duplicates, a set built from any collection has one entry per distinct value; the book later uses this on frequencies.
options: The number of addresses in the original list
The number of addresses that were repeated
The number of different addresses in the list
The number of times the most common address appears
optionExplain: Repeats do not add entries.
Repeated and unrepeated values each get one entry.
Right: a set keeps one entry per distinct value.
Sets do not track frequency.
questions.teaches: Because a set ignores duplicates, putting a collection into a set leaves one entry per distinct value, so its length counts the distinct values; the book later uses this on frequencies.
questions.rule: A set records presence, not how many times an element was added.

questions.q: To count how many times each word occurs in a text, which structure fits?
questions.explain: Counting needs a value per key. The card next shows why.
options: A set of words
A set of counts
A hash map from word to count
An array indexed by words
optionExplain: It cannot hold counts.
Counts without words lose which word they belong to.
Right: each word needs a number attached.
Words are not integer indices.
questions.rule: Use a set for presence; use a hash map when each key carries a value.

questions.q: True or false: a set is basically a hash map if you only consider the keys.
questions.explain: A set keeps keys only, with no values.
questions.rule: Set = keys of a map.

questions.q: Sort each task by the structure it needs.
questions.explain: Presence tasks need only keys. Counts, prices and positions are values attached to keys.

items.t: Has this email been used before?
How many orders did each customer place?
What is the price of each product code?
Has this word appeared earlier?
At which index did each number last appear?
Is this card id already registered?

questions.rule: Presence: set. Attached data: map.

questions.q: A routine uses a set to check whether a name was seen. The task now also needs how many times each name appeared. What changes?
questions.explain: A new requirement for a value means a map.
options: Replace the set with a hash map from name to count
Add a second set for the counts
Keep the set and add the name again each time
Sort the names and count in place
optionExplain: Right: the count is the new value to attach.
A set cannot store a number per name.
Repeated adds change nothing.
Sorting is not needed and costs more.
questions.rule: Use a set for presence; use a hash map when each key carries a value.

questions.q: A coder keeps a hash map, writes True for every key, and only ever checks whether a key exists. What is the best note?
questions.explain: The code is not wrong, only more roundabout.
options: It fails, because maps cannot check whether a key exists
It fails, because the stored value True is mutable
It works, but a set is more convenient for existence
It is slower than scanning an array of the same keys
optionExplain: Maps can check existence in O(1).
A value can be anything.
Right: sets are the convenient choice for presence.
Both are constant time and faster than an array scan.
questions.rule: Use a set for presence; use a hash map when each key carries a value.

questions.q: A cache must remember which URLs were fetched, and a second feature must remember the response size per URL. Which pair is a good fit?
questions.explain: Match the structure to what each feature remembers.
options: A hash map for both, with identical values stored
A set for the first feature and a map for the second
A single set used for both of the features
A single array shared by both of the features
optionExplain: The first feature needs no value.
Right: presence for one, a value per key for the other.
A set cannot hold response sizes.
URLs are not integer indices.
questions.teaches: A set is more convenient when you only care about checking whether elements exist, while a hash map is needed to remember data tied to keys.
questions.rule: Use a set for presence; use a hash map when each key carries a value.

questions.q: In Python, how can you use the list [1, 51, 163] as a hash map key?
questions.explain: Immutability decides the answer. The card shows the options.
options: Use the list itself
Append a trailing item to it
Use its first element only
Convert it to a tuple first
optionExplain: Lists are mutable and are not accepted as keys.
Appending leaves it a mutable list.
That loses the other elements and may collide.
Right: a tuple is immutable.
questions.rule: Convert a mutable array to a tuple or a delimited string, then use that as the key.

questions.q: In Python, tuple(arr) converts an array into an ____ key.
questions.explain: A tuple cannot be changed after creation, so it works as a key.
questions.rule: Tuple the array, or join it with a delimiter.

questions.q: Select the values that are acceptable as a key for a hash map, in a Python-style language.
questions.explain: Convert to a tuple or a delimited string; the original mutable list does not qualify.
options: The list [3, 7, 9] itself
A list of lists such as [[3], [7, 9]]
The tuple (3, 7, 9)
The string 3,7,9 built by joining with commas
optionExplain: Lists are mutable.
Still mutable.
Right: tuples are immutable.
Right: strings are immutable and the delimiter keeps elements apart.
questions.rule: Convert a mutable array to a tuple or a delimited string, then use that as the key.

questions.q: What does the code print?
questions.explain: The delimiter keeps neighbouring numbers apart.
optionExplain: That would drop the commas.
That is the list printed, not the joined key.
That would print key1, not key2.
Right: join with commas.

arr = [1, 51, 163]
key1 = tuple(arr)

questions.rule: Convert a mutable array to a tuple or a delimited string, then use that as the key.

questions.q: A coder converts arrays by joining with no delimiter, so [1, 23] and [12, 3] both become 123. What is wrong?
questions.explain: A delimiter that cannot appear in any element prevents collisions.
options: The joined result is not a string at all
Without a delimiter, different arrays can share a key
The joined key is mutable, so it cannot be used
Arrays of two numbers cannot be turned into keys
optionExplain: Join always gives a string.
Right: 1,23 and 12,3 differ only with the commas.
A string is immutable.
They can, with a safe conversion.
questions.rule: Convert a mutable array to a tuple or a delimited string, then use that as the key.

questions.q: In C++ you meet std::map, which lets you associate mutable data structures with values. How does the book classify it?
questions.explain: Some languages offer a different structure that accepts mutable keys, but it is not a hash map.
options: A hash map with faster resizing than the built-in
A hash map restricted to integer keys only
Not a hash map, but it can solve similar problems
A set that stores whole arrays as its members
optionExplain: It is not a hash map.
It is not a hash map.
Right: the book notes it is not a hash map.
It associates keys with values.
questions.teaches: In C++ std::map allows mutable data structures to be associated to values; it is not a hash map but can be used to solve similar problems.
questions.rule: Convert a mutable array to a tuple or a delimited string, then use that as the key.

questions.q: Which Java HashMap method checks whether a key exists?
questions.explain: The name tells you what it checks. The card next shows why.
options: contains
exists
containsKey
hasValue
optionExplain: Plausible, but the method is specifically for keys.
Java's HashMap does not have an exists method.
Right: it takes a key and returns true or false.
That would test values, not keys.
questions.rule: Know how your language checks, reads, writes, deletes, counts and iterates a hash map.

questions.q: Match each Java HashMap call to what it does.
questions.explain: These four cover existence, read, delete and count.
pairs: reads the value of a key
questions.rule: containsKey, get, put, remove, size.

questions.q: What does the code print?
questions.explain: Track each change: update 5, add 9, delete 9.
optionExplain: Right: the map ends with keys 1, 5 and 7 and d[5] is 6.
Key 9 was deleted, so there are three keys.
d[5] was updated to 6.
Key 9 was removed before printing.
questions.rule: Know how your language checks, reads, writes, deletes, counts and iterates a hash map.

questions.q: To add a new pair or update an existing one, Java's HashMap uses the method ____.
questions.explain: put inserts when the key is new and updates the value when the key exists.
questions.rule: put adds or updates.

questions.q: A coder writes dic.append(3, 4) to add the pair 3 and 4 to a Python dictionary. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Match the language's own operation names.
options: The key must be a string
Pairs can only be added when the dictionary is created
A dictionary has no append; add a pair by assigning dic[3] = 4
append works but is O(n)
optionExplain: Integer keys are fine.
You can add pairs at any time.
Right: assignment is the add (put) operation.
The method does not exist on dictionaries.
questions.rule: Know how your language checks, reads, writes, deletes, counts and iterates a hash map.

questions.q: A stock counter holds key 5 with value 3. The program now calls put(5, 6). What results?
questions.explain: If the key already exists, the value is updated; if not, the pair is inserted.
options: A second entry for key 5 with value 6
The map still has the same number of keys and key 5 now holds 6
An error, because key 5 already exists
Nothing changes; the first value stays
optionExplain: Keys are unique.
Right: put on an existing key updates its value.
put does not fail.
put overwrites.
questions.teaches: Calling put on a key that already exists updates its value, while a new key is inserted as a new pair.
questions.rule: Know how your language checks, reads, writes, deletes, counts and iterates a hash map.

questions.q: A loop runs n times and, in each iteration, scans an array of n items for a value. What is the total time?
questions.explain: Nested loops multiply. The card shows how a hash structure fixes this.
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n squared)
O(2n)
optionExplain: That would hold only if each scan were constant time.
Nothing here is sorted or halved.
Right: n iterations of an O(n) scan.
That treats the scan as a single step.
questions.rule: Store the elements in a set or hash map so that each repeated existence check takes O(1).

questions.q: Replacing an inner O(n) search with a hash lookup usually turns O(n squared) into O(____).
questions.explain: n iterations of constant-time lookups give O(n).
questions.rule: Repeated exists checks: use a set or map.

questions.q: Order the steps for speeding up a slow duplicate check.
questions.explain: Spot the pattern, pick the structure, swap the check, then recompute the cost.
items: Notice that the inner loop only asks whether a value exists
Choose a set to hold the values already seen
Replace the inner loop with a membership test
Re-derive the cost as n iterations of O(1) work
questions.rule: Spot, store, swap, recompute.

questions.q: With no duplicates in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], the code compares a[j] with a[i] ____ times in total.
questions.explain: The inner loop runs 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 times, which grows like n squared; a set would need only 5 lookups.
questions.rule: Store the elements in a set or hash map so that each repeated existence check takes O(1).

questions.q: A student replaces the inner loop with x in lst, where lst is still a list, and claims the algorithm is now O(n). What is wrong?
questions.explain: Only a hash-based set or map makes the check O(1).
options: The check should use a double loop to be fast
Lists cannot hold integer values in Python
The result is O(n log n) because lists are sorted
Membership in a list is still a scan; it needs a set
optionExplain: A double loop is the problem, not the fix.
They can.
No sorting occurs.
Right: the structure must be hash-based.
questions.rule: Store the elements in a set or hash map so that each repeated existence check takes O(1).

questions.q: The set-based fix is applied. Which cost does it add that the slow version did not have?
questions.explain: Time is traded for space. In the book's third example the set occupies O(n) space.
options: About O(n) extra space to hold the set
About O(n squared) extra space for the set
Extra time per check, O(n), for each lookup
No extra cost at all, since the set is free
optionExplain: Right: the set stores up to n elements.
A set of n elements takes O(n) space.
Each check is O(1).
The set must be stored somewhere.
questions.teaches: Converting the input into a set makes each check cost O(1) but the set occupies O(n) space, so the speed-up trades memory for time.
questions.rule: Store the elements in a set or hash map so that each repeated existence check takes O(1).

questions.q: Two numbers must add up to 9. You are looking at 4. What value are you hoping to find?
questions.explain: The complement is target minus the current number. The card next shows why.
optionExplain: Right: 9 minus 4.
Using the same number needs a second copy and rarely fits.
That is the target itself.
That adds instead of subtracting.
questions.rule: At each element, look up target minus the element in a map of the values seen so far.

questions.q: True or false: at each element num, the hash map is searched for the key target + num.
questions.explain: The complement is target - num, because num plus (target - num) equals the target.
questions.rule: Look up target - num.

questions.q: What does the code return for nums [3, 2, 4] and target 6?
questions.explain: Trace the map: {3:0}, then {3:0, 2:1}, then 4 finds 2.
optionExplain: 3 and 2 sum to 5.
Right: at index 2 the number 4 finds 2, stored at index 1.
The check comes before the insert, so 3 does not pair with itself.
The function returns the current index first: [2, 1].
questions.rule: At each element, look up target minus the element in a map of the values seen so far.

questions.q: For nums [5, 1, 4, 8] and target 12, the function returns [3, ____].
questions.explain: At index 3 the number 8 finds its complement 4, which was stored at index 2.
questions.rule: At each element, look up target minus the element in a map of the values seen so far.

questions.q: A variant stores seen[num] = i before testing comp in seen. Which input exposes the bug?
questions.explain: Testing first guarantees the match came from an earlier index.
options: nums [3, 5], target 6, giving [0, 0] with one index twice
nums [2, 7], target 9, where the pair is found normally
nums [4, 5, 6], target 11, where the pair is found normally
nums [1, 2, 3], target 7, where no pair exists at all
optionExplain: Right: 3 finds itself as its complement.
It still returns the valid [1, 0].
It still returns the valid [2, 1].
It correctly finds no pair.
questions.rule: At each element, look up target minus the element in a map of the values seen so far.

questions.q: The input has 1,000,000 numbers and no pair adds up to the target. Roughly how many entries does the map end up with?
questions.explain: The book says the solution uses O(n) space because the number of keys scales linearly with the input.
options: Only 2 entries, since the final pair is all that is kept
About 1,000, the square root of the input size
Up to 1,000,000, one per distinct number
None, since lookups need no stored numbers at all
optionExplain: No pair was found; every number was stored.
Nothing here takes a square root.
Right: space grows linearly with the input.
Lookups need the stored values.
questions.teaches: Two Sum with a hash map uses O(n) space because the number of keys stored scales linearly with the input size.
questions.rule: At each element, look up target minus the element in a map of the values seen so far.

questions.q: A Two Sum variant must return True or False for whether any pair adds up to the target. What must you store?
questions.explain: Match the stored data to the answer. The card next shows why.
options: Each number together with its index in the array
Each number together with how often it appears
Every pair of numbers whose sum is computed
The numbers already seen, with no extra data
optionExplain: The index is not needed for a yes or no.
Counts are not needed.
That is O(n squared) memory.
Right: presence is enough.
questions.rule: Ask what the answer must report: presence needs a set; positions need a map.

questions.q: True or false: returning the indices of the pair requires remembering where each number was seen, so a set alone is not enough.
questions.explain: A set holds presence only, so it cannot give the index of the earlier number.
questions.rule: Indices need a map.

questions.q: Sort each Two Sum variant by the structure it needs.
questions.explain: Presence answers need the set. Anything about position needs the map.

items.t: Return True if a pair exists
Return the indices of the pair
Return the position of the earlier number
Return False if no pair exists
Return the index where the match was found
Return whether any two values sum to the target

questions.rule: Presence: set. Position: map.

questions.q: True or false: with nums [8, 3, 5] and target 8 the code returns True.
questions.explain: At the number 5 the complement 3 is already in the set, since 3 + 5 = 8.
questions.rule: Ask what the answer must report: presence needs a set; positions need a map.

questions.q: A coder swaps the dictionary for a set in the indices version but keeps the line return [i, seen[comp]]. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: The structure must carry a value per key.
options: The set is slower than a dictionary for lookups
The set cannot be searched by the complement
The loop skips the very first element in the list
A set stores no values, so seen[comp] reads nothing
optionExplain: Sets are O(1) too.
The membership test would work.
The loop is unchanged.
Right: indexing needs a mapping.
questions.rule: Ask what the answer must report: presence needs a set; positions need a map.

questions.q: A variant returns the two numbers themselves, not their indices. Which structure does the book say is enough?
questions.explain: The book says that if the question wanted a boolean or the numbers themselves, a set would do.
options: A hash map, so that positions can be remembered
A set, since the numbers need no positions
A sorted array searched with binary search
A set, but only if all the numbers are distinct
optionExplain: Positions are not asked for.
Right: the numbers themselves need no index.
A set is simpler and faster.
Duplicates do not change the set approach.
questions.teaches: If the question wanted a boolean indicating whether a pair exists, or the numbers themselves, a set would be enough; only indices force a hash map.
questions.rule: Ask what the answer must report: presence needs a set; positions need a map.

questions.q: Scanning a string left to right, what do you need to remember to spot a second appearance?
questions.explain: The card shows how to store them.
options: The count of every character in the whole string
The characters already seen
Only the previous character
The longest run of equal characters
optionExplain: Counting the whole string first is unnecessary.
Right: a repeat is a character that was seen before.
Repeats need not be adjacent.
That is a different problem.
questions.rule: Check the set first, then add: the first hit is the first second appearance.

questions.q: True or false: the code tests whether the character is in the set before adding it.
questions.explain: Test first, add after. Otherwise the character would always be found.
questions.rule: Check, then add.

questions.q: What does first_repeat return for the string abcbca?
questions.explain: Scan until the first character is found in the set.
options: a
c
b
The empty string
optionExplain: The first a does repeat later, but at index 5, after b has already repeated.
The second c arrives at index 4, after the second b.
Right: the second b at index 3 is the first repeat to complete, before any second a or c.
The string does contain a repeat.
questions.rule: Check the set first, then add: the first hit is the first second appearance.

questions.q: For the string abcbca, the set holds ____ characters at the moment the function returns.
questions.explain: At index 3 the set contains a, b and c; the second b is found and returned.
questions.rule: Check the set first, then add: the first hit is the first second appearance.

questions.q: A variant calls seen.add(c) before testing c in seen. What does it return for abcbca?
questions.explain: Adding before testing makes every test succeed.
options: a, the very first character
b, the correct repeat
The empty string
c, the last distinct character
optionExplain: Right: after adding, the character is always found.
The early add makes the first test succeed.
The loop returns at the first character.
The first character already succeeds.
questions.rule: Check the set first, then add: the first hit is the first second appearance.

questions.q: If the input might have no repeated character, what must the code handle?
questions.explain: The problem statement guarantees a duplicate, so the fallback is never reached; remove the guarantee and it matters.
options: Nothing: the loop returns a character on every input
An empty set, which raises an error when read
A second full pass over the whole string
The end of the loop with no repeat, needing a fallback return
optionExplain: That is only so when a duplicate is guaranteed.
An empty set is fine.
A second pass is not needed.
Right: the book's code returns a blank character after the loop.
questions.teaches: The book's solution still ends with a fallback return (a blank character) after the loop; it is never reached because the problem guarantees a duplicate.
questions.rule: Check the set first, then add: the first hit is the first second appearance.

questions.q: A string of length 1,000,000 uses only lowercase English letters. How many entries can a set of its characters hold?
questions.explain: Distinct letters, not string length, decide the size. The card next shows why.
options: At most 26
Exactly 1,000
optionExplain: Duplicates collapse into one entry.
Right: a set keeps one entry per distinct letter.
Nothing here halves the length.
No such limit exists.
questions.rule: A set limited to a fixed alphabet takes O(1) space.

questions.q: A set of English letters holds at most ____ entries.
questions.explain: There are 26 letters in the English alphabet.
questions.rule: Distinct letters are bounded by 26.

questions.q: The first-repeat solution runs on a 10,000-character string of lowercase English letters. What is the space used by the set?
questions.explain: Fixed alphabet, fixed bound.
options: About 10,000 entries, one per character
At most 26 entries, a constant
About 5,000 entries, one per pair of characters
Zero entries, since sets use no space
optionExplain: Only distinct letters are stored.
Right: it does not grow with the string.
No halving happens.
A set uses memory.
questions.rule: A set limited to a fixed alphabet takes O(1) space.

questions.q: A solution uses a set of the letters in a string over the English alphabet. Which description of its space is accepted by the book as technically correct?
questions.explain: Space depends on distinct characters, which are bounded.
options: O(1), since the alphabet is bounded by a constant
O(n), since the string has n characters
O(n squared), from the nested comparison it replaced
It cannot be stated
optionExplain: Right: a bounded alphabet makes space constant.
The set stores distinct characters only.
The nested loop is gone.
It can be stated.
questions.rule: A set limited to a fixed alphabet takes O(1) space.

questions.q: True or false: the set is O(n) space because the string has n characters, and every character is stored.
questions.explain: A set stores distinct characters only, so with a bounded alphabet it holds at most 26 entries.
questions.rule: Space follows distinct values.

questions.q: Input digits are limited to 0 to 9. A set of seen digits is used. How should an interview answer be framed?
questions.explain: The general bound m is the number of allowable characters, which is 10 here.
options: O(n), since the digits repeat along the string
O(10 n), since each digit costs ten steps
Only O(1); mentioning m would be a mistake
O(1), and note the general bound O(m) as well
optionExplain: Repeats do not add entries.
Space does not scale with length.
The general form is also correct.
Right: give the constant answer and note the general one.
questions.teaches: In an interview you should also note that the space could be O(m), where m is the number of allowable characters; this is a more general answer and also technically correct.
questions.rule: A set limited to a fixed alphabet takes O(1) space.

questions.q: To find numbers whose neighbours x + 1 and x - 1 are absent, what makes the neighbour checks cheap?
questions.explain: Membership questions suggest a set. The card next shows why.
options: Sorting the numbers into a list before the loop
Using a nested loop over every pair of numbers
Adding 1 to every number before the loop starts
Putting the numbers in a set before looping
optionExplain: Sorting costs O(n log n) and still needs a search.
That is O(n squared).
That does not enable lookup.
Right: the set answers membership in O(1).
questions.rule: Build a set first, then answer each neighbour question in O(1).

questions.q: True or false: the solution converts the array into a set before testing neighbours.
questions.explain: The set is built first so that each test of x + 1 or x - 1 is O(1).
questions.rule: Build the set first.

questions.q: For the input [1, 2, 4, 7, 7, 9, 10], the function returns ____ values.
questions.explain: The set is {1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 10}. Only 4 and 7 have neither neighbour present.
questions.rule: Build a set first, then answer each neighbour question in O(1).

questions.q: Which values does the function return for [3, 4, 9, 9, 15, 16, 20]?
questions.explain: Check each distinct value for x - 1 and x + 1 in the set.
options: 3 and 4 and 15 and 16
9 and 9 and 20
9 and 20
20 only
optionExplain: Those are exactly the ones with a neighbour.
Each valid value is reported once.
Right: 3 and 4, and 15 and 16, are neighbours of each other.
9 has neither 8 nor 10.
questions.rule: Build a set first, then answer each neighbour question in O(1).

questions.q: A variant loops over nums (not the set) in the final step. What changes for [7, 7, 20]?
questions.explain: The set removes duplicates; the array does not.
options: 20 is missed because it has no neighbours at all
7 is reported twice instead of once
The neighbour checks become O(n) each, as in a list
Nothing changes in the result for this input
optionExplain: 20 has no neighbours and is still found.
Right: the array visits both copies.
The checks still use the set.
Duplicates now show up twice.
questions.rule: Build a set first, then answer each neighbour question in O(1).

questions.q: A calendar tool must list booked days whose previous and next day are both free. Days are stored in an array. What is the first step?
questions.explain: Making a lookup structure before the main loop is called pre-processing.
options: Build a set of the booked days before the loop
Sort the days and then scan through them twice
Loop over the days, scanning the array for day plus 1
Count the booked days with a hash map first
optionExplain: Right: building a lookup first is pre-processing.
Costs more and is unnecessary.
That is O(n squared).
Counts are not needed.
questions.teaches: Converting the input into a set beforehand is another example of pre-processing.
questions.rule: Build a set first, then answer each neighbour question in O(1).

questions.q: To count how often each word occurs in a text, the hash map should map each word to...
questions.explain: A number per key is the guess; the card names it.
options: A list of every position of the word
The word's length in letters
An integer: the number of times it appeared
True, once the word has been seen
optionExplain: Positions are not counts, and a count is all that is required.
Length says nothing about frequency.
Right: the value is the frequency.
That records presence only, which is a set's job.
questions.rule: To count anything, map each key to its frequency in a hash map.

questions.q: True or false: in a counting hash map, the value stored for a key is the number of times that key has been seen.
questions.explain: Keys map to integer frequencies.
questions.rule: Counting map: key to frequency.

questions.q: What does the code print?
questions.explain: Count each letter, then count the keys.
optionExplain: Right: banana has a three times and three distinct letters.
6 is the length of the word, not the number of keys.
a appears three times, not twice.
1 would be the count after the first a only.
questions.rule: To count anything, map each key to its frequency in a hash map.

questions.q: Counting the letters of mississippi, the largest frequency is ____.
questions.explain: i appears 4 times and s appears 4 times; p appears 2 times and m once.
questions.rule: Count each key, then compare frequencies.

questions.q: A Python coder writes counts[c] += 1 on an empty dictionary. What happens at the first new character?
questions.explain: A new key needs an initial count.
options: It sets the count to 1 automatically for new keys
It silently ignores the new character
It raises an error, as the key has no starting count
It sets the count to the character's numeric code
optionExplain: A plain dictionary does not create the key.
It raises an error instead.
Right: start from 0 with get, or use a defaultdict.
No such conversion exists.
questions.rule: To count anything, map each key to its frequency in a hash map.

questions.q: Which sliding window constraint needs a hash map, rather than a single integer variable?
questions.explain: A single counter works when only one element matters.
options: At most k zeros in the window
At most k distinct characters in the window
The window length is at most k
The window sum is at most k, with positives
optionExplain: A single integer can count only the zeros.
Right: it involves several different elements.
That needs only the indices.
A running sum is a single integer.
questions.teaches: A hash map opens the door to sliding window problems whose constraint involves multiple elements; a constraint on one element, such as at most k zeros, only needs an integer.
questions.rule: To count anything, map each key to its frequency in a hash map.
