questions.q: A window may hold at most k distinct characters. How can you check this quickly after each slide?
questions.explain: A per-character count is the guess; the card shows the details.
options: Keep a count per character in the window and read how many keys exist
Rescan the whole window from its left edge every time
Compare the length of the window with the number k
Sort the characters of the window and compare neighbours
optionExplain: Right: the number of keys is the number of distinct characters.
That is O(n) per step.
Length is not the number of distinct characters.
Sorting is slow and unnecessary.
questions.rule: Keep a counts map for the window; shrink from the left whenever it has more than k keys.

questions.q: True or false: the window is invalid when counts has more than k keys.
questions.explain: More than k keys means more than k distinct characters.
questions.rule: Invalid when counts has more than k keys.

questions.q: What does longest(s, k) return for s = aabbcc and k = 2?
questions.explain: Longest window with at most 2 distinct letters.
optionExplain: A window of 3 is valid but not the longest.
Five characters would include three distinct letters.
The full string has three distinct letters.
Right: aabb and bbcc both have 4 characters and 2 distinct letters.
questions.rule: Keep a counts map for the window; shrink from the left whenever it has more than k keys.

questions.q: For s = eceba and k = 2, after processing index 3 (the letter b) the left pointer sits at index ____.
questions.explain: Adding b gives 3 keys; removing e then c leaves {e, b}, with left at 2.
questions.rule: Keep a counts map for the window; shrink from the left whenever it has more than k keys.

questions.q: A coder checks the distinct-character constraint by scanning the whole window with a set at every step. What is the cost?
questions.explain: Recomputing from scratch undoes the benefit of the window.
options: O(1) per step, the same as the counts map
O(n) per step, so about O(n squared) overall
O(log n) per step, as with a balanced search
O(k) per step, so O(n) overall
optionExplain: Rebuilding a set walks the window.
Right: the map makes the check constant time.
No halving occurs.
The window can be longer than k.
questions.rule: Keep a counts map for the window; shrink from the left whenever it has more than k keys.

questions.q: A stream tool finds the longest run of days using at most 3 different songs. For this problem, what is the constraint metric and its restriction?
questions.explain: The book frames the check as a constraint metric with a numeric restriction; here it is distinct songs, at most 3.
options: The number of distinct songs in the window, at most 3
The number of days in the window, at most 3
The total number of plays in the window, at most 3
The most played song in the window, at most 3 plays
optionExplain: Right: that is what the window must keep small.
That would limit the length, not the variety.
Plays are not the stated limit.
Counts per song are the means, not the limit.
questions.teaches: Name the constraint metric (what you measure about the window) and its numeric restriction; in this problem the metric is the number of unique characters and the restriction is at most k.
questions.rule: Keep a counts map for the window; shrink from the left whenever it has more than k keys.

questions.q: The last copy of letter q leaves the window, but its key stays in the map with count 0. What does counting keys now overcount?
questions.explain: A stale key inflates the count. The card gives the fix.
options: The total length of the current window
The number of times q appeared before
Nothing: zero entries are skipped automatically
Distinct characters: q is still listed
optionExplain: Length comes from the pointers, not from keys.
The count was decremented to 0.
The key still occupies the map.
Right: the key count would include q.
questions.rule: Delete a key when its frequency reaches zero so that the number of keys stays honest.

questions.q: True or false: when a character's frequency in the window becomes 0, the character is no longer in the window.
questions.explain: Zero means no copies remain inside the window.
questions.rule: Frequency 0 means absent.

questions.q: The code removes one a from the map. It prints the number of keys left: ____.
questions.explain: The count of a falls to 0, so the key is deleted; only b remains.
questions.rule: Delete a key when its frequency reaches zero so that the number of keys stays honest.

questions.q: With k = 2 the window holds x and y, then z arrives and the single x leaves. Which keys should counts hold afterwards?
questions.explain: Keys mirror the characters now inside the window.
options: x, y and z
y and z
only z
x and z
optionExplain: x has no copies left and should be deleted.
Right: x was deleted at zero.
y is still in the window.
x left and y stayed.
questions.rule: Delete a key when its frequency reaches zero so that the number of keys stays honest.

questions.q: A solution decrements counts but leaves zero-count keys in the map. For abaccc with k = 2 it returns 3 instead of 4. Why?
questions.explain: Stale keys make the validity test wrong.
options: The window does not shrink at all and keeps growing
The loop reads past the end of the string
The map overflows once it passes k keys in size
Zero-count keys inflate the key count, so the window shrinks too far
optionExplain: It shrinks more than it should.
No indexing error is involved.
A map has no such limit; the stale keys are the cause.
Right: stale keys make the window look invalid.
questions.rule: Delete a key when its frequency reaches zero so that the number of keys stays honest.

questions.q: A tool measures distinct customers in the last 3 orders using a counts map over a moving window. When an old order leaves, what should happen?
questions.explain: The number of keys is the number of distinct customers in the window, but only if zero counts are removed.
options: Delete the customer's key at once, whatever its count
Leave the count unchanged until the end of the run
Decrement the customer's count and delete the key at zero
Reset the whole map and rebuild it from the window
optionExplain: Other orders from the same customer may remain.
The map would describe the wrong window.
Right: keys must mirror the customers still in the window.
That loses the other customers' counts.
questions.teaches: The number of keys in counts is the number of distinct elements in the window, but only if a key is removed as soon as its frequency becomes zero.
questions.rule: Delete a key when its frequency reaches zero so that the number of keys stays honest.

questions.q: A window keeps at most k distinct characters in a counts map. How does the map's size scale?
questions.explain: The map cannot hold more than about k keys. The card explains.
options: With the input length n
With k, not with the input length
With n squared
It stays at size 1
optionExplain: Keys are removed as characters leave.
Right: it is trimmed back to k keys.
The map never holds more than distinct characters.
Up to k different keys are held.
questions.rule: With O(1) map operations the sliding window is O(n) time and O(k) space.

questions.q: The counts map in the sliding window uses O(____) space.
questions.explain: It holds about k keys because zero-count keys are deleted.
questions.rule: Space is O(k).

questions.q: n = 1,000,000 characters and k = 3. Which statement about the map is accurate?
questions.explain: Space follows k, not n.
options: It holds a handful of keys, about k at a time
It holds up to 1,000,000 keys at the end of the run
It holds exactly 3 keys at every moment of the run
It holds no keys between steps of the loop
optionExplain: Right: a few entries, not a million.
Only the characters currently inside the window are held.
It can briefly hold k + 1 before shrinking.
The window's characters stay in the map.
questions.rule: With O(1) map operations the sliding window is O(n) time and O(k) space.

questions.q: Suppose each map operation took O(n) instead of O(1). What would the total time of the sliding window become?
questions.explain: The sliding window is linear only because each step is constant.
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(k)
O(n squared)
optionExplain: That relies on O(1) operations.
No sorting or halving happens.
k bounds the space, not the time.
Right: n steps of O(n) work each.
questions.rule: With O(1) map operations the sliding window is O(n) time and O(k) space.

questions.q: True or false: the while loop inside the for loop makes the algorithm O(n squared), since it is a loop in a loop.
questions.explain: The left pointer only moves forward, so across the whole run each element is removed at most once. Total work stays O(n).
questions.rule: Count total pointer moves, not loop nesting.

questions.q: A window algorithm does a constant-time update each time it adds or removes an element. What is the time complexity, and why?
questions.explain: Sliding window problems are O(n) if the work in each iteration is amortized constant.
options: O(n squared), since the loop is nested
O(n), as the work per iteration is amortized constant
O(log n), since the window halves each time
O(k), since the map has k keys
optionExplain: Nesting alone does not decide the cost.
Right: the book gives this as the condition for linear time.
A window does not halve.
k bounds space, not time.
questions.teaches: Sliding window problems run in O(n) if the work done inside each for loop iteration is amortized constant, which hash map operations make true.
questions.rule: With O(1) map operations the sliding window is O(n) time and O(k) space.

questions.q: Every array holds distinct numbers. A number's total count across n arrays equals n. What does this tell you?
questions.explain: Distinct values per array is what makes the count meaningful. The card next shows why.
options: It appears in only one array, n times
It appears in all n arrays
It is the largest number
It appears an odd number of times
optionExplain: Arrays have distinct values, so one array adds at most 1.
Right: once per array, with no repeats inside any array.
Counts say nothing about size.
The parity of n is not the point.
questions.rule: Count all elements; the ones whose count equals the number of arrays are in every array.

questions.q: A number is in every array exactly when its count equals the ____ of arrays.
questions.explain: Each array contributes at most one occurrence, so n occurrences means all n arrays.
questions.rule: Count equals n means present in all.

questions.q: What does the code return for [[5, 6], [6, 7], [6, 8], [9, 6]]?
questions.explain: Only 6 reaches count 4.
optionExplain: Right: 6 has count 4, equal to the 4 arrays.
5 appears only once.
6 appears in all four arrays.
Those are all numbers, not the ones in every array.
questions.rule: Count all elements; the ones whose count equals the number of arrays are in every array.

questions.q: True or false: if an inner array can repeat a value, as in [[1, 1], [2, 3]], a count equal to n still proves a number is in every array.
questions.explain: Here 1 reaches a count of 2, equal to the number of arrays, though it is missing from the second array. The distinct-values guarantee matters.
questions.rule: Distinctness inside each array makes count equal n valid.

questions.q: For 3 arrays of 4 elements each, building the counts map takes ____ updates.
questions.explain: One update per element: 3 x 4 = 12.
questions.rule: n arrays of m elements cost n x m updates.

questions.q: The answer is sorted at the end. With n arrays of average length m, why is the sort O(m log m) and not larger?
questions.explain: Only numbers common to all arrays are in the answer, so at most m of them are sorted.
options: Sorting costs O(m log m) whatever is being sorted
The counts map holds only m keys in total
A number in every array appears in each, so at most m qualify
The arrays are already sorted before counting
optionExplain: Sort cost depends on the input size being sorted.
It can have up to n x m keys.
Right: the answer cannot exceed one array's length.
Nothing says the arrays are sorted.
questions.teaches: At most m elements can be in the answer when it is sorted, so the sort costs O(m log m) even though the map may hold up to n x m keys.
questions.rule: Count all elements; the ones whose count equals the number of arrays are in every array.

questions.q: Counting values 2, 4, 6 and 800 with an array indexed by value needs at least how many slots?
questions.explain: The biggest value sets the array size. The card next shows why.
optionExplain: Four values do not mean four indices; the value itself is the index.
Index 800 needs a slot, so one more.
That adds the values together.
Right: indices 0 to 800.
questions.rule: A counting map costs space for the keys present; a counting array costs space for the largest key.

questions.q: True or false: a hash map used for counting stores one entry per distinct key that occurs.
questions.explain: Keys that never occur have no entry.
questions.rule: Map size follows the number of distinct keys.

questions.q: Values 3, 8 and 2000 are counted in an array indexed by value. It needs at least ____ slots.
questions.explain: Indices 0 to 2000 are needed.
questions.rule: Array size = largest key + 1.

questions.q: Values 1, 2, 3 and 5000 are counted in an array. How many slots stay unused?
questions.explain: Only the slots at the four values are used.
optionExplain: That ignores the used slots.
It undercounts the slots by one.
Most slots are empty.
Right: 5,001 slots minus 4 used.
questions.rule: A counting map costs space for the keys present; a counting array costs space for the largest key.

questions.q: A coder counts integers with an array because keys are integers. A hidden test contains 10 to the power 11. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Sparse keys make arrays wasteful.
options: Integers that big cannot be counted in any structure
The array would need over 100 billion slots, nearly all empty
The array would be too short by exactly one slot
The counts would become negative for large keys
optionExplain: A hash map handles them.
Right: size follows the biggest key.
It would be short by billions.
Counts do not go negative.
questions.rule: A counting map costs space for the keys present; a counting array costs space for the largest key.

questions.q: Keys are integers 0 to 25 with a very large input. What is the fair comparison of an array and a hash map?
questions.explain: Sometimes an array is more efficient because of the hash map's overhead, but overall a hash map is much safer.
options: An array can win on overhead, though a map is safer
Only a hash map can count them correctly
An array is unusable for counting such keys
They are identical in memory used and in speed
optionExplain: Right: a known small range favours an array.
An array of 26 slots works.
It counts fine here.
A hash map carries overhead.
questions.teaches: Sometimes an array is more efficient than a hash map because of the hash map's overhead, but a hash map is much safer when the key range is unknown.
questions.rule: A counting map costs space for the keys present; a counting array costs space for the largest key.

questions.q: A map shows a:2, b:2, c:2. How can you check cheaply that all counts are equal?
questions.explain: Use the way a set treats duplicates. The card next shows why.
options: Put the counts in a set and see that it has one element
Sort the letters and compare neighbours
Add up the counts and compare with the number of letters
Check that the map has three keys
optionExplain: Right: duplicates collapse into one entry.
Sorting letters does not compare counts.
A sum cannot show that each count is the same.
Keys do not show equal counts.
questions.rule: Count with a map, then check that the set of counts has size one.

questions.q: True or false: the set of frequencies has exactly one element when all characters have the same frequency.
questions.explain: Equal frequencies collapse into one entry in the set.
questions.rule: One distinct frequency means all equal.

questions.q: True or false: for the string aabbbcc the function returns False.
questions.explain: Counts are a:2, b:3, c:2, so the set of counts is {2, 3} with two elements, giving False.
questions.rule: Count with a map, then check that the set of counts has size one.

questions.q: For s = abcabcab the counts are a:3, b:3, c:2, so the set of frequencies has ____ elements.
questions.explain: The distinct frequencies are 3 and 2.
questions.rule: Set size = number of distinct frequencies.

questions.q: A coder puts the characters of the string in a set and tests that its size is 1 to check equal frequencies. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Put the frequencies, not the characters, into the set.
options: A set of characters cannot be built from a string
It tests for a single distinct character, not equal frequencies
Sets can only hold numbers, not characters
The size of the set should be 26 and not 1
optionExplain: It can be built.
Right: the set must hold the counts.
Sets hold any hashable key.
26 is the English alphabet size, not the test.
questions.rule: Count with a map, then check that the set of counts has size one.

questions.q: A teacher checks whether every student handed in the same number of assignments, given a list of student names, one per submission. What approach follows?
questions.explain: Counting plus a set of counts solves the whole family of problems.
options: Put the names in a set and check that its size is one
Sort the names and compare the first and last entries
Count submissions per name and check that the map has one key
Count per name, put the counts in a set and check its size is one
optionExplain: That checks for a single student.
Sorting does not give counts.
That checks for a single student, not equal counts.
Right: same pattern as the characters problem.
questions.teaches: Populating the counts map costs O(n) and converting its values into a set costs another O(n), so the whole check is O(n).
questions.rule: Count with a map, then check that the set of counts has size one.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: Count the subarrays of positive numbers whose sum is less than k. Which technique is the natural choice?
questions.explain: Shrinking helps when the constraint is an upper bound. The card next shows why.
options: A prefix-sum hash map for exact differences
Sorting the array first
Sliding window
Binary search on the answer
optionExplain: Exact matching is for sum equal to k.
Sorting would break the subarray order.
Right: shrinking a valid window keeps its sum below k.
Nothing here is monotone in that sense.
questions.rule: Sliding window needs a constraint that stays true when a valid window shrinks; exact constraints do not.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: True or false: for sum exactly k, a valid window from left to right stays valid when its left end moves to any i up to right.
questions.explain: Dropping elements changes the sum, so the exact value of k is lost. The property holds for sum less than k with positives only.
questions.rule: Exact constraints are not preserved by shrinking.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: Sort each counting task by the method that suits it.
questions.explain: Upper bounds on positives survive shrinking. Exact values do not, so they use prefix sums with a map.
groups: Prefix sums with a hash map

items.t: Subarrays of positive numbers with sum less than k
Subarrays with sum exactly equal to k
Subarrays with exactly k odd numbers
Subarrays of positive numbers with sum at most k
Subarrays with sum equal to k, negatives allowed

questions.rule: Upper bound: window. Exact value: prefix sums and map.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: True or false: for nums [1, 2, 1] and k = 3, the windows over indexes 0 to 1 and over index 1 alone both sum to 3.
questions.explain: The first window sums to 3 but the window of index 1 alone sums to 2.
questions.rule: Shrinking breaks an exact sum.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: A student reasons: 'sum less than k works with sliding window, so sum equal to k works the same way.' What is wrong?
questions.explain: Strict constraints do not preserve the window property.
options: A valid window with an exact sum can turn invalid when it shrinks
Sliding window only works on strings, not on arrays
An exact sum needs the array sorted before any scan
An exact sum is O(n squared) for any possible method
optionExplain: Right: exact constraints do not keep the property.
It also works on arrays.
Sorting breaks the subarray structure.
A hash map solves it in O(n).
questions.rule: Sliding window needs a constraint that stays true when a valid window shrinks; exact constraints do not.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: Count the subarrays with exactly k zeros. Which approach does the unit's pattern suggest?
questions.explain: The book says these problems may seem hard at first, but the pattern is simple, and the code is similar across problems.
options: A sliding window that shrinks when zeros exceed k
Prefix counts of zeros with a hash map
Sorting the zeros to the front of the array
A set of the zeros seen so far in the array
optionExplain: That counts at most k zeros; exact is not preserved.
Right: an exact count is an exact constraint.
Sorting loses subarray positions.
Positions and counts are needed.
questions.teaches: Exact-constraint counting problems may seem difficult at first, but the pattern is very simple and the code looks similar from one problem to the next.
questions.rule: Sliding window needs a constraint that stays true when a valid window shrinks; exact constraints do not.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: The prefix sum before a subarray is 11 and the prefix sum at its end is 14. What is the subarray's sum?
questions.explain: A subarray sum is a difference of prefix sums. The card next shows why.
optionExplain: Right: 14 minus 11.
That adds the prefix sums.
That is the sum before the subarray.
That is the sum including everything up to the end.
questions.rule: At each index, the number of earlier prefix sums equal to curr - k is the number of subarrays with sum k ending here.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: True or false: at each index the answer grows by counts[curr + k].
questions.explain: The matching earlier prefix is curr - k: subtracting it leaves a subarray of sum k.
questions.rule: Look up curr - k.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: What does the code return for nums [1, 2, 1, 2, 1] and k = 3?
questions.explain: Trace curr and counts, checking curr - 3 each step.
optionExplain: That misses the subarray starting at index 0, which the empty prefix finds.
That counts only one orientation.
Right: [1, 2] twice and [2, 1] twice.
Only four subarrays sum to 3.
questions.rule: At each index, the number of earlier prefix sums equal to curr - k is the number of subarrays with sum k ending here.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: For nums [3, 4, 7, 2, -3, 1, 4, 2] and k = 7, the code returns ____.
questions.rule: At each index, the number of earlier prefix sums equal to curr - k is the number of subarrays with sum k ending here.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: A coder records counts[curr] before computing ans += counts[curr - k]. For nums [5] and k = 0, what goes wrong?
questions.explain: Look up before recording so that a prefix is not paired with itself.
options: It returns 1 instead of 0, as the prefix matches itself
It returns 0 here, which happens to be correct
It raises an error because the array is empty
It returns -1 to signal that no subarray was found
optionExplain: Right: no subarray sums to 0, but the early record counts one.
The early record makes it return 1.
The array is not empty.
The code never returns a negative.
questions.rule: At each index, the number of earlier prefix sums equal to curr - k is the number of subarrays with sum k ending here.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: How does this approach relate to Two Sum?
questions.explain: The book draws this link: the lookup key is a complement, but computed on prefix sums.
options: Two Sum uses sorting and the prefix method does not
Two Sum uses a set and the prefix method uses an array
They are unrelated problems with no shared pattern
Two Sum looks up target minus num; here we look up curr minus k
optionExplain: Neither uses sorting.
Two Sum used a hash map here too.
The structure of the lookup is shared.
Right: the same pattern applied to prefix sums.
questions.teaches: This is the Two Sum pattern applied to prefix sums: Two Sum locks in a number and searches for target minus num, while here we lock in curr and search for curr minus k.
questions.rule: At each index, the number of earlier prefix sums equal to curr - k is the number of subarrays with sum k ending here.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: nums is [2, 1] and k = 3. The only subarray with sum 3 is the whole array. Which earlier prefix pairs with the prefix 3?
questions.explain: A prefix before the first element must exist. The card next shows why.
options: The prefix [2], with sum 2
The prefix [2, 1], with sum 3
No prefix: the array cannot match
The empty prefix, with sum 0
optionExplain: 3 minus 2 is 1.
3 minus 3 is 0, which is not k.
The empty prefix does match.
Right: 3 minus 0 is 3.
questions.rule: Start the counts map with 0: 1 so that subarrays beginning at index 0 are found.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: The map is started with counts[0] = ____.
questions.explain: One empty prefix has sum 0.
questions.rule: counts starts as {0: 1}.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: Remove the initial counts[0] = 1 from the algorithm. What does it return for nums [1, 2, 1, 2, 1] and k = 3?
questions.explain: The book finds three prefix differences of 3 and the fourth needs the empty prefix.
optionExplain: That is the correct answer with the initialisation.
Right: it loses [1, 2] at the start of the array.
It still finds three subarrays.
Only one subarray is lost.
questions.rule: Start the counts map with 0: 1 so that subarrays beginning at index 0 are found.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: For nums [5, 2, 3] and k = 5, the correct answer with the initialisation is ____.
questions.explain: The subarrays are [5] and [2, 3]; without the initialisation [5] is lost.
questions.rule: Include the empty prefix.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: True or false: the initialisation counts[0] = 1 is needed only when the array contains zeros.
questions.explain: It is needed for any subarray that starts at index 0, whatever the array contains.
questions.rule: Empty prefix matters at the start.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: The empty prefix [] represents what in the algorithm, and what does it pair with?
questions.explain: The book describes the empty prefix [] as having sum 0, so a prefix equal to k finds it.
options: A prefix with sum 0, matched by a prefix with sum k
The last prefix, matched against the first prefix
A prefix with sum k, matched against a prefix with sum 2k
A prefix of unknown sum, matched against any prefix
optionExplain: Right: curr - k = 0 means the prefix itself sums to k.
No such pairing exists.
The pairing is against curr - k.
Its sum is 0.
questions.teaches: The empty prefix [] has sum 0, so a prefix whose sum equals k finds it as curr - k = 0, which is how subarrays starting at index 0 are counted.
questions.rule: Start the counts map with 0: 1 so that subarrays beginning at index 0 are found.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: The prefix sums of [2, -2, 2] are 2, 0, 2. What does the repeat of 2 mean for the counting map?
questions.explain: Repeats are possible with negative numbers. The card next shows why.
options: The input is invalid and must be rejected
Two different starting points share a prefix sum
One of the two 2s can be safely ignored
The map must be kept sorted by prefix sum
optionExplain: Negatives are allowed.
Right: the map must record both.
Both are real starting points.
Order is not needed.
questions.rule: Repeated prefix sums create several subarrays, so store frequencies, not mere presence.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: True or false: when all numbers are positive, the prefix sums strictly increase, so no prefix sum repeats.
questions.explain: Each added number raises the sum, so every prefix sum is new.
questions.rule: Positive input: prefix sums never repeat.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: For nums [1, -1, 1, -1] and k = 0, what does the counts-map algorithm return?
questions.explain: The prefix sums 1, 0, 1, 0 give two earlier 0s at the end.
optionExplain: That is what a set of prefix sums would return.
That counts only the pairs.
Several subarrays sum to 0.
Right: [1, -1] twice, [-1, 1] once and the whole array.
questions.rule: Repeated prefix sums create several subarrays, so store frequencies, not mere presence.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: The prefix sums of [3, -3, 0, 3] are 3, 0, 0, 3. The prefix sum 0 occurs ____ times.
questions.explain: It appears at indexes 1 and 2 (not counting the empty prefix).
questions.rule: Count how often each prefix sum occurs.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: Seen prefix sums are kept in a set instead of a map. For [1, -1, 1, -1] and k = 0 this counts 3, not 4. Why is that wrong?
questions.explain: Presence is not enough when several starts share a prefix.
options: The set loses the sign of the numbers it stores
The set is far too slow for this input
Two earlier 0 prefixes exist, but the set counts them once
The set cannot hold the value 0 as an element
optionExplain: Signs are kept in the prefix sums.
Speed is not the problem.
Right: the true answer is 4.
It can hold 0.
questions.rule: Repeated prefix sums create several subarrays, so store frequencies, not mere presence.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: A problem states -1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000. How does this constraint affect the choice between a set and a counts map?
questions.explain: Read the constraints first.
options: Only a set works, because the range of values is small
Negatives are allowed, so prefix sums repeat and need counting
The constraint is irrelevant to the choice of structure
An array of size 2000 is required for the prefix sums
optionExplain: Range size does not stop repeats.
Right: the constraints reveal whether repeats can occur.
It shows that negatives can occur.
Prefix sums can leave that range.
questions.teaches: Read the problem constraints: a lower bound below zero, such as -1000 <= nums[i], means prefix sums can repeat and the map must count frequency.
questions.rule: Repeated prefix sums create several subarrays, so store frequencies, not mere presence.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: For exactly k odd numbers in a subarray, what should the running value curr record?
questions.explain: Match curr to the constraint metric. The card next shows why.
options: The sum of all the numbers so far
The number of odd numbers in the prefix
The number of elements so far in the prefix
The largest odd number so far in the prefix
optionExplain: A sum does not isolate odd numbers.
Right: differences of it count odd numbers in subarrays.
Length is not the constraint.
A maximum cannot be subtracted to give a count.
questions.rule: Change what curr measures; the counts-map lookup stays the same.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: True or false: adding num % 2 to curr adds 1 for each odd number and 0 for each even number.
questions.explain: An odd number leaves remainder 1 when divided by 2, and an even number leaves 0.
questions.rule: curr += num % 2.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: What does the code return for nums [2, 1, 1, 2, 1] and k = 2?
questions.explain: Trace the prefix odd counts 0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3 and look up curr - 2.
optionExplain: That undercounts the subarrays that include leading or trailing evens.
Right: five subarrays contain exactly two odd numbers.
That is what summing the numbers would give.
Five subarrays qualify.
questions.rule: Change what curr measures; the counts-map lookup stays the same.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: For the binary array [1, 0, 1, 0, 1], the number of subarrays with exactly two ones is ____.
questions.explain: Counting ones is counting odd numbers: the answer is 4.
questions.rule: Change what curr measures; the counts-map lookup stays the same.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: A coder writes curr += num, not curr += num % 2. For [2, 1, 1, 2, 1] and k = 2 it returns 3, not 5. Why?
questions.explain: The tracked quantity decides what the difference means.
options: The map starts at the wrong initial value
The loop skips the last element of the array
The value of k is read incorrectly in the loop
It tracks the sum, not the odd count, so differences mislead
optionExplain: The initialisation is unchanged.
All elements are visited.
k is used the same way.
Right: the metric must match the constraint.
questions.rule: Change what curr measures; the counts-map lookup stays the same.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint
questions.q: To count subarrays with exactly k even numbers, which line replaces curr += num % 2?
questions.explain: Not all problems of this pattern use identical code, but they are very similar: only the quantity added to curr changes.
options: curr += 1 - num % 2
curr += num // 2
curr += num
curr += num % 2
optionExplain: Right: an even number gives 1 and an odd number gives 0.
That adds half of each number.
That sums the values.
That counts odd numbers.
questions.teaches: While not every problem in this pattern uses identical code, they are all very similar; usually only the quantity that curr tracks changes.
questions.rule: Change what curr measures; the counts-map lookup stays the same.

questions.q: Which value is the same for every anagram of the word bcab?
questions.explain: Something about the letters, not their order. The card next shows why.
options: The word's first letter
The word spelled backwards
The word with its letters sorted: abbc
The word's position in the list
optionExplain: Anagrams can start with different letters.
Reversal differs between anagrams.
Right: every anagram sorts to the same string.
Position has nothing to do with letters.
questions.rule: Use a canonical form shared by the whole group, such as the sorted string, as the hash map key.

questions.q: True or false: sorting the letters of the word tea and of the word eat gives the same string.
questions.explain: Both sort to aet, and every anagram of a word sorts to the same string.
questions.rule: Sorted string is the group key.

questions.q: For the strings eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat, the code returns ____ groups.
questions.explain: The keys are aet, ant and abt, so there are three groups.
questions.rule: Use a canonical form shared by the whole group, such as the sorted string, as the hash map key.

questions.q: For listen, silent, enlist, google and gogole the code returns ____ groups.
questions.explain: listen, silent and enlist share the sorted key eilnst; google and gogole share eggloo.
questions.rule: Use a canonical form shared by the whole group, such as the sorted string, as the hash map key.

questions.q: A coder uses each string's length as the map key. Why does this fail?
questions.explain: The key must separate every non-anagram pair.
options: Strings of different lengths can still be anagrams of each other
Lengths cannot be hashed into a key at all
Equal-length strings that are not anagrams, like tea and tan, would share a group
The map would be unordered, so groups could not be read
optionExplain: Anagrams always have equal length; the failure is the opposite.
Integers hash fine.
Right: length is not a complete identifier.
That is true of every hash map and not the cause of the error.
questions.rule: Use a canonical form shared by the whole group, such as the sorted string, as the hash map key.

questions.q: The book rejects comparing two character-count hash maps for each pair of strings. Why?
questions.explain: A group needs one identifier, which both sorted strings and count-based keys provide.
options: It is cumbersome to write and gives no single identifier for a group of more than two strings
Hash maps cannot count the characters of a string at all, so a different structure is required for the job
It makes every comparison slower than O(n squared) whatever the lengths of the strings
It requires the strings to be sorted before their characters can be counted at all
optionExplain: Right: pairwise comparison does not give each group an identifier.
They can; counting is a core use.
Speed is not the reason given.
Sorting is not required for counting.
questions.teaches: The book says counting characters in two hash maps and comparing them is cumbersome and does not help group strings when a group has more than two, because each group needs a single identifier.
questions.rule: Use a canonical form shared by the whole group, such as the sorted string, as the hash map key.

questions.q: Instead of sorting, what else could identify a group of anagrams?
questions.explain: Anagrams contain the same letters in the same quantities. The card next shows why.
options: How many times each letter occurs
The number of distinct letters
The first and last letter
The string length
optionExplain: Right: anagrams have identical letter counts.
Different strings can share this.
Anagrams can differ in both.
Equal length is not enough.
questions.rule: A 26-count tuple key gives O(n x m) but with a larger constant and a 26-letter assumption.

questions.q: True or false: two strings are anagrams exactly when their 26-count tuples are equal.
questions.explain: Equal counts for every letter means the same letters in the same quantities.
questions.rule: Equal counts identify anagrams.

questions.q: In the 26-count tuple for the string abb, the entry for the letter b is ____.
questions.explain: b appears twice in abb.
questions.rule: Each entry counts one letter.

questions.q: True or false: the count-tuple key is faster than sorting on every input, since O(n x m) is below O(n x m log m).
questions.explain: Big O ignores constants. For short strings the 26 counts can cost more than a small sort.
questions.rule: Big O hides constants.

questions.q: A follow-up question allows any Unicode character, not only 26 letters. Which key is the more resistant?
questions.explain: The tuple assumes 26 possible characters, which is less general.
options: The sorted string, as it assumes no fixed alphabet
The 26-count tuple, because 26 is a constant
The string's length, because every string has one
Both are equally resistant to a bigger alphabet
optionExplain: Right: the count tuple would need an entry for every possible character.
It only covers 26 characters.
Length does not identify anagrams.
The count tuple has the built-in assumption.
questions.teaches: The count-tuple key assumes the strings use only 26 different characters; that is valid here but less general and less resistant to follow-up questions.
questions.rule: A 26-count tuple key gives O(n x m) but with a larger constant and a 26-letter assumption.

questions.q: The shortest subarray that contains a duplicate will have what at its two ends?
questions.explain: Trim anything that is not needed. The card next shows why.
options: The smallest and largest elements
The first and last elements of the whole array
Two different elements
The two equal elements
optionExplain: Size has no role.
That is the longest option.
The duplicate must be at the edges.
Right: anything beyond them could be trimmed.
questions.rule: The shortest repeating subarray is the shortest gap between two equal elements, found with a map from value to index.

questions.q: True or false: the shortest subarray containing a duplicate starts and ends with the two equal elements.
questions.explain: Otherwise an end element could be removed and the duplicate would remain.
questions.rule: Equal pair at the ends.

questions.q: For cards [1, 2, 6, 2, 1] the function returns ____.
questions.explain: The 2s sit at indices 1 and 3, a subarray of length 3; the 1s at indices 0 and 4 give 5.
questions.rule: The shortest repeating subarray is the shortest gap between two equal elements, found with a map from value to index.

questions.q: What does the function return for cards [5, 1, 5, 9, 1, 1]?
questions.explain: Check the gap between neighbouring occurrences of each value.
optionExplain: The 5s at indices 0 and 2 give 3, but a shorter pair exists.
The 1s at indices 1 and 4 give 4, which is not the shortest.
Duplicates exist.
Right: the last two 1s at indices 4 and 5 are adjacent.
questions.rule: The shortest repeating subarray is the shortest gap between two equal elements, found with a map from value to index.

questions.q: A variant uses i - last[c] without the plus one. For [1, 2, 6, 2, 1] it returns 2 instead of 3. What is the bug?
questions.explain: Subarray length counts both ends.
options: It stores the wrong index for each value
It returns a distance, not the subarray length
It skips the first element of the array
It returns -1 for input that is valid
optionExplain: last[c] is updated correctly.
Right: length is distance plus one.
All elements are visited.
It returns 2 here.
questions.rule: The shortest repeating subarray is the shortest gap between two equal elements, found with a map from value to index.

questions.q: To find the shortest gap between equal elements, how many indices per value does the map really need?
questions.explain: Keep only the latest index for each value. This keeps the average space smaller, while worst-case space stays O(n).
options: Only the most recent one, saving space on average
All of them, kept in a list for each value
Only the first one seen for each value
None: the values alone are enough to measure
optionExplain: Right: each new occurrence only needs the previous one.
The list version also works, but it keeps more than needed.
A later pair can be closer than a pair with the first.
Indices are needed to measure a gap.
questions.teaches: You do not need to store all indices for a value, only the most recent one; this improves the average space complexity (the worst case is still O(n) when there are no duplicates).
questions.rule: The shortest repeating subarray is the shortest gap between two equal elements, found with a map from value to index.

questions.q: Which key groups the numbers 18, 36 and 63 for this problem?
questions.explain: Use the property the problem names. The card next shows why.
options: Their number of digits
Their digit sum, 9
Their last digit
Their remainder when divided by 9, ignoring the digits
optionExplain: That groups by length only.
Right: all three sum to 9.
The last digits differ.
The digit sum is the stated key.
questions.rule: Group by an identifier that numbers in a group share, then pick the best pair per group.

questions.q: True or false: numbers with equal digit sums fall into the same group when the digit sum is the key.
questions.explain: The key decides the group. For example 478 has digit sum 4 + 7 + 8 = 19.
questions.rule: Digit sum is the group identifier.

questions.q: What does the function return for [18, 43, 36, 13, 7]?
questions.explain: Compare the best pair in each digit-sum group.
optionExplain: Right: 18 and 36 share digit sum 9; 43 and 7 share 7 (sum 50).
That is the pair 43 and 7, which is not the largest.
Those numbers are not paired by digit sum.
Pairs exist.
questions.rule: Group by an identifier that numbers in a group share, then pick the best pair per group.

questions.q: For [51, 71, 17, 42] the function returns ____.
questions.explain: 51 and 42 share digit sum 6, giving 93; 71 and 17 share digit sum 8, giving 88. The larger is 93.
questions.rule: Best pair within each digit-sum group.

questions.q: A variant uses best[ds] = num, overwriting with the latest number. For [90, 9, 18] it returns 99 instead of 108. What is the bug?
questions.explain: Store the largest number per group.
options: It forgets to compute the digit sum of each number
It keeps the latest number, not the largest, in each group
It returns -1 even when pairs exist in the input
It pairs a number with itself when it is stored
optionExplain: The digit sum is computed.
Right: 90 was overwritten by 9.
It returned 99 here.
The check happens before the store.
questions.rule: Group by an identifier that numbers in a group share, then pick the best pair per group.

questions.q: The first approach sorts every group. The book improves it by saving only what for each digit sum?
questions.explain: Keep only the biggest value per group; each new number pairs with it.
options: Every number in the group, but kept unsorted
The smallest number seen so far in the group
The count of numbers seen so far in the group
The largest number seen so far in the group
optionExplain: Storing everything keeps the space high.
The best pair uses the largest numbers.
A count cannot give the sum.
Right: no sorting is needed.
questions.teaches: Only the largest number seen so far for each digit sum needs saving; this improves the time complexity to O(n) and the average space, since no group needs to be stored or sorted.
questions.rule: Group by an identifier that numbers in a group share, then pick the best pair per group.

questions.q: Three rows equal [1, 2, 3] and two columns also equal [1, 2, 3]. How many equal (row, column) pairs do they form?
questions.explain: Every row can pair with every matching column. The card next shows why.
optionExplain: That adds 3 + 2.
Right: each of the 3 rows pairs with each of the 2 columns.
That counts only the rows.
That counts only the columns.
questions.rule: Count rows by key, count columns by key, and add the product of the two counts for every shared key.

questions.q: True or false: a row stored as a plain list can be used directly as a hash map key.
questions.explain: Lists are mutable. Convert the row to a tuple or a delimited string first.
questions.rule: Convert arrays to hashable keys.

questions.explain: Count identical keys, multiply counts, and sum.
optionExplain: That misses one match.
Right: the repeated row 2,4,2,2 twice matches column 2, and row 3,1,2,2 matches column 0.
Only three row-column pairs match.
More than one pair matches.
questions.rule: Count rows by key, count columns by key, and add the product of the two counts for every shared key.

questions.q: For the grid [[1, 2], [2, 1]] the number of equal row and column pairs is ____.
questions.explain: Row [1, 2] equals column [1, 2], and row [2, 1] equals column [2, 1].
questions.rule: Count rows by key, count columns by key, and add the product of the two counts for every shared key.

questions.q: A coder adds the row count and the column count for each shared key. With 2 identical rows and 3 identical columns of the same array, what is wrong?
questions.explain: Pairs are combinations of one row and one column.
options: It gets 6 pairs, which happens to be correct
It gets 1 pair, because keys in a map are unique
It cannot handle repeated rows or columns at all
It gets 5 pairs, not 6: the counts should multiply
optionExplain: Adding gives 5.
Both counts are used.
The maps count repeats.
Right: x times y.
questions.rule: Count rows by key, count columns by key, and add the product of the two counts for every shared key.

questions.q: A grid is n by n and every row and column is unique. What does each of the two maps hold, and what is the total space?
questions.explain: Each map has n keys; every key is an array of n values.
options: n keys of length n each, so O(n squared)
n keys of length 1, so O(n)
1 key, so O(1)
n squared keys, so O(n cubed)
optionExplain: Right: n squared numbers are stored across the keys.
Each key has n elements.
Unique rows give n separate keys.
There are only n rows and n columns.
questions.teaches: If all rows and columns are unique, each of the two hash maps grows to n keys with each key of length n, so the space complexity is O(n squared).
questions.rule: Count rows by key, count columns by key, and add the product of the two counts for every shared key.

questions.q: How does the book describe the place of hash maps in the rest of the course?
questions.explain: The chapter ends by saying they keep appearing. The card next shows why.
options: They are used in this chapter only and then dropped
They are replaced by sorting later in the course
They are used only in string problems from now on
They are used again and again in many algorithms
optionExplain: The book says it will keep using them.
No such replacement is described.
They appear across problem types.
Right: the book says they are nearly ubiquitous.
questions.rule: Recognise the pattern (exists, count, exact prefix, group by identifier) and reach for a set or map.

questions.q: True or false: after this chapter the course stops using hash maps.
questions.explain: The book says hash maps will continue to be used for the rest of the course.
questions.rule: Hash maps keep reappearing.

questions.q: Match each task to the hashing pattern that suits it.
questions.explain: Presence, frequency, exact prefix differences and grouping each have a standard shape.
pairs: How many times does each word occur?
a map from key to count
Count subarrays with sum exactly k
prefix sums and a counts map
a map keyed by a shared identifier
questions.rule: Match the question to the pattern.

questions.q: A new problem asks for the longest substring with at most k distinct characters. Which chapter pattern applies?
questions.explain: Match the constraint's shape to the pattern.
options: A sliding window with a counts map of its characters
A set of the characters seen so far
Prefix sums with a counts map of earlier sums
An identifier key used to group anagram strings
optionExplain: Right: the constraint involves several different elements.
A set cannot count characters leaving the window.
That is for exact constraints.
No grouping is asked for.
questions.rule: Recognise the pattern (exists, count, exact prefix, group by identifier) and reach for a set or map.

questions.q: A problem does not mention hashing, but your brute force has an inner loop that searches for a value. What does the closing advice suggest?
questions.explain: The book says there are unlimited ways to incorporate hash maps, so look for the search or count.
options: Sort the data and avoid any hashing
Hashing is unlikely, as the problem does not mention it
Consider a hash map or set, as they appear in many algorithms
Replace the inner loop with another inner loop
optionExplain: Sorting is not the book's advice here.
The book says hash maps appear in many unexpected places.
Right: the book describes hash maps as ubiquitous.
That only makes it slower.
questions.teaches: There are an unlimited number of ways to incorporate hash maps into an algorithm, so a problem does not need to mention hashing for one to help.
questions.rule: Recognise the pattern (exists, count, exact prefix, group by identifier) and reach for a set or map.

questions.q: A linked list keeps values in order. What is the link from one value to the one after it?
options: Each node stores its position number, and nodes sit sorted in memory
Each node holds a reference to the node that follows it
Nodes sit exactly 4 bytes apart, so the next one is found by adding 4
A separate table lists every position and the address of its node
optionExplain: Position numbers belong to arrays; a node in a linked list does not need one, and nodes can sit anywhere.
Right: the order lives in references from node to node, not in where nodes sit in memory.
Fixed spacing is how array elements are located, and it is exactly what a linked list does not rely on.
A position table would work as an index, but a linked list has no such table; each node points on instead.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The order is carried by pointers between nodes; the card shows how.
questions.rule: A linked list is nodes joined by next pointers, with null marking the end.

questions.q: The field of a node that refers to the following node is usually called ____.
questions.explain: The book names it next. The node after the last one does not exist, so the last node's next is null.
questions.rule: Each node has val and next.

questions.q: True or false: in a playlist stored as nodes A, B, C, D, each pointing to the following track, only node D has a next of null.
questions.explain: Null marks the end, so only the final node has it. A points to B, B to C and C to D.
questions.rule: The end of the chain is the node with next set to null.

questions.q: The code below prints ____.
questions.code:
a = ListNode(5)
b = ListNode(8)
c = ListNode(2)
a.next = b
b.next = c
print(a.next.val)
questions.explain: a.next refers to b, whose val is 8.
questions.rule: x.next moves one node forward; .val reads the value there.

questions.q: A 32-bit integer array starts at address 1000, and each element takes 4 bytes. At what address does arr[6] sit?
optionExplain: Adding the index alone ignores the 4-byte element size.
1028 is the address of arr[7], one element too far.
1032 is the address of arr[8].
Right: arr[6] is 6 elements along, 6 x 4 = 24 bytes, so 1000 + 24.
questions.explain: The address is the start plus index times element size, so the machine gets there with one calculation.
questions.rule: Contiguous storage lets an array jump to any index by arithmetic.
questions.teaches: Array elements sit contiguously, each 4 bytes (32 bits) from its neighbour for 32-bit integers, which is what allows indexing such as arr[6]; linked list nodes have no such spacing.

questions.q: A treasure hunt gives each clue the next hiding place, and the last clue says the hunt is done. Which linked list idea does that final clue match?
options: A node whose next is null, ending the chain
A node whose val is 0, holding no data
A head that points back to the first clue
A pointer that jumps to any clue by number
optionExplain: Right: the final clue is the last node, with no successor to point to.
Null is the empty next pointer; val still holds the clue.
A pointer back to the start would make a cycle, and the hunt would never end.
Jumping by number needs an index, which a chain of pointers does not offer.
questions.explain: Each clue plays the part of a node, and the missing next hiding place plays the part of null.
questions.rule: Follow next until null to finish.
questions.teaches: A node is an abstract idea: an element together with more than its bare value, so an array element can be viewed as a node holding the value and its index, and a list node as a value and a next pointer.

questions.q: A program holds a pointer to the third node of a singly linked list with five nodes. Which nodes can it reach by following next?
options: All five nodes, as the list is one chain
The first, second and third nodes only
The third, fourth and fifth nodes only
Only the third node, as pointers cannot be followed
optionExplain: The nodes are one chain, but links only run from earlier nodes to later ones.
That would need pointers to run backward, which a singly linked list lacks.
Right: next pointers run forward, so only the node itself and those after it.
Following next is how traversal works; the node reaches the ones after it.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. Links run one way, which is why the head matters; the card explains.
questions.rule: Keep a reference to the head so that no element of the list is lost.

questions.q: True or false: the head is the only node from which every element of a singly linked list can be reached.
questions.explain: Every other node is reached by following next from some earlier node, so only the head reaches all of them.
questions.rule: All nodes are reachable from the head.

questions.q: A cache keeps entries as a singly linked list, but its code stores only a pointer to the middle entry. A request needs the first entry. What follows?
options: It is reached by following prev from the middle entry
It is reached in O(1), as the middle entry stores the head's address
The first entry cannot be reached from the middle pointer
It is reached by following next, which wraps around to the start
optionExplain: A prev pointer exists only in a doubly linked list, not in this one.
A node stores only its value and its next pointer, not the head's address.
Right: next only moves forward, so the earlier nodes are out of reach.
Wrapping would need a cycle; this list ends in null.
questions.explain: Without a reference to the head, the nodes before the middle cannot be found.
questions.rule: Hold the head, or lose the nodes before your current position.

questions.q: The variable head holds the list 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7, and the code runs head = head.next twice. Which values can the program still reach?
options: 6 and 7
4 and 5
7 only
optionExplain: Right: head now refers to 6, and no variable refers to 4 or 5.
Moving head does not rebuild the list; the first two nodes are no longer referred to.
Those are the nodes left behind, and nothing points to them.
7 is reachable, but head sits on 6, which still points to 7.
questions.explain: Each assignment moves head one node forward, and the nodes it leaves are no longer reachable.
questions.rule: Moving your only reference forward loses the nodes behind it.

questions.q: A list has 1,000 nodes and the program holds only the head. How many next-steps lead to the last node, the tail? Answer with a number: ____
questions.explain: The k-th node is k - 1 steps from the head, so the last of 1,000 is 999 steps away.
questions.rule: From the head, node k is k - 1 steps away.
questions.teaches: The end of a list is called the tail, and from a bare head reference reaching the tail means walking the whole list, n - 1 steps for n nodes.

questions.q: A music player walks a playlist stored as a singly linked list. A user taps the restart button during track 7. What does restarting need?
options: A prev pointer on track 7 that leads back to track 6 and on to the start
A new list built from the tracks already played
Nothing, because the list stores its own start
A saved reference to the head, so it can begin again
optionExplain: One prev step reaches only track 6, and the list is singly linked.
Rebuilding costs extra space and time, and the head makes it unnecessary.
Nodes store only a value and a next pointer; the start must be held by the program.
Right: with the head saved, the walk can begin again at the first track.
questions.explain: A held head reference is what makes starting again possible.
questions.rule: The head you kept is the way back to the start.
questions.teaches: Keeping the head also lets a program start over from the first element at any time, while a separate moving pointer does the walking.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: A linked list holds 200,000 values and the program holds only the head. It needs the 150,000th value. What is usually the best option?
options: Compute its address in one step from the head
Walk from the head, taking about 150,000 steps
Binary search the list in about 18 steps
Read it in O(1) from the list's built-in index
optionExplain: Address arithmetic works for arrays because elements are contiguous, not for scattered nodes.
Right: with only the head, the program iterates from the start.
Binary search needs to jump to the middle, which the list cannot do.
A linked list has no index to read from.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. Position access is the weak spot of a linked list; the card explains why.
questions.rule: A linked list wins at changing a position you already hold and loses at reaching a position by number.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: Match each operation to its cost.
pairs: Index into a linked list from its head
Insert after a node you already hold
Insert at an arbitrary position of a dynamic array
questions.explain: Arrays index by address in O(1) but shift elements on insertion, O(n). A list must walk to a position, O(n), but rewires in O(1) from a held node.
questions.rule: Match cost to how elements are stored.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: A text editor keeps lines as a singly linked list, and the cursor holds the line before the insertion point. Inserting a line costs O(____) time.
questions.explain: With the previous node in hand, insertion is a fixed number of pointer changes, so O(1).
questions.rule: Held reference: O(1). No reference: O(n) to find it.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: A program makes 1,000,000 reads by position and almost no insertions. Which structure suits it?
options: A dynamic array, as indexing is O(1)
A linked list, as every read is O(1) once the head is held
A linked list, as it never needs resizing
Either, as both index in the same time
optionExplain: Right: the workload is read-heavy by position, which arrays serve in O(1).
Only the head is O(1); position k costs O(k).
Avoiding resizing is a plus, but a million slow reads outweigh it.
Their indexing costs differ: O(1) for an array, O(n) for a list.
questions.explain: Reads by position favour the structure with O(1) indexing.
questions.rule: Many positional reads point to an array.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: A student writes: inserting in the middle of a list is O(1), so a list beats an array in every case. What is the flaw?
options: Inserting in a list moves every later node, so it is O(n)
The array beats the list because arrays index in O(log n)
Finding the middle from the head costs O(n) if no reference is held
Pointers cannot be changed after the list is built
optionExplain: Nodes do not move; only pointers change.
Array indexing is O(1), and that is not the flaw anyway.
Right: the O(1) holds only once the reference to the position is in hand.
Pointer fields can be reassigned, and insertion does exactly that.
questions.explain: The student left out the cost of getting a reference to the insertion point.
questions.rule: Check where the reference comes from before claiming O(1).
questions.hint: Ask how the program gets to the middle in the first place.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: A leaderboard of 5 million players is a singly linked list. A request asks for rank 3,000,000. What does this cost, and why?
options: One step, as the rank is stored in the node and read directly from it
About 3,000,000 steps, as the list is walked from the head
About 22 steps, as the walk can halve the list
About 3,000,000 steps, as arrays also walk to a rank
optionExplain: A node holds a value and next, not its own position.
Right: reaching position k means k - 1 steps from the head.
Halving needs a jump to the middle, which a list cannot make.
An array reaches a rank directly, without walking.
questions.explain: Cost grows with the position asked for, so late ranks are the expensive ones.
questions.rule: Reading position k from the head takes about k steps.
questions.teaches: The cost of reaching an element grows with its position: the 150,000th element of a long list usually takes 150,000 iterations from the head.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: A program stores 1,000,000 boolean flags. Which structure carries more storage overhead per element?
options: An array, as every slot adds a pointer
Neither, as both store only the flag
They match, as the element counts are equal, so the storage is too
A singly linked list, as every node adds a pointer
optionExplain: Array slots hold the elements side by side with no pointer.
A node must store its next reference as well as its data.
The counts match, but the storage per element does not.
Right: the pointer stored beside each flag is the extra cost.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. Each node must carry a pointer; the card shows the consequence.
questions.rule: Lists grow without resizing but spend extra storage on a pointer per element.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: True or false: in most linked list problems, you decide whether a linked list is the right structure.
questions.explain: Almost all such problems hand you the list as part of the input, so you are forced to use it.
questions.rule: Most list problems give you the list.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: Assume a character takes 1 byte and a pointer 8 bytes, and ignore other overhead. A list of 1,000 characters takes ____ bytes.
questions.explain: Each node holds 1 + 8 = 9 bytes, and 1,000 nodes give 9,000 bytes against 1,000 bytes for an array of characters.
questions.rule: Small items, big pointers: the overhead dominates.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: A dynamic array with a fixed allocation of 4 slots is full and receives a fifth item. What happens under the hood?
options: The item is stored in a new node linked to the fourth
A new, larger allocation is made, which is expensive
The array grows by one slot at no cost
The item is dropped because arrays cannot resize
optionExplain: Linking in a new node is how a linked list grows, not an array.
Right: once the size is exceeded the array is resized, and that is costly.
Growth is not free: the array must be resized.
Dynamic arrays can be resized, which is what makes them dynamic.
questions.explain: A dynamic array still has a fixed allocation under the hood and pays when it is exceeded.
questions.rule: Arrays pay at resize time; lists pay per node.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: A candidate defends using a linked list for its flexible size, yet the problem gives the list as input. What is the weak point?
options: Lists have a fixed size, so they cannot grow
Flexible size makes list indexing O(1)
Lists need less storage per element than arrays
The input already is a list, so there is no choice to defend
optionExplain: Lists grow node by node; fixed size is the array's trait.
Indexing a list still takes O(n) however it grows.
Each node adds a pointer, so a list needs more storage.
Right: when the list comes as input, the structure is forced.
questions.explain: The defence answers a question the problem never asks.
questions.rule: Check whether the problem leaves you any choice.

questions.section: Advantages and disadvantages compared to arrays
questions.q: An interviewer asks you to compare a linked list and an array for 10 million booleans. Which answer fits the book's trade-offs?
options: The list grows without resizing but spends a pointer on each boolean
The list is smaller, since it stores only the booleans that are true
The array must be rebuilt for each boolean it stores
The list is better, since indexing it takes O(1)
optionExplain: Right: flexible size against pointer overhead is the trade-off for small items.
A list stores a node for every item it holds, true or false.
An array is rebuilt only when it outgrows its allocation.
Indexing a list is O(n), not O(1).
questions.explain: Small items make pointer overhead the main cost of the list.
questions.rule: For tiny items, a pointer per node can outweigh the data.
questions.teaches: Linked list advantages and disadvantages may be asked as trivia in an interview even though algorithm problems rarely give you a choice.

questions.q: Variable ptr is set equal to head, which refers to the node holding 1. Then head is set to head.next and then to null. What is ptr.val?
options: An error, as head is null
optionExplain: 2 would be right only if ptr followed head forward.
3 is two nodes further than head ever moved.
Right: ptr was set once, to the node holding 1, and nothing assigned to ptr afterwards.
Setting head to null does not touch ptr.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card explains why ptr stays where it was.
questions.rule: A variable stays at its node until that same variable is assigned.

questions.q: True or false: after ptr = head, a later head = head.next also moves ptr to the second node.
questions.explain: ptr refers to the node it was given. Only an assignment to ptr itself can move it.
questions.rule: Assigning one variable leaves the others where they are.

questions.q: A list holds 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40. What are cur.val and mark.val after the code runs?
questions.code:
cur = head
mark = head.next
cur = cur.next.next
options: 30 and 30
20 and 20
30 and 20
10 and 20
optionExplain: mark was set to head.next once; it does not follow cur.
cur moved two steps from the head, not one.
Right: cur ends two nodes along, and mark was fixed at the second node when set.
cur does not stay at the head; it was assigned cur.next.next.
questions.explain: mark is set once to the second node. cur starts at 10 and then moves two nodes on to 30.
questions.rule: Trace each variable by itself.

questions.q: A list holds 1 -> 2 -> 3, with head at node 1. The code below prints ____.
questions.code:
ptr = head
ptr.next = ptr.next.next
print(head.next.val)
questions.explain: Assigning to a field edits the shared node, so head sees it too. Assigning to a variable would not.
questions.rule: Changing a field is visible to every variable that refers to the node.

questions.q: A student says: ptr = head ran earlier, so after head = head.next, ptr refers to the second node as well. Which fix is right?
options: ptr was assigned once; only an assignment to ptr moves it
ptr moves along with head, because both were linked when ptr = head ran
ptr is right, as pointers always follow the head
ptr holds a copy of the whole list at that time
optionExplain: Right: ptr stays on the first node unless ptr is assigned.
The names are separate variables with their own references.
Variables follow nothing; each holds one reference.
ptr holds a reference to a node, not a copy of the list.
questions.explain: Moving head changes head's reference only.
questions.rule: A variable moves only when you assign to it.

questions.q: Two bookmarks open the same web page. One bookmark is re-pointed to a new page. What happens to the other bookmark?
options: It now opens the new page, as both followed one link
It opens a blank page, as the link was cut
It opens a copy of the original that cannot be edited
It still opens the original page
optionExplain: That would match a shared name for one variable, not two variables.
Nothing cuts the second link; only the first bookmark changed.
Both bookmarks share the real page, not a copy.
Right: re-pointing one bookmark does not touch the other, in the same way that head = head.next leaves ptr alone.
questions.explain: A bookmark is a variable and a page is a node: re-pointing a variable never moves another.
questions.rule: Variables are separate; nodes are shared.
questions.teaches: In languages without explicit pointers, all non-primitive variables, such as custom class objects, behave as pointers; C++ writes them with an asterisk.

questions.q: A list holds 1 -> 2 -> 3, with head at the node 1. Which node does head.next.next refer to?
options: The node holding 2
The node holding 3
The node holding 1
Null
optionExplain: head.next alone gives the node 2.
Right: head.next is the node 2, and its next is the node 3.
head itself is the node 1.
Null is 3's next, one more .next away.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. Each .next moves one node on; the card shows the pattern.
questions.rule: In a chain of .next, all but the last name a node, and the last is the field you read or write.

questions.q: On 1 -> 2 -> 3 with head at 1, the expression head.next names the node holding ____.
questions.explain: head is the node 1, so head.next is the node after it, which holds 2.
questions.rule: head.next is one node ahead of head.

questions.q: A list holds 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 8 -> 9, with head at 5. What is head.next.next.next.val?
optionExplain: Right: three .next steps from 5 land on 8.
7 is two steps from the head.
9 is four steps from the head.
6 is one step from the head.
questions.explain: Count one node per .next: 6, 7, 8.
questions.rule: k times .next lands k nodes ahead.

questions.q: A list holds 1 -> 2 -> 3. The code head.next.next = None runs. Which values does a walk from head visit?
optionExplain: 3 is detached, so the walk does not reach it.
Node 1 still points to node 2.
Right: node 2's next now holds null, so the walk stops after 2.
The walk starts at head, which is still node 1.
questions.explain: The assignment changes the next field of node 2.
questions.rule: Setting a next field to null ends the list at that node.

questions.q: True or false: head.next.next.val fails on the two-node list 1 -> 2 because head.next.next is null.
questions.explain: Node 2's next is null, and reading val from null is an error. The first .next is fine; the second reaches null.
questions.rule: Check for null before a chained read.

questions.q: A list holds A -> B -> C, with head at A. What does head.next.next = head do?
options: It makes node A's next refer to C
It makes node B's next refer to A, cutting B's link to C
It reads the node C and stores it in head
It does nothing, as the two sides name different nodes and nothing is changed
optionExplain: That would be head.next = head.next.next.
Right: the left side is B's next field, and it is assigned the node A.
A read happens on the right side of an assignment, not the left.
Both sides name nodes, but the left side is a field that changes.
questions.explain: On the left of =, the chain names the field being set. On the right, it names the node being read.
questions.rule: Left of =: the field you change. Right of =: the node you read.
questions.teaches: The same expression, head.next.next, changes B's next node when it stands before the assignment operator, and refers to the node that follows B when it stands after.

questions.q: A loop visits every node of a list of n nodes exactly once. About how many loop steps does it take?
options: log n
n squared
n
optionExplain: log n belongs to halving searches, which a list cannot do.
Squared would mean n steps for each node.
One step reaches only the first node.
Right: one step per node.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card shows what ends the loop.
questions.rule: Walk until the pointer is null, using each node once.

questions.q: Put the steps of an iterative sum over a linked list in order.
items: Test that the current node is not null
Add the current node's val to the total
Return the total once the loop ends
questions.explain: Initialise, test, use the node, advance, and repeat; after null, return.
questions.rule: Test, use, advance.

questions.q: A list holds 3 -> 1 -> 4 -> 1 -> 5. The sum loop returns ____.
questions.explain: 3 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 5 = 14: each node is added once.
questions.rule: The sum counts every node once.

questions.q: The recursive sum runs on a list of 4 nodes. How many calls happen, counting the final call on null?
optionExplain: 4 forgets the call on null that stops the recursion.
Right: one call per node plus one more on null, which returns 0.
3 skips both the first node and the null call.
6 counts a call that never happens.
questions.explain: Each call handles one node and calls on the next; the call on null ends the chain.
questions.rule: n nodes make n + 1 calls.

questions.q: This loop should sum 2 -> 4 -> 6 to 12, but returns 6. What is wrong?
options: The loop never moves head forward
ans starts at the wrong value
The loop runs one step past the end and tries to add the null node's value
The test stops at the last node before its value is added
optionExplain: head = head.next is there; the loop does advance.
ans starts at 0, which is correct for a sum.
The loop stops early, not late.
Right: head.next is null at the last node, so the loop ends before adding 6.
questions.explain: Testing head.next instead of head leaves the last node out.
questions.rule: Test the current node, not its successor.

questions.q: A bug links the last node of a 3-node list back to the first. What does the sum loop do?
options: It never stops, as the pointer never becomes null
It stops after 3 steps, as the list has 3 nodes
It stops at once, as the first node repeats
It returns the sum of 3 values, then raises an error
optionExplain: Right: with no node whose next is null, the loop has nothing to end on.
Stopping after the node count needs a counter the loop does not have.
A repeated node does not stop the loop; it only revisits.
No error arises; the loop keeps adding.
questions.explain: The loop's only exit is reaching null, and a cycle has no end.
questions.rule: No null, no exit.
questions.teaches: If a list has a cycle, traversal never ends: it moves around the circle forever, which is why the end-of-list test cannot be trusted on a cycle.

questions.q: To insert a new element at position i of a singly linked list, which existing node must you hold?
options: The node at position i + 1
The tail of the list
The node at position i - 1
The node at position i + 2
optionExplain: A node after the new one cannot point backward at it.
The tail matters only for appending at the end.
Right: only the node before the new one can have its next pointer relinked to it.
A node two places on is no help to the node before.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card shows why the previous node is the one needed.
questions.rule: Hold the node before the position; when inserting, point the new node at the old successor before relinking prev.

questions.q: Put the steps of inserting a new node after the held node prev in order.
items: Hold the node prev at position i - 1
Point the new node's next at prev's current next
Point prev's next at the new node
questions.explain: The new node must take over the old successor first. Then prev can safely be pointed at it.
questions.rule: New node first, prev second.

questions.q: A list holds 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40. delete_node runs with prev set to the node holding 20. Which values remain?
optionExplain: That would delete 20, not the node after prev.
That would delete 40; the deleted node is prev.next.
Right: prev.next skips 30 and points at 40.
