That would delete 10, the head.
questions.explain: delete_node removes the node after prev, which is the one holding 30.
questions.rule: delete_node(prev) removes prev.next.

questions.q: In this insert, the two lines run in the wrong order. What goes wrong?
options: The new node ends up pointing at itself, losing the old successor
The new node points at the old successor, which is correct
prev is left pointing at the old successor
The old successor is deleted from memory and the new node becomes the end of the list
optionExplain: Right: after prev.next = n, reading prev.next gives n, so n.next = n.
That is the right order, not the wrong one.
prev is already pointing at the new node after its first line.
The old successor is not deleted; it is only unreachable, and n loops on itself.
questions.explain: Relinking prev first erases the only reference to the old successor.
questions.rule: Save the old successor before you overwrite the link to it.

questions.q: True or false: holding the node at position 2,000 of a singly linked list is enough to delete that same node in O(1).
questions.explain: Deletion relinks the node before the target, at position 1,999, and holding the target gives no way back to it. Finding it takes about 2,000 steps from the head.
questions.rule: Hold the node before the target, not the target itself.

questions.q: While walking a list to remove every node equal to 7, which node should the loop track besides the current one?
options: The next node, so the current one can be skipped from ahead
The head only, as all deletions are relinked from the start
The tail, as removed nodes are moved to the end
The previous node, so it can skip the current one
optionExplain: The next node is needed to move on, but cannot relink the one before.
The head alone gives no access to the node before the current one.
Removed nodes are unlinked, not moved.
Right: deleting current means setting prev.next to current.next.
questions.explain: A deletion needs the node before the target, which the walk can keep as it goes.
questions.rule: Walk with prev behind current.
questions.teaches: Typically these operations are done on the fly while iterating through the list, rather than with a pointer given in advance to the node at i - 1.

questions.q: A singly linked delete needs the node at i - 1. In a doubly linked list, which node is enough to delete node i?
options: Node i + 1 alone, since next leads on
Node i alone, since its prev leads to node i - 1
The head, since every edit starts there
No node at all, as a doubly linked list rewires itself after a request
optionExplain: Node i + 1 would need prev to reach the node before i, and that still takes two steps.
Right: node i holds prev, so node i - 1 is one step away.
The head would force a walk of about i steps.
Pointers change only when code assigns them.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The extra pointer is what makes the difference; the card shows how.
questions.rule: A prev pointer lets you edit from the node itself, at the price of updating links in both directions.

questions.q: The extra pointer in a doubly linked node, which refers to the node before it, is usually called ____.
questions.explain: The book names it prev, and it allows iteration in both directions.
questions.rule: next goes forward; prev goes back.

questions.q: How many pointer fields does the doubly linked add_node on the card assign when it inserts one node?
optionExplain: Right: node_to_add.next, node_to_add.prev, prev_node.next and node.prev.
2 is the count for the doubly linked delete, not the insert.
Three links are fewer than the four that need a new value.
One is the count for a singly linked delete.
questions.explain: The new node needs both of its pointers, and each of its two new neighbours needs one.
questions.rule: Doubly linked insert: four assignments.

questions.q: A list reads 1 <-> 2 <-> 3. After delete_node on the node holding 2, what values does a walk visit going backward from 3?
optionExplain: 2 would remain only if prev were left unchanged.
The walk continues past 3 to the node 1.
Right: both neighbours were relinked, so 3's prev is now 1.
Going backward starts at 3, not at 1.
questions.explain: The delete sets 1.next to 3 and 3.prev to 1.
questions.rule: Both directions must agree after an edit.

questions.q: True or false: if delete_node sets only prev_node.next = next_node, walking forward skips the deleted node but walking backward can still reach it.
questions.explain: next_node.prev still points at the deleted node, so a backward walk passes through it.
questions.rule: Update next and prev together.

questions.q: A list reads 1 <-> 2 <-> 3. delete_node from the card runs on the node holding 3. What happens?
options: The node is removed and the list is 1 <-> 2
next_node is null, so assigning next_node.prev raises an error
Nothing changes, as the last node of a list cannot be deleted by this code
The node holding 1 is removed instead
optionExplain: That is the intended result; the plain code does not reach it.
Right: the last node has no successor to update.
The code does not check for the end, so it tries and fails.
Deletion acts on the node given, not the head.
questions.explain: At the ends, next_node or prev_node is null, which the plain code does not handle.
questions.rule: Ends need special handling in the plain version.
questions.teaches: The plain doubly linked edits are error-prone at the ends of the list: deleting the last node leaves nextNode null, and using it fails.

questions.q: In a doubly linked list, what could make deleting the last node as safe as deleting a middle node?
options: A larger value stored in the last node
A second head pointer stored in the first node
Deleting the node twice to be sure
A tail node after it, so its next is never null
optionExplain: The value is irrelevant to the pointer problem.
A second head does nothing about the missing node after the end.
Repeating a deletion would hit the same null.
Right: with a node always after it, the last real node has a successor to update.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. A placeholder node at each end is the idea; the card shows it.
questions.rule: Sentinel nodes make every real node an interior node, so the ends need no special case.

questions.q: True or false: the sentinel head and tail nodes are part of the data the list stores.
questions.explain: They only mark the ends. The real first node is head.next and the real last is tail.prev.
questions.rule: Sentinels frame the list; they are not in it.

questions.q: A list with sentinels is empty. Then head.next refers to the ____ sentinel.
questions.explain: The setup links head.next = tail and tail.prev = head, which is the empty state. Null would bring back the end cases that sentinels avoid.
questions.rule: Empty list: head.next is tail.

questions.q: Nodes 1, 2, 3 are added with add_to_end, then remove_from_end runs once. Which values lie between the sentinels, front to back?
optionExplain: That is the list before the removal.
Right: add_to_end appends at the back, and remove_from_end drops the last one, 3.
That would come from removing the front.
Removal acts at the end, so the middle stays.
questions.explain: The back is tail.prev, which is the node holding 3 when removal runs.
questions.rule: add_to_end then remove_from_end undoes the last add.

questions.q: remove_from_end loses its first check and runs on an empty list with sentinels. What happens?
questions.code:
def remove_from_end():
    node = tail.prev
    node.prev.next = tail
    tail.prev = node.prev
options: It returns quietly, as the list is already empty
It removes the tail sentinel and leaves head.next null
It deletes the last real node, which does not exist
It treats the head sentinel as a real node and fails on its missing prev
optionExplain: Without the check there is no quiet return.
The code reads tail.prev, so the tail is not the node removed.
No real node exists to delete; the code reaches a sentinel instead.
Right: tail.prev is the head sentinel, whose prev is null, so node.prev.next fails.
questions.explain: The check head.next is tail stops the removal from reaching the sentinels.
questions.rule: Sentinels need an empty-list check before removal.

questions.q: A print queue adds jobs at the back and removes them from the front, both in O(1). Which structure fits?
options: A doubly linked list with sentinel head and tail
A singly linked list with only a head pointer
A dynamic array, where removing the front is O(1)
A linked list searched for the front each time
optionExplain: Right: sentinels give O(1) access to both ends.
Reaching the back from the head alone takes O(n).
Removing the front of an array shifts every other element, O(n).
Searching from the head to the front is not needed; sentinels give it directly.
questions.explain: Both ends are always held, so adding at one and removing at the other are each a fixed number of pointer changes.
questions.rule: Held ends make end operations O(1).
questions.teaches: A deque, a structure covered later in the book, can be implemented with a linked list.

questions.q: A function sums a list and must then reverse it, starting from the first node. How should it do the sum walk?
options: Move the head variable along the list, then rebuild the list afterwards
Walk twice with the head variable
Move a second variable and leave the head variable alone
Copy the list into an array and discard the nodes
optionExplain: Moving head would lose the first node and force a rebuild.
A second walk with the same variable would start where the first ended.
Right: the head variable stays on the first node for later use.
Discarding the nodes would lose the list itself.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. A spare pointer is the answer; the card shows it.
questions.rule: Walk with a spare pointer and keep head where it is.

questions.q: Walking with a dummy pointer set to head leaves the head variable on the ____ node.
questions.explain: Only the dummy moves, so head still refers to the first node.
questions.rule: Dummy walks; head stays.

questions.q: A list holds 7 -> 8 -> 9, with head at 7. The code below runs. What do head.val and dummy.val read?
questions.code:
dummy = head
dummy = dummy.next
dummy = dummy.next
options: 9 and 9
7 and 8
7 and 9
8 and 9
optionExplain: head is never assigned, so it cannot be at 9.
dummy was moved twice, ending at 9, not 8.
Right: dummy moved twice, head not at all.
head stays on the first node, 7.
questions.explain: dummy = head and two dummy.next steps: dummy ends at the third node.
questions.rule: Only the assigned variable moves.

questions.q: Loop A: while head: head = head.next. Loop B: dummy = head, then while dummy: dummy = dummy.next. Run alone, which loop leaves head on the first node?
options: Only loop B
Only loop A
Both loops
Neither loop
optionExplain: Right: loop A moves head itself to null, while loop B moves dummy.
Loop A overwrites head on every step.
Loop A consumes head, so both is wrong.
Loop B keeps head untouched.
questions.explain: A loop that moves head also destroys head; moving a spare keeps it.
questions.rule: Move the spare, not the head.

questions.q: True or false: starting the walk at dummy = head.next, to keep head safe, still visits every node.
questions.explain: The walk starts at the second node, so the first node is never visited. dummy should start at head itself; head stays safe anyway, because only dummy moves.
questions.rule: dummy = head, not head.next.

questions.q: A function must double every value in a list, then return the head to its caller. How should the loop be written?
options: Walk with head itself, then return head
Walk with head itself, then rebuild the list
Copy each node into a new array, then return it
Walk with a spare pointer, and return the untouched head
optionExplain: After walking, head would be null.
A rebuild is unneeded and repeats the work.
An array is O(n) extra space, and the function must return a list.
Right: the spare pointer finds every node, and head is still the first node at the end.
questions.explain: Editing values in place needs a walker, and returning the head needs a variable still on the first node.
questions.rule: Edit with the dummy, return the head.
questions.teaches: A large part of linked lists is moving pointers around, so build intuition by watching the process step by step and working through examples.

questions.q: A problem asks for the middle value of a linked list, and one solution copies the values into an array. How does the book rate it?
options: As the best solution, since arrays index in O(1)
As cheating that would not pass in an interview
As equal to any pointer solution in every way
As required, since lists cannot be walked twice
optionExplain: Indexing is fast, but the extra space and the missed skill cost more.
Right: the book calls it basically cheating.
Time may match, but space does not: O(n) against O(1).
A list can be walked as often as you like with a spare pointer.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the book's view and the reason.
questions.rule: Aim for clean pointer manipulation in O(1) space; copying the list into an array is the shortcut to avoid.

questions.q: True or false: according to the author, the point of most linked list problems is usually to manipulate pointers cleanly in O(1) space.
questions.explain: The author says the point is clean pointer manipulation using O(1) space.
questions.rule: Pointers in O(1) space is the target.

questions.q: A list has 1,000,000 nodes. Copying its values into an array needs O(____) extra space.
questions.explain: One array slot per node, so the space grows with n. A few spare pointers would need O(1).
questions.rule: Copy: O(n) space. Pointers: O(1).

questions.q: Two solutions both run in O(n) time. Solution X copies the list into an array. Solution Y uses three pointer variables. Which does the book prefer?
options: Y, as it uses O(1) extra space
X, as arrays index in O(1)
X, as arrays are easier to write
Neither, as equal time means equal quality
optionExplain: Right: equal time, so the O(1) space decides it.
Fast indexing helps X, but pointers are what the problem tests.
Ease of writing is not the stated criterion.
Time ties, but space and the tested skill differ.
questions.explain: When time ties, space and skill break the tie.
questions.rule: Tied on time: choose the smaller space.

questions.q: A candidate says both approaches are O(n) time, so the choice of array or pointers does not matter. What does this overlook?
options: The array takes O(n squared) time
The pointer approach takes O(log n) time
The array needs O(n) extra space, and the problem tests pointer skill
Arrays cannot store the values of a list
optionExplain: Copying a list into an array takes O(n), not O(n squared).
A pointer walk still visits every node, which is O(n).
Right: time ties, but space and the intent differ.
An array can hold the values; that is the shortcut.
questions.explain: Time is not the only measure; space and the intended skill matter.
questions.rule: Compare space as well as time.

questions.q: Your array solution passes all tests with ten minutes left in an interview. According to the book, which next step fits?
options: Stop, since passing tests is what counts
Present it, then redo it with pointers in O(1) space
Delete it and say nothing about the array idea
Explain that arrays are always better than lists, so the solution is complete
optionExplain: The book says the array route will almost guarantee failure.
Right: the book values the pointer solution and explicit thinking.
Hiding your thinking helps neither you nor the interviewer.
The book makes no such claim; it values pointer skill.
questions.explain: The array idea shows you can solve it; the pointer version shows the skill being tested.
questions.rule: Reach for pointers once the array idea works.
questions.teaches: Many linked list solutions are difficult to reach because of their elegance, even though they are usually simple once found.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: On a 9-node list, two pointers start at the head: one moves 2 nodes per step, the other 1. Where is the slow one when the fast one reaches the end?
options: Still at the head
At the end as well
One node before the end
About halfway along the list
optionExplain: It has moved with every step, so it has left the head.
It moves at half the speed, so it is far behind the end.
That would need it to move almost as fast as fast.
Right: slow has taken half as many steps as fast.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. Half the speed means half the distance; the card builds on that.
questions.rule: Move fast two nodes and slow one, and loop while both fast and fast.next exist.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: True or false: the loop test while fast and fast.next stops the code from reading fast.next.next when fast.next is null.
questions.explain: If fast is on the last node, fast.next is null. The test ends the loop before fast.next.next is read.
questions.rule: Test fast and fast.next before moving two nodes.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: The skeleton loop runs on a list of 10 nodes. It takes ____ iterations.
questions.explain: Fast moves 1 to 3 to 5 to 7 to 9 and then off the end: five moves. Each iteration moves fast two nodes, so n nodes take about n / 2 iterations.
questions.rule: About n / 2 iterations.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A list holds 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40 -> 50 -> 60. Where does slow stand when the skeleton loop ends?
options: On the node holding 30
On the node holding 40
On the node holding 50
On the node holding 60
optionExplain: 30 is the lower of the two middle nodes, but slow moves three times.
Right: three iterations move slow from the first node to the fourth.
50 would need four iterations.
60 is where fast would be if it moved one node at a time.
questions.explain: Fast takes 3 iterations to leave a 6-node list, so slow moves 3 nodes to the fourth.
questions.rule: Trace slow once per iteration.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A loop tests only while fast and then sets fast = fast.next.next. On a 3-node list it raises an error. Why?
questions.code:
while fast:
    fast = fast.next.next
options: fast starts as null, so the first step fails
fast.next.next is never valid on a list of 3 nodes
The loop runs one step too few and leaves a node unvisited
On the last node, fast.next is null, so fast.next.next reads a field of null
optionExplain: fast starts at the head, which exists.
The first step is valid; the failure comes at the last node.
The failure is an error, not a missed node.
Right: the test fast passes on the last node, then fast.next.next fails.
questions.explain: Fast can stand on the last node with fast.next null, and that case needs the second test.
questions.rule: Test fast.next as well as fast.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A variant moves fast three nodes per iteration. Which loop test keeps it from reading a field of null?
options: Test that fast, fast.next and fast.next.next all exist
Test only that fast exists
Test fast and fast.next only, as in the two-node case, since they cover each read
Test only that fast.next.next exists
optionExplain: Right: each node the pointer reads through must exist before the step.
On the last node, fast.next is null and the step fails.
Two checks cover a two-node step; a three-node step reads one node further.
If fast is null, reading fast.next.next fails before the test is reached.
questions.explain: The test must cover every .next the step reads through.
questions.rule: Check as many links as the step crosses.
questions.teaches: Two nodes versus one is the usual speed pairing, but the book notes it is not always the case, so the test depends on the step size.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: Which approach finds the middle of a list of unknown length in one pass with two variables?
options: Copy the list into an array and index its centre
Count the nodes first, then walk half of them
Move one pointer at twice the speed of the other
Store every node in a set and take the middle one
optionExplain: That uses O(n) extra space.
That takes two passes.
Right: when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow one is halfway.
A set has no order and costs O(n) space.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. Speed ratio replaces the count; the card shows how.
questions.rule: When fast reaches the end, slow stands at the middle.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: Match each way of finding the middle to its main trait.
pairs: Copy into an array and index it
Count the length, then walk half of it
questions.explain: The array trades space for ease, the count needs a second walk, and fast and slow pointers need neither.
questions.rule: One pass, O(1) space: fast and slow.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A list holds 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40 -> 50 -> 60 -> 70 -> 80 -> 90. What does get_middle return?
optionExplain: 40 would come from stopping one iteration early.
60 would come from one more iteration than fast allows.
Right: slow takes 4 steps while fast takes 4 double steps off the end.
90 is the last value, where fast stands, not slow.
questions.explain: Fast moves 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and stops on the last node; slow has moved 4 times to the fifth node.
questions.rule: Trace both pointers per iteration.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A list has 101 nodes. The middle is found after ____ loop iterations.
questions.explain: Fast moves 50 double steps from node 1 to node 101, and slow stands on node 51, the middle.
questions.rule: About n / 2 iterations.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A student returns fast.val after the loop on 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5. What comes back, and why is it wrong?
options: 5, the last value, as fast ends on the final node and slow on the middle
3, the middle value, which is correct
Null, as fast ends one step past the final node
4, as fast ends one node before the final node
optionExplain: Right: with an odd count fast stops on the last node, so slow.val is the one to return.
3 is what slow.val gives, not fast.val.
Null is where fast would end in an even-length list, but this one is odd.
Fast lands on node 5, not node 4, in this list.
questions.explain: Fast ends at the end of the list, and slow at its middle.
questions.rule: Return slow, not fast.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: Our reading: get_middle runs on 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4, which has an even number of nodes. What does it return?
options: An error, as the middle is undefined
optionExplain: 2 is the first of the two middle nodes, which this loop never selects.
4 is where fast would be with one more step.
The code runs without error; fast becomes null and the loop ends.
Right: slow moves twice and stands on the node holding 3, the second of the two middle nodes.
questions.explain: With 4 nodes the loop runs twice, leaving slow on the third node.
questions.rule: Even length: slow lands on the later middle.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A program counts the length n of a list with a dummy pointer, then walks from the head. For n = 7, how many steps reach the middle?
optionExplain: 4 is the position of the middle node, not the number of steps to it.
Right: length // 2 steps from the head, and 7 // 2 is 3.
7 would walk the whole list.
2 would stop at the third node.
questions.explain: The two-pass method walks length // 2 steps after the count, so the node reached is the fourth.
questions.rule: Two passes: count, then walk half.
questions.teaches: The two-pass alternative counts the length with a dummy pointer, then walks length // 2 steps from the head; it works but needs a second traversal.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A program follows next 1,000,000 times from the head and, if null has not been reached, reports a cycle. What is the risk?
options: A long list with no cycle is wrongly reported as cyclic
A short list with a cycle is reported as acyclic
The program reports the cycle but cannot find where it starts
The program fails on every list longer than 100 nodes
optionExplain: Right: an acyclic list longer than the cutoff looks the same as a cycle.
A cycle never reaches null, so it always passes the cutoff.
The risk here is about the verdict, not the cycle's start.
The cutoff is 1,000,000, not 100, so shorter lists work.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The cutoff confuses long with endless; the card explains.
questions.rule: A fixed iteration cutoff cannot prove that a list has a cycle.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: True or false: a list has a cycle if some node can be reached again by continuously following next.
questions.explain: That is the definition: following next leads back to a node already visited.
questions.rule: A cycle is a node reachable again.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: True or false: with a cutoff of 10 million steps, a 12-million-node list with no cycle is wrongly reported as having a cycle.
questions.explain: The test runs out of steps before the list ends and guesses a cycle, so the verdict is wrong.
questions.rule: Long is not the same as endless.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A developer fixes the cutoff by raising it to 10 billion. What is still wrong?
options: 10 billion is too small for any computer
Raising the cutoff makes cycles harder to find
A longer acyclic list can be passed in, and the loop is impractical
The cutoff now misses lists with a cycle
optionExplain: The size of the number is not the issue; the existence of a longer list is.
A cycle is still found, because iteration never reaches null.
Right: any cutoff has a longer list that defeats it.
Cycles never end, so they are still caught by any cutoff.
questions.explain: No fixed number removes the weakness.
questions.rule: No cutoff covers every list.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: The cutoff is 10 steps. An acyclic list of 20 nodes is judged by the cutoff test to have a ____.
questions.explain: 20 nodes exceed the cutoff but the list has an end, so the test misjudges it. A real cycle or a short list is judged correctly.
questions.rule: False alarms come from long acyclic lists.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A web crawler follows links and reports a link loop once it has visited 10,000 pages. What is wrong with the rule?
options: A site with a loop is never flagged
A large site with no loop is wrongly flagged as a loop
A site with 5 pages is wrongly flagged
Every site with fewer than 10,000 pages is wrongly flagged as a loop
optionExplain: A loop keeps adding pages, so it reaches 10,000.
Right: the same flaw as the cutoff on a list.
Five pages never reach the cutoff.
Small sites stay below the cutoff.
questions.explain: The crawler confuses a large site with a loop, in the same way the cutoff confuses a long list with a cycle.
questions.rule: Large is not looped.
questions.teaches: Hard-coding such a limit is a terrible practice, in the author's words.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: Two runners of different speeds race on a straight track and then on a circular one. What happens on the circular track?
options: The slower runner finishes first
The runners never meet, as speeds differ
The faster runner stops at the starting line
The faster runner eventually laps the slower one
optionExplain: A circle has no finish, so no one finishes.
Different speeds on a loop lead to a meeting, not a standoff.
Nothing stops the faster runner.
Right: on a circle the faster runner comes up behind the slower one.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card uses this picture for pointers.
questions.rule: Fast and slow pointers meet if the list has a cycle, and fast reaches null if it does not.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: True or false: if the fast pointer reaches null, the list has no cycle.
questions.explain: A cycle has no end, so a pointer cannot reach null on a cyclic list.
questions.rule: Null means an end, so no cycle.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: Node 5 of the list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 points back to node 3. Fast and slow start at node 1. At which node do they meet?
optionExplain: Node 3 is where the cycle starts, but they are not both there together.
Right: after iterations (2,3), (3,5), they land together on 4.
Node 5 is where fast stands after two iterations, with slow on 3.
Node 2 is slow after one iteration, with fast on 3.
questions.explain: Trace: slow and fast stand on (2,3), then (3,5), then (4,4).
questions.rule: Trace both pointers each iteration.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A list has 7 nodes, and node 7 points back to node 4. Slow and fast meet after ____ loop iterations.
questions.explain: Slow and fast both stand on node 5 after four iterations. Fast enters the cycle first and then gains one position on slow per iteration.
questions.rule: Count the iterations by tracing.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A version checks slow is fast before moving the pointers, in the first line of the loop. What goes wrong?
options: It never reports a cycle, as the pointers start apart
It reports a cycle only on lists with an even length
It reports a cycle only when the cycle starts at the head, where both pointers begin
It reports a cycle on every list, as both pointers start at the head
optionExplain: They start together, not apart.
Length parity is unrelated to the early check.
Equality holds at the start on every list.
Right: both start at the head, so they are equal before any move.
questions.explain: The meeting must be a meeting after moving.
questions.rule: Check equality after the move, not before.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: Inside a cycle, fast stands 5 positions behind slow, and both are on the loop. How many iterations until they meet?
options: They never meet
optionExplain: Right: fast gains exactly one position each iteration.
Fast gains one per iteration, not a half.
The gap shrinks one each time, so it reaches zero after five.
Fast cannot step over slow, so the gap closes to zero.
questions.explain: Fast moves two and slow moves one, so the gap falls by one each iteration.
questions.rule: The gap closes by one per iteration.
questions.teaches: After looping around the cycle once, fast moves exactly one step closer to slow each iteration, so it cannot skip over slow.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A program adds each visited node to a set and stops when it meets a node already in the set. What does stopping mean?
options: The list is sorted
The list has an even number of nodes
The list has a cycle
The list has no cycle
optionExplain: Nothing about order is recorded in the set.
A repeat has nothing to do with the count of nodes.
Right: a repeated node can only come from a loop.
A list with no cycle ends in null instead of repeating.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. A repeat means the pointers looped; the card explains.
questions.rule: A set finds a cycle by spotting a repeated node, at the price of O(n) space.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: The set-based cycle check uses O(____) extra space for n nodes.
questions.explain: Every node may be stored before the walk ends, so the space grows with n.
questions.rule: Set: O(n) space.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A list of 1,000,000 nodes has no cycle. How many nodes does the set hold when the walk reaches null?
optionExplain: One would be enough only if the walk stopped at once.
Two nodes are what fast and slow pointers store, not a set.
Right: each node is added once as it is visited.
Half of them would need the walk to stop at the middle.
questions.explain: The walk visits every node and stores each one.
questions.rule: Set size grows with the list.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: Two cycle tests both run in O(n) time: one keeps a set of seen nodes, one moves fast and slow pointers. Which does the book call better, and why?
options: The pointer test, since it uses less space
The set test, since it finds the cycle sooner
The set test, since it needs no extra pointers
Neither, since equal time means equal quality
optionExplain: Right: the book says the first solution is better as it uses less space.
Neither is claimed to find a cycle sooner.
The set uses more storage, not fewer pointers.
Time ties, and space breaks the tie.
questions.explain: O(1) space beats O(n) space at the same time cost.
questions.rule: Same time: pick less space.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: True or false: storing node values instead of nodes in the set reports a cycle on 1 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3, which has no cycle.
questions.explain: The second 1 is a different node with an equal value, but the set treats it as a repeat. A cycle is about the same node twice, not the same value twice.
questions.rule: Store nodes, not values.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A URL redirects to B, B to C and C back to A. Which method spots the loop, and what does it store?
options: A set of URLs already seen; it stores only the first URL
A count of redirects; it stores no URLs
A sorted list of all URLs on the internet
A set of URLs already seen; it stores each URL visited
optionExplain: Storing only the first URL would miss a loop that avoids it, such as B to C to B.
A count cannot tell a long chain from a loop, as with the cutoff idea.
The full internet is not needed; only the visited URLs matter.
Right: meeting A a second time reveals the loop.
questions.explain: A redirect chain behaves like a list, and a repeat means a loop.
questions.rule: Seen before means looped.
questions.teaches: Following next from the head leaves exactly two possibilities: reach null, so there is no cycle, or eventually visit some node twice, so there is one.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: Pointer P starts k nodes ahead of pointer Q in a long list, and both then move one node per step. How far ahead is P after 10 steps?
options: k + 10 nodes ahead
Still k nodes ahead
k - 10 nodes ahead
Level with Q
optionExplain: Only a faster P would widen the gap.
Right: equal speeds keep the gap fixed.
Only a faster Q would shrink the gap.
The gap does not close unless Q is faster.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. A fixed gap is the heart of the method; the card builds on it.
questions.rule: Open a gap of k, then move both pointers together until fast falls off the end.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: Put the steps of finding the k-th node from the end in order.
items: Set both pointers at the head
Move fast ahead by k nodes
Move both pointers one node per iteration
Return the node slow points at
questions.explain: First the gap is opened, then both move together, and slow is read when fast runs off the end.
questions.rule: Gap first, then move together.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A list holds 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 and k = 3. Which node does find_node return?
options: The node holding 4
The node holding 3
The node holding 5
The node holding 6
optionExplain: Right: the 3rd node from the end of six nodes is the fourth.
3 is the 3rd node from the start, not the end.
5 is the 2nd from the end.
6 is the 1st from the end.
questions.explain: Counting from the end: 6 is first, 5 second, 4 third.
questions.rule: k-th from the end is position n - k + 1.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A list has 100 nodes and k = 10. Slow takes ____ steps in the second loop.
questions.explain: After the head start fast is at node 11 and has 90 steps left before it is null, so slow also moves 90.
questions.rule: Second loop: n - k steps.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A version gives fast a head start of k + 1 nodes. On 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 with k = 2, which node comes back, and why?
options: The node holding 4, as intended
The node holding 5, since the gap is too small
The node holding 3, since the gap is one too large
An error, since fast starts beyond the end of the list and is null at once
optionExplain: 4 needs a gap of exactly 2.
A smaller gap would return a later node; this gap is larger.
Right: a gap of 3 puts slow on the 3rd node from the end.
Fast begins on node 4 and does not run past the end.
questions.explain: The returned node is as many positions from the end as the gap.
questions.rule: Gap size equals k.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers
questions.q: A list has 12 nodes. The length-first method counts the nodes, then walks from the head. How many steps reach the 3rd node from the end?
optionExplain: 3 counts steps from the end, not from the head.
Right: 12 - 3 = 9 steps from the head.
12 would walk off the end.
10 would reach the 2nd from the end.
questions.explain: The k-th from the end is n - k steps from the head.
questions.rule: Two-pass: count n, then walk n - k.
questions.teaches: The book's alternatives to the gap method are converting the list to an array or counting the length in one pass and then walking to the node in a second pass.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: A singly linked list is reversed in place, without creating new nodes. What extra space is possible?
options: O(n), one new node per old node
O(log n), a stack of halves
O(n squared), every pair of nodes
O(1), a few pointer variables
optionExplain: O(n) is what copying into a new list or array costs.
Halving is not part of reversal.
Pairs of nodes never need to be stored.
Right: the same nodes are relinked, so only a few variables are needed.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. In-place relinking needs few variables; the card shows the loop.
questions.rule: Save the next node, flip the arrow, then advance prev and curr.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: Put the four lines of the reversal loop body in order.
questions.explain: The next node is saved before the arrow is flipped. prev and curr then advance, prev first, so prev still gets the old curr.
questions.rule: Save, flip, advance prev, advance curr.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: A list holds 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4. After the first loop iteration, what do prev and curr hold, and where does node 1 point?
options: prev is node 2, curr is node 3, and node 1 points to null
prev is node 1, curr is node 2, and node 1 points to null
prev is node 1, curr is node 2, and node 1 points to node 2
prev is null, curr is node 1, and node 1 points to node 2
optionExplain: That is the state after the second iteration.
Right: node 1's arrow is flipped to null, the old prev, and the walk moves on.
Node 1's arrow was flipped, so it no longer points to node 2.
That is the state before the first iteration.
questions.explain: The first pass flips node 1's arrow to prev (null), sets prev to 1 and moves curr to 2.
questions.rule: After k passes, prev is the k-th node.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: A list has 100 nodes. The reversal assigns curr.next exactly ____ times.
questions.explain: One assignment per node, so the loop body runs 100 times.
questions.rule: n nodes: n arrow flips.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: A student returns curr instead of prev after the loop. What does the function return?
options: The new head, which is correct
The old head, with its next set to null
The middle node of the list
Null, since curr is null when the loop ends
optionExplain: The new head is prev, not curr.
The old head is the last node of the new list, and curr has moved past it.
The loop ends beyond the last node, not at the middle.
Right: the loop runs until curr is null, so prev holds the new head.
questions.explain: The loop ends when curr falls off the list; the last node visited is in prev.
questions.rule: Return prev.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: An app stores history newest first in a singly linked list. A screen must show it oldest first, with O(1) extra space. What fits?
options: Reverse the list in place, taking O(n) time
Copy it into an array and read it backward
Follow prev pointers from the head
Do nothing, since lists can be read from the end
optionExplain: Right: in-place reversal needs O(n) time and O(1) space.
An array costs O(n) extra space.
A singly linked list has no prev pointers.
A singly linked list can only be read forward.
questions.explain: Reversal turns the last node into the first, which makes oldest-first reading possible.
questions.rule: Reverse in place to read backward.
questions.teaches: Reversing a list is a common problem in itself, but it is also a technique that can be a step in solving different problems.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: In the reversal loop, curr.next is set to prev before the old curr.next has been saved. What is lost?
options: The node before curr
The value stored in curr
The rest of the list after curr
The head variable
optionExplain: The node before curr is held by prev.
The value is untouched; only the pointer changes.
Right: curr.next was the only link to the rest.
head is a separate variable and is not affected.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card shows why the save comes first.
questions.rule: Each line depends on the one before it: save, flip, then advance.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: Match each line of the reversal loop to its job.
pairs: Keeps the rest of the list reachable
Flips the arrow at this node
Moves on along the original list
questions.explain: Each line has one job, and the order follows what each line needs.
questions.rule: Each line serves one need.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: A version flips the arrow first and saves next_node afterwards. What does it return for 1 -> 2 -> 3?
questions.code:
curr.next = prev
next_node = curr.next
prev = curr
curr = next_node
options: 3 -> 2 -> 1, as normal
A list holding only 3
A list holding only 1
An endless loop over all three nodes
optionExplain: The normal result needs the save before the flip.
The loop stops at the first node, and the new head is node 1, not 3.
Right: next_node is read after the flip, so it is prev, which is null, and the loop ends after node 1.
next_node is null, so the loop stops at once.
questions.explain: Saving after the flip reads the new value of curr.next, which is prev.
questions.rule: Save the next node before changing it.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: A version moves prev = curr before the flip curr.next = prev. After the loop on 1 -> 2 -> 3, where does node 1's next point?
options: At node 1 itself
At null
At node 2
At node 3
optionExplain: Right: prev is already curr when the flip runs, so each node points at itself.
Null is the correct result for the first node, but this version overwrites prev first.
Node 2 was the original successor, but the flip changes it.
Node 3 is reached by neither the original nor the flipped arrows.
questions.explain: The flip reads prev, which has already been replaced by curr.
questions.rule: Do not overwrite a value before a later line reads it.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: True or false: reversing a list of 1,000,000 nodes in place creates no new nodes.
questions.explain: Only the next arrows change, so the same nodes are relinked and the extra space is O(1).
questions.rule: In place: no new nodes.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: A coworker lists the needs of the reversal. Which need leads to introducing the prev pointer?
options: The loop must stop when the list ends
The value of each node must be copied
The head must be returned at the end
At the current node, next must refer to the node visited immediately before
optionExplain: The stop test uses curr, not prev.
Values are not copied in reversal.
The new head is prev's final value, but the need for prev comes from the flip.
Right: a singly linked node cannot look back, so the previous node is tracked.
questions.explain: Listing needs shows which variables are required.
questions.rule: Each need suggests a variable or a line.
questions.teaches: Solutions to linked list problems are usually simple and elegant, and the way to reach them is to think about what you need and solve the problem one step at a time.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: Swapping the pairs of 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 gives 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3. Which node of the original list is the new head?
options: The first node, holding 1
The second node, holding 2
The last node, holding 4
The third node, holding 3
optionExplain: The first node moves behind the second.
Right: the first pair swaps, so its second node leads the result.
Node 4 leads the second pair, not the whole list.
Node 3 leads the second pair, not the whole list.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card shows why the function must remember it.
questions.rule: Save what follows the pair, flip the pair, and reconnect the previous pair to it.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: True or false: after swapping the first pair, the function can still return the original head.
questions.explain: The original head is now the second node of the first pair. The new head is the original second node, so the function must remember it.
questions.rule: Save the new head before it is lost.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: The card's swap_pairs runs on 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5. Which values does the result hold, in order?
optionExplain: Right: the two pairs swap and the lone last node stays.
The last node would be lost; head.next = next_node keeps it linked.
Only the first pair would be swapped.
The first pair is swapped, so 2 comes first.
questions.explain: Pairs (1,2) and (3,4) swap; node 5 has no partner.
questions.rule: Odd count: the last node stays in place.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: Put the lines of the swap_pairs loop body in order.
items: Link the previous pair's first node to this pair's second node
Remember this pair's first node as prev
Save the node after the pair
Point the second node back at the first
Point the first node at the saved node
Move head to the saved node
questions.explain: Each line uses a value that earlier lines have kept safe: the saved node, then the pair flip, then the move on.
questions.rule: Reconnect, remember, save, flip, relink, advance.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: A version returns the original head instead of the saved second node. What does it return for 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4?
options: 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3, as intended
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4, unchanged
1 -> 4 -> 3, with node 2 lost
An empty list
optionExplain: The intended answer needs the new head returned.
The list was changed in place, so it is not unchanged.
Right: node 1 now points at 4, so node 2 cannot be reached from it.
Node 1 still leads to nodes 4 and 3.
questions.explain: The original head is the first node of the first pair, which is now second.
questions.rule: Return the node saved before the loop.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: On 1 -> 2 -> 3, which line keeps the unpaired node 3 linked after node 1?
options: head = next_node, which moves past the first pair
head.next = next_node, which sets node 1's next to node 3
prev = head, which remembers node 1
head.next.next = head, which points node 2 back at node 1 and cuts node 3 off
optionExplain: That moves head but changes no link from node 1.
Right: the line sets A.next to C, so the odd leftover stays attached.
prev only stores node 1.
That sets node 2's next, not node 1's.
questions.explain: Without it node 1 would still point at node 2, and the list would loop between them.
questions.rule: Link the first node to the saved node.
questions.teaches: Setting A.next to the saved node is overridden by prev.next = head.next in the next swap when another pair remains, so it matters only when none does.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: You meet an unfamiliar linked list problem. According to the book, which first move helps most?
options: Write the code at once, then fix it step by step whenever the tests fail
Copy the list into an array to see the values
Memorise the solution of the most similar problem
List what you need to accomplish and how each need can be met
optionExplain: Wrong-answer feedback helps later, but planning comes first.
The book calls the array route a shortcut that misses the point.
Solutions are found by reasoning, not by recall.
Right: the book says to break the problem down into needs and steps.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the book's method.
questions.rule: List your needs, turn each into a pointer step, order the steps by what they depend on, and test on a small example.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: True or false: the steps of a pointer solution run in the same order in which you first thought of them.
questions.explain: The book says the order of thinking need not match the order of execution, so steps are sequenced after they are listed.
questions.rule: Think in needs; run in dependency order.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: A function must delete the node after prev and also return its value. Which step must come before prev.next is changed?
options: Setting the doomed node's next to null
Reading and keeping the doomed node's value
Moving prev to the doomed node
Returning from the function
optionExplain: That is unneeded, as the node is already cut off.
Right: after prev.next skips it, the node can no longer be reached from the list.
Moving prev there would delete the wrong node.
Returning first would leave the deletion undone.
questions.explain: Listing needs shows that the value must be read while the node is still reachable.
questions.rule: Read what you need before you cut the link.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: The book suggests working through a small example such as 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4, ideally on ____.
questions.explain: A small example on paper lets you test each step and exposes missed cases such as the last node.
questions.rule: Test on a small example.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: A student codes pair-swapping lines in the order they were thought of, and it fails. What is the best fix?
options: Add more variables so every line is repeated
Use an array instead of pointers
Delete the lines that fail first
Reorder the lines by what each one depends on
optionExplain: More variables do not fix wrong order.
The array route avoids the skill the problem tests.
Deleting lines removes needs.
Right: sequence the steps by dependency, not by when you thought of them.
questions.explain: Thinking order and execution order often differ.
questions.rule: Order by dependency.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.3 Reversing a linked list
questions.q: In an interview you have missed a pointer step. According to the book, what should you do?
options: Speak your thought process aloud so the interviewer can help fill the gap
Stay silent until you are certain
Switch to an array solution at once
Submit the first version and wait for a wrong answer
optionExplain: Right: the book advises being vocal about your thinking.
Silence gives the interviewer nothing to help with.
The book says the array route almost guarantees failure.
A wrong-answer submission is how LeetCode points out missed steps, not an interview.
questions.explain: Talking through your needs shows where a step is missing.
questions.rule: Think aloud.
questions.teaches: In an interview, be vocal about your thought process, and the interviewer should help you fill any gaps.

questions.section: Reversal as only part of an algorithm
questions.q: Using only the list's own nodes, which approach finds the maximum twin sum in O(1) extra space?
options: Copy the list into an array and index both ends
Store every node in a set along with its position and look up each twin
Find the middle, reverse the second half, then add mirror pairs
Sort the values and add the largest to the smallest
optionExplain: That uses O(n) extra space.
A set also uses O(n) space and does not give positions.
Right: the three tools of this chapter, combined.
Sorting loses which nodes are twins.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card combines two tools from earlier ideas.
questions.rule: Reversal can be one step: find the middle, reverse the second half, then read mirror pairs at a fixed offset.

questions.section: Reversal as only part of an algorithm
questions.q: Put the steps of the twin-sum algorithm in order.
items: Find the middle with fast and slow pointers
Reverse the second half of the list
Place a second pointer n / 2 ahead of the first
Add each pair of values, n / 2 times, tracking the maximum
questions.explain: The middle comes first, then the reversal makes twins a fixed distance apart, and then the sums are read.
questions.rule: Middle, reverse, offset, sum.

questions.section: Reversal as only part of an algorithm
questions.q: A list holds 3 -> 7 -> 1 -> 9 -> 4 -> 6. What is its maximum twin sum?
optionExplain: 9 is only the first pair.
10 is only the third pair.
Right: the twin sums are 3 + 6 = 9, 7 + 4 = 11 and 1 + 9 = 10.
13 is the sum of values that are not twins, 9 + 4.
questions.explain: Each node is paired with its mirror node, and the largest of the three sums is 11.
questions.rule: Pair first with last, second with second-last.

questions.section: Reversal as only part of an algorithm
questions.q: A list has 100,000 nodes. After the reversal, the sums are read ____ times.
questions.explain: There are n / 2 twin pairs, so 100,000 / 2 = 50,000 sums.
questions.rule: n nodes: n / 2 twin pairs.

questions.section: Reversal as only part of an algorithm
questions.q: A student skips the reversal and offsets the second pointer by n / 2. For 3 -> 7 -> 1 -> 9 -> 4 -> 6, what maximum comes out?
options: 12, from the pair 3 and 9, which are not twins
11, the correct twin maximum
9, from the pair 3 and 6
10, from the pair 1 and 9
optionExplain: Right: with no reversal, the pairs are 3 + 9, 7 + 4 and 1 + 6.
The correct answer needs the reversal.
3 and 6 are twins, but this pairing does not select them.
1 and 9 are twins, but this pairing does not select them.
questions.explain: Without the reversal, the offset joins first-half nodes to nodes in the wrong order.
questions.rule: The reversal makes the offset hit the twin.

questions.section: Reversal as only part of an algorithm
questions.q: Which combination of this chapter's tools checks whether a list reads the same forward and backward, with O(1) extra space?
options: Copy the list to an array and compare its ends
Run a cycle test with fast and slow pointers
Delete every second node, then compare the lengths
Find the middle, reverse the second half, then compare the halves
optionExplain: That works but uses O(n) space.
A cycle test answers a different question.
Deleting nodes loses the values to compare.
Right: the same two tools, with comparison in place of sums.
questions.explain: Mirror positions are compared after the second half is reversed.
questions.rule: Middle plus reversal gives mirror access.
questions.teaches: Unlike the earlier examples, the reversal is not the whole point of the problem but a tool used to arrive at a better solution.

questions.q: A browser tab visits site A, then B, then C. The back arrow is pressed once. Which site leaves the history?
options: Site A, the first one visited
Site C, the most recent one
Site B, the middle one
All three sites, since back clears the tab
optionExplain: It seems natural that the oldest page goes first, but removal happens at the end where pages were added.
Right: back removes the latest page, which is the top of the history.
Nothing in a history lets you remove from the middle with one step.
Back removes one page per press; the earlier pages stay.
questions.explain: Back undoes the latest visit, so the page added last leaves first. The card next names this pattern.
questions.rule: The newest item leaves first.

questions.q: A stack removes items in last in, first out order, which is shortened to ____.
questions.explain: LIFO means last in, first out: the last element placed inside is the first to come out.
questions.rule: A stack is LIFO.

questions.q: Start with an empty stack. Push 4, push 9, push 2, pop once, then push 7. Order the remaining items from top to bottom.
questions.explain: The pop removes 2, the latest item. Pushing 7 puts it on top of 9, which sits on 4, so from top to bottom the stack reads 7, 9, 4.
questions.rule: Pop removes the item pushed last.
questions.hint: Trace each push and pop on the top end.

questions.q: Dee pushes 5, 6, 7 in that order, pops once and says the result is 5 because it went in first. What is wrong?
options: Pop returns the middle item, 6, because it is neither first nor last
Pop returns 5, but only when the stack uses a linked list underneath
Pop returns nothing until peek has been called on the top item
Pop removes from the end where items are added, so it returns 7, the last one pushed
optionExplain: Middle access is not part of a stack's interface.
The interface fixes the order; the storage underneath does not change it.
Peek is optional; it reads the top without removing it and is not needed before pop.
Right: the end used for pushing is the end used for popping.
questions.explain: Dee describes first in, first out. In a stack, items leave from the same end they entered, so 7 comes out first.
questions.rule: Pops and pushes share one end.

questions.q: True or false: a plain Python list, with append to push and pop to remove, is a valid stack.
questions.explain: Any dynamic array can serve as a stack. What makes something a stack is that elements are added and removed only at the same end, which append and pop on a list do.
questions.rule: A stack is defined by its interface, not by what stores it.
questions.teaches: In Python a list with append and pop is enough, because a stack is an abstract interface: the only requirement is adding and removing at the same end.

questions.q: A help desk stores tickets T1, T2, T3 (in arrival order) on a stack. Which ticket is answered first?
options: T3, the latest, so the desk would not serve in arrival order
T1, because it arrived first and a stack keeps the first item on top
T2, because a stack serves the middle item when there are three
Any of them, since a stack does not fix the order of removal
optionExplain: Right: a stack serves the newest first, which is the opposite of arrival order.
Pushing T1 first puts it at the bottom, not on top.
A stack has no middle rule; only the top is reachable.
A stack fixes the order exactly: last in, first out.
questions.explain: Pushing T1, T2, T3 leaves T3 on top, so the first pop gives T3. Arrival order needs first in, first out, which uses opposite ends.
questions.rule: A stack cannot give first come, first served.
questions.teaches: First come, first served is the first in, first out pattern, which needs additions and removals at opposite ends: that structure is a queue.

questions.q: A stack is stored in a dynamic array. How much work does one push take, in big-O terms?
options: O(n), since the array must be shifted to make room
O(log n), because the stack keeps its items ordered
O(1), a single step at the end of the array
O(n squared), because every older item is compared with the new one
optionExplain: Shifting happens when you insert at the front, not at the end.
A stack is ordered by arrival, not sorted, so no halving is involved.
Right: appending at the end of a dynamic array moves nothing else.
A push compares nothing; it only adds at the top.
questions.explain: Pushing writes one new slot at the end. The card next gives the cost of every stack operation.
questions.rule: Push is a one-step action at the top.

questions.q: Searching for a value in an array-backed stack costs O(____).
questions.explain: Search has no shortcut, so in the worst case it looks at all n elements.
questions.rule: Search is linear.

questions.q: A browser keeps 10,000 pages in an array-backed stack. How does checking for one site compare with a push?
options: Both are O(1) because a stack only touches the top
The check is O(log n) because the pages were added in order
The check is O(n), far more than the O(1) push
The check is O(1) because the top page is checked first
optionExplain: Only push, pop and peek stay at the top; looking for a value is a different operation.
Order of arrival does not sort the pages by name, so halving is not possible.
Right: the site could be anywhere, so up to 10,000 pages may be examined.
The top is checked first, but a missing or deep site forces more checks.
questions.explain: Search is O(n) in the worst case, while push is O(1). Treat the stack as a structure for the top, not for lookup.
questions.rule: Use a stack for the top, not for finding values.

questions.q: Which operations on an array-backed stack are O(1)? Select all that apply.
options: Push a new element
Pop the top element
Read the element at a known index
Search for a given value
Remove the bottom element and keep the rest in order
optionExplain: Right: appends at the end.
Right: removes the last slot.
Right: random access on a dynamic array is O(1).
Search is O(n): it may scan everything.
Removing from the front of an array shifts every other element, which is O(n).
questions.explain: Operations at the end, and reading by index, are constant time. Searching, or removing at the opposite end, is not.
questions.rule: Only the top end is cheap.

questions.q: True or false: a stack can also be implemented with a linked list that keeps a tail pointer.
questions.explain: The book notes that a stack may be built on a linked list with a tail pointer. Either way it stays a stack as long as additions and removals share one end.
questions.rule: The interface decides what a stack is.
questions.teaches: Besides a dynamic array, a stack may sit on a linked list with a tail pointer; the stack is the same abstract interface either way.

questions.q: A drawing app stores strokes on an array-backed stack. A user undoes 500 strokes in a row. How does the total work grow?
options: O(k) for k undos, since each pop is O(1)
O(k squared), since each undo shifts the strokes behind it
O(1) overall, since a stack handles any number of pops in one step
O(n) for n strokes drawn, whatever k is
optionExplain: Right: k constant-time pops add up to work proportional to k.
Nothing shifts when the last slot is popped.
Each pop is one step, but 500 steps still add up.
The work follows the pops performed, not the whole history.
questions.explain: Total cost is the number of operations times the cost of each. With O(1) pops, k undos cost O(k).
questions.rule: Add up the operations: k times O(1) is O(k).
questions.teaches: Counting operations and multiplying by their O(1) cost is how a whole stack-based algorithm gets its total, for example O(n) when each element is pushed and popped once.

questions.q: Function a calls b, and b calls c. Which call finishes first?
options: Call a, since it started first
Call b, because it sits between the other two
All three finish together at the end of the program
Call c, the one started last
optionExplain: a must wait for b, and b must wait for c.
b is waiting for c, so it cannot finish before c.
Each call returns on its own, in reverse order of starting.
Right: c is on top of the call stack, so it returns first.
questions.explain: The latest call is the first to finish. The card next explains how a stack models this.
questions.rule: The newest call finishes first.

questions.q: The call at the ____ of the call stack is the active one.
questions.explain: The top call is the one running; the calls below it are waiting.
questions.rule: The top call is active.

questions.q: Order the lines this program prints, first to last.
questions.code:
def a():
    print('a start')
    b()
    print('a end')

def b():
    print('b start')
    c()
    print('b end')

def c():
    print('c')

a()
questions.explain: a starts and calls b, which starts and calls c. c prints and returns first, then b finishes, then a: the calls unwind in reverse.
questions.rule: Calls unwind in reverse order.
questions.hint: Follow the call stack: a, then b on top, then c on top.

questions.q: A student says: when g returns, f, the function that called g, is popped as well. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: a return pops every call below the top as well
Only g's call is popped; f stays on the stack and becomes active again
f is popped first, because it was called before g
g stays on the stack until f returns, to hold its result
optionExplain: A return pops only the call that is finishing.
Right: f was waiting under g and continues from where it stopped.
The older call is lower in the stack and cannot leave before g.
A finished call is popped when it returns; it does not wait.
questions.explain: A return pops only the top call. The caller underneath is then on top, so it is the active call again.
questions.rule: A return pops one call only.

questions.q: A function has no return statement. When is its call popped from the call stack?
options: When the end of the function body is reached
Never, since only a return statement pops a call
When the next function in the file is called
When the program ends, together with all other calls
optionExplain: Right: reaching the end pops the call as a return statement does.
Running off the end of the body also finishes the call.
The next call is pushed on top; it does not pop the current one.
A call is popped as soon as it finishes, not at the end of the program.
questions.explain: A call is popped when a return statement runs or when the end of the function is reached.
questions.rule: Both a return and the end of the body pop the call.
questions.teaches: A call is popped in two cases: on a return statement, and when the end of the function is reached.

questions.q: countdown(3) calls countdown(2), which calls countdown(1), which calls countdown(0). How many calls are on the stack while countdown(0) is active?
options: 1: only the active call is on the stack
3: the calls for 3, 2 and 1, since 0 is a stopping case
4: countdown(3), (2), (1) waiting and (0) on top
0: the stack is empty once the last call is active
optionExplain: Calls that are waiting have not returned, so they still occupy the stack.
The call for 0 is also pushed; it is the one on top.
Right: every caller stays on the stack beneath the active call.
A running call is on the stack; the stack is empty only when nothing is running.
questions.explain: No call has returned yet, so all four are on the stack, with countdown(0) on top.
questions.rule: Waiting callers stay under the active call.
questions.teaches: Calls that have started but not returned stay on the stack, waiting beneath the active call, so the depth is the number of nested calls in progress.

questions.q: Which task is the best fit for a stack?
options: Serve customers in the order they joined the line
Match each closing bracket with the latest bracket still open
Find the largest value in an unsorted list by a single scan
Look up a phone number given a contact name
optionExplain: Oldest first is the opposite of what a stack gives.
Right: the most recent open bracket must be closed first.
A single running maximum is enough; no past elements need to wait.
Lookup by key is a job for hashing, not a stack.
questions.explain: Matching nested items needs the newest unresolved one first, which is what a stack provides. The card next states the signal.
questions.rule: Newest unresolved first signals a stack.

questions.q: A stack is a good option whenever you can recognise the ____ pattern in a problem.
questions.explain: LIFO, last in first out, is the recognition signal for a stack.
questions.rule: Spot LIFO, then use a stack.

questions.q: Sort each task by whether its pattern calls for a stack.

items.t: Undo the most recent edit in a document first
Check that nested sections of a report are closed in reverse order of opening
Evaluate a bracketed arithmetic expression such as (2 + 3) * 4
Print jobs in the order they were submitted
Serve the person who has waited longest at a bakery
Look up a price by product code

questions.explain: Undo, nested sections and bracketed expressions all resolve the newest open item first. Oldest-first service and key lookup do not.
questions.rule: Ask: is the newest unresolved item next?

questions.q: A learner reasons: the earliest element must be handled first, so a stack fits. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Nothing is wrong: the first element pushed is on top
A stack handles the middle element first, so neither end applies
The reasoning is right, but only for stacks held in linked lists
Earliest first is first in, first out, the opposite of what a stack provides
optionExplain: The first element pushed sits at the bottom.
Only the top is reachable in a stack.
The order is part of the interface, not the storage.
Right: a stack hands back the newest element first.
questions.explain: A stack fits when the latest item is handled first. Earliest-first points to a queue, taught later in this unit.
questions.rule: Earliest first is not a stack pattern.

questions.q: Which interactions between input elements does the book list as signs that a stack might help? Select all that apply.
options: Matching elements together
Asking how far away the next largest element is
Evaluating a mathematical equation given as a string
Computing the sum of an array in one pass
Choosing the median by sorting the whole input first
optionExplain: Right: for example opening and closing brackets.
Right: a property query like this is a stack signal.
Right: expression strings are on the book's list.
A running total needs no waiting elements.
Sorting does not leave elements waiting in LIFO order.
questions.explain: The book lists matching, querying a property such as the next larger element, evaluating a string equation, and comparing elements.
questions.rule: Interacting elements are the clue.
questions.teaches: Besides matching and comparing, the book names querying a property such as how far the next largest element is, and evaluating a math equation given as a string, as stack signals.

questions.q: A config file nests blocks: begin report, begin table, end table, end report. Each end must close the latest open begin. Which tool fits?
options: A queue: the first begin seen must be matched first
A hash set of names seen so far, to detect repeats
A sorted list of block names, scanned from the start
A stack: push each begin, pop on each end and compare names
optionExplain: First-opened-first-closed would accept crossed blocks such as begin report, begin table, end report.
Presence alone loses the nesting order.
Sorting destroys the order in which blocks were opened.
Right: the latest open block is the first to close.
questions.explain: Nesting is LIFO: the innermost open block closes first, so the top of a stack names the block that must close next.
questions.rule: Nested open and close pairs are LIFO.
questions.teaches: Nested open and close markers are a typical hidden LIFO: each closer must match the most recent opener still unclosed, which is the top of the stack.

questions.q: A program scans a string with a stack. At each step, what is the current character compared with?
options: The first character of the input string
The character on top of the stack
The bottom of the stack, the oldest saved character
The next unread character of the input
optionExplain: The first character is an old fixed point and says little about the recent history.
Right: the top is the latest character still unresolved.
Only the top of a stack is reachable without removing items.
Looking ahead is not part of the pattern; the stack looks back.
questions.explain: String problems with stacks compare the top of the stack, the latest unresolved character, with the current one. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Compare with the top of the stack.

questions.q: A stack helps with string matching because it saves a ____ of the previous characters.
questions.explain: The stack keeps the history of earlier characters, newest on top.
questions.rule: A stack stores history.

questions.q: A scan pushes each letter unless it equals the top, in which case it pops. What does the stack hold after mnnmpq?
options: m n n m p q
m m p q
p q
n n p q
optionExplain: That is every letter pushed with no cancelling.
The pair n, n cancels, and then the two m's become adjacent and cancel too.
Right: n, n cancel, then m, m cancel, leaving p and q.
The two n's cancel as soon as the second one arrives.
questions.explain: The second n equals the top, so both go. The next m then equals the new top m and both go. Then p and q are pushed.
questions.rule: Cancel the top when it equals the current letter.

questions.q: True or false: comparing with the first input character finds the same cancellations as comparing with the top of the stack.
questions.explain: The first character is an old fixed point. The cancellations depend on the most recent unresolved character, which is on top of the stack.
questions.rule: The top is the key comparison point.

questions.q: A scan pushes every character and pops nothing, as in abcdef where no letters cancel. How many characters are on the stack at the end?
options: 6, so in the worst case the stack holds as many characters as the input
1, since only the most recent character is kept
3, since a stack keeps half of the input at most
0, since the stack is emptied when the scan ends
optionExplain: Right: nothing cancelled, so every character stays.
A stack keeps every unresolved character, not only the latest.
No rule limits it to half.
Unresolved characters are not removed at the end.
questions.explain: With no cancelling, each character stays. The stack can therefore grow to n, so extra space is O(n).
questions.rule: Worst case, the stack holds n characters.
questions.teaches: Because the stack can hold every character of the input, a string-scan stack uses O(n) extra space in the worst case.

questions.q: A tool cancels a lowercase letter directly followed by its capital twin, such as aA. Scanning abBAc with a stack, what is left?
options: abBAc, since no two equal letters are adjacent
c, since bB cancels and then aA cancels
aAc, since only bB is adjacent at the start
abc, since the capitals are deleted but lowercase stays
optionExplain: Equality is not the test here; twins cancel, so bB and aA go.
Right: after bB leaves, a and A become adjacent.
Once bB cancels, aA is adjacent and cancels too.
Both letters of a twin pair are removed, not only the capital.
questions.explain: Push a, push b, then B cancels b, then A cancels a, then c is pushed. The loop is the same; only the matching test differs.
questions.rule: Change the test, keep the stack loop.
questions.teaches: The stack supplies the most recent unresolved character; the test applied to it (equality, a bracket-pair lookup, a twin check) is chosen by the problem.

questions.q: A string opens ( then { then [. In what order must the matching closers appear for the string to be valid?
options: ) then } then ]
} then ] then )
Any order, as long as each type appears once
], then }, then )
optionExplain: That closes the oldest opener first, which crosses the nested pairs.
The middle opener cannot close before the one nested inside it.
Order matters: crossed pairs such as ( ] are not valid.
Right: the bracket opened last must be closed first.
questions.explain: Nested brackets close in reverse order of opening. The card next shows how a stack enforces that.
questions.rule: Closers come in reverse order of openers.

questions.q: True or false: when a closing bracket arrives, the item popped is the most recent opening bracket that is still unmatched.
questions.explain: The top of the stack is the most recent unmatched opener, and it is the one the closer must match.
questions.rule: The top is the latest open bracket.

questions.q: After the scan processes the prefix ({[] , what does the stack hold from bottom to top?
optionExplain: Right: ] matched and removed [, leaving ( and {.
The closer ] pops the [ at once, so it is no longer there.
The popped item is the top, which is [, not the middle one.
Closers are never stored on the stack in this method.
questions.explain: Three openers are pushed. The ] pops the top, [, and it matches. The remaining stack is ( then {.
questions.rule: A matched pair is popped.

questions.q: This version drops the empty-stack check before popping. Which input makes it fail by popping an empty stack?
optionExplain: The stack holds ( when ] arrives, so the pop works and the mismatch is reported.
A leftover opener at the end is caught by the final check, not by a pop.
Right: after {} the stack is empty, and ] tries to pop from it.
Every closer finds a waiting opener, so no pop is attempted on an empty stack.
questions.explain: In {}] the first pair empties the stack, then ] pops with nothing left to pop. The guard returns False first in the full solution.
questions.rule: Guard against an empty stack before popping.

questions.q: To check a closing bracket quickly, the book looks up the popped opener in a hash ____ that stores each opener's closer.
questions.explain: A hash map pairs each opener with its closer. After popping the top, look it up and compare the result with the current character.
questions.rule: Map each opener to its closer.
questions.teaches: A hash map from each opening bracket to its closing bracket lets you use the popped opener as the key and compare the value with the current closer.

questions.q: Openers a and b close with A and B. Scanning abBAa, no pop meets a wrong type. Is the string valid?
options: Yes: no pair was mismatched, so nothing is wrong
No: the closer A comes after the closer B, so the order is wrong
No: the final a is never closed, so the stack is not empty at the end
Yes: a string may end with an opener when the last character is lowercase
