optionExplain: The scan has a second condition: openers left at the end make a string invalid.
A and B close in the correct nested order here.
Right: every closer matched, yet one opener is left over.
Case plays no role: every opener needs its closer.
questions.explain: After abBA the stack is empty, then a is pushed and nothing closes it. The final answer is that the string is valid only if the stack is empty at the end.
questions.rule: Empty stack at the end, or the string is invalid.
questions.teaches: A bracket string can fail without any mismatch: openers left on the stack at the end, as in (){, make the string invalid, so the stack must be empty to accept.

questions.q: True or false: a bracket string is valid whenever no closing bracket meets a wrong opener, as in (){.
questions.explain: The string (){ has no mismatch but ends with an unclosed opener. The card next lists all three ways a string fails.
questions.rule: Leftover openers also make a string invalid.

questions.q: A bracket scan of a string with n characters takes O(____) time.
questions.explain: Each character is pushed at most once and popped at most once.
questions.rule: The scan is linear.

questions.q: Match each string to the way the scan rejects it.
pairs: A closer arrives with an empty stack
A closer meets a different type on top
An opener is left on the stack at the end
questions.explain: In {}] the first pair empties the stack, so ] has nothing to match. In (] the top is ( but the closer is ]. In (){ the opener { is never closed.
questions.rule: Three distinct ways to reject.

questions.q: The scan reads ((([]))){}. What is the largest number of items the stack holds at once?
optionExplain: Right: three ( and one [ are open together before the first closer.
The three round openers are counted, but [ is pushed before any closer arrives.
Only four openers come before the first closer; the later { is pushed after the stack has emptied.
That counts every opener in the string, but most are popped before { arrives.
questions.explain: The first four characters are all openers, so the stack reaches 4. Then each closer pops one, and { and } each need only one slot.
questions.rule: Peak size is the deepest nesting.

questions.q: A student says the bracket scan is O(n squared) because every closer triggers a pop inside the loop. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong: a pop inside a loop always makes it quadratic
The pops are free, so the scan is O(1) overall
The scan is O(n squared) only when the stack uses a linked list
Each character is pushed at most once and popped at most once, so the total work is linear
optionExplain: A pop is one step; the loop does not rescan the stack.
Each character still has to be read, so at least O(n) is needed.
Both array and linked-list stacks have O(1) push and pop here.
Right: pops are O(1) and are bounded by the number of pushes.
questions.explain: Pushes and pops are O(1) each and number at most n each, so total time is O(n).
questions.rule: Count pushes and pops, not loops.

questions.q: A log of 1,000,000 characters holds 500,000 openers followed by their 500,000 closers. What is the peak size of the stack?
options: 1, since closers are matched one at a time
500,000, so memory grows with the input
1,000,000, since every character is stored
About 1,000, the square root of the input size
optionExplain: Closers come after all the openers, so the stack is full by then.
Right: all openers are on the stack before the first closer.
Closers are not stored; they pop openers.
No rule gives a square root; the stack holds every open opener.
questions.explain: All 500,000 openers are pushed before any closer, so the stack peaks at 500,000. This is why space is O(n).
questions.rule: Worst-case memory is linear.
questions.teaches: The stack's size can grow linearly with the input, so the space complexity of the bracket scan is O(n), even though only openers are stored.

questions.q: In the string abbaca you delete bb and get aaca. Which pair can be deleted next?
options: aa
ca
ac
None: after one deletion the process stops
optionExplain: Right: removing bb made the two a's adjacent.
c and a are different letters, so they do not form a pair.
a and c are different letters, so they do not form a pair.
The process continues until no equal neighbours remain.
questions.explain: Deleting a pair can create a new adjacent pair. The card next shows how a stack keeps track of that.
questions.rule: A deletion can expose a new pair.

questions.q: True or false: when the top of the stack equals the current character, the method pops instead of pushing.
questions.explain: Equal characters on top and at hand are adjacent at this moment, so both are deleted: the top is popped and the current one is not pushed.
questions.rule: Equal top and current means delete both.

questions.q: Removing adjacent duplicates from qrssrtuut leaves the string ____.
questions.explain: ss goes, then the two r's meet and go, then uu goes, then the two t's meet and go, leaving q.
questions.rule: Work from the middle outwards: each deletion can expose a new pair.

questions.q: A keypad filter deletes pairs of identical digits that touch. What is left of the input 1223321?
options: (empty)
optionExplain: Only one digit left would need the 2 and the final 1 to cancel, but they are different digits.
That deletes nothing; 22 and 33 are adjacent and must go.
Right: 22 goes, then 33 goes, leaving 1, 2, 1.
The final 2 and 1 have no partners, so something remains.
questions.explain: Push 1, push 2, 2 cancels, push 3, 3 cancels, push 2, push 1. The stack reads 1, 2, 1.
questions.rule: Trace pushes and pops one character at a time.

questions.q: A student scans abba once, removing only pairs that touch in the original string, and returns aa. What did the student miss?
options: The pair aa was fine to keep because it is not adjacent in abba
After bb is deleted the two a's touch, so a single pass without a stack misses that pair
The answer should be bb, since the inner pair is deleted last
Nothing: the answer aa is correct because deletions are done only once
optionExplain: Once bb is gone, the a's are adjacent, and the task says to continue.
Right: new adjacencies appear as deletions happen.
The inner pair is deleted first.
The task repeats the deletion until none remain.
questions.explain: A deletion in the middle can make outer characters adjacent. The stack remembers the outer characters until that happens.
questions.rule: Deleting can create new pairs.

questions.q: Boxes arrive as R G B B G R, and touching boxes of one colour are removed. In what order are the colours removed?
options: R, then G, then B
G, then B, then R
All three pairs at the same moment
B, then G, then R
optionExplain: R and R are far apart at the start and cannot touch until the inside is gone.
G and G are separated by B and B at the beginning.
Only B and B touch at the start, so only that pair can go first.
Right: the innermost pair is removed first, the outermost last.
questions.explain: BB touch first. After they go, the two G's touch, and after they go, the two R's touch. Deletion order is the reverse of arrival order.
questions.rule: Inner pairs go first.
questions.teaches: In a string such as abccba the deletion order is c, then b, then a: the character that arrived last among the waiting ones is deleted first, which is why a stack fits.

questions.q: True or false: the stack in a string problem must be an object of a dedicated Stack class.
questions.explain: A stack is a pattern of use. The card next shows structures that serve as one.
questions.rule: A stack is an interface, not a class.

questions.q: In Python, the list method that pushes an item onto the end used as the stack top is ____.
questions.explain: append adds at the end and pop() removes from the end, so together they give the stack interface.
questions.rule: Use the same end for both.

questions.q: The list out is used as a stack. What does this program print?
options: heo
hello
he
o
optionExplain: Each l removes a character, so both h and e leave.
The l branch pops, so the output is shorter than the input.
The final o is pushed after the l characters, so it is in the output.
Right: h, e are pushed; each l pops one; o is pushed.
questions.explain: Push h and e. The first l pops e, the second l pops h. Then o is pushed. The list holds only o.
questions.rule: Trace the list from the end.

questions.q: A text field deletes one character for each x typed. A dev uses a list with append and pop. What does abxxcx leave?
options: c
(empty)
abc
ab
optionExplain: The last x removes c, so c does not stay.
Right: a, b pushed; x pops b; x pops a; c pushed; x pops c.
x characters are not stored; they delete earlier ones.
The first x removes b, the second removes a, so ab does not remain.
questions.explain: Each x pops the most recent character: after abxx nothing is left, then c is pushed and the last x pops it.
questions.rule: Each x removes the latest character.

questions.q: True or false: a learner who pushes with append but removes with pop(0) is still using a stack.
questions.explain: append works on the last position and pop(0) on the first, so adding and removing happen at opposite ends. That is a queue, not a stack.
questions.rule: Both operations must share one end.

questions.q: The book's Java solution for removing adjacent duplicates keeps the stack in a StringBuilder. What does this choice give?
options: Constant-time search for any character
A guarantee that the result is sorted
The answer string is available at the end without copying characters from a separate stack
A faster algorithm than O(n)
optionExplain: Search stays linear for a builder or an array.
Nothing sorts the characters; the order is the order of arrival.
Right: a StringBuilder is a convenient way to get the answer in string format.
The scan must read every character, so O(n) is a lower bound.
questions.explain: The builder acts as the stack, since it supports adding and deleting the last character, and it also produces the result string directly.
questions.rule: Choose a container that also yields the answer.
questions.teaches: The book uses a Java StringBuilder as the stack because it is a convenient way to get the answer in string format at the end, and a C++ string can be used the same way because C++ strings are mutable.

questions.q: In an empty editor you type a, b, #, c, where # is a backspace. What text is shown?
options: ac
bc
abc
c
optionExplain: Right: the backspace deletes b, the latest character.
The backspace removes the latest character, not the first.
The hash sign deletes a character; it is not typed as text.
Only one character is deleted by one backspace.
questions.explain: A backspace deletes the character typed last. The card next shows how a stack does this.
questions.rule: Backspace removes the latest character.

questions.q: To simulate a backspace on the stack of typed characters, you ____ the stack.
questions.explain: Pop removes the most recently typed character.
questions.rule: Backspace is pop.

questions.q: Typing a, #, #, b into an empty editor, with the second # having nothing to delete. What text is shown?
options: ab
b
a
(empty)
optionExplain: The hash signs are backspaces; a is deleted.
Right: the first # deletes a, the second does nothing, then b is typed.
The first backspace removes a; b is typed afterwards.
b is typed after the backspaces, so it stays.
questions.explain: Push a, pop it, ignore the backspace on empty text, push b. The stack holds b.
questions.rule: A backspace on empty text is a no-op.

questions.q: Which pairs of typed strings show the same text? Select all that apply.
options: ab#c and ad#c
a##c and #a#c
a#c and b
ab## and c#d#
abc# and abd
optionExplain: Right: both give ac.
Right: both give c.
These give c and b.
Right: both end up empty.
These give ab and abd.
questions.explain: Build each string with the stack and compare the results: three pairs match and two do not.
questions.rule: Build each string and compare.

questions.q: This build function pops on every hash sign without checking the stack. Which input makes it fail?
options: ab#
a#b
ab##
#a
optionExplain: One backspace after two characters pops b without trouble.
The backspace pops a, which is on the stack, so nothing fails.
Two backspaces after two characters empty the stack but never pop an empty one.
Right: the first backspace meets an empty stack.
questions.explain: Only an input that begins with a backspace, or has more backspaces than characters so far, pops an empty stack.
questions.rule: Guard the pop for empty text.

questions.q: Two input strings each hold 1,000,000 characters. At most how many stack operations does the method perform in total?
options: About 2,000,000, one push or one pop per character
About 1,000,000 times 1,000,000, since each string is compared with the other
About 1,000, the square root of the length
About 1,000,000, since the second string reuses the first result
optionExplain: Right: each character causes at most one stack operation, and each operation is O(1).
The comparison happens once, after both builds, and costs linear time.
No such reduction exists; every character is read.
Each string is built on its own, so both are processed.
questions.explain: Every character leads to one push or one pop at most, so two strings of a million give at most two million operations: linear in the input sizes.
questions.rule: Linear total for linear input.
questions.teaches: Because stack operations are O(1), building both strings costs time and space linear in the two input sizes, so this approach scales as O(n + m).

questions.q: Deli tickets 41, 42 and 43 are taken in that order and served by arrival. Which ticket is served first?
options: 43, the latest to arrive
42, the middle ticket
41, the first to arrive
Whichever ticket is peeked at first
optionExplain: That is last in, first out, which is the stack's order.
No rule serves the middle ticket first.
Right: the first in is the first served.
Peeking only looks; it does not decide who is served.
questions.explain: Serving by arrival order is first in, first out. The card next names the structure.
questions.rule: Arrival order is service order.

questions.q: FIFO stands for first in, first ____.
questions.explain: FIFO means first in, first out: the oldest element leaves first.
questions.rule: A queue is FIFO.

questions.q: Start with an empty queue. Enqueue 5, 8, 1 and 6, then dequeue once. Order the remaining items from front to back.
questions.explain: Dequeue removes the front item, 5. The queue then reads 8, 1, 6 from the front to the back.
questions.rule: Remove from the front; add at the back.
questions.hint: Which end does a dequeue use?

questions.q: Sort each task by the structure that fits it.

items.t: Answer support callers in the order they called
Take turns on a shared printer in the order jobs were sent
Close nested brackets in reverse order of opening
Undo the latest edit in a document
Seat restaurant guests in the order they joined the waiting list
Go back one page in a browser tab

questions.explain: Where the oldest item goes first, use a queue. Where the latest goes first, use a stack.
questions.rule: Oldest first is a queue; newest first is a stack.

questions.q: A developer calls a structure a queue, yet removes items from the same end where they are added. What does it really behave as?
options: A queue, since any structure with an add and a remove operation is a queue
A deque that has lost one of its ends
A stack, since adding and removing at one end gives last in, first out
A sorted list, since the newest is always the largest
optionExplain: A queue needs additions and removals at opposite ends.
A deque allows both ends; this has one working end only, which is a stack.
Right: sharing one end gives LIFO order.
Order of arrival does not sort the items.
questions.explain: Opposite ends make a queue; the same end makes a stack.
questions.rule: Opposite ends: queue. Same end: stack.

questions.q: A team uses a Python list: append to add, pop(0) to remove. It is slow on large lists. Is it still a queue?
options: Yes: it adds at one end and removes at the opposite end, whatever its speed
No: a queue needs a linked list underneath
No: a slow structure cannot be called a queue
Yes, but only if the list holds numbers
optionExplain: Right: the interface defines a queue.
The book says a queue is defined by its abstract interface, not by one storage choice.
Speed does not change which element leaves first.
The contents do not matter; the end used does.
questions.explain: Append at the back and pop(0) from the front is first in, first out, so it is a queue. Its slowness is a separate matter of implementation.
questions.rule: Interface defines a queue.
questions.teaches: A queue is defined by its abstract interface, adding and removing at opposite sides, and there are several ways to implement it with different performance.

questions.q: A queue is stored in a dynamic array with its front at position 0. How much work does one dequeue take in big-O terms?
options: O(1), since only one item is removed
O(log n), since the array can be halved
O(n squared), since every pair is compared
O(n), since every remaining item shifts forward
optionExplain: That is true at the end of the array, but not at the front.
Nothing in a dequeue halves the array.
No comparisons are made; it is a shift of the elements.
Right: removing at the front of an array moves all other elements.
questions.explain: Removing the front element shifts everything else. The card next explains the usual fix.
questions.rule: The front of an array is the slow end.

questions.q: Removing the first element of a dynamic array holding n items costs O(____).
questions.explain: All remaining elements have to move one place, so the cost grows with n.
questions.rule: Front removal on an array is linear.

questions.q: A queue on a plain array holds n jobs and all n are dequeued one after another. What is the total work?
options: O(n), since each job is removed once
O(n squared), since each of n dequeues costs O(n)
O(n log n), since the array is rebuilt in halves
O(1), since a queue is a fast structure
optionExplain: That would need O(1) per dequeue, which a plain array does not give at the front.
Right: n operations times O(n) each.
Nothing in this process halves anything.
A queue's speed depends on its implementation.
questions.explain: Each dequeue shifts up to n elements. Doing it n times costs n times n.
questions.rule: Multiply the cost per operation by the number of operations.

questions.q: Which storage choice gives O(1) enqueue and O(1) dequeue?
options: A doubly linked list with pointers to head and tail
A dynamic array with the front at position 0
A sorted array of the jobs
A hash set of the job names
optionExplain: Right: both ends are reached directly and nodes can be added or deleted at a known location.
Front removal shifts all elements, so it is O(n).
Keeping jobs sorted adds work and does not fix the front shift.
A set has no order, so it cannot tell which job is the oldest.
questions.explain: A doubly linked list with head and tail pointers can add at one end and delete at the other in constant time.
questions.rule: Pointers to both ends make both ends cheap.

questions.q: True or false: the book says the doubly linked list used as a queue usually has sentinel nodes at its head and tail.
questions.explain: The list keeps pointers to the head and tail, usually with sentinel nodes at the two ends.
questions.rule: Head and tail, usually with sentinel nodes.
questions.teaches: The doubly linked list queue maintains pointers to the head and the tail, usually with sentinel nodes marking both ends.

questions.q: A Python program must hold 10 million tasks in a queue. Why is collections.deque better than a list with pop(0)?
options: A deque keeps the tasks sorted by size
A deque stores each task only once and removes duplicates
A deque dequeues from the front in O(1), while pop(0) on a list is O(n)
A deque makes enqueue O(n) but search O(1)
optionExplain: A deque keeps arrival order, not size order.
A deque keeps duplicates like any queue.
Right: the book says deque allows O(1) dequeue from the front.
Enqueue is O(1) and search is not improved.
questions.explain: With 10 million tasks, each front removal on a list would shift millions of items. The deque is built for cheap work at the front.
questions.rule: Pick a structure whose front is cheap.
questions.teaches: In Python, collections.deque implements the queue because it performs dequeue operations from the front in O(1).

questions.q: True or false: a deque can remove elements from both its front and its back.
questions.explain: A deque is a double-ended queue. The card next lays out what it allows.
questions.rule: A deque is open at both ends.

questions.q: Deque is short for ____-ended queue.
questions.explain: Double-ended means elements can be added and removed at both ends.
questions.rule: Deque means double-ended queue.

questions.q: Empty deque: add 3, 5 at the back, 7 at the front, remove the back, add 2 at the back. Order front to back.
questions.explain: After the first three steps the deque is 7, 3, 5. Removing from the back drops 5; adding 2 at the back gives 7, 3, 2.
questions.rule: Track which end each operation uses.

questions.q: Sort each operation by what it needs.

items.t: Add an item at the back
Remove an item from the front
Look at the front item
Remove an item from the back
Add an item at the front

questions.explain: A plain queue adds at the back and removes from the front. Touching the opposite ends, removing from the back or adding at the front, needs a deque.
questions.rule: A queue uses its ends in one direction only.

questions.q: True or false: a deque is the same thing as a queue, since both have a front and a back.
questions.explain: A queue adds at one end and deletes at the other. A deque can add and delete at both ends.
questions.rule: A queue uses each end for one job; a deque for both.

questions.q: A dealer adds and draws cards at the top or bottom of a pile. Which structure models it, and how is its name said?
options: A queue, pronounced like cue
A deque, pronounced like deck
A stack, pronounced like stack
A deque, pronounced like dee-queue
optionExplain: A queue works one way; this pile works at both ends.
Right: both ends take adds and removals, and deque sounds like deck.
A stack uses one end only, but the dealer uses both.
The structure is right, but the book gives deck as the pronunciation.
questions.explain: Open at both ends means deque. The word is pronounced like deck, which suits a pile of cards.
questions.rule: Both ends open: deque.
questions.teaches: Deque is pronounced deck.

questions.q: According to the book, what is the most common use of a queue in algorithm problems?
options: Checking that brackets are balanced
Sorting an array in place
Looking up a value by key
Implementing breadth-first search
optionExplain: That is a stack job, based on last in, first out.
Sorting is not described as a queue's main use.
Lookup by key is a hashing job.
Right: the book says a queue is mostly used to implement BFS.
questions.explain: The book names BFS as the usual home of the queue. The card next sets out the picture.
questions.rule: Queue means BFS first.

questions.q: True or false: according to the book, queues appear more often than stacks in algorithm problems.
questions.explain: The book says queues are less common than stacks, and that few problems focus mainly on a queue.
questions.rule: Queues are rarer than stacks.

questions.q: Match each structure to the use the book gives it.
pairs: Matching each closing bracket with the latest open one
Tracking which function is active during recursion
questions.explain: A stack suits the newest-first matching of brackets, a queue suits BFS, and the call stack records the active function in recursion.
questions.rule: Each structure has a home pattern.

questions.q: A learner says: since many things come in order, queue problems should be as common as stack problems. What does the book say?
options: Queues are more common but easier than stacks
Queues and stacks are equally common in problems
Queues never appear in problems at all
Queues are less common, and mostly serve BFS
optionExplain: The book says the opposite on both counts.
The book says queues are less common.
Queues do appear: the book gives examples and BFS.
Right: few problems have a queue as their main focus.
questions.explain: The book says queues are less common, and the problems are generally more difficult.
questions.rule: Expect fewer queue problems than stack problems.

questions.q: According to the book, how do problems that use queues compare in difficulty with stack problems?
options: They are generally easier, since the order is obvious
They are generally more difficult
They are the same, since both are linear structures
They are easier only when BFS is not involved
optionExplain: The book says they are more difficult.
Right: the book says queue problems are generally more difficult.
The book makes no such claim.
The book ties difficulty to queues generally, not to BFS.
questions.explain: The book groups two facts about queues: they come up less often, and the problems tend to be harder.
questions.rule: Queue problems: rarer and harder.
questions.teaches: Queue problems are generally more difficult than stack problems, as well as less common.

questions.q: Several people send documents to one shared office printer, which prints them in the order they arrive. Which structure models the printer's job list?
options: A stack: the latest document prints first
A hash map from document to owner
A queue: first come, first served
A deque, because documents may be added at either end
optionExplain: That would make early senders wait indefinitely.
A map stores lookups; it does not decide the order of service.
Right: the book names this printer case as a practical use of a queue.
Arrival order only needs one end for adding and the other for removal.
questions.explain: A system that handles jobs first come, first served is a queue. This is the practical software use; BFS is the algorithm-problem use.
questions.rule: First come, first served: queue.
questions.teaches: Outside algorithm problems, any system that handles jobs on a first come, first served basis, such as people sharing a printer, is a practical use of a queue.

questions.q: Calls arrive with increasing times and only the last 3000 time units matter. Which stored calls can be discarded once they are outdated?
options: The oldest calls, because later pings can never count them
The newest calls, because they have not been checked yet
Every second call, to halve the storage
None of them: all calls must be kept for the final count
optionExplain: Right: times only increase, so an outdated call stays outdated.
The newest calls are the ones certain to count.
Dropping at random would give wrong counts.
Outdated calls never count again, so keeping them only costs time.
questions.explain: Old calls are gone for good once they fall outside the window. The card next gives the queue method.
questions.rule: Drop what can never count again.

questions.q: On each ping the outdated timestamps are removed from the ____ of the queue.
questions.explain: The oldest timestamp is at the front, so the front is where outdated ones are dropped.
questions.rule: Outdated timestamps are at the front.

questions.q: Pings arrive at times 1, 100, 3001 and 3002. What does the ping at 3002 return?
optionExplain: That counts all four calls, but 1 is outside the window ending at 3002.
Right: 1 is older than 3002 - 3000 = 2 and is dropped; 100, 3001 and 3002 remain.
100 and 3001 and 3002 are all inside the window, which makes three.
Only the new call would remain if every older one were dropped, but 100 and 3001 are recent enough.
questions.explain: The window for 3002 starts at 2. The timestamp 1 is dropped. The queue holds 100, 3001, 3002.
questions.rule: Drop those below t minus 3000.

questions.q: A limiter counts requests in the last 60 seconds. Requests come at seconds 5, 20, 62, 70, 90. How many count at 90?
optionExplain: That counts every request, but 5 and 20 are older than 30.
The request at 20 is older than second 30 and is dropped.
The requests at 62, 70 and 90 are all within 60 seconds of 90.
Right: the window starts at 30, so 62, 70 and 90 count.
questions.explain: At 90 the cut-off is 30. The queue drops 5 and 20 and keeps 62, 70 and 90.
questions.rule: Window start = t minus the window size.

questions.q: True or false: outdated timestamps should be removed from the back of the queue, because the back holds the oldest call.
questions.explain: The back holds the newest timestamp and the front holds the oldest. Removing from the back would delete the call that was added last.
questions.rule: Outdated entries are at the front.

questions.q: Suppose pings could arrive with times that do not increase. Would checking only the front still find every outdated timestamp?
options: No: the front would no longer be guaranteed to hold the oldest timestamp
Yes: the front is always the oldest item of any queue
Yes: but only if the queue is stored in a dynamic array
No: but only because a queue cannot hold timestamps
optionExplain: Right: the sorted order came from increasing times.
The front is the oldest by arrival, not necessarily by timestamp.
The storage does not change what the front holds.
A queue can hold any values; the issue is the order of the times.
questions.explain: The method relies on arrival order matching time order. Without that, an old timestamp might sit behind a newer one and be missed.
questions.rule: The front check needs sorted times.
questions.teaches: The queue is in sorted order, with the oldest call at the front, only because the calls come with increasing t; this is what makes checking the front enough.

questions.q: A stack receives push 1, push 2, push 3, then pop, then pop. Which value does peek show?
options: Nothing: peek is only allowed on an empty stack
optionExplain: The second pop removes 2 as well.
3 was the first value popped.
Right: 3 and 2 are removed, leaving 1 on top.
Peek reads the top of a stack that has at least one item.
questions.explain: Two pops remove 3 and then 2. The remaining top is 1. The card next lists the operations and their names.
questions.rule: Peek reads, pop removes.

questions.q: Match each Java stack method to its Python list counterpart.
questions.explain: Push is append, pop is pop, peek is reading the last item, and size is len.
questions.rule: Same operations, different names.

questions.q: Order the lines this program prints, first to last.
questions.code:
stack = []
stack.append(1)
stack.append(2)
stack.append(3)
print(stack.pop())
print(stack.pop())
print(stack.pop())
stack.append(5)
print(stack[-1])
questions.explain: The three pops print 3, 2 and 1. Then 5 is pushed, and the peek at the end prints 5.
questions.rule: Pops come out newest first.

questions.q: A browser needs to show the current page without leaving it. Which stack operation fits the history?
options: Pop, which reads the top and removes it
Push, which adds a copy of the top
Peek, which reads the top without removing it
Size, which tells how many pages there are
optionExplain: Pop would leave the page; the history would lose it.
Push adds an item; it is not a way to read.
Right: the page stays in the history.
Size gives a count, not the page.
questions.explain: Peek reads the top and leaves it in place, which is what showing the current page needs.
questions.rule: Use peek to look without changing.

questions.q: True or false: after peek is called on a stack of 3 items, the stack holds 2 items.
questions.explain: Peek only reads the top, so the stack still holds 3 items. Pop would reduce it to 2.
questions.rule: Peek never changes the stack.

questions.q: A loop must process every item on a stack, newest first, and stop when none are left. Which loop is safe?
options: Repeat while the stack is not empty: pop an item and process it
Repeat for the original number of items, popping each time, without checking
Repeat forever and pop, stopping when an error stops the program
Peek once, then process the top until the end
optionExplain: Right: the emptiness check comes before each pop.
This works only if no one else changes the stack in between.
Popping an empty stack is the failure that a check avoids.
Peeking does not remove anything, so the same item is processed again and again.
questions.explain: Checking the stack with empty before each pop avoids popping nothing. The bracket solution does the same before popping.
questions.rule: Check for empty, then pop.
questions.teaches: Java's empty method reports whether the stack has no elements, and the bracket solution calls it before popping so that a closer with nothing to match returns false.

questions.q: Enqueue 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, then dequeue twice. Which element is now at the front?
optionExplain: 5 is at the back, the most recently added.
2 was removed by the second dequeue.
1 was the first to leave.
Right: 1 and 2 were removed from the front.
questions.explain: Two dequeues take away 1 and 2, so the front is 3. The card next gives the operation names.
questions.rule: Dequeue removes the front.

questions.q: Match each Java queue method to its Python deque counterpart.
questions.explain: Offer is append at the back, poll is popleft at the front, peek reads the front item, and size is len.
questions.rule: Same operations, different names.

questions.q: What does this program print?
questions.code:
from collections import deque

queue = deque([1, 2, 3])
queue.append(4)
queue.append(5)
queue.popleft()
queue.popleft()
print(queue[0], len(queue))
optionExplain: 1 was removed by the first popleft.
Right: after two popleft calls the deque holds 3, 4, 5, so the front is 3 and the length is 3.
queue[0] is the front, not the back.
Two items were removed, so the length is 3, not 5.
questions.explain: The deque starts as 1, 2, 3, then 4 and 5 are appended, giving five items. Two popleft calls remove 1 and 2.
questions.rule: popleft removes the front.

questions.q: A café app must show who is next in line without calling them yet. Which queue operation fits?
options: Peek, which reads the front without removing it
Poll, which reads the front and removes it
Offer, which adds a customer at the back
Size, which tells how long the line is
optionExplain: Right: the customer stays in the line until served.
That would take the person out of the line before they are called.
Offer adds a new person; it does not read.
Size gives the length, not the person.
questions.explain: Peek returns the next element to be removed and leaves the queue unchanged.
questions.rule: Peek reads the front.

questions.q: True or false: calling pop() on a Python deque is the correct way to dequeue the oldest element.
questions.explain: pop() removes from the back, the newest element, so it behaves like a stack. popleft() removes from the front.
questions.rule: Dequeue uses popleft, not pop.

questions.q: A task runner must process every job, oldest first, and stop when none remain. Which Python loop shape fits?
options: Repeat while the deque is not empty: pop and process
Repeat while the deque is not empty: read queue[0] and process it
Repeat while the deque is not empty: popleft and process
Repeat a fixed 100 times: popleft and process
optionExplain: pop takes the newest job, which turns the queue into a stack.
Reading does not remove, so the same job would be processed forever.
Right: dequeue from the front until nothing remains.
A fixed count fails when there are fewer or more jobs than that.
questions.explain: The loop checks emptiness, then removes from the front so the oldest job is processed first, as in the book's example of polling until the queue is empty.
questions.rule: Loop until empty, removing from the front.
questions.teaches: The book drains a queue with a loop that runs while the queue is not empty, removing from the front each time and ending with a message when the queue is empty.

questions.q: A stack that must stay increasing from bottom to top holds [2, 6, 9]. The value 5 arrives. What does the stack hold afterwards?
optionExplain: Pushing without removing leaves 9 above 5, which breaks the increasing order.
Right: 9 and 6 are larger than 5 and are removed first.
Items are added at the top, not the bottom.
6 is also larger than 5, so it must be removed as well.
questions.explain: Elements larger than the new one violate the order, so they leave before 5 is pushed. The card next gives the full rule.
questions.rule: Remove violators first, then push.

questions.q: Before pushing onto an increasing stack, you pop the elements that are ____ than the new one.
questions.explain: A larger element left below a smaller new one would break the increasing order.
questions.rule: Pop what breaks the order.

questions.q: An increasing stack holds [2, 6, 9, 12] and the price 7 arrives. What does the stack hold afterwards?
optionExplain: No elements are removed here, so the order breaks.
6 is smaller than 7 and does not break the increasing order, so it stays.
Only larger elements are removed; 2 and 6 stay.
Right: 12 and 9 are larger than 7 and go; 6 is smaller and stays.
questions.explain: Pop 12 and 9, the elements larger than 7, then push 7.
questions.rule: Pop strictly larger elements.

questions.q: Feed 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, 9, 7, 8 in this order into an increasing stack. Order the final stack from bottom to top.
questions.explain: 1 removes 3; 2 removes 4; 5 and 9 are pushed; 7 removes 9; 8 is pushed. The stack is 1, 2, 5, 7, 8.
questions.rule: Pop larger elements before each push.
questions.hint: Which elements does each new value remove?

questions.q: True or false: popping while the top is smaller than the new value (stack[-1] < num) still gives an increasing stack.
questions.explain: Popping smaller elements keeps larger ones below the new value, which gives a decreasing stack. For an increasing stack the loop must pop elements that are larger.
questions.rule: The comparison decides the direction.

questions.q: A decreasing stack (bottom to top) holds [9, 6, 4] and 7 arrives. What does it hold afterwards?
optionExplain: That leaves 4 below 7 in a decreasing stack, which breaks the order.
9 is larger than 7 and does not break a decreasing order, so it stays.
6 is smaller than 7, so it also has to go.
Right: 4 and 6 are smaller than 7 and are removed.
questions.explain: For a decreasing stack the test flips: pop elements smaller than the new one, then push. This is the direction the next ideas use.
questions.rule: Flip the test for a decreasing stack.
questions.teaches: Whether the stack is increasing or decreasing depends on the algorithm: for a decreasing stack the loop pops the elements smaller than the new one.

questions.q: A for loop over n numbers has an inner while loop that pops stack elements. What is the best bound on total time?
options: O(n squared)
O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
optionExplain: Nested loops often mean n squared, but here the inner loop shares a budget of n pops.
Right: each element is popped at most once overall.
Every element is read, so at least n steps are needed.
No sorting or halving step is involved.
questions.explain: The inner loop cannot run more than n times in total. The card next gives the argument.
questions.rule: Count pops over the whole run.

questions.q: In the template, each element is pushed once and popped at most ____ time.
questions.explain: An element that has been popped is gone, so it cannot be popped again.
questions.rule: Popped means gone.

questions.q: An increasing stack processes 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 6 in that order. The total number of pops is ____.
questions.explain: Each of 4, 3, 2 and 1 removes the one before it: four pops. The final 6 removes nothing. Pops never exceed the number of pushes.
questions.rule: Count pops against pushes.

questions.q: An increasing stack processes the six numbers 5, 1, 6, 2, 7, 3. How many pops happen in total?
optionExplain: Several values are larger than the next one, so pops do happen.
Each element is popped at most once, and the last element stays, so six is impossible.
Right: 1 removes 5, 2 removes 6, and 3 removes 7.
Every pop needs a larger element on top of a smaller arrival; only three arrivals find one.
questions.explain: 5 pops when 1 arrives, 6 pops when 2 arrives, 7 pops when 3 arrives. Three pops, below the six pushes.
questions.rule: Pops cannot exceed pushes.

questions.q: True or false: because the while loop sits inside the for loop, the monotonic stack template takes O(n squared) time.
questions.explain: The while loop does not start from scratch each time. Every pop removes an element for good, so over the whole run it runs at most n times.
questions.rule: Total pops are bounded by n.

questions.q: A cleaner scans 1,000,000 entries, adding each once and possibly deleting older ones. What is the most deletions in total?
options: 1,000,000, one per entry added
1,000,000 times 1,000,000, since each scan step may delete many
500,000, since only half the entries can be older
As many as the buffer's size at the end
optionExplain: Right: an entry can be deleted at most once, so deletions never exceed additions.
A step may delete many, but the total over the whole run is capped.
No such limit exists; the cap is the number of entries added.
Deleted entries are no longer in the buffer, so its final size says nothing of the total.
questions.explain: Some steps delete many entries and others none. Counted over the whole run, the average is constant per step, which is what amortized O(1) means.
questions.rule: Average over the whole run, not the worst step.
questions.teaches: A single iteration may pop many elements, yet each iteration is amortized O(1) because the pops over the whole run total at most n.

questions.q: For each day in a list of temperatures, you must report how many days pass before a warmer day. Which structure fits best?
options: A hash map from temperature to day
A monotonic stack
A queue serving days in order
A sorted array of all temperatures
optionExplain: Temperatures repeat, and a map cannot tell which later day is the first warmer one.
Right: it finds the next greater element for every day in one pass.
A queue gives arrival order and does not compare temperatures.
Sorting loses the day positions that the answer depends on.
questions.explain: Next-greater queries are the typical home of monotonic stacks. The card next states the pattern.
questions.rule: Next greater element: monotonic stack.

questions.q: Which tasks suit a monotonic stack or queue? Select all that apply.
options: For each item, find the next larger item to its right
Report the maximum of every window of fixed size
Count how often each value appears
Report the minimum of a window that grows and shrinks
Reverse a string in place
optionExplain: Right: next greater element.
Right: a window maximum.
Counting is a job for hashing.
Right: a dynamic window minimum.
Reversal does not need ordered history.
questions.explain: Next-greater queries and maxima or minima of a changing window are the book's two uses.
questions.rule: Two patterns: next greater, window extreme.

questions.q: Sort each task by whether a monotonic stack or queue is a good tool.

items.t: For each day, how many days until a higher stock price
Highest reading in each hour-long window of a sensor stream
Smallest price in each moving 7-day window
Number of times each product code appears
Check that a username is not taken
Reverse the words of a sentence

questions.explain: Next-greater queries and window extremes suit the pattern. Counting, lookup and reversal are other tools' jobs.
questions.rule: Match the problem pattern to the tool.

questions.q: Task 1: the next larger element for each element. Task 2: the maximum of every window of size k. Which structures does the book use?
options: A monotonic deque for (1) and a plain stack for (2)
A plain queue for both
A hash map for both
A monotonic stack for (1) and a monotonic deque for (2)
optionExplain: This reverses the roles: next greater uses the stack.
A plain queue does not keep the order needed for either.
A map cannot find the next larger element or the window maximum.
Right: the stack handles next-greater, the deque handles the sliding window.
questions.explain: Both tasks need a sorted order of candidates, but the window needs removal from the front as well, which a deque offers.
questions.rule: Window problems need both ends.

questions.q: True or false: a monotonic stack is the right tool for finding the sum of each window of size k.
questions.explain: A sum needs every element in the window, not only the candidates for an extreme. A sliding window or a prefix sum fits better.
questions.rule: It helps with extremes, not with sums.

questions.q: A problem asks for the longest stretch whose largest and smallest values differ by at most a limit. How is a monotonic structure used?
options: As one part of a sliding window, tracking the window's maximum and minimum
As the whole algorithm, with no window needed
It would not be used, since a gap needs sorting
Only to count how many elements are in the array
optionExplain: Right: the book uses monotonic structures inside a larger sliding-window algorithm.
The window still decides which subarray is examined.
Sorting would lose the positions the stretch depends on.
Counting needs no monotonic structure.
questions.explain: The monotonic deques keep the maximum and minimum of the changing window available; the sliding window decides what to add and remove.
questions.rule: Combine patterns when needed.
questions.teaches: In more advanced problems a monotonic stack or queue is only one part of the algorithm, for example inside a sliding window that needs the window's maximum and minimum.

questions.q: Temperatures for two days are [30, 40]. What answer array reports the days to wait for a warmer day?
optionExplain: That swaps the days: the second day has nothing after it.
Day 1 has no later day, so its answer is 0.
Right: day 0 waits 1 day for 40, and day 1 has no warmer day after it.
The warmer day is the next one, so the wait is 1, not 2.
questions.explain: Day 0 is followed at once by a warmer day; the last day has no later day. The card next shows the stack method.
questions.rule: No warmer day means 0.

questions.q: The stack stores ____ instead of temperatures, because the answer is a number of days between two days.
questions.explain: Given an index, the temperature is easy to read from the input, and the distance i - j comes straight from the indices.
questions.rule: Store indices when the answer is a distance.

questions.q: For temperatures [40, 35, 32, 37, 50], which answer array does the method produce?
optionExplain: The first day does not get a warmer day on the next day; it waits for 50.
The decreasing run does not mean every day waits for the last one.
Right: 50 is 4 days after 40, 37 is 2 after 35, 37 is 1 after 32, 50 is 1 after 37.
Warmer days exist later, so most answers are not 0.
questions.explain: At 37 the stack pops 32 (wait 1) and 35 (wait 2). At 50 it pops 37 (wait 1) and 40 (wait 4). Order: [4, 2, 1, 1, 0].
questions.rule: Distance = current index minus popped index.

questions.q: A weather desk applies the method to [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]. Which array does it produce?
optionExplain: Right: each entry is the gap to the next strictly warmer day.
The day with 75 waits for 76 at index 6, which is 4 days, not 3.
The day with 72 is followed by 76, one day later; the 76 has no warmer day.
The day with 74 is followed at once by 75, so its wait is 1.
questions.explain: Trace: 74 resolves day 0, 75 resolves day 1, 72 resolves 69 (1 day) and 71 (2 days), and 76 resolves 72 (1 day) and 75 (4 days). The last 73 and 76 stay unresolved.
questions.rule: Check each answer as the gap to the next warmer day.

questions.q: True or false: with the comparison reversed as shown, the input [30, 40] still returns [1, 0].
questions.explain: With the comparison reversed, a day is popped when the current day is colder. For [30, 40], 40 is not colder than 30, so nothing is popped and the result is [0, 0].
questions.rule: Pop when today is warmer than the top.

questions.q: River levels are [5, 4, 6, 3, 2] and the method finds days until a higher level. How many answers are 0?
options: 0: every day eventually gets a higher level
2: the days with levels 3 and 2
5: no day finds a higher level
3: the days with levels 6, 3 and 2
optionExplain: The level 6 is followed only by lower levels, so it never finds a higher one.
The day with level 6 also has no higher level after it.
The levels 5 and 4 both reach 6.
Right: no higher level follows them, so they remain on the stack.
questions.explain: The answers are [2, 1, 0, 0, 0]. Indices still on the stack when the loop ends found nothing higher, so they keep their default answer, 0.
questions.rule: Left on the stack means no answer.
questions.teaches: Indices still on the stack when the loop ends have no warmer day after them, so they keep the default answer 0.

questions.q: True or false: if 32 is not warmer than 33, and 33 is not warmer than 34, then 32 is not warmer than 34.
questions.explain: If 32 is at most 33 and 33 is at most 34, then 32 is at most 34. The card next uses this to explain the stack.
questions.rule: Not warmer than is transitive.

questions.q: The temperature at the top of the stack is the ____ of the days still waiting for a warmer one.
questions.explain: The stack is ordered so that temperatures never increase toward the top, so the top is the coldest waiting day.
questions.rule: The top is the coldest waiting day.

questions.q: The stack holds the days with temperatures 40, 35 and 32 (top). A day with 34 arrives. Which waiting days does it resolve?
options: The days with 32 and 35
Only the day with 32
All three days
None, because 34 is not warmer than the day before it
optionExplain: 34 is not warmer than 35, so the day with 35 keeps waiting.
Right: 34 beats 32, but 35 is warmer than 34, so the check stops.
34 is not warmer than 40 or 35.
The comparison is with the top, 32, and 34 is warmer than 32.
questions.explain: 34 > 32 pops the day with 32. Next the top is 35, and 34 is not above it, so the loop stops. The stack becomes 40, 35, 34.
questions.rule: Stop at the first day that is not beaten.

questions.q: The temperatures are 34, 33, 32, 31, 30, 50. How many days does the final 50 pop from the stack?
optionExplain: Right: all five earlier days are still waiting and 50 beats every one.
50 beats the top, and then the next top, and so on until the stack is empty.
50 is warmer than every earlier day, so pops do happen.
The 50 itself is pushed, not popped, so only the five earlier days leave.
questions.explain: Each earlier day is colder than the one before, so they all stay on the stack until 50 arrives and clears them.
questions.rule: One warm day can clear a long run of cooler days.

questions.q: True or false: for the temperatures 34, 30, 32, 33, the last day resolves the first day, because 33 is warmer than 30 and 32.
questions.explain: 33 is not warmer than 34, so the first day is still waiting. At 33 the stack holds the days with 34 and 32; 33 beats 32 only. A day is resolved only by a warmer day.
questions.rule: Compare with the top only, and stop at the first day not beaten.

questions.q: Prices are 100, 90, 95, 105 and the stack finds days until a higher price. Which waiting prices does 105 resolve?
options: All of 100, 90 and 95
Only 95, the top of the stack
95 and 100, because 90 was already resolved by 95
Only 100, the oldest price
optionExplain: 90 left the stack when 95 arrived.
The check repeats on the next top, 100, which 105 also beats.
Right: both remaining days are below 105.
The newest waiting price, 95, is checked first and is also beaten.
questions.explain: 95 resolved 90 earlier. At 105 the stack holds 100 and 95, and 105 beats both. Because every new day is checked against the top, each day it pops has met its first higher price.
questions.rule: Each pop records the first higher day.
questions.teaches: Because the check against the top runs on every iteration, the current day is the first warmer day for every index it pops.

questions.q: True or false: the list [5, 3, 3, 2] is monotonically decreasing in the strict mathematical sense.
questions.explain: Strictly decreasing would need each item below the one before, but 3 followed by 3 is not a decrease. The card next gives the exact term.
questions.rule: Equal neighbours are not strictly decreasing.

questions.q: Strictly speaking, the list [5, 3, 3, 2] is monotonically non-____.
questions.explain: It never increases, but it does not always decrease, so non-increasing is the exact term.
questions.rule: Never increases: non-increasing.

questions.q: The strict comparison is used on temperatures [70, 70, 71]. The first entry of the answer array is ____.
questions.explain: The first 70 is not beaten by the second 70, so both stay on the stack. 71 resolves them after 2 days and 1 day.
questions.rule: Equal days do not pop each other.

questions.q: True or false: with the comparison written as shown, the input [70, 70, 71] still gives the correct answer [2, 1, 0].
questions.explain: With <= the second 70 pops the first 70 and records 1 day, but an equal temperature is not warmer. The result is [1, 1, 0], not [2, 1, 0].
questions.rule: Use a strict comparison for warmer.

questions.q: An increasing-stack template pops while the top is greater than the new value. Which change makes it refuse equal elements in the stack?
options: Pop while the top is less than the new value
Pop while the top is greater than or equal to the new value
Pop only when the stack is empty
Push twice when the values are equal
optionExplain: That reverses the direction of the stack and does not address equals.
Right: > becomes >=, so an equal top is popped as well.
An empty stack has nothing to pop.
That puts more equal elements on the stack, not fewer.
questions.explain: Changing the operator > to >= (or < to <= for the other direction) makes equal elements pop each other.
questions.rule: Add equality to the pop test to forbid equals.
questions.teaches: To build a monotonic stack that cannot have equal elements, change the comparison from > to >= (or from < to <=).

questions.q: A heating log shows plateaus: 20, 20, 20, 25. The strict method finds the days until a warmer day. What is the answer array?
optionExplain: Equal days do not resolve each other, so the first 20 waits for 25.
25 is warmer than all three, so they have answers.
Each 20 waits a different number of days for the 25.
Right: all three 20s wait for 25, so they remain on the stack together.
questions.explain: The three 20s stack up (equal days stay) and the 25 pops all three: 3, 2 and 1 days after them. The last entry is 0.
questions.rule: Equal days stay until a warmer one arrives.
questions.teaches: In the daily temperatures problem the stack may hold equal temperatures at the same time, since an equal day is not warmer, so the comparison stays strict.

questions.q: A window holds [5, 3, 7, 1] and then 6 arrives. Which of these numbers can still become the maximum of a later window?
options: Only 6, because it is the newest
5 and 3, because they are the oldest
7 and 6
optionExplain: 5, 3 and 1 are smaller than the newer 6, so they leave the window first and never lead.
7 is larger than 6 and stays in the window until it expires.
Older and smaller than 6 means they expire first and never lead.
Right: 7 is larger and 6 will outlast 5, 3 and 1.
questions.explain: An element smaller than a newer one can never be the maximum. 7 is larger than 6, so both remain candidates. The card next builds on this.
questions.rule: Smaller and older means never a maximum.

questions.q: The front of the deque holds the index of the ____ in the current window at every step.
questions.explain: The deque is decreasing, so its front is the largest value in the window.
questions.rule: The front is the window maximum.

questions.q: For nums = [4, 1, 5, 2, 7, 3, 6] and k = 3, after six elements, which values does the deque hold?
optionExplain: 6 has not been processed yet; it is the seventh element.
Right: 7 is the maximum and 3 is a candidate behind it.
The deque holds only candidates, not the whole window.
5 and 2 were removed from the back when the larger 7 arrived.
questions.explain: 7 removed 2 and 5 from the back; 3 is smaller than 7 and stays behind it. Both are inside the window of the last three elements.
questions.rule: Smaller values behind a larger one stay.

questions.q: A thermostat logs [4, 1, 5, 2, 7, 3, 6] and reports the maximum of every 3 consecutive readings. What does it report?
optionExplain: The last window 7, 3, 6 still holds the 7.
The first window includes 5, so its maximum is 5.
Right: the windows are 4,1,5 then 1,5,2 then 5,2,7 then 2,7,3 then 7,3,6.
That picks the last element of each window instead of the maximum.
questions.explain: Windows of three: maxima 5, 5, 7, 7, 7. Seven readings with window 3 give five windows.
questions.rule: n - k + 1 windows.

questions.q: True or false: without removing expired indices, this version returns [9, 2, 3] for nums = [9, 1, 2, 3], k = 2.
questions.explain: The index of 9 is never removed, so it stays at the front and every window reports 9. The result is [9, 9, 9]. The correct answer is [9, 2, 3].
questions.rule: Remove expired indices from the front.

questions.q: Using k = 3 on a stream of 1,000,000 numbers, what is the most indices the deque holds at the end of any iteration?
options: 3, the window size
1,000,000, the number of elements
1, since only the maximum is kept
About 1,000, the square root of the stream length
optionExplain: Right: only indices inside the current window can stay.
Indices that have left the window are removed from the front.
The deque keeps every candidate that can still become a maximum, so it can hold several.
No square-root bound applies; the window size is the bound.
questions.explain: Indices outside the window are dropped from the front, so no more than k remain. Space is O(k), not O(n).
questions.rule: Space follows the window size.
questions.teaches: The space complexity is O(k), because the deque cannot grow beyond the size of the window.

questions.q: A window is acceptable when every pair of its elements differs by at most limit. Which single quantity decides this?
options: Its average minus its median
Its maximum minus its minimum
The difference between its first and last elements
Its length
optionExplain: These can be small even when the extremes are far apart.
Right: the largest pair difference is max minus min.
The extremes need not be at the ends.
A window of any length can pass or fail depending on its values.
questions.explain: If the largest and smallest values are within the limit, so is every other pair. The card next uses this in a sliding window.
questions.rule: The widest pair is max minus min.

questions.q: The length of a window running from left to right is right - left + ____.
questions.explain: Both ends are included, so the count is one more than the difference of the indices.
questions.rule: Length = right - left + 1.

questions.q: For nums = [10, 1, 2, 4, 7, 2] and limit = 5, what is the length of the longest acceptable subarray?
optionExplain: A longer window, 2, 4, 7, 2, still has a gap of 5.
Any window of five includes 10 with 2 or 1 and has a gap of at least 8, or includes 1 with 7.
The whole array has maximum 10 and minimum 1.
Right: the window 1, 2, 4, 7 has maximum 7 and minimum 1, a difference of 6; the window 2, 4, 7, 2 has 7 and 2, a difference of 5.
questions.explain: The window 2, 4, 7, 2 has a gap of 5, so it is allowed and has length 4. No window of length 5 has a gap of 5 or less.
questions.rule: Check max minus min for each candidate window.

questions.q: Readings [21, 25, 23, 22, 30, 24] are stable if highest minus lowest is at most 3. What is the longest stable stretch?
optionExplain: Right: 25, 23, 22 has a gap of 3.
Adding 21 or 30 widens the gap beyond 3.
A longer stretch, 25, 23, 22, already works.
The whole day has readings from 21 to 30.
questions.explain: The stretch 25, 23, 22 has a gap of 3. Extending it to 21 gives a gap of 4, and extending it to 30 gives 8.
questions.rule: Test max minus min against the limit.

questions.q: True or false: a single decreasing deque, which gives the maximum, is enough to test whether the window's gap is within limit.
questions.explain: The gap needs the minimum as well. A second, increasing deque supplies the minimum at its front.
questions.rule: Two extremes need two deques.

questions.q: In the sliding window maximum the deque is bounded by k. Here, with a window that grows and shrinks, how large can the deques become?
options: At most limit elements
At most 2, one for the maximum and one for the minimum
Up to n, the size of the array
At most log n, since the deques are sorted
optionExplain: The limit is a bound on values, not on how many elements.
Each deque keeps every candidate extreme, not only one.
Right: the window has no fixed size, and in a long run of acceptable elements it can cover almost the whole array.
Sorted order does not bound the length of the deque.
questions.explain: The window length is not fixed, so the deques may hold up to n elements. Time and space are both O(n).
questions.rule: No fixed window means no k bound.
questions.teaches: With a variable-size window the deques can grow to size n, so the space complexity here is O(n) rather than O(k), while time stays O(n).

questions.q: Which earlier skill do tree problems lean on most?
options: Sliding a window across a sorted array of values
Thinking recursively about a smaller copy of the problem
Keeping running prefix sums over a long array
Counting repeated values with a hash map of frequencies
optionExplain: Windows suit sequences, and a tree is not a flat sequence.
Right: tree solutions call themselves on the children.
Prefix sums answer range questions on arrays, not tree shape.
Counting helps in many topics but is not the tree skill.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the skill the chapter expects.
questions.rule: Trees and graphs are the most common interview topic, and the chapter assumes you can read recursion.

questions.q: True or false: according to the book, many interview problems give a tree or graph as the input and focus entirely on it.
questions.explain: The book says a huge number of problems do this, which is why mastering the topic is crucial.
questions.rule: Many problems are about a tree or graph from start to finish.

questions.q: A learner who finds ____ shaky is told to review the first chapter's introduction to it before reading this chapter.
questions.explain: The chapter's very first note points back to the recursion article.
questions.rule: Review recursion first if it is shaky.

questions.q: Which reading fits the claim that trees and graphs are 'probably the most common type of interview question'?
options: It is a proven count taken over every interview ever held
It applies only to companies that ask about hash maps
It means arrays and strings are never asked in interviews
It is the authors' view of interviews, softened by the word probably
optionExplain: No survey or number is given, so it cannot be a proven count.
The book says hash maps are not a type, so they play no role.
It calls array and string too broad a label, not unasked.
Right: the book hedges with 'probably' and offers no count.
questions.explain: The sentence is advice with a hedge, so test it as an opinion.
questions.rule: Read a hedge such as 'probably' as opinion, not as data.

questions.q: A reader says: 'Trees need no recursion, so I will ignore the recursion article.' What is wrong with this?
options: The chapter says it makes heavy use of recursion throughout
Recursion is only needed for graphs, never for trees
The article is about loops, which trees do not use
Recursion is optional for every tree problem in the book
optionExplain: Right: the chapter's first line says the whole chapter relies on it.
Tree DFS is the first place the chapter uses recursion.
The article is about recursion, not loops.
Iterative versions exist but the main solutions are recursive.
questions.explain: The book itself states the dependence on recursion up front.
questions.rule: Trees and graphs are the most common interview topic, and the chapter assumes you can read recursion.
questions.hint: Reread the first line of the chapter.

questions.q: A friend asks why the book can single out trees and graphs as a question type but not hash maps. Which reply fits the book?
options: Hash maps are too hard to be asked in interviews
Hash map questions only appear after graphs in the course
A hash map is a tool used across topics, so it is not itself a question type
A hash map is slower than an array, so it is left out
optionExplain: Nothing in the book calls hash maps too hard for interviews.
The order of chapters has no bearing on question types.
Right: the book says hash maps are not really a type of question.
Speed is not the reason the book gives.
questions.explain: The book says hash maps are not really a type, and array or string is too broad.
questions.rule: Trees and graphs are the most common interview topic, and the chapter assumes you can read recursion.
questions.teaches: The book says hash maps are not really a question 'type', and 'array' or 'string' is too broad a label, which is why trees and graphs head its list.

questions.q: True or false: a node can store only an integer as its data.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. A node may store any data, such as a hash map or a custom object. The card states this.
questions.rule: A node is data plus pointers to other nodes.

questions.q: A node stores data and ____ to other nodes.
questions.explain: The second part of a node is its pointers, which link it to other nodes.
questions.rule: Node = data + pointers.

questions.q: A node must represent a city holding its name and its population. Which design fits the book's node idea?
options: Store only the name, since data must be a single integer
Store only pointers, since a node holds no data
Store name and population as the data, and pointers to neighbouring cities
Store the population, with the name kept outside every node
optionExplain: The data can be any type, including several fields.
A node always has a data part besides its pointers.
Right: data may be several values, and pointers connect to other nodes.
Nothing forces the name outside; the data part can hold it.
questions.explain: Data can be rich, and pointers give the links.
questions.rule: A node is data plus pointers to other nodes.

questions.q: A node holds a list of tags as data and no pointers. What structure can it form with other nodes?
options: None, since without pointers it links to nothing
A binary tree, since tags give the child links
A linked list, since the tags give the next node
A graph, since every node counts as a vertex already
optionExplain: Right: with no pointers the node is an isolated value.
Child links are pointers, and tags are data.
The next node is also reached by a pointer, which is absent.
A graph needs connections between nodes, which are absent.
questions.explain: Pointers are what connect nodes, so no pointer means no structure.
questions.rule: No pointers, no structure.

questions.q: True or false: a node's data value decides which other nodes it connects to.
questions.explain: Connections come from pointers. The data is the payload the node carries.
questions.rule: Pointers carry connection, data carries content.

questions.q: A team stores each employee as a node with name data and a pointer to the manager node. Which idea from the book does this reuse?
options: Nodes with data only, as in an array of employees, where each name is stored without any link
A hash map, which cannot hold pointers at all, so each employee has to be looked up by name
A sorted list, which ignores node links entirely, so each employee is found by position
Nodes with pointers, as in linked lists, but with a different pointer pattern
optionExplain: An array has no pointers between employees, but this design has a pointer to the manager.
A node may hold a hash map as data, so that is no obstacle.
Sorting is unrelated to how nodes link.
Right: it is the same node idea, with pointers pointing upward to managers.
questions.explain: The node concept is the shared base for lists, trees and graphs.
questions.rule: A node is data plus pointers to other nodes.
questions.teaches: The book says a node's data can even be a hash map, and one node may mix several kinds of data, so a node can be as rich as the problem needs.

questions.q: True or false: a linked list counts as a graph.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. A list is made of nodes and pointers, which is all a graph needs. The card gives the definition.
questions.rule: A graph is any collection of nodes and the pointers between them; lists and trees are graphs.

questions.q: A graph is any collection of nodes and their ____ to other nodes.
questions.explain: The definition is nodes plus the pointers between them.
questions.rule: Graph = nodes + pointers.

questions.q: Which collection fits the book's definition of a graph?
options: An array of five integers with no pointers at all
Five nodes in which some nodes point to others
One integer stored in a single variable
A string made of five characters in a row
optionExplain: An array has no nodes pointing to one another.
Right: nodes joined by pointers are a graph.
A single value has no pointers or other nodes.
Characters in a string are not nodes with pointers.
questions.explain: Count nodes and pointers; if both are there, it is a graph.
questions.rule: A graph is any collection of nodes and the pointers between them; lists and trees are graphs.

questions.q: Which statement relates linked lists, trees and graphs?
options: Lists and trees are graphs whose pointers follow extra restrictions
Graphs are a special case of trees with extra pointers
Lists are graphs but trees are a separate kind of structure
Graphs are linked lists that happen to have loops in them
optionExplain: Right: graphs are the general case.
The direction is reversed: trees are the special case.
The book says linked lists and trees are both types of graphs.
Loops do not make a graph a list; lists are one special shape.
questions.explain: Think general to special: graph, then tree or list.
questions.rule: A graph is any collection of nodes and the pointers between them; lists and trees are graphs.

questions.q: True or false: a structure with only one pointer in each node cannot be a graph.
questions.explain: A graph may have any pattern of pointers, so one pointer per node still gives a graph (a linked list is an example).
questions.rule: The definition asks only for nodes and pointers, in any pattern.

questions.q: A reader wants every known theorem about nodes and their connections. What does the book say exists for that?
options: A single article in the linked lists chapter
A rule that applies only to binary trees
A whole field of study called graph theory
Nothing, because graphs are too small a topic
optionExplain: The lists chapter introduces nodes, not all of graph theory.
Graph theory is not limited to binary trees.
Right: graphs are broad enough to have their own field.
The book calls graphs extremely broad, not small.
questions.explain: The chapter covers only the part of graph theory that interview problems use.
questions.rule: A graph is any collection of nodes and the pointers between them; lists and trees are graphs.
questions.teaches: Graphs are such a broad topic that there is an entire field of study dedicated to them, called graph theory.

questions.q: A road map is modelled as a graph with towns as nodes. What does a road correspond to?
options: A vertex that stores the road length
An edge connecting two vertices
A node that sits between the towns
A subtree rooted at the larger town
optionExplain: Vertices stand for towns, not roads.
Right: the connection between nodes is an edge.
A road joins two towns; it is not a third node.
Subtrees belong to trees, and are not part of this question.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the term.
questions.rule: Nodes are vertices, pointers are edges.

questions.q: Match each graph word with its other name.
questions.explain: Vertices are nodes, and edges are the pointers between nodes.
questions.rule: Node = vertex, pointer = edge.

questions.q: A graph has 7 vertices and 6 edges. It has ____ nodes.
questions.explain: Vertices and nodes are the same thing, so 7 vertices means 7 nodes.
questions.rule: Vertex is another word for node.

questions.q: A learner reads about an edge to vertex 4 and says a vertex is a different kind of thing from a node. What fixes this?
options: A vertex is a node that has no pointers at all
A vertex is a pointer between two nodes
A vertex is the first node of a linked list only
Vertex is another name for node; the words are interchangeable
optionExplain: A node with no pointers is still a node.
The pointer between nodes is the edge, not the vertex.
Vertices are not limited to a list's first node.
Right: vertices are nodes.
questions.explain: Two words, one thing.
questions.rule: Nodes are vertices, pointers are edges.

questions.q: In a graph with vertices A, B and C, the pointers go A to B and B to C. How many edges and vertices?
options: 3 edges and 2 vertices
2 edges and 3 vertices
2 edges and 2 vertices
3 edges and 3 vertices
optionExplain: The counts are swapped.
Right: count nodes for vertices and pointers for edges.
C is also a vertex, so there are 3.
Only two pointers are listed, so there are 2 edges.
questions.explain: Vertices count nodes; edges count pointers.
questions.rule: Nodes are vertices, pointers are edges.

questions.q: How does the book say vertices and edges are usually drawn?
options: Vertices as squares, and edges as the words inside them
Vertices as arrows, and edges as circles between them
Vertices as numbers in a row, with no lines at all
Vertices as circles, and edges as lines or arrows between circles
optionExplain: The book names circles for nodes, not squares.
The roles are reversed in this option.
Drawings include the connecting lines or arrows.
Right: circles joined by lines or arrows.
questions.explain: Circles are vertices; lines or arrows are edges. The book adds that directed edges are drawn as arrows and undirected edges as straight lines.
questions.rule: Nodes are vertices, pointers are edges.
questions.teaches: Edges can be directed, drawn as arrows, or undirected, drawn as straight lines; with an arrow you can move only one way along the edge.

questions.q: True or false: because a tree is a graph, interview problems treat trees and graphs as one topic.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The book says they are considered different topics. The card gives the order of study.
questions.rule: Trees are graphs, but they are taught first and treated as their own topic.

questions.q: The course teaches ____ first and graphs afterwards.
questions.explain: Trees come first.
questions.rule: Start with the simpler case.

questions.q: A friend says: 'I will read the graph articles first; a tree is only a graph, so I can skip trees.' What is the book's likely reply?
options: Study trees first, because the course teaches them before graphs
Skip trees, since graphs include everything inside them
Study graphs only if no tree article exists
Read both together and ignore the order of the articles
optionExplain: Right: the course orders topics from easier to harder.
The course treats trees as the stepping stone.
Both topics exist in the course, in a set order.
The order is deliberate, not arbitrary.
questions.explain: Trees are the on-ramp to graphs.
questions.rule: Trees are graphs, but they are taught first and treated as their own topic.

questions.q: True or false: algorithm problems treat trees and graphs as different topics, although a tree is a type of graph.
questions.explain: Type-of does not mean same-topic: the book files them separately.
questions.rule: Type-of does not mean same-topic.

questions.q: A learner meets a new problem about a company where every employee has exactly one manager. Which topic label does the course give it?
options: A graph problem, since graphs cover all structures
A recursion problem, with no structure involved
A tree problem, since one parent per node fits a tree
A sorting problem, since people are ranked
optionExplain: Though a tree is a graph, the course files it as a tree.
Recursion is a technique and not the structure.
Right: this is a tree, which the course treats as its own topic.
Ranking is not the point of the problem.
questions.explain: Match the structure to the narrowest topic name.
questions.rule: Trees are graphs, but they are taught first and treated as their own topic.
questions.hint: Each employee has exactly one manager.

questions.q: A learner finds trees easy and graphs harder. What do the book's words about the two predict?
options: That is unusual, since the book calls graphs easier
That is a sign the tree material was skipped
That is expected, since graphs are the more advanced topic
That is expected, since trees contain graphs inside them
optionExplain: The book calls graphs the harder topic.
The experience matches the book rather than signalling a skip.
Right: graphs are the more advanced and difficult topic.
The containment runs the other way: trees sit inside graphs.
questions.explain: Graphs are the more advanced topic, so expect more effort. The reason is that a tree is a graph with restrictions, and lifting them lets graphs take many more forms.
questions.rule: Trees are graphs, but they are taught first and treated as their own topic.
questions.teaches: A binary tree is a graph with restrictions: every node has at most one parent and at most two children; lifting the restrictions gives general graphs.

questions.q: What would you call the first node of a binary tree, as the linked list calls its first node the head?
options: The root
The tail
The leaf
The trunk
optionExplain: Right: the start of a binary tree is the root.
A tail is the end of a list.
A leaf is a node at the bottom with no children.
The book uses root, not trunk.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the term.
questions.rule: The root is the first node of a tree, the counterpart of a list's head.

questions.q: The start of a linked list is the head; the start of a binary tree is the ____.
questions.explain: The root is the tree's starting node.
questions.rule: Head for lists, root for trees.

questions.q: A function receives one argument, a reference to the first node of a tree. Which name fits that argument?
options: tail
leaf
next
root
optionExplain: Tail names the last node of a list.
A leaf is at the far end of a tree.
Next is the pointer in a list node.
Right: the root is what a tree problem hands you.
questions.explain: Tree problems come with the root.
questions.rule: The root is the first node of a tree, the counterpart of a list's head.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches the list term with the tree term that plays the same role?
options: head in a list, leaf in a tree
head in a list, root in a tree
next pointer in a list, root in a tree
tail in a list, root in a tree
optionExplain: A leaf is where a tree ends.
Right: both name the starting node.
