The next pointer is a link, not a start.
A tail is the end of a list.
questions.explain: Starts match starts.
questions.rule: The root is the first node of a tree, the counterpart of a list's head.

questions.q: True or false: a tree can have two roots, because two nodes may each start the tree.
questions.explain: A tree has one starting node, the root. Two starting points would describe two separate trees.
questions.rule: The root is the first node of a tree, the counterpart of a list's head.
questions.hint: Recall that a tree has one starting node.

questions.q: A reader asks which node in a binary tree has no parent. What does the book say?
options: The root is the only node with no parent
Every leaf has no parent
The last child added has no parent
All nodes have a parent, even the first
optionExplain: Right: the root is the only parentless node.
Leaves have no children but do have a parent.
Insertion order does not decide who has a parent.
The first node has no one above it.
questions.explain: The root is the only node with no parent. It is also the entry point: the book says every node can be reached from it, and most tree questions hand it over as the input.
questions.rule: The root is the first node of a tree, the counterpart of a list's head.
questions.teaches: Every node in the tree is accessible starting from the root, and in most tree questions the root is given as the input.

questions.q: In a tree, node X has a pointer to node Y. What is Y to X?
options: A parent
The root
A child
A leaf, whatever its pointers
optionExplain: The pointer starts at X, so X is the parent.
The root is the start of the whole tree, not any pointed-to node.
Right: the node pointed to is the child.
A leaf is judged by its own pointers, not by being pointed to.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the direction.
questions.rule: If A points to B, then A is B's parent and B is A's child.

questions.q: If node A points to node B, then A is the ____ of B.
questions.explain: The node that points is the parent; the node pointed to is the child.
questions.rule: Pointer goes from parent to child.

questions.q: In a folder tree, the folder photos points to the folders 2023 and 2024. What are 2023 and 2024 to photos?
options: Parents of photos
Children of photos
Roots of the tree
Leaves that have no parent
optionExplain: Parents point at children, not the other way round.
Right: the folders pointed to are children.
The root is the top folder, which is not named here.
A node pointed to by photos has a parent: photos.
questions.explain: Follow the pointer to find the child.
questions.rule: If A points to B, then A is B's parent and B is A's child.

questions.q: A tree node M points to nodes N and P. Which statement must be true?
options: N is the parent of M
N and P are parents of each other
M is a child of N and P
M is the parent of both N and P
optionExplain: N is pointed to by M, so N is M's child.
Siblings are not parent and child.
The pointers run from M to N and P.
Right: M points to N and P.
questions.explain: The pointing node is the parent.
questions.rule: If A points to B, then A is B's parent and B is A's child.

questions.q: True or false: in a tree, each node holds a pointer to its parent.
questions.explain: Tree pointers lead from a node to its children. The parent is the node that points to it.
questions.rule: Pointers go down, not up.

questions.q: What does the book say about how many parents a tree node can have?
options: Any number, as long as one is the root
At most one: a node cannot have more than one parent
Exactly two, matching its two children
None, since only the root has a parent
optionExplain: More than one parent is not allowed in a tree.
Right: a node cannot have more than one parent.
The two-child limit concerns children, not parents.
Every node except the root has a parent.
questions.explain: One parent at most.
questions.rule: If A points to B, then A is B's parent and B is A's child.
questions.teaches: In a tree, a node cannot have more than one parent.

questions.q: What makes a tree 'binary'?
options: Each node has exactly one parent and one child
The tree has exactly two levels
Each node stores one of two values
Each node has at most two children
optionExplain: That describes a list.
Binary does not restrict the number of levels.
Binary does not restrict what a node stores.
Right: the limit is on children.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card states the limit.
questions.rule: A binary tree allows each node at most two children: a left child and a right child.

questions.q: True or false: a node in a binary tree may have a single child.
questions.explain: At most two children includes one child and zero children.
questions.rule: At most two, so 0, 1 or 2.

questions.q: Which number of children is NOT allowed for a node in a binary tree?
options: Three
Zero
One
Two
optionExplain: Right: three exceeds the limit.
Zero is a leaf and is allowed.
One child is allowed.
Two children is the maximum.
questions.explain: Zero, one or two children only.
questions.rule: A binary tree allows each node at most two children: a left child and a right child.

questions.q: A binary tree node has both its left pointer and its right pointer filled. It has ____ children.
questions.explain: A left child and a right child make two children.
questions.rule: Two named slots, so at most two children.

questions.q: A learner says: 'A binary tree node must have exactly two children.' What is wrong?
options: The rule is at least two, so more are fine
The rule is exactly one child per node
The rule is at most two, so fewer children are fine
The rule counts parents rather than children
optionExplain: There is no minimum and no allowance for more than two.
A list has one child per node, which is a different structure.
Right: leaves have no children and still belong to a binary tree.
The limit applies to children.
questions.explain: Check the limit: at most two.
questions.rule: A binary tree allows each node at most two children: a left child and a right child.

questions.q: What does the book say about the difference between a left child and a right child?
options: The left child must hold the smaller value
The right child is the parent of the left child
No real difference; the names are a convention that suits drawings
The left child is always visited by a different rule
optionExplain: That rule belongs to binary search trees, not binary trees generally.
Siblings are not parent and child.
Right: the left and right names are a convention.
The book gives no such rule for plain binary trees.
questions.explain: Left and right are labels, not meanings.
questions.rule: A binary tree allows each node at most two children: a left child and a right child.
questions.teaches: There is not really a difference between a child being on the left or the right; the names are convention and convenient for graphical representations.

questions.q: Which description matches a binary tree?
options: Each node has 0 to 2 children and every node but the root has one parent
Each node has exactly 2 children and one parent, so the tree grows evenly at every node
Each node has 1 child and 2 parents, so a node is reached from two directions at once
Each node has 0 to 2 parents and no children, so the limit is on how many nodes point to it
optionExplain: Right: it limits children and parents together.
Exactly 2 children would leave no leaves.
Two parents are not allowed.
The limit is on children, and a node has at most one parent.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives both conditions.
questions.rule: Every node has 0 to 2 children, and every node except the root has exactly one parent.

questions.q: In a binary tree every node except the root has exactly ____ parent.
questions.explain: Every non-root node has exactly one parent.
questions.rule: One parent each, except the root.

questions.q: Nodes P, Q, R and S: P points to Q and R; Q points to S; R points to S. Is this a binary tree?
options: Yes, since each node has at most two children
No, since P has two children
Yes, since S is a leaf and leaves are allowed
No, since S has two parents
optionExplain: Child counts are fine, but the parent rule fails.
Two children are allowed.
Leaves must still have only one parent.
Right: S is pointed to by both Q and R.
questions.explain: Check parents as well as children.
questions.rule: Every node has 0 to 2 children, and every node except the root has exactly one parent.

questions.q: A structure has nodes A, B, C where A points to B and C points to B. Is it a binary tree with A as root?
options: Yes, since no node has more than two children
No, since B has two parents and C is unreachable from A
Yes, since B is a leaf
No, since a root must have exactly two children
optionExplain: The parent rule is also needed.
Right: B has two parents.
A leaf still has exactly one parent.
A root may have zero, one or two children.
questions.explain: Check both conditions.
questions.rule: Every node has 0 to 2 children, and every node except the root has exactly one parent.

questions.q: True or false: a structure in which each node has at most three children counts as a binary tree.
questions.explain: Binary needs at most two children per node, so a node with three children breaks the rule.
questions.rule: Binary means two, not three.

questions.q: The book says linked lists have several types. What does it say about trees?
options: There are several types of trees too, and the course focuses on binary trees
There is exactly one type of tree, the binary tree, so the word tree always means binary
Trees have types, but the course ignores all of them and teaches graphs in their place
Binary trees are the only type of graph, so every graph in the course is a binary tree
optionExplain: Right: binary trees are one type among several.
Other types of tree exist.
The course focuses on binary trees specifically.
Graphs include many other structures.
questions.explain: Binary is the chosen type.
questions.rule: Every node has 0 to 2 children, and every node except the root has exactly one parent.
questions.teaches: Like linked lists, trees come in multiple types, and this course focuses on binary trees.

questions.q: In a comment thread on a social app, which item is the root of the tree?
options: The newest reply
The longest comment
The original post
The user who viewed it last
optionExplain: Newest replies are leaves or near leaves.
Length has nothing to do with the structure.
Right: everything hangs below the original post.
Viewing is not part of the structure.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card pairs each structure with its root.
questions.rule: File systems, comment threads and org charts are trees, each with a root and children.

questions.q: Match each real structure with the node that serves as its root.
questions.explain: Each structure has one top element from which everything else descends.
questions.rule: Find the top element to find the root.

questions.q: A course catalogue lists prerequisites so that each course has exactly one required course above it, apart from one starting course. Which structure is this?
options: A list, since it has only one course
A tree, with the starting course as the root
A graph that cannot be a tree
A binary tree, since it has two levels
optionExplain: There are many courses, not one.
Right: one parent each except one root.
Trees are graphs, so a tree fits.
Binary needs a limit of two children, which is not given.
questions.explain: One parent each plus one root means a tree.
questions.rule: File systems, comment threads and org charts are trees, each with a root and children.

questions.q: Which real-life tree is least likely to be a binary tree?
options: A tournament bracket where two players meet in each match
A game tree in which every move offers two choices
A set of yes/no questions leading to answers
A company with a CEO who has six direct reports
optionExplain: Two players per match fit two children.
Two choices give two children per node.
Yes/no questions give two branches per question.
Right: six direct reports exceed two children.
questions.explain: Count the children per node.
questions.rule: File systems, comment threads and org charts are trees, each with a root and children.

questions.q: True or false: an org chart in which managers have many direct reports cannot be a tree.
questions.explain: Many children are allowed in a tree. Only a binary tree caps the children at two.
questions.rule: Tree is wider than binary tree.

questions.q: In a computer's file system modelled as a tree, what are the root and the children?
options: The newest file is the root; older files are the children
The root directory is the root; its subfolders and files are the children
The largest file is the root; smaller ones are the children
Each file is a root of its own tree with no children
optionExplain: Age does not decide who is the root.
Right: the root directory has folders and files below it.
Size does not decide who is the root.
A file system hangs everything from one top directory.
questions.explain: Root directory on top, contents below.
questions.rule: File systems, comment threads and org charts are trees, each with a root and children.
questions.teaches: In a file system tree the root is the root directory, and its children are the subfolders and files.

questions.q: In a company tree where an edge A to B means A manages B, which person is the root?
options: The newest hire at the bottom
The manager with the most direct reports
Every person who manages someone
The person whom no one manages, the CEO
optionExplain: Newest hires are near the leaves.
Count of reports does not pick the root.
Many managers are children of someone else.
Right: the root has no parent, so nobody manages the CEO.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card ties root to the unmanaged top.
questions.rule: In an org chart tree, edges run from a manager to each direct report, and the unmanaged CEO is the root.

questions.q: In the company tree, an edge from A to B means that A ____ B.
questions.explain: An edge points from a manager to each direct report.
questions.rule: Edges point from manager to report.

questions.q: A school tree: the principal points to heads of department, who point to teachers. What is a head of science to the principal?
options: A child
The parent
The root
A sibling
optionExplain: Right: the principal points to the head, who is therefore a child.
The principal is above, so the principal is the parent.
The principal is the root, as nobody manages that person.
Siblings share a parent; the principal is that parent.
questions.explain: Follow the edge from manager to report.
questions.rule: In an org chart tree, edges run from a manager to each direct report, and the unmanaged CEO is the root.

questions.q: True or false: if edges are drawn from each employee to their manager, the structure still follows the book's rule that an edge A to B means A manages B.
questions.explain: That rule puts the edge from the manager to the report. Drawing the other way reverses parent and child.
questions.rule: Keep edges pointing from manager to report.

questions.q: A company has one CEO, three managers under the CEO, and two staff under each manager. How many nodes does the tree have?
optionExplain: That counts only 1 + 3 + 2.
That leaves out the CEO.
That adds one extra person.
questions.explain: Add the root, the middle level and the lowest level.
questions.rule: In an org chart tree, edges run from a manager to each direct report, and the unmanaged CEO is the root.

questions.q: In the book's company example, a C-suite member has VPs reporting to them. What sits below those VPs?
options: The CEO again
Nothing, since VPs are always leaves
Directors, and so on down the levels
Other C-suite members
optionExplain: The CEO is at the top, not below.
VPs have directors reporting to them.
Right: directors report to VPs.
C-suite members sit above VPs.
questions.explain: The tree deepens with each management layer.
questions.rule: In an org chart tree, edges run from a manager to each direct report, and the unmanaged CEO is the root.
questions.teaches: In the book's company tree, VPs report to the C-suite and directors report to the VPs, so each management layer adds a level.

questions.q: A CEO has six direct reports. Is the company tree a binary tree?
options: No, because the CEO has more than two children
Yes, because every company is a binary tree
Yes, because the CEO has a left and a right report
No, because the CEO is the root
optionExplain: Right: six children exceed two.
Binary needs at most two children, so size matters.
Six reports do not fit in left and right.
A root can belong to a binary tree.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the rule.
questions.rule: More than two children at any node means a tree is not binary.

questions.q: True or false: one node with three children is enough to stop a tree from being binary.
questions.explain: Binary allows at most two children for every node, so one violation breaks it.
questions.rule: One bad node is enough.

questions.q: A manager has 5 direct reports. In the company tree that manager has ____ children.
questions.explain: Each direct report is a child.
questions.rule: Reports are children.

questions.q: In a company tree the CEO has 6 direct reports and each of them has 3 VPs. How many VPs in total?
optionExplain: That is 6 + 3.
That is 6 x 2.
That is 6 x 4.
Right: 6 x 3 = 18.
questions.explain: Multiply reports by VPs per report.
questions.rule: More than two children at any node means a tree is not binary.

questions.q: A reader says: the CEO has six children, so this structure is not a tree at all. What is the mistake?
options: Six children are fine because binary allows six, so the structure is a tree and a binary one
Six children break only the binary rule; the structure is still a tree
A CEO cannot be a root of any tree, since a root is a node that a manager has to appoint
A tree must have exactly six children at its root, so a CEO with fewer would break the tree
optionExplain: Binary allows at most two children.
Right: too many children means not binary, not not-a-tree.
The CEO is the root: nobody manages them.
No such requirement exists.
questions.explain: Keep tree and binary apart.
questions.rule: More than two children at any node means a tree is not binary.

questions.q: What change to the company would make its tree binary?
options: Every manager would have at most two direct reports
Every manager would have at least six direct reports
The CEO would manage nobody
Every person would have two managers
optionExplain: Right: cap children at two per node.
More reports moves further from binary.
That would leave a one-node tree, which is binary but not the same company.
Two parents break the tree rule.
questions.explain: Cap the children per node at two.
questions.rule: More than two children at any node means a tree is not binary.
questions.teaches: In the book's example the CEO's six children are the C-suite, people such as the CFO, COO and CTO, who each have their own reports.

questions.q: True or false: a company where each person has exactly one manager and everyone is linked to the CEO forms a tree.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. One manager each plus connection are the two properties named on the card.
questions.rule: A tree needs one parent per node and one connected structure.

questions.q: In the company tree, each person has only one ____.
questions.explain: The single manager is the node's parent.
questions.rule: One manager, one parent.

questions.q: In a club, member M is supervised by two co-leaders. Which tree property fails?
options: Connection, since M is cut off
Binary shape, since M has two children
One parent per node, since M has two supervisors
Root count, since there are two co-leaders
optionExplain: M is linked to the leaders, so it is connected.
The binary rule concerns children.
Right: two supervisors mean two parents.
The co-leaders issue concerns M's parents.
questions.explain: Count parents.
questions.rule: A tree needs one parent per node and one connected structure.

questions.q: Match each situation with the tree property it breaks.
pairs: A team with no link to anyone above
questions.explain: Two managers break the parent rule, a cut-off team breaks connection, and six reports break neither.
questions.rule: Check parents, check connection, then check child counts.

questions.q: A new team is added to the chart with its own head, but nobody links the head to the CEO. What property fails?
options: One manager per person, since the head has no manager
The structure is no longer connected
The root rule, since the team has no root
The binary rule, since the head has no children
optionExplain: The head has zero managers, not two; that is not what breaks.
Right: the team is separate from the rest.
The team does have a head, which acts as its own top.
The binary rule is about children.
questions.explain: Cut-off group means not connected.
questions.rule: A tree needs one parent per node and one connected structure.

questions.q: The book gives a quick test for connection. Which is it?
options: Count the people and check the total is even, since an even head count means everyone has a pair
Check that every manager has exactly two reports, since a full set of pairs shows no one is left out
Sort the people by name and compare neighbours, since neighbours in the list should be linked
Start at anyone and repeatedly follow managers; you always end up at the CEO
optionExplain: Counting does not test connection.
That checks a binary shape, not connection.
Sorting does not test links.
Right: tracing upward must end at the single top.
questions.explain: Following managers upward from anyone ends at the CEO. The CEO is the root of the company tree because no other employee manages them.
questions.rule: A tree needs one parent per node and one connected structure.
questions.teaches: The CEO is the root because they are at the top and are not managed by any other employee.

questions.q: A tree question gives you one reference. Which node is it most likely to be?
options: A random leaf
The root
The deepest node
The node with the largest value
optionExplain: A leaf cannot reach the other nodes.
Right: the root reaches every node.
The deepest node is a leaf.
Values do not decide what is given.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card says what the input is.
questions.rule: Every node of a tree is reachable from the root, so the root is usually all you are given.

questions.q: True or false: every node in a tree can be reached by starting from the root.
questions.explain: That is what makes the root enough as an input.
questions.rule: Root reaches all.

questions.q: A function holds the root of a 10,000-node tree. It needs ____ extra node references to reach every node.
questions.explain: The root reaches every node, so no extra reference is needed.
questions.rule: One reference, whole tree.

questions.q: A function is handed a leaf node of a tree and no other reference. Which nodes can it reach through child pointers?
options: The whole tree
Every node above it
Its siblings
Only that leaf itself
optionExplain: Only the root reaches everything.
Child pointers lead down, not up.
Siblings are reached through the parent.
Right: a leaf has no child pointers to follow.
questions.explain: Child pointers go down.
questions.rule: Every node of a tree is reachable from the root, so the root is usually all you are given.

questions.q: A function receives a middle node and claims it can total the values of the entire tree. What is wrong?
options: It can reach only the nodes below that node, not the parent or the rest
It can reach every node, since a tree is connected
It can reach everything, but only by recursion
It must be a root, because middle nodes do not exist
optionExplain: Right: child pointers lead down, so only descendants are reachable.
Connected is not the same as reachable from every node.
Recursion does not add upward links.
Middle nodes exist in every large tree.
questions.explain: Reachable from the root only.
questions.rule: Every node of a tree is reachable from the root, so the root is usually all you are given.

questions.q: In a binary tree, after you move from a node to its child, what can you do?
options: You can move back using a parent pointer, which every node of a binary tree stores
You can move to any sibling directly, since the two children of a node are linked to each other
You cannot move back to the parent, because edges point only downward
You can jump to the root directly, since every node keeps a pointer to the top of the tree
optionExplain: The node stores child pointers only.
Siblings are not linked to each other.
Right: the book says you can't access a node's parent.
No pointer to the root is stored.
questions.explain: No way back up without extra work.
questions.rule: Every node of a tree is reachable from the root, so the root is usually all you are given.
questions.teaches: Edges in a binary tree are directed downward: you can't access a node's parent, and once you move to a child you can't move back.

questions.q: What do you call a node of a tree that has no children?
options: A root
A parent
A leaf
A subtree
optionExplain: The root starts the tree.
A parent has at least one child.
Right: a childless node is a leaf.
A subtree is a node with all its descendants.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the term.
questions.rule: A leaf is a node with no children.

questions.q: A node with no children is called a ____ node.
questions.explain: Childless nodes are leaves.
questions.rule: No children means leaf.

questions.q: Tree: 1 is the root with children 2 and 3; 2 has children 4 and 5; 3 has only a right child 6. The tree has ____ leaves.
questions.explain: The nodes 4, 5 and 6 have no children, so there are 3 leaves.
questions.rule: Count childless nodes.

questions.q: A binary tree has 7 nodes, and every node with children has exactly two. How many leaves?
optionExplain: Right: root, two children, four grandchildren; the four are leaves.
That counts only the middle level.
That counts one node too many.
Only four nodes lack children.
questions.explain: Draw the three levels: 1, 2 and 4 nodes.
questions.rule: A leaf is a node with no children.

questions.q: True or false: in the tree above, node 3 is a leaf because it has fewer than two children.
questions.explain: A leaf has no children, and node 3 has one (node 6). Fewer than two is not the test.
questions.rule: Leaf means zero children.

questions.q: A problem asks for the longest path from the root to a leaf. Why is the leaf the end of that path?
options: A leaf has the largest value, so the path stops
A leaf has no parent, so the path starts there
A leaf points back to the root, so the path ends
A leaf has no children, so the path cannot continue further down
optionExplain: Leaves do not have to hold large values.
Leaves have parents.
Pointers do not lead back.
Right: with no children there is no next step downward.
questions.explain: Paths run down to a leaf.
questions.rule: A leaf is a node with no children.
questions.teaches: Many tree problems measure paths from the root to a leaf, such as the maximum depth problem, which asks for the longest such path.

questions.q: What depth does the root of a tree have?
options: The number of leaves
The number of children
optionExplain: Depth 1 belongs to the root's children.
Right: the root is zero steps from itself.
Leaf counts do not set depth.
The count of children is unrelated.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the convention.
questions.rule: A node's depth is its parent's depth plus 1, with the root at 0.

questions.q: A child's depth is its parent's depth plus ____.
questions.explain: Each step down adds one.
questions.rule: Child depth = parent depth + 1.

questions.q: Node 1 is the root with children 2 and 3. Node 2 has children 4 and 5; node 3 has a right child 6. The depth of node 6 is ____.
questions.explain: Node 3 has depth 1, so its child 6 has depth 2.
questions.rule: Add one per step down.

questions.q: Order these nodes from the smallest depth to the largest, using the tree where 1 is the root, 2 and 3 are its children, and 4 is a child of 2.
questions.explain: Node 1 has depth 0, node 3 has depth 1 (a child of the root), and node 4 has depth 2 (a child of node 2).
questions.rule: Smaller depth means closer to the root.

questions.q: A learner computes depth by counting the nodes on the path from the root, so the root gets depth 1. Under the usual definition, what is off?
options: The usual definition counts steps, so the root has depth 0
The root should have depth 2, because the usual definition counts the root and its first child
Depth counts leaves, not nodes, so the path from the root should be measured in leaves reached
Depth is the number of children, so the root should get the depth that matches how many it has
optionExplain: Right: depth counts edges from the root.
Nothing sets the root to 2; the root is the start, at distance 0.
Depth does not count leaves.
The number of children is a separate quantity.
questions.explain: Depth counts edges, not nodes.
questions.rule: A node's depth is its parent's depth plus 1, with the root at 0.

questions.q: A problem asks for the number of nodes on the longest path from the root to a leaf. A chain of 3 nodes is given. What is the answer?
options: 2, because the deepest node has depth 2 and the path is measured in steps
0, because the root has depth 0 and the longest path starts and ends there
3, because the problem counts nodes and the root counts as 1
1, because only the leaf is counted and the nodes above it are only on the way
optionExplain: Depth 2 is a step count, not a node count.
Zero would count no nodes at all.
Right: the problem counts nodes, so the root contributes 1.
The path has three nodes.
questions.explain: Count nodes if the problem asks for nodes.
questions.rule: A node's depth is its parent's depth plus 1, with the root at 0.
questions.teaches: In the maximum depth problem, the root's depth is defined as 1 because the question asks for the number of nodes on the path.

questions.q: A subtree rooted at a node includes which nodes?
options: Only the node and its direct children
The node and all of its descendants
The node and its parent
Every node in the tree
optionExplain: Grandchildren and deeper nodes belong too.
Right: all descendants are included.
Parents are outside the subtree.
That describes the subtree of the root only.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the definition.
questions.rule: A node's subtree is that node plus everything beneath it.

questions.q: True or false: the subtree of a leaf node consists of that leaf alone.
questions.explain: A leaf has no descendants, so only the leaf itself belongs to the subtree.
questions.rule: A leaf is a one-node subtree.

questions.q: Node 1 is the root with children 2 and 3. Node 2 has children 4 and 5; node 3 has a right child 6. The subtree rooted at node 2 has ____ nodes.
questions.explain: Nodes 2, 4 and 5 are in it.
questions.rule: Count the node and its descendants.

questions.q: Using the same tree, the subtree rooted at node 3 has ____ nodes.
questions.explain: Nodes 3 and 6 are in it.
questions.rule: Count the node and its descendants.

questions.q: A learner says the subtree of a node is its parent plus its children. What is wrong?
options: A subtree contains only the node's siblings, which are the nodes at the same level
A subtree contains the whole tree each time, which is why it can reach the parent
A subtree contains only leaves, which are the nodes at the bottom below the chosen node
A subtree contains the node and all descendants, never the parent
optionExplain: Siblings are outside the subtree.
Only the root's subtree is the whole tree.
Subtrees include internal nodes as well as leaves.
Right: it points downward from the chosen node.
questions.explain: A subtree hangs below its root.
questions.rule: A node's subtree is that node plus everything beneath it.

questions.q: What is the subtree rooted at the right child of the root called?
options: The root's parent, which is not a tree, since a parent sits above the root of the tree
The right subtree of the root, and it is itself a binary tree
The right leaf, which is not a tree, since a subtree is only the single node at the end
The inverse tree, a different structure, since the right side is a mirror of the left
optionExplain: The root has no parent.
Right: a subtree is a smaller binary tree.
The right child need not be a leaf.
No such structure appears in the book.
questions.explain: A right subtree is itself a binary tree.
questions.rule: A node's subtree is that node plus everything beneath it.
questions.teaches: The subtree rooted at a node's right child is called the right subtree of that node, and it is itself a binary tree.

questions.q: You cut the link between the CTO and the SVP of engineering. What is the SVP's group now?
options: A broken structure that is no longer a tree
A list ordered by seniority
An empty tree
A valid smaller tree rooted at the SVP
optionExplain: Each node keeps one manager, and the top node needs none.
The shape is still a branching tree.
There are still people in it.
Right: the SVP's group is a tree with its own root.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card shows the cut.
questions.rule: Cut a node from its parent and its subtree is a smaller, valid tree.

questions.q: True or false: every subtree of a binary tree is a binary tree.
questions.explain: Each subtree has one top node, one parent per other node and at most two children per node.
questions.rule: Subtrees are trees.

questions.q: A tree has 12 nodes. The left child of its root starts a subtree of 5 nodes. The right subtree of the root contains ____ nodes.
questions.rule: Total = root + left subtree + right subtree.

questions.q: A function correct for any whole binary tree is called on a node's left child. What does it compute?
options: The answer for the left subtree, as if that subtree were the whole input
The answer for the whole tree again, because the function always starts from the root
The answer for the right subtree, because a left child can also see its sibling's side
The answer for the parent only, because the child call walks back up to the node above
optionExplain: Right: the left child is the root of a smaller tree.
It sees only its own subtree.
The right subtree is not reachable from the left child.
The parent is not reachable by child pointers.
questions.explain: Hand a child's subtree to the same function.
questions.rule: Cut a node from its parent and its subtree is a smaller, valid tree.

questions.q: A learner says: a subtree cut from a bigger tree is not a real tree, since it lost its parent. What is wrong?
options: Every tree must keep a parent for its top node
A tree needs at least two roots
The cut node becomes a root, and a root needs no parent
A cut tree is a list instead
optionExplain: The root of a tree has no parent.
A tree has one root.
Right: a root is the one node with no parent.
Branching children keep it a tree.
questions.explain: A root is allowed to have no parent.
questions.rule: Cut a node from its parent and its subtree is a smaller, valid tree.

questions.q: Why does treating a subtree as its own tree help in solving tree problems?
options: It lets you sort the nodes in linear time, because each subtree can be ordered on its own
It removes the need to visit leaves, because a subtree is described by its root alone
The same logic can be applied to each child, so the problem is solved recursively
It guarantees every tree is balanced, because every subtree has the same shape as the whole
optionExplain: Sorting is not the point.
Leaves still have to be handled; they are the base of the recursion.
Right: this is the basis for recursive solutions.
Shape is not changed by looking at a subtree.
questions.explain: Same problem, smaller tree.
questions.rule: Cut a node from its parent and its subtree is a smaller, valid tree.
questions.teaches: Treating any node as its own tree is the most fundamental idea for solving tree problems, because it allows you to solve them in a recursive manner.

questions.q: Which fields would you expect a binary tree node to hold?
options: A value, a left child and a right child
A value and a next node
A value and a list of all ancestors
A left child and a right child, but no value
optionExplain: Right: data plus two child links.
Next is the list pointer.
Ancestors are not stored.
A node carries data.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card shows the class.
questions.rule: A TreeNode holds val, left and right.

questions.q: In the TreeNode class, the field holding the data is called ____.
questions.explain: The data field is val.
questions.rule: val, left, right.

questions.q: root = TreeNode(5), then root.left = TreeNode(3) and root.right = TreeNode(8). What is root.right.val?
questions.code:
root = TreeNode(5)
root.left = TreeNode(3)
root.right = TreeNode(8)
print(root.right.val)
options: None
optionExplain: 3 is the left child's value.
5 is the root's value.
root.right was assigned, so it is not None.
Right: root.right is the node holding 8.
questions.explain: Read the chain from root to right to val.
questions.rule: A TreeNode holds val, left and right.

questions.q: After root.left.left = TreeNode(1) on the tree above, what does root.left.left.val give?
questions.code:
root = TreeNode(5)
root.left = TreeNode(3)
root.right = TreeNode(8)
root.left.left = TreeNode(1)
print(root.left.left.val)
options: None
optionExplain: 3 is the value of root.left.
Right: the new node holds 1.
5 is the root value.
The new node has a val of 1.
questions.explain: Follow each dot one step down.
questions.rule: A TreeNode holds val, left and right.

questions.q: True or false: after root = TreeNode(5), the line print(root.left.val) prints None.
questions.code:
root = TreeNode(5)
print(root.left.val)
questions.explain: root.left is None, and reading val from None raises an error instead of printing None.
questions.rule: Check for None before reading val.

questions.q: A new TreeNode(4) is created and given no other assignments. What children does it have?
options: None, because both child fields start empty
A left child equal to 4
A right child equal to 4
Two children, each copying its parent
optionExplain: Right: the constructor sets only val.
No child is created automatically.
The same applies to the right field.
Nothing is copied.
questions.explain: A fresh node is a leaf.
questions.rule: A TreeNode holds val, left and right.
questions.teaches: The constructor sets only the node's value, so a newly created node starts with no children.

questions.q: Given the root of a tree, how would you reach the root's left child?
options: root.next
root.parent
root.left
root.first
optionExplain: Next is the list pointer.
Nodes have no parent field.
Right: left is the left child field.
No first field exists.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the fields.
questions.rule: Start at the root and use .left and .right to move down, reading val at each node.

questions.q: The data of the node in a variable node is read with node.____.
questions.explain: val holds the data.
questions.rule: val holds the data.

questions.q: Tree: root 4 has children 2 (left) and 7 (right); 2 has children 1 and 3; 7 has children 6 and 9. What is root.left.right.val?
optionExplain: 1 is root.left.left.
Right: the left child 2 has right child 3.
2 is root.left.
6 is root.right.left.
questions.explain: Follow left, then right.
questions.rule: Start at the root and use .left and .right to move down, reading val at each node.

questions.q: With the same tree, what is root.right.left.val?
optionExplain: 7 is root.right.
9 is root.right.right.
3 is root.left.right.
Right: 7 is the right child and its left child is 6.
questions.explain: Go right, then left.
questions.rule: Start at the root and use .left and .right to move down, reading val at each node.

questions.q: True or false: with only the root of a tree, you can read the value of any node by chaining .left and .right.
questions.explain: Every node lies on a downward path from the root.
questions.rule: Root reaches everything.

questions.q: With the same tree, someone writes root.left.left.left.val. What happens?
options: It gives 1, the value of the deepest node
It fails, because the node with value 1 has no left child
It gives 0, the default value
It gives 4, wrapping around to the root
optionExplain: The node 1 is root.left.left, one step short.
Right: the third .left lands on None, which has no val.
No default value exists.
Chains do not wrap.
questions.explain: A chain stops at empty children.
questions.rule: Start at the root and use .left and .right to move down, reading val at each node.
questions.teaches: A missing child shows up as null, so a chain that steps onto a missing child cannot read a value from it.

questions.q: In code, what does node.left hold when a node has no left child?
options: Zero
The node itself
The parent
null
optionExplain: Zero is a number, not a missing node.
A node does not point to itself here.
Parent pointers do not exist.
Right: an empty child pointer is null.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the convention.
questions.rule: A missing child is null, and a leaf has two null children.

questions.q: True or false: a node is a leaf when both node.left and node.right are null.
questions.explain: No children in either slot means a leaf.
questions.rule: Both null means leaf.

questions.q: Which test finds leaves in code?
questions.code:
def is_leaf(node):
    return node.left is None and node.right is None
options: node.left is None and node.right is None
node.left is None or node.right is None
node.left is not None and node.right is not None
node.val is None
optionExplain: Right: both children must be missing.
Or also accepts a node with one child.
That describes a node with two children.
val is the data, not the children.
questions.explain: Use and, not or.
questions.rule: A missing child is null, and a leaf has two null children.

questions.q: A node has a left child but node.right is null. The call is_leaf(node) returns ____ (True or False).
questions.code:
def is_leaf(node):
    return node.left is None and node.right is None
questions.explain: Both children must be null for a leaf, and the left child exists.
questions.rule: Test both fields.

questions.q: A learner writes: if node.left is None or node.right is None: it is a leaf. What case does this misclassify?
options: The root of a one-node tree
A node with no children
A node with exactly one child
A node with two children
optionExplain: A single node has two null children and passes correctly.
A node with no children is a true leaf.
Right: one child is present, so it is not a leaf.
Two children fail the or, so they are classed non-leaf correctly.
questions.explain: Or accepts too much.
questions.rule: A missing child is null, and a leaf has two null children.

questions.q: In a linked list the tail's next is null. Which tree node plays a similar role?
options: The root, whose parent is null
The node with the largest val
A leaf, whose children are null
Any node with a null left
optionExplain: The root has no parent field in code.
Values do not decide structure.
Right: both are the end of the structure.
One null child does not end a branch.
questions.explain: A leaf has both children null, like a list tail whose next is null. The book also notes that a problem gives you only the root, and you reach the rest with root.left and root.right.
questions.rule: A missing child is null, and a leaf has two null children.
questions.teaches: In a binary tree problem you are given only a reference to the root; the left subtree is root.left and the right subtree is root.right.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Which traversal style does the book say is the usual one for binary trees?
options: Recursive, calling the function on the children
Iterative, using one while loop and a next pointer
Sorting the nodes first, then scanning the sorted nodes
Hashing the nodes, then reading them back
optionExplain: Right: trees are usually traversed recursively.
A single next pointer is the list traversal.
Sorting is not a traversal and is not used.
Hashing does not move through the tree.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card contrasts lists with trees.
questions.rule: To traverse a tree, start at the root and follow .left and .right, usually with recursion.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: a tree traversal starts at the root and moves with the child pointers .left and .right.
questions.explain: The root plays the role of the head, and child pointers play the role of next.
questions.rule: Root first, then children.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: To move from a tree node to its right child, use node.____.
questions.explain: The right child is stored in node.right.
questions.rule: Move with .left and .right.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A linked list holds 3, 5, 2. What does the list traversal sum code return?
optionExplain: That leaves out one value.
That is only the middle value.
That is only the first value.
questions.explain: Add each value as the head moves along.
questions.rule: To traverse a tree, start at the root and follow .left and .right, usually with recursion.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Match each structure with how it is moved through.
pairs: Start at root, follow left and right
Start at its own top node
questions.explain: A list needs one pointer to move; a tree uses the two child pointers, and any subtree starts from its own top node.
questions.rule: Start at the top, follow the pointers.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the list traversal, when is a node visited?
options: When the node's value is the largest
When the head variable refers to that node
When the node has no next pointer
When the loop is finished
optionExplain: Values do not decide a visit.
Right: each node has a moment where the variable references it.
Only the last node has no next.
The loop ends after all visits.
questions.explain: A visit is a moment when a variable points at the node.
questions.rule: To traverse a tree, start at the root and follow .left and .right, usually with recursion.
questions.teaches: For each node there is a moment in the code's execution where the variable (such as head) is referencing that node; that moment is the visit.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: How many ways to perform DFS on a binary tree does the book name?
options: Three: preorder, inorder and postorder
Two: left-first and right-first
One: the recursive form
Four: one for each level of the tree
optionExplain: Right: three DFS forms.
Left and right priority is a different split.
Recursive and iterative are ways to code it.
Levels relate to BFS.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names them.
questions.rule: Traversals are DFS or BFS, and DFS on a binary tree comes in preorder, inorder and postorder forms.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The other main type of tree traversal, besides depth-first search, is ____-first search.
questions.explain: Breadth-first search is the other main type.
questions.rule: DFS and BFS.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Sort each traversal name into its family.

items.t: preorder
inorder
postorder
breadth-first
level-first
random

questions.explain: Preorder, inorder and postorder are the three DFS forms. Breadth-first is the other family.
questions.rule: Three DFS forms, one BFS.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A problem only requires visiting every node of a binary tree once. Which DFS form should you choose?
options: Only preorder, since the others skip nodes
Only postorder, since it ends at the root
Any of the three, since the choice rarely matters here
Only inorder, since it needs a stack
optionExplain: Preorder does not visit more nodes than the others.
The root is last in postorder, which is not an advantage here.
Right: all three visit the same nodes.
Inorder does not require a different stack.
questions.explain: If every node is visited, order may not matter.
questions.rule: Traversals are DFS or BFS, and DFS on a binary tree comes in preorder, inorder and postorder forms.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: preorder, inorder and postorder DFS visit different sets of nodes.
questions.explain: All three visit every node. Only the order of the visits differs.
questions.rule: Same nodes, different order.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A teammate worries about memorising three DFS types. What does the book say?
options: Always use postorder, since it is the standard
Do not worry; the type you choose rarely matters
Memorise inorder only, since the others are rare
Ignore DFS and use BFS for every tree problem
optionExplain: No type is declared the standard.
Right: the choice rarely matters.
No single form is singled out.
BFS is not recommended for every problem.
questions.explain: The book says not to worry.
questions.rule: Traversals are DFS or BFS, and DFS on a binary tree comes in preorder, inorder and postorder forms.
questions.teaches: The book says not to worry about the three DFS types because the type you choose rarely matters.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In a left-priority DFS, which part of the tree is explored completely first?
options: The right subtree of the root
The nodes at depth 1 only
Whichever subtree holds more nodes
The left subtree of the root
optionExplain: The right subtree comes later.
Depth 1 only would be a level-by-level search.
Size of subtrees plays no role.
Right: it goes left until that subtree is exhausted.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card says what DFS prioritises.
questions.rule: DFS follows one direction to the bottom before trying the other direction.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: DFS prioritises ____, going as far down as it can before moving sideways.
questions.explain: Depth is prioritised.
questions.rule: Depth first.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Node 1 has children 2 and 3, and node 2 has children 4 and 5. Order the nodes as a left-priority DFS first reaches them.
questions.explain: From 1 it goes left to 2, then left to 4, back to 5, and only then to 3.
questions.rule: Finish the left side first.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Using the same tree, a right-priority DFS reaches the nodes in which order?
optionExplain: That is level order, not DFS.
Right: it goes right to 3, then returns to 2 and takes 5 before 4.
Inside the left subtree the right child 5 should come first.
The root is still visited first.
questions.explain: Mirror the left-priority order.
questions.rule: DFS follows one direction to the bottom before trying the other direction.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A reader says: DFS visits every node at depth 1 before any node at depth 2. What is wrong?
options: That describes preorder DFS exactly
That is correct for DFS on any tree
That describes DFS only on a list
That describes breadth-first search, not DFS
optionExplain: Preorder still dives down before moving across.
DFS dives first.
The statement is about trees, and not lists.
Right: DFS goes down a branch first.
questions.explain: Breadth first is level by level.
questions.rule: DFS follows one direction to the bottom before trying the other direction.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: On a large tree, how do the depths of nodes in the order a DFS visits them tend to start?
options: Increasing steadily, like 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Repeating a level, like 0, 1, 1, 2, 2
Staying at 0 until every node is seen
Falling from the leaves up, like 5, 4, 3
optionExplain: Right: DFS keeps going deeper first.
Level repeats describe BFS.
Depth changes as DFS moves.
A preorder walk begins at the root, not the leaves.
questions.explain: Depth climbs as DFS dives.
questions.rule: DFS follows one direction to the bottom before trying the other direction.
questions.teaches: On a large tree a DFS visits nodes whose depths look like 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, whereas a breadth-first search shows depths like 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: What does DFS do when it reaches a leaf?
options: It stops the whole search
It restarts from the root
It backtracks up until it finds an unexplored branch
It jumps to the deepest unexplored leaf
optionExplain: Other branches still need visiting.
Restarting would repeat work.
Right: it backs up to the nearest branch not yet explored.
It searches nearby first, not the deepest.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card describes the backtracking.
questions.rule: DFS dives down a branch, then backtracks to the nearest unexplored branch, remembered by a stack.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: DFS is typically implemented with recursion, whose call stack remembers the way back up.
questions.explain: The call stack holds the pending calls to return to.
questions.rule: Recursion supplies the stack.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A tree has root 1 with children 2 and 3. Node 2 has one child, 4. After DFS finishes node 4, where does it go next?
options: Straight to 3 without returning to 2
Back to 4 again
Back to 2, then to the unexplored branch at 3
To the root's parent
optionExplain: It must return through 2 to reach 3.
Node 4 is finished.
Right: it backs up from 4 to 2, which has no other child, then to 1 and 3.
The root has no parent.
questions.explain: Backtrack until a branch is unexplored.
questions.rule: DFS dives down a branch, then backtracks to the nearest unexplored branch, remembered by a stack.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A DFS reaches a leaf at depth 4 and then backs up. It first returns to depth ____.
questions.explain: A leaf's parent is one level up.
questions.rule: Backtracking goes up one step at a time.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A learner says DFS needs no stack because it only moves down. What is wrong?
options: It must come back up after each dead end, and a stack remembers where
It needs a queue to remember which nodes come next
It needs a stack only on lists
It remembers nothing and revisits from the root
optionExplain: Right: the stack holds the way back up.
A queue belongs to breadth-first search.
Lists do not need backtracking.
Restarting from the root would waste work.
questions.explain: No stack, no way back.
questions.rule: DFS dives down a branch, then backtracks to the nearest unexplored branch, remembered by a stack.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Which implementation does the book say is the typical one for DFS?
options: A queue, though recursion is also used
Sorting the tree, then scanning
A hash set, with no other structure
Recursion, though iterative DFS with a stack is also used
optionExplain: Queues belong to breadth-first search.
Sorting plays no role.
A set records visited nodes but does not move through the tree.
Right: recursion is typical, iteration with a stack is the alternative.
questions.explain: DFS must back up after reaching the end of a branch. Recursion does that with the call stack, a stack under the hood, so the iterative form uses an explicit stack.
questions.rule: DFS dives down a branch, then backtracks to the nearest unexplored branch, remembered by a stack.
questions.teaches: Recursion uses a stack under the hood, which is why an iterative DFS uses an explicit stack to do the same backing up.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In a recursive DFS on a tree, what should happen when the function receives an empty node?
options: It calls itself on the same empty node
It returns immediately
It raises an error
It restarts from the root
optionExplain: That would never stop.
Right: an empty node is the base case.
An empty child is expected at every leaf.
Restarting would loop forever.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the base case.
questions.rule: A recursive DFS stops at an empty node and calls itself on the left and right child.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the recursive DFS, the function returns at once when the node is ____.
questions.explain: The base case is an empty node.
questions.rule: Check for an empty node first.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The recursive DFS runs on a tree with 5 real nodes, 2 and 3 being children of the root and 4 and 5 children of 2. Counting calls on empty nodes too, dfs is called ____ times in total.
questions.explain: Each of the 5 nodes gets a call, and there are 6 empty child slots, giving 5 + 6 = 11.
questions.rule: Calls = nodes + empty children.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: dfs runs on a tree with root 1 and children 2 (left) and 3 (right). Which call happens right after dfs(1)?
options: dfs(2)
dfs(3)
dfs(None) for the root's parent
dfs(1) again
optionExplain: Right: the left child is called first.
The right child is called after the left subtree.
The root has no parent call.
The root is only called once.
questions.explain: Left first.
questions.rule: A recursive DFS stops at an empty node and calls itself on the left and right child.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: dropping the None check from dfs is harmless, since leaves have no children to call.
questions.explain: A leaf still has left and right fields, which are None. The calls on them would read fields of None and fail.
questions.rule: Keep the base case.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A tree has n real nodes. What is true about the calls on empty children?
options: Empty children are skipped before the call, since the parent checks them and does not call
Only leaves call empty children, since a node with a child has no empty child to call
Each real node calls both children, and the empty ones hit the base case
Empty children make the function run forever, since there is no node left to stop at
optionExplain: The call is made first; the check is inside the call.
Every node calls both children, not only leaves.
Right: both calls are made, and missing children return at once.
The base case ends the recursion.
questions.explain: Every real node makes two calls.
questions.rule: A recursive DFS stops at an empty node and calls itself on the left and right child.
questions.teaches: A leaf has no children, so both of its calls hit the base case immediately and return.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In a recursive tree function, which step usually comes first?
options: Recurse on the children
Handle the base case, usually an empty tree
Return the final answer
Do logic for the root only
optionExplain: Recursion without a base case never ends.
Right: the base case is checked before any work.
Returning comes last.
Logic is done for every node, not only the root.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the four steps.
questions.rule: Base case, logic, recursion on children, return: the shape of nearly every tree DFS.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the four-step template, the base case is usually an ____ tree, where the node is null.
questions.explain: An empty tree is the usual base case.
questions.rule: Base case first.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A function must count the nodes of a tree. In the template, which step holds the +1 for the current node?
options: Step 1, the base case
Step 3, the calls on the children
Step 4, the return only
Step 2, the logic for the current node
optionExplain: The base case returns 0 for an empty tree.
The children calls count their own subtrees.
The return carries the combined result.
Right: the current node's own contribution is its logic.
questions.explain: Count the node itself in step 2.
questions.rule: Base case, logic, recursion on children, return: the shape of nearly every tree DFS.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A problem needs the logic to run after both child calls come back. How does the template change?
options: Step 1 moves to the end, so the base case is checked after the recursive calls come back
Steps 2 and 3 swap, so the logic runs after the recursion
Step 4 moves to the start, so the return happens before the child calls are made at all
The template cannot do this, since the logic always has to run before the recursive calls
optionExplain: The base case stays at the start; without it the calls would never end.
Right: the order of steps 2 and 3 may differ.
Returning first would skip the work.
The book says the order of steps 2 and 3 may swap.
questions.explain: Only steps 2 and 3 swap.
questions.rule: Base case, logic, recursion on children, return: the shape of nearly every tree DFS.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: the base case check can safely come after the recursive calls on the children.
questions.explain: The calls on an empty node would run before the check and fail, so the base case belongs first.
questions.rule: Step 1 comes first.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Which parts of the template change from one tree problem to another?
options: The base case being an empty tree
Whether the function calls itself
The number of children visited
The logic at the current node and the value returned
optionExplain: The empty tree is the usual base case.
Recursion is the usual tool.
A binary tree has two children.
Right: the rest of the structure stays the same.
questions.explain: The logic and the return value vary.
questions.rule: Base case, logic, recursion on children, return: the shape of nearly every tree DFS.
questions.teaches: The structure for performing a DFS is very similar across all problems; steps 2 and 3 may happen in different orders.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A function node_count(node) is meant to count nodes. What does node_count(root.left) return?
options: The number of nodes in the left subtree
The number of nodes in the whole tree
The number of leaves in the tree
The depth of the left child
optionExplain: Right: a call answers for the subtree at its argument.
The call sees only its own subtree.
It counts nodes, not leaves.
It returns a count, not a depth.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the contract.
questions.rule: A call on a node returns the answer for the subtree rooted at that node.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: each recursive call solves the problem as if the subtree rooted at the current node were the whole input.
questions.explain: That is the central rule for tree recursion.
questions.rule: A call answers for its subtree.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: node_count(root.left) returns 4 and node_count(root.right) returns 2. Then node_count(root) returns ____.
questions.explain: Add both subtrees and the root itself: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7.
questions.rule: Combine children answers with the node's own logic.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A function max_val(node) returns the largest value in a subtree. Its children return 9 and 3, and the node holds 5. What does it return?
optionExplain: 17 adds values instead of taking the maximum.
5 ignores the larger children values.
Right: the maximum of 9, 3 and 5.
3 is the smaller child's answer.
questions.explain: Combine according to the question asked.
questions.rule: A call on a node returns the answer for the subtree rooted at that node.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A learner writes a function whose call on a child returns the answer for the whole tree. Why does the recursion break?
options: The child call is allowed to know the parent, so it is fine to answer for the whole tree
The function would never reach a leaf, since each child call restarts from the root
The child call must answer for its own subtree, or the combined result is wrong
The answer would be correct but slow, since the whole tree is counted again at each call
optionExplain: The contract forbids that: a call sees only its own subtree.
Leaves are still reached.
Right: mixing scopes gives wrong totals.
It breaks correctness, not only speed.
questions.explain: Keep each call about its own subtree.
questions.rule: A call on a node returns the answer for the subtree rooted at that node.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Why can you trust a recursive call on a child without tracing it?
options: The function is meant to be correct for any subtree, so the call returns the right answer
The call is guaranteed to be fast, because a subtree is always much smaller than the whole tree
The child is always a leaf, so the call only has to check a single value and can return at once
The call returns the parent's answer, so the child's result can be reused as the parent's own
optionExplain: Right: if the function is correct on any tree, it is correct on a child.
Trust concerns correctness, not speed.
Children are not always leaves; a child can root a large subtree.
A child's call returns the answer for its own subtree, not the parent's.
questions.explain: Trust the recursion; do not trace it all.
questions.rule: A call on a node returns the answer for the subtree rooted at that node.
questions.teaches: You do not need to worry about the cascading calls: you know that making the call will give you the answer you need.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: While DFS is at a leaf at depth 3, how many calls to dfs are waiting on the call stack from the root down to it?
options: 1, since only the leaf is active
3, one for each level below the root
The number of nodes in the whole tree
4, one for each node on the path from the root
optionExplain: The parents' calls are still pending.
The root's call is pending too, so four.
Only the nodes on the path are pending.
Right: root, depth 1, depth 2 and the leaf make four.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card says many calls coexist.
questions.rule: Each pending call has its own node and variables, which is why recursion on a tree works.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: each DFS call has its own version of the node variable.
questions.explain: Each call stores its own variables.
questions.rule: Own call, own variables.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: DFS is paused at a node of depth 5. Counting the call for this node, ____ calls are pending on the call stack.
questions.explain: The root at depth 0 up to depth 5 makes 6 calls.
questions.rule: Pending calls = depth + 1.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: DFS has reached a leaf, and its call returns. What happens to the parent's variables?
options: They are overwritten by the leaf's variables, since the leaf returns last and writes its own
They are still intact, because the parent's call has its own copy
They are deleted with the leaf, since the leaf and its parent share one stored frame
They are shared with the leaf's variables, since a call uses the variables of the caller
optionExplain: Each call has separate variables.
Right: calls do not overwrite each other's variables.
The parent's call is still running.
Sharing would break the recursion.
questions.explain: Own copy per call.
questions.rule: Each pending call has its own node and variables, which is why recursion on a tree works.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A learner says: the node variable holds one value during the entire DFS. What is wrong?
options: Each call has its own node, so many different nodes are held at once
The node variable changes only at leaves, so above the leaves it keeps its first value
The node variable is global to the program, so every call reads the same shared value
The node variable is identical in every call, so there is only one node being held
optionExplain: Right: every pending call refers to a different node.
It differs in every call, not only at leaves.
It is local to each call, not global.
The values differ by call.
questions.explain: Many calls, many nodes.
questions.rule: Each pending call has its own node and variables, which is why recursion on a tree works.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A recursive maximum-depth function stores the results of its child calls in local variables left and right. A leaf sits at depth 3. How many versions of left exist while the leaf's call runs?
options: 1, because the variable is shared by all calls
3, because the leaf's own call has none
4, one in the call of each node on the path from the root
2, one for each child of the leaf
optionExplain: Each call keeps its own copy.
The leaf's call has its own left too, so it counts.
Right: root, depth 1, depth 2 and the leaf each hold one.
Children are counted by calls, not by sibling count.
questions.explain: One copy per pending call.
questions.rule: Each pending call has its own node and variables, which is why recursion on a tree works.
questions.teaches: In the book's maximum depth example, when the recursion reaches the node labeled 6, there are 4 different values of left existing simultaneously.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In a preorder traversal, when is the current node's value printed?
options: After both child calls return
Before the calls on its children
Between the left and right calls
Only when the node is a leaf
optionExplain: That is postorder.
Right: pre means before the children.
That is inorder.
Preorder prints every node, not only leaves.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the position of the logic.
questions.rule: Preorder handles the node, then the left subtree, then the right subtree.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In preorder, the node is handled ____ its children.
questions.explain: Pre means before the children are visited.
questions.rule: Pre: before children.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In which order does preorder print the nodes of the tree with root 5, left child 3 and right child 8, where 3 has children 1 and 4?
questions.explain: Preorder: 5, then the whole left subtree (3, 1, 4), then 8.
questions.rule: Node, left subtree, right subtree.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Preorder runs on the tree with root 5, left child 3 and right child 8, where 3 has children 1 and 4 and 8 has a right child 9. Which node prints last?
optionExplain: 8 is printed before its child 9.
4 ends the left subtree, not the tree.
5 is first in preorder.
Right: the sequence is 5, 3, 1, 4, 8, 9.
questions.explain: Write out the whole sequence.
questions.rule: Preorder handles the node, then the left subtree, then the right subtree.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: this function prints the leaves of a subtree before its root, so it is a preorder traversal.
questions.explain: Printing after the child calls is postorder. Preorder prints the node before its children.
questions.rule: Pre means print first.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In preorder, how does the order in which nodes are handled compare with the order in which the function calls happen?
options: They are reversed, since the work waits until the calls return
They are the same, since the work is done right at the start of each call
They differ only for leaves
They are unrelated, since recursion reorders them
optionExplain: Work done at the end of a call would be reversed, but preorder works at the start.
Right: each node is handled the moment its call begins.
Leaves follow the same rule.
The sequences line up.
questions.explain: Preorder does its work at the start of each call, so handling order equals call order. On the book's example tree this prints 0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 2, 5.
questions.rule: Preorder handles the node, then the left subtree, then the right subtree.
questions.teaches: On the book's example tree, preorder prints the nodes in the order 0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 2, 5.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In inorder traversal, the current node's value is printed at which moment?
options: Before either child is called, so that the value appears ahead of both subtrees
After both children are called, so that the value appears behind both subtrees
Only for the left child, since the right child is handled by a different traversal
Between the call on the left child and the call on the right child
optionExplain: That is preorder.
That is postorder.
Inorder prints every node.
Right: in means in the middle.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card places the logic.
questions.rule: Inorder handles the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Inorder handles the left subtree, then the node, then the ____ subtree.
questions.explain: Right comes last.
questions.rule: Left, node, right.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In which order does inorder print the nodes of the tree with root 5, left child 3 and right child 8, where 3 has children 1 and 4 and 8 has a right child 9?
questions.explain: Left subtree first (1, 3, 4), then 5, then the right subtree (8, 9).
questions.rule: Left, node, right at every node.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Inorder runs on the tree with root 7, left child 2 and right child 6; 2 has a right child 4; 6 has children 5 and 9. Which node prints first?
optionExplain: Right: 2 has no left child, so it is the first node reached with nothing left to print.
7 waits for its whole left subtree.
4 waits for node 2 to print.
5 belongs to the right subtree.
questions.explain: Go left until you cannot.
questions.rule: Inorder handles the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A learner says that inorder prints the root of the whole tree first. What is wrong?
options: The root prints last, after the right subtree
The root prints first only on trees with two nodes
The root prints only after its entire left subtree has been printed
The root is skipped in inorder
optionExplain: That is postorder.
No such special case exists.
Right: the left subtree comes first.
Inorder visits all nodes.
questions.explain: Left subtree before node.
questions.rule: Inorder handles the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In inorder, which node's logic runs before all the others?
options: The root, because it starts the traversal
The first leaf on the right side
The first node reached that has no left child
The node with the smallest value
optionExplain: The root waits for its left subtree.
The right side comes last.
Right: no logic runs until a node without a left child is reached.
Values do not decide the order in a plain tree.
questions.explain: Dive left until you cannot go further.
questions.rule: Inorder handles the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.
questions.teaches: No logic is done in an inorder traversal until we reach a node without a left child, since calling on the left child takes priority over performing logic.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In postorder traversal, when is the current node's value printed?
options: After the calls on both children
Before the calls on the children
Between the two child calls
Only for nodes with a right child
optionExplain: Right: post means after the children.
That is preorder.
That is inorder.
Postorder prints every node.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

Left stays before right.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Two functions use the same two recursive calls (left, then right). What can differ between them?

Only where the line handling the current node sits relative to the calls

Call counts are equal.

questions.rule: Pre, in and post say whether the node's work comes before, between or after its child calls.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A function prints node.val first and then calls on the left and right children. On a root with children 2 and 3, what prints first?

The root, as this is preorder

questions.rule: Pre, in and post say whether the node's work comes before, between or after its child calls.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

questions.teaches: An inorder DFS that goes left before right on a BST handles the nodes in sorted order.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: For a single node tree holding 4, what do the three traversals output?

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Write the preorder of this tree: root 1 with children 2 and 3; 2 has a left child 4; 3 has children 5 and 6.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

questions.explain: Left subtree, right subtree, then the node.
questions.rule: Left, right, node.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: 4, 2, 1, 5, 3, 6 is the postorder of that tree.
