questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the inorder list of any binary tree, what do you know about the root's position?
options: Every node of the left subtree comes before it, and every node of the right subtree after it
It is always first, because a node is handled before the subtrees that hang below it in the tree
It is always last, because a node is handled only after all of the nodes beneath it are done
It is always in the exact middle of the list, because the two subtrees are split evenly around it
optionExplain: Right: the root sits between the two subtree lists.
That describes preorder, not inorder.
That describes postorder, not inorder.
The middle only occurs when both subtrees have equal size.

questions.rule: Write the node in front of, between or behind its left and right subtree lists.
questions.teaches: In inorder, a node's value is not printed until all values in its left subtree have been printed, and values in its right subtree are not printed until after it.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: in many tree problems it does not matter whether you use preorder, inorder or postorder DFS.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: With recursion, switching between the DFS types is ____ because only the position of the logic changes.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A problem asks you to count how many nodes have an even value. Which DFS form is needed?

questions.rule: Pick any DFS order that fits the logic; for visit-everything problems the order does not matter.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Which problem is the most sensitive to the order in which nodes are visited?

Add up every value in the tree, since a sum depends on which values are added first
Print the values so that a node always appears after both of its children
Check whether any node holds the value 7, since the search must meet the nodes in a fixed order
optionExplain: Counts do not depend on order.
Sums do not depend on order.

questions.rule: Pick any DFS order that fits the logic; for visit-everything problems the order does not matter.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: to total every value in a tree you must choose the right one of the three DFS orders very carefully.

questions.rule: Do not over-invest in the order.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: What does the book say the differences between the three DFS types are mostly good for?
options: Trivia, such as answering an interviewer's question about them
Deciding every tree problem's time complexity
Choosing between stacks and queues
Making recursion unnecessary
optionExplain: Right: knowing the differences is mostly good for trivia.
Complexity is the same for the three.
Stack versus queue separates DFS from BFS.
All three still use recursion or a stack.

questions.rule: Pick any DFS order that fits the logic; for visit-everything problems the order does not matter.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

questions.explain: An empty tree has no nodes on any path.
questions.rule: Base case: 0.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A tree has root 3 with children 9 and 20, and 20 has children 15 and 7. The maximum depth, counted in nodes, is ____.

questions.rule: Add 1 for each level on the deeper side.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Our reading: a student replaces max with min in the formula to get the shortest root-to-leaf path. For a root with only a right child that is a leaf, what does 1 + min(left, right) give?

1, which is wrong because the empty side hides the real path
0, because the empty side wins
It crashes on the empty side

The result is 1, not 0.
The empty side returns 0, not an error.
questions.explain: An empty side is not a path.
questions.rule: maxDepth(node) = 1 + max(maxDepth(left), maxDepth(right)), and 0 for an empty tree.
questions.hint: Think about what the empty side returns.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: a version that returns max(left, right) without adding 1 gives 0 for a chain of 3 nodes.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

Adding would overflow the integer type, so the sum is avoided for the sake of safety
The sum would count the node itself twice, so the answer would be too big by exactly one

Sides are generally unequal.

The node's own +1 is added once either way; the real problem is counting both sides.

questions.teaches: The + 1 performed at each node propagates upward from the leaves, so each ancestor adds one to its deeper child's value.

questions.q: What does the maximum depth recursion return for a leaf?

questions.rule: Empty children return 0.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

Right: each level adds 1 to the returned depth below.
Values would not grow without adding.
The order is reversed.

questions.rule: A leaf returns 1, and each ancestor returns one more than its deeper child.

questions.q: True or false: the 1 added at each node is passed down from the root to the leaves.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Which direction does the value carry in this recursion?
options: Down: each node passes its depth to its children
Sideways: siblings exchange depths
Nowhere: the answer is stored in a global
Up: each node uses the results of its children and adds 1

Siblings are independent.
The answer is returned by the calls.
Right: the +1 propagates upward from the leaves.
questions.explain: Answers climb back up the call stack.
questions.rule: A leaf returns 1, and each ancestor returns one more than its deeper child.
questions.teaches: The +1 performed at each node propagates upwards from the leaves.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the recursive maximum depth solution, when does a node compute its own answer?
options: Before any child is called
After its children's calls return
Between the two child calls, always
Only when the node is the root
optionExplain: It cannot know the child depths yet.
Right: it needs both child depths first.
It needs both before computing.
Every node computes its own.

questions.rule: When a node needs its children's answers first, its logic runs after the child calls: postorder.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The maximum depth solution is a ____order traversal.
questions.explain: Its logic comes after the child calls.
questions.rule: Logic after calls is postorder.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A function returns the number of nodes in a subtree as 1 + count(left) + count(right). Which DFS form is it?
options: Preorder, since the node is counted first
Inorder, since the node sits between the sums
Level order, since each level is counted

The expression has no step between the calls.

questions.rule: When a node needs its children's answers first, its logic runs after the child calls: postorder.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A function needs only to print the depth of each node on the way down, where depth is passed as an argument. Which form fits?

Postorder, since the children must report back before the node can print its depth
Inorder, since both children must be seen before a middle print can show the depth
None of them, since recursion cannot pass an argument such as depth down to a child
optionExplain: Right: the data arrives from above, so no waiting is needed.
Nothing needs to come from the children, so no waiting is needed.
A middle print is not needed; the depth is already known on arrival.
Arguments can be passed in recursion.

questions.rule: When a node needs its children's answers first, its logic runs after the child calls: postorder.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: because the recursive maximum depth solution returns after the calls, it is a preorder traversal.

questions.rule: After the calls means postorder.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

options: Postorder is very easy; the others are complicated
All three are equally complicated
Preorder is very easy; inorder and postorder are more complicated
None of them can be done iteratively
optionExplain: Postorder is among the harder ones.
The book rates preorder as easy.
Right: preorder is the easy one.
All three can be done with a stack.
questions.explain: Iterative preorder is the simple case.
questions.rule: When a node needs its children's answers first, its logic runs after the child calls: postorder.
questions.teaches: All three types of DFS can be implemented iteratively, but postorder and inorder are more complicated to implement than preorder, which is very easy.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Which structure replaces the call stack in an iterative DFS?

Sorting plays no role.

A set does not give an order of visits.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

questions.explain: Children are one deeper: depth + 1.
questions.rule: Children get depth + 1.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The iterative code runs on a chain of 4 nodes. It returns ____.
questions.explain: The deepest popped entry has depth 4, counted in nodes.
questions.rule: Take the largest depth seen.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The stack in the iterative code is changed into a queue that serves the oldest entry first. What traversal results?
options: A breadth-first one, level by level
Still depth-first, only mirrored
A traversal that visits nodes twice
No traversal; the loop never ends
optionExplain: Right: a queue gives level order.
Mirroring comes from the push order, not from the container.
Each node is still pushed once.
The loop ends when the container is empty.

questions.rule: Iterative DFS: push (node, depth), pop one, update the answer, push its children.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

Use recursion instead, as stacks cannot hold two values
Skip the depth and recompute it from the root each time

A stack can hold pairs.
Recomputing from the root is wasteful.

questions.rule: Iterative DFS: push (node, depth), pop one, update the answer, push its children.
questions.teaches: An iterative DFS is much less common than a recursive one and should be used only if an interviewer asks for it.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In an iterative DFS, what does a single pass of the while loop correspond to?
options: The whole traversal
One recursive call, handling one node
One level of the tree
Only the leaf nodes
optionExplain: The loop repeats until all nodes are done.
Right: one iteration equals one call.
Levels belong to breadth-first search.
Every node is handled, not only leaves.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card maps loops to calls.
questions.rule: In iterative DFS, popping a node is the same as entering a call, and pushing children is the same as calling on them.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: the loop in iterative DFS runs until the stack is empty.
questions.explain: No entries left means every pushed node has been handled.
questions.rule: Loop until the stack is empty.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A tree has 6 nodes. The iterative DFS loop body runs ____ times.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: An iterative DFS has the stack [A] at the start of a pass, and A has children B and C. Which entries are on the stack after the pass?
options: B and C, because A was popped and its children pushed
A, B and C, because the node stays on the stack while its children are pushed above it
Only A, because the node is pushed back on the stack until both children are finished
Only the leaf nodes, because internal nodes are never kept on the stack between the passes

A has been popped at the start of the pass, so it is no longer there.
The stack changes each pass: A leaves and its children enter.
B and C may be internal nodes; the stack holds whatever is pushed.
questions.explain: Pop one, push its children.
questions.rule: In iterative DFS, popping a node is the same as entering a call, and pushing children is the same as calling on them.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A loop pops a node and returns the answer from the first pass, to match the recursive version's return. What goes wrong?
options: It visits the nodes twice, because the first pass handles a node and the return handles it again
It never terminates, because nothing removes nodes from the stack once the loop has begun
It stops after one node, while the recursive version collects results across all calls
It works unchanged on any problem, because a return inside a loop behaves like a return from a call
optionExplain: Each node is still handled at most once; the trouble is that the loop ends too soon.
It stops after the first pass, so termination is not the problem.
Right: the loop must keep going until the stack is empty.
Returning early skips most nodes, so it does not work unchanged.
questions.explain: Return after the loop, not inside it, unless an answer is found.
questions.rule: In iterative DFS, popping a node is the same as entering a call, and pushing children is the same as calling on them.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the path sum problem, the iterative version keeps a running sum for each node. Where is it kept?
options: In a global that all passes update
On the stack, paired with the node
In a queue next to the stack
Nowhere; it is recomputed from the root
optionExplain: A single global would mix paths.
Right: the stack entry carries the sum.
No queue is used.
The sum is stored, not recomputed.
questions.explain: State that a call would carry travels on the stack.
questions.rule: In iterative DFS, popping a node is the same as entering a call, and pushing children is the same as calling on them.
questions.teaches: The format for performing the traversal with the stack can be reused between problems: a stack, a while loop until it is empty, and all of the function's logic done inside the loop.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: An iterative DFS pushes the left child and then the right child. Which child is popped first?
options: The left child
Whichever has the smaller value

questions.rule: Trees p and q are the same when p.val equals q.val and both pairs of subtrees are the same.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Two trees are the same if the roots hold equal values, the left subtrees are the same and the right subtrees are the ____.
questions.explain: Both pairs of subtrees must be the same.
questions.rule: Roots, left, right.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Tree A is root 1 with left child 2 and right child 3. Tree B is root 1 with left child 3 and right child 2. Are they the same?
options: Yes, since both hold 1, 2 and 3
No, since the left subtrees hold different values
Yes, since the roots match
No, since the roots differ
optionExplain: Position matters.
Right: matching positions must agree.
Matching roots are only one of three conditions.
The roots both hold 1.
questions.explain: Compare position by position.
questions.rule: Trees p and q are the same when p.val equals q.val and both pairs of subtrees are the same.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Tree A is root 1 with only a left child 2. Tree B is root 1 with only a right child 2. Are they the same?
options: No, since the shapes differ: one has a left child, the other a right child
Yes, since both trees have the same two values, and the order of the nodes does not matter
Yes, since the roots match, and a matching root means that the rest of the trees will match too
No, since the values differ between the trees, as the child sits in a different position
optionExplain: Right: the left subtrees differ (one is empty).
Shape counts as well as values.
Roots are not enough; the subtrees must match as well.
The values are the same; it is the shape that differs.
questions.explain: Structure must be identical.
questions.rule: Trees p and q are the same when p.val equals q.val and both pairs of subtrees are the same.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: to test whether two trees are the same, it is enough to check that they contain the same values.
questions.explain: Equal values in different positions give different trees.
questions.rule: Match position and value.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Why can the function itself be used to check the two pairs of subtrees?
options: Subtrees are always identical, so the same function can be applied to either pair
The function ignores the subtrees, so only the two root values are ever compared in the end
The subtrees are binary trees, so the same function answers the question for them
Subtrees are checked by sorting their values, so the function is applied to the sorted lists
optionExplain: They are identical only when the trees are, which is what is being tested.
They are checked, not ignored; that is what the recursive calls do.
Right: a subtree is a tree of its own.
No sorting is used; the shape of the subtrees matters as well.
questions.explain: A smaller instance of the same question.
questions.rule: Trees p and q are the same when p.val equals q.val and both pairs of subtrees are the same.
questions.teaches: Because the function being implemented tells whether two trees are the same, it can be used to answer the conditions on the left and right subtrees.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Two empty trees are compared. What should the function return?
options: False, since there is nothing to compare
True, since two empty trees are the same
None
It depends on the values
optionExplain: There is nothing different between them.
Right: empty equals empty.
A boolean is expected.
No values exist.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives both-null.
questions.rule: Both null is true; one null is false; otherwise compare values and recurse.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: If exactly one of the two nodes is null, the function returns ____ (True or False).
questions.explain: One empty and one real tree differ.
questions.rule: One null: false.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Two one-node trees both hold 7. What does the check return, and why?
options: False: a one-node tree has no children to compare
True: but only because the roots are leaves
False: single nodes cannot be compared
True: the values match and both pairs of children are empty
optionExplain: Empty pairs return true.
The reason is the same either way, yet the check relies on the base case.
Single nodes can be compared.
Right: the two child calls hit both-null and return true.
questions.explain: Walk through a one-node case.
questions.rule: Both null is true; one null is false; otherwise compare values and recurse.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The check meets p as a node holding 2 and q as null. What does it return, without reading further?
options: True
False
It compares p.val with q.val
It raises an error
optionExplain: The trees differ.
Right: exactly one null means different trees.
q has no val to read.
The guard returns before reading.
questions.explain: One null returns false.
questions.rule: Both null is true; one null is false; otherwise compare values and recurse.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: placing the one-null check first, without the both-null check, still returns True for two empty trees.
questions.explain: With only the either-null check, two empty trees would return False, so both-null must come first.
questions.rule: Both null first.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Why is thinking about a one-node tree a good way to test a base case?
options: It guarantees the code is fast, since a tiny case shows how many calls the recursion makes
It avoids recursion, since a single node can be compared without calling the function again
It proves the code for all sizes, since every larger tree is built from one-node trees
Its children are empty, so it exercises the base case directly
optionExplain: Speed is a different matter.
Recursion still happens on the two empty children.
A test case is not a proof.
Right: a small case reveals the base logic.
questions.explain: Test the smallest case first.
questions.rule: Both null is true; one null is false; otherwise compare values and recurse.
questions.teaches: A good way to think about base cases is to think about a tree with only one node.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The left subtrees are the same, but the right subtrees differ. What does the recursion return for the whole trees?
options: False
True
It depends on the roots
It returns the left answer
optionExplain: Right: all conditions must hold.
One failed pair is enough to fail.
Equal roots do not rescue it.
The right answer is also needed.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the operator.
questions.rule: Same trees need every pair to match, so combine the results with and.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The recursion combines the answers for the two subtree pairs with ____.
questions.explain: Both pairs must be the same.
questions.rule: Every pair: and.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The left pair returns true and the right pair returns true, and the root values are equal. What does the call return?
options: False
Only the left answer
True
It depends on the depth
optionExplain: Nothing has failed.
Both sides matter.
Right: all three conditions hold.
Depth plays no role.
questions.explain: true and true = true.
questions.rule: Same trees need every pair to match, so combine the results with and.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The iterative version pops a pair where one node is null and the other is not. What does it do?
options: Skips the pair
Pushes the children anyway
Returns false at once
Returns true
optionExplain: Only a both-null pair is skipped.
A null has no children.
Right: a structural mismatch ends the search.
A mismatch means the trees differ.
questions.explain: Early false on any mismatch.
questions.rule: Same trees need every pair to match, so combine the results with and.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: if a learner uses or instead of and for the two child answers, the code accepts only trees that are completely identical.
questions.explain: With or, one matching pair of subtrees is enough, so trees that differ on the other side would be accepted.
questions.rule: Or accepts partial matches.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the iterative same-tree code, a popped pair where both nodes are null is handled how?
options: It is skipped with continue, and the loop moves on
It returns true immediately, since a pair of empty nodes means the two trees match
It returns false immediately, since an empty pair means a node is missing from both
It is pushed back on the stack, since its children still have to be paired and checked
optionExplain: Right: an empty pair adds nothing to check.
Other pairs may still differ, so it cannot return yet.
That would reject equal trees.
That would loop forever.
questions.explain: Both null is fine; keep going.
questions.rule: Same trees need every pair to match, so combine the results with and.
questions.teaches: In the iterative version, a pair where both nodes are null is skipped with continue, a false is returned the moment any condition is broken, and true is returned only after the loop finishes.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In a tree, p is in the left subtree of a node and q is in its right subtree. Which is the lowest common ancestor?
options: The root of the whole tree, whatever it is
The parent of that node
The deepest leaf
That node, the point where the two subtrees connect
optionExplain: A lower node already has both, unless this is the root.
The parent is higher.
Leaves have no descendants.
Right: it is the lowest node with both as descendants.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives three cases.
questions.rule: The LCA is the first node where p and q split, or a node that is p or q itself.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the LCA definition, a node counts as a descendant of ____.
questions.explain: So if p is an ancestor of q, the LCA is p.
questions.rule: A node is its own descendant.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the tree 3 (children 5, 1), 5 has children 6 and 2, and 2 has children 7 and 4, what is the LCA of 6 and 4?
optionExplain: 3 is a common ancestor, but 5 is lower.
Right: 6 is in 5's left side, and 4 is in 5's right side, so 5 is the split point.
2 does not contain 6.
6 does not contain 4.
questions.explain: Find where the two paths split.
questions.rule: The LCA is the first node where p and q split, or a node that is p or q itself.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the same tree, what is the LCA of 5 and 4?
options: 5, since 5 is itself an ancestor of 4
3, the root
2, the parent of 4
optionExplain: Right: case 1, the node is p or q.
3 is higher than 5, which already has both.
2 does not contain 5.
4 does not contain 5.
questions.explain: A node is its own descendant.
questions.rule: The LCA is the first node where p and q split, or a node that is p or q itself.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: if the current node is p, the answer might be found in a subtree below it.
questions.explain: Anything below the node would lack the node itself as a descendant, so the answer cannot be lower.
questions.rule: Case 1: stop at p or q.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: p and q both lie in the left subtree of the current node. What follows?
options: The current node is the answer, since it is an ancestor of both p and q and sits on the path
The answer is in the right subtree, since the left one was already searched and nothing was found
The current node is not the answer, since a lower node in the left subtree already has both
No answer exists, since both nodes sit on one side and no node splits them between two sides
optionExplain: It is a common ancestor, but a lower common ancestor exists inside the left subtree.
The right subtree holds neither p nor q, so it cannot hold the answer.
Right: look inside the left subtree.
The LCA always exists when both nodes are in the tree; here it lies in the left subtree.
questions.explain: When both nodes are in one subtree, the answer lies lower, inside that subtree. The book adds that an iterative solution is significantly more difficult and cumbersome.
questions.rule: The LCA is the first node where p and q split, or a node that is p or q itself.
questions.teaches: An iterative solution of the LCA problem exists but is significantly more difficult and cumbersome than the recursive one.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the recursive LCA function, a call returns non-null for a subtree only when...
options: That subtree is a leaf
That subtree contains p or q
That subtree has more than one node
That subtree has the larger values
optionExplain: Leaves can hold neither target.
Right: non-null signals a target is inside.
Size is irrelevant.
Values are irrelevant.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card defines the return.
questions.rule: Each call returns null if p and q are absent from its subtree; two non-null child results make this node the LCA.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: For an empty tree the LCA function returns ____.
questions.explain: An empty tree contains neither p nor q.
questions.rule: Empty: null.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: At a node the left call returns a node and the right call returns null. What does the node return?
options: The node itself
Null
The right result
The left result
optionExplain: Only two non-null results make the node the answer.
That would lose the found result.
The right result is null.
Right: both targets (or the answer) are in the left subtree.
questions.explain: Pass a single non-null result upward.
questions.rule: Each call returns null if p and q are absent from its subtree; two non-null child results make this node the LCA.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: At a node the left call returns a node and the right call returns a node. What does the node return?
options: The left result, since the left call came first and so its node is the answer found
The node itself, as the connection point
The right result, since the right call came last and so its node is the answer found
Null, since two non-null results cancel out and no single node can be returned
optionExplain: That would ignore the right target.
Right: p and q are on different sides.
That would ignore the left target.
That would lose the answer.
questions.explain: Two non-null results: this node.
questions.rule: Each call returns null if p and q are absent from its subtree; two non-null child results make this node the LCA.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: after a node is found equal to p, the function should still search its subtrees for q.
questions.explain: If p is the node, the answer is at least as high as p (and is p when q is below it), so p can be returned without searching below.
questions.rule: Return at once on a match.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The LCA function runs on a tree of n nodes. What are its time and the stack space?
options: O(log n) time, since it searches one side
O(n squared) time, since it checks pairs
O(1) space, since it keeps no data
O(n) time, with up to O(n) space for the call stack
optionExplain: It may visit both subtrees.
No pair checking is done.
The call stack grows with the height.
Right: each node is visited at most once.
questions.explain: Each node is visited at most once with constant work, giving O(n) time, and the call stack can reach O(n) space. The book keeps this problem as a bonus because it is a classic.
questions.rule: Each call returns null if p and q are absent from its subtree; two non-null child results make this node the LCA.
questions.teaches: The LCA problem was going to be removed from the course as significantly more difficult, and is kept only as a bonus because it is a classic.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In a region of the tree with neither p nor q, what do the two child calls of a node return?
options: Null from both
The node itself from both
Null from one and a node from the other
An error
optionExplain: Right: neither target is below.
Nodes are returned only when a target is found.
A target must be below for that to occur.
Empty results are normal.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card describes this region.
questions.rule: If both child results are null, the node returns null, meaning neither target lies below.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: True or false: when both child calls return null, the node returns null.
questions.explain: That is the value that means neither target is below.
questions.rule: Null from both: null.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A subtree contains neither p nor q. Its call returns ____.
questions.explain: Null signals that no target is inside.
questions.rule: No targets: null.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A node has left null. Which statement about its right call is correct?
options: It must be non-null, because the right subtree is where both of the targets have to be
It must be null, because a null left side means the answer was already found
It may be null or non-null, depending on whether a target lies in the right subtree
It must be the node itself, because one empty side leaves the node as the answer

A null left call says nothing about the right side: a target may still be there.
Right: both being null is possible.
Nothing forces the node itself; the node is returned only when both calls are non-null or it is p or q.
questions.explain: Left null does not decide the right.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: The video claims that if the left call is null, the right call is not null. What does the book say about that?
options: It is correct for every node, so the code can rely on the right call being non-null
It is wrong, so the code fails on any tree where both calls come back null together
It is a small mistake, because both can be null, yet the code still works
It only applies to leaves, so the code is wrong only for nodes without any children
optionExplain: Both may be null in a part of the tree with neither p nor q.
The code does not depend on the claim; it returns null in that case.
Right: the implementation returns null in that case, which is the desired result.
It is not specific to leaves.
questions.explain: The code holds even though the remark is loose.
questions.rule: If both child results are null, the node returns null, meaning neither target lies below.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A node is reached whose subtree holds neither p nor q, so the final line returns right, which is null. Why is that fine?
options: Null is the agreed signal that neither target is in this subtree
Null means the node is the answer, since a node with no targets below it ends the search
Null is ignored by the parent, since the parent only looks at the non-null child values
The parent will search again, since a null result sends the same call back down this side
optionExplain: Right: the signal matches the definition.
The answer is non-null; null means nothing was found.
The parent reads null as absence, and that is how it tells the cases apart.
No second search happens.
questions.explain: Null keeps one meaning: neither target is below. The book also defines the LCA so that a node is a descendant of itself, so a node equal to p or q is returned straight away.
questions.rule: If both child results are null, the node returns null, meaning neither target lies below.
questions.teaches: The LCA definition counts a node as a descendant of itself, which is why the code can return a node at once when it is p or q.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the path sum problem, the running sum travels in which direction?
options: Up, as a return value
Sideways between siblings
It is not stored anywhere
Down, as an argument to each call
optionExplain: The booleans travel up.
Siblings do not talk.
It is stored in the argument.
Right: curr is passed from parent to child.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names both directions.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Match each tree problem with what is passed down as an argument.
pairs: Sum of the path so far
The matching node of the other tree
questions.explain: Each problem needs different context from above. Maximum depth needs none.
questions.rule: Ask what the node must know from its ancestors.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In maximum depth, which direction does information travel?
options: Down: each node passes the depth to its child
Up: each node returns a depth that its parent uses
Sideways: siblings compare their depths
Neither direction
optionExplain: The recursion needs no depth argument.
Right: the depth is built from the leaves upward.
Siblings are combined by the parent.
The return value flows upward.

questions.rule: Pass context down in arguments and report results up in return values.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: Sort each item by how it travels in a tree recursion.

items.t: Sum of the path so far
Maximum value so far
Count of good nodes below
Whether a path was found
Depth of a subtree

questions.rule: Down for context, up for results.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: A problem asks for the number of nodes whose value exceeds their parent's value. What must each call know from above?
options: The parent's value
The sum of the whole tree
The number of leaves
Nothing
optionExplain: Right: the comparison needs the parent's value, passed down.
No total is needed.
Leaf counts do not help.
The comparison needs a value from above.
questions.explain: Decide what the node must know.
questions.rule: Pass context down in arguments and report results up in return values.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS
questions.q: In the good nodes problem, what is each call's return value and what is its extra argument?
options: It returns the maximum, and takes the count as the argument
It returns a boolean, and takes the node count
It returns a count of good nodes, and takes the maximum so far as the argument
It returns nothing, and takes both
optionExplain: The roles are swapped.
A boolean is not the result.
Right: the count flows up, the maximum flows down.
A count is returned.
questions.explain: Down: context. Up: result.
questions.rule: Pass context down in arguments and report results up in return values.
questions.teaches: In the good nodes problem, dfs(node, maxSoFar) returns the number of good nodes in the subtree rooted at node, given the greatest value seen so far on the path.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A BFS reaches the root's children. Which nodes does it visit next?
options: The left child's whole subtree
All the nodes at depth 2, before any at depth 3
The leftmost leaf of the tree
The nodes with the largest values
optionExplain: That would be depth-first behaviour.
Right: it finishes a level before going deeper.
Reaching a leaf early also describes depth-first.
Values do not decide the order.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the order.
questions.rule: BFS visits every node at depth d before any node at depth d + 1.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: BFS visits all nodes at depth d before any node at depth ____.
questions.explain: It moves one level down at a time.
questions.rule: Finish a level, then go one deeper.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: Order in which BFS visits the nodes of the tree with root 1, children 2 and 3, and 2 has a left child 4 while 3 has children 5 and 6 (left to right in each level).
questions.explain: Level 0 is 1, level 1 is 2 and 3, and level 2 is 4, 5 and 6.
questions.rule: Level by level.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: In the perfect tree with root 1, children 2 and 3, and leaves 4, 5, 6, 7, which node is third, in BFS and in left-first preorder DFS?
options: BFS reaches 4 third; preorder reaches 3 third
Both reach 3 third
Both reach 4 third
BFS reaches 3 third; preorder reaches 4 third
optionExplain: The orders are the other way round.
Preorder dives into the left subtree.
BFS finishes level 1 first.
Right: BFS is 1, 2, 3, ...; preorder is 1, 2, 4, ...
questions.explain: Write both sequences.
questions.rule: BFS visits every node at depth d before any node at depth d + 1.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: True or false: a BFS on a large tree visits nodes whose depths look like 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, going straight down.
questions.explain: That pattern belongs to DFS. A BFS repeats each depth for all its nodes before moving on.
questions.rule: BFS repeats a depth; DFS climbs depths.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: In a complete binary tree, the first two levels are full, and the last level has two nodes placed under the left child. Is it complete, and why?
options: No: a complete tree must have all levels full including the last, so this tree has a gap
Yes: every level but the last is full, and the last level's nodes are as far left as possible
No: the last level must have nodes under the right child, since that is where a gap is closed
Yes: any tree with two full levels is complete, whatever the third level looks like at all
optionExplain: Only the last level may be partly filled.
Right: the last level may be partial if packed to the left.
The packing runs to the left, not the right.
Two full levels are not enough; the last level must be packed left.
questions.explain: Complete means packed left in the last level.
questions.rule: BFS visits every node at depth d before any node at depth d + 1.
questions.teaches: A complete binary tree is one where every level except possibly the last is full, and all the nodes in the last level are as far left as possible.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: Which data structure is used to implement BFS?
options: A stack
A sorted array
A binary search tree
A queue
optionExplain: A stack gives depth-first order.
Sorting does not give level order.
A search tree is the thing being traversed.
Right: BFS serves nodes first in, first out.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the structure.
questions.rule: BFS is iterative and uses a queue; DFS is recursive or uses a stack.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: Match each traversal with the structure behind it.
questions.explain: Depth-first work goes back up like a stack; breadth-first work goes in arrival order like a queue.
questions.rule: Stack for DFS, queue for BFS.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A BFS processes node A, then adds A's children B and C. Another node D was already waiting before them. Which is served next?
options: D, because it was added before B and C
B, since it is A's first child
C, since it was added last
Whichever has the smaller value
optionExplain: Right: a queue serves the oldest entry first.
B is behind D.
The most recent entry waits longest.
Values do not decide the order.
questions.explain: Oldest first.
questions.rule: BFS is iterative and uses a queue; DFS is recursive or uses a stack.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: Nodes are removed from the left end of the queue and added at the right end. After all nodes of one level are removed, what does the queue hold?
options: All the nodes of the same level
Only the leaves
All the nodes of the next level
Nothing
optionExplain: Those nodes have been removed.
Internal nodes are included.
Right: the children were added behind the level being processed.
The children were added, so it is not empty.
questions.explain: Removing from one end and adding to the other keeps levels apart.
questions.rule: BFS is iterative and uses a queue; DFS is recursive or uses a stack.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: True or false: the book recommends a recursive BFS because it is simpler than the iterative one.
questions.explain: A recursive BFS is possible but much more difficult, with no benefit, so the book uses iterative code.
questions.rule: BFS is iterative.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: JavaScript has no built-in efficient queue. What does the book suggest for BFS there?

Give up BFS in JavaScript

A workaround exists.

questions.rule: BFS is iterative and uses a queue; DFS is recursive or uses a stack.
questions.teaches: For JavaScript users, since there is no built-in efficient queue, BFS can use a second array nextQueue as a workaround.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: In the BFS loop, why is the queue size stored before the inner for loop?

So leaves are counted twice, since a stored size makes each leaf appear in two levels

The root is handled in the first pass.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS

questions.explain: The snapshot covers the current level.
questions.rule: Queue = current level.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS

items: Run the logic for the current level
Remove a node from the front
Add its children to the back

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: BFS runs on the tree with root 1, children 2 and 3, and 2 has a child 4. What are the queue sizes recorded at the start of each pass?

The second level has two nodes.
The first pass holds the root alone.
Right: the levels hold 1, 2 and 1 nodes.
questions.explain: Count nodes per level.
questions.rule: Snapshot the queue size, process exactly that many nodes, and queue their children.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A learner reads len(queue) inside the for loop condition on every iteration instead of storing it first. What goes wrong?

Children are added, so the queue does not stay empty.
The loop would run past the level, so the result differs.
questions.explain: Snapshot before the loop.
questions.rule: Snapshot the queue size, process exactly that many nodes, and queue their children.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A problem only needs every node visited and does not care about levels. How can the template change?
options: Drop the for loop and loop while the queue is not empty
Switch to a stack, since a stack visits every node without any need for levels
Add a second queue, so one holds the visited nodes while the other holds the rest
Run it twice, so the first run visits the nodes and the second one checks them
optionExplain: Right: the per-level loop is only for level logic.
A stack would change the traversal into a DFS.
One queue is enough.
Once is enough; each node is visited once.
questions.explain: Use the for loop only when levels matter.
questions.rule: Snapshot the queue size, process exactly that many nodes, and queue their children.
questions.teaches: When we do not care about levels as a whole, as in the shortest-path BFS, we do not need the for loop, only the while loop on a queue.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: At the start of the first while iteration of a tree BFS, what does the queue hold?

The root's children
Only the root
Every node

The children are added during the pass.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: True or false: nodes are removed from one end of the queue and added to the opposite end.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A level has 5 nodes and each has 2 children. After the for loop finishes, the queue holds ____ nodes.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS

questions.rule: Each pass leaves the queue holding exactly the next level.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A learner adds children to the front of the queue while removing from the front. What breaks?

The queue no longer keeps the current level apart, and the traversal turns depth-first

No sorting occurs; the queue behaves like a stack.

questions.rule: Each pass leaves the queue holding exactly the next level.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: Which kinds of problems benefit from having a whole level in the queue at the top of the loop?
options: Those that sort a tree, because a level is a group of nodes that are already in sorted order
Those that handle nodes by level, such as the rightmost node per level
Those that count leaves only, because the leaves all sit together at the bottom level
Those that never visit the root, because the first level is handled before the loop runs
optionExplain: Sorting is not a level question.
Right: level-based questions fit.
Leaves can be counted with any traversal, and they need not share a level.
Every traversal begins at the root.
questions.explain: Think level by level.
questions.rule: Each pass leaves the queue holding exactly the next level.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A problem wants the largest value on each level of a tree. Which traversal fits best?
options: DFS, since recursion is shorter
Inorder DFS, since it gives sorted output
Neither; trees have no levels
BFS, since it handles one level at a time
optionExplain: Shorter code does not fit levels.
Inorder is sorted only for search trees.
Trees have levels by depth.
Right: level-based problems suit BFS.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card ties BFS to levels.
questions.rule: Use DFS for plain visits because it is shorter; use BFS when the problem is about levels.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: For a problem that only needs every node visited, most people choose ____ because it needs less code.
questions.explain: DFS is shorter, especially with recursion, and the order is irrelevant here.
questions.rule: Visit-all: DFS for brevity.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: You must sum every value in a tree. Which choice does the book's reasoning favour?
options: DFS, since the order does not matter and it needs less code
BFS, since it handles the nodes level by level and so every value is added exactly once
BFS, since DFS is slower, because it has to climb back up the tree after each branch
Neither works for sums, since a sum needs the nodes to be visited in sorted order

No levels are involved in a plain sum.
Both have the same time complexity.
Both can sum; a sum does not depend on the order.
questions.explain: Take the shorter code when order is irrelevant.
questions.rule: Use DFS for plain visits because it is shorter; use BFS when the problem is about levels.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: Which problem needs BFS rather than DFS?
options: Count the nodes in the tree, since a count needs the nodes to be grouped by level
Find the maximum value, since the largest value tends to sit at the deepest level
Return the values of the nodes at each depth as separate lists
Check whether a value is present, since a presence check needs to go through the levels in order
optionExplain: A count ignores order.
A maximum ignores order.
Right: the answer is organised by level.
A presence check ignores order.

questions.rule: Use DFS for plain visits because it is shorter; use BFS when the problem is about levels.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: True or false: because BFS visits nodes in a different order from DFS, it can miss some nodes.
questions.explain: Both traversals visit every node. They differ only in the order of visits.
questions.rule: Same nodes, different order.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: How rare does the book say it is for DFS to be better than BFS in binary tree problems?
options: Common, with DFS using less time since it does not have to scan every level in order
Common, with DFS visiting fewer nodes because it can stop before reaching the deepest level
Very rare, with DFS chosen mainly because it is quicker to write
Impossible, since BFS always wins because it reaches every node in the fewest steps
optionExplain: Time is the same for both.
Both visit all nodes when everything must be seen.
Right: the preference is about convenience, not power.
The book says DFS is usually quicker to implement, so people still choose it.
questions.explain: DFS is rarely better on capability, but it takes less code. The book also says BFS written recursively is much harder with no benefit, so BFS is taught iteratively.
questions.rule: Use DFS for plain visits because it is shorter; use BFS when the problem is about levels.
questions.teaches: BFS can be written with recursion, but that is a lot more difficult without any benefit, so the course shows only iterative BFS.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A huge tree holds the sought value in the root's right child. A left-first DFS searches for it. What happens?
options: It explores the whole left subtree first, wasting a lot of work
It finds the value at once, since DFS checks the nodes closest to the root before others
It skips the left subtree, since DFS can tell from the root which side holds the value

optionExplain: Right: left-first DFS finishes the left side before the right.
The value is on the other side, so the left-first search does not reach it at once.
DFS has no shortcut for skipping a side.
DFS starts at the root.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A left-first DFS searching for a value stored in the root's right child explores the whole ____ subtree first.

questions.rule: DFS can waste time on the wrong side.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: The target is a leaf at the very bottom of a very tall tree. Which traversal tends to spend more effort on the shallow levels?

DFS, because it uses a queue
BFS, which checks every level above before reaching the bottom

DFS uses a stack.

questions.rule: DFS can waste time exploring a deep wrong branch; BFS can waste time on shallow levels when the target is deep.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: The sought node is one step below the root, on the side DFS visits last. Which drawback is this?
options: The BFS drawback: it needs a queue

No drawback; both are equally fast

BFS explores levels from the top.

questions.rule: DFS can waste time exploring a deep wrong branch; BFS can waste time on shallow levels when the target is deep.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: Which statement fits the book about choosing between BFS and DFS for finding a value?
options: The better choice depends on whether the target tends to be near the root or deep
Always choose BFS, because it checks every level in order and so finds a value after the least work
Always choose DFS, because it dives straight to the leaves where a value is most likely to be
Choose by tree height only, because a taller tree always favours the traversal that goes deeper

DFS wastes work on a huge subtree when the target is one step from the root.

questions.rule: DFS can waste time exploring a deep wrong branch; BFS can waste time on shallow levels when the target is deep.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS

questions.rule: DFS space follows the height; BFS space follows the widest level, so either can win.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A queue's remove-from-front takes O(n) time. What happens to the BFS time?

It falls to O(1), since the removal is the only operation that takes any time at all
It becomes O(log n), since a slow removal still halves the queue on every step
It grows beyond O(n), since each removal is costly

Visiting n nodes cannot be constant.

questions.rule: With an O(1) queue, BFS visits each node once for O(n) total, like DFS.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: True or false: BFS is slower than DFS by a factor of the tree's height, because it checks each level.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS
questions.q: A BFS must sort the values of each level, costing k log k for a level of k nodes. What is the effect on the total time?

It leaves the total at O(n) exactly
It makes the traversal O(1)
It removes the need for the queue

Visiting n nodes cannot be constant.

questions.rule: With an O(1) queue, BFS visits each node once for O(n) total, like DFS.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.3 Binary trees - BFS

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Root 10 has left child 5 and right child 15; 5 has children 2 and 7; 15 has children 12 and 20. Is it a BST?
options: No, since 7 is greater than 5, and a left subtree may not hold a value greater than its parent
Yes, since every node is greater than its left subtree and smaller than its right
No, since 12 is smaller than 15, and a right-hand part of the tree may not hold smaller values
No, since a BST needs two levels only, and this tree has three levels of nodes below the root
optionExplain: 7 sits in the right subtree of 5, where greater is correct.
Right: all values respect their ancestors.
12 is in the left subtree of 15, where smaller is correct.
BSTs can have any number of levels.
questions.explain: Check each node against its subtrees.
questions.rule: In a BST every left-subtree value is smaller and every right-subtree value is larger than the node.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Root 10 has left child 5 and right child 15; 5 has children 2 and 12. Is this a BST?
options: Yes, since 12 is greater than its parent 5, and a right child only has to beat its parent
Yes, since 12 is smaller than 15, and the right-hand node 15 is the one that bounds it
No, since 2 is smaller than 5, and a left child may not be smaller than its own parent
No, since 12 lies in the left subtree of 10 but is greater than 10
optionExplain: The parent comparison is fine, but the ancestor comparison fails.
15 is not an ancestor of 12.
2 is correctly placed as a left child of 5.
Right: the ancestor 10 bounds the whole left subtree.
questions.explain: Compare with every ancestor.
questions.rule: In a BST every left-subtree value is smaller and every right-subtree value is larger than the node.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: a tree is a BST whenever each node is greater than its left child and smaller than its right child.
questions.explain: The rule covers the whole subtree. A deeper node can break an ancestor's bound.
questions.rule: Check whole subtrees, not only children.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A BST holds the numbers 1 to 7. Which node can be the root?
options: Only 4, the middle one, because a BST must be balanced with equal parts on both sides of the root
Any of them, provided the subtrees split the rest accordingly
Only 1, the smallest, because the root of a BST must be smaller than everything beneath it
Only 7, the largest, because the root of a BST must be larger than everything beneath it
optionExplain: The tree need not be balanced.
Right: the root only needs smaller values on its left and larger on its right.
A BST puts larger values to the right of the root, and root 1 is allowed, but it is not the only choice.
Root 7 is allowed, with every other value in its left subtree, but it is not the only choice.
questions.explain: The root can be any value, with subtrees to match.
questions.rule: In a BST every left-subtree value is smaller and every right-subtree value is larger than the node.
questions.teaches: The BST property holds at any given node, so all subtrees of a BST are themselves BSTs.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Can a BST built under the book's property hold the value 5 twice?
options: Yes, on the left side
Yes, on the right side
Yes, as two children of the same node
No, since neither side permits an equal value
optionExplain: Left requires strictly less.
Right requires strictly greater.
Both children sit on strict sides.
Right: left must be less and right must be greater.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card applies the property.
questions.rule: Strict less-than and greater-than mean a BST holds no duplicates.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: The BST property implies that the values in a BST must be ____.
questions.explain: Strict inequalities leave no place for a repeat.
questions.rule: No duplicates.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A tree holds the values 8, 3, 8, 1. Could it be a BST?
options: No, since 8 appears twice
Yes, as long as the second 8 is on the right
Yes, as long as the second 8 is on the left
Yes, as long as the 8s are leaves
optionExplain: Right: duplicates break the property.
Equal values are not greater.
Equal values are not less.
Leaves still need strict order.
questions.explain: Look for repeats.
questions.rule: Strict less-than and greater-than mean a BST holds no duplicates.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Root 5 has a right child 5. What does the BST check say about this tree?
options: It is a BST, since 5 is not less than 5, and so the right child respects the root
It is a BST, since a root can repeat, and the equal value is allowed on either side
It is not a BST, since the right child is not greater than the root
It is a BST, since both nodes are leaves, and a tree of leaves cannot break the rule
optionExplain: The rule demands greater, not not-less.
Roots follow the same rule as other nodes.
Right: equal is not greater.
The right child is a leaf, but the rule still fails.
questions.explain: Strict means strict.
questions.rule: Strict less-than and greater-than mean a BST holds no duplicates.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: a BST may contain two nodes with the same value as long as they are in different subtrees.
questions.explain: Under this property every value must be unique, wherever it sits.
questions.rule: Unique values.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A system stores student IDs in a BST. Two students share an ID. What does the property suggest?
options: Nothing; the BST places both IDs on the left, because an equal value counts as smaller
Nothing; the BST places both IDs on the right, because an equal value counts as larger
The structure needs a different rule for ties, since this BST requires unique values
Nothing; the BST stores one ID and drops the other silently, because it keeps the first
optionExplain: Left does not allow an equal value; left means strictly smaller.
Right does not allow an equal value; right means strictly greater.
Right: ties are outside this property.
Dropping data silently is not part of the property.
questions.explain: The property needs unique values, so ties need another rule. The book adds that with unique ordered values a BST supports search, add and remove in O(log n) on average.
questions.rule: Strict less-than and greater-than mean a BST holds no duplicates.
questions.teaches: In a BST, searching, adding and removing take O(log n) time on average, using something called binary search.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Searching a BST for the value 20, you are at a node holding 23. Which subtree can you ignore?
options: The right subtree, since all its values exceed 23
The left subtree, since all its values are below 23
Neither; both may hold 20
The whole tree, since 23 is not 20
optionExplain: Right: 20 is smaller than 23, so it can only be on the left.
The left subtree is where 20 must be.
The property rules out one side.
The tree is not exhausted.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the rule.
questions.rule: At each node, compare the target and go left if it is smaller, right if it is larger.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: In a BST search, if the target is smaller than the current node, move to the ____ child.
questions.explain: Smaller values live on the left.
questions.rule: Smaller: go left.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Order the nodes visited when searching for 12 in the tree with root 10, children 5 and 15, where 5 has children 2 and 7 and 15 has children 12 and 20.
questions.explain: 12 is greater than 10 so go right to 15, then 12 is smaller than 15 so go left to 12.
questions.rule: Compare, then pick a side.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Using the same tree, how many nodes does a search for 8 visit before giving up?
options: 3: nodes 10, 5 and 7
optionExplain: It continues until a null.
It goes past 5.
It does not visit the whole tree.
Right: 8 < 10 go left, 8 > 5 go right to 7, 8 > 7 and 7 has no right child.
questions.explain: Follow the comparisons to a missing child.
questions.rule: At each node, compare the target and go left if it is smaller, right if it is larger.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: after finding the target is greater than the current node, the search should still check the left subtree in case of duplicates.
questions.explain: Under the BST property the left subtree holds only smaller values, and values are unique.
questions.rule: Discard the wrong side.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A BST has no right children at all: each node has only a left child. A search for its smallest value visits about how many of its n nodes?
options: About log n of them, since each step discards a side
All n of them, since the tree is a straight line like a linked list
About n over 2, since half are skipped
Exactly 1, since the smallest is near the root
optionExplain: Halving needs both sides to be used.
Right: with a line, nothing is discarded.
Nothing is skipped on a line.
The smallest is at the end of the line.
questions.explain: A line has no side to discard.
questions.rule: At each node, compare the target and go left if it is smaller, right if it is larger.
questions.teaches: In the worst case, such as a tree with no right children that is a straight line (basically a linked list), the search time is O(n).

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: What is the average time to search a BST with n nodes?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n squared)
optionExplain: Right: each step discards a side.
That is the worst case.
Constant time is not possible for a large tree.
Nothing is quadratic.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives both cases.
questions.rule: BST operations cost the tree's height: O(log n) on average and O(n) for a lopsided line.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: In the worst case, a BST that is a straight line takes O(____) time to search.
questions.explain: A line of n nodes needs up to n steps.
questions.rule: Worst case: n.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are inserted in increasing order into an empty BST. What shape results, and what is a worst-case search?
options: A balanced tree, with 2 or 3 steps
A straight line to the left, with up to 5 steps
A straight line to the right, with up to 5 steps
A star, with 1 step
optionExplain: Increasing insertion does not balance the tree.
Larger values go to the right.
Right: each new value goes right of the last.
Each node has at most two children.
questions.explain: Sorted insertion builds a line.
questions.rule: BST operations cost the tree's height: O(log n) on average and O(n) for a lopsided line.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A BST holds n nodes in a straight line. How does a search compare with a linked list search?
options: It is faster: log n steps
It is the same: up to n steps
It is slower: n squared steps
It is instant: 1 step
optionExplain: The speed-up needs balance.
Right: the line behaves like a linked list.
Nothing here is quadratic.
Constant time would need a direct hit on the root.
questions.explain: A line is a linked list.
questions.rule: BST operations cost the tree's height: O(log n) on average and O(n) for a lopsided line.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: because a BST discards a side at each step, searching it takes O(log n) on every BST.
questions.explain: The halving holds only for balanced shapes. A line-shaped BST needs O(n).
questions.rule: O(log n) is an average.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Which named technique does the book say a BST's average O(log n) operations rely on?
options: Breadth-first search, covered in the previous article
Hashing, covered in an earlier chapter
Sorting, covered in the arrays chapter
Binary search, which has a chapter of its own later in the course
optionExplain: BFS visits level by level and does not discard sides.
Hashing uses a different structure.
Sorting is not the technique at work.
Right: discarding one side at each step is binary search.
questions.explain: BST operations follow a binary search.
questions.rule: BST operations cost the tree's height: O(log n) on average and O(n) for a lopsided line.
questions.teaches: Searching, adding and removing in a BST rely on binary search, which is the focus of an upcoming chapter.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: An inorder DFS runs on a BST. In what order are the values handled?
options: Largest to smallest
Sorted, from smallest to largest
Root first, then level by level
In the order they were inserted
optionExplain: That would need right before left.
Right: left, node, right yields ascending order.
That is breadth-first order.
Insertion order is not stored.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the property.
questions.rule: Inorder on a BST visits the values from smallest to largest.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: To get ascending order from a BST, use an ____order traversal.
questions.explain: Inorder gives ascending order.
questions.rule: Inorder = sorted.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: List the values of the BST with root 10, children 5 and 15, where 5 has children 2 and 7 and 15 has a left child 12, in inorder.
questions.explain: Inorder visits the left subtree (2, 5, 7), then 10, then the right subtree (12, 15).
questions.rule: Left, node, right.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A BST has the inorder sequence 3, 8, 12, 20. What is the smallest value, and where is it in the tree?
options: 20, the leftmost node, because inorder lists the nodes from the largest value down to the smallest
3, the root, because the smallest value of a BST always sits at the very top of the tree
12, the leftmost node, because the middle of the inorder list is where the left spine ends
3, the leftmost node (it may not be a leaf if it has a right child)
optionExplain: 20 is the largest, and inorder lists values from smallest to largest.
The root is not necessarily the smallest.
12 is not the smallest value in the sequence.
Right: the first value in inorder is the end of the left spine.
questions.explain: First in inorder is smallest.
questions.rule: Inorder on a BST visits the values from smallest to largest.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: an inorder traversal of any binary tree produces its values in sorted order.
questions.explain: Only a BST has that property. In a general tree the order depends on how values were placed.
questions.rule: Sorted order needs the BST property.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A tree's inorder output is 4, 9, 6, 12. What do you conclude?
options: It is not a BST, since a BST's inorder output is sorted
It is a BST, since inorder is always unsorted
It is a BST, since 4 is smaller than 12
Nothing; inorder says nothing about BSTs
optionExplain: Right: 9 before 6 breaks the order.
BST output is sorted.
The ends are in order, but not the middle.
Inorder reveals this property.
questions.explain: A non-sorted inorder rules out a BST.
questions.rule: Inorder on a BST visits the values from smallest to largest.
questions.teaches: An inorder DFS traversal prioritising left before right on a BST will handle the nodes in sorted order, which is trivia worth knowing.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: While summing values in the range [7, 15] on a BST, you reach a node holding 5. Which subtree can you skip?
options: The right subtree, since it holds larger values
Neither; both may hold values in range
The left subtree, since all its values are below 5
The node itself
optionExplain: The right side may reach into the range.
The BST property rules out the left.

The node's own value is checked separately.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the pruning rule.
questions.rule: Visit the left side only if low is less than the node, and the right side only if the node is less than high.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: The left subtree is visited only if low is ____ than the current value.
questions.explain: Otherwise everything on the left is below the range.
questions.rule: low < val: go left.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: BST with root 10, children 5 and 15, then 3 and 7 under 5, and 18 under 15. The sum of values in [7, 15] is ____.
questions.explain: The values 7, 10 and 15 sum to 32.
questions.rule: Add the in-range nodes.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: For the same tree and the range [7, 15], which nodes does the pruned code skip entirely?
options: Node 7, since it is the lowest in range
Node 15, since it is the highest in range
Node 3, since 5 is below low and its left side cannot be in range
Nodes 10 and 15, since they lie on the boundary
optionExplain: 7 is in range.
15 is in range.
Right: at node 5, low is not less than 5, so its left child is skipped.
Both are inside the range.
questions.explain: Pruning skips the wrong side.
questions.rule: Visit the left side only if low is less than the node, and the right side only if the node is less than high.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: the pruning rules would be valid on any binary tree, not only on a BST.
questions.explain: They rely on the BST property that the left subtree is smaller and the right is larger.
questions.rule: Pruning needs the BST property.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: The same range sum is asked on a binary tree that is not a BST. What must change?
options: Every node must be visited, with no pruning
The same pruning works
Only the left subtree needs visiting
Only leaves need visiting
optionExplain: Right: without the property no side can be ruled out.
The pruning depends on order.
No side is privileged.
Interior nodes may be in range.
questions.explain: No order, no pruning.
questions.rule: Visit the left side only if low is less than the node, and the right side only if the node is less than high.
questions.teaches: The trivial approach is a normal BFS or DFS that visits every node and adds those within the range; the BST property improves on it.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A range covers every value in the BST. What is the time of the pruned range sum?
options: O(log n), since pruning always helps
O(1), since the range is full
O(n squared), since pruning adds cost
O(n), since every node is visited
optionExplain: Pruning needs values outside the range.
A full sum touches every node.
Pruning does not add a loop.
Right: with nothing to prune, all nodes are summed.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the worst case.
questions.rule: Pruning cuts work on average, but the worst case stays O(n).

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: The extra space used by the stack or recursion in the pruned range sum is O(____).
questions.explain: The stack can grow with the tree.
questions.rule: Space: O(n).

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A full tree has 1,000,000 nodes and the root's value exceeds high. The right subtree of about ____ nodes is skipped.
questions.explain: The root's right subtree holds about half of the remaining nodes.
questions.rule: Skip a whole half at once.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A BST of n nodes is a straight line, and the range is all values. What is the stack depth?
options: Up to 1 entry
Up to n entries
About log n entries
Exactly 2 entries
optionExplain: The line is tall.
Right: a line makes the recursion n deep.
Log n needs a balanced tree.
Two is only the child count.
questions.explain: Space follows height.
questions.rule: Pruning cuts work on average, but the worst case stays O(n).

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: pruning guarantees the range sum runs in O(log n) time.
questions.explain: Pruning helps on average; with the whole tree in range the cost is still O(n).
questions.rule: Average gain, worst-case equal.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Which change makes pruning save the most on a BST?
options: A narrow range that excludes most of the values
A range that covers every value
A tree with duplicate values
A range chosen after the traversal
optionExplain: Right: more excluded subtrees mean more skipped work.
Nothing is excluded then.
BSTs have unique values.
The range must be known first.
