questions.explain: A narrow range lets whole subtrees be skipped. The book notes the time can still be O(n) when all nodes lie in the range, and the space is O(n) for the stack or call stack.
questions.rule: Pruning cuts work on average, but the worst case stays O(n).
questions.teaches: The space complexity of the pruned range sum is O(n), for the stack or the recursion call stack.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: To find the minimum difference between two values, which pair of values in the sorted list needs to be compared?
options: The smallest and the largest
Every pair
Adjacent values only
The first and last of each half
optionExplain: That pair has the largest gap.
That works but is slower.
Right: the closest pair is adjacent.
That pairs distant values.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the argument.
questions.rule: The closest pair of values is always adjacent in sorted order.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Comparing every pair of n values costs O(n ____).
questions.explain: n(n-1)/2 pairs is quadratic.
questions.rule: All pairs: quadratic.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: The sorted values are 2, 9, 11, 20. The minimum difference between any two values is ____.
questions.explain: Adjacent gaps are 7, 2 and 9, so the smallest is 2.
questions.rule: Check the gaps between neighbours.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A tree holds 1,000 values. Roughly how many pair comparisons does the naive method need?
options: About 1,000
About 500,000
About 10,000
optionExplain: That is one per value.
Right: 1000 x 999 / 2 is about 500,000.
That is only 10 per value.
That is far too many.
questions.explain: Count the pairs.
questions.rule: The closest pair of values is always adjacent in sorted order.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: after sorting, the minimum difference could lie between two values that are not neighbours.
questions.explain: If another value sat between them, it would form a smaller gap with one of them.
questions.rule: Closest means adjacent.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: What time does the sort-then-compare approach take, and what dominates it?
options: O(n), dominated by the comparisons
O(n squared), dominated by the sort
O(log n), dominated by the first value
O(n log n), dominated by the sort
optionExplain: The scan is linear, but the sort costs more.
Sorting is not quadratic here.
Every value has to be read.
Right: the sorting step costs more than the linear scan.
questions.explain: The sort is the bottleneck.
questions.rule: The closest pair of values is always adjacent in sorted order.
questions.teaches: One approach is to put all values in an array and loop over all pairs, which is O(n squared); sorting the array and iterating over the adjacent elements improves it to O(n log n) because of the sort.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: In a BST, which traversal gives the values in sorted order without sorting?
options: Preorder DFS
Inorder DFS
Postorder DFS
Breadth-first search
optionExplain: Preorder puts the root first.
Right: left, node, right ascends.
Postorder puts the root last.
BFS goes level by level.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card relies on the sorted property.
questions.rule: Inorder gives the values sorted for free, so only the neighbour gaps need scanning.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: After the inorder walk, the minimum difference is found by scanning ____ pairs of values in the list.
questions.explain: Only neighbours need comparing.
questions.rule: Scan neighbours.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A BST has root 4, children 2 and 6, and 1 and 3 under 2. The inorder list is 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, so the minimum difference is ____.
questions.explain: Adjacent gaps are 1, 1, 1 and 2.
questions.rule: Take the smallest gap.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: How much time does the inorder method take on a BST with n nodes?
options: O(n log n)
O(n squared)
O(log n)
O(n), with no sorting step
optionExplain: That includes a sort that is not needed.
Pairs are not compared.
Every node is read.
Right: one walk and one scan.
questions.explain: Linear walk plus linear scan.
questions.rule: Inorder gives the values sorted for free, so only the neighbour gaps need scanning.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: using preorder instead of inorder in this solution still gives correctly sorted values.
questions.explain: Preorder lists the root first, so the list is not in sorted order and neighbour gaps would be wrong.
questions.rule: Use inorder for sorted values.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: The same task is posed for a binary tree that is not a BST. What is the best approach from the book's ideas?
options: Collect the values, sort them, and compare neighbours, for O(n log n)
Use inorder and compare neighbours, for O(n), since inorder lists any tree's values in order
Compare only parents with children, since the closest values must sit on neighbouring nodes
Return the root minus its left child, since the two closest values are always at the top
optionExplain: Right: without the BST property the sort is needed.
Inorder is sorted only for a BST.
Close values may be anywhere in the tree.
That ignores most pairs.
questions.explain: No BST, no free order.
questions.rule: Inorder gives the values sorted for free, so only the neighbour gaps need scanning.
questions.teaches: Because the inorder traversal on a BST visits the nodes in sorted order, we get the sorted nodes without the O(n log n) sort, giving an overall time complexity of O(n).

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: In iterative inorder, what happens when curr is not empty?
options: The node is recorded at once, since its value is added to the result before the walk goes on
The walk moves to the right child, since the right side is the next part still to be handled
The node is pushed and the walk moves to its left child
The stack is cleared, since a non-empty curr means the pending nodes are no longer needed
optionExplain: Recording happens after popping.
The right child comes later.
Right: each node waits until its left subtree is done.
The stack holds the pending nodes.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the loop.
questions.rule: Iterative inorder pushes the left spine, then pops, records and moves right.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: When curr is empty, the code ____ a node from the stack.
questions.explain: The most recent pending node is taken.
questions.rule: Empty curr: pop.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Trace the iterative inorder on the tree with root 2 and children 1 and 3. Order in which values are recorded.
questions.explain: Push 2 and 1, pop and record 1, pop and record 2, move right to 3, push, pop and record 3.
questions.rule: Left spine, then pop and go right.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: On a tree with root 5 and only a right child 8, what is the first value recorded?
options: Nothing
Both together
optionExplain: 8 comes after 5.
5 is recorded first.
Right: 5 has no left child, so it is popped at once.
Values are recorded one at a time.
questions.explain: No left child means pop immediately.
questions.rule: Iterative inorder pushes the left spine, then pops, records and moves right.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: the loop condition can test only that the stack is non-empty, because curr can be ignored after the first pass.
questions.explain: At the start the stack is empty while curr holds the root, and after a pop curr may hold a right child, so both must be checked.
questions.rule: Check the stack and curr.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: An interviewer asks for a tree's inorder sequence without saying how. What does the book advise?
options: Use recursion if given the option, but know the iterative version
Always write the iterative version, since the iterative form is the one interviewers expect
Refuse, since inorder cannot be recursive and so must always be written with a stack
Use BFS instead, since a level-by-level pass gives the values in sorted order directly
optionExplain: Right: iterative inorder is a lot more complicated.
Iterative is the less common choice.
Recursion handles inorder well.
BFS does not give inorder.
questions.explain: Prefer the simple recursive form.
questions.rule: Iterative inorder pushes the left spine, then pops, records and moves right.
questions.teaches: If ever given the option, you should stick with recursion for inorder, since the iterative version is a lot more complicated, although you could be asked to do both in an interview.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: To validate a BST, what must be true of a node deep in the left subtree of the root?
options: Its value is below its parent only, since the parent is the one node it is directly compared with
Its value is above the root's value, since a deep node has to be larger than the node at the top
Its value equals its parent's value, since the parent and the child on one side must match exactly
Its value is below the root's value, as well as fitting its own parent
optionExplain: The root's bound applies too, not only the parent's.
Left means smaller than the root, not larger.
Equal values are not allowed here.
Right: all ancestors impose bounds.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card passes bounds down.
questions.rule: Each node must lie strictly between the lower and upper bounds inherited from its ancestors.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: The bounds for the root are minus infinity and ____.
questions.explain: The root has no ancestors, so it can be any value.
questions.rule: Root: unbounded.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: At node 8 with bounds (3, 20), the left child is called. What bounds does it receive?
optionExplain: That is the right child's bounds.
Right: going left lowers the upper bound to 8.
Bounds must tighten.
That leaves no room.
questions.explain: Left: large becomes node.val.
questions.rule: Each node must lie strictly between the lower and upper bounds inherited from its ancestors.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Root 10 has left child 5 and right child 15; 5 has a right child 12. What does the code return?
options: False, since 12 arrives with bounds (5, 10) and is not below 10
True, since 12 is above its parent 5, and a right child only has to be above its own parent
True, since 12 is below 15, and the right-hand node 15 sets the upper bound for the whole tree
False, since 5 is below 10, and a left child may not sit under a root that is larger than it
optionExplain: Right: the upper bound 10 comes from the root.
The bound inherited from the root also applies, and it fails.
15 is not an ancestor of 12, so it sets no bound.
5 itself is valid; the problem is the node 12 below it.
questions.explain: Follow the bounds down.
questions.rule: Each node must lie strictly between the lower and upper bounds inherited from its ancestors.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: checking only that each node is between its parent and its other child is enough to validate a BST.
questions.explain: Deeper nodes must also respect the bounds of all their ancestors.
questions.rule: Pass bounds from every ancestor.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: The same tree has the value 5 at the root and 5 as its left child. What does the bounds check return?
options: True, since equal values are allowed
True, since left children may match
False, since 5 is not below the bound 5
False, since 5 is below minus infinity
optionExplain: The property is strict.
Left must be less.
Right: the interval is open.
5 is above minus infinity.
questions.explain: Open intervals reject ties.
questions.rule: Each node must lie strictly between the lower and upper bounds inherited from its ancestors.
questions.teaches: The bounds small and large define an exclusive range (small, large); a value outside it violates the BST property, and the root starts with small = -infinity and large = infinity because it has no parent.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: What should the BST check return for an empty tree?
options: False, since there are no values to compare
True, since an empty tree is technically a BST
None
It depends on the bounds
optionExplain: With no values, nothing violates the property.
Right: empty is valid.
A boolean is expected.
No node means no bound check.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the base case.
questions.rule: Empty is a valid BST; a tree is valid only if the node, left subtree and right subtree are all valid.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: The answers for the left and right subtrees are combined with ____.
questions.explain: Both subtrees must be valid.
questions.rule: Every subtree valid: and.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: A single node tree is checked. What do its two child calls return, and what does the whole call return?
options: False from both, so the call returns False
True from one and False from the other
They are not called for a single node
True from both, so the call returns True
optionExplain: Empty trees are valid.
Both children are empty.
The calls are made and answered by the base case.
Right: empty children are valid.
questions.explain: A single node is always valid.
questions.rule: Empty is a valid BST; a tree is valid only if the node, left subtree and right subtree are all valid.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: The left subtree is a valid BST, the right subtree is not, and the node's own value is in bounds. What does the call return?
options: True
False
It returns the left answer
It depends on the depth
optionExplain: One invalid subtree makes the whole invalid.
Right: and needs every part to be valid.
The right answer matters too.
Depth does not matter.
questions.explain: True and False is False.
questions.rule: Empty is a valid BST; a tree is valid only if the node, left subtree and right subtree are all valid.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: True or false: using or to combine the two subtree answers would correctly reject a tree whose right subtree is invalid.
questions.explain: With or, a valid left subtree would be enough to accept the whole tree.
questions.rule: All subtrees must hold: and.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees
questions.q: Which earlier problem uses the same pattern of returning true for empty and combining child answers with and?
options: Path sum, which returns true for an empty tree and combines the child answers with and
Maximum depth, which returns true for an empty tree and combines the answers with and
Right side view, which returns true for an empty tree and combines the answers with or
Same tree, which returns true for two empty trees and combines the child answers with and
optionExplain: Path sum returns false for an empty tree and combines with or.
Maximum depth returns 0 for an empty tree and takes a maximum.
Right side view is a BFS and returns a list, not a boolean.
Right: both problems demand that every part holds.
questions.explain: Every-part problems share a shape.
questions.rule: Empty is a valid BST; a tree is valid only if the node, left subtree and right subtree are all valid.
questions.teaches: If a tree rooted at a node is a BST, then node.left and node.right must also be BSTs, which gives the same recursive way of looking at the problem as in the same-tree example.

questions.q: Which description makes a graph a binary tree?
options: Each node has at most one parent and at most two children
Each node has exactly two neighbours
The graph has no vertices with children
The graph has more edges than vertices
optionExplain: Right: those are the prominent restrictions.
Neighbours are not limited that way.
Trees do have children.
A tree has fewer edges than vertices.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the two restrictions.
questions.rule: A binary tree is a graph limited to one parent and two children per node.

questions.q: Every node in a binary tree has at most ____ parent(s).
questions.explain: A node in a tree cannot have more than one parent.
questions.rule: At most one parent.

questions.q: In a graph, node C is pointed to by both A and B. Can this graph be a binary tree?
options: Yes, since each node has at most two children
Yes, since C is a leaf
No, since C would have two parents
No, since C has no children
optionExplain: Child count is fine, but the parent restriction fails.
Leaves still have one parent.
Right: the one-parent restriction is broken.
Having no children is allowed.
questions.explain: Check parents first.
questions.rule: A binary tree is a graph limited to one parent and two children per node.

questions.q: A node in a graph points to four other nodes. What does this say about the graph?
options: It is not a graph at all, since a node in a graph may not point to that many other nodes
It is a binary tree with a root, since a node of a binary tree may point to up to four children
It is not a binary tree, since a node has more than two children
It is a tree with four parents, since the four pointed-to nodes each count as a parent of it
optionExplain: Graphs allow any number of edges.
The limit for a binary tree is two children.
Right: four outgoing edges exceed the child limit.
Parents are a separate count; pointing to four nodes makes four children.
questions.explain: Count outgoing edges.
questions.rule: A binary tree is a graph limited to one parent and two children per node.

questions.q: True or false: every graph is a tree, because trees are the general case.
questions.explain: Trees are the restricted case. A graph can have nodes with several parents and many children.
questions.rule: Trees are special graphs.

questions.q: How many edges can leave a node in a general graph?
options: Any number, since a node can have any number of edges connected to it
At most two, as in a binary tree, since every node of a graph has a left and a right edge
Exactly one, as in a list, since each node of a graph points to the single node after it
At most three, since a node needs room for a left pointer, a right pointer and a parent
optionExplain: Right: the restrictions are lifted.
That is the binary tree limit.
That is the list limit.
A general graph has no such limit.
questions.explain: A general graph lifts the restrictions, so a node can have any number of edges. In a binary tree each node has at most one parent and at most two children.
questions.rule: A binary tree is a graph limited to one parent and two children per node.
questions.teaches: A binary tree is a graph with restrictions, the most prominent being at most one parent and at most two children per node.

questions.q: A map shows airports and the direct flights between them. How is it modelled as a graph?
options: Flights as nodes, airports as edges
Only the busiest airport as a node
Passengers as nodes, tickets as edges only
Airports as nodes, flights as edges
optionExplain: Roles are swapped.
The model covers all airports.
Passengers are not part of the map.
Right: places are nodes and links are edges.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the pattern.
questions.rule: Model things as nodes and their relationships as edges to see a graph in everyday systems.

questions.q: In a social network graph, each person is a ____.
questions.explain: People are nodes; friendships are edges.
questions.rule: Things are nodes.

questions.q: Match each system with the thing that becomes an edge.
questions.explain: In each system the relationships between items are the edges.
questions.rule: Edges are relationships.

questions.q: A city's one-way streets are modelled as a graph. What type of edges do they need?
options: Undirected edges, since streets connect places
Directed edges, since each street allows movement one way
No edges, since streets are nodes
Edges of equal length only
optionExplain: Undirected edges allow both ways.
Right: one-way travel is directed.
Junctions are the nodes.
Length is a separate matter.
questions.explain: Direction matches the movement allowed.
questions.rule: Model things as nodes and their relationships as edges to see a graph in everyday systems.

questions.q: True or false: graphs appear only in computer science problems and not in daily life.
questions.explain: Social networks, roads and internet traffic are everyday graphs.
questions.rule: Graphs appear everywhere.

questions.q: Which of these does the book also list as something modelled with graphs?
options: Circuit boards, crypto blockchains and models in biology
Only sorted lists of numbers, because a graph needs its nodes to be put in ascending order
Only linked lists of text, because every graph is a chain with one pointer from node to node
Only trees of folders, because a graph needs a root directory and a pointer for each file
optionExplain: Right: graphs reach well beyond social media.
Lists are special graphs, but the book lists wider uses.
Lists of text are special cases; graphs are broader.
Folder trees are graphs, but the book's list is wider.
questions.explain: The range of uses is wide.
questions.rule: Model things as nodes and their relationships as edges to see a graph in everyday systems.
questions.teaches: The book also lists circuit boards, crypto blockchains and models in biology as practical applications of graphs.

questions.q: A directed edge goes from node A to node B. Which moves are allowed?
options: B to A only
Both A to B and B to A
A to B only
Neither
optionExplain: That is the reverse.
That describes an undirected edge.
Right: a directed edge allows one direction.
The edge permits A to B.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the definition.
questions.rule: Directed edges go one way; undirected edges go both ways.

questions.q: An edge you can traverse in both directions is called ____.
questions.explain: Undirected edges go both ways.
questions.rule: Undirected: both ways.

questions.q: A one-way street connects junction P to junction Q. Which edge type models it?
options: An undirected edge between P and Q
A directed edge from P to Q
A directed edge from Q to P
No edge, since junctions are not nodes
optionExplain: That would allow driving both ways.
Right: movement is allowed from P to Q only.
That reverses the street.
Junctions are natural nodes.
questions.explain: Match the movement allowed.
questions.rule: Directed edges go one way; undirected edges go both ways.

questions.q: A graph has the single directed edge A to B. Starting at B, which nodes can you reach?
options: A and B
A only
Every node
Only B itself
optionExplain: A is not reachable from B.
B is already there.
No other nodes exist.
Right: the edge cannot be followed backwards.
questions.explain: Follow arrows forwards only.
questions.rule: Directed edges go one way; undirected edges go both ways.

questions.q: True or false: with a directed edge from A to B, you can still move from B back to A.
questions.explain: A directed edge is one-way. You can move from A to B but not from B to A.
questions.rule: Directed means one way.

questions.q: How are directed and undirected edges drawn in a graph picture?
options: Directed edges as circles, undirected edges as squares
Directed edges as arrows, undirected edges as straight lines
Directed edges as straight lines, undirected edges as arrows
Both as arrows
optionExplain: Circles are nodes.
Right: arrows show a direction.
The two are swapped.
Undirected edges have no arrowhead.
questions.explain: Arrow means direction.
questions.rule: Directed edges go one way; undirected edges go both ways.
questions.teaches: In graphical representations, directed edges are arrows between nodes and undirected edges are straight lines.

questions.q: A graph has two separate clusters of nodes with no edge between the clusters. How many connected components does it have?
options: One
Three
Zero
Two
optionExplain: The clusters are not joined.
Only two clusters exist.
Clusters count as components.
Right: each cluster is a component.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card defines a component.
questions.rule: A connected component is a group of nodes linked by edges, and a tree has exactly one.

questions.q: A binary tree has exactly ____ connected component(s).
questions.explain: All nodes are reachable from the root.
questions.rule: A tree: one component.

questions.q: Six cities are joined by roads as follows: A-B, B-C, D-E, and F has no road. The graph has ____ connected components.
questions.explain: The groups are {A, B, C}, {D, E} and {F}.
questions.rule: Count groups.

questions.q: One road is added between C and D in that map. How many components remain?
optionExplain: Right: the groups {A, B, C} and {D, E} merge into one, leaving {F} separate.
Merging reduces the count.
F still stands alone.
Merging does not add components.
questions.explain: A connecting edge merges two groups.
questions.rule: A connected component is a group of nodes linked by edges, and a tree has exactly one.

questions.q: True or false: a graph with 100 nodes and 5 isolated nodes still has exactly one connected component.
questions.explain: Each isolated node is its own component, so the graph has at least six.
questions.rule: Isolated nodes count.

questions.q: In the provinces problem, each group of directly or indirectly linked cities is one province. What graph idea does a province correspond to?
options: A cycle
A leaf
A connected component
An indegree
optionExplain: A cycle is a loop.
A leaf is a node with no children.
Right: a province is a component.
Indegree counts incoming edges.
questions.explain: A province is a connected component. The book also names connected nodes neighbors, so in A <-> B <-> C node B has two neighbors.
questions.rule: A connected component is a group of nodes linked by edges, and a tree has exactly one.
questions.teaches: Nodes joined by an edge are called neighbors: in A <-> B <-> C, B is a neighbor of A and of C.

questions.q: A node has three edges leaving it and one entering it. What are its outdegree and indegree?
options: Outdegree 1, indegree 3
Outdegree 4, indegree 0
Outdegree 3, indegree 1
Outdegree 3, indegree 3
optionExplain: The numbers are swapped.
Total edges is not the outdegree.
Right: out counts leaving edges and in counts entering ones.
Only one edge enters.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card defines both.
questions.rule: Indegree counts edges coming in, outdegree counts edges going out, and neighbours share an edge.

questions.q: The number of edges that can be used to reach a node is its ____degree.
questions.explain: Indegree counts edges entering.
questions.rule: In = entering.

questions.q: Directed edges: 0 to 1, 0 to 2, 1 to 2, 3 to 2. The indegree of node 2 is ____.
questions.explain: Nodes 0, 1 and 3 each point to 2.
questions.rule: Count edges entering.

questions.q: For the same edges, which node has an indegree of 0?
options: Nodes 0 and 3
Node 2 only
Node 1 only
Nodes 1 and 2
optionExplain: Right: nothing points to 0 or 3.
Node 2 has three incoming edges.
Node 1 receives from 0.
Both receive edges.
questions.explain: Zero indegree means nothing points to the node.
questions.rule: Indegree counts edges coming in, outdegree counts edges going out, and neighbours share an edge.

questions.q: True or false: in A <-> B <-> C, node A is a neighbour of C because they are in the same graph.
questions.explain: Neighbours share an edge. A and C are linked only through B.
questions.rule: Neighbours share an edge.

questions.q: In the directed graph above, how many neighbours does node 2 have by the book's definition, which counts nodes connected by an edge?
options: Zero, since node 2 has no outgoing edge
One, since only one edge is drawn
Four, since all nodes are neighbours
Three: nodes 0, 1 and 3, because they share edges with it
optionExplain: The edges enter it, so it still has neighbours.
Three edges touch it.
Node 2 is not its own neighbour.
Right: neighbours are nodes connected by an edge, in either direction here.
questions.explain: Count nodes sharing an edge.
questions.rule: Indegree counts edges coming in, outdegree counts edges going out, and neighbours share an edge.
questions.teaches: Nodes that are connected by an edge are called neighbors; in A <-> B <-> C, B is a neighbor of both A and C while A and C are not neighbors of each other.

questions.q: Edges go A to B, B to C, and C to A. Is this graph cyclic?
options: No, since every node has one outgoing edge
Yes, since the path returns to A
No, since all edges are directed
It depends on the node values
optionExplain: One outgoing edge each still forms a loop here.
Right: following the edges loops forever.
Directed graphs can have cycles.
Values do not matter.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card defines a cycle.
questions.rule: A cycle is a loop of edges; a graph without any is acyclic.

questions.q: A graph with no cycle is called ____.
questions.explain: Acyclic means without a cycle.
questions.rule: No cycle: acyclic.

questions.q: Edges go A to B, B to C and A to C. Is the graph cyclic?
options: No, since no path leads back to the node it started from
Yes, since there are three edges for three nodes
Yes, since A has two outgoing edges
Yes, since C has two incoming edges
optionExplain: Right: all edges point forward.
Edge counts alone do not make a cycle.
Two outgoing edges do not form a loop.
Two incoming edges do not form a loop.
questions.explain: Look for a way back.
questions.rule: A cycle is a loop of edges; a graph without any is acyclic.

questions.q: An undirected edge joins A and B. Is this graph cyclic as the book describes it?
options: Acyclic, because there is only one edge and a single edge cannot form a loop on its own
Acyclic, because it has fewer than three nodes and a loop needs at least three nodes
Cyclic in the sense that a traversal can go A to B and back again without end
Neither, because cycles need directed edges and an undirected edge has no direction to follow
optionExplain: One undirected edge already allows a walk back and forth.
Size does not decide; the walk A to B and back is endless.
Right: undirected edges let a walk move back and forth forever.
The book says an undirected edge A <-> B is an infinite loop for a naive walk.
questions.explain: Back-and-forth is a loop for an unmarked walk.
questions.rule: A cycle is a loop of edges; a graph without any is acyclic.

questions.q: True or false: a binary tree can contain a cycle if a leaf points back to the root.
questions.explain: By definition a binary tree has no cycle, and a node cannot have a parent below it.
questions.rule: Trees are acyclic.

questions.q: Which statement about trees follows from the book?
options: Binary trees may contain cycles at leaves
Binary trees by definition cannot have a cycle
Binary trees contain exactly one cycle
Binary trees are cyclic when they have many nodes
optionExplain: Leaves have no outgoing edges.
Right: trees are acyclic.
No cycle exists in a tree.
Size does not create a cycle.
questions.explain: No cycle can occur in a binary tree. In an undirected graph or one with cycles, a tree-style DFS would loop forever unless a seen set is used.
questions.rule: A cycle is a loop of edges; a graph without any is acyclic.
questions.teaches: In any undirected graph or directed graph with cycles, a tree-style DFS loops forever; a seen set prevents this.

questions.q: In a binary tree, what is the indegree of a node other than the root?
options: Any number
1, from its parent
optionExplain: Only the root has indegree 0.
Two parents are not allowed.
The tree fixes it at 1.
Right: each non-root node has exactly one parent.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the degrees.
questions.rule: A binary tree is a directed, connected, acyclic graph in which only the root has indegree 0 and every outdegree is at most 2.

questions.q: In a binary tree a node with an outdegree of 0 is a ____.
questions.explain: No outgoing edges means no children.
questions.rule: Outdegree 0: leaf.

questions.q: A tree node has outdegree 2 and indegree 1. What can you say about it?
options: It is the root, since the root is the node with two children and therefore the one with the most edges
It is an internal node with a parent and two children
It is a leaf, since a leaf has an edge entering it and the two edges leaving it come from its parent
It is an isolated node, since an isolated node has the same number of edges in as out of it
optionExplain: The root has indegree 0.
Right: indegree 1 means a parent, outdegree 2 means two children.
Leaves have outdegree 0.
Isolated nodes have no edges.
questions.explain: Read the degrees.
questions.rule: A binary tree is a directed, connected, acyclic graph in which only the root has indegree 0 and every outdegree is at most 2.

questions.q: A directed graph has a node with indegree 2. Can it be a binary tree?
options: Yes, since a binary tree allows two incoming edges
Yes, if the node is a leaf
Yes, if the node is the root
No, since a tree node has at most one incoming edge
optionExplain: Two refers to children, not parents.
Leaves have one parent too.
The root has indegree 0.
Right: a tree node has one parent.
questions.explain: One parent at most.
questions.rule: A binary tree is a directed, connected, acyclic graph in which only the root has indegree 0 and every outdegree is at most 2.

questions.q: True or false: in a binary tree, you can reach a node's parent by following an edge from the node.
questions.explain: Tree edges point from parent to child, so you cannot move from a node to its parent.
questions.rule: Tree edges point downward.

questions.q: Which terms are used for a node's connected nodes in tree problems versus general graph problems?
options: Parent and child in trees, neighbours in graphs
Neighbours in trees, parent and child in graphs
Root and leaf in both
Vertex and edge in trees, node in graphs
optionExplain: Right: trees have a hierarchy.
The terms are swapped.
Root and leaf name positions, not relations.
Vertex and node mean the same.
questions.explain: Hierarchy gives parent and child.
questions.rule: A binary tree is a directed, connected, acyclic graph in which only the root has indegree 0 and every outdegree is at most 2.
questions.teaches: Specific to trees, the parent and child terms are used instead of neighbors, which graphs use for nodes connected by an edge.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A graph problem begins with a reference to the first node of a graph, as tree problems begin with the root. Is that typical?
options: Yes, graph problems always give a root, since every graph has one node that every other node hangs from
Yes, graph problems give a head as lists do, which is the first node of the graph in the input
No, a graph problem gives information about the graph, not node objects
No, they give nothing, so you must build the whole graph from the problem statement alone
optionExplain: Graphs do not have a single root.
A head belongs to linked lists.
Right: the graph exists as an idea derived from the input.
Some information is given, such as edges or a matrix.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card describes the difference.
questions.rule: A graph problem gives data about a graph, not node objects; you choose how to represent it.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A graph problem gives ____ about the graph; the graph itself does not exist in memory as objects.
questions.explain: Only the idea of the graph exists; the input describes it.
questions.rule: The graph is an idea.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A statement says: there are n cities labelled from 0 to n - 1. What should you treat each city as?
options: An edge with a weight
A connected component
A node with a unique label
A cycle
optionExplain: Edges are the connections between cities.
Components are groups.
Right: cities become nodes.
Cycles are loops.
questions.explain: Story objects become nodes.
questions.rule: A graph problem gives data about a graph, not node objects; you choose how to represent it.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A problem says nothing about graphs but mentions towns joined by roads. What should you suspect?
options: A graph, with towns as nodes and roads as edges
A sorting problem
A tree with exactly one parent each
A string problem
optionExplain: Right: a story can hide a graph.
Nothing sorts here.
Roads need not form a tree.
No strings are involved.
questions.explain: Look for objects and links.
questions.rule: A graph problem gives data about a graph, not node objects; you choose how to represent it.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: True or false: the first sentence of a graph problem states that the input is a graph.
questions.explain: The statement may or may not say so; sometimes a story must be recognised as a graph.
questions.rule: Recognise the graph from the story.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: Why must you decide how to represent a graph in code?
options: Because graphs cannot be stored in memory unless they are first converted into a tree
Because all graphs are too large to be held, so only part of each one can be stored
Because nodes have no labels, so you have to invent a name for each node before storing it
Because the input only describes the graph and gives no node objects to follow
optionExplain: Graphs can be stored with the right structure, such as a map or array.
Size is not the reason.
Nodes are usually labelled; the labels are part of the input.
Right: the representation is your choice.
questions.explain: Description in, representation out.
questions.rule: A graph problem gives data about a graph, not node objects; you choose how to represent it.
questions.teaches: The problem statement may or may not explicitly say that the input is a graph; sometimes a story tells you, and you have to determine that the input is a graph.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: The graph input is an array of edges. Finding the neighbours of one node by scanning the array takes about how long?
options: Constant time
Time proportional to the number of edges
Time proportional to the node's label
Time proportional to the number of components
optionExplain: Scanning is not constant.
Right: every edge must be inspected.
The label does not set the scan length.
Components do not set it.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card describes the scan.
questions.rule: Build a neighbour lookup first so each node's neighbours are one access away.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: To get a node's neighbours at once, preprocess the edges into a ____ map.
questions.explain: A hash map from node to a list of neighbours gives them in O(1).
questions.rule: Preprocess into a hash map.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A graph has 1,000 edges and the traversal visits 500 nodes, rescanning the edge array at each. About how many edge inspections is that?
options: About 500,000
About 1,500
About 1,000
About 500
optionExplain: Right: 500 nodes x 1,000 edges.
That adds instead of multiplying.
That scans only once.
That counts nodes only.
questions.explain: Multiply scans by edges.
questions.rule: Build a neighbour lookup first so each node's neighbours are one access away.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: After preprocessing, a hash map graph is available. What does graph[0] give?
options: The number of nodes
The edge array
The list of neighbours of node 0
The first edge only
optionExplain: The map holds neighbours, not a count.
The original array is separate.
Right: one access returns all neighbours.
It returns a full list.
questions.explain: Key in, neighbours out.
questions.rule: Build a neighbour lookup first so each node's neighbours are one access away.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: True or false: scanning the edge array at every node is fine, since it needs only O(1) work per node.
questions.explain: Each scan inspects every edge, so the work per node is proportional to the number of edges.
questions.rule: A scan is not constant.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: The book compares an edge array to finding your friends on Facebook. What is the point?
options: Friends lists are always smaller than edge arrays, so Facebook stores fewer items per person than a graph would
Without a prebuilt friends list, you would scan every connection in the world to find yours
Facebook stores its graph as a tree, so every person has exactly one parent who lists their friends
Friends should be kept sorted alphabetically, so that a person can be found by halving the list each time
optionExplain: Size is not the point; the point is how you find one person's connections.
Right: a prebuilt structure answers at once.
Facebook is a graph, not a tree.
Sorting is not the point; a prebuilt structure answers at once.
questions.explain: Prebuilt lookups avoid full scans.
questions.rule: Build a neighbour lookup first so each node's neighbours are one access away.
questions.teaches: Imagine Facebook kept its graph as an array of edges: you would need to look at every connection in the world to find your friends, whereas a prebuilt graph lets you open your friends list.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In an edge array, what does the element [3, 7] mean?
options: Node 3 has the value 7
Node 3 is the parent of 7 in a tree
There are 3 nodes and 7 edges
There is an edge between node 3 and node 7
optionExplain: Pairs are connections, not values.
Direction is not stated by the pair alone.
Counts are not encoded this way.
Right: the pair names the two endpoints.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card defines the format.
questions.rule: An edge array lists pairs [x, y]; the statement says whether they are directed.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: The problem statement says whether the edges in an edge array are directed or ____.
questions.explain: The description decides.
questions.rule: Statement decides direction.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: edges = [[0, 1], [1, 2]] and the statement says the edges are undirected. Can you walk from 2 to 0?
options: No, since no edge starts at 2
Yes, through 1, since undirected edges work both ways
Yes, directly, since 2 and 0 share an edge
No, since undirected graphs forbid walks
optionExplain: That is true only if the edges were directed.
Right: 2 to 1 to 0 is possible.
No edge joins 2 and 0 directly.
Walks are allowed.
questions.explain: Undirected means both ways.
questions.rule: An edge array lists pairs [x, y]; the statement says whether they are directed.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: edges = [[0, 1], [1, 2]] with directed edges. Starting at 2, which nodes can you reach?
options: 0, 1 and 2
1 and 2
0 only
Only 2 itself
optionExplain: Edges cannot be followed backwards.
1 is behind 2.
0 is behind 2.
Right: no directed edge leaves 2.
questions.explain: Follow arrows forward only.
questions.rule: An edge array lists pairs [x, y]; the statement says whether they are directed.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: True or false: the array [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 0], [2, 3]] exists in memory as four linked node objects.
questions.explain: It exists only as an array; the graph is an idea derived from it.
questions.rule: The graph is an idea.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A statement says [x, y] means highway between city x and city y, with no mention of direction. What should you ask?
options: Whether highways can be driven both ways, since the description sets direction
Whether the array is sorted by city, since a sorted array would show which way each pair points
Whether city labels are even numbers, since the parity of a label would decide the direction
Whether the highways form cycles, since a cycle would tell you which end each pair starts from
optionExplain: Right: direction comes from the description.
Sorting is not the issue; direction comes from the description.
Labels do not set direction.
Cycles are a separate property from direction.
questions.explain: Check the statement for direction.
questions.rule: An edge array lists pairs [x, y]; the statement says whether they are directed.
questions.teaches: Using the cities example, the story for an edge array would be something like [x, y] means there is a highway connecting city x and city y, and the problem description tells you whether edges are directed.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: For a directed edge [x, y], where is y stored in the neighbour map?
options: In the list for y
In both lists
In the list for x
In neither list
optionExplain: That would let you leave y towards y.
Both lists apply only to undirected edges.
Right: you can leave x towards y.
The edge must be recorded.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the rule.
questions.rule: For each pair [x, y] add y to graph[x], and x to graph[y] too if edges are undirected.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: For an undirected edge [x, y], y is added to graph[x] and ____ is added to graph[y].
questions.explain: An undirected edge works from both ends.
questions.rule: Undirected: add both ways.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: Directed edges [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 0], [2, 3]] are loaded. What does graph[2] hold?
optionExplain: 1 points to 2, but the edge is directed.
A node is not its own neighbour here.
Right: node 2 has edges to 0 and 3.
1 does not leave 2.
questions.explain: Collect the edges leaving 2.
questions.rule: For each pair [x, y] add y to graph[x], and x to graph[y] too if edges are undirected.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: Undirected edges [[0, 1], [1, 2]] are loaded. What does graph[1] hold?
optionExplain: Right: both edges touch 1.
The edge to 0 also counts.
The edge to 2 also counts.
A node is not its own neighbour here.
questions.explain: Undirected edges are recorded twice.
questions.rule: For each pair [x, y] add y to graph[x], and x to graph[y] too if edges are undirected.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: True or false: for undirected edges it is enough to add y to the list of x only.
questions.explain: Without adding x to the list of y, you could not move from y back to x.
questions.rule: Undirected: add both ways.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: Why does the code also create an empty list for y when only x has an outgoing edge?
options: Because y must have a neighbour, as every node needs at least one entry in the map
Because the map needs sorted keys, and an empty list keeps the keys in order
Because empty lists save memory, as they take less room than a missing key
So that looking up y later finds an empty list, not a missing key
optionExplain: A node with no outgoing edge has no neighbours; the list is empty.
Order is not needed in a map.
Empty lists use memory; they do not save any.
Right: the lookup then works for every node.
questions.explain: Every node needs an entry.
questions.rule: For each pair [x, y] add y to graph[x], and x to graph[y] too if edges are undirected.
questions.teaches: After building the hash map, graph[0] immediately gives all the neighbors of node 0, and nodes with no neighbours need empty lists so lookups never fail.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In an adjacency list graph, how do you get all the neighbours of node 6?
options: Scan every pair of the array
Read graph[6]
Read graph[6][6]
Sort the array first
optionExplain: That is the edge array approach.
Right: the list is already indexed by node.
That is the matrix approach.
No sorting is needed.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the format.
questions.rule: In an adjacency list, graph[i] holds the neighbours of node i directly.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: An adjacency list needs no ____ before the traversal starts.
questions.explain: The neighbours are already accessible.
questions.rule: No preprocessing.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: graph = [[1, 2], [3], [3], []]. What are the neighbours of node 0?
options: Nodes 1 and 2
Node 3 only
Nodes 0 and 3
No nodes
optionExplain: Right: graph[0] is [1, 2].
3 is reached by the neighbours of 0.
A node is not its own neighbour.
graph[0] is not empty.
questions.explain: Read the row.
questions.rule: In an adjacency list, graph[i] holds the neighbours of node i directly.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In graph = [[1], [2], [0, 3], []], which node has no outgoing edges?
options: Node 0, whose list is [1], so it has no outgoing edge since its only link points inward
Node 1, whose list is [2], so it has no outgoing edge since its only link is a loop
Node 3, whose list is empty
Node 2, whose list is [0, 3], so it has no outgoing edge as both entries point back
optionExplain: graph[0] lists node 1, so node 0 has an outgoing edge.
graph[1] lists node 2, so node 1 has an outgoing edge.
Right: graph[3] is [].
graph[2] lists two nodes, so it has two outgoing edges.
questions.explain: An empty list means no outgoing edge.
questions.rule: In an adjacency list, graph[i] holds the neighbours of node i directly.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: True or false: an adjacency list must first be converted into a hash map before it can be traversed.
questions.explain: It is already in that form, so graph[i] gives the neighbours immediately.
questions.rule: No conversion needed.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In the keys and rooms problem, rooms[i] holds the keys found in room i. Which format is this?
options: An edge array, since each room is listed together with the rooms it leads to
An adjacency list, with rooms as nodes and keys as edges
An adjacency matrix, since each room has a row showing which rooms its keys open
A grid of squares, since the rooms lie next to each other in rows and columns
optionExplain: An edge array lists pairs, not one list per node.
Right: rooms[i] lists the nodes reachable from i.
A matrix is n by n with ones and zeros.
The squares of a grid are a different input format.
questions.explain: Rows of neighbours form an adjacency list.
questions.rule: In an adjacency list, graph[i] holds the neighbours of node i directly.
questions.teaches: In the keys and rooms problem, rooms[i] is an array of other rooms we can visit from room i, so the graph is given as an adjacency list and needs no conversion.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In an adjacency matrix, what does graph[2][5] == 1 tell you?
options: Node 2 has the value 5
Node 5 is the parent of node 2
There are five nodes
There is an edge from node 2 to node 5
optionExplain: The cell holds an edge flag.
Direction goes from the row to the column.
Counts are not stored.
Right: row is the source, column the target.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card defines the cells.
questions.rule: graph[i][j] == 1 means an edge from i to j; either scan the row or convert to neighbour lists.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: An adjacency matrix for n nodes has size n by ____.
questions.explain: It is a square matrix.
questions.rule: n by n.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: graph = [[0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1], [1, 0, 0]]. What are the neighbours of node 0?
options: Nodes 0 and 1
Nodes 1 and 2
Node 2 only
No nodes
optionExplain: graph[0][0] is 0.
Right: graph[0][1] and graph[0][2] are 1.
Node 1 also counts.
Row 0 has two ones.
questions.explain: Read the ones in the row.
questions.rule: graph[i][j] == 1 means an edge from i to j; either scan the row or convert to neighbour lists.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: For the same matrix, how many edges does the graph have?
optionExplain: That counts rows.
That counts one too many.
That counts all cells.
Right: there are four ones.
questions.explain: Count the ones.
questions.rule: graph[i][j] == 1 means an edge from i to j; either scan the row or convert to neighbour lists.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: True or false: building a neighbour map from an n by n matrix takes O(n) time, since there are n nodes.
questions.explain: Every cell must be examined, which costs O(n squared).
questions.rule: A matrix scan is quadratic.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A graph has 10,000 nodes and each node has about 3 neighbours. Why might you still convert the matrix to neighbour lists?
options: To avoid looping over 10,000 cells at every node during the traversal
To reduce the cost of building below O(n squared)
To make the graph undirected
To remove all edges
optionExplain: Right: the conversion pays off when nodes have few neighbours and n is large.
Building still costs n squared.
Direction is unchanged.
The edges are preserved.
questions.explain: Few neighbours, big n: convert.
questions.rule: graph[i][j] == 1 means an edge from i to j; either scan the row or convert to neighbour lists.
questions.teaches: Converting is especially useful when nodes have only a few neighbors and n is large, since the traversal then avoids iterating n times at every node.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In a grid problem, where do the edges come from?
options: From the values inside the squares, since a value of 1 always links a cell to the next one
From a separate array of edges that comes with the grid, as in the earlier graph problems
From the problem description, such as adjacency above, below, left and right
From the row numbers alone, since cells in the same row are always connected to each other
optionExplain: Values may or may not matter; the description defines the neighbours.
The grid is the whole input; no separate edge array is given.
Right: the story defines the neighbours.
Row numbers alone do not define adjacency.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card states the source of edges.
questions.rule: In a grid problem every cell is a node and the statement defines its neighbours.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In a grid graph, each ____ of the matrix is a node.
questions.explain: The squares are the nodes.
questions.rule: Cells are nodes.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: The cell (2, 3) has four-direction neighbours. Its neighbour below is (____, 3).
questions.explain: Below means row + 1.
questions.rule: Below: row + 1.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In a grid with 3 rows and 3 columns, how many in-bounds neighbours (four directions) does the corner (0, 0) have?
optionExplain: That ignores the bounds.
Only two directions stay inside.
Right: only right and down are in bounds.
Two directions remain.
questions.explain: Corners have fewer neighbours.
questions.rule: In a grid problem every cell is a node and the statement defines its neighbours.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: True or false: in a grid problem every cell has exactly four neighbours.
questions.explain: Cells on the border have fewer in-bounds neighbours.
questions.rule: Check bounds.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A problem lets a chess knight move between squares of a board. What are the edges?
options: The knight moves, as the problem description defines them
The squares sharing a row, since the knight stays on one row until it reaches the end
The squares of equal colour only, since a knight can reach only squares of its own colour
No edges exist, since a board is a grid of values and the knight is not a node of any graph
optionExplain: Right: the statement tells the moves, which become edges.
Rows are not the described moves.
Colour is not the described move.
The moves exist, and each one is an edge.
questions.explain: The edges come from the problem description, here the knight's moves. In the book's village example the neighbours of (row, col) are the four adjacent cells that are in bounds.
questions.rule: In a grid problem every cell is a node and the statement defines its neighbours.
questions.teaches: In a matrix graph the neighbours of (row, col) are (row - 1, col), (row, col - 1), (row + 1, col) and (row, col + 1), when in bounds.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In a graph traversal, how do you visit the neighbours of the current node?
options: With node.left and node.right
With exactly three calls
By sorting the neighbours first
With a loop over all neighbours
optionExplain: Those are tree fields.
The count is not fixed.
Sorting is not part of the traversal.
Right: the count of neighbours varies.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card compares the two.
questions.rule: Loop over neighbours instead of two children, convert the input if needed, and choose the start yourself.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A tree traversal begins at the ____, but a graph may lack an obvious start.
questions.explain: Trees come with a root.
questions.rule: Graph start is a decision.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A problem gives an array of edges. Before a DFS, what is a typical first step?
options: Sort the edges by length
Convert the edges into a hash map of neighbours
Add parent pointers to every node
Delete half of the edges
optionExplain: Edge length is not the issue.
Right: the traversal needs quick neighbour access.
Parent pointers are a different technique.
Deleting edges changes the graph.
questions.explain: Prepare neighbour lookup first.
questions.rule: Loop over neighbours instead of two children, convert the input if needed, and choose the start yourself.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A recursive tree DFS is copied directly to an undirected graph with no other change. What can happen?
options: It can run forever by moving back and forth along an edge
It visits each node exactly once, since a recursive call never returns to a node it came from
It skips the start node, since the first call is made on a neighbour instead of the start
It becomes breadth-first, since an undirected edge makes the calls alternate between sides
optionExplain: Right: with cycles and undirected edges, the walk loops.
Nothing marks nodes as visited, so nodes can be visited again.
The start is visited first.
The recursion remains depth-first.
questions.explain: Loops need protection.
questions.rule: Loop over neighbours instead of two children, convert the input if needed, and choose the start yourself.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: True or false: a graph traversal must start from node 0.
questions.explain: The start depends on the problem; sometimes the statement names it, sometimes you must work it out.
questions.rule: Choose the start from the problem.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In a graph DFS that follows the template, which step sits inside a loop over the neighbours?
options: The base case
The final return
The recursive call on each neighbour
The reading of the input
optionExplain: The base case runs once per call.
The return runs once per call.
Right: step 3 now repeats for every neighbour.
Input is read before the traversal.
questions.explain: The loop replaces the two fixed calls.
questions.rule: Loop over neighbours instead of two children, convert the input if needed, and choose the start yourself.
questions.teaches: Implementation of DFS for graphs is similar to trees: check the base case, recursively call on all neighbors, do some logic to calculate the answer, and return the answer; you can also do it iteratively with a stack.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: Two nodes A and B are joined by an undirected edge. A DFS has no record of visited nodes. What happens?
options: It visits A and B once and stops
It moves between A and B forever
It skips B
It visits only the root
optionExplain: Nothing stops the return.
Right: each can reach the other again.
B is reachable from A.
Both are reachable.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card describes the problem.
questions.rule: Mark a node as seen before visiting it, so each node is visited once and cycles end.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: To visit each node at most once, keep a set called ____.
questions.explain: Check it before visiting a node.
questions.rule: Use a seen set.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: At node X, a neighbour Y is already in seen. What should the DFS do?
options: Visit Y again
Remove Y from seen
Stop the whole traversal
Skip Y
optionExplain: That risks looping.
Removing it would allow revisits.
Other neighbours still matter.
Right: it has been handled.
questions.explain: Skip what is seen.
questions.rule: Mark a node as seen before visiting it, so each node is visited once and cycles end.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: A directed graph has edges 0 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 0. A DFS from 0 with a seen set visits which nodes, in what count?
options: 0 only
0, 1 and 2, each once
0, 1 and 2, repeated forever
1 and 2 only
optionExplain: It continues around the loop once.
Right: the seen set cuts the cycle.
That is what happens without the set.
The start is visited too.
questions.explain: Each node once.
questions.rule: Mark a node as seen before visiting it, so each node is visited once and cycles end.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: True or false: a seen set was needed in binary tree DFS, since the same node could be reached twice.
questions.explain: In a tree the edges only point downward, so once you leave a node you cannot reach it again.
questions.rule: Trees have no way back.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?
questions.q: In a language like C++, how might seen be stored for nodes labelled 0 to n - 1, and what changes?
options: As a queue, which changes the algorithm, since a queue remembers the order of arrival
As a sorted tree, which changes the answer, since the nodes then come out in label order
Not at all, since arrays cannot mark nodes and only a hash set can hold visited labels
As an array, which may run faster, with no change to the algorithm
optionExplain: A queue is not a set.
The answer stays the same.
Arrays can mark labelled nodes.
Right: the array is an implementation detail.
questions.explain: Same idea, different container.
questions.rule: Mark a node as seen before visiting it, so each node is visited once and cycles end.
questions.teaches: In languages where the range of states is known, such as C++ with nodes numbered 0 to n - 1, an array for seen may be faster than a set, though the time complexity and the algorithm are unchanged.

questions.q: An undirected graph has two separate groups of nodes. A DFS starts in the first group. Which nodes does it visit?
options: Exactly the nodes of the first group
All nodes in both groups
Only the start node
Only the leaves of the first group
optionExplain: Right: it cannot cross to the other component.
No edge joins the groups.
It follows edges to reach the whole group.
It visits internal nodes too.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card ties DFS to components.
questions.rule: A traversal from any node of an undirected graph visits exactly its whole connected component.

questions.q: After a DFS finishes on an undirected graph, all nodes of one connected ____ are in seen.
questions.explain: The DFS has covered the whole component.
questions.rule: DFS covers a component.

questions.q: Nodes 0-1-2 form a path, and nodes 3-4 are joined to each other but not to the rest. A DFS from 1 visits how many nodes?
optionExplain: It cannot reach 3 or 4.
Node 2 and node 0 are both reachable.
Right: it covers 0, 1 and 2.
It continues beyond the start.
questions.explain: Stay inside the component.
questions.rule: A traversal from any node of an undirected graph visits exactly its whole connected component.

questions.q: A graph has 3 components. How many separate DFS starts are needed to visit every node?
options: 3, one in each component
As many as there are edges
optionExplain: One DFS covers only one component.
Three groups need three starts.
Right: one start per component.
Edges do not set the number.
questions.explain: One DFS per component.
questions.rule: A traversal from any node of an undirected graph visits exactly its whole connected component.

questions.q: True or false: starting a DFS from node 0 in an undirected graph visits every node of the graph, whatever its shape.
questions.explain: It visits only the component of node 0. Other components need their own starts.
questions.rule: A DFS covers one component.

questions.q: With directed edges, a DFS from node A reaches fewer nodes than A's component. Why?
options: Directed edges can only be followed forward, so some nodes in the component are behind the arrows
Directed edges cannot be followed at all by a DFS, so it can never leave the node it began on
Directed graphs have no components, so there is no group of nodes that the DFS could cover fully
The DFS stops at the first leaf it reaches, so the other branches are never explored afterwards or visited
optionExplain: Right: reachability follows arrows.
They can be followed forward, which is how the DFS moves.
Components exist in directed graphs too, so this is not the reason.
The DFS continues past leaves by backtracking to unexplored neighbours.
questions.explain: Direction limits reach.
questions.rule: A traversal from any node of an undirected graph visits exactly its whole connected component.
questions.teaches: A traversal on an undirected graph visits every node in the connected component; this is a property you can memorize, but it also makes sense because a traversal from the root of a binary tree visits every node of that tree.

questions.q: A loop meets an unseen node while counting components. What does it do?
options: Skips it, since it is unseen
Adds 1 only after the whole loop
Runs a DFS without counting
Adds 1 to the count and runs a DFS from it
optionExplain: Unseen nodes are the ones to process.
The count grows at discovery.
The count marks each component.
Right: an unseen node begins a new component.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the loop.
questions.rule: Loop over the nodes; each time you find an unseen one, add 1 and DFS its component.

questions.q: After the DFS from an unseen node, every node in that node's component is in ____.
questions.explain: The seen set marks them.
questions.rule: DFS fills seen.

questions.q: isConnected = [[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,1]]. What does the code return?
optionExplain: Node 2 is separate.
Right: nodes 0 and 1 are linked, and node 2 stands alone.
Nodes 0 and 1 count as one.
At least one province exists.
questions.explain: Group the linked cities.
questions.rule: Loop over the nodes; each time you find an unseen one, add 1 and DFS its component.

questions.q: isConnected is the 3 by 3 identity matrix (ones on the diagonal only). What does the code return?
optionExplain: Right: no city is linked to another.
That would need all cities linked.
Each city is its own province.
Cells are not provinces.
questions.explain: Self-links alone give single-city provinces.
questions.rule: Loop over the nodes; each time you find an unseen one, add 1 and DFS its component.

questions.q: True or false: marking seen only inside the DFS, and not for the starting node, still counts every component exactly once.
questions.explain: The starting node must also be marked, or a later neighbour could reach it and count the component again.
questions.rule: Mark the start as seen.

questions.q: Which change makes the code count components of a graph given as an edge array?
options: Replace the DFS with sorting, since sorted edges put each component next to its neighbours
Count the edges instead of the nodes, since each edge marks the start of one component
Build the neighbour map from the edges instead of from the matrix
Remove the seen set, since an edge array already stops any node from being visited twice
optionExplain: Sorting does not find components.
Edges are not components.
Right: the counting loop is unchanged.
Without seen, components are counted wrongly.
questions.explain: Only the graph building changes.
questions.rule: Loop over the nodes; each time you find an unseen one, add 1 and DFS its component.
questions.teaches: The use of the set (or boolean array) seen will prevent us from counting the same component more than once, and the same loop works whatever format the graph arrives in once a neighbour map exists.

questions.q: In a graph DFS for n cities labelled 0 to n - 1, what is the argument of dfs?
options: A TreeNode object
The integer label of the node
The array of edges
The number of components
optionExplain: No node objects are given.
Right: nodes are identified by label.
The edges live in the neighbour map.
The count is kept outside.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card states the argument.
questions.rule: A graph DFS takes the node's integer label; the iterative form replaces recursion with a stack inside dfs.

questions.q: In an iterative graph DFS, each pass of the loop pops a node from the ____.
questions.explain: The popped node is like a call argument.
questions.rule: Pop = call.

questions.q: A graph problem labels 8 junctions from 0 to 7. How is the junction 5 passed to the DFS?
options: As a TreeNode holding 5
As a list of its edges
As the string 'junction'
As the integer 5
optionExplain: No TreeNode objects exist.
Edges come from the map.
Labels are numbers.
Right: the label identifies the node.
questions.explain: Pass the label.
questions.rule: A graph DFS takes the node's integer label; the iterative form replaces recursion with a stack inside dfs.

questions.q: What must change in the recursive graph DFS to make it iterative, according to the book?
options: The whole program, including the graph building, since a loop needs a different input
Only the dfs function: use a stack, and keep everything else the same
The seen set must be dropped, since the stack already prevents a node being visited twice
A queue must replace the loop over neighbours, since that is how an iterative DFS is made
optionExplain: Graph building is separate and stays the same.
Right: the rest of the code is reusable.
Seen is still needed.
A queue changes the traversal order; a stack keeps it depth-first.
questions.explain: Swap recursion for a stack inside dfs.
questions.rule: A graph DFS takes the node's integer label; the iterative form replaces recursion with a stack inside dfs.

questions.q: True or false: in a graph problem the graph exists in memory as linked node objects, like a binary tree.
questions.explain: Only the idea of the graph exists; the input describes it and you build a representation.
questions.rule: The graph is an idea.

questions.q: Why can graph problems with nodes labelled 0 to n - 1 reuse so much of the same logic?
options: Every such graph is a tree, so the same tree traversal code can be copied from problem to problem
Every such graph has no cycles, so a seen structure is never needed in the traversal code at all
Every such graph has exactly n edges, so the same neighbour loop fits each of these problems
Labels are integers that index maps or arrays, so the code looks alike across problems
optionExplain: Graphs are not all trees; the labels are only integers.
Cycles are allowed, which is why seen is used.
Edge counts vary from graph to graph.
Right: integer labels make neighbour maps and seen arrays easy.
questions.explain: Integer labels give a shared pattern.
questions.rule: A graph DFS takes the node's integer label; the iterative form replaces recursion with a stack inside dfs.
questions.teaches: Thankfully, most graph problems have the nodes labeled 0 to n - 1, so a lot of the logic can be reused between problems.

questions.q: A graph DFS visits n nodes, and the for loop over neighbours runs e times in total. What is the time complexity?
options: O(n + e)
O(n times e)
O(n)
O(e squared)
optionExplain: Right: n visits plus e edge looks.
The loop is not repeated per node over all edges.
Edges are also examined.
Nothing is squared here.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the total.
questions.rule: Graph DFS visits each node once and each edge once, so it costs O(n + e).

questions.q: In a graph DFS each node is visited at most ____.
questions.explain: The seen set prevents repeats.
questions.rule: Once per node.

questions.q: A graph has 10 nodes and 15 edges. The DFS does about ____ units of node and edge work (n + e).
questions.rule: Add nodes and edges.

questions.q: Every node in a graph of n nodes is connected to every other node. What is e, roughly, and the DFS time?
options: About n edges, so O(n) time
About log n edges, so O(log n) time
About n squared edges, so O(n squared) time
Exactly 1 edge, so O(1) time
optionExplain: That is a sparse graph.
No edge count is logarithmic here.
Right: e is about n squared here.
Many edges exist.
questions.explain: Dense graphs make e large.
questions.rule: Graph DFS visits each node once and each edge once, so it costs O(n + e).

questions.q: True or false: because the DFS has a for loop inside the function, graph DFS must cost n times the number of neighbours of the busiest node.
questions.explain: Each edge is looked at once across the entire run, so the total is n + e.
questions.rule: Count total edge looks.

questions.q: In the provinces problem the input is an n by n matrix, so building the map costs O(n squared). What is the overall time?
options: O(n), since DFS is linear in the nodes and the matrix is read as part of that work
O(n + e) with e unknown, since the number of edges is not bounded by the input
O(n squared), since e is at most n squared and the matrix must be read
O(log n), since the components are few and each DFS skips most of the matrix
optionExplain: Reading the matrix takes more than O(n).
The matrix already bounds e, so it is not unknown.
Right: reading the matrix dominates.
No halving occurs.
questions.explain: Input format can set the bound.
questions.rule: Graph DFS visits each node once and each edge once, so it costs O(n + e).
questions.teaches: Technically in the provinces problem the time complexity is O(n squared) because the input is an adjacency matrix, so building the hash map always needs O(n squared), and e is dominated by n squared.

questions.q: Which parts make up the extra space of a graph DFS?
options: The neighbour map, the call stack and the seen set
Only the seen set
Only the call stack
The input matrix and nothing else
optionExplain: Right: all three grow with the graph.
The map and stack also count.
The map and seen also count.
The built map is separate from the input.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card lists the three.
questions.rule: Space is the neighbour map plus the stack plus seen: O(n + e).

questions.q: The space complexity of the graph DFS with a neighbour map is O(n + ____).
questions.explain: Nodes plus edges.
questions.rule: Space: n + e.

questions.q: A graph has 1,000 nodes but only 1,200 edges. About how much space does the neighbour map need?
options: About 1,000,000 entries, as n squared, since each node needs room for every other node
About 1,000 entries only, since the map holds one entry for each of the nodes
About 12,000 entries, since the edge count is multiplied by ten for the lists
About 1,200 list entries, plus bookkeeping for 1,000 nodes
optionExplain: That would be a dense graph; this one has few edges.
Edges also take entries, so 1,000 is too few.
No factor of ten applies.
Right: it grows with existing edges.
questions.explain: Count the edges that exist.
questions.rule: Space is the neighbour map plus the stack plus seen: O(n + e).

questions.q: A dense graph has e close to n squared. What is its DFS space?
options: O(n), because the map keeps one entry per node and the edge lists add nothing
O(n squared), because the map stores about n squared edges
O(log n), because each step of the DFS cuts the remaining graph in half
O(1), because the DFS only keeps the current node and not any other data
optionExplain: The map still has e entries, and here e is about n squared.
Right: e is large here.
No halving occurs in a DFS over a graph.
The map and the seen structure are not constant.
questions.explain: Space follows e.
questions.rule: Space is the neighbour map plus the stack plus seen: O(n + e).

questions.q: True or false: the space of a graph DFS built from a matrix equals O(n squared) in every case, because the matrix has n squared cells.
questions.explain: The map built from it grows only with the edges that exist, so the space is O(n + e).
questions.rule: The map grows with edges.

questions.q: Why does the book separate time from space in the provinces problem?
options: Reading the matrix always costs n squared time, but the map only grows with existing edges
Time and space always match, because every edge that is read is also stored once in the map
Space is always larger than time, because the map must hold a list for every possible pair
The matrix is not read at all, because the DFS works on a map that is somehow already built
optionExplain: Right: reading costs time, storing costs space.
