They differ here: reading the whole matrix is quadratic, while the map holds only the edges that exist.
Time is quadratic, and the map holds only existing edges, so space may be smaller than time.
The matrix must be read once to build the map, and that reading is where the time goes.
questions.explain: Reading the matrix always costs n squared, while the map holds only existing edges. The book notes that scanning graph[node] and pre-processing into a hash map both take O(n squared) time.
questions.rule: Space is the neighbour map plus the stack plus seen: O(n + e).
questions.teaches: Both ways of using an adjacency matrix, scanning graph[node] or building a hash map first, take O(n squared) time.

questions.q: What does the directions array hold in a grid DFS?
options: The cell values of the grid, copied so that each neighbour can be read without indexing
The list of visited cells, so that each neighbour is checked against the ones already seen
Coordinate changes for each neighbour, such as (0, 1) for right
The sizes of the rows, so that each neighbour can be tested against the edge of the grid
optionExplain: Cell values are in the grid.
Visited cells are in seen.
Right: each pair is a step to a neighbour.
Row sizes are separate.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card describes it.
questions.rule: Loop over a directions list and test each neighbour with a valid helper.

questions.q: The valid helper first checks that the cell is in ____.
questions.code:
directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]

def valid(row, col, grid):
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    return 0 <= row < m and 0 <= col < n and grid[row][col] == '1'
questions.explain: Out-of-range cells are not nodes.
questions.rule: Check bounds first.

questions.q: From the cell (2, 2), the direction (-1, 0) leads to which neighbour?
questions.code:
directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]

def valid(row, col, grid):
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    return 0 <= row < m and 0 <= col < n and grid[row][col] == '1'
options: (3, 2), the cell below
(1, 2), the cell above
(2, 1), the cell to the left
(2, 3), the cell to the right
optionExplain: Down adds 1 to the row.
Right: row minus 1 is up.
Left changes the column.
Right changes the column.
questions.explain: Add the change to each coordinate.
questions.rule: Loop over a directions list and test each neighbour with a valid helper.

questions.q: In a 3 by 3 grid, valid is called for (-1, 0). What does it return?
questions.code:
directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]

def valid(row, col, grid):
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    return 0 <= row < m and 0 <= col < n and grid[row][col] == '1'
options: True, since the row is within the grid
An index error, since row -1 does not exist
True, since the cell is land
False, since the row is out of bounds
optionExplain: Row -1 is above the grid.
The bounds check protects the access.
The cell does not exist.
Right: the bounds check fails first.
questions.explain: Bounds first.
questions.rule: Loop over a directions list and test each neighbour with a valid helper.

questions.q: True or false: valid may test grid[row][col] before the bounds check, because the grid indexes safely.
questions.explain: Reading outside the grid can fail or give a wrong cell, so the bounds must be tested first.
questions.rule: Bounds before value.

questions.q: A problem allows diagonal moves as well. What changes in the helpers?
options: valid must be removed, since diagonal cells are always inside the grid and need no check
The directions array gains the four diagonal changes
The grid must be transposed, since the diagonal cells are found by swapping rows and columns
The seen set must be dropped, since a diagonal move cannot take the walk back to a cell
optionExplain: valid still guards the bounds for diagonal cells.
Right: only the list of steps changes.
No transposing is needed.
Seen is still needed.
questions.explain: Edit the directions list.
questions.rule: Loop over a directions list and test each neighbour with a valid helper.
questions.teaches: Declaring a directions array (a very common practice) makes the code cleaner when iterating over the neighbors, and a helper such as valid makes it more modular, though neither is necessary.

questions.q: Which earlier problem is counting islands equivalent to?
options: Finding the maximum depth
Validating a binary search tree
Computing a path sum
Counting connected components, as with provinces
optionExplain: Depth belongs to trees.
BST validation uses bounds.
Path sum sums values.
Right: islands are components of land cells.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the match.
questions.rule: Islands are connected components of land cells; scan the grid and DFS from each unseen land cell.

questions.q: In the islands grid, only cells holding ____ (land) are nodes.
questions.explain: Water cells are never nodes.
questions.rule: Land cells are the nodes.

questions.q: Grid rows: 11000, 11000, 00100, 00011. How many islands?
optionExplain: Right: the 2 by 2 block, the single middle cell and the bottom-right pair are separate.
Three separate groups exist.
The middle cell touches no other land.
More than one group exists.
questions.explain: Count groups of touching land.
questions.rule: Islands are connected components of land cells; scan the grid and DFS from each unseen land cell.

questions.q: Grid rows: 101, 010, 101 (diagonals only touch). How many islands under four-direction moves?
optionExplain: Diagonals do not connect.
Each land cell is alone.
Right: no two land cells share a side.
Water cells are not islands.
questions.explain: Only side-by-side land connects.
questions.rule: Islands are connected components of land cells; scan the grid and DFS from each unseen land cell.

questions.q: True or false: incrementing the island count for every land cell, not only for unseen ones, still returns the number of islands.
questions.explain: That would count land cells, not groups. Only an unseen land cell starts a new island.
questions.rule: Count unseen starts only.

questions.q: The problem now allows diagonal connections. What is the smallest code change?
options: Replace the DFS with sorting, since diagonal land cells are found by ordering the cells
Count only the water cells, since diagonal links are decided by the cells between the land
Add the four diagonal steps to the directions list
Remove the seen set, since a diagonal step cannot lead back to a cell that was seen
optionExplain: Sorting does not find groups.
Water is not counted.
Right: only the neighbour definition changes.
Seen is still required.
questions.explain: Neighbours come from the directions list, so diagonal links add four steps. The book stresses that in a matrix graph the problem description, not the input, decides the edges.
questions.rule: Islands are connected components of land cells; scan the grid and DFS from each unseen land cell.
questions.teaches: In a matrix input the edges are determined by the problem description, not by the input, so a diagonal rule adds neighbours.

questions.q: An m by n grid DFS visits each cell once and each cell has at most four neighbours. What is the time?
options: O(m times n)
O(m plus n)
O(m squared times n squared)
O(log(m times n))
optionExplain: Right: constant work for each of m times n cells.
That is far smaller than the cell count.
Cells are not compared in pairs.
Every cell is read.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the bound.
questions.rule: Islands cost O(m x n) because each cell has at most four neighbours.

questions.q: A grid cell has at most ____ edges when moves go up, down, left and right.
questions.explain: Four directions give at most four neighbours.
questions.rule: At most four.

questions.q: A grid has 30 rows and 40 columns. The number of cells the DFS can visit is ____.
questions.rule: Rows times columns.

questions.q: Instead of a seen set, the code sets visited land cells to 0. What is the main risk?
options: The DFS visits land twice, because the zeroed cells can still be reached from their neighbours
The island count grows, because every zeroed cell is counted again as a fresh piece of land
The recursion never ends, because a cell turned to 0 keeps sending calls to its neighbours
The input grid is changed, which an interviewer may not allow
optionExplain: Zeroed cells are not land again.
The count is unaffected.
Zero cells stop the walk.
Right: the caller's data is modified.
questions.explain: Mutating input has a cost.
questions.rule: Islands cost O(m x n) because each cell has at most four neighbours.

questions.q: True or false: because a node can have any number of neighbours, the island DFS should still be quoted as O(nodes + edges) with unknown edges per node.
questions.explain: Here each cell has at most four neighbours, so the per-cell work is constant and the total is O(m x n).
questions.rule: Bounded degree gives O(cells).

questions.q: A problem allows moves in 8 directions. How does the time bound change?
options: It becomes O(8 to the power m times n)
It stays O(m times n), since 8 is still a constant
It becomes O(m + n)
It becomes constant
optionExplain: No exponent arises.
Right: a fixed number of directions is a constant factor.
Cells must still be visited.
All cells may be visited.
questions.explain: Constant neighbours, same order.
questions.rule: Islands cost O(m x n) because each cell has at most four neighbours.
questions.teaches: We can avoid using the set by modifying the input: instead of putting a square in seen, change that square's value to 0, although some interviewers may not want you to modify the input.

questions.q: n cities are joined by n - 1 roads, with exactly one way between any two cities. What shape is this graph?
options: A tree, with city 0 as the root
A graph with many cycles
Several unconnected components
A single cycle
optionExplain: Right: n nodes with n - 1 edges and one route each form a tree.
One route between cities means no cycles.
All cities are connected.
A cycle would give two routes.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card describes the shape.
questions.rule: DFS from 0 over undirected roads; each road crossed that exists as given, pointing away from 0, is flipped.

questions.q: The DFS treats the roads as ____ so it can reach every city from city 0.
questions.explain: Directed roads would block the walk.
questions.rule: Make it undirected for traversal.

questions.q: Roads: 1 to 0, 1 to 2, 3 to 2, 3 to 4 (five cities). How many roads must be reversed?
optionExplain: Some roads point away from 0.
Only some need reversing.
Right: walking from 0, the step 1 to 2 and the step 3 to 4 follow original roads, so both are flipped.
Not all roads point away.
questions.explain: Walk from 0 and compare each step with the original road.
questions.rule: DFS from 0 over undirected roads; each road crossed that exists as given, pointing away from 0, is flipped.

questions.q: Roads: 1 to 0 and 2 to 0. How many reversals does the code report?
options: 1, since the DFS meets one road that points away from city 0 on its way down
0, since both roads already point toward city 0
2, since both roads touch city 0 and every road at the start must be reversed
3, since the two roads and the starting city each cost one reversal in the count
optionExplain: No step away from 0 follows an original road, so nothing is counted.
Right: the DFS steps 0 to 1 and 0 to 2 are not original roads.
Road 1 to 0 already points to 0, so it needs no reversal.
Road 2 to 0 already points to 0 too, and a city is not a road.
questions.explain: Check the stepping direction against the originals.
questions.rule: DFS from 0 over undirected roads; each road crossed that exists as given, pointing away from 0, is flipped.

questions.q: True or false: the roads set can be dropped because the undirected graph already records which roads were reversed.
questions.explain: The undirected graph loses direction; the original set is how a step that follows a road is recognised.
questions.rule: Keep the original directions.

questions.q: Why is the answer O(n) time when the input has n - 1 roads?
options: Each road is checked n times, once from every city, so the total is linear in the roads
The DFS visits every pair of cities, and n - 1 roads keep the number of pairs small
Sorting the roads dominates, so the total follows the n log n cost of the sort
Each city is visited once and the number of edges is linear in n
optionExplain: No repeated checks occur: each road is looked at from its two ends only.
Pairs of cities are not examined.
No sorting happens.
Right: n + (n - 1) is linear.
questions.explain: n nodes and n - 1 edges.
questions.rule: DFS from 0 over undirected roads; each road crossed that exists as given, pointing away from 0, is flipped.
questions.teaches: The time and space complexity of this algorithm is O(n), because we only visit each node once, do constant work, and are told the number of edges is n - 1, which is O(n).

questions.q: Each city has only one road path to city 0. For a city to reach city 0, which direction must the roads on that path point?
options: Away from city 0
Toward city 0
Any direction
Alternating directions
optionExplain: That leads away from the goal.
Right: you can only follow a road in its direction.
Direction decides whether travel is possible.
A single wrong road blocks the trip.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card builds on this fact.
questions.rule: With one route per city, a road must be flipped exactly when it points away from city 0.

questions.q: The reorder problem asks for the ____ number of roads to flip.
questions.explain: The goal is a minimum count.
questions.rule: Count only the roads that must flip.

questions.q: Roads in a 4 city tree rooted at 0: 0 to 1, 2 to 1, 1 to 3. Which roads point away from 0 and must be flipped?
options: 2 to 1 only
All three roads
None of the roads
0 to 1 and 1 to 3
optionExplain: The road 2 to 1 is fine; the others are not.
One road is already correct.
Some roads point away.
Right: 2 to 1 already points toward 0, and the other two point away.
questions.explain: Compare each road with the way toward 0.
questions.rule: With one route per city, a road must be flipped exactly when it points away from city 0.

questions.q: A 5 city tree has 4 roads. All 4 point toward city 0. What is the minimum number of flips?
optionExplain: Right: nothing blocks any city.
Nothing needs flipping.
Flipping any would hurt.
There are only 4 roads.
questions.explain: Every road is already correct.
questions.rule: With one route per city, a road must be flipped exactly when it points away from city 0.

questions.q: True or false: a road that already points toward city 0 may still need flipping, because a city beyond it could use another route.
questions.explain: There is only one route per city, so a road pointing toward 0 is already as needed.
questions.rule: Single route means one right direction.

questions.q: Why is it enough to test each road against a set of the original roads during the DFS?
options: Sets sort the roads by direction, so the roads pointing away from 0 are listed first
Sets stop the DFS from revisiting nodes, so the same test removes repeated roads as well
The set answers in O(1) time whether the road we crossed existed in that direction
Sets store the number of cities, so the DFS can tell when every city has been reached
optionExplain: Sets do not sort.
Seen stops revisits; the set of roads answers a different question.
Right: crossing node to neighbour matches an original road exactly when it points away from 0.
The count of cities is n, not stored in the roads set.
questions.explain: Fast membership checks.
questions.rule: With one route per city, a road must be flipped exactly when it points away from city 0.
questions.teaches: To check in O(1) time whether a given edge is in connections, put the original directed edges in a set called roads.

questions.q: In the keys and rooms problem, what do the nodes and edges of the graph represent?
options: Keys are nodes and rooms are edges
Doors are nodes and floors are edges
Rooms are nodes and keys are edges
Rooms are edges and corridors are nodes
optionExplain: The roles are the other way round.
Doors and floors are not in the input.
Right: a key leads from the room holding it to the room it opens.
Rooms are the things visited.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the model.
questions.rule: DFS from room 0 and check that the number of seen rooms equals the number of rooms.

questions.q: After the DFS, the answer is True when the size of ____ equals the number of rooms.
questions.explain: Each visited room was added to seen.
questions.rule: Compare len(seen) with n.

questions.q: rooms = [[1], [2], [3], []]. What does the code return?
options: True
False
An error, because the last list is empty
optionExplain: Right: 0 opens 1, 1 opens 2, 2 opens 3, so all four rooms are seen.
All four are reached.
An empty list means no keys.
It returns a boolean.
questions.explain: Follow the keys from room 0.
questions.rule: DFS from room 0 and check that the number of seen rooms equals the number of rooms.

questions.q: rooms = [[1, 3], [3, 0, 1], [2], [0]]. What does the code return?
options: True
An infinite loop
False
optionExplain: Room 2 is never opened.
The result is a boolean.
Seen prevents looping.
Right: room 2 holds only its own key, and no other room has a key to it.
questions.explain: Which room has no key leading to it?
questions.rule: DFS from room 0 and check that the number of seen rooms equals the number of rooms.

questions.q: True or false: because rooms is already an adjacency list, the code must first build a hash map from it.
questions.explain: The input already gives the neighbours of room i as rooms[i], so no map is needed.
questions.rule: Use the adjacency list directly.

questions.q: Why does this problem need less extra space than the provinces problem with an adjacency matrix?
options: It uses a queue instead of a stack, so fewer nodes wait to be handled at once
The adjacency list can be used as the graph, so only seen and the stack are extra
It never stores a seen set, so no memory is spent on tracking visited rooms
It visits fewer rooms than a matrix has cells, so the DFS has less work to remember
optionExplain: The stack-or-queue choice is not the reason.
Right: no new graph is built.
Seen is still used.
The saving is in not building a graph.
questions.explain: No graph is built.
questions.rule: DFS from room 0 and check that the number of seen rooms equals the number of rooms.
questions.teaches: Adjacency lists are the most convenient input when nodes are numbered 0 to n - 1, because the input is basically already a hash map and no conversion is needed.

questions.q: The indegree of a node is the number of what?
options: Edges entering the node
Edges leaving the node
Nodes in its component
Leaves below it
optionExplain: Right: in means arriving at the node.
That is the outdegree.
That counts nodes, not edges.
Leaves are a tree idea.

questions.q: Nodes in the smallest set have indegree ____.

questions.rule: Indegree 0 means a mandatory start.

questions.q: n = 6 and edges [[0,1],[0,2],[2,5],[3,4],[4,2]]. Which nodes form the smallest set?

0, 2 and 3
0 and 3
Only 0
optionExplain: Those nodes all have edges entering them.
Node 2 is reached from 0 and 4.
Right: nodes 1, 2, 4 and 5 each have an incoming edge, while 0 and 3 have none.
Node 3 is not reachable from 0.

questions.rule: Count how many edges enter each node; the nodes with count 0 are the answer.

questions.q: A directed graph with 3 nodes is a cycle: 0 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 0. What does the code return?
options: [0], since node 0 is where the cycle starts and so nothing is counted as entering it
An empty list, since every node has indegree 1
[0, 1, 2], since every node of the cycle can be reached only from the other nodes beyond it
[2], since node 2 is the last node of the cycle and the edge out of it closes the loop
optionExplain: Node 0 has an incoming edge from 2.

Node 2 has an incoming edge from 1.

questions.q: Why does this problem not need a DFS at all?
options: Graphs with cycles cannot be traversed, so the graph would have to be cut up before a DFS
The edges are undirected, so every node could be reached from every other node directly
A DFS cannot count nodes, since it only visits them and has no place to keep a count
The answer depends only on counting edges entering each node
optionExplain: The graph is acyclic here, and cyclic graphs can be traversed with seen.
The edges are directed.
A DFS can count; it is not needed here.
Right: a single pass over the edges is enough.

questions.rule: Count how many edges enter each node; the nodes with count 0 are the answer.
questions.teaches: This example does not require a DFS, but it is a good exercise for understanding the mechanics of graphs.

questions.q: A BFS starts at node S. Which nodes does it visit before any node two steps away?
options: Only the leaves
Every node one step from S
The deepest node first
Nodes with the smallest label
optionExplain: Leaves are not the order.
Right: closer levels come first.
BFS does not go deep first.
Labels do not set the order.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the order.
questions.rule: The first time BFS visits a node, it has used the minimum number of steps from the start.

questions.q: BFS visits nodes in order of their ____ from the start.
questions.explain: Level by level means by distance.
questions.rule: Closest nodes first.

questions.q: In a graph, S has neighbours A and B. A has neighbour C. B has neighbour D. Which level is C on?
options: Level 1
Level 3
Level 0
Level 2
optionExplain: Level 1 holds A and B.
Only a longer chain reaches level 3.
Level 0 holds only the start.

questions.explain: Count steps from S.
questions.rule: The first time BFS visits a node, it has used the minimum number of steps from the start.

questions.q: A node can be reached from S in 2 steps or in 5 steps. After BFS reaches it, how many steps does the BFS record for it?
optionExplain: Right: the shorter route is explored first.
The longer route is explored later.
A mix of the routes is not used.
Steps are not added.
questions.explain: First arrival is the shortest.
questions.rule: The first time BFS visits a node, it has used the minimum number of steps from the start.

questions.q: True or false: on a graph, BFS may reach a node first by a path that is longer than the shortest one.
questions.explain: Levels are visited in order of distance, so the first arrival uses the fewest steps.
questions.rule: First arrival is shortest.

questions.q: A graph is not shaped like a tree. Why does the level idea still apply?
options: The graph can be rearranged into a tree first, and then the usual levels of that tree are used
BFS only runs on trees, so the level idea never reaches a graph that has other kinds of edges
Treat the start as a root: its neighbours are level 1, and their unseen neighbours are level 2
Levels are decided by node labels, so the nodes with the smallest labels form level 1 first
optionExplain: No rearranging is done; levels come from distance in the graph itself.
BFS runs on graphs too, with a seen set.
Right: levels are defined by distance, not by shape.
Labels do not matter; levels are distances from the start.
questions.explain: Levels come from distance.
questions.rule: The first time BFS visits a node, it has used the minimum number of steps from the start.
questions.teaches: 99% of the time a graph will not have a tree structure, but the level logic still holds if you imagine the start node as a root.

questions.q: Which search is the better fit for finding the fewest steps between two nodes of a graph?
options: DFS
Either, with no difference
BFS
Neither, since graphs are unordered
optionExplain: DFS may find a longer path first.
They differ on shortest paths.
Right: BFS explores by distance.
Graphs can be searched in order.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card makes the case.
questions.rule: Use BFS for shortest paths on graphs; a DFS may find a longer path first.

questions.q: A DFS goes down one path as far as it can, so the first path it finds may be ____ than needed.
questions.explain: It has no ordering by distance.
questions.rule: DFS first path is not best.

questions.q: A square graph has edges 0-1, 1-2, 2-3, 3-0. A DFS from 0 tries node 1 first. How many steps does it use to reach 3?
optionExplain: Right: it goes 0, 1, 2, 3.
That is the BFS answer.
It does not skip node 2.
Only three edges are crossed.
questions.explain: Follow the DFS order.
questions.rule: Use BFS for shortest paths on graphs; a DFS may find a longer path first.

questions.q: Same square graph. How many steps does BFS from 0 report for node 3?
optionExplain: That is the DFS answer.
3 is next to 0.
Zero is the start.
Right: 3 is a neighbour of 0.
questions.explain: Check the neighbours of 0.
questions.rule: Use BFS for shortest paths on graphs; a DFS may find a longer path first.

questions.q: True or false: in a binary tree, a DFS can reach a node by a longer path than the shortest one.
questions.explain: A tree has only one path from the root to any node, so there is no longer or shorter choice.
questions.rule: One path means no choice.

questions.q: Why did DFS and BFS agree on the depth of every node in a binary tree?
options: Trees are always balanced
A tree has only one possible path from the root to any node
BFS and DFS use the same data structure
Trees have no leaves to confuse the search
optionExplain: Trees need not be balanced.
Right: with one path there is nothing to compare.
They use a queue and a stack.
Leaves do not matter.
questions.explain: One path means one answer.
questions.rule: Use BFS for shortest paths on graphs; a DFS may find a longer path first.
questions.teaches: The first-visit guarantee held even for DFS on binary trees because there is only one possible path from the root to a node, whereas in a graph there can be many paths.

questions.q: In the binary matrix path problem, which cells are nodes?
options: Cells whose value is 0
Cells whose value is 1
Only the corners
Only the border cells
optionExplain: Right: a clear path uses 0 cells only.
Those are the blocked cells.
Interior cells can be on the path.
Cells inside count as well.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card states the rule.
questions.rule: BFS from the top left with a (cell, steps) queue; return the steps when the bottom right is reached.

questions.q: Each queue entry holds a cell and the number of ____ taken to reach it.
questions.explain: The steps are stored beside the cell.
questions.rule: Queue entries carry the steps.

questions.q: grid = [[0,0,0],[1,1,0],[1,1,0]]. What does the code return?
optionExplain: Three cells cannot join the corners here.
A diagonal step shortens the walk.
Right: the path (0,0), (0,1), (1,2), (2,2) has four cells.
A clear path exists.
questions.explain: Use the diagonal step.
questions.rule: BFS from the top left with a (cell, steps) queue; return the steps when the bottom right is reached.

questions.q: grid = [[1,0,0],[1,1,0],[1,1,0]]. What does the code return?
options: 0, since the start is already the target when no step has been taken yet in the grid
-1, since the start cell is blocked
1, since the start cell counts as one step and the path ends where it began at once
3, since the grid is three cells wide and the shortest route crosses three cells
optionExplain: Zero is not a path length here.
Right: the first line of the code returns -1.
The start cell is a 1, so the code returns before counting a step.
No path is searched: the first line returns -1.
questions.explain: Check the start cell first.
questions.rule: BFS from the top left with a (cell, steps) queue; return the steps when the bottom right is reached.

questions.q: True or false: the code needs a for loop over each level, since the answer depends on whole levels.
questions.explain: Only the target matters, so a steps value stored per entry is enough.
questions.rule: No level loop is needed.

questions.q: An all-zero 3 by 3 grid is searched with 8 directions. What does the code return?
optionExplain: Two cells cannot reach the opposite corner.
That is a longer route.
That counts every cell.
Right: the diagonal from corner to corner has three cells.
questions.explain: BFS reaches the corner in the fewest steps, here 3 by moving diagonally. The book shows that a DFS path of 11 squares can use up squares of the optimal 7-square path.
questions.rule: BFS from the top left with a (cell, steps) queue; return the steps when the bottom right is reached.
questions.teaches: In the book's example the optimal path has 7 squares, while a DFS path found 11 squares and used up squares of the optimal path.

questions.q: A shortest-path BFS needs only the step count of the target. Which design is enough?
options: Sort the queue after each pass
Store a steps value with each queue entry
Run a second BFS from the target
Keep a separate list of all paths
optionExplain: Sorting is not needed.
Right: return the steps when the target arrives.
A second search is unnecessary.
Listing paths is extra work.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the choice.
questions.rule: Store steps per node when only the target matters; loop by level when levels are analysed together.

questions.q: The other style keeps a ____ counter and raises it after each pass of the while loop.
questions.explain: Each pass is one level.
questions.rule: One pass, one level.

questions.q: Which problem needs the for loop over the queue size?
options: Finding the shortest path from the top-left to the bottom-right
Testing whether a node is reachable
Counting provinces
Finding the maximum value on each level of a binary tree
optionExplain: A target-only search can store steps.
Reachability needs no levels.
Provinces use DFS and seen.
Right: the whole level is examined together.
questions.explain: Which one treats levels as groups?
questions.rule: Store steps per node when only the target matters; loop by level when levels are analysed together.

questions.q: A level counter starts at 0 and is raised at the end of each while pass. The target is dequeued during the third pass. What is the counter?
optionExplain: Right: two passes have ended, so the counter reads 2.
Three would need the third pass to have ended.
Only one pass is counted.
The counter has moved from its start.
questions.explain: Count completed passes.
questions.rule: Store steps per node when only the target matters; loop by level when levels are analysed together.

questions.q: True or false: storing steps in each queue entry gives wrong shortest paths, so the level loop is required.
questions.explain: Both designs are correct; steps per entry is easier when only the target matters.
questions.rule: Both designs work.

questions.q: A problem asks for the sum of each level of a graph reached from a start node. Which design fits?
options: Steps in each entry, with no loop, since the step count already tells which level it is
A DFS with recursion only, since the sums can be added up as the recursion comes back up
The level loop, since each level is processed as a whole
Sorting the nodes by label, since nodes with nearby labels are on the same level
optionExplain: Steps alone do not group the nodes into whole levels for a sum.
DFS does not group by level.
Right: sums need all nodes of one level together.
Labels do not give levels.
questions.explain: A level sum needs each level as a whole, so the level loop fits. The book adds that in graphs BFS is mostly the better choice when you are asked to find the shortest path.
questions.rule: Store steps per node when only the target matters; loop by level when levels are analysed together.
questions.teaches: In graphs BFS is mostly better than over DFS when asked to find the shortest path.

questions.q: In a binary tree, what stops a BFS from the target node from reaching every node?
options: Trees have no edges, so a search from one node has nothing to follow to its neighbours
Leaves have too many neighbours, so the search cannot decide which of them to follow first
Nodes point only to their children, so the parent cannot be reached
BFS cannot run on trees, because trees are not graphs and have no levels to go through
optionExplain: Trees do have edges.
Leaves have none below them.
Right: movement is only downward.
BFS runs on trees.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the obstacle.
questions.rule: Record each node's parent with a DFS, then BFS from the target for k levels; the queue holds the answer.

questions.q: To move upward, first record each node's ____ with a traversal from the root.
questions.explain: The parent map gives the upward edge.
questions.rule: Parent record first.

questions.q: The tree is [3,5,1,6,2,0,8,null,null,7,4]. Target 5, k = 2. Which values does the code return?
options: 7, 4 and 1 in some order
6 and 2
3 only
0 and 8
optionExplain: Right: 7 and 4 are below 2, and 1 is reached through the parent 3.
Those are one step from 5.
3 is one step from 5.
Those are further away than 2 steps.

questions.rule: Record each node's parent with a DFS, then BFS from the target for k levels; the queue holds the answer.

questions.q: Same tree, target 5 and k = 1. Which values does the code return?
options: 7 and 4
1 only
6, 2 and 3 in some order
optionExplain: Those are two steps away.
Node 1 is two steps away.
The target is distance 0.

questions.explain: Three neighbours: left, right and parent.
questions.rule: Record each node's parent with a DFS, then BFS from the target for k levels; the queue holds the answer.

questions.q: True or false: without parent pointers, the nodes at distance k from the target can all be found by a BFS in the target's subtree.
questions.explain: Some nodes at distance k lie outside the subtree and are reached only through the parent.
questions.rule: Parents add the upward edges.

questions.q: Why does the code stop after the while loop and return the queue contents?
options: The queue holds all nodes of the tree, so the loop ends once every node has been taken out
After k levels the queue holds exactly the nodes at distance k
The queue holds the parents only, so the nodes at distance k are the ones above the target
The queue holds nodes sorted by value, so the nodes at distance k are the ones at the front
optionExplain: Only one level is held at a time.
Right: level k is the last level processed.
Both children and parents are held.
The queue is not sorted; it is in the order of discovery.
questions.explain: The queue is the current level.
questions.rule: Record each node's parent with a DFS, then BFS from the target for k levels; the queue holds the answer.
questions.teaches: Assigning new attributes like parent to node objects may be seen as bad practice in an interview, so a hash map from node to parent is the safer approach.

questions.q: A BFS queue begins with three nodes, all at step 0. What does each later node's step count measure?
options: The distance from the nearest of the three starting nodes
The distance from the first node only
The sum of distances to all three
The number of nodes seen so far
optionExplain: Right: all three are level 0.
The others are sources too.
Distances are not added.
Count of nodes is not distance.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the meaning.
questions.rule: Put every starting node in the queue at level 0; each node is then reached from its nearest source.

questions.q: In multi-source BFS, level ____ contains every starting node.
questions.explain: All sources are at distance zero.
questions.rule: Sources are level 0.

questions.q: A path of 5 nodes is numbered 0 to 4. A BFS starts from nodes 0 and 4. What is the BFS distance of node 2?
optionExplain: Node 1 and node 3 are one step away.
That would be too far from the nearest end.
Right: node 2 is two steps from each end.
Node 4 is the other end.
questions.explain: Use the nearest source.
questions.rule: Put every starting node in the queue at level 0; each node is then reached from its nearest source.

questions.q: A path of 6 nodes is numbered 0 to 5, with BFS sources 0 and 5. Which node has the largest distance?
options: Node 3 only, at distance 3
Node 2 or node 3, both at distance 2
Node 1, at distance 1
Node 0, at distance 0
optionExplain: Node 3 is only 2 from node 5.
Right: min(2, 3) = 2 for node 2 and min(3, 2) = 2 for node 3.
Node 1 is the closest to 0.
A source has distance 0.
questions.explain: Take the nearest source for each node.
questions.rule: Put every starting node in the queue at level 0; each node is then reached from its nearest source.

questions.q: True or false: starting a BFS from several nodes breaks the guarantee that each node is reached in the fewest steps.
questions.explain: The guarantee holds from the nearest source, since all sources form level 0.
questions.rule: All sources are level 0.

questions.q: Why must the starting nodes be placed in seen before the loop starts?
options: So the queue is sorted
So the target is found sooner
So their neighbours are skipped
So they are not queued again with a larger distance
optionExplain: Sorting is not needed.
It does not affect the target.
Neighbours must still be explored.
Right: it protects their distance 0.
questions.explain: Seen protects the sources.
questions.rule: Put every starting node in the queue at level 0; each node is then reached from its nearest source.
questions.teaches: There is nothing stopping us from having multiple nodes in the 0th level; the single source in earlier examples was only a special case.

questions.q: To find the nearest 0 for every cell, where does the BFS start?
options: At the top-left cell only
At all the 0 cells together
At each 1 cell in turn
At the largest cell
optionExplain: One cell is not enough.
Right: all zeros are sources at level 0.
Separate searches repeat work.
Size is not a criterion.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the start.
questions.rule: Queue every 0 at level 0; the first time BFS reaches a 1, its steps value is the answer.

questions.q: When BFS first reaches a 1, its answer is the current number of ____.
questions.explain: The steps value is the distance.
questions.rule: First arrival gives distance.

questions.q: mat = [[0,1,1,1]]. What does the code return?
optionExplain: Only the first 1 is at distance 1.
Distances grow away from the 0.
The 0 stays 0.
Right: the distances from the single 0 grow by 1.
questions.explain: Count steps from the 0.
questions.rule: Queue every 0 at level 0; the first time BFS reaches a 1, its steps value is the answer.

questions.q: mat = [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,1,0]]. What does the top-left cell become?
optionExplain: Right: it is 2 rows and 2 columns from the 0, so 4 steps.
That is too small to reach.
It would need a diagonal move.
The cell is not a 0.
questions.explain: Add the row and column gaps.
questions.rule: Queue every 0 at level 0; the first time BFS reaches a 1, its steps value is the answer.

questions.q: True or false: seen is not needed in this BFS, since each 1 is reached once anyway.
questions.explain: Without seen, cells could be queued repeatedly and answers overwritten by larger values.
questions.rule: Seen protects the first answer.

questions.q: A matrix has no 0 at all. What does a BFS started from all zeros do?
options: It visits every cell once
It sets every cell to 0
It starts with an empty queue and changes nothing
It raises an error at the first row
optionExplain: There is no start cell.
Cells keep their values.
Right: nothing can be queued.
The loop does not run.
questions.explain: Think about an empty queue.
questions.rule: Queue every 0 at level 0; the first time BFS reaches a 1, its steps value is the answer.
questions.teaches: If a square x with value 1 has its nearest 0 at y, walking x to y and y to x take the same number of steps, so it makes no difference which way you search.

questions.q: You may remove up to k obstacles on the way. What must each BFS entry hold besides the cell?
options: The cell's colour
The row number alone
How many removals remain
The total number of obstacles
optionExplain: Colour does not matter.
The row is part of the cell.
Right: the rules depend on the removals left.
That count is fixed.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card defines state.
questions.rule: If the node does not fully describe your options, extend the state and store the whole state in seen.

questions.q: Seen must store the whole ____, not only the node.
questions.explain: States are what must not repeat.
questions.rule: Seen stores states.

questions.q: Moving from (r, c) with remain = 2 onto an obstacle cell. What state comes next?
options: The new cell with remain = 1
The new cell with remain = 2
The new cell with remain = 3
No move is allowed
optionExplain: Right: removing an obstacle costs one removal.
That is the move onto a 0.
Removals do not increase.
remain is above 0, so it is allowed.
questions.explain: Walls cost a removal.
questions.rule: If the node does not fully describe your options, extend the state and store the whole state in seen.

questions.q: From (r, c) with remain = 0, a neighbour is an obstacle. What does the code do with it?
options: Queues it with remain = -1
Queues it with remain = 0
Stops the whole search
Skips it
optionExplain: That would break the rule.
That would keep removals unused.
Other neighbours remain.
Right: the else branch continues.
questions.explain: No removals, no wall.
questions.rule: If the node does not fully describe your options, extend the state and store the whole state in seen.

questions.q: True or false: the same cell reached with remain = 2 and with remain = 0 counts as the same state.
questions.explain: The two states differ in what can be done next, so seen must keep them apart.
questions.rule: States differ if options differ.

questions.q: A 2D grid search also lets you break at most 3 walls and carries a count of walls broken. What does seen hold?
options: Only (row, column) pairs
(row, column, walls broken) triples
Only the walls-broken counts
Only the cells that are walls
optionExplain: That loses the count.
Right: all three values define the state.
That loses the cell.
That loses non-wall cells.
questions.explain: Everything in the state goes in seen.
questions.rule: If the node does not fully describe your options, extend the state and store the whole state in seen.
questions.teaches: Seen actually prevents us from visiting the same state twice; we only used nodes before because the node entirely described the state.

questions.q: Seen stops any state from being visited twice. What does the BFS cost therefore depend on?
options: The number of states
The number of leaves
The largest node label
The depth of recursion
optionExplain: Right: each state is processed once.
Leaves are a tree idea.
Labels do not set the cost.
BFS does not recurse.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the count.
questions.rule: The cost is the number of states times the work per state.

questions.q: With state (node, remain), the number of states is nodes times the number of ____ values.
questions.explain: Each pair is a state.
questions.rule: Multiply the ranges.

questions.q: A 10 by 20 grid with k = 3 has a state count of ____ if remain takes the k values.
questions.rule: m times n times k.

questions.q: A 5 by 5 grid is searched with state (cell, colour) and 2 colours. How many states exist at most?
optionExplain: That ignores the colour.
That adds instead of multiplying.
Right: 25 x 2 = 50.
That is neither product nor sum.
questions.explain: Cells times colours.
questions.rule: The cost is the number of states times the work per state.

questions.q: True or false: adding a state variable with range 2 changes the order of the time complexity.
questions.explain: A factor of 2 is a constant, so the order stays the same.
questions.rule: Constant factors do not change the order.

questions.q: In the obstacle problem, k is raised from 5 to 10. What happens to the worst-case number of states?
options: It stays the same
It doubles
It grows by 5
It grows by a factor of 10
optionExplain: k is part of the product.
Right: the count is m x n x k.
Adding 5 to k is a doubling here.
k alone changes by a factor of 2.
questions.explain: Proportional to k.
questions.rule: The cost is the number of states times the work per state.
questions.teaches: The time complexity for graph algorithms is O(nodes + edges) in theory, but technically it should be written with s, the number of states, in place of nodes.

questions.q: Edges must alternate in colour along the path. Which extra value does the BFS state need?
options: The number of red edges in the graph
The label of node 0
The weight of each edge
The colour of the next edge to use
optionExplain: That count is fixed.
The start is known.
Edges are unweighted.
Right: it decides which edges are allowed.

questions.rule: Use (node, colour, steps) states, flip the colour on each move, and keep the minimum steps per node.

questions.q: To flip a colour coded as 0 or 1, use 1 ____ colour.

questions.q: n = 3, red edges [[0,1],[1,2]], no blue edges. What does the code return?
optionExplain: That uses two red edges in a row.
Right: after the red edge 0 to 1, a blue edge is needed to reach 2, and none exists.
Node 1 is reached with the red edge.
Node 2 is unreachable.
questions.explain: Alternate the colours.
questions.rule: Use (node, colour, steps) states, flip the colour on each move, and keep the minimum steps per node.

questions.q: n = 3, red [[0,1]], blue [[1,2]]. What does the code return?
optionExplain: Node 2 is reachable.
Node 1 is reachable.
Node 2 needs two steps.
Right: red then blue alternates.
questions.explain: Red, then blue.
questions.rule: Use (node, colour, steps) states, flip the colour on each move, and keep the minimum steps per node.

questions.q: True or false: the queue should start with only (0, 0, 0), because node 0 has one colour.
questions.explain: Node 0 can leave by either colour, so both starting states are queued.
questions.rule: Start with both colours.

questions.q: Why is the initial queue allowed to hold two entries for node 0?
options: The level 0 can contain any number of states
Node 0 is visited twice by design
Two nodes share the label 0
The graph has two copies of node 0
optionExplain: Right: level 0 is a set of starting states.
Seen records states, so both are new.
There is only one node 0.
There is one graph.
questions.explain: Level 0 is not limited to one entry.
questions.rule: Use (node, colour, steps) states, flip the colour on each move, and keep the minimum steps per node.
questions.teaches: It doesn't matter which colour is coded as 0 and which as 1, since the code only needs the two values to be different.

questions.q: Which question is not part of the BFS setup checklist?
options: What are the nodes?
What are the edges?
How many comments the code will have
Where should the BFS start?
optionExplain: Nodes must be named.
Edges must be named.
Right: comments do not shape the algorithm.
The start must be chosen.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card lists the questions.
questions.rule: Before coding a BFS, say what the nodes, edges, extra state and start are.

questions.q: One question asks whether a state ____ is needed besides the node.
questions.explain: Extra state may be needed.
questions.rule: Check for extra state.

questions.q: In the 01 Matrix problem, where should the BFS start?
options: At the top-left cell
At the bottom-right cell
At all the 0 cells
At the largest 1
optionExplain: That is the binary matrix start.
No fixed corner is the source.
Right: the source is the set of zeros.
Size is not a criterion.
questions.explain: Use the checklist.
questions.rule: Before coding a BFS, say what the nodes, edges, extra state and start are.

questions.q: In the obstacle problem, what are the nodes of the BFS?
options: (cell, removals remaining) pairs
Rows only
Obstacles only
Whole paths
optionExplain: Right: the state includes the remaining removals.
Rows alone lose the column.
Open cells are nodes too.
Paths are not nodes.
questions.explain: Think about the state.
questions.rule: Before coding a BFS, say what the nodes, edges, extra state and start are.

questions.q: True or false: every BFS problem needs a state variable besides the node.
questions.explain: Many problems need only the node. A state variable is added when the rules need one.
questions.rule: Add state only when needed.

questions.q: A problem has a robot that moves on a grid and carries a key, which changes what cells are open. What goes in the state?
options: The cell only
The key only
The step count only
The cell and whether the key is held
optionExplain: Key matters.
The cell matters.
Steps are not state.
Right: openness depends on the key.
questions.explain: Include what changes your options.
questions.rule: Before coding a BFS, say what the nodes, edges, extra state and start are.
questions.teaches: Every problem in the previous article on graph DFS could also have been solved with a BFS.

questions.q: A problem has no graph in its input but moves between states. How can it be modelled as a graph?
options: States are edges and transitions are nodes
States are nodes and transitions are edges
Only arrays can be nodes
It cannot be modelled as a graph
optionExplain: The roles are swapped.
Right: this is the card's rule of thumb.
Any element can be a node.
A graph is any abstract relationship.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the mapping.
questions.rule: If a problem moves between states, model the states as nodes and the transitions as edges.

questions.q: A problem asking for the fewest operations is a strong candidate for ____.
questions.explain: BFS finds the minimum steps.
questions.rule: Fewest steps suggests BFS.

questions.q: A puzzle asks for the minimum number of moves to turn one word into another, changing one letter at a time. What are the edges?
options: Pairs of words that differ by one letter
Pairs of words with the same length
Every pair of words
Words that start with the same letter
optionExplain: Right: one move links two words.
That would join almost everything.
That links every word to every other.
That is not a move.
questions.explain: Edges are single moves.
questions.rule: If a problem moves between states, model the states as nodes and the transitions as edges.

questions.q: A state graph has 10 readings and each reading connects to its 4 single-turn neighbours. Which search fits a fewest-moves question?
options: Sorting the readings
A DFS taking the first path found
BFS from the starting reading
Counting the edges only
optionExplain: Sorting does not give moves.
The first path may be long.
Right: BFS gives the minimum number of moves.
Counting edges gives no path.
questions.explain: Fewest moves means BFS.
questions.rule: If a problem moves between states, model the states as nodes and the transitions as edges.

questions.q: True or false: every graph problem gives its input as an adjacency list, a matrix or an array of edges.
questions.explain: Implicit graphs are given in other forms, and the graph must be recognised by modelling the states.
questions.rule: Model states and transitions.

questions.q: In earlier graph problems, what usually made it easy to see that a graph was involved?
options: The answer was always a number
The input format matched a known graph format
The input was sorted
The input was small
optionExplain: Answers vary.
Right: it was usually a giveaway.
Sorting is unrelated.
Size is unrelated.
questions.explain: Look at the input format.
questions.rule: If a problem moves between states, model the states as nodes and the transitions as edges.
questions.teaches: In earlier problems the input format was usually a giveaway: some problems told us explicitly we were dealing with a graph, while others had a story like cities connected by roads.

questions.q: In the lock problem, two lock readings are joined by an edge when what is true?
options: They have the same digit sum
They share the first digit
Their difference is 1000
They differ in exactly one wheel, by 1
optionExplain: That is not a move.
A move may change any wheel.
That is only one kind of move.
Right: that is one move.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card defines the edges.
questions.rule: BFS from 0000 over single-wheel turns, with deadends already in seen.

questions.q: The BFS starts from the reading ____.
questions.explain: The lock starts at 0000.
questions.rule: Start at 0000.

questions.q: With no deadends and target 1111, How many moves does the code return?
optionExplain: One move changes one wheel.
Right: each of four wheels needs one turn.
Two wheels remain.
That would turn too many times.
questions.explain: One turn per wheel.
questions.rule: BFS from 0000 over single-wheel turns, with deadends already in seen.

questions.q: With the single deadend 8888 and target 0009, what does the code return?
optionExplain: That wheel wraps in one step.
The target is reachable.
The target is not the start.
Right: turning the last wheel from 0 down to 9 is one move.
questions.explain: Wrap-around makes 0 and 9 neighbours.
questions.rule: BFS from 0000 over single-wheel turns, with deadends already in seen.

questions.q: True or false: a BFS may visit a deadend reading as long as it does not stop there.
questions.explain: A blocked lock cannot turn, so deadends are treated as already seen and never entered.
questions.rule: Deadends are never visited.

questions.q: What does the code return when 0000 is in deadends?
options: -1, because the lock cannot move at all
The distance to target ignoring the deadend
An error from the queue
optionExplain: Right: the first line checks it.
Zero would mean the target is 0000.
The deadend blocks the start.
A check prevents an error.
questions.explain: Check the start first.
questions.rule: BFS from 0000 over single-wheel turns, with deadends already in seen.
questions.teaches: The solution adds an early check: if the start reading 0000 is itself a deadend, return -1 before any search.

questions.q: How many neighbours does a lock reading have, ignoring deadends?
optionExplain: That counts only one direction.
10 is the number of digits.
Right: 4 wheels, up and down.
That multiplies 4 and 10.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card counts them.
questions.rule: Each reading has 8 neighbours from 4 wheels turned up or down with modulo 10; put deadends in seen first.

questions.explain: Modulo wraps the digit.
questions.rule: Wrap-around uses modulo 10.

questions.q: From the reading '0000', which neighbour is produced by turning the first wheel down by 1?
optionExplain: That turns it up.
That changes the last wheel.
Right: (0 - 1) % 10 = 9 in the first position.
That is the reading itself.
questions.explain: Change only the first digit.
questions.rule: Each reading has 8 neighbours from 4 wheels turned up or down with modulo 10; put deadends in seen first.

questions.q: How many distinct neighbours does '0000' have?
optionExplain: Right: the first, second, third and fourth wheel each give an up and a down reading.
Up and down both exist.
Wrap-around gives both directions.
Each wheel gives two.
questions.explain: Four wheels, two directions.
questions.rule: Each reading has 8 neighbours from 4 wheels turned up or down with modulo 10; put deadends in seen first.

questions.q: True or false: the modulo operator is needed only for the digit 9.
questions.explain: It is needed for both ends: 9 wraps to 0 on the way up and 0 wraps to 9 on the way down.
questions.rule: Both ends wrap.

questions.q: What is the benefit of putting deadends into seen before the search?
options: The search becomes depth-first, since marked nodes are handled before the unmarked ones
The queue no longer needs steps, since each deadend already stores the distance in seen
Deadends are removed from the target, so the search can end on any of the other nodes
No separate deadend check is needed when queuing neighbours
optionExplain: The queue keeps its order, so the search stays breadth-first.
Steps are still tracked.
The target is unchanged.
Right: seen already blocks them.
questions.explain: Seen already stops visits, so deadends placed in it need no extra check. The book notes the lock states are nodes and the allowed moves are edges.
questions.rule: Each reading has 8 neighbours from 4 wheels turned up or down with modulo 10; put deadends in seen first.
questions.teaches: If a problem involves transitioning between states, the states can be nodes and the transition criteria can be edges.

questions.q: A lock has n wheels with 10 digits each. How many different readings (states) exist?
options: 10 times n
10 to the power n
n squared
n factorial
optionExplain: That is linear in n.
Right: each wheel has 10 values.
That ignores the 10 digits.
Order is not relevant.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card counts states.
questions.rule: Time is the number of states times the work per state: 10^n states, O(n^2) each.

questions.q: A 4-wheel lock has ____ states in total.
questions.rule: 10 to the n.

questions.q: A lock has 3 wheels. How many readings are there?
optionExplain: Right: 10^3.
That is 10 x 3.
That is 10^2.
That is 10^4.
questions.explain: Raise 10 to the number of wheels.
questions.rule: Time is the number of states times the work per state: 10^n states, O(n^2) each.

questions.q: Per state, the code loops over n wheels and builds a string of length n for each of 2 turns. What is the work per state?
options: O(n)
O(n squared)
O(2 to the n)
optionExplain: That leaves out string copying.
It depends on n.
Right: n wheels times O(n) string work.
No exponent arises.
questions.explain: n loops, each O(n).
questions.rule: Time is the number of states times the work per state: 10^n states, O(n^2) each.

questions.q: True or false: the lock BFS cost depends on the number of deadends only when the number of wheels grows.
questions.explain: The deadend set costs O(d) at any wheel count, and the rest is constant for 4 wheels.
questions.rule: O(d) is separate.

questions.q: In a language with mutable strings, building a neighbour costs O(1) per changed digit. How does the per-state work change?
options: It stays O(n squared)
It reduces to O(n)
It becomes O(1)
It becomes O(10 to the n)
optionExplain: The string copy no longer costs O(n).
Right: only the loop over wheels remains.
The wheel loop still runs.
That is the state count.
questions.explain: Mutable strings remove the copy cost per neighbour. The book adds that with 4 wheels the time is technically O(d), for turning deadends into a set.
questions.rule: Time is the number of states times the work per state: 10^n states, O(n^2) each.
questions.teaches: With a fixed 4 wheels the time is technically O(d) for building the deadends set, because everything else is constant.

questions.q: In the division equations problem, what does a node of the graph stand for?
options: An equation
A query
A value from the values array
A variable
optionExplain: Equations are edges.
Queries are traversals.
Values are weights.
Right: the equations connect variables.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card names the nodes.
questions.rule: Variables are nodes; each equation adds a weighted edge and its reciprocal; each query is a traversal.

questions.q: For the equation x / y = val, the edge from y to x has weight 1 / ____.
questions.explain: The reverse ratio is the reciprocal.
questions.rule: Add the reciprocal edge.

questions.q: equations [['a','b'],['b','c']] and values [2.0, 3.0]. What does the query ['a','c'] return?
optionExplain: Weights are multiplied, not added.
Right: 2.0 times 3.0 = 6.0.
That divides them.
A path from a to c exists.
questions.explain: Multiply the weights on the path.
questions.rule: Variables are nodes; each equation adds a weighted edge and its reciprocal; each query is a traversal.

questions.q: Same equations. What does the query ['b','a'] return?
optionExplain: That is a / b.
A reverse edge exists.
That would be b / b.
questions.explain: Use the reciprocal edge.
questions.rule: Variables are nodes; each equation adds a weighted edge and its reciprocal; each query is a traversal.

questions.q: True or false: edges can be directed only, because a / b = 2 says nothing about b / a.
questions.explain: It does imply b / a = 1 / 2, so the graph needs both directions.
questions.rule: Add reciprocal edges.

questions.q: Equations: a / b = 2.0 and c / d = 3.0. What does the query ['a','d'] return?
options: -1, since a and d are in different components
6.0, since a / d is the product of the two ratios 2.0 and 3.0 that were given
0.67, since a / d is the ratio 2.0 divided by 3.0, which is what the two equations give
1.0, since the query starts and ends on the same kind of letter so the ratio is one
optionExplain: Right: no path joins them, so no value can be derived.
That multiplies ratios of unrelated pairs; no path joins a and d.
That divides unrelated ratios; no path joins a and d.
A ratio of 1.0 is for a / a, and a and d are different variables.
questions.explain: Look for a path.
questions.rule: Variables are nodes; each equation adds a weighted edge and its reciprocal; each query is a traversal.
questions.teaches: The graph can be stored as a hash map where each node maps to another hash map holding its relationships; for example a maps to a hash map holding b: 5.

questions.q: A traversal for a query starts at the numerator. What is the starting ratio?
options: The first weight
optionExplain: Zero would erase every product.
No weight is used yet.
Right: a / a = 1.
-1 means no answer.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card states it.
questions.rule: Carry a running product from the numerator; the product on reaching the denominator is the answer.

questions.q: Chaining a / b and b / c cancels the variable ____.
questions.explain: The middle variable cancels.
questions.rule: The middle cancels.

questions.q: a / b = 5 and b / c = 2. What is a / c?
optionExplain: That adds the ratios.
That divides them.
Right: 5 x 2.
That subtracts them.
questions.explain: Multiply the ratios.
questions.rule: Carry a running product from the numerator; the product on reaching the denominator is the answer.

questions.q: a / b = 4 and c / b = 2. What does the traversal return for a / c?
optionExplain: Right: a -> b gives 4, then b -> c gives 1 / 2, so 4 x 0.5 = 2.0.
That multiplies 4 and 2.
That is c / a.
That adds them.
questions.explain: Use the reciprocal for b to c.
questions.rule: Carry a running product from the numerator; the product on reaching the denominator is the answer.

questions.q: True or false: the traversal must add the weights along the path.
questions.explain: Ratios chain by multiplication, so the weights are multiplied.
questions.rule: Multiply the weights.

questions.q: Does it matter whether the traversal for each query is a BFS or a DFS?
options: Yes, only BFS finds the right product, because it reaches the denominator by the shortest path
Yes, only DFS multiplies correctly, because it follows one path all the way to the denominator
Yes, a stack changes the weights, because the edges are multiplied in the reverse order
No, because any path to the denominator gives the same product
optionExplain: BFS is not required; any path gives the same product.
DFS is not required either.
The weights do not change with the data structure.
Right: only reachability and the product matter.
questions.explain: Any path will do.
questions.rule: Carry a running product from the numerator; the product on reaching the denominator is the answer.
questions.teaches: For this problem, doing a BFS or DFS for each query does not matter; the code uses a stack.

questions.q: What is a weight in a graph?
options: The number of nodes
A value associated with an edge
A label on the root
The degree of a node
optionExplain: That is the graph size.
Right: weights belong to edges.
Roots are a tree idea.
Degree counts edges.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card defines it.
questions.rule: A weight is a value on an edge; plain BFS and DFS treat every edge alike.

questions.q: An unweighted graph treats every edge as one ____.
questions.explain: All edges count equally.
questions.rule: No weights means one step per edge.

questions.q: In the equation graph, a / b = 4. What is the weight of the edge from b to a?
optionExplain: That is the forward edge.
Ratios are positive here.
That would be a / a.
questions.explain: Take the reciprocal.
questions.rule: A weight is a value on an edge; plain BFS and DFS treat every edge alike.

questions.q: Edge costs differ: one path has 2 edges costing 10 and 10. Another has 3 edges costing 1 each. Which has the smaller total?
options: The 2-edge path, which costs 20
They tie at 3
The 3-edge path, which costs 3
The 2-edge path, which costs 2
optionExplain: BFS would pick this one.
The totals are not equal.
Right: fewer edges does not mean smaller cost.
20 is the larger total.
questions.explain: Add the weights.
questions.rule: A weight is a value on an edge; plain BFS and DFS treat every edge alike.

questions.q: True or false: plain BFS gives the smallest total weight in any weighted graph.
questions.explain: BFS minimises the number of edges, not the sum of weights.
questions.rule: BFS counts edges.

questions.q: Why does the division problem not need a weighted shortest path algorithm?
options: The weights are all equal, so every path gives the same product however it is chosen
It needs any path's product, not the cheapest one
The graph has no edges, so the weights are looked up from a table in place of a path
The answer is always 1, so no weight has to be multiplied along any of the paths
optionExplain: Weights differ from edge to edge.
Right: all paths give the same product.
Equations are edges.
Answers vary with the query.
questions.explain: Any path gives the same product, so no cheapest path is needed. In the book's example a / b = 5 and b / c = 2, so the multiplier along a, b, c is 10.
questions.rule: A weight is a value on an edge; plain BFS and DFS treat every edge alike.
questions.teaches: In the book's example a / b = 5 and b / c = 2, so moving from a to b to c multiplies by 5 times 2 = 10, which gives a / c = 10.

questions.q: Each query runs one full traversal costing O(n + e). With q queries, what is the total time?
options: O(n + e + q)
O(q squared)
O(n times e)
O(q times (n + e))
optionExplain: That adds instead of multiplying.
q alone does not capture the graph.
It is not a product of n and e.
Right: q traversals.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card gives the bound.
questions.rule: Time is O(q(n + e)) because every query runs its own traversal.

questions.q: The graph is built ____ and reused by all queries.
questions.explain: Only the traversals repeat.
questions.rule: Build once, search q times.

questions.q: With n + e = 50 and q = 20 queries, the number of node-and-edge visits in the worst case is ____.
questions.rule: q times (n + e).

questions.q: The number of queries doubles and the graph stays the same. What happens to the time?
options: It stays the same
It doubles
It quadruples
It halves
optionExplain: Each new query adds a traversal.
Right: it is linear in q.
The growth is linear.
More queries cost more.
questions.explain: q is a linear factor.
questions.rule: Time is O(q(n + e)) because every query runs its own traversal.

questions.q: True or false: the seen set is shared by all queries to save time.
questions.explain: Each query needs its own fresh seen set, because a node seen by one query may be needed by the next.
questions.rule: Fresh seen per query.

questions.q: Which structures account for the O(n + e) space of the solution?
options: Only the queries
Only the output
The sorted equations
The graph, the seen set and the stack
optionExplain: Queries are separate input.
The output is not counted as extra.
The equations are not sorted.
Right: all three grow with n and e.
questions.explain: Three structures use the space: the graph, seen and the call stack, giving O(n + e). The book adds that either BFS or DFS can answer each query.
questions.rule: Time is O(q(n + e)) because every query runs its own traversal.
questions.teaches: A query can be answered by a BFS or a DFS; the book says it does not matter which one is used.

questions.q: A program keeps a changing collection of 1,000,000 numbers. How many steps should reading the smallest one take, with the best-suited structure?
options: About 20 steps, the logarithm of the size
About 1,000 steps, the square root of the size
A constant number of steps, whatever the size
About 1,000,000 steps, one look at every number
optionExplain: Logarithmic time is the cost of adding or removing, not of reading the minimum.
Nothing in a heap's costs involves a square root.
Right: a heap keeps its minimum ready, so reading it is O(1).
Looking at everything is what an unordered list needs, not a heap.
questions.explain: A heap keeps its minimum at the top, so finding it is O(1). The card next shows what it costs to keep it there.
questions.rule: A heap finds its minimum in O(1) and adds or removes in O(log n).

questions.q: Removing the minimum element from a heap of n elements takes O(____) time.
questions.explain: The heap must repair itself after the removal, which costs logarithmic time.
questions.rule: Add and remove are O(log n); find is O(1).

questions.q: A scheduler keeps job deadlines in a heap of n entries, earliest on top. It adds one deadline, then reads the earliest. What is the cost of those two steps?
options: O(log n), because the add costs that much and the read is constant
O(1), because the earliest deadline is always ready and so is the add
O(n), because the add must scan the whole heap for a place
O(n log n), because reading the top re-sorts every entry first
optionExplain: Right: O(log n) for the add plus O(1) for the read is O(log n).
The read is O(1), but the add is O(log n), so the total is not constant.
An add repairs the heap along one path; it does not scan everything.
Reading the top is a lookup, and nothing is re-sorted.
questions.explain: An add costs O(log n) and a read of the minimum costs O(1); the larger term decides the total.
questions.rule: Add the costs and keep the larger term.

questions.q: True or false: In this course a heap is the abstract idea and a priority queue is the particular data structure that implements it.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: a priority queue is the abstract data structure and a heap is one way to implement it. People use the terms interchangeably, and the course says heap.
questions.rule: A priority queue is abstract; a heap implements it.

questions.q: True or false: Because a heap finds its minimum in O(1), it can also check whether a given value is stored in O(1).
questions.explain: The O(1) promise is for the minimum only. Add, remove the minimum and find the minimum are the listed operations; none of them is a lookup of another value (our reading).
questions.rule: O(1) is promised for the extreme element only.

questions.q: A game must serve the highest score first. What does the course say about a heap for this?
options: A heap only ever finds minimums, so the scores need a different structure
It can, but only by re-sorting the scores each time the top is read
It can, but reading the top then costs O(log n) instead of O(1)
It can be set up to find and remove the maximum, as a max heap
optionExplain: The card listed only the min operations, but the heap is not limited to them.
No sorting is needed; the heap keeps the extreme ready on its own.
The costs stay the same for a max heap.
Right: the same container can be set up to find and remove the maximum.
questions.explain: A heap can be configured to find and remove the maximum instead of the minimum. The min version is called a min heap and the max version a max heap, with the same costs.
questions.rule: A heap finds its minimum in O(1) and adds or removes in O(log n).
questions.teaches: A heap can be configured to find and remove the maximum instead of the minimum; the min version is called a min heap and the max version a max heap.

questions.q: In most problems that use a heap, what role does the heap play, according to the course?
options: The whole solution: the task is only to build the heap and read it
A helper inside a larger algorithm that supplies extremes
A replacement for hash maps, which it makes unnecessary in every problem
A way to sort the final answer once the real work is complete
optionExplain: Most problems also need counting, simulating or comparing around the heap.
Right: like a hash map, a heap is usually only a tool used within an algorithm.
The course treats the two as tools that often appear together, not rivals.
The heap is used while the algorithm runs, not only at the end.
questions.explain: The course says that, as with hash maps, a problem that uses a heap is normally not solely about the heap; the heap helps the algorithm do something efficiently.
questions.rule: A heap finds its minimum in O(1) and adds or removes in O(log n).
questions.teaches: As with a hash map, a heap is usually a tool inside a larger algorithm: when a heap is used, the problem is normally not solely focused on the heap.

questions.q: A min heap is stored in an array. Where is its smallest element?
options: At the last position, since elements are appended in order
At the first position, index 0, the root of the tree
At the middle position, so both halves are balanced
Anywhere; its position depends on the order of insertion
optionExplain: Appending puts new elements at the end, but the heap rearranges them.
Right: the root is the first array element and holds the minimum.
Nothing in a heap aims at a balanced middle.
The minimum is always reachable at the same place, whatever the insertion order.
questions.explain: The smallest element is always the root, at index 0. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A binary heap is a complete binary tree in an array where every parent is no larger than its children, so the root is the minimum.

questions.q: In a binary heap stored as an array, the root is the element at index ____.
questions.explain: Index 0 holds the root, and the rest of the tree is laid out after it.
questions.rule: The root sits at index 0.

questions.q: Which description is a valid min-heap tree?
options: Root 1 with children 4 and 2; node 4 has a single child 3
Root 5 with children 3 and 8; node 3 has a single child 9
Root 2 with children 6 and 3; node 6 has children 4 and 7
Root 1 with children 4 and 2; node 4 has children 9 and 6
optionExplain: 3 is larger than the root 1, but smaller than its own parent 4, so the rule fails at that node.
The root 5 is larger than its child 3, so the root is not the minimum.
Node 6 has a child 4 that is smaller than it, which breaks the rule at that node.
Right: every parent, 1 and 4, is no larger than its children.
questions.explain: Check each parent against its own children, not only against the root.
questions.rule: Compare every parent with its own children.

questions.q: True or false: In a min heap stored in an array of three elements, the second element must not be larger than the third.
questions.explain: Only parents are compared with their children. The array 1, 3, 2 is a valid min heap although 3 comes before 2 (our reading: no rule orders siblings).
questions.rule: The array of a heap is not sorted.

questions.q: Why does the rule that every parent is no larger than its children put the minimum at the root?
options: Every node reaches the root through parents that are no larger
The array is kept fully sorted, so its first element is the smallest
The root is picked as the smallest when the heap is built and never changes
Each node is compared with all of its siblings, which forces the order
optionExplain: Right: following the chain of parents upward never goes below the root's value.
A heap keeps only the parent-child order, not a full sort.
Adds and removals change the root, so it is kept right by the rule, not fixed once.
Siblings are not compared with each other.
questions.explain: The parent rule applies along every path to the root, so the root cannot be beaten by any descendant.
questions.rule: The parent rule, applied along each path, makes the root the minimum.

questions.q: Is a binary heap in an array the only way to implement a heap?
options: Yes; every heap is by definition a binary tree stored in an array
No; the most popular way is a hash map from each priority to its items
No; several exist, and the array-based binary heap is the most popular
Yes; the child positions can only be found through index arithmetic
optionExplain: The card described one implementation, not the definition of a heap.

questions.q: In an array heap the root is at index 0. Which two indices hold the root's children?

Indices 0 and 1

Indices 1 and 3

questions.q: A teammate adds left and right pointer fields to every element of an array-based heap. How does the course make the links instead?

questions.q: One more element is added to a min heap of 1,000,000 elements. How does the number of repair operations grow with the size?

In proportion to the logarithm of the size

questions.explain: Repairs scale logarithmically with the size. The card next gives the costs.
questions.rule: Adds and removals repair the heap in O(log n), and an existing array becomes a heap in O(n).

questions.q: Converting an existing array of n elements into a heap takes ____ time.
questions.explain: The course says an existing array can be converted in linear time.
questions.rule: Building from an array is O(n).

questions.q: A job system adds n jobs one at a time to an empty heap, each add costing O(log n) at most. What is the total worst-case time?
