O(n log n), since there are n adds of O(log n) each
O(n), because each add is a single swap on average
O(n^2), because each add rescans the whole heap
optionExplain: Each add still pays its own logarithmic cost.
Right: n adds times O(log n) gives O(n log n). Our reading: this is an upper bound.
Worst-case adds are logarithmic, not constant; an average of one swap does not bound the worst case.
An add repairs one path, never a full rescan.
questions.explain: Multiply the number of adds by the cost of one add. Converting the whole array at once is the O(n) alternative.
questions.rule: n adds of O(log n) each cost O(n log n).

questions.q: True or false: After a new smallest value is added to a min heap, finding the new minimum still takes O(1).
questions.explain: The add pays O(log n) to repair the heap, and then the minimum is at the top again, so reading it is O(1).
questions.rule: Repair on change, constant lookup afterwards.

questions.q: A reviewer says adding to a heap is O(1), because reading the minimum is O(1). What is the flaw?
options: Adds are O(1), but removals shift the whole array, so they cost O(n)
Reading the minimum is really O(log n), so adds cannot be cheaper
An add compares the new element with every other one, so it costs O(n)
Reading is O(1), but each add needs a repair that costs O(log n)
optionExplain: Removals are repaired along a path too and cost O(log n).
The read of the minimum is the O(1) operation.
An add follows one path; it does not compare against every element.
Right: the O(1) read is paid for by O(log n) work on each change.
questions.explain: The heap keeps its minimum ready by doing logarithmic repair work at every add and removal.
questions.rule: Cheap reads are paid for by repairs on each change.

questions.q: A service must build a heap from 2 million existing scores at startup. What does the course say about doing that?
options: Add the scores one by one, because no faster way to build a heap exists
Sort the array first, since a heap can only be built from sorted data

questions.rule: Adds and removals repair the heap in O(log n), and an existing array becomes a heap in O(n).
questions.teaches: Converting an array into a heap in linear time is complicated, but some major programming languages have built-in methods to do it.

questions.q: An algorithm finds the largest of n numbers by scanning, removes it, and repeats until none are left. What is its total time?

O(n log n), since each scan of the numbers is logarithmic
O(log n), since each scan stops as soon as it meets the largest

A scan of unordered numbers is linear, not logarithmic.
A scan has to look at every number to be sure of the largest.

questions.rule: If a problem needs the max or min of a changing collection again and again, a heap turns O(n^2) into O(n log n).

questions.q: Repeating a full scan of n items n times takes O(____) time.
questions.explain: n scans of n items each is n times n.
questions.rule: n scans of n items cost O(n^2).

questions.q: For n = 1,000,000, about how many times fewer steps is n log2(n) than n^2?

questions.rule: The gain is n / log2(n).

questions.q: Which tasks suit a heap? Select all that apply.

Report the smallest of a fixed list once

questions.q: n drops from 1,000,000 to 1,000. About how many times fewer steps is n log2(n) than n^2 now?

About 100 times fewer, so the gain is smaller
About 10 times fewer
About 1,000 times fewer

questions.q: A print shop prints its longest job next each time. Each printed job leaves a smaller job that rejoins the queue. Why does sorting the jobs once not replace a heap?

A sorted list cannot report its largest in constant time
Sorting works only on whole numbers, not on job lengths
optionExplain: A sort costs O(n log n), not O(n^2).

questions.q: Your language's built-in heap is a min heap, but you need the largest number first. What is the easy trick for numbers?

Pop the heap n times and use the last value that comes out

It is a min heap by default; Comparator.reverseOrder() gives a max heap

questions.q: A solver must repeatedly find the two heaviest stones of a pile whose contents keep changing. Which structure gives each one in logarithmic time?

A max heap

questions.q: A learner stops the stone problem to study how a heap rearranges its elements internally. What does the course advise?

questions.teaches: While solving a problem, do not focus on what happens under the hood of a heap: remember what it can do for you and how to use its operations.

questions.q: Each smash among n stones destroys at least one stone. At most how many smash rounds can happen?
options: At most n^2

As many as the largest stone weight
At most n

Weights do not decide how many stones exist.

questions.explain: With at least one stone destroyed per round, the number of rounds cannot exceed n. The card next gives the argument.

questions.q: True or false: The number of smash rounds depends on how large the stone weights are.

questions.q: Stones 9, 3, 5 and 1 are smashed with a max heap until the heap holds zero or one stone. How many rounds does that take?

One round cannot use up four stones that survive as three.
After two rounds two stones of weight 1 remain, so a third round is needed.
Four rounds would need each round to destroy no stones.

questions.q: Put the steps of the O(n log n) argument in order.
items: Each smash destroys at least one stone
So the stone count drops by at least one per round
So there are at most n rounds
Each round costs O(log n) in heap operations
So the total time is O(n log n)

questions.rule: Rounds times cost per round.

questions.q: A student argues: the loop runs n times and each round re-sorts the heap in O(n log n), so the total is O(n^2 log n). What is the flaw?
options: The loop actually runs only log n times, which cancels the extra factor
A heap never re-sorts; each round is a few O(log n) operations
Sorting a heap costs O(n), so the total is O(n^2)
The rounds overlap, so only the first round's cost counts

Right: the heap's pops and pushes are O(log n), so each round is cheap.
No sort happens in the algorithm at all.
Every round pays its own cost.

questions.rule: A round costs a few O(log n) heap operations.

questions.q: A Python solution turns the input list into the heap in place, creating no new list. How does the course say to count its space?
options: Count it as O(1), because no new list was created by the code
Count it as O(log n), the depth of the heap
Count it as O(n) anyway, since the reused input is the heap
Count it as O(n^2), because every round copies the whole heap
optionExplain: Reusing the input is exactly the case the course says to count.
Depth of the tree is not the space the heap uses.
Right: the course counts the reused input toward the space complexity here.
No round copies the heap.

questions.teaches: In Python the input is reused as the heap, so it counts toward the space complexity, which would not normally be done.

questions.q: To reach half the starting sum in the fewest halvings, which number should the next halving target?

The smallest number, to avoid wasting a large one
The number nearest the average, to keep the sum balanced
The first unused number in the original order
optionExplain: Right: the biggest number gives the biggest reduction.
Halving a small number removes only a small amount.
The average is not special for the amount removed.

questions.q: Halving a number x reduces the total by ____.
questions.explain: The number goes from x to x / 2, so the sum falls by x / 2.
questions.rule: Halving x removes x / 2.

Five halvings would be more than needed.

questions.q: A student halves each number once, largest first, without putting halves back. For 8, 1, 1, 1, 1 she needs 5 halvings, though 2 suffice. Why?

Halving the same number twice is not allowed by the problem statement
Sorting in ascending order would reach the target in two halvings here

Right: the sum is 12, so 6 must go. Halving 8 removes 4 and halving the new 4 removes 2, which is enough.
The problem lets any number be chosen in each operation.
Halving the small numbers first removes far less.

questions.rule: Halved values must go back into the pool.

questions.q: For nums = [1000000, 1, 1], the big number needs many halvings to become tiny. Can the loop need more than n operations?
options: Yes; the largest number must be halved over and over until it is below 1
Yes, but the heap makes each extra halving cost only O(1) time
No; the loop always stops after about log n operations whatever the input
No; halving every number once already removes half the sum
optionExplain: Each halving of a huge number also removes a huge amount.
Heap operations cost O(log n), not O(1).
The number of operations depends on the input, not always log n.
Right: the target is reached after one halving of every number at the latest.
questions.explain: The course argues that you could always perform the operation on each number once, which removes exactly half the sum. So the operation count cannot exceed n.
questions.rule: To cut the sum in the fewest halvings, always halve the current largest number, using a max heap.
questions.teaches: The number of operations is at most n, because halving each number once already removes half of the sum.

questions.q: Numbers keep arriving, and the median must be available quickly. Which pair of heaps puts the middle value within reach?

One max heap holding everything and an empty min heap
A max heap of the lower half and a min heap of the upper half
A min heap of the lower half and a max heap of the upper half
optionExplain: Two min heaps show the two smallest values of each half, not the middle.
One heap exposes only its own extreme, not a middle.
Right: the two tops then sit next to the middle of the sorted data.
That pairing exposes the ends of the data, not its middle.
questions.explain: The tops must face each other at the middle: the largest of the lower half and the smallest of the upper half. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Keep a max heap of the lower half and a min heap of the upper half in balance, and the median sits at the tops.

questions.q: The heap that holds the smaller half of the numbers is a ____ heap.
questions.explain: Its top must be the largest of the lower half, so it is a max heap.
questions.rule: Lower half: max heap. Upper half: min heap.

questions.q: The max heap holds 2, 4 and 6, and the min heap holds 9, 11 and 15. What is the median?
optionExplain: Right: the counts are equal, so the median is the average of the two tops, (6 + 9) / 2 = 7.5.
6 is only the lower top; with equal sizes the median uses both tops.
9 is only the upper top.
10 is the average of 9 and 11, which are not the middle values.
questions.explain: Equal sizes mean an even count, so average the two tops.
questions.rule: Equal sizes: average the two tops.

questions.q: Six numbers arrive: 12, 3, 21, 8, 17, 5. Which heap holds each one when the halves are balanced?
questions.explain: Sorted, the numbers are 3, 5, 8, 12, 17, 21. The lower three go to the max heap and the upper three to the min heap.
questions.rule: Split the sorted data in half.

questions.q: The max heap holds 5, 8 and 9, and the min heap holds 7, 10 and 11. A student reports (9 + 7) / 2 = 8 as the median. What is wrong?
options: The median should be the average of the two largest numbers in the data
The heaps must have different sizes for their tops to give the median
The max heap should hold the larger half of the numbers, not the smaller half
The 8 and 9 in the max heap exceed the min heap's 7, so the halves overlap
optionExplain: The median is built from the middle values, not the largest ones.
Equal sizes are fine for an even count.
The max heap holds the lower half so that its top is the largest of that half.
Right: the halves must not overlap. Sorted, the data is 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, so the median is 8.5.
questions.explain: The condition that every min-heap element is at least as large as every max-heap element was broken.
questions.rule: Every min-heap element is at least as large as every max-heap element.

questions.q: A monitoring service lets the min heap hold the extra element when the count is odd. Does that break the method?
options: Yes; only the max heap can hold the extra element, or the tops would not touch
No; the extra element may go in either heap, so the median is the min top
Yes; with an odd count the heaps must be exactly equal in size to work
No; but the median is then the average of both tops of the heaps
optionExplain: The tops still touch at the middle with either choice.
Right: the choice is arbitrary, as long as the sizes differ by at most one and the halves stay ordered.
An odd count cannot be split into equal sizes.
With an odd count one top alone is the median.
questions.explain: The course picks the max heap for the extra element arbitrarily and says it does not matter which heap is chosen.
questions.rule: Keep a max heap of the lower half and a min heap of the upper half in balance, and the median sits at the tops.
questions.teaches: It does not matter which heap stores the extra element when the count is odd; the course arbitrarily picks the max heap.

questions.q: The lower half holds numbers up to 7 and the upper half starts at 13. A new number, 50, is pushed onto the max heap only. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; the max heap may hold any number, large or small, without harm
The max heap now holds a number above the whole upper half
The min heap loses its smallest element to the max heap at once
The max heap quietly turns into a min heap once 50 enters
optionExplain: The lower half must stay below the upper half.
Right: 50 belongs in the upper half, but it sits in the lower half's heap.
Pushing onto one heap does not remove anything from the other.
A heap keeps its kind whatever is pushed.
questions.explain: A number pushed straight onto the max heap can land in the wrong half. The card next shows the fix.
questions.rule: Push to the max heap, move its top to the min heap, then move one back if the min heap is larger.

questions.q: Put the three steps of addNum in order.
items: Push the number onto the max heap
Pop the max heap's top and push it onto the min heap
If the min heap is larger, pop its top and push it onto the max heap
questions.explain: The first step enters the number, the second restores the order between halves, the third restores the size balance.
questions.rule: Push, move across, rebalance.

questions.q: The max heap holds 2, 4 and 6, and the min heap holds 9, 12 and 15. After addNum(10), what is the median?
optionExplain: 6 was the median's lower top before the add.
10 is the min heap's top, but the max heap has the extra element.
7.5 was the median before the add.
Right: step 1 gives max {2, 4, 6, 10}; step 2 moves 10 to the min heap; step 3 moves 9 back. The max heap is {2, 4, 6, 9}, the min heap {10, 12, 15}, and the max heap holds the extra 9.
questions.explain: After the steps the max heap has 4 elements and the min heap 3, so the median is the max heap's top.
questions.rule: Odd count: the max heap's top is the median.

questions.q: Starting empty, addNum(5), addNum(1) and addNum(8) are called. findMedian then returns ____.
questions.explain: The sorted data is 1, 5, 8, so the median is 5, the max heap's top after the three adds.
questions.rule: Three numbers: the middle one.

questions.q: A buggy addNum skips step 2, moving the max heap's top onto the min heap, on every add. After adding 2, 4 and 6 it reports 6. Why is that wrong?
options: The 6 sits in the max heap above the min heap's 4; the true median is 4
6 is correct, since the max heap holds the extra element when the count is odd
The median should be 5, the average of 4 and 6, as for an even count
findMedian should average the two tops of the heaps instead of using one
optionExplain: Right: the buggy rule only moves the top when the max heap gets too big, so 6 never reaches the upper half.
The extra element is only the median when the halves are ordered.
With three numbers the median is the middle value, 4, not an average.
Averaging is only for an even count.
questions.explain: Without the move in step 2, a large number can stay in the lower half's heap and the tops stop being the middle.
questions.rule: Step 2 keeps the halves ordered.

questions.q: After 1,000,000 calls to addNum, a team says the next call costs O(log n). What does n stand for in that bound?
options: The size of the larger of the two heaps only
The largest number that has been added so far
The number of times addNum has been called so far
The number of calls made to findMedian, not addNum
optionExplain: The two heaps together hold all n numbers, and the bound is stated in terms of that total.
The values added play no part in the cost.
Right: n counts the numbers added so far.
findMedian is O(1) whatever n is.
questions.explain: The course states the costs in terms of n, the number of times addNum has been called so far.
questions.rule: Push to the max heap, move its top to the min heap, then move one back if the min heap is larger.
questions.teaches: In the costs of the two-heap method, n is the number of times addNum has been called so far.

questions.q: Which approach finds the 5 largest of 1,000,000 numbers and improves on sorting them all?
options: Keep a max heap of at most 5 numbers and pop when it grows past 5
Keep a hash map from each number to its rank
Sort all numbers with a custom comparator, then read the last five
Keep a min heap of at most 5 numbers and pop when it grows past 5
optionExplain: A max heap would pop the largest, so it would keep the smallest numbers.
A hash map has no notion of rank.
Sorting everything is the O(n log n) baseline that this improves on.
Right: a bounded min heap keeps the five largest and costs O(n log 5).
questions.explain: A min heap capped at k drops the smallest element each time. The card next explains why that keeps the best.
questions.rule: To get the k best in O(n log k), keep a min heap of at most k elements and pop whenever it grows past k.

questions.q: With a heap capped at k elements, each heap operation costs O(log ____).
questions.explain: The heap never holds more than about k elements, so its operations are O(log k).
questions.rule: A bounded heap makes each operation O(log k).

questions.q: A min heap capped at 3 processes 4, 9, 2, 7, 5, 8 in that order. Put the values popped in the order they come out.
questions.explain: The heap fills with 4, 9, 2; adding 7 pops 2; adding 5 pops 4; adding 8 pops 5. It ends holding 7, 8, 9.
questions.rule: Each pop removes the smallest held value.

questions.q: With n = 1,000,000 and k = 8, by about what factor is log2(k) smaller than log2(n)?
options: About 6.6 times smaller
About 125,000 times smaller
About 20 times smaller
About 1.3 times smaller
optionExplain: Right: log2(1,000,000) is about 19.93 and log2(8) is 3, a ratio of about 6.6.
That is n / k, which is not the ratio of the logarithms.
20 is log2(n) alone.
That ratio would apply if k were close to n.
questions.explain: Divide the two logarithms: 19.93 / 3 is about 6.6.
questions.rule: Compare log n with log k.

questions.q: To find the 3 largest of 4, 9, 2, 7, 5, 8, a student keeps a max heap capped at 3, popping its top when too big. What does it end up holding?
options: 7, 8 and 9, the three largest, because a max heap favours big values
2, 4 and 5, the three smallest, as each pop removes the largest
4, 5 and 7, the middle values, because pops take both ends
2, 4 and 9, the first three numbers read, because later ones are dropped
optionExplain: The max heap's pop removes its top, which is the largest, so large values are the ones dropped.
Right: the cap with a max heap drops the largest each time, leaving the smallest.
A pop takes only the top, never both ends.
Later numbers are pushed in too; they are not skipped.
questions.explain: A bounded heap keeps what its pop does not remove. To keep the largest, pop the smallest, so use a min heap.
questions.rule: To keep the best, pop the worst.

questions.q: With n = 10,000 and k = 100, a teammate says plain sorting is fine. Which view matches the course?
options: The heap gives a massive speedup, as when O(n^2) becomes O(n log n) here
Sorting is faster, because each heap operation costs O(n)
Little gain in practice, as log is so fast, yet interviewers look for it
Sorting is wrong here, because it cannot return the top k
optionExplain: The gain here is from O(n log n) to O(n log k), which is small.
A heap operation is O(log k), not O(n).
Right: logically k < n so the heap is better, but practically the gain is probably small.
Sorting does return the top k, at O(n log n) cost.
questions.explain: The course says the improvement is logical but, because log is so fast, probably not a big deal in speed; interviewers still look for these small gains.
questions.rule: To get the k best in O(n log k), keep a min heap of at most k elements and pop whenever it grows past k.
questions.teaches: Because log grows so slowly, the speed gain of the heap over sorting is probably small in practice, but interviewers look for it.

questions.q: In a heap-based solution to the k most frequent elements, what should the heap compare entries by?
options: How often each element occurs
The value of each element
The position where each element first appears
The hash code of each element
optionExplain: Right: the heap must rank elements by frequency.
Value says nothing about how common an element is.
First position is unrelated to frequency.
A hash code does not measure frequency.
questions.explain: The heap should rank elements by how often they occur. The card next shows how a pair makes that happen.
questions.rule: Count with a hash map, then keep the k most frequent in a min heap of at most k pairs keyed by frequency.

questions.q: Each heap entry is a pair, and the ____ must come first so the heap orders by it.
questions.explain: A heap compares pairs starting with the first entry, so the frequency goes first.
questions.rule: Put the ranking key first in the pair.

questions.q: The array has 5 six times, 7 five times, 9 four times, 4 three times, 8 twice and 6 once; k = 3. Where does each element end up?

items.t: 5 (6 times)
7 (5 times)
9 (4 times)
4 (3 times)
8 (2 times)
6 (1 time)

questions.explain: Each pop removes the least frequent pair held. With six elements and k = 3, the three least frequent are popped.
questions.rule: The k most frequent are never popped.

questions.q: A variation asks for the k LEAST frequent elements. Which heap suits (frequency, element) pairs?
options: A min heap, exactly as in the original problem with no change
A min heap, but popping whenever the size is below k
A max heap, so each pop removes the most frequent pair held
A max heap, but popping the least frequent pair
optionExplain: The original min heap drops the least frequent, which keeps the most frequent.
Popping below k would empty the heap.
Right: to keep the rarest, pop the most frequent.
A max heap pops its top, which is the most frequent pair.
questions.explain: Flip the heap type: the heap must pop the worst by the new criterion.
questions.rule: Pop what you do not want to keep.

questions.q: A student pushes (element, frequency) pairs onto a Python min heap capped at k = 2. For 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4 what goes wrong?
options: It keeps 2 and 4, the two least frequent elements in the array
It orders by element value, so it keeps 3 and 4 rather than 1 and 3
It keeps 1 and 3 correctly, since pair order makes no difference to a heap
It fails with an error, because pairs cannot be pushed onto a heap
optionExplain: Those are not even the elements the value order would keep.
Right: the first entry of each pair decides the order, so the heap compares elements, not frequencies.
The order inside a pair decides what the heap compares.
Pairs can be pushed; the problem is only what they compare.
questions.explain: The course stresses that the frequency has to come first. Reversed, the heap ranks by value.
questions.rule: Frequency first.

questions.q: Counting the frequencies costs O(n). How does that compare with the overall cost O(n log k)?
options: It adds to the total, making the whole bound O(n^2) in the end
It replaces the heap loop, so the total becomes only O(n) overall
It must cost O(n log n), since a hash map keeps keys sorted
It is dominated by the heap loop, so the total stays O(n log k)
optionExplain: Adding O(n) to O(n log k) does not give a square.
The heap loop still runs over the elements.
A hash map does not keep its keys sorted.
Right: O(n) is smaller than O(n log k), so it drops out of the bound.
questions.explain: The course notes that counting the frequencies only costs O(n), which is dominated by the main loop.
questions.rule: Count with a hash map, then keep the k most frequent in a min heap of at most k pairs keyed by frequency.
questions.teaches: Counting the frequencies costs only O(n), which is dominated by the O(n log k) main loop.

questions.q: While finding the k elements closest to x, the heap grows past k. Which element should it pop?
options: The one closest to x
The smallest value
The one farthest from x
The most recently added
optionExplain: Popping the closest would keep the farthest.
Value alone ignores the distance from x.
Right: popping the farthest keeps the closest.
Arrival order has no link to distance.
questions.explain: To keep the closest, remove the farthest. The card next shows the heap that does it.
questions.rule: For the k smallest distances, use a max heap on distance, break ties by value, and sort the survivors.

questions.q: True or false: To keep the k closest elements, the heap should be a max heap on distance from x.
questions.explain: A max heap puts the largest distance on top, so each pop removes the farthest element.
questions.rule: Max heap on distance, pop the farthest.

questions.q: For arr = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10], x = 7 and k = 3, which elements does the method return?
optionExplain: Right: 6 and 8 are at distance 1; 4 and 10 tie at distance 3, and the smaller value, 4, wins.
That would keep 10 on the tie, but the smaller element wins.
2 is at distance 5, the farthest of all.
10 loses the tie with 4, and 8 is closer than 10.
questions.explain: Distances are 5, 3, 1, 1, 3. The three smallest are 1, 1 and a tie at 3 that goes to 4.
questions.rule: Break distance ties toward the smaller value.

questions.q: With x = 5, the values 3 and 7 are both at distance 2. If only one fits, the tie rule keeps ____.
questions.explain: The rule takes the smaller element on a tie, so 3 is kept and 7 is popped first.
questions.rule: Tie: keep the smaller element.

questions.q: A Python solution pushes (abs(num - x), num) onto a min heap capped at k and pops when too big. For 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, x = 7, k = 3, what does it keep?
options: 6, 8 and 4, the closest elements
6, 8 and 10, the closest elements after the tie rule is applied
2, 4 and 6, the three smallest values in the array
2, 4 and 10, the farthest, as each pop removes the closest
optionExplain: That is the correct answer, which this min heap does not produce.
The tie rule cannot rescue a heap that pops the closest.
Value order plays no part in this heap.
Right: a min heap on distance pops the closest, so it keeps the farthest.
questions.explain: The distance must be on top as the largest, so negate it or use a max heap.
questions.rule: Pop the farthest, not the closest.

questions.q: A Java developer must break distance ties by value inside a heap. What does the course say is needed?
options: Nothing; Java's heap compares pairs entry by entry as Python's does
A custom comparator that says how to rank two elements on a tie
A tuple of (distance, value), exactly as in Python
A second pass that sorts the tied elements after the heap finishes
optionExplain: Entry-by-entry comparison is what Python and C++ do with ordered collections.
Right: in Java the tie-break must be spelled out in a comparator.
Java has no tuple to put in a heap in the course's example.
The tie must be decided while the heap decides which element to pop.
questions.explain: In Python or C++ an ordered collection such as a tuple is compared entry by entry. In Java you write a comparator that explicitly handles the tie.
questions.rule: For the k smallest distances, use a max heap on distance, break ties by value, and sort the survivors.
questions.teaches: In Python or C++ a tuple in a heap is compared entry by entry, so ties resolve by the next entry; in Java a custom comparator must handle the tie explicitly.

questions.q: At each step an algorithm takes the best-looking option available right then and does not revisit it. What is this style called?
questions.explain: Taking the best visible option step by step is called greedy. The card next defines it.
options: Exhaustive search: every complete plan is compared before one is chosen
Greedy: the choice is the best one visible at that step
Divide and conquer: the input is split in halves and solved separately
Backtracking: each choice is undone when it leads to a dead end
optionExplain: This also seeks the best, but it looks at whole plans, not at one step.
Right: picking the best available option step by step is the greedy style.
Splitting is a different idea and says nothing about picking the best option now.
Backtracking does revisit choices, which is the opposite of this style.
questions.rule: A greedy algorithm takes the best option visible at this step, as the problem defines best, without looking ahead.

questions.q: True or false: a decision is local when it weighs the consequences that may follow from it in later steps.
questions.explain: A local decision considers only the options available at the current step. Weighing later consequences would make it a look-ahead decision.
questions.hint: Think about what information a local decision is allowed to use.
questions.rule: A greedy algorithm takes the best option visible at this step, as the problem defines best, without looking ahead.

questions.q: A cashier hands back change by giving, at each step, the largest coin that fits the remaining amount. What makes each handover local?
questions.explain: Each handover looks at the coins that fit the current remainder and nothing else.
options: It first lists every way to make the total and takes the shortest list
It uses the coins that earlier customers received in the same shift
It checks that the final number of coins will be the smallest possible
It compares only the coins that fit the amount still owed right now
optionExplain: That compares complete plans, so it is not a local decision.
Past customers are unrelated information, and a local choice would not use it.
That needs to know the end result, which a local choice does not see.
Right: the choice uses only the current options and the current remainder.
questions.rule: A greedy algorithm takes the best option visible at this step, as the problem defines best, without looking ahead.

questions.q: Sort each step into greedy (best option visible now) or not greedy.
questions.explain: A greedy step uses only what is visible at the current step. Comparing whole plans or simulating later steps looks ahead.

items.t: Take the cheapest item left on the shelf
Hand over the largest coin that fits the remaining change
Play the highest-scoring card in your hand right now
Try every complete order of visits and keep the shortest
Pick the move after simulating every later reply to the end
Choose the step after planning all later steps to get the best total

questions.rule: A greedy algorithm takes the best option visible at this step, as the problem defines best, without looking ahead.

questions.q: A problem asks only whether every task can be finished, and a smallest-task-first rule is proposed. Does the yes-or-no question rule out greedy?
questions.explain: Most greedy problems ask for a maximum or minimum, but a decision problem can be greedy too.
options: No: most greedy problems ask for a maximum or minimum, but not all of them
Yes: greedy needs the problem to ask for a maximum or minimum, so a yes-or-no question is excluded
Yes: a yes-or-no answer cannot depend on a local choice at all
No: greedy applies only when the answer is a yes or no
optionExplain: Right: the book says most, not all, and the asteroid problem later returns true or false.
This is the common belief, but the book says most greedy problems do so, not every one.
The answer can depend on a sequence of local choices, such as an order of tasks.
This reverses the pattern; many greedy problems ask for a number that is largest or smallest.
questions.teaches: Most greedy problems ask for the maximum or minimum of something, but not all: a problem that asks a yes-or-no question can also be solved greedily.
questions.rule: A greedy algorithm takes the best option visible at this step, as the problem defines best, without looking ahead.

questions.q: A courier visits five houses, each time driving to the nearest unvisited one. Is the total trip guaranteed to be the shortest possible?
questions.explain: Nearest-first is not guaranteed to give the shortest trip. The card next tells the story.
options: Yes, since every leg is the shortest one available at that step
Yes, since the driver compares all five houses before leaving
No: a nearest-first choice can force much longer legs later
Only if the driver restarts from the depot after each stop
optionExplain: Each leg is shortest locally, but the sum of legs can still be larger than another order gives.
Comparing houses one step at a time is not the same as comparing whole routes.
Right: the shortest next leg may leave the remaining houses badly placed.
Returning to the depot adds distance and does not fix the choice rule.
questions.rule: A strategy that picks the best option step by step is trustworthy only once you have a reason that it reaches the best whole.

questions.q: True or false: the courier's nearest-first choices were local, yet the total trip was not the shortest.
questions.explain: The courier compared only the next house, so each choice was local, but a different order using the bridge was shorter overall.
questions.rule: A strategy that picks the best option step by step is trustworthy only once you have a reason that it reaches the best whole.

questions.q: For coins 1, 3 and 4 and the amount 6, greedy_coins([1, 3, 4], 6) returns ____.
questions.explain: The function takes 4, then 1, then 1: three coins. Two coins of 3 would make 6, so the greedy count is not the smallest.
questions.hint: Take the largest coin that fits, then repeat with what is left.
questions.rule: A strategy that picks the best option step by step is trustworthy only once you have a reason that it reaches the best whole.

questions.q: Ravi finds largest-coin-first best for coins 1, 3, 4 on amounts 1 to 5 and calls it correct. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Matching the best answer on small inputs is not a reason to trust the rule. Amount 6 with coins 1, 3, 4 is a counterexample.
options: Coins 1, 3 and 4 are too few coins for any greedy rule to be tested fairly
Nothing is wrong, because five correct cases cover every amount up to 5
Five small passing cases prove nothing: amount 6 breaks the rule
He should have tested only amounts that are larger than every coin
optionExplain: The number of coins is not the issue; the rule fails for a legal input.
They cover only those amounts, and the claim was about the rule in general.
Right: agreement on small cases is not a reason; amount 6 needs 3 coins by greedy and 2 by 3 + 3.
Larger amounts are no better as a test; a reason for the rule is what is missing.
questions.rule: A strategy that picks the best option step by step is trustworthy only once you have a reason that it reaches the best whole.

questions.q: A quick greedy route planner gives routes about a quarter longer than the best. For whom is that acceptable?
questions.explain: In real life a fast greedy answer that is a little off can beat an exact answer that takes far too long.
options: A delivery firm that needs a good route fast for many stops
A proof that claims the route found is the shortest
A contest judge who compares routes character by character
A grader that accepts only the single shortest possible route
optionExplain: Right: a quick, close-enough answer is useful when an exact one is too costly to compute.
The route is longer, so it cannot be offered as the shortest.
An exact-match judge is the setting where close but wrong fails.
A grader that needs the exact answer would mark a longer route wrong.
questions.teaches: In real life greedy gives good approximations with far less computation: for the travelling salesman problem it is usually only about 25% wrong at O(n squared), while no classical exact algorithm faster than O(2 to the n) is known.
questions.rule: A strategy that picks the best option step by step is trustworthy only once you have a reason that it reaches the best whole.

questions.q: Coins 1, 5, 12, amount 15: largest-first gives 12, 1, 1, 1, but three 5s do better. How does LeetCode grade the greedy answer?
questions.explain: The greedy answer is 4 coins against a best of 3. It is close and still wrong, and grading for exact answers rejects it.
options: As wrong only when the amount is larger than 100 coins or more
As correct, because it is within one coin of the best possible answer
As correct, since a greedy answer is accepted whenever it is reasonable
As wrong: near the best still fails when exact is required
optionExplain: The amount does not matter here; 15 already breaks the rule.
Near-correct answers earn nothing when the grader wants the exact best.
Greedy is not accepted for being greedy alone; the answer must be right.
Right: 4 coins is near 3, but a close answer still fails when the exact one is required.
questions.teaches: In many problems a greedy approach gives an answer very close to the correct one but still wrong, and on LeetCode only fully correct solutions count.
questions.rule: A strategy that picks the best option step by step is trustworthy only once you have a reason that it reaches the best whole.

questions.q: Many greedy solutions begin by sorting the input. What does sorting make convenient?
questions.explain: Sorted input makes extreme elements easy to take. The card next gathers the clues.
options: Checking whether any element is repeated anywhere in the input
Taking the largest or smallest remaining element at each step
Skipping the need to explain why the strategy works
Reducing the memory used to a single variable in every case
optionExplain: Sorting does bring equal values together, but this is not the reason greedy solutions sort.
Right: sorted input puts the extremes at the ends.
Sorting is only preparation; the justification is still needed.
Sorting does not reduce memory to a single variable.
questions.rule: When a problem wants a maximum or minimum from step-by-step choices, sort the input and test a rule that takes the extreme option each time.

questions.q: Greedy solutions often start by ____ the input, so that the largest or smallest elements are easy to take.
questions.explain: Sorting turns each take-the-extreme step into reading one end of the array.
questions.rule: When a problem wants a maximum or minimum from step-by-step choices, sort the input and test a rule that takes the extreme option each time.

questions.q: Given the prices of items and a budget, buy as many items as possible. Which first move best fits the greedy clues?
questions.explain: Buying the cheapest first needs the prices in ascending order, so sort first.
options: Sort the prices descending and buy from the dearest downward
Pick items at random until the budget runs out
Put the prices in a hash set and look each one up
Sort the prices ascending and buy from the cheapest upward
optionExplain: Dear items use the budget up fast, so fewer items fit.
Random picks give no reason the count is the largest.
A set removes repeats and gives no order for picking extremes.
Right: the cheapest items leave the most budget for more items.
questions.rule: When a problem wants a maximum or minimum from step-by-step choices, sort the input and test a rule that takes the extreme option each time.

questions.q: Put the steps of a typical greedy solution in order.
questions.explain: First recognise the clue, then propose a rule, then justify it, and only then write the sort and loop.
items: Notice that the problem asks for a maximum or minimum
Propose a rule that takes the extreme option at each step
Find a reason the rule reaches the best answer
Sort the input and loop, taking the extreme option each time
questions.rule: When a problem wants a maximum or minimum from step-by-step choices, sort the input and test a rule that takes the extreme option each time.

questions.q: A leaderboard service repeatedly removes the top score from a max heap to give out prizes. How does the author classify heap-based processing like this?
questions.explain: Many heap algorithms pick the max or min each step, which makes them greedy. The author says most of the previous chapter qualifies.
options: It is never greedy, since greedy requires that the whole input is sorted first
It is often greedy: a heap hands over the max or min that a greedy step takes
It is not greedy, because a heap is a data structure and not a strategy at all
It is greedy only when the heap holds fewer than ten items at a time
optionExplain: Sorting is a common helper, but a heap delivers extremes without sorting everything.
Right: heaps give the extreme element directly, which is what greedy steps need.
A heap is a structure, but the way it is used in repeated max picks is the greedy part.
Heap size does not decide whether a step is greedy.
questions.teaches: A lot of algorithms involving heaps can be considered greedy, because a heap gives the maximum or minimum element and greedy approaches choose max or min at each step; most algorithms in the heap chapter fit.
questions.rule: When a problem wants a maximum or minimum from step-by-step choices, sort the input and test a rule that takes the extreme option each time.

questions.q: A teammate asks which library function implements the greedy algorithm. What is the best reply?
questions.explain: Greedy is neither a data structure nor a single algorithm. The main thing to practise is spotting when it applies.
options: The sort function, since greedy is the name of the sorting method used
The heap class, since greedy is a kind of heap that returns extremes
None: greedy is an approach to problems, not one algorithm or structure
The hash map class, since greedy means keeping a running count of each item
optionExplain: Sorting often helps greedy solutions, but greedy is not a sorting method.
Heaps often appear in greedy code, but greedy is not a heap.
Right: the skill is to recognise when the approach applies.
Counting is used in some problems and is not what greedy means.
questions.teaches: Greedy is not a data structure or any single algorithm but a way to approach a problem, so there is little to learn about it directly and the main skill is recognising when it applies.
questions.rule: When a problem wants a maximum or minimum from step-by-step choices, sort the input and test a rule that takes the extreme option each time.

questions.q: A programmer finishes a greedy solution in ten lines. According to the author, which part of the work is typically the hard one?
questions.explain: The author says coding is typically easy and the strategy is the hard part. The card next explains.
options: Realising that the strategy actually works and why
Typing out the loop that makes each choice
Picking a programming language that supports sorting
Making the program run in linear time on a small input
optionExplain: Right: the author says implementing is typically easy and the hard part is realising or proving the strategy works.
The author says implementing a greedy algorithm is typically very easy.
Nearly every language sorts; this is not the hard part.
Greedy solutions are usually efficient, so speed is not the main difficulty.
questions.rule: Writing a greedy loop is the easy part; the work is showing that the greedy choice is safe.

questions.q: According to the author, writing a greedy algorithm is typically ____, while realising that the strategy works is the hard part.
questions.explain: Implementation is typically easy; realising or proving that the strategy works is the hard part.
questions.rule: Writing a greedy loop is the easy part; the work is showing that the greedy choice is safe.

questions.q: Mia's greedy solution passes all 12 sample cases. Which next step best matches the author's advice?
questions.explain: The sample cases do not settle correctness; an argument about the choice does.
options: Look for a reason that no other choice at a step can do better
Replace the sort with a heap to make it run faster
Rewrite the loop in a different language to be safe
Submit it, since twelve passing samples show the rule is correct
optionExplain: Right: the open question is whether the strategy works, which needs an argument.
Speed is not the open question.
The language does not change whether the strategy is right.
Samples can pass while the rule still fails on another input.
questions.rule: Writing a greedy loop is the easy part; the work is showing that the greedy choice is safe.

questions.q: True or false: a student reasons that greedy rules are efficient, so any greedy rule they code must be correct. This is sound.
questions.explain: Speed says nothing about correctness: a greedy rule can run fast and still give wrong answers, as the courier and coin examples show.
questions.rule: Writing a greedy loop is the easy part; the work is showing that the greedy choice is safe.

questions.q: According to the author, how detailed must the justification of a greedy rule be to count as sufficient in a coding interview?
questions.explain: The author gives explanations of why greedy works and notes they are not formal proofs but are enough for an interview.
options: A complete formal mathematical proof, written out line by line with all steps
Only a passing run on the examples given in the problem statement itself
No justification, because the code itself shows that the rule is right
A clear logical explanation of why it works; a formal proof is not needed
optionExplain: The author states that a formal proof is not needed there.
Examples alone are not an explanation of why it works.
Code shows what the rule does, not why it works.
Right: the author calls such an explanation sufficient for an interview, though not a formal proof.
questions.teaches: A logical explanation of why the greedy strategy works is not a formal mathematical proof, but the author says it would be a sufficient explanation in an interview.
questions.rule: Writing a greedy loop is the easy part; the work is showing that the greedy choice is safe.

questions.q: A scheduling rule has been argued correct and is greedy. A teammate suggests a slower exhaustive search instead. What follows from the author's view?
questions.explain: With a justified greedy rule you keep correctness and gain efficiency, which is why it matters to recognise these problems.
options: Prefer the exhaustive search, since greedy rules are usually slow in practice
Prefer the greedy rule: it is usually very efficient
Prefer the exhaustive search, since a justified rule can still turn out wrong
Either is equal, since efficiency is not a reason to choose between them
optionExplain: The author says greedy algorithms are usually very efficient.
Right: once the rule is justified its efficiency is the benefit.
A rule with a valid argument is right; the doubt applies to rules without one.
Efficiency is the stated reason to recognise greedy problems.
questions.teaches: Greedy algorithms are usually very efficient, so if a problem can be solved greedily it is important to recognise it.
questions.rule: Writing a greedy loop is the easy part; the work is showing that the greedy choice is safe.

questions.q: Planet mass 10; asteroids 30, 4, 12 and 6, met in any order you choose. Which first step shows what the planet can take now?
questions.explain: Sorting ascending puts the asteroids the planet can take first. The card next shows the loop.
options: Add all the masses and compare the total with 10
Sort the masses descending so the heaviest come first
Sort the masses ascending so the lightest come first
Pick the asteroid closest to 10 each time
optionExplain: The total ignores that the planet grows only as it absorbs asteroids.
The heaviest asteroid is the one the planet is least able to take.
Right: the lightest asteroids are the ones the planet can take, and sorting lines them up.
Closeness to the planet's mass is not what decides which asteroids it can take.
questions.rule: Sort ascending and absorb asteroids in that order; answer no at the first one heavier than the current mass.

questions.q: True or false: the loop answers no the first time the next asteroid in sorted order is heavier than the planet's current mass.
questions.explain: The sorted order means every later asteroid is at least as heavy, so the first asteroid that is too heavy ends the attempt.
questions.rule: Sort ascending and absorb asteroids in that order; answer no at the first one heavier than the current mass.

questions.q: Planet mass 5 meets asteroids of mass 14, 3, 9 and 5. Put them in the order the greedy loop meets them.
questions.explain: The loop works through the sorted list 3, 5, 9, 14. The planet grows 5, 8, 13, 22, 36 and every asteroid is taken.
questions.rule: Sort ascending and absorb asteroids in that order; answer no at the first one heavier than the current mass.

questions.q: Planet mass 3 meets asteroids of mass 2, 6, 4 and 30. The loop stops at the asteroid of mass ____.
questions.explain: Sorted: 2, 4, 6, 30. The planet grows 3, 5, 9, 15, and 15 is below 30, so the loop returns False at 30.
questions.hint: Add the masses in sorted order until one is heavier than the total.
questions.rule: Sort ascending and absorb asteroids in that order; answer no at the first one heavier than the current mass.

questions.q: Planet mass 8 meets asteroids 5, 9 and 6. Meeting 6 first, then 5, then 9 also destroys all. Does that contradict smallest-first?
questions.explain: Many orders can lead to a correct answer. Smallest-first is chosen because it is easy to see and to code.
options: Yes: only the smallest-first order can ever destroy every asteroid, so 6, 5, 9 must fail
No: several strategies are correct; smallest-first is chosen as easy to implement
Yes: smallest-first gave a smaller final mass than the order 6, 5, 9 does
No: it fails to destroy all, so the loop is wrong for this input
optionExplain: Other orders work here; the planet only needs to afford each asteroid when it meets it.
Right: 6, 5, 9 and 5, 6, 9 both work, so more than one order is correct.
Both orders end at the same total mass, 28, since all asteroids are absorbed.
The sorted loop destroys all three here.
questions.teaches: Although many strategies can lead to a correct solution, the author chooses greedily taking the smallest remaining asteroid because it is intuitive and easy to implement.
questions.rule: Sort ascending and absorb asteroids in that order; answer no at the first one heavier than the current mass.

questions.q: The asteroid check is ported to a language whose sort is quicksort-based. The loop needs O(1) extra space. What sets the total extra space?
questions.explain: The extra space is whatever the language's sort uses, since the loop itself adds only a few variables.
options: The loop, which stores every asteroid it has absorbed so far
A heap, which the check builds to find the lightest asteroid
Nothing: the check is in place, so the extra space is zero whatever sort the language uses
The language's sort: O(log n) for quicksort-based, up to O(n) for Python's timsort
optionExplain: The loop keeps one running mass, not a list of absorbed asteroids.
This version uses a sort and no heap.
Sorting can need extra space, so it cannot be ignored.
Right: the loop adds O(1), so the sort decides the extra space.
questions.teaches: The space used depends on the language: Python implements timsort, which uses up to O(n) space, while a language that uses quicksort uses O(log n).
questions.rule: Sort ascending and absorb asteroids in that order; answer no at the first one heavier than the current mass.

questions.q: True or false: when the planet can destroy both a 3 and a 7 now, their order can decide whether all asteroids are destroyed.
questions.explain: Absorbing either one only adds mass, so the other stays destroyable. The card next gives the reason.
questions.rule: Mass only increases, so an asteroid that can be destroyed now can be destroyed later, and the order among destroyable ones does not matter.

questions.q: Each time the planet absorbs an asteroid, its mass can only ____.
questions.explain: Absorbed mass is added and never removed, so the planet only gets heavier.
questions.rule: Mass only increases, so an asteroid that can be destroyed now can be destroyed later, and the order among destroyable ones does not matter.

questions.q: Planet mass 5 can destroy asteroids 4 and 5. Which statement about the order of these two is correct?
questions.explain: Both orders add 4 and 5 to 5 and reach 14, so no later asteroid can tell them apart.
options: Either order leaves the mass at 14, so later asteroids see the same planet
Meeting 4 first leaves a lighter planet than meeting 5 first would
Meeting 5 first could make the 4 undestroyable afterwards, so the 4 should go first
The order matters only when the planet is lighter than both asteroids
optionExplain: Right: 5 + 4 + 5 is 14 whichever comes first.
Both orders add the same two masses, so the totals match.
The planet is heavier after the 5, so the 4 is still easy.
Equal masses are no different; the total is the same.
questions.rule: Mass only increases, so an asteroid that can be destroyed now can be destroyed later, and the order among destroyable ones does not matter.

questions.q: True or false: Dev worries that meeting the 4 before the 6 may make the 6 undestroyable, and this worry is sound.
questions.explain: Meeting the 4 first only raises the mass, so an asteroid that was destroyable before is still destroyable.
questions.rule: Mass only increases, so an asteroid that can be destroyed now can be destroyed later, and the order among destroyable ones does not matter.

questions.q: Planet mass 4 meets asteroids of mass 4 and 8. A planet is destroyed only if its mass is less than the asteroid's. What happens?
questions.explain: Equal mass is survived because only a lighter planet is destroyed, so the check is mass less than the asteroid.
options: The planet is destroyed by the first asteroid, since the two masses are equal
The 4 is absorbed, but the 8 destroys the planet at mass 4
The 4 is absorbed (equal mass is survived), then the 8, ending at mass 16
Neither asteroid can be taken until the planet is heavier than both
optionExplain: Only a lighter planet is destroyed, and equal is not lighter.
After the 4 the planet has mass 8, which is not less than 8.
Right: 4 is not less than 4, so the planet survives and grows to 8, then 16.
The planet needs to be at least as heavy as each asteroid when it meets it.
questions.teaches: The planet is destroyed only if its mass is less than the asteroid's, so an asteroid of exactly equal mass is absorbed rather than fatal.
questions.rule: Mass only increases, so an asteroid that can be destroyed now can be destroyed later, and the order among destroyable ones does not matter.

questions.q: A hero of strength 7 faces monsters 9, 12, 8, 30 in any order and loses to a stronger one. Can all be beaten?
questions.explain: The weakest remaining monster, 8, already beats the hero of 7. Every other monster is at least as strong, so no order can start.
options: Yes: the monsters can be fought in the order that suits the hero
Yes: fighting the 9 first then the 12 raises strength enough for the 8
No: every monster is at least 8, so no order lets the hero get started
Only if the 30 is fought last, since it is the strongest
optionExplain: Any order must start with some monster, and every one is too strong.
The 9 beats a hero of 7, so that order cannot begin.
Right: if the smallest remaining one is too strong, all the rest are too.
The order of the 30 does not matter when the hero cannot beat anyone.
questions.teaches: If at any step the smallest remaining asteroid is heavier than the planet, destroying all of them is impossible, because no order of asteroids would allow the planet to continue.
questions.rule: Mass only increases, so an asteroid that can be destroyed now can be destroyed later, and the order among destroyable ones does not matter.

questions.q: Split 10, 1, 12, 5, 3 and 14 into groups whose largest and smallest values differ by at most 4. What is the fewest groups?
questions.explain: Two groups are enough: 1 to 5 and 10 to 14. The card next shows how to find them.
optionExplain: The values from 1 to 14 span 13, far more than 4.
Right: 1, 3, 5 fit one group and 10, 12, 14 fit another.
Three groups is possible but not the fewest; 1, 3, 5 and 10, 12, 14 suffice.
Four groups would split values that can share a group.
questions.rule: Sort, start a group at the smallest unused value x, absorb everything up to x plus k, then start again at the first value beyond.

questions.q: True or false: in partition_array a new group starts when v minus x is greater than k.
questions.explain: Once a value is more than k above the group's smallest value x, it cannot join the group, so it starts a new one and becomes x.
questions.rule: Sort, start a group at the smallest unused value x, absorb everything up to x plus k, then start again at the first value beyond.

questions.q: For nums 7, 2, 9, 4, 12, 1, 8 and k = 3, partition_array returns ____.
questions.explain: Sorted: 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 12. The group of 1 takes 1, 2, 4; the group of 7 takes 7, 8, 9 (up to 10); then 12 starts a third.
questions.hint: Sort first, then start a group at x and take everything up to x + 3.
questions.rule: Sort, start a group at the smallest unused value x, absorb everything up to x plus k, then start again at the first value beyond.

questions.q: Temperature readings 20, 22, 31, 18, 35, 23 and 30 go into bins that each span at most 5 degrees. How few bins are needed?
questions.explain: Sorted: 18, 20, 22, 23, 30, 31, 35. The bin starting at 18 holds up to 23, and 30 starts a second that holds the rest.
optionExplain: Right: 18 to 23 is one bin and 30 to 35 is another.
The readings range from 18 to 35, which is more than 5.
A third bin is not needed because 18 to 23 and 30 to 35 cover everything.
Four bins would split readings that fit together.
questions.rule: Sort, start a group at the smallest unused value x, absorb everything up to x plus k, then start again at the first value beyond.

questions.q: This version returns 1 for nums 10, 1, 12, 5, 3, 14 and k = 4, but the answer is 2. Which change fixes it?
questions.explain: The loop increments only when a new group starts, so the first group must be counted before the loop.
options: Start the count at 1, since the first group exists before any comparison
Sort the array in descending order so the largest value starts each group
Change the test to v - x >= k so that groups close one value sooner than now
Reset x to nums[0] at every step so each group starts from the first value
optionExplain: Right: the loop only counts new groups, so the first one has to be counted at the start.
Descending order breaks the idea of starting at the smallest value.
That changes which values share a group, not the missing first group.
x must move forward when a group closes, not back.
questions.rule: Sort, start a group at the smallest unused value x, absorb everything up to x plus k, then start again at the first value beyond.

questions.q: After the group starting at x has taken every value up to x plus k and those are set aside, what is left to solve?
questions.explain: Setting aside a finished group leaves the same problem on fewer values, which is why one loop with a moving x suffices.
options: A different problem with new rules, which needs a new algorithm
A harder problem, because the values set aside must be revisited at the end
Nothing is left, because the first group takes every value in the array
The same problem on the remaining values, with a new smallest value as x
optionExplain: It is the same question on a smaller input.
Set aside values are finished; they do not return.
Values beyond x plus k cannot join, so more groups may be needed.
Right: the leftover values pose the same question again.
questions.teaches: After taking all values in [x, x + k] we can erase them from the array, and we have the same problem again with a different x.
questions.rule: Sort, start a group at the smallest unused value x, absorb everything up to x plus k, then start again at the first value beyond.

questions.q: True or false: sorting nums can change the fewest number of groups, because the groups must be subsequences that keep the original order.
questions.explain: Only the largest and smallest of each group matter, so the arrangement does not change the count. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Order inside a group is irrelevant, and leaving out a value within k of the group's smallest only makes later groups worse.

questions.q: True or false: the order of the elements inside a group changes whether the group's largest minus smallest is at most k.
questions.explain: Largest minus smallest depends on which values are in the group, not on how they are arranged.
questions.rule: Order inside a group is irrelevant, and leaving out a value within k of the group's smallest only makes later groups worse.

questions.q: Values 2, 3, 4, 9, 10 with k = 2: if the first group leaves 4 out, the total number of groups is ____.
questions.explain: Group {2, 3}; the rest 4, 9, 10 needs {4} and {9, 10}. That is 3 groups, against 2 when the first group takes 2, 3, 4.
questions.hint: Count the first group, then group what remains.
questions.rule: Order inside a group is irrelevant, and leaving out a value within k of the group's smallest only makes later groups worse.

questions.q: Values 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, k = 2. The group of 1 takes 3, 2 or 1 values; each adds one group. What decides?
questions.explain: The current group costs one in every case, so the best choice is the one that leaves the least work.
options: Pick the option taking one element only, which keeps each group small and safe
Pick the option that leaves the smallest remaining problem: take all three
Pick the option that leaves the largest remaining problem, so more is learned
Any option, since all three add one and give the same final total
optionExplain: Smaller groups leave more values to group later.
Right: the count rises by one in every case, so leave the least to solve afterwards.
A bigger leftover problem can only need as many groups or more.
The first group adds one each time, but the leftover differs in size and can need more groups.
questions.teaches: In every case the answer goes up by one for the current group, so we may as well choose the case where the remaining problem is the smallest, which means taking as many numbers as we can.
questions.rule: Order inside a group is irrelevant, and leaving out a value within k of the group's smallest only makes later groups worse.

questions.q: Lena proposes leaving 3 out of the group starting at 2 (k = 2) so it can join the next group. What is the flaw?
questions.explain: Leaving a value out drags the next group's start down, which shrinks the range it can cover and cannot reduce the count.
options: Groups must have an even number of elements
The 3 cannot be in two groups, so it would be counted twice
The 3 is further from 2 than k allows, so it cannot be in that group at all
The next group would start at a smaller value, so it covers less range
optionExplain: The problem sets no rule about group size.
Each value belongs to exactly one group in either plan.
A gap of 1 is within k = 2, so the 3 could join.
Right: starting lower limits how many later values it can hold.
questions.rule: Order inside a group is irrelevant, and leaving out a value within k of the group's smallest only makes later groups worse.

questions.q: Suppose each group had to be a block of neighbouring elements of the original array. Would sorting still be safe?
questions.explain: Without an order requirement a subsequence is a subset, so sorting is free. A block of neighbours is not a subset.
options: Yes: only the maximum and minimum matter, so any rearrangement is fine
No: with positions required, a group is more than a set of values
Yes: sorting keeps neighbouring values together, so blocks survive
No: sorting makes the maximum and minimum harder to find
optionExplain: That holds for sets of values, not for blocks of neighbours.
Right: subsequence equals subset only when no order or position is required.
Sorting moves neighbours apart as well as together.
Sorting makes them easier to find; the issue is positions.
questions.teaches: Without the order requirement, a subsequence is the same as a subset, so only then can the array be sorted without changing the problem.
questions.rule: Order inside a group is irrelevant, and leaving out a value within k of the group's smallest only makes later groups worse.

questions.q: Capital 10, two projects allowed. Projects as (needs, profit): (5, 3), (10, 8), (12, 20), (8, 4). Which should be done first?
questions.explain: Among the affordable ones, profit 8 is the largest. The card next gives the rule.
options: The one needing 12 with profit 20
The one needing 5 with profit 3
The one needing 10 with profit 8
The one needing 8 with profit 4
optionExplain: It has the most profit, but 12 is more than the capital of 10, so it is not affordable.
It is the cheapest, and cheapness is not the goal.
Right: it is the most profitable project that is affordable with capital 10.
It is affordable, but a better affordable project exists.
questions.rule: Among the projects you can afford, take the one with the most profit, and repeat up to k times.

questions.q: True or false: the greedy rule picks, among affordable projects, the one with the lowest capital requirement.
questions.explain: The rule picks the highest profit among the affordable projects. The requirement only decides which projects are affordable.
questions.rule: Among the projects you can afford, take the one with the most profit, and repeat up to k times.

questions.q: Start capital 3, three projects allowed, projects as (needs, profit): (2, 4), (3, 2), (8, 9), (15, 6). Greedy ends with capital ____.
questions.explain: Capital 3 affords (2, 4) and (3, 2): take profit 4, capital 7. Then (3, 2) only: capital 9. Now (8, 9) is affordable: capital 18.
questions.hint: Pick the largest profit among those you can afford, update the capital, and repeat.
questions.rule: Among the projects you can afford, take the one with the most profit, and repeat up to k times.

questions.q: Capital 6 and one project allowed. Projects as (needs, profit): (2, 3), (6, 7), (9, 5). Which is chosen, and what is the final capital?
questions.explain: With one project left to do, take the most profitable affordable one: profit 7, so 6 + 7 = 13.
options: The one needing 6 with profit 7, final capital 13
The one needing 9 with profit 5, final capital 11
The one needing 2 with profit 3, final capital 9
The one needing 6 with profit 7, final capital 7
optionExplain: Right: the project needing 9 is not affordable, and 7 beats 3.
It needs 9, more than the capital of 6.
It is affordable but has a smaller profit than another affordable project.
The profit is added to the capital of 6, giving 13, not 7.
questions.rule: Among the projects you can afford, take the one with the most profit, and repeat up to k times.

questions.q: Why does the author prefer the most profitable affordable project to a cheaper one with less profit?
questions.explain: More profit means more capital now and, because capital opens options, at least as many projects next.
options: It gives the most gain now and opens the most projects next
It is the only choice that cannot be undone later, unlike the others
It keeps the number of projects done as small as possible
It leaves the most expensive projects until last
optionExplain: Right: higher profit serves the goal and raises capital the most, so more projects become affordable.
Choices here are final for every option, so this is not a distinguishing reason.
The goal is final capital, not fewer projects.
Which projects come last is not the reason.
questions.teaches: The most profitable affordable project is best not only because the answer wants the maximum capital, but because it also opens the door to the most projects for the next decision.
questions.rule: Among the projects you can afford, take the one with the most profit, and repeat up to k times.

questions.q: A freelancer with savings of 4 may take up to 3 jobs, each needing savings of at least 10. What does greedy end with?
questions.explain: Up to k projects means fewer are allowed. With none affordable the process stops and the answer is the capital so far.
options: Savings of 10, since that is the requirement
Savings of 4 plus the profit of the best of the three jobs
Nothing: the process has no answer unless all 3 allowed jobs are done
Savings of 4: nothing is affordable, so the process stops there
optionExplain: Meeting the requirement is not the same as having it; savings stay at 4.
No job can be started with savings of 4.
The limit is up to 3, so doing fewer is allowed.
Right: up to 3 jobs allows fewer, and none can start.
questions.teaches: If no project is affordable, the process stops and the answer is the current capital, even when fewer than k projects have been done.
questions.rule: Among the projects you can afford, take the one with the most profit, and repeat up to k times.

questions.q: At each step you need the largest profit among the projects affordable now, and new projects join as capital grows. Which structure suits?
questions.explain: A max heap returns the largest value fast. The card next shows how it is fed.
options: A queue of profits in the order they became affordable
A max heap of profits
A stack of profits in the order they became affordable
A hash set of the affordable projects
optionExplain: A queue returns the oldest entry, not the largest.
Right: it hands over the largest profit quickly and accepts new entries.
A stack returns the newest entry, not the largest.
A set tests membership; it does not give the largest quickly.
questions.rule: Sort by capital, move a pointer to add newly affordable profits to a max heap, and pop the largest each step.

questions.q: The projects are sorted by ____ so that a pointer can find the ones that have become affordable.
questions.explain: Sorting by the capital a project needs makes the affordable ones a prefix, which a forward pointer can walk.
questions.rule: Sort by capital, move a pointer to add newly affordable profits to a max heap, and pop the largest each step.

questions.q: Start capital 5, three projects allowed, projects as (needs, profit): (4, 3), (5, 4), (11, 20), (40, 1). Order the profits taken.
questions.explain: Capital 5 affords profits 3 and 4: take 4 (capital 9), then 3 (capital 12). Now the project needing 11 is affordable: take 20 (capital 32).
questions.rule: Sort by capital, move a pointer to add newly affordable profits to a max heap, and pop the largest each step.

questions.q: With n = 100,000 projects and k = 1,000, which cost fits the heap solution?
questions.explain: The sort and the n pushes cost O(n log n), and the k pops cost O(k log n), which is smaller when k is small.
options: O(k log n), because only k projects are done
O(n times k), because each step scans every project
O((k + n) log n), which is about O(n log n) here
O(n squared), because sorting and pushing multiply
optionExplain: All n projects may be pushed to the heap, not only the k that are done.
The heap avoids scanning every project at each step.
Right: n pushes, k pops and the sort are all at most O(n log n) once k is small.
Sorting and pushing are added, not multiplied.
questions.rule: Sort by capital, move a pointer to add newly affordable profits to a max heap, and pop the largest each step.

questions.q: With k=2, w=10, profits [3, 8, 20, 4], capital [5, 10, 12, 8] this code returns 17, not 38. What is the bug?
questions.explain: heapq pops the smallest value first, so without negation each step takes the least profitable project.
options: It sorts by profit, so affordable projects are missed
It pushes plain profits, so the min heap pops the smallest
The while loop stops too early and misses affordable projects
The for loop should run n times instead of k
optionExplain: It sorts by capital, as the idea requires.
Right: a min heap needs negated profits to behave as a max heap.
The loop correctly advances while the next project is affordable.
k is the cap on projects done, so k iterations are right.
questions.rule: Sort by capital, move a pointer to add newly affordable profits to a max heap, and pop the largest each step.

questions.q: Suppose the projects were not sorted by capital. What would the pointer lose?
questions.explain: Sorted by capital, the first too-expensive project means all after it are too expensive, so the pointer can wait there.
options: The guarantee that profits are in descending order
The ability to keep profits in a heap at all, since a heap needs sorted input
The ability to count how many projects have been done
Knowing that once a project is too costly, all later ones are too
optionExplain: Sorting by capital never ordered the profits.
A heap works on any list of profits; it does not need the sort.

questions.q: From 5, 5, 5, 2, 2, 3 you must remove exactly 3 elements. What is the fewest distinct values that can remain?

questions.q: People weigh 2, 2, 3, 7 and 8, and a boat holds two people up to a total of 10. What is the fewest boats?

questions.q: A sorted list holds 1,000,000 names. Which method can find one name with about 20 looks?

questions.rule: Binary search needs a sorted search space, and then answers in O(log n) time with O(1) extra space.

questions.rule: Binary search needs a sorted search space, and then answers in O(log n) time with O(1) extra space.

questions.q: About how many looks does binary search need, at most, for 1,000,000,000 sorted entries?

Four million more passes, one for each new score

questions.q: The flattened search replaces nums[mid] from the 1D search. What else has to change in the loop?
questions.explain: Once an index converts to a cell, the earlier search applies unchanged.
options: The bounds must move by whole rows instead of single indexes
The comparison must test the row and the column separately
Nothing else: only the way the middle value is read changes
The loop must run once for every row in the matrix
optionExplain: The bounds still move by single indexes in the flattened array.
One value is compared with the target, as before.
Right: bounds, comparisons and updates are the same as in the 1D search.
A single loop over the flattened indexes is enough.
questions.teaches: The authors reduce the matrix problem to the previous 1D example: with a way to convert an index to a row and column, the same binary search applies unchanged.
questions.rule: Binary search the indexes 0 to m * n - 1 and read each middle from row = mid // n, col = mid % n.

questions.q: A grid has 6 columns and is numbered 0, 1, 2 and so on, row by row. Which index starts row 3?
questions.explain: Count the cells that come before the row. The card next explains the pattern.
optionExplain: Right: three full rows of 6 cells come before it.
This is the row number itself, not the index of its first cell.
Row 2 covers indexes 12 to 17, so 15 is inside row 2, not the start of row 3.
Row 3 covers indexes 18 to 23, so 21 is inside row 3, not its start.
questions.rule: Floor division by the row length gives the row, and the remainder gives the column.

questions.q: True or false: in a grid with n columns, row 0 uses indexes 0 to n - 1 and row 1 starts at index n.
questions.explain: Each row holds n cells, so the numbering moves to the next row after every n indexes.
questions.rule: Floor division by the row length gives the row, and the remainder gives the column.

questions.q: A theatre has 8 rows of 25 seats numbered 0 to 199 row by row. Which cell is seat index 137?
questions.explain: Quotient is the row and remainder is the column.
options: Row 12, column 5
Row 4, column 37
Row 5, column 12
Row 6, column 12
optionExplain: This swaps the quotient and the remainder.
Column 37 does not exist; the row has only 25 seats.
Row 6 starts at index 150, so seat 137 is still in row 5.
questions.rule: Floor division by the row length gives the row, and the remainder gives the column.

questions.q: In a grid with 7 columns, the cell in row 4, column 3 has flat index ____.
questions.explain: Four full rows of 7 cells come first, which is 28 indexes, and the column adds 3, so the index is 4 * 7 + 3 = 31.
questions.rule: Floor division by the row length gives the row, and the remainder gives the column.

questions.q: Dividing by the row count 3 instead of the column count 4, which of indexes 0 to 3 first maps to a wrong cell?
questions.explain: The divisor must be the row length. A wrong divisor stays right only while the index is below it.
options: Index 0, which maps to (0, 0) instead of (0, 3)
Index 1, which maps to (0, 1) instead of (1, 0)
Index 2, which maps to (0, 2) instead of (0, 3)
Index 3, which maps to (1, 0) instead of (0, 3)
optionExplain: Index 0 maps to (0, 0) correctly with either divisor.
Index 1 is at row 0, column 1 in both versions.
Index 2 is at row 0, column 2 in both versions.
Right: with divisor 3, index 3 gives row 1, column 0, but its true cell is row 0, column 3.
questions.rule: Floor division by the row length gives the row, and the remainder gives the column.

questions.q: An image 640 pixels wide is stored row by row in one flat list. At which index is the pixel in row 3, column 7?
questions.explain: The index is the cells above plus the column.
optionExplain: Right: three rows of 640 pixels come before row 3, so 3 * 640 + 7.
This is 2 * 640, the start of row 2, with no offset.
This is 640 + 7, which is row 1, column 7.
This is 3 * 640, the start of row 3, without the column offset.
questions.teaches: A cell in row r has r * n cells above it, so its index is r * n + col, which is why dividing the index by n recovers r.
questions.rule: Floor division by the row length gives the row, and the remainder gives the column.

questions.q: Potions [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 20] are sorted, and a spell needs a potion of at least 10. How many potions qualify?
questions.explain: Count from the first potion that reaches the threshold to the end. The card next shows how to find it fast.
optionExplain: This counts 8 as well, but 8 is below 10.
This leaves out one of the three potions that reach 10.
This counts every potion except the weakest, which includes values below 10.
Right: 11, 14 and 20 are at least 10.
questions.rule: The count for a spell is the number of potions minus the insertion index of success / spell in the sorted potions.

questions.q: True or false: with insertion index i for the threshold in m sorted potions, m - i potions reach the threshold.
