questions.explain: Indexes i to m - 1 hold values at or above the threshold, and that range has m - i entries.
questions.rule: The count for a spell is the number of potions minus the insertion index of success / spell in the sorted potions.

questions.q: Sorted potions [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 20], success 40, spell 10. How many potions pair successfully?
questions.explain: Divide success by the spell, find the insertion index, and subtract it from the number of potions.
optionExplain: The weakest potion, 2, gives a product of 20, which is below 40.
Right: the spell needs a potion of at least 4, and the insertion index of 4 is 1, so 6 - 1 = 5.
This counts from the wrong insertion index; the first potion at least 4 is 5, at index 1.
This is the insertion index, not the count.
questions.rule: The count for a spell is the number of potions minus the insertion index of success / spell in the sorted potions.

questions.q: With sorted potions [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 20] and success 40, a spell of strength 2 pairs with ____ potion(s).
questions.explain: The spell needs a potion of at least 20. The insertion index of 20 is 5, so 6 - 5 = 1 potion qualifies.
questions.rule: The count for a spell is the number of potions minus the insertion index of success / spell in the sorted potions.

questions.q: Potions [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 20], success 44, spell 4: testing with > instead of >= gives 2, not 3. Why?
questions.explain: At least means that equal counts, so use the left-most test with >=.
options: The potions should be sorted in descending order for this kind of test
The need should be 44 * 4, since success scales with the spell
Equal products count, so the test must be >= and potion 11 must stay
The loop should end at len(potions) - 1, not len(potions)
optionExplain: Ascending order is what the search needs.
The need is success divided by the spell, which is 11.
Right: 4 * 11 = 44 reaches success, but > drops the potion equal to 11.
The upper bound is len(potions) so the insertion index can be one past the end.
questions.rule: The count for a spell is the number of potions minus the insertion index of success / spell in the sorted potions.

questions.q: A shop keeps gift-card balances sorted and, for each purchase price, counts the cards whose balance covers it. What role does binary search play?
questions.explain: Sometimes binary search is the whole answer; here it is a tool inside a larger loop.
options: It replaces the loop over purchases and gives the final answer directly
It sorts the balances so that no other step is needed
A tool that speeds up the per-purchase count inside a larger algorithm
It checks every balance against every purchase to count them
optionExplain: The algorithm still handles each purchase one at a time.
Sorting is a separate step done once before the searches.
Right: the loop over purchases stays, and each count uses a search.
That is the brute-force approach the search avoids.
questions.teaches: Sometimes you directly binary search for the answer, and other times binary search is only a tool that speeds up your algorithm.
questions.rule: The count for a spell is the number of potions minus the insertion index of success / spell in the sorted potions.

questions.q: There are n spells and m potions. How many pairs does the brute-force check examine?
questions.explain: Each spell meets each potion once. The card next compares this with sorting and searching.
options: n + m
n * m
n log m
m log n
optionExplain: This counts each item once, not each pair.
Right: every spell is paired with every potion.
This is the cost of one binary search per spell, not of the pairs.
This swaps the roles and does not count pairs.
questions.rule: Pay for one sort, and then each query costs only a logarithm.

questions.q: True or false: each of the n binary searches over the sorted potions costs O(log m).
questions.explain: Each search halves a space of m potions, so each costs O(log m), and n searches cost O(n log m).
questions.rule: Pay for one sort, and then each query costs only a logarithm.

questions.q: With n = m = 1,000,000, put the approaches in order from least to most work.
questions.explain: Sorting costs about m log m and the searches about n log m, which is near 40 million here, far below the 10 to the power 12 pairs.
items: One scan of the potions: about 1 million steps
Sort once, then search for each spell: about 40 million steps
Check all pairs: about 1 trillion steps
questions.rule: Pay for one sort, and then each query costs only a logarithm.

questions.q: True or false: with a single spell and 1,000,000 potions, sorting the potions first is cheaper than one scan of them.
questions.explain: Sorting costs about m log m, which is more than one scan of m potions. The saving appears only with many queries.
questions.rule: Pay for one sort, and then each query costs only a logarithm.

questions.q: A developer says the whole algorithm costs O(n log m), because each search is O(log m) and sorting is free. What is missing?
questions.explain: Sorting is a cost term of its own.
options: The cost of reading each spell, which is O(n log n)
The cost of dividing success by each spell, which is O(m)
The cost of building the answer array, which is O(n * m)
The O(m log m) cost of sorting the potions once
optionExplain: Reading the spells is O(n), and it is dominated by the searches.
There is one division per spell, so O(n) in total.
The answer array has one entry per spell and costs O(n).
Right: the sort has a real cost, and the total is (m + n) log m.
questions.rule: Pay for one sort, and then each query costs only a logarithm.

questions.q: A team claims the pairs algorithm uses O(1) extra space, because binary search does. Is that right?
questions.explain: Check the space of every step, not only the search.
options: No: sorting may use extra space, depending on the algorithm
Yes: the sort works in place, so no language adds extra space
No: each search needs an array of size m to track bounds
Yes: the answer array is part of the input, so it is not counted
optionExplain: Right: the search is O(1), but the whole algorithm includes the sort.
The space of a sort depends on the algorithm and the language.
The search keeps only a few integer variables.
The answer array is new storage built by the algorithm.
questions.teaches: Because the input is sorted, some space is used that depends on the sorting algorithm of the language, so the whole algorithm is not O(1) in extra space.
questions.rule: Pay for one sort, and then each query costs only a logarithm.

questions.q: A problem asks for the smallest box capacity that fits all items within a trip limit. Which fact points to binary search on the capacity?
questions.explain: The search needs results that change only once along the range of capacities. The card next lists the conditions.
options: If a capacity works, every larger capacity works as well
The items can be listed in alphabetical order by name
The number of items is even, so the range halves cleanly
The capacity must be a power of two, so few values exist
optionExplain: Right: working values then form one block above the answer.
The order of the items says nothing about how capacities behave.
Parity of the item count is unrelated to the search.
The capacity can be any integer, and a power of two is not required.
questions.rule: Binary search the answers when a quick check exists and the results change only once along the range.

questions.q: A check function used in a solution-space search must test one candidate in O(n) or ____ time.
questions.explain: If the check is slow, O(log k) repetitions of it will be slow as well, so it must be O(n) or better.
questions.rule: Binary search the answers when a quick check exists and the results change only once along the range.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether it meets the conditions for binary searching the answer.
questions.explain: The conditions are a quick check and one-way results. A value that works and fails alternately breaks the second condition, and a very slow check breaks the first.

items.t: Smallest speed that arrives on time: a speed that works also works for every higher speed
Largest ribbon length that still gives 8 pieces: a length that works also works for every shorter one
Smallest box size that holds all items: if a size fits them, every bigger size fits them
A value that works at 36, fails at 37 and works again at 38
A check that must try every subset of the items, so it takes exponential time
Prime numbers: 7 works, 8 and 9 fail, and 11 works again

questions.rule: Binary search the answers when a quick check exists and the results change only once along the range.

questions.q: A bakery asks for the largest slice width that still serves at least 20 customers. Which fact makes binary search on the width valid?
questions.explain: For a maximum, a working value makes all smaller values work.
options: If a width serves 20 customers, every wider width does too
If a width serves 20 customers, every narrower width does too
The widths are given in sorted order in the input of the problem
The number of customers is a power of two, so halving fits
optionExplain: Wider slices serve fewer customers, so this is the opposite direction.
Right: for a maximum, working values extend downward from the answer.
The input order does not matter; the property of the candidates does.
The number of customers has no bearing on the structure of the answers.
questions.rule: Binary search the answers when a quick check exists and the results change only once along the range.

questions.q: A student says: for a minimum, if the task is possible for x, it is possible for every number less than x. What is wrong?
questions.explain: A minimum search relies on larger values working once a smaller one does.
options: Nothing is wrong: a minimum always works for every smaller number
It should say every number less than x is impossible as well
For a minimum, a working x means every larger number works
It should say possible at x means x is the answer
optionExplain: If smaller numbers always worked, the minimum would be the lowest number, so the search would be pointless.
Smaller numbers can be either possible or impossible, and the minimum search relies on the larger side.
Right: smaller numbers may fail, which is why x is only a candidate for the minimum.
A possible value need not be the smallest possible one.
questions.rule: Binary search the answers when a quick check exists and the results change only once along the range.

questions.q: You must write the check for a largest-ribbon-length problem. According to the authors, what kind of algorithm does check usually use?
questions.explain: The check can often be a simple greedy pass over the input.
options: A second binary search nested inside the first
Dynamic programming over every subset of the pieces
A full sort of the candidate answers
A greedy one
optionExplain: Nested searches are not what the authors describe for the check.
This would make the check very slow, against the quick-check condition.
The candidates are consecutive numbers and need no sort.
Right: the authors say that in most cases the algorithm inside check is a greedy one.
questions.teaches: In most cases the algorithm used inside the check function is a greedy one.
questions.rule: Binary search the answers when a quick check exists and the results change only once along the range.

questions.q: Speeds 1 to 4 all miss a deadline and every speed from 5 up meets it. Which value would a minimum-speed question ask for?
questions.explain: The answer sits where the results switch. The card next names this switch.
options: The highest speed that was tried
optionExplain: This is the highest speed in the impossible zone, so it misses the deadline.
This is the lowest candidate, but it is not possible.
Right: it is the lowest speed in the zone where the task is possible.
The highest tried speed meets the deadline but is not the lowest one that does.
questions.rule: Possible and impossible answers form two gap-free zones, and a minimum or maximum is the value at the point where they meet.

questions.q: True or false: the possible zone and the impossible zone overlap in a few values near the threshold.
questions.explain: The zones have no breaks and no overlap: every candidate belongs to exactly one of them.
questions.rule: Possible and impossible answers form two gap-free zones, and a minimum or maximum is the value at the point where they meet.

questions.q: Candidates 10 to 100 in tens give N N N N Y Y Y Y Y Y (Y is possible). A minimum search returns ____.
questions.explain: For a minimum, the answer is the first candidate in the possible zone, which is 50.
questions.hint: Which candidate is the first one marked Y?
questions.rule: Possible and impossible answers form two gap-free zones, and a minimum or maximum is the value at the point where they meet.

questions.q: Over the candidates 1 to 8, which pattern of check results has a usable threshold?
questions.explain: A usable pattern changes only once.
options: Y N Y N Y N Y N
N Y N Y Y Y N N
Y Y N N Y Y N N
N N N Y Y Y Y Y
optionExplain: The results alternate, so there are many switches and no single threshold.
The zones are broken into several pieces.
The pattern changes three times, so there are no two zones.
Right: one impossible block followed by one possible block.
questions.rule: Possible and impossible answers form two gap-free zones, and a minimum or maximum is the value at the point where they meet.

questions.q: Candidates 1 to 8 give Y Y Y Y Y N N N, and a maximum search returns 6. What is the error?
questions.explain: A maximum is the end of the possible zone; the threshold lies right after it.
options: The answer is 1, the first value that works, since a maximum starts low
The answer is 5, the last value that works, not the first failure
The answer is 8, the last value tested
Nothing is wrong, since 6 is where the pattern changes
optionExplain: The first value that works is the lowest, not the highest.
Right: for a maximum, the answer is the last candidate in the possible zone.
Eight fails the check.
The pattern changes at 6, but the answer is the last value that works, which is 5.
questions.rule: Possible and impossible answers form two gap-free zones, and a minimum or maximum is the value at the point where they meet.

questions.q: For a minimum search, which pair of facts together guarantees two gap-free zones?
questions.explain: The two facts for the same direction fit together.
options: Possible at x means possible for all larger values, and impossible at x means impossible for all smaller values
Possible at x means possible for all smaller values, and impossible at x means impossible for all larger values
Possible at x means possible for all larger values, and impossible at x means impossible for all larger values
Possible at x means impossible for every other value, and the reverse
optionExplain: Right: working values extend upward and failing values extend downward.
This pair holds for a maximum, not a minimum.
The second statement contradicts the first for larger values.
This would give a single possible value, not a zone.
questions.teaches: The second and third requirements together imply that there are two zones, one possible and one impossible, with no breaks and no overlap.
questions.rule: Possible and impossible answers form two gap-free zones, and a minimum or maximum is the value at the point where they meet.

questions.q: A check costs O(n), and the answer lies in a range of k candidate values. What does binary searching the range cost?
questions.explain: The number of passes is logarithmic in the range, and every pass runs the check. The card next confirms this.
options: O(n * k)
O(k log n)
O(n log k)
O(n + k)
optionExplain: This is the cost of trying every candidate once.
This swaps the roles of n and k.
Right: about log k passes, each with one check of cost O(n).
This adds the two sizes as if the check ran only once.
questions.rule: Start at the smallest and largest possible answers; the total cost is log k checks, each costing as much as one check.

questions.q: In O(n log k), the letter k stands for the size of the solution ____.
questions.explain: The solution space is the range of candidate answers, and k is how many candidates it holds.
questions.rule: Start at the smallest and largest possible answers; the total cost is log k checks, each costing as much as one check.

questions.q: A check scans 200,000 weights, and the answer lies between 1 and 1,000,000,000. Roughly how many steps does the whole search take?
questions.explain: Passes times the cost of one check.
options: About 200 billion
About 6 million
About 200,000
About 30
optionExplain: This multiplies the weights by a billion candidates, which is a scan of the whole range.
Right: about 30 passes, each scanning 200,000 weights.
This counts one check only.
This counts the passes, not the steps within each check.
questions.rule: Start at the smallest and largest possible answers; the total cost is log k checks, each costing as much as one check.

questions.q: Put the steps of a solution-space binary search in order.
questions.explain: The bounds come first, then each pass picks a middle, checks it and keeps the useful half, until left passes right.
items: Find the smallest and largest possible answers
Take the middle candidate of the current range
Keep the half of the range that can hold the threshold
questions.rule: Start at the smallest and largest possible answers; the total cost is log k checks, each costing as much as one check.

questions.q: A minimum-speed search starts with left = 1 and right = 5, but the true answer is 8. What does the minimum template return?
questions.explain: If the range misses the answer, the result looks like a normal number but is wrong.
options: 8, because the check eventually finds the answer
-1, because the loop reports a missing answer
5, the largest value in the range, where the loop stops
6, a wrong value, since the range missed the answer
optionExplain: The check can only test values inside the range, and 8 is outside it.
The template returns a pointer value and does not signal failure.
Left moves above right when all checks fail, so it returns 6.
Right: every check fails, so left climbs past right to 6.
questions.rule: Start at the smallest and largest possible answers; the total cost is log k checks, each costing as much as one check.

questions.q: The possible range of answers grows from 1,000,000 to 1,000,000,000,000. At most how many more checks does the search make?
questions.explain: A bigger range adds one pass per doubling.
options: About a million more
About 1,000 times as many
About 20 more
None, since the range does not change the passes
optionExplain: A million times more candidates adds only a few passes under halving.
The count of passes grows by one for every doubling, not in proportion to the range.
Right: log2 of a million is about 20, and log2 of a trillion is about 40.
The range sets the number of halvings.
questions.teaches: Even if the possible solution space is huge, logarithms run so fast that the search stays very efficient.
questions.rule: Start at the smallest and largest possible answers; the total cost is log k checks, each costing as much as one check.

questions.q: Koko eats from one pile per hour at 3 bananas per hour. How many hours does a pile of 8 bananas take?
questions.explain: A leftover part of a pile still costs a whole hour. The card next uses this in the check.
optionExplain: Right: two hours eat 6 bananas, and the last 2 need a third hour.
This ignores the 2 bananas left after 6 are eaten.
Hours here are whole; she cannot share an hour between piles.
Three hours already eat 9 bananas, which covers the 8.
questions.rule: Count ceil(pile / k) hours for each pile, and search speeds 1 to max(piles) for the smallest speed within h.

questions.q: True or false: the lowest eating speed worth testing in the search is 1 banana per hour.
questions.explain: A speed of 0 would eat nothing, and the speed must be a positive whole number, so the search starts at 1.
questions.rule: Count ceil(pile / k) hours for each pile, and search speeds 1 to max(piles) for the smallest speed within h.

questions.q: For piles [5, 8, 12] and an eating speed of 7, the hours needed are ____.
questions.explain: Round each pile on its own: 1 hour for the 5, 2 hours for the 8 and 2 hours for the 12. Rounding the total 25 / 7 would give 4 and undercount.
questions.rule: Count ceil(pile / k) hours for each pile, and search speeds 1 to max(piles) for the smallest speed within h.

questions.q: For piles [7, 4, 9, 3] and h = 8 hours, what is the minimum eating speed?
questions.explain: Test speeds from low to high and keep the first one within 8 hours.
optionExplain: At speed 3 the piles need 9 hours, which is over the limit of 8.
Right: at speed 4 the piles take 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 7 hours, but at speed 3 they take 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 9.
Speed 5 works, but 4 works as well and is lower.
This is the largest pile, an upper bound but not the minimum.
questions.rule: Count ceil(pile / k) hours for each pile, and search speeds 1 to max(piles) for the smallest speed within h.

questions.q: A check uses ceil(sum(piles) / k). For piles [3, 3, 3], k = 2, h = 5 it says the speed works. What is wrong?
questions.explain: A pile left over at the end of an hour wastes the rest of that hour.
options: The sum should be divided by h and not by k, since h is the time limit
The ceiling should be a floor, giving 4 hours for the total
Nothing is wrong, since 9 / 2 rounds up to 5
Piles round up one by one, so the real time is 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 hours
optionExplain: The time for a speed is bananas over speed, not over hours.
A floor would undercount even more.
The total 9 / 2 gives 5, but piles cannot share an hour, so 5 is too low.
Right: 6 hours is over the limit of 5.
questions.rule: Count ceil(pile / k) hours for each pile, and search speeds 1 to max(piles) for the smallest speed within h.

questions.q: Jobs have different page counts and a printer does one job per hour at k pages per hour. What is the highest speed worth testing?
questions.explain: Once every pile takes only one hour, a faster speed cannot save any more time.
options: The total number of pages in all jobs
The page count of the largest job
The page count of the smallest job
The number of jobs
optionExplain: Even a speed this high can do no better than one hour per job.
Right: at that speed every job already takes one hour, so a faster speed gains nothing.
Larger jobs would then take several hours, so faster speeds could still help.
The number of jobs says nothing about page speed.
questions.teaches: The maximum possible answer is max(piles), because a faster speed cannot help once every pile already takes one hour.
questions.rule: Count ceil(pile / k) hours for each pile, and search speeds 1 to max(piles) for the smallest speed within h.

questions.q: A path's effort is the largest height change between consecutive cells. A path steps by 1, then 4, then 2. What is its effort?
questions.explain: Effort is a maximum over the path, not a sum. The card next searches for the least effort.
optionExplain: Right: the largest single change is 4.
This adds the changes; effort is the largest single one.
This is the last step, not the largest.
This is the first step, not the largest.
questions.rule: Make the check a reachability search that crosses only steps within the allowed effort, and binary search for the smallest effort that reaches the goal.

questions.q: True or false: if a path exists when the allowed difference is e, a path also exists when the allowed difference is e + 1.
questions.explain: The same path stays valid when steps are allowed to be a little larger, so working efforts extend upward.
questions.rule: Make the check a reachability search that crosses only steps within the allowed effort, and binary search for the smallest effort that reaches the goal.

questions.q: For the grid [[1, 3, 5], [2, 8, 3], [4, 6, 4]], the minimum effort from the top left to the bottom right is ____.
questions.explain: The path 1, 2, 4, 6, 4 changes by 1, 2, 2 and 2. With effort 1 the search reaches 2 and cannot move on, since both next cells differ by 2 or more.
questions.rule: Make the check a reachability search that crosses only steps within the allowed effort, and binary search for the smallest effort that reaches the goal.

questions.q: A 1000 by 1000 grid has heights up to 1,000,000. About how many cell visits does the whole search make, ignoring constants?
questions.explain: Passes (about log2 of the largest height) times cells.
options: About 1 million
About 20 million
About a trillion
About 20 thousand
optionExplain: This counts only one search of the grid.
Right: about 20 passes of the search, each visiting up to a million cells.
This is the cost of searching for every effort in turn, about 10 to the power 6 times 10 to the power 6.
This counts the passes by the number of rows.
questions.rule: Make the check a reachability search that crosses only steps within the allowed effort, and binary search for the smallest effort that reaches the goal.

questions.q: A developer starts the search with left = 1 as the lowest effort. For a grid where every cell holds 7, what does it return?
questions.explain: The lowest possible effort is 0, so the range must begin at 0.
options: 0, because the search finds it anyway
7, the height of every cell
1, but the true minimum effort is 0
-1, because the path does not exist
optionExplain: The search cannot test 0 if it starts at 1.
Effort is a difference, and all differences are 0.
Right: every step changes by 0, so effort 0 already works, and the range must include 0.
A path exists, and the code has no -1 result here.
questions.rule: Make the check a reachability search that crosses only steps within the allowed effort, and binary search for the smallest effort that reaches the goal.

questions.q: If heights could be negative, running from -5 to 8, is the largest height 8 still a safe upper bound for the effort?
questions.explain: The upper bound is the largest possible difference, which depends on the range of the heights.
options: No: a step from -5 to 8 differs by 13, more than 8
Yes: effort can never exceed the largest height
Yes: negative heights lower the differences
No: the upper bound must be the sum of all the heights
optionExplain: Right: with negative values, differences can exceed the largest value.
This holds only when heights are not negative.
A negative height raises the difference with a high neighbour.
The effort is a single difference, not a sum.
questions.teaches: Heights are not negative in this problem, so no difference between two cells can exceed the largest number, which makes it a safe upper bound.
questions.rule: Make the check a reachability search that crosses only steps within the allowed effort, and binary search for the smallest effort that reaches the goal.

questions.q: Trains leave only at whole hours. You leave at hour 0 and arrive after a 1.5-hour ride. When can the next train leave?
questions.explain: The wait rounds the elapsed time up. The card next puts this in the check.
options: At hour 1.5, immediately
At hour 3, one full wait after the arrival
At hour 1, which is before the arrival
At hour 2, after waiting half an hour
optionExplain: Trains leave only at whole hours.
Hour 2 is the next whole hour, so there is no need to wait longer.
You cannot leave before you arrive.
Right: the next whole hour after 1.5 is 2.
questions.rule: Round the elapsed time up before each ride but not after the last, and return -1 when there are more trains than the rounded-up limit.

questions.q: True or false: the check rounds up the time of the last ride before comparing it with the limit.
questions.explain: No further train has to be caught after the last ride, so its time is added without rounding.
questions.rule: Round the elapsed time up before each ride but not after the last, and return -1 when there are more trains than the rounded-up limit.

questions.q: For distances [2, 3, 5] at speed 2, the arrival time in hours is ____.
questions.explain: The first ride ends at 1. The second starts at 1 and ends at 2.5. The third waits until 3 and ends at 5.5, which is over the limit of 4.5.
questions.rule: Round the elapsed time up before each ride but not after the last, and return -1 when there are more trains than the rounded-up limit.

questions.q: For distances [2, 3, 5] and a limit of 4.5 hours, what is the minimum whole-number speed?
questions.explain: Check speeds from low to high and keep the first that arrives on time.
optionExplain: At speed 2 the arrival time is 5.5 hours, which is over the limit.
Speed 4 works, but 3 works as well and is lower.
Right: at speed 3 the arrival time is about 3.67, and at speed 2 it is 5.5.
Speed 5 works, but lower speeds do too.
questions.rule: Round the elapsed time up before each ride but not after the last, and return -1 when there are more trains than the rounded-up limit.

questions.q: A developer says 4 trains can make a 2.9-hour limit at speed 10,000,000, as rides take almost no time. What is wrong?
questions.explain: With more trains than ceil(hour), the answer is -1 whatever the speed.
options: The speed limit should be a float rather than an integer
The fourth train cannot leave before hour 3, past 2.9
The rides must be rounded after the last train as well
Nothing is wrong, since a fast enough speed arrives on time
optionExplain: A larger speed does not help, whatever its type.
Right: three rides each need a whole-hour departure, so the fourth leaves at hour 3 at the earliest.
The last ride is not rounded, so this is not the cause.
Waiting for departure hours does not depend on speed.
questions.rule: Round the elapsed time up before each ride but not after the last, and return -1 when there are more trains than the rounded-up limit.

questions.q: The problem statement gives no upper limit on the answer. Where should right start?
questions.explain: When no maximum is given, use an arbitrarily large bound.
options: At a huge value above any answer, such as 10 to the power 10
At the largest distance in the input, since no ride needs more
At the number of trains, since each train adds an hour of waiting
At the time limit, since the speed cannot exceed it
optionExplain: Right: logarithms are so fast that a large bound hardly costs anything.
A tight time limit can need a speed far above any single distance.
The number of trains says nothing about how fast the speed must be.
The limit is a time, not a speed.
questions.teaches: If you cannot find a maximum possible answer from the input, you can use an arbitrarily large number for right, such as 10 to the power 10, because logarithms are so fast that it hardly makes a difference.
questions.rule: Round the elapsed time up before each ride but not after the last, and return -1 when there are more trains than the rounded-up limit.

questions.q: A search for the largest passing value sets left = mid + 1 whenever check passes. When the loop ends, which pointer holds the answer?
questions.explain: Think about which pointer last stepped past the answer. The card next explains it.
options: left
right
mid
Neither, because the loop returns a flag
optionExplain: Left has moved one past the answer, since it was pushed up after each pass.
Right: the pointer that kept getting pulled down by failures is the one that ends on the last passing value.
The variable mid exists only inside the loop and is not the final answer.
The template returns a pointer value.
questions.rule: Return left for a minimum and right for a maximum, because the pointer that moved past the answer ends right beside it.

questions.q: True or false: when looking for a minimum, the loop returns the left pointer.
questions.explain: For a minimum, left climbs until it equals the answer, so left is returned.
questions.rule: Return left for a minimum and right for a maximum, because the pointer that moved past the answer ends right beside it.

questions.q: For the largest x with x * x <= 50 over 0 to 50, what are left and right when the loop ends?
questions.explain: The loop ends when the pointers cross, with right on the last value that passes.
options: left = 7 and right = 8
left = 7 and right = 7
left = 8 and right = 8
left = 8 and right = 7
optionExplain: The loop ends with left greater than right, so left cannot be the smaller one.
Left ends one past the last passing value.
The right pointer ends on the last passing value, 7.
Right: check(7) passes and check(8) fails, so right ends on 7 and left ends on 8.
questions.rule: Return left for a minimum and right for a maximum, because the pointer that moved past the answer ends right beside it.

questions.q: Searching for the smallest x with x * x >= 50 over the range 0 to 50, the minimum template returns ____.
questions.explain: 7 * 7 is 49, below 50, and 8 * 8 is 64. The loop ends with left = 8 and right = 7, and the minimum template returns left.
questions.rule: Return left for a minimum and right for a maximum, because the pointer that moved past the answer ends right beside it.

questions.q: A developer returns left from a search for the largest x with x * x <= 50 and gets 8. Why is that wrong?
questions.explain: For a maximum, return right.
options: Left ends one past the last passing value, so the answer is 7
The loop condition should be left < right, which would give 7
The check should use < instead of <=, which would give 7
Nothing is wrong, since 8 squared is close enough to 50
optionExplain: Right: for a maximum, the answer is held by right.
The condition is not the cause; the choice of the pointer is.
This changes the problem, not the choice of the returned pointer.
The task asks for the largest value that satisfies the check.
questions.rule: Return left for a minimum and right for a maximum, because the pointer that moved past the answer ends right beside it.

questions.q: A ribbon search over 1 to 40 wants the longest length. check(12) passes; check(13) and above fail. Which pointer holds the answer?
questions.explain: The mirror rule uses right for any maximum.
options: left, holding 13
right, holding 12
right, holding 13
left, holding 12
optionExplain: This is the pointer of the minimum case, and 13 fails the check.
Right: a maximum is held by right, and 12 is the last length that works.
The right pointer ends on the passing value, not on the failing one.
Left ends one past the last passing value, so it holds 13.
questions.teaches: For a maximum, check(x) passing sets left = x + 1, which leaves the answer outside the search space; later checks fail and pull right down until right = x and the loop ends because right < left.
questions.rule: Return left for a minimum and right for a maximum, because the pointer that moved past the answer ends right beside it.

questions.q: You must list every 4-letter string over a to z that meets some rule. An exhaustive search first generates how many candidate strings?
questions.explain: Every position can take any letter, so the choices multiply. The card next shows the cost.
options: 104 strings, because 4 positions times 26 letters gives 104
30 strings, because there are 26 letters and 4 positions
456,976 strings, because each of the 4 positions has 26 letters
24 strings, because 4 letters can be put in 4 factorial orders
optionExplain: Adding or multiplying the counts treats the positions as one choice each; the choices combine, so they multiply per position.
Adding 26 and 4 mixes two different counts; neither is the number of ways to fill the positions.
Right: 26 choices in each of 4 positions multiply to 26 to the power 4.
Factorial counts reorderings of 4 fixed letters; here each position may take any of 26 letters.
questions.rule: Exhaustive search generates every candidate and checks each one afterwards, so its cost is the number of candidates times the cost of one check.

questions.q: Exhaustive search generates all possibilities and only afterwards ____ each one for a solution.
questions.explain: The defining feature is the order of the two steps: generate everything, then check each candidate.
questions.rule: Exhaustive search generates every candidate and checks each one afterwards, so its cost is the number of candidates times the cost of one check.

questions.q: A lock has 4 dials of digits 0 to 9. Every setting is listed, then each is tested. How many settings are listed?
questions.explain: Exhaustive search generates all 10 to the power 4 settings, then tests each one.
options: 10,000 settings, since each of the 4 dials has 10 digits
5,040 settings, since the digits on the dials must differ
40 settings, since 4 dials times 10 digits each gives 40
The settings with digit sum 20, since the others are dropped
optionExplain: Right: 10 choices on each of 4 dials give 10 to the power 4, before any test.
The rule says nothing about distinct digits; every digit may repeat across the dials.
Multiplying dials by digits counts the faces, not the combined settings.
The test happens after generation, so the failing settings are generated first.
questions.rule: Exhaustive search generates every candidate and checks each one afterwards, so its cost is the number of candidates times the cost of one check.

questions.q: Strings over 26 letters grow from length 3 to length 4. The number of candidates is multiplied by ____.
questions.explain: \(26^4 / 26^3 = 26\): each extra position multiplies the candidates by 26.
questions.rule: Exhaustive search generates every candidate and checks each one afterwards, so its cost is the number of candidates times the cost of one check.

questions.q: True or false: when one check costs k steps, saying exhaustive search over length-n strings costs \(O(26^n)\) is complete.
questions.explain: The check cost multiplies the number of candidates, so the cost is \(O(k \cdot 26^n)\). Dropping k hides work that grows with the cost of a check.
questions.hint: Count the work per candidate as well as the number of candidates.
questions.rule: Exhaustive search generates every candidate and checks each one afterwards, so its cost is the number of candidates times the cost of one check.

questions.q: Strings of length 4 must now use only vowels. A plain exhaustive search still starts by generating how many candidate strings?
questions.explain: A constraint does not shrink the work of exhaustive search; it only changes which candidates pass the check.
options: 5, because a single vowel string is the only valid answer
625, because only the 5 vowels can be used at each position
104, because the constraint cuts the choices per position
456,976, because the constraint is applied only afterwards
optionExplain: Several strings are valid, and anyway valid strings are found only after the full list exists.
Only a search that rejects bad letters while building produces 625; exhaustive search does not.
The constraint changes which strings pass the check, not how many are generated.
Right: all 26 to the power 4 strings are produced, then the non-vowel ones are rejected.
questions.teaches: Adding a constraint does not reduce the number of candidates exhaustive search generates; it still produces all of them and then checks each one, so a tight constraint saves no work.
questions.rule: Exhaustive search generates every candidate and checks each one afterwards, so its cost is the number of candidates times the cost of one check.

questions.q: In the tree of all strings built one letter at a time, what does the path from the root to a node stand for?
questions.explain: The path from the root spells the candidate so far. The card next defines the tree.
options: The number of strings that are still possible
The letters chosen so far, in order
Only the last letter that was chosen
The shortest route back to an answer
optionExplain: A count belongs to a subtree, not to a path; the path itself is a sequence of choices.
Right: following the choices from the root spells the partial string.
The last letter is only the final step; the whole path is the string being built.
The tree has no notion of a route back to an answer; the path records choices made.
questions.rule: Picture the possibilities as a tree whose root is the empty candidate and whose paths from the root spell the candidates being built.

questions.q: In the tree of all strings over a to z, every node has ____ children.
questions.explain: One child exists for each letter that could come next, so every node has 26 children.
questions.rule: Picture the possibilities as a tree whose root is the empty candidate and whose paths from the root spell the candidates being built.

questions.q: Codes of length 3 use digits 0, 1 and 2. In the tree of all codes, what are the children per node and the depth?
questions.explain: Children match the choices for the next piece, and depth matches the length of the finished candidate.
options: Three children per node; depth 2
Three children per node; depth 3
Three children per node; depth 9
Two children per node; depth 3
optionExplain: The root is the empty code at depth 0, and each of the 3 positions adds one level, so the depth is 3, not 2.
Right: one child per digit, and one level per position in the code.
Nine would be digits times positions; depth counts positions only.
There are 3 digits available, so each node has 3 children, not 2.
questions.rule: Picture the possibilities as a tree whose root is the empty candidate and whose paths from the root spell the candidates being built.

questions.q: Order the nodes on the root-to-node path that spells the string gp, from the root downward.
questions.explain: Each step adds one letter: the root is empty, its child g spells g, and the child of g reached by p spells gp.
questions.hint: The path grows one letter at a time.
questions.rule: Picture the possibilities as a tree whose root is the empty candidate and whose paths from the root spell the candidates being built.

questions.q: True or false: in the tree of 2-letter strings, the nodes g and p lie on one path, both at depth 1.
questions.explain: Depth-1 nodes are the single letters, and they are all children of the root, so g and p are on different paths. The node gp is the child of g at depth 2.
questions.hint: Both are children of the same parent.
questions.rule: Picture the possibilities as a tree whose root is the empty candidate and whose paths from the root spell the candidates being built.

questions.q: Words of length 3 are built from the letters a and b. In the tree of all such words, which nodes are the finished candidates?
questions.explain: Interior nodes are partial candidates; the leaves at the full depth are the complete ones.
options: The 2 children of the root, one for each letter
Every node, since each path spells some string
Only the root, since it holds all the strings
Only the 8 leaf nodes at depth 3
optionExplain: Those are partial candidates of length 1; the words are not complete yet.
Every path spells a partial string, but only a path of full length is a finished word.
The root is the empty candidate, the starting point of the build.
Right: a finished candidate has all 3 letters, so it sits at the deepest level.
questions.teaches: The leaf nodes of the tree represent the answers: a complete candidate sits at the full depth, while the nodes above it are partial candidates.
questions.rule: Picture the possibilities as a tree whose root is the empty candidate and whose paths from the root spell the candidates being built.

questions.q: You build a 4-letter string that may use only vowels, and you have written the letter b. What should an efficient search do next?
questions.explain: A path that has already broken the rule can be dropped together with everything below it. The card next names this.
options: Drop every string that begins with b and move on
Finish all 26 cubed completions of b, then reject them
Replace b with a vowel and carry on from that string
Start again from the empty string with a new rule
optionExplain: Right: no extension of b can be all vowels, so the whole group is skipped at once.
Generating them first is exactly the waste that an early stop avoids.
Changing the letter in place builds a different candidate; the search should visit the other letters in turn.
Restarting loses the work on the other letters and solves nothing.
questions.rule: Prune a path the moment it cannot lead to a solution, which skips every candidate below it.

questions.q: True or false: pruning a path discards the whole subtree below that path, not only the node where the path was abandoned.
questions.explain: The candidates below a pruned node all begin with the same bad path, so none of them is generated.
questions.hint: Think about what every string below the bad node has in common.
questions.rule: Prune a path the moment it cannot lead to a solution, which skips every candidate below it.

questions.q: A 3-digit code uses odd digits only. A search drops any even digit as it builds. How many codes does it build?
questions.explain: With pruning, each position offers only the 5 odd digits, so the count is 5 cubed.
options: 500, since half the digits are dropped from the 1,000 codes
15, since there are 5 odd digits and 3 positions
125, since 5 odd digits are available at each of 3 positions
1,000, since pruning changes only the order of the search
optionExplain: Halving once would be right for one position; the drop applies at each position, so it compounds.
Multiplying choices by positions is not how choices combine.
Right: 5 choices per position multiply to 5 cubed.
Pruning removes candidates; it does more than reorder them.
questions.rule: Prune a path the moment it cannot lead to a solution, which skips every candidate below it.

questions.q: Vowel-only strings of length 4: exhaustive search builds 456,976 candidates, backtracking 625. Rounded down, backtracking builds ____ times fewer.
questions.explain: \(456976 / 625 = 731.16\), so backtracking generates about 731 times fewer candidates.
questions.rule: Prune a path the moment it cannot lead to a solution, which skips every candidate below it.

questions.q: A solver searching for 5-letter words drops any partial string that is not itself a word, such as sp. What is wrong with this pruning?
questions.explain: A pruning rule must be certain: only abandon a path when no extension can succeed.
options: It prunes too little, since non-words should be kept to the end
It prunes after the base case, which is too late to save work
It stops pruning once a word is found, so duplicates appear
A partial string that is not a word can still grow into one
optionExplain: Keeping non-words to the end is the exhaustive search the pruning is meant to avoid.
The base case is not involved; the fault is the condition used for pruning.
Duplicates are a separate matter; this rule fails on correctness, not on repeats.
Right: sp is no word, yet it extends to spin, so abandoning it loses answers.
questions.rule: Prune a path the moment it cannot lead to a solution, which skips every candidate below it.

questions.q: You search a binary search tree for a value x, and the root holds a value greater than x. Which part can be ignored?
questions.explain: Skipping a whole subtree because of what you know about its root is the same move as pruning.
options: The entire left subtree of the root
The entire right subtree of the root
Nothing, because every node must be compared with x
Only the root itself, and nothing below it
optionExplain: Values smaller than the root are where x could be, so the left subtree must be searched.
Right: every value there is greater than the root, hence greater than x.
A search tree is ordered precisely so that whole parts can be skipped.
The root alone is checked; the rule lets you skip the whole right side too.
questions.teaches: Pruning resembles searching a binary search tree for x: if the root is greater than x, you ignore the entire right subtree without looking inside it.
questions.rule: Prune a path the moment it cannot lead to a solution, which skips every candidate below it.

questions.q: Both methods solve the same constrained problem. How do they differ in the way they treat candidates?
questions.explain: They differ in when failing candidates are removed. The card next compares them.
options: Backtracking finds fewer solutions, because pruning discards answers
Exhaustive search drops bad paths while building; backtracking builds all first
Exhaustive search builds all, then checks; backtracking prunes while building
Exhaustive search needs a tree, and backtracking does not use one
optionExplain: Pruning only removes paths that cannot succeed, so the answers are the same.
This swaps the two methods.
Right: the difference is when the bad candidates are removed.
Both can be pictured as a tree; they differ in how much of it they build.
questions.rule: Backtracking finds the same answers as exhaustive search while generating only the paths that can still succeed.

questions.q: Match each term with its meaning.
questions.explain: The card defines the two methods, the pruning step and the vowel example.
pairs: Generate all possibilities, then check each one
Prune paths that cannot lead to a solution
Abandoning a path that cannot succeed
Candidates grow as 5 to the power n
questions.rule: Backtracking finds the same answers as exhaustive search while generating only the paths that can still succeed.

questions.q: A 5-digit code may use only the digits 0 to 4. A backtracking search that rejects other digits as it builds generates ____ candidates.
questions.explain: Each of the 5 positions has 5 choices, so \(5^5 = 3125\). Exhaustive search would generate \(10^5 = 100000\).
questions.rule: Backtracking finds the same answers as exhaustive search while generating only the paths that can still succeed.

questions.q: True or false: for vowel-only strings, one more position multiplies exhaustive search by 26 and backtracking by 5.
questions.explain: Exhaustive search grows as \(26^n\) and backtracking as \(5^n\), so one more position multiplies them by 26 and 5.
questions.rule: Backtracking finds the same answers as exhaustive search while generating only the paths that can still succeed.

questions.q: Program A builds all 3-letter strings and keeps those with only vowels. Program B only ever appends a vowel. Which statement is correct?
questions.explain: The test is when the failing strings are removed: before they are built, or after.
options: B is backtracking and builds 125 strings; A builds 17,576
A is backtracking, since it keeps only the strings that pass
Both are backtracking, since both return the same strings
B is exhaustive, since it appends one letter at a time
optionExplain: Right: B prunes as it builds, so it never produces a string with a consonant.
Keeping only passing strings is a filter after generation, which is the exhaustive style.
Same output does not make same method; they differ in how many candidates are built.
Building piece by piece is common to both; the prune on bad letters is what marks B.
questions.rule: Backtracking finds the same answers as exhaustive search while generating only the paths that can still succeed.

questions.q: In a 26-way tree with leaves at depth 4, how many leaves go with a prune at depth 1, and at depth 3?
questions.explain: The earlier a path is pruned, the larger the subtree that is skipped.
options: 17,576 leaves at depth 1, but only 26 at depth 3
26 leaves at depth 1, and 17,576 at depth 3
The same number at both depths, since each prune is one node
456,976 leaves at depth 1, and 26 at depth 3
optionExplain: Right: a subtree at depth d holds 26 to the power (4 minus d) leaves.
This reverses the depths; a node near the root has far more below it.
A prune removes the whole subtree, and subtrees differ in size with depth.
The full 456,976 is the whole tree; a depth-1 subtree is a 26th of it.
questions.teaches: Because the number of nodes in each subtree is exponential relative to its depth, pruning near the root saves huge amounts of computation, while pruning near the leaves saves little.
questions.rule: Backtracking finds the same answers as exhaustive search while generating only the paths that can still succeed.

questions.q: A problem gives n up to 12 and asks for every arrangement of the items that meets a rule. Which method suits it?
questions.explain: Find-all problems with tiny limits suit backtracking. The card next lists the signals.
options: A sliding window, which scans the items once from the left
Binary search, which halves the range of possible answers
Backtracking, which can afford exponential work at small n
A prefix sum, which answers each range query in constant time
optionExplain: A window scans for one best stretch; it does not generate every arrangement.
Binary search needs an ordered range of answers; here the output is a list of arrangements.
Right: asking for every arrangement with a tiny limit is the classic backtracking signal.
Prefix sums serve repeated range totals, not the generation of arrangements.
questions.rule: Reach for backtracking when the task is to find all of something and the input is small enough for exponential work.

questions.q: Which features of a problem point toward backtracking? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Two features of the task and one feature of the limits make up the book hints.
options: The input limit is very small, around n of 15 or less
No clear route to an answer exists without trying the logical possibilities
The task is to find all of something
The input is already sorted and one target must be found
The input has 100,000 elements and the answer is one number
optionExplain: Right: small limits allow exponential time.
Right: that is the second signal.
Right: listing every solution is the first signal.
A sorted input with a target suggests binary search.
A large input with a single numeric answer calls for a faster method.
questions.rule: Reach for backtracking when the task is to find all of something and the input is small enough for exponential work.

questions.q: Sort each task by whether backtracking fits it or a different method is the better choice.
questions.explain: Find-all tasks on tiny inputs suit backtracking; one value from a big input has a direct, faster method.

items.t: List every way to seat 8 guests at a table
Return all subsets of an array of 10 ids
Generate every valid placement of 8 queens on a board
Find the largest of 100,000 prices in a list
Check if x is in a sorted list of a million values
Sum the sales figures for 200,000 receipts

questions.rule: Reach for backtracking when the task is to find all of something and the input is small enough for exponential work.

questions.q: A backtracking search visits about \(2^n\) nodes. For n = 15 it visits about ____ nodes. Give a whole number.
questions.explain: \(2^{15} = 32768\), which is small. For n = 40 the same method would need over a trillion nodes, which is why small limits matter.
questions.rule: Reach for backtracking when the task is to find all of something and the input is small enough for exponential work.

questions.q: A student sees an array of 200,000 numbers and a request to return all subsets, and calls it ideal for backtracking. What is wrong?
questions.explain: The task fits backtracking, but the limit does not. Both hints should agree.
options: Subsets cannot be generated by backtracking, whatever the input size
The huge limit removes the small-n hint, and the work will not finish
Backtracking works only when the input array is already sorted
Backtracking can return only one subset, not all of them
optionExplain: Subsets are a standard find-all task; the trouble is only the size.
Right: the number of subsets doubles with every element, so 200,000 is far out of reach.
Order of the input is not a condition for using backtracking.
It can return every subset; that is what a find-all task is.
questions.rule: Reach for backtracking when the task is to find all of something and the input is small enough for exponential work.

questions.q: In an interview the limits are not stated, and the interviewer says to do your best. What can you still use to choose backtracking?
questions.explain: Without stated limits, you recognise backtracking from the kind of task.
options: A guaranteed small n, which the interviewer will confirm if asked
The size of the sample input printed with the problem
The language the interviewer asks you to write the code in
The shape of the task: find all of something, or check all options
optionExplain: Asking tends to bring a vague answer, so you cannot count on it.
A sample is usually tiny and says little about the real limits.
The language has no bearing on which algorithm fits.
Right: the task itself carries the hint when the limits are missing.
questions.teaches: In an interview you are usually not told the constraints, and asking tends to get a vague answer, so you must recognise when to use backtracking from the problem itself.
questions.rule: Reach for backtracking when the task is to find all of something and the input is small enough for exponential work.

questions.q: In the general backtracking function, what runs right after the recursive call inside the loop?
questions.explain: The undo is what lets the loop try the next choice. The card next shows the whole function.
options: The check of the base case for the new curr
The undo of the modification made to curr
The recording of curr into the list of answers
A second recursive call with the same curr
optionExplain: The base case is checked at the top of each call, not after returning.
Right: the choice is taken back so the next one starts from the same state.
Recording happens in the base case, before the loop.
One call per choice is made; calling twice would repeat the same subtree.
questions.rule: Backtracking checks the base case, then for each choice modifies curr, recurses, and undoes the change.

questions.q: Put the steps of one backtrack call in the order they run when the base case does not hold.
questions.explain: The base case is checked first. Then each loop iteration modifies, recurses, then undoes.
items: Check the base case at the top of the call
Modify curr with the next choice
Call backtrack on the modified curr
Undo the modification before the next choice
questions.rule: Backtracking checks the base case, then for each choice modifies curr, recurses, and undoes the change.

questions.q: The template builds all binary strings of length 3. Its base case holds when len(curr) equals ____.
questions.explain: A finished string has the full length, 3, so there is nothing more to add. Before that, the loop must keep extending curr.
questions.rule: Backtracking checks the base case, then for each choice modifies curr, recurses, and undoes the change.

questions.q: What is out after this code runs?
questions.explain: The loop runs a then b at each of two positions, producing the four pairs in that order.
options: aa, ab, ba, bb, in that order
ab, ba, in that order
aa, bb, in that order
ba, bb, ab, aa, in that order
optionExplain: Right: the first position takes a then b, and under each the second position takes a then b.
Pairs with equal letters are valid too; nothing here forbids repeats.
Only the repeated pairs would appear if the second letter had to match the first.
The loop tries a before b at each position, so the order starts with aa.
questions.rule: Backtracking checks the base case, then for each choice modifies curr, recurses, and undoes the change.

questions.q: The undo line is missing from this code. After the first answer [a, a] is recorded, what happens next?
questions.explain: Without the undo, curr is no longer the partial candidate of the current node.
options: The code still returns all four pairs, only in a different order of listing
The code returns the four pairs plus a second copy of [b, b]
The code returns only [a, a] and then stops without an error
curr grows past 2, so the base case is missed and the recursion never ends
optionExplain: Without the undo the state is wrong, so more than a reordering results.
No further pair is recorded, because the length passes 2 and never equals it again.
It would stop cleanly only if the recursion ended; here it continues without limit.
Right: stale choices stay in curr, so its length skips over 2 and the base case is missed.
questions.rule: Backtracking checks the base case, then for each choice modifies curr, recurses, and undoes the change.

questions.q: A teammate proposes writing the backtracking template with a plain loop and no recursion. What does the book say about this?
questions.explain: The recursion is what makes the undo step natural: each call returns to its parent.
options: Recursion is needed only when the base case adds to the answer list
Recursion is optional, and an iterative version is the usual choice
It is almost always recursive; iteration does not make sense
Recursion is used only for counting, and not for building lists
optionExplain: The need for recursion does not depend on what the base case does.
The book says the opposite about what is usual.
Right: the book says backtracking is almost always implemented with recursion.
Both counting and building lists use the same recursive form.
questions.teaches: Backtracking is almost always implemented with recursion, because each call stands for a node of the tree and returning is the move back to the parent; doing it iteratively does not make sense.
questions.rule: Backtracking checks the base case, then for each choice modifies curr, recurses, and undoes the change.

questions.q: In the tree picture of backtracking, which part of the code moves from a child back up to its parent?
questions.explain: The undo is the step back up. The card next maps each part of the code.
options: The header of the for loop over the choices
The check of the base case at the top of the call
The line that undoes the modification to curr
The recursive call to backtrack in the loop
optionExplain: The header selects the next child; it does not return to the parent.
The check only decides whether this node is complete.
Right: undoing the last choice is the step back to the parent.
The call moves down to a child, the opposite direction.
questions.rule: A call is a node, a loop iteration is a child, the recursive call goes down, and the undo goes back up.

questions.q: Match each part of the code with what it does in the tree.
questions.explain: Calls are nodes, iterations are children, the recursive call goes down, and the undo goes up.
pairs: One iteration of the for loop
A child of the current node
The recursive call inside the loop
The line that undoes the modification
Moving back up to the parent
questions.rule: A call is a node, a loop iteration is a child, the recursive call goes down, and the undo goes back up.

questions.q: Strings of length 2 are built from a and b with the template. Counting the first call, backtrack is called ____ times.
questions.explain: One root call, 2 calls for the first letter, then 2 for each of those: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7. Each call is one node of the tree.
questions.rule: A call is a node, a loop iteration is a child, the recursive call goes down, and the undo goes back up.

questions.q: The template builds length-2 strings from a and b. Put these events in the order they happen.
questions.explain: After the leaf [a, a] is recorded, the call returns, the undo restores [a], and the next iteration adds b.
items: curr is [a, a] and the answer is recorded
curr becomes [a] after the undo line
curr becomes [a, b] in the next loop iteration
questions.hint: After a leaf, the search first climbs to the parent.
questions.rule: A call is a node, a loop iteration is a child, the recursive call goes down, and the undo goes back up.

questions.q: A student says the undo line moves the search down the tree to the next child. What is wrong?
questions.explain: The path from the root to the node is curr, so removing the last choice is exactly one step up.
options: The undo moves up to the parent; the call moves down
The undo moves to the root, whatever the depth
The undo does not move at all, since it only edits curr
The undo moves sideways to a sibling directly
optionExplain: Right: down is the call, up is the undo.
It steps back one level only, to the parent of the current node.
Editing curr is how the move is carried out; the path shrinks with it.
The sibling is reached next by the following loop iteration, after the climb to the parent.
questions.rule: A call is a node, a loop iteration is a child, the recursive call goes down, and the undo goes back up.

questions.q: In the tree of a backtracking run, what does the root stand for?
questions.explain: The root has no choices on its path, so its candidate is empty.
options: The first complete solution found by the whole search run
The last choice made before the search returns to the caller
The base case, which is reached and ends the whole search
An empty candidate, the scope of the first backtrack call
optionExplain: Solutions sit at leaves; the root is where the build starts.
The last choice is deep in the tree, not at the root.
The base case is reached at leaves, not at the root.
Right: nothing has been chosen at the root, and it is where the original call is made.
questions.teaches: The root of the tree is an empty candidate and represents the scope from which the original backtrack call is made.
questions.rule: A call is a node, a loop iteration is a child, the recursive call goes down, and the undo goes back up.

questions.q: For nums = [1, 2, 3], how many permutations are there?
questions.explain: Choices shrink as numbers are used up. The card next shows how the code builds them.
options: 3, since each number leads the list once
6, since there are 3 choices, then 2, then 1
8, since each number is either used or not used
9, since 3 positions each take one of 3 numbers
optionExplain: Each leading number is followed by several orders of the rest.
Right: each position has one fewer unused number than the one before.
That counts subsets; a permutation must use every number.
That allows repeats, but a number cannot be reused within a permutation.
questions.rule: To build permutations, loop over the whole input at every call and add only numbers that are not yet in curr.

questions.q: True or false: every call of the permutations code loops over the whole input and adds only numbers not yet in curr.
questions.explain: The loop covers all numbers at every position, since any unused number may come next; the in-curr check enforces use-once.
questions.rule: To build permutations, loop over the whole input at every call and add only numbers that are not yet in curr.

questions.q: Arranging 4 distinct books on a shelf in every order with this method gives ____ complete arrangements.
questions.explain: There are 4 choices for the first slot, 3 for the second, 2 for the third and 1 for the last: 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24.
questions.rule: To build permutations, loop over the whole input at every call and add only numbers that are not yet in curr.

questions.q: Put these three permutations of [1, 2, 3] in the order the code adds them to the answer.
questions.explain: The loop tries 1 first, so [1, 2, 3] and [1, 3, 2] come before any list that starts with 2.
questions.rule: To build permutations, loop over the whole input at every call and add only numbers that are not yet in curr.

questions.q: The check num not in curr is removed. For nums = [1, 2], what does the code return?
questions.explain: The check is what makes each number appear once in a permutation.
options: [1, 2] and [2, 1], the same two permutations as before
[1, 1], [1, 2], [2, 1], [2, 2]: some lists repeat a number
[1, 2] only, because the loop stops at the first full list
Nothing, because curr can never reach the length of nums
optionExplain: The check is what rules out [1, 1] and [2, 2], so its removal changes the output.
Right: without the check, each position takes any number, so repeats appear.
The loop does not stop at the first answer; it continues through all choices.
curr still reaches length 2, since every call adds a number.
questions.rule: To build permutations, loop over the whole input at every call and add only numbers that are not yet in curr.

questions.q: The code runs on [1, 2, 3] and has recorded [1, 3, 2] as its latest answer. What happens next?
questions.explain: The traversal is depth first: a subtree is completed before the next sibling begins.
options: It restarts from an empty list with the input reversed
It records [2, 1, 3] at once without leaving the current call
It tries 1 in the first position again with the rest reversed
It climbs back to the root, then places 2 first in a new subtree
optionExplain: The input is never reversed; the loop moves on to the next number.
A new first number needs a return to the root first.
Every ordering starting with 1 is already done.
Right: the whole subtree under 1 is finished before 2 is tried in the first position.
questions.teaches: After all possibilities with the first number in the first position are tried, the code goes back up and tries the second number there, going through a whole subtree again, exactly like DFS.
questions.rule: To build permutations, loop over the whole input at every call and add only numbers that are not yet in curr.

questions.q: A list ans stores curr itself, and then curr is changed. What does ans hold?
questions.explain: A stored reference follows the list it points to. The card next shows the fix.
options: The same list as curr, so it shows the later change
A frozen snapshot of curr as it was when it was stored
An empty list, because storing curr clears it
A separate list that is updated only on request
optionExplain: Right: ans holds a reference to the one list, so every change shows through.
A snapshot needs a copy; storing curr itself does not make one.
Storing a list does not empty it.
No separate list exists unless a copy is made.
questions.rule: Record a copy of curr, because curr is only a reference to one list that keeps changing.

questions.q: When recording an answer, add a ____ of curr, not curr itself.
questions.explain: A copy is a separate list, so later changes to curr do not alter the recorded answer.
questions.rule: Record a copy of curr, because curr is only a reference to one list that keeps changing.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: A reference shows later changes; a copy made earlier does not.
optionExplain: This swaps the two: the reference follows curr, the copy does not.
Only a copy of both would stay unchanged; the first entry is a reference.
Right: the first entry is curr itself and grows; the second is a copy and stays as it was.
The copy was made before w was added, so it does not contain w.
questions.code:
curr = ['x', 'y', 'z']
saved = [curr]
saved.append(curr[:])
curr.append('w')
print(saved)
questions.rule: Record a copy of curr, because curr is only a reference to one list that keeps changing.

questions.q: The template builds strings of length 2 from a and b, but records out.append(curr) without a copy. What is out at the end?
questions.explain: All four entries point at the same list, and by the end it has been emptied.
options: [a, a], [a, b], [b, a], [b, b], as one would expect
Four copies of [b, b], which was the last list built
Only [a, a], because the first record blocks all the later ones
Four empty lists, since the undos empty the shared list
optionExplain: The expected result needs copies; stored references do not keep the answers.
The last list is undone too, so the shared list ends empty rather than at [b, b].
Recording does not stop the search; four entries are added.
Right: all four entries are the same list, which ends empty after every undo.
questions.rule: Record a copy of curr, because curr is only a reference to one list that keeps changing.

questions.q: True or false: a function that only counts the solutions with a counter still needs to make a copy of curr at each base case.
questions.explain: A copy matters only when curr is stored. A counter stores no list, so there is nothing to protect.
questions.hint: What does the base case do with curr in a counting problem?
questions.rule: Record a copy of curr, because curr is only a reference to one list that keeps changing.

questions.q: The subsets code records a copy of curr at each of its 2^n nodes. Why does that add a factor to the running time?
questions.explain: Recording an answer is not free; its cost depends on how long the answer is.
options: A copy takes constant time, so it adds no factor
A copy takes time proportional to the length of curr
Copying doubles the number of nodes in the tree
The copies force every recursive call to run twice
optionExplain: A copy must visit every element, so its time grows with the length.
Right: each copy costs time that grows with the size of curr.
The tree is the same size; the copy is extra work at each node.
Calls are not repeated; the copy is extra work inside each call.
questions.teaches: Copying curr costs time proportional to its length, so the copy made at each node adds a factor to the time complexity (for subsets, O(n) per node).
questions.rule: Record a copy of curr, because curr is only a reference to one list that keeps changing.

questions.q: The root call of the permutations code on n numbers makes n recursive calls. How many does each of those calls make?
questions.explain: The count of choices drops by one per level. The card next multiplies the levels.
options: 1, since only the next unused number is tried
n, since the loop runs over the whole input again
n - 1, since one number is already used
n / 2, since half of the numbers are used by then
optionExplain: Every unused number is tried, not only the next one.
The loop runs n times, but the used number does not start a call.
Right: the used number is skipped, so one fewer choice remains.
The count falls by one each level, not by half.
questions.rule: The permutations code makes about n! calls of about \(n^2\) work each, which is an estimate and not an exact count.

questions.q: Choices n, then n - 1, then n - 2, down to 1, multiply to give n ____, which sets the number of calls.
questions.explain: The product \(n \cdot (n-1) \cdots 1\) is the factorial, written \(n!\).
questions.rule: The permutations code makes about n! calls of about \(n^2\) work each, which is an estimate and not an exact count.

questions.q: The code is run on 6 distinct numbers. It records ____ permutations in total.
questions.explain: \(6! = 6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 720\). The whole tree has 1957 calls, of which 720 are leaves.
questions.rule: The permutations code makes about n! calls of about \(n^2\) work each, which is an estimate and not an exact count.

questions.q: Each call loops over n numbers, and each in-curr check scans curr in O(n). What is the cost of one call?
questions.explain: Work per call is the loop length times the cost of the membership check.
options: About \(O(n^2)\): n steps, each with a linear scan
About \(O(n!)\): each call lists all permutations itself
About \(O(1)\): one call adds a single number
About \(O(n)\): the loop is the only cost
optionExplain: Right: n steps times a check of cost n gives n squared.
The factorial counts calls in the whole tree, not the work in one call.
The call still runs a loop of n steps with a scan in each.
This leaves out that each loop step runs a scan of curr.
questions.rule: The permutations code makes about n! calls of about \(n^2\) work each, which is an estimate and not an exact count.

questions.q: True or false: the permutations code makes only n calls in total, since its loop runs n times.
questions.explain: The loop runs n times in every call, and each iteration that is allowed starts a new call, so the calls multiply to about n!.
questions.hint: Count the calls made by the calls.
questions.rule: The permutations code makes about n! calls of about \(n^2\) work each, which is an estimate and not an exact count.

questions.q: To speed up the in-curr check, a separate hash set of the numbers in curr is kept. What does this do to the estimate?
questions.explain: Reducing the cost of one call reduces the total in the same proportion.
options: Each check becomes \(O(1)\), so the total is \(O(n \cdot n!)\)
The total becomes \(O(n!)\), because checks cost nothing
The total becomes \(O(n^3 \cdot n!)\), because the set adds a loop
The total is unchanged at \(O(n^2 \cdot n!)\), as the loop dominates
optionExplain: Right: with a constant-time check, the loop alone costs n per call.
The loop of n steps per call still costs n, so a factor n remains.
A hash set lookup is a constant-time step, not another loop.
The scan was the source of the second factor n, and the set removes it.
questions.teaches: Keeping the numbers in curr in a separate hash set makes the in-curr check O(1), which lowers the estimate from O(n^2 * n!) to O(n * n!).
questions.rule: The permutations code makes about n! calls of about \(n^2\) work each, which is an estimate and not an exact count.

questions.q: For nums = [1, 2, 3], how many subsets are there, counting the empty subset and the whole array?
questions.explain: Each number is in or out of a subset. The card next sets subsets beside permutations.
options: 7, since every non-empty choice counts and the empty one does not
6, since there are 3 x 2 x 1 orderings
8, since each number is either in or out
3, since one subset exists for each number
optionExplain: The empty subset is a valid subset and counts.
That counts permutations, which use all numbers in some order.
Right: two choices for each of three numbers give eight subsets.
Subsets can hold several numbers, and the empty one counts as well.
questions.rule: A subset has any length and ignores order, so every node holds an answer and each set must be built in only one order.

questions.q: Sort each description into permutations or subsets.
questions.explain: Permutations fix the length and respect order; subsets allow any length and ignore order.

items.t: [1, 2, 3] and [3, 2, 1] count as different results
Every result has the same length as the input
[1, 2, 3] and [3, 2, 1] count as one result
Results can have any length from 0 up to n

questions.rule: A subset has any length and ignores order, so every node holds an answer and each set must be built in only one order.

questions.q: A club picks members for a committee, and the committee [Ann, Bo] is the same as [Bo, Ann]. Which model fits, and why?
questions.explain: Ask whether the same items in another order are a new answer.
options: Permutations, since each member must appear once
Subsets, since the order of members is irrelevant
Permutations, since the committee has a fixed size
Subsets, since the committee must contain every member
optionExplain: Using each member once holds for subsets too; the deciding point is whether order matters.
Right: when order does not matter, the same group in another order is not a new answer.
A fixed size is not what makes permutations; their order matters.
A subset need not contain every member; that is a trait of permutations.
questions.rule: A subset has any length and ignores order, so every node holds an answer and each set must be built in only one order.

questions.q: True or false: if curr is recorded only at length 3, nums = [1, 2, 3] yields the single subset [1, 2, 3].
questions.explain: Only the whole array has length 3, so every shorter subset would be missed. Subsets must be recorded at nodes of every length.
