questions.explain: Base cases plus the recurrence relation define the algorithm.
options: The hash map and the recursion
The array and the nested loops
The base cases and the recurrence relation
The number of states and the language used
optionExplain: These are implementation choices for top-down.
These are implementation choices for bottom-up.
Right: these two pieces define the algorithm whatever the style.
The number of states sets the cost; neither defines the algorithm.
questions.rule: Top-down and bottom-up differ only in implementation; the base cases and the recurrence relation define the DP algorithm.

questions.q: Sort each description into top-down or bottom-up.
questions.explain: Top-down recurses from the original problem with a cache. Bottom-up iterates from the base cases over the states.

items.t: Starts with a call for the original problem
Caches answers in a hash map
Reaches the base cases last
Fills an array from the base cases
Is also called tabulation
Uses loops over the state variables

questions.rule: Top-down and bottom-up differ only in implementation; the base cases and the recurrence relation define the DP algorithm.

questions.q: A top-down solution has base case dp(0) = 0 and dp(i) = dp(i - 1) + 2. What does its bottom-up version use?
questions.explain: The base case and the recurrence relation stay the same; only the evaluation order changes.
options: Set dp[0] = 0, then loop i upward with dp[i] = dp[i + 1] + 2
Set dp[n] = 0, then loop i downward with dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + 2
Rewrite the recurrence, since a loop cannot use dp[i - 1]
Set dp[0] = 0, then loop i upward with dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + 2
optionExplain: The recurrence itself must not change; it still reads i - 1.
The base case stays at 0 and the loop must run from it outward.
A loop reads the earlier cell without trouble.
Right: the base case and recurrence carry over unchanged.
questions.rule: Top-down and bottom-up differ only in implementation; the base cases and the recurrence relation define the DP algorithm.

questions.q: True or false: moving from top-down to bottom-up changes the recurrence relation, because loops cannot call themselves.
questions.explain: The recurrence is the same equation in both versions; calls to dp(...) become reads of dp[...]. The relation defines the algorithm, not the control flow.
questions.rule: Top-down and bottom-up differ only in implementation; the base cases and the recurrence relation define the DP algorithm.

questions.q: In an interview you wrote a memoized top-down solution, and the interviewer asks for the other approach too. What carries over to it?
questions.explain: The same base cases and recurrence relation are reused.
options: The hash map and the recursive calls
The base cases and the recurrence relation
The call stack and the order of visits
Nothing, since it is a different algorithm
optionExplain: These belong to the top-down style and are replaced.
Right: they define the algorithm, so they are reused.
Both change in the iterative version.
It is the same algorithm in a different implementation.
questions.teaches: Sometimes an interviewer asks for both the top-down and the bottom-up approach, and a top-down solution can be converted to a bottom-up one by a general method.
questions.rule: Top-down and bottom-up differ only in implementation; the base cases and the recurrence relation define the DP algorithm.

questions.q: Two correct solutions to the same DP problem use the same states. Which is usually faster?
questions.explain: Iteration has less overhead than recursion. The card next gives both claims.
options: The top-down one, since recursion skips unneeded states
The top-down one, since a hash map is faster than an array
The bottom-up one, since a loop has less overhead than recursion
Neither, since DP time does not depend on implementation
optionExplain: Both visit the same states, so skipping does not apply to the comparison.
An array is typically as fast or faster than a hash map.
Right: per-call overhead is the usual difference.
The time class is the same, but overhead differs.
questions.rule: Bottom-up usually runs faster; top-down is usually easier to write.

questions.q: True or false: according to the book, a top-down approach is usually easier to write than a bottom-up one.
questions.explain: With recursion the order in which states are visited does not matter, which usually makes top-down easier to write.
questions.rule: Bottom-up usually runs faster; top-down is usually easier to write.

questions.q: You must write a DP solution under time pressure for a problem with three state variables. Which style does the book suggest is easier?
questions.explain: Recursion removes the need to choose a loop order, which is why top-down is usually easier to write.
options: Top-down, so you do not have to arrange three nested loops
Bottom-up, since loops are simpler than recursion
Either, since the two styles need the same code
Neither, since three variables need a different method
optionExplain: Right: recursion removes the need to choose the loop order.
The book says that arranging loops for multiple state variables can be hard.
The code differs even though the algorithm is the same.
The framework works for any number of state variables.
questions.rule: Bottom-up usually runs faster; top-down is usually easier to write.

questions.q: Lee says bottom-up is faster because it computes fewer states than top-down. What is wrong with the reason?
questions.explain: The two styles share the states; they differ in overhead.
options: Both compute the same states; iteration has less overhead
Nothing is wrong, since bottom-up skips base cases
Top-down computes fewer states, so it is faster
Bottom-up is faster only for one state variable
optionExplain: Right: the number of states is the same, the overhead differs.
Both handle the base cases.
The states are the same in both.
The reason is overhead, which does not depend on the number of variables.
questions.rule: Bottom-up usually runs faster; top-down is usually easier to write.

questions.q: In a language that implements tail recursion, the usual speed advantage of bottom-up is ____ impactful.
questions.explain: Tail recursion reduces the overhead of recursion, so the gap shrinks.
questions.teaches: The speed advantage of bottom-up is less impactful if the language implements tail recursion.
questions.rule: Bottom-up usually runs faster; top-down is usually easier to write.

questions.q: A DP has state (i, j, k). Why might a top-down version be easier than a bottom-up one?
questions.explain: The order of visiting is the hard part of bottom-up in several dimensions.
options: Recursion uses less memory, so it is the simpler choice
Bottom-up cannot handle three variables, only top-down can
Recursion needs no loop order; loops must order the states
Top-down code runs faster for three variables
optionExplain: Memory does not decide ease of writing, and recursion adds stack use.
Bottom-up works; it is only harder to arrange.
Right: with iteration the right loop configuration can be hard to find.
It usually runs slower because of overhead.
questions.teaches: With iteration, if you have a multi-dimensional problem, it can sometimes be difficult to figure out the correct configuration of your for loops.
questions.rule: Bottom-up usually runs faster; top-down is usually easier to write.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: Which question most strongly hints that dynamic programming might fit?
questions.explain: A count of ways or an optimum is the usual opening. The card next lists the openings.
options: Which position in this list holds the value that was typed in first by the user?
Does this string read the same forwards as it does backwards when printed?
How many different ways can a path be chosen through this grid?
What is the title of the first section stored in this sorted file of records?
optionExplain: This is a lookup of one element, not an optimum or a count.
This is a yes-or-no check on one string, not an optimum or a count of ways.
Right: a count of ways is one of the two typical openings.
This is a lookup, with no optimum and no count of ways.
questions.rule: A question that asks for an optimum or a number of ways is a first hint of DP, to be confirmed by the second sign.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: Which three phrasings match the first sign of a DP problem?
questions.explain: The openings ask for a minimum, a maximum, a longest, or a count of ways.
options: What is the minimum cost of doing something
Print every node of the tree in order
Is the given string empty
Return the first element that matches a test
What is the longest possible version of something
How many ways are there to do something
optionExplain: Right: a minimum is an optimal value.
A traversal reports items; it does not ask for an optimum or a count of ways.
A yes-or-no check is neither an optimum nor a count.
A first match is a search, not an optimum or a count.
Right: a longest is a maximum.
Right: a number of ways is the other opening.
questions.rule: A question that asks for an optimum or a number of ways is a first hint of DP, to be confirmed by the second sign.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: Sort each question by whether it has the first sign of a DP problem.
questions.explain: Cheapest, how many ways and longest are the typical openings. A duplicate check, a middle node and a reversal are not optimum or counting questions.

items.t: What is the cheapest route through the grid?
In how many ways can 10 be written as a sum of 1s and 2s?
What is the longest run of rising prices?
Does the list contain a duplicate?
Return the middle node of the list
Reverse the string

questions.rule: A question that asks for an optimum or a number of ways is a first hint of DP, to be confirmed by the second sign.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: Jordan says: this problem asks for the maximum of something, so it must be solved with DP. What is wrong with the claim?
questions.explain: The wording is a hint, not a proof.
options: A maximum is a DP sign only when the answer is also a count of ways
The wording counts only when it is a minimum, and not for a maximum
Nothing is wrong, since the wording fully decides the method used
The book says not all problems in these formats are meant to be solved with DP
optionExplain: Either an optimum or a count of ways is enough for the first sign.
Maximum and minimum are both named as optimal values.
The wording is a guideline, and the second sign must also hold.
Right: a maximum of an array is found by one pass.
questions.rule: A question that asks for an optimum or a number of ways is a first hint of DP, to be confirmed by the second sign.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: True or false: a problem that does not ask for an optimum or a number of ways cannot be a DP problem.
questions.explain: The book says not all DP problems are in one of those formats, so the wording is only a guideline.
questions.teaches: Not all problems in these formats are meant to be solved with DP, and not all DP problems are in one of those formats.
questions.rule: A question that asks for an optimum or a number of ways is a first hint of DP, to be confirmed by the second sign.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: A task asks for the largest number in an unsorted array. It matches the first sign. What is the sensible conclusion?
questions.explain: Check the second sign before choosing DP.
options: Use DP, since the first sign alone is enough to decide the method used
Only a hint: one pass finds the largest, so DP is not needed here
Use DP with a table over the array, as any maximum needs a recurrence
Reject DP, since arrays cannot be the input of a DP problem
optionExplain: The first sign alone does not settle the method.
Right: the second sign, decisions that affect each other, is missing.
A maximum over independent values needs no recurrence or table.
Arrays are common inputs of DP problems; this one does not need it.
questions.teaches: The two characteristics, an optimum or count plus decisions that affect each other, hold up very well as a general guideline.
questions.rule: A question that asks for an optimum or a number of ways is a first hint of DP, to be confirmed by the second sign.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: In which problem does a decision affect future decisions?
questions.explain: Rule-outs between choices make decisions interact. The card next states this.
options: Adding up all the positive numbers in a list, one number at a time
Choosing houses to rob, where no two neighbouring houses may both be robbed
Counting the vowels in a word from the first letter to the last
Printing every name in a list in the order the names were entered
optionExplain: Each number is added or skipped on its own, whatever the others are.
Right: taking one house rules out its neighbours.
Each letter is judged alone, so nothing it does affects another letter.
Printing one name does not change what can be printed next.
questions.rule: If taking one option changes which options remain later, the decisions interact and DP is likely to fit.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: True or false: in House Robber, robbing one house changes which houses are allowed to be robbed afterwards.
questions.explain: Robbing two neighbouring houses sets off the alarm, so one robbery takes the neighbours out of play.
questions.rule: If taking one option changes which options remain later, the decisions interact and DP is likely to fit.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: Sort each task by whether a decision in it affects later decisions.
questions.explain: Seats that may not touch, a shared budget and overlapping lessons each shut out other choices. Summing positives, counting and unlimited stickers leave later choices untouched.

items.t: Pick seats in a row where no two chosen seats may touch
Choose gifts for friends from one shared budget
Pick lessons where overlapping ones cannot both be taken
Add every positive number of a list to a total
Count how many words in a list start with a vowel
Give each of five friends any one sticker from an unlimited pile

questions.rule: If taking one option changes which options remain later, the decisions interact and DP is likely to fit.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: The alarm rule is removed from House Robber, so neighbouring houses may both be robbed. What is the best strategy?
questions.explain: Without the rule the second sign disappears, and the problem becomes a sum.
options: Rob every other house, since the old pattern still holds
Rob only the richest house, since more houses mean more risk
Use the same DP, since the recurrence stays the same
Rob every house, since no choice rules out any other
optionExplain: The pattern existed only because of the alarm rule.
There is no risk without the alarm rule.
The recurrence depended on the rule; independent choices need no DP.
Right: with no rule-outs the decisions are independent.
questions.rule: If taking one option changes which options remain later, the decisions interact and DP is likely to fit.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: The book mentions what a single decision could be in these problems. Which is one such decision?
questions.explain: A decision in the problem could be picking between two elements, as in take this one or that one.
options: Picking between two elements
Choosing the programming language for the solution
Deciding how large the input will be before the run
Selecting whether to cache results or to recompute them
optionExplain: Right: a decision could be picking between two elements.
That is a choice about code, not a decision inside the problem.
The input is given, not decided.
That is a choice of implementation, not a decision in the problem.
questions.teaches: A decision could be picking between two elements.
questions.rule: If taking one option changes which options remain later, the decisions interact and DP is likely to fit.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: A tour operator picks events for a day, and any two events that overlap in time cannot both be chosen. Does the second sign hold?
questions.explain: Any rule-out between choices makes decisions interact.
options: No: the events are listed once, so each choice is independent
No: only choices about money can affect later choices
Yes: choosing an event shuts out every event that overlaps it
Yes, but only if the number of events is very large
optionExplain: Listing them once does not make the choices independent.
The book names no such limit; any rule-out counts.
Right: a choice changes which options remain, as a robbed house does.
Size does not create the property; the rule-out does.
questions.teaches: Decisions affecting future decisions could be something like: if you take an element x, then you cannot take an element y in the future.
questions.rule: If taking one option changes which options remain later, the decisions interact and DP is likely to fit.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: In House Robber with nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1], a greedy robber takes the 7 over the 2. What happens to the 9?
questions.explain: The 7 and the 9 are neighbours, so taking one blocks the other. The card next shows the result.
options: The 9 can still be taken together with the 7 since the 3 is between them
The 9 is taken next, as greedy prefers the largest number left
The 9 is skipped by the rules, since greedy cannot read past two houses
The 9 can no longer be taken, because it is next to the 7
optionExplain: The 9 is directly next to the 7, so the alarm sounds.
Taking it would break the alarm rule after the 7 is taken.
The rule that blocks it is the alarm rule, not a reading limit.
Right: that is how a local choice shuts out a later one.
questions.rule: When decisions affect each other, a locally best choice can lose, so use DP instead of greedy.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: True or false: the second sign usually separates DP problems from greedy problems.
questions.explain: Whether decisions affect future decisions is what usually differentiates DP from greedy.
questions.rule: When decisions affect each other, a locally best choice can lose, so use DP instead of greedy.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: For nums = [5, 9, 8, 1, 6], the greedy function shown returns ____.
questions.explain: The function takes the larger of a house and the next one, then skips a neighbour: it takes 9, skips 8, then takes 6 for a total of 15; the best total is 19 (5 + 8 + 6).
questions.rule: When decisions affect each other, a locally best choice can lose, so use DP instead of greedy.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: For nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1], greedy gets 10. Which set of houses gives the best total without setting off the alarm?
questions.explain: The best set starts with the smaller 2 so that the 9 stays open.
options: The 7 and the 3, for a total of 10
The 2, the 9 and the 1, for a total of 12
The 7, the 9 and the 1, for a total of 17
The 2, the 7 and the 3, for a total of 12
optionExplain: That is the greedy total; 12 is higher.
Right: giving up the 7 keeps the 9 available.
The 7 and the 9 are neighbours, so they cannot both be taken.
The 2 and the 7 are neighbours, so that set sets off the alarm.
questions.teaches: For nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] the best answer takes the 2, the 9 and the 1, giving up the larger 7 at the start.
questions.rule: When decisions affect each other, a locally best choice can lose, so use DP instead of greedy.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: Which statement about a new problem points to DP rather than greedy?
questions.explain: Interacting decisions point to DP; independent decisions point to greedy.
options: Every choice can be made without looking at any other choice
The answer is requested as a single number at the end
Taking one element can rule out taking another one later
The input is an array of integers with no repeated values
optionExplain: Independent choices are where greedy works.
Greedy problems also return one number.
Right: this is the second sign, and greedy cannot see it.
Greedy and DP both accept such input.
questions.rule: When decisions affect each other, a locally best choice can lose, so use DP instead of greedy.

questions.section: When should I consider using DP?
questions.q: Pick any three items to get the highest total value; no other rule applies. Which method fits?
questions.explain: Without rule-outs between choices, greedy is enough.
options: Greedy: take the three highest, as choices are independent
DP, since the problem asks for the maximum total value
DP, since each item is either taken or left out of the set
Neither, since greedy cannot give a maximum on any problem
optionExplain: Right: independent decisions need no DP.
A maximum is only the first sign; the second sign is missing.
A take-or-leave choice with no rule-outs is still independent.
Greedy gives the right maximum when choices are independent.
questions.teaches: The idea behind greedy is that local decisions do not affect other decisions.
questions.rule: When decisions affect each other, a locally best choice can lose, so use DP instead of greedy.

questions.q: In a DP algorithm, what is a state?
questions.explain: The state is the set of variables that describe a scenario. The card next defines it.
options: A list of every value the recursion has returned so far, in order
A flag that tells the program whether it is in top-down or bottom-up mode
A set of variables that fully describes one scenario of the problem
A name for the last line of the recurrence relation of the problem
optionExplain: That is the history of returns, not what describes a scenario.
That is a style choice, not a description of a scenario.
Right: the arguments of dp are the state.
The recurrence relation is a rule linking states, not a state.
questions.rule: Choose state variables that fully describe a scenario, and let dp(state) answer the original problem for it.

questions.q: A call to dp(state) should return the answer to the original problem as if state were the ____.
questions.explain: The state stands in for the input: dp(state) answers the original problem for the situation the state describes.
questions.rule: Choose state variables that fully describe a scenario, and let dp(state) answer the original problem for it.

questions.q: A robot on a grid has a battery that drains by one per move. Which variables fully describe its situation for a DP?
questions.explain: The state needs the variables that affect future options and nothing else.
options: Its row, its column and the battery charge left
Its row and column only, since the battery does not change the choices
Its row, its column and the colour painted on its case
The list of every square it has visited, with the time of each visit
optionExplain: Right: position and charge decide what it can still do.
The battery limits future moves, so leaving it out merges different scenarios.
The colour changes nothing about what the robot can do.
That records history that does not alter what the robot can do next.
questions.rule: Choose state variables that fully describe a scenario, and let dp(state) answer the original problem for it.

questions.q: True or false: two calls with the same state values may need different answers because the earlier calls that led to them were different.
questions.explain: A state fully describes the scenario, so the answer depends only on the state values, not on how the calls got there. That is why a cached value can be reused.
questions.rule: Choose state variables that fully describe a scenario, and let dp(state) answer the original problem for it.

questions.q: According to the book, what is the first step to creating a DP algorithm?
questions.explain: The state comes first because the function, the recurrence and the base cases are all written in terms of it.
options: Write the loops that fill a table from the base cases
Pick the programming language and the type of cache to use
Count how many states there are and the work at each state
Decide which state variables are necessary
optionExplain: The loops come last, during conversion to bottom-up.
These are implementation details chosen after the state.
The count follows from the state variables, so it cannot come first.
Right: the framework starts from the state.
questions.teaches: The first step to creating DP algorithms is deciding on what state variables are necessary.
questions.rule: Choose state variables that fully describe a scenario, and let dp(state) answer the original problem for it.

questions.q: A tree function dfs(node, depth) returns an answer for the subtree at node. By the book, what is its state?
questions.explain: In trees and in DP alike, the arguments of the recursive call form the state.
options: Only node, since depth is not a tree variable but a count
Both node and depth, the arguments of the call
Only the return value, since the state is what the call gives back
Neither, since tree problems have no state
optionExplain: A depth argument is part of the call, so it is part of the state.
Right: every argument of the recursive call is part of the state.
The return value is the answer, not the state.
Tree functions have states too; they do not repeat.
questions.teaches: In tree problems every recursive call to dfs took node, and maybe other variables, as arguments, and these arguments represent the state.
questions.rule: Choose state variables that fully describe a scenario, and let dp(state) answer the original problem for it.

questions.q: Which kind of state variable appears in almost every DP problem?
questions.explain: The index along the input is the usual state variable. The card next explains what it means.
options: A random number chosen at the start of each recursive call
An index along the input array, string or number
The memory address of the array that holds the cached answers
The name of the language in which the solution is written
optionExplain: DP states are fixed values describing the scenario, not random.
Right: it is the most common state variable.
Addresses are an implementation detail, not part of the scenario.
The language does not describe the scenario of the problem.
questions.rule: An index state i means: treat the input as if it ended at position i.

questions.q: With nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] and i = 2, the state acts as if nums had ____ elements.
questions.explain: The state i = 2 stands for the input up to and including index 2, which is [0, 1, 2].
questions.rule: An index state i means: treat the input as if it ended at position i.

questions.q: With nums = [7, 3, 9, 4] and the state i = 1, which input does dp(1) treat as the whole array?
questions.explain: The usual meaning of the index state is the prefix ending at i.
options: [3], the single element at index 1 and nothing before it
[7], the elements strictly before index 1 and nothing from it on
[3, 9, 4], the elements from index 1 up to the end of the array
[7, 3], the elements from index 0 up to and including index 1
optionExplain: The index marks the end of a prefix, not one lone element.
The prefix includes index 1 itself.
That is a suffix; the usual meaning is the prefix.
Right: the state covers the prefix ending at i.
questions.rule: An index state i means: treat the input as if it ended at position i.

questions.q: An input array has 8 elements and the only state variable is the index i. How many different states are there?
questions.explain: One index running over n positions gives n states.
options: 8, one for each index from 0 to 7
7, one for each gap between neighbouring elements
16, one for the prefix and one for the suffix of each index
64, one for every pair of an index and an element
optionExplain: Right: one state per index value.
States are indices, not gaps between them.
The state has one meaning, so one state per index.
That counts pairs, which would need two variables.
questions.rule: An index state i means: treat the input as if it ended at position i.

questions.q: True or false: for nums = [4, 8, 1, 6, 2], the state i = 3 stands for the input [6] alone.
questions.explain: The index state means the input up to and including index 3, here [4, 8, 1, 6], not the single element.
questions.rule: An index state i means: treat the input as if it ended at position i.

questions.q: For s = banana and the state i = 3, which part of the string is the input of dp(3)?
questions.explain: Strings work like arrays: the index state means the prefix up to i.
options: ban, the letters at positions 0 to 2
ana, the letters at positions 3 to 5
a, the single letter at position 3
bana, the letters at positions 0 to 3
optionExplain: Position 3 is included in the prefix.
That is a suffix, which is not the usual reading.
The state covers every letter up to position 3.
Right: the prefix up to and including index 3.
questions.teaches: An index along the input will be a state variable in almost all problems, and is frequently the only state variable.
questions.rule: An index state i means: treat the input as if it ended at position i.

questions.q: With nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] and two state indices i = 1 and j = 3, which input is being considered?
questions.explain: Both bounds are inclusive. The card next states the meaning.
options: [2]: only the element strictly between the two indices
[1, 2, 3]: the elements from index 1 through index 3
[0, 1, 2, 3]: everything up to index 3 and nothing else
[1, 2]: the elements from index 1 up to but not including 3
optionExplain: Both indices themselves belong to the piece.
Right: both bounds are included.
The left bound i cuts the start off.
The right bound is included in the piece.
questions.rule: Two indices mark both ends of the piece of input a state stands for.

questions.q: With nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4], i = 1 and j = 3, the state considers ____ elements.
questions.explain: Indices 1, 2 and 3 are included, so three elements are in play.
questions.rule: Two indices mark both ends of the piece of input a state stands for.

questions.q: For s = racecar, the state (i, j) = (2, 5) means which piece of the string?
questions.explain: Read the piece from the left bound through the right bound, both included.
options: cec, the letters at positions 2 through 4
rac, the letters at positions 0 through 2
ceca, the letters at positions 2 through 5
aceca, the letters at positions 1 through 5
optionExplain: Position 5 is included.
The left bound is 2, not 0.
Right: the letters from i through j, both included.
The left bound is 2, so the letter at 1 is outside.
questions.rule: Two indices mark both ends of the piece of input a state stands for.

questions.q: A state is a pair (i, j) with i at most j on an input of 5 elements. How many different pairs are there?
questions.explain: Counting the pairs gives 15, and for larger n it is about n squared halves.
options: 15, since there are 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 valid pairs
25, since each index can pair with all five indices
10, since pairs are chosen from five items in two ways
5, since the pieces are named by one index each
optionExplain: Right: each i pairs with the j values from i to 4.
This ignores the rule that i is at most j.
That counts pairs with i different from j and leaves out the single-element pieces.
Two indices give more than one state per index.
questions.rule: Two indices mark both ends of the piece of input a state stands for.

questions.q: True or false: two state indices over n elements give 2n states, since each index has n values.
questions.explain: The ranges multiply, so up to n times n pairs are possible. States are combinations of values, not a sum of ranges.
questions.rule: Two indices mark both ends of the piece of input a state stands for.

questions.q: To compare two strings, abcde and ace, a DP needs a position in each. Which state describes this?
questions.explain: Two inputs need two positions.
options: One index, since the strings are compared character by character
Two indices, both walking along the first string only
Two indices: one for the first string, one for the second
Three indices: one per string and one for the answer
optionExplain: Each string needs its own position, so one index is not enough.
The second string needs its own position.
Right: a second index can walk a second input.
The answer is returned, not part of the state.
questions.teaches: In a problem with two strings, one index variable is used for each string.
questions.rule: Two indices mark both ends of the piece of input a state stands for.

questions.q: A problem lets you remove at most k obstacles on a route. What would a state variable for k track?
questions.explain: The variable counts the allowance that is left. The card next gives the idea.
options: How many obstacles the route contains in total from start to end
How many more obstacles you are still allowed to remove
The index of the obstacle removed most recently along the route
Whether the current square holds an obstacle or not
optionExplain: That is fixed by the input and does not change during the walk.
Right: it counts the remaining allowance.
The index of the last removal does not limit future removals.
That is a property of the square, not of the allowance.
questions.rule: Add a variable for a limit that shrinks or a status that flips whenever it changes what you can do later.

questions.q: True or false: a boolean state variable can describe a status such as holding a package or not.
questions.explain: The book uses a boolean for a status such as true if currently holding a package and false if not.
questions.rule: Add a variable for a limit that shrinks or a status that flips whenever it changes what you can do later.

questions.q: A courier may make at most 3 express deliveries and either carries a parcel or not. Along with the index, which state variables fit?
questions.explain: A limit and a status are both worth a variable when they change what is allowed.
options: The total number of parcels, and the courier's name
Only the express limit, since carrying a parcel is not a status
The list of all earlier deliveries, in the order made
Express deliveries left, and a boolean for carrying a parcel
optionExplain: Neither changes what the courier can do next.
Carrying or not is a status that changes the allowed moves.
The list is history; the two variables summarise what matters.
Right: a limit and a status each change the later options.
questions.rule: Add a variable for a limit that shrinks or a status that flips whenever it changes what you can do later.

questions.q: Match each piece of information to the kind of state variable it becomes.
questions.explain: Positions are indices, a shrinking allowance is a numerical constraint, and a yes-or-no condition is a boolean status.
pairs: How many more obstacles may be removed
questions.rule: Add a variable for a limit that shrinks or a status that flips whenever it changes what you can do later.

questions.q: An input has n = 10 positions, a limit k = 3 and a boolean status. By the book's counting, how many states are there?
questions.explain: Count the product of the ranges: 10 * 3 * 2 = 60.
options: 15, since 10 plus 3 plus 2 is 15
30, since the boolean adds no new states
60, since 10 times 3 times 2 is 60
13, since the limit and the input are counted together
optionExplain: States multiply across variables; they do not add.
A boolean doubles the count.
Right: multiply the range of each variable.
Counting them together would be adding; the ranges multiply.
questions.rule: Add a variable for a limit that shrinks or a status that flips whenever it changes what you can do later.

questions.q: In the stock problem, k transactions are allowed, and the book tracks them with a variable named remain. What does it hold?
questions.explain: The numerical constraint is stored as what remains.
options: How many transactions are still available on the current day
How many transactions have been made since day zero
The profit made so far from the completed transactions
The index of the day on which the last sale took place
optionExplain: Right: it is the allowance that is left.
It counts the allowance left, not the used part.
Profit is the return value, not a state variable.
That records history; the variable tracks the allowance.
questions.teaches: In the stock problem the numerical constraint is a variable named remain that counts how many transactions are left, along with a boolean holding and the day index i.
questions.rule: Add a variable for a limit that shrinks or a status that flips whenever it changes what you can do later.

questions.q: A DP algorithm uses the three state variables i, holding and remain. How is it described?
questions.explain: Each state variable counts once. The card next defines dimensionality.
options: It is one-dimensional, since only i walks along the input
It is two-dimensional, since a boolean is not a real dimension
It is six-dimensional, since the variable ranges add up to six
It is three-dimensional, because it has three state variables
optionExplain: Every state variable counts, whatever its range.
The boolean is a state variable and counts.
Ranges are not added; the variables are counted.
Right: dimensionality is the count of state variables.
questions.rule: Dimensionality is the count of state variables.

questions.q: An algorithm whose state is the pair (i, j) is ____-dimensional.
questions.explain: Two state variables make the algorithm two-dimensional.
questions.rule: Dimensionality is the count of state variables.

questions.q: Sort each algorithm by its dimensionality.
questions.explain: One state variable means one-dimensional. Two or three variables make an algorithm multi-dimensional.

items.t: House Robber with the state i
Longest increasing subsequence with the state i
Climbing stairs with the state i
Longest common subsequence with the state (i, j)
Stock trading with the state (i, holding, remain)
Piles of coins with the state (i, remain)

questions.rule: Dimensionality is the count of state variables.

questions.q: A one-dimensional algorithm gets one extra boolean state variable. What is its dimensionality afterwards?
questions.explain: Count the variables, not their ranges.
options: Still one-dimensional, since a boolean has only two values
Two-dimensional: the boolean is a second state variable
Three-dimensional, since a boolean counts as two variables
Zero-dimensional, since the boolean replaces the index
optionExplain: The number of values does not change the count of variables.
Right: the count of variables goes from one to two.
A boolean is one variable.
The index is still there; the boolean is added.
questions.rule: Dimensionality is the count of state variables.

questions.q: A learner says (i, holding, remain) has 2 times n times k dimensions. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Dimensions count variables; states multiply their ranges.
options: Nothing is wrong, since the dimension is the product of the ranges
Dimensions count variables, here 3; 2 * n * k counts states
The dimensionality is n * k because holding does not count
The dimensionality is 2, since a boolean has two values
optionExplain: The product is the number of states, not the dimensions.
Right: the product is the state count.
Every variable counts, including holding.
The count is of variables, not of values.
questions.rule: Dimensionality is the count of state variables.

questions.q: How many state variables, at most, does the book say some problems might require?
questions.explain: Some problems need as many as five dimensions.
options: Exactly two, an index and a limit
Only one, an index along the input
There is no upper limit of any kind at all
As many as five
optionExplain: Problems with three variables appear in this chapter.
Many problems need more than the index.
The book gives five as the high end.
Right: the book says some problems might require as many as five dimensions.
questions.teaches: Some problems might require as many as five dimensions.
questions.rule: Dimensionality is the count of state variables.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: A memoized DP has 1,000 possible states, and each state does 50 steps of its own. About how many steps does it take in total?
questions.explain: Each state does its work once, so multiply. The card next states the formula.
options: 1,050, since the work of the states is added to the state count
1,000, since memoization leaves one step for each state
50,000, since 1,000 states times 50 steps is 50,000
50, since only one state does real work and the rest read the cache
optionExplain: Work per state is repeated for every state, so it multiplies.
Each state still does its own 50 steps once.
Right: states times work per state.
Every distinct state does its work once.
questions.rule: DP time is the number of states times the work done at one state.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: With N states and F work at each state, the time is O(N * ____).
questions.explain: The time is the number of states times the work per state, O(N * F).
questions.rule: DP time is the number of states times the work done at one state.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: A DP has n * m states, and each state loops over x options doing O(1) work per option. What is the time?
questions.explain: Multiply the number of states by the work at each state.
options: O(n * m * x), because the work per state is x
O(n * m), because the states set the time on their own
O(n + m + x), because the three sizes are added together
O(x), because the cache removes the loop from later states
optionExplain: Right: states times work per state.
The loop makes each state cost x, not 1.
Sizes multiply when states each do work.
The cache skips repeat visits, not the loop inside a first visit.
questions.rule: DP time is the number of states times the work done at one state.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: A DP is changed so each state does twice as much work, with the same states. What happens to the total time?
questions.explain: Time scales with the work per state.
options: It stays the same, since the states are unchanged
It about squares, since work is repeated for each state
It about halves, since the cache removes half of the work
It about doubles
optionExplain: The states are the same but each costs more.
Doubling F doubles N * F; it does not square it.
The cache removes repeat visits and does not lower the work of a first visit.
Right: time is N * F and F doubled.
questions.rule: DP time is the number of states times the work done at one state.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: True or false: a memoized DP repeats the full work of a state every time it visits that state.
questions.explain: A repeat visit reads the stored value. The full work of a state is done once, which is why time is N * F.
questions.rule: DP time is the number of states times the work done at one state.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: A DP has n states, but each state scans all earlier states in a loop. What is the time, and why?
questions.explain: The work per state can be larger than O(1).
options: O(n), since the cache stores each answer once
O(n^2): the work per state is linear in n and there are n states
O(2^n), since every state calls the earlier states again
O(n log n), since scanning earlier states is a search
optionExplain: The cache saves repeat visits, not the scan inside a state.
Right: N * F = n * n.
The cache stops repeated calls, so the growth is not exponential.
A plain scan over n items is linear, not logarithmic.
questions.teaches: Notice that the O(n^2) arises because the work done at each state is linear with n and there are n states.
questions.rule: DP time is the number of states times the work done at one state.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: A DP has 1,000 states, and each answer is one number. How does the plain solution's space grow with the number of states?
questions.explain: One value per state gives linear space. The card next states this.
options: Quadratically, since each state stores its relation to every other state
Not at all, since the recursion already keeps all the answers
Logarithmically, since the cache can be compressed by hashing
Linearly, with one stored number per state
optionExplain: A state stores its own answer only.
The recursion does not keep answers; the cache does.
Hashing does not shrink the number of stored answers.
Right: space is O(N).
questions.rule: A plain DP stores one value per state, so its space is O(N).

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: True or false: in top-down DP, the hash map ends up holding every state that was visited.
questions.explain: Each visited state is cached, so by the end the hash map stores all the states.
questions.rule: A plain DP stores one value per state, so its space is O(N).

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: A bottom-up table over states (i, j) with i from 0 to 19 and j from 0 to 29 has ____ cells.
questions.explain: The array is as large as the number of states: 20 values of i times 30 values of j is 600.
questions.rule: A plain DP stores one value per state, so its space is O(N).

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: Memoized fib(6) has finished. How many results are stored in the memo?
questions.explain: Only states that needed recursive work are stored: 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
options: 5, one each for fib(2) to fib(6)
7, one for each value from fib(0) to fib(6)
25, one for each call that was made without a cache
11, one for each time the function was entered
optionExplain: Right: the base cases are returned without being stored.
The base cases return directly and are not cached.
That is the call count of plain recursion.
Cache hits do not store new results.
questions.rule: A plain DP stores one value per state, so its space is O(N).

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: According to the book, which implementation can often use less than O(N) space for a DP problem?
questions.explain: Bottom-up can often drop states it no longer needs.
options: Top-down, but not bottom-up
Both, by deleting entries whenever the cache gets large
Bottom-up, but not top-down
Neither, since both must store every state until the end
optionExplain: The book says the improvement is possible only in bottom-up.
Deleting entries would break the top-down cache for later states.
Right: the bottom-up table can often be reduced.
The book says bottom-up can improve in many problems.
questions.teaches: In many problems the space complexity can be improved when implementing bottom-up, but not top-down.
questions.rule: A plain DP stores one value per state, so its space is O(N).

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: A top-down DP needs only the last two answers at any time. Can the recursive version reach O(1) space?
questions.explain: The recursion itself costs space, whatever the cache holds.
options: Yes: delete the older entries from the hash map as the recursion goes
Yes: switch to a smaller hash map type that stores two values
No: the hash map grows to O(n^2) when entries are deleted
No: the recursion call stack uses O(n) space, even without a hash map
optionExplain: The call stack still holds one frame per level.
The stack depth is unchanged by the map type.
Deleting entries does not make the map larger.
Right: the stack depth cannot be avoided.
questions.teaches: The recursion call stack uses O(n) space and cannot be avoided, even if no hash map were needed.
questions.rule: A plain DP stores one value per state, so its space is O(N).

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: A state has variables i (n values), k (k values) and a boolean. How many states are there?
questions.explain: The number of states is the product of the ranges. The card next shows the example.
options: n + k + 2, the sum of the ranges of the variables
n * k * 2, the product of the ranges
n * k, since a boolean has no effect on the count
3, the number of variables in the state
optionExplain: Combinations multiply; they do not add.
Right: multiply the numbers of values.
A boolean doubles the count.
That is the dimensionality, not the number of states.
questions.rule: Multiply the ranges of the state variables to get the number of states.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: A state has variables i from 0 to 49 and k from 1 to 4. The number of states is ____.
questions.explain: There are 50 values of i and 4 values of k, and 50 * 4 = 200.
questions.rule: Multiply the ranges of the state variables to get the number of states.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: An index over 30 items, a limit with 5 values and a boolean make the state. With O(1) work per state, what is the time?
questions.explain: Count the states with the product, then multiply by the work per state.
options: O(n + k): about 30 + 5 + 2 = 37 states
O(2^n): the boolean doubles the work at every item
O(n * k): about 30 * 5 * 2 = 300 states
O(1): the limit and the boolean are fixed in the input
optionExplain: Ranges multiply; they do not add.
It doubles the count once, not at each item.
Right: the boolean is a constant factor.
They are fixed, but they still multiply the states.
questions.rule: Multiply the ranges of the state variables to get the number of states.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: A problem adds a second boolean to the state i, k, holding. How does the number of states change?
questions.explain: Each added variable multiplies the count by its number of values.
options: It doubles, from n * k * 2 to n * k * 4
It adds 2 states, from n * k * 2 to n * k * 2 + 2
It stays the same, since booleans carry no information
It squares, from n * k * 2 to (n * k * 2) squared
optionExplain: Right: another boolean multiplies by 2.
Added variables multiply the count.
Each boolean doubles the count.
A boolean doubles; it does not square.
questions.rule: Multiply the ranges of the state variables to get the number of states.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: True or false: the number of states for the variables i, k and holding is n + k + 2.
questions.explain: States are all combinations of values, so the ranges multiply: n * k * 2.
questions.rule: Multiply the ranges of the state variables to get the number of states.

questions.section: Time and space complexity of DP algorithms
questions.q: The state is an index i over n items plus a limit k, with x choices tried per state. What are the time and space?
questions.explain: Time is states times work per state, and space is states.
options: Time O(n * k) and space O(n * k * x), as the choices must be stored
Time O(n * k * x) and space O(x), as only the choices need space
Time O(n * k * x) and space O(n * k)
Time O(n + k + x) and space O(n + k), as sizes are added
optionExplain: Choices are tried, not stored, so space stays at one value per state.
The table still has one cell per state.
Right: the n * k states each do x work; the table stores one value per state.
Both time and space come from products here.
questions.teaches: The number of states is the product of the ranges of the state variables, and with a loop of x steps inside each state the time gains a factor of x while the space does not.
questions.rule: Multiply the ranges of the state variables to get the number of states.

questions.q: Which trio describes the components the book says every DP algorithm needs?
questions.explain: A function, a recurrence relation and base cases. The card next explains each.
options: A greedy rule for each step, a sorting key, and a priority queue
A loop over the input, a stack of pending items, and a final pass
A function for any state, a recurrence relation, and base cases
A hash function, a table size, and a rule for handling collisions
optionExplain: These belong to greedy methods, not to the DP framework.
These are generic control-flow parts, not the DP components.
Right: these are the three components of the framework.
These describe a hash map, which is only one way to cache.
questions.rule: Write three things for any DP: what the function returns for a state, how states connect, and where it stops.

questions.q: Match each framework component to its job.
questions.explain: The function says what a state means, the recurrence connects states, and the base cases supply known values.
pairs: Holds or computes the answer for any given state
Give actual values so the recursion ends
questions.rule: Write three things for any DP: what the function returns for a state, how states connect, and where it stops.

questions.q: You must count the ways to climb n stairs with steps of 1 or 2. Which plan covers all three components?
questions.explain: Check that you can name what dp returns, how a state follows from others, and the base values.
options: dp(i) is the number of ways to reach step i; dp(i) = dp(i - 1) + dp(i - 2); dp(0) = dp(1) = 1
dp(i) is the number of ways to reach step i; dp(i) = dp(i - 1) + dp(i - 2); no base cases are needed
dp(0) = dp(1) = 1; dp(i) = dp(i - 1) + dp(i - 2); the value returned is left undefined
dp(i) is the number of ways to reach step i; dp(0) = dp(1) = 1; the steps are tried in any order
optionExplain: Right: it names the function, the recurrence and the base cases.
Without base cases the recursion cannot return actual values.
The function must say what it returns for a state.
There is no recurrence relation to link the states.
questions.rule: Write three things for any DP: what the function returns for a state, how states connect, and where it stops.

questions.q: True or false: a function and a recurrence relation are enough for a working DP algorithm; base cases are optional.
questions.explain: Without base cases the recursion keeps asking for smaller states and does not reach an actual value.
questions.rule: Write three things for any DP: what the function returns for a state, how states connect, and where it stops.

questions.q: The three parts are in place and the function is plain recursion. What does the book say not to forget before analysing the time?
questions.explain: Memoization is the step that makes the three parts efficient.
options: Sort the input array, which improves the time from O(n^2) to O(n log n)
Memoize the function, which improves the time from O(2^n) to O(n)
Convert to bottom-up, which improves the time from O(n) to O(1)
Add a second recurrence relation, which improves the time to O(log n)
optionExplain: The framework does not rely on sorting.
Right: the cache turns exponential recursion into linear time.
The conversion changes style and sometimes space, not the time class.
A second recurrence is not part of the framework.
questions.teaches: Do not forget to memoize the function to improve the time complexity from O(2^n) to O(n), where n is the length of the input array.
questions.rule: Write three things for any DP: what the function returns for a state, how states connect, and where it stops.

questions.q: A friend says the framework suits only counting problems. How does the book describe its reach?
questions.explain: The framework applies whatever the question asks for.
options: It works for counting problems only, and other DP problems need a different method
It works for any DP problem and gives a systematic way to build an algorithm
It works only in one dimension, with at most one state variable
It gives a correct answer but cannot give the running time
optionExplain: The same three parts are used for minimum and maximum problems.

questions.code:
def rob(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    dp = [0] * n
    dp[0] = nums[0]
    dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1])
    for i in range(2, n):
        dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + nums[i])
    return dp[n - 1]
questions.teaches: The bottom-up solution returns nums[0] when there is only one house, to avoid an out of bounds error from setting the second base case.
questions.rule: The recurrence looks back two houses, so houses 0 and 1 get their answers directly.

def most_points(questions):
    n = len(questions)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)

        dp[i] = max(questions[i][0] + dp[min(j, n)], dp[i + 1])
    return dp[0]

options: The table has n + 1 cells, one more than House Robber
The recurrence is not static: the reach depends on the input
The recurrence takes a maximum of two terms, as House Robber does
The base case is at the end, and ends cannot be dropped
optionExplain: One extra cell does not prevent the saving.
Right: the reach varies from state to state.
House Robber takes a maximum of two terms too.
The direction does not decide whether states can be dropped.
questions.teaches: Because the recurrence relation is not static, since it depends on questions[i][1], the space complexity cannot be improved in the bottom-up implementation.
questions.rule: Base case at and past the end, an extra cell at index n, and a clamp on the jump.

questions.q: To compare two strings with DP, which state fits best?
questions.explain: Each string needs its own position. The card next defines dp(i, j).
options: One index into the shorter string only
The pair of letters that were compared last
One index into each string
The length of the common subsequence found so far
optionExplain: The other string needs a position too.
The letters do not say how much is left to compare.
Right: a position in text1 and a position in text2.
That is the answer being built, not the state.
questions.rule: Match: add 1 and move both indices. Mismatch: take the better of moving either index.

questions.q: True or false: when text1[i] equals text2[j], the book sets dp(i, j) = 1 + dp(i + 1, j + 1).
questions.explain: A match adds one to the length, and both strings move to the next character.
questions.rule: Match: add 1 and move both indices. Mismatch: take the better of moving either index.

questions.q: For text1 = stone and text2 = longs, the longest common subsequence has length ____.
questions.explain: The letters o and n appear in both strings in the same order, and no longer common subsequence exists.
questions.rule: Match: add 1 and move both indices. Mismatch: take the better of moving either index.

questions.q: For text1 = cat and text2 = act, the first letters c and a differ. Which two values does dp(0, 0) take the max of?
questions.explain: On a mismatch, try dropping the current letter of either string.
options: dp(1, 0) and dp(0, 1)
dp(1, 1) and dp(0, 0)
dp(1, 1) only
dp(0, 2) and dp(2, 0)
optionExplain: Right: move either index forward by one.
Moving both indices is the match case, and dp(0, 0) is the call itself.
A mismatch leaves two ways to move on, one for each string.
The indices move by one, not by two.
questions.rule: Match: add 1 and move both indices. Mismatch: take the better of moving either index.

questions.q: On a mismatch this version moves both indices. What does it return for text1 = ab and text2 = ba?
questions.explain: Try both single moves on a mismatch.
options: 1, the same as the correct version
2, since both letters are in both strings
It does not finish, since the indices do not reach the end
0, but the correct answer is 1, because a common letter is skipped
optionExplain: Both mismatches move to the end and return 0.
The letters are in a different order, so only one can count.
The indices increase by one and do reach the end.
Right: moving both indices past a mismatch can lose a match.
questions.rule: Match: add 1 and move both indices. Mismatch: take the better of moving either index.

questions.q: In the version that considers text1 from 0 to i and text2 from 0 to j, where is the base case?
questions.explain: The base case moves to wherever the recursion stops.
options: At i equal to the length of text1 or j equal to the length of text2
At i equal to -1 or j equal to -1, the empty strings
At i equal to 0 and j equal to 0 only
There is no base case, since the strings meet in the middle
optionExplain: That is the base case of the version that moves forward.
Right: the recurrence uses i - 1 and j - 1.
A single character is not an empty string.
The recursion still needs a place to stop.
questions.teaches: In the opposite direction dp(i, j) considers text1 from 0 until i and text2 from 0 until j, the base case is i == -1 or j == -1 (empty strings), and the recurrence uses dp(i - 1, j), dp(i, j - 1) and dp(i - 1, j - 1).
questions.rule: Match: add 1 and move both indices. Mismatch: take the better of moving either index.

questions.q: In the LCS recurrence, text1[i] equals text2[j]. Does the recurrence also try the option of skipping that match?
questions.explain: A match can only help. The card next explains why.
options: Yes: it compares taking and skipping, like House Robber
No: taking the match cannot be worse than skipping it
Yes: the match may be part of a shorter subsequence only
No: a match ends the recursion at once
optionExplain: House Robber must compare, because taking blocks others; here it does not.
Right: skipping gains nothing.
A match adds to a common subsequence and does not make it shorter.
A match moves both indices; the recursion goes on.
questions.rule: Take every match, and return 0 once either string is used up.

questions.q: When one of the strings has no characters left, dp(i, j) returns ____.
questions.explain: With no characters left in one string, there are no common characters.
questions.rule: Take every match, and return 0 once either string is used up.

questions.q: For text1 = abc and text2 = abd, dp(0, 0) equals ____.
questions.explain: a matches a and b matches b, so 1 + 1; then c and d differ and both indices reach the end, giving 0. The total is 2.
questions.rule: Take every match, and return 0 once either string is used up.

questions.q: The match case becomes max(1 + dp(i + 1, j + 1), dp(i + 1, j), dp(i, j + 1)). What happens to the answers?
questions.explain: Extra options that cannot win only add work.
options: They become larger, since more options are compared
They become smaller, since skipping lowers the count
They become wrong, since a match must not be compared
They stay the same, but each state does extra work
optionExplain: More options cannot beat the match, so the answer does not grow.
The max keeps the match result.
The answers are still correct; the extra terms are redundant.
Right: skipping a match cannot beat taking it.
questions.rule: Take every match, and return 0 once either string is used up.

questions.q: True or false: returning 1 instead of 0 when a string is used up still gives the correct length.
questions.explain: The base value is added to every path, so a wrong base value spreads. For text1 = a and text2 = b the code returns 1 where the answer is 0.
questions.rule: Take every match, and return 0 once either string is used up.

questions.q: Why can a match not add more than 1 to the length in one step?
questions.explain: A match gains one letter, so no later option can do better by skipping it.
options: Because each string can be used only once
Because the recursion stops after the first match
One matched pair of characters adds one letter to the subsequence
Because two matches cannot be next to each other
optionExplain: Strings are read many times as the indices move.
It continues from the next characters.
Right: that is why taking it at once is safe.
Matches can follow one another, as in abc and abc.
questions.teaches: We cannot increase our length by more than 1 at any given step, so when we have the opportunity to take a match, we should take it.
questions.rule: Take every match, and return 0 once either string is used up.

questions.q: The LCS table covers strings of lengths n and m, with O(1) work per cell. What are the time and space?
questions.explain: One cell per pair of positions. The card next shows the table.
options: Time O(n + m) and space O(n + m)
Time O(n * m) and space O(n + m)
Time O(2^n) and space O(n * m)
Both O(n * m)
optionExplain: The table has a cell for every pair of positions, not for each position.
The plain table holds all n * m cells.
The cache prevents the repeated work.
Right: one cell per pair of positions.
questions.rule: Fill the (n + 1) by (m + 1) table from the last row and column back to dp[0][0].

questions.q: For strings of lengths 5 and 7, the table has ____ cells.
questions.explain: The table is (5 + 1) by (7 + 1), which is 6 * 8 = 48 cells.
questions.rule: Fill the (n + 1) by (m + 1) table from the last row and column back to dp[0][0].

questions.q: For text1 = abcde and text2 = ace, the cell dp[1][0] (bcde against ace) holds ____.
questions.explain: The common subsequence ce has length 2, and nothing longer is shared by bcde and ace.
questions.rule: Fill the (n + 1) by (m + 1) table from the last row and column back to dp[0][0].

questions.q: For two strings of length 2, put the cells in the order the loops fill them (n = m = 2).
questions.explain: i runs 1 then 0 and j runs 1 then 0 inside it, so the order is (1, 1), (1, 0), (0, 1), (0, 0).
questions.rule: Fill the (n + 1) by (m + 1) table from the last row and column back to dp[0][0].

questions.q: The table is made with n rows and m columns, without the extra row and column. What happens when the loops run?
questions.explain: The table needs a base row and a base column.
options: Nothing: the loops stop before the last row and column
The reads at dp[i + 1][j + 1] go past the table
The code runs but returns a smaller answer
The code runs and returns the correct answer
optionExplain: The loops start from the last character, which reads one cell further.
Right: the extra row and column hold the base cases.
It raises an error instead.
The base cells do not exist.
questions.rule: Fill the (n + 1) by (m + 1) table from the last row and column back to dp[0][0].

questions.q: In the version of LCS that considers the strings from 0 until i and j, in which direction should the bottom-up loops run?
questions.explain: Start the loops at the base cases of the definition you chose.
options: Downward, as in the forward version
Either way, since the order of loops does not matter in a table
Upward, starting from the base cases at the small indices
Diagonally, since the matches lie on diagonals
optionExplain: In this definition the base cases are at the small indices.
The order matters because each cell reads others.
Right: loops must start from the base cases.
The loops run along rows and columns.
questions.teaches: Bottom-up needs to start iterating from the base cases, whichever direction the definition of dp takes.
questions.rule: Fill the (n + 1) by (m + 1) table from the last row and column back to dp[0][0].

questions.q: A trader holds at most one unit of stock and has k transactions. Which facts decide what she can do on a given day?
questions.explain: Day, holding status and transactions left. The card next explains each.
options: The day and the price paid for the stock she holds
Only the day, since prices are given for each day
The day, whether she holds stock, and how many transactions are left
The day, the profit so far, and the lowest price seen
optionExplain: The price paid is not needed; only whether she holds counts.
The day alone does not say whether she may buy or sell.
Right: these three settle the possible moves and the future.
These summarise the past and do not change what is allowed.
questions.rule: The state is the day, whether you hold stock, and how many transactions remain.

questions.q: Match each state variable of the stock problem to its kind.
questions.explain: The day is an index, holding is a boolean status, and remain is the explicit numerical constraint from the problem.
questions.rule: The state is the day, whether you hold stock, and how many transactions remain.

questions.q: A bakery stores one batch of dough at a time and may make 3 resale trades over daily prices. Which state fits?
questions.explain: Day, holding and trades left apply to any one-unit trading problem with a trade limit.
options: The day, whether a batch is held, and the number of trades left
The day and the profit made so far from the trades
The day and the number of trades left, without a flag for holding a batch
The day, the price of the batch held, and the lowest price seen
optionExplain: Right: the same three variables.
The profit is what dp returns, not part of the state.
Without the flag the DP cannot tell whether to buy or sell.
These add detail that does not change the allowed moves.
questions.rule: The state is the day, whether you hold stock, and how many transactions remain.

questions.q: Counting states as the product of the ranges, n = 50 days, k = 4 and a boolean give ____ states.
questions.rule: The state is the day, whether you hold stock, and how many transactions remain.

questions.q: A learner uses only (i, remain) as the state, leaving out holding. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Each variable must separate situations that allow different moves.
options: Nothing: holding can be inferred from remain
The DP needs one more state variable for the price
The profit cannot be added, as the state has two variables
Holding or not looks the same, so buy and sell blur
optionExplain: remain does not say whether stock is held on this day.
Prices are fixed inputs and not part of the state.
A state may have any number of variables.
Right: holding changes which move is allowed.
questions.rule: The state is the day, whether you hold stock, and how many transactions remain.

questions.q: For 8 daily prices and k = 2, which call gives the answer to the whole problem?
questions.explain: The answer starts at the first day with nothing held.
options: dp(7, true, 0): the last day, holding stock, no transactions left
dp(0, false, 2): day 0, not holding stock, 2 transactions remaining
dp(0, true, 2): day 0, already holding stock
dp(8, false, 2): the day after the last, with all transactions left
optionExplain: That is near the end, not the start.
Right: you start the first day with nothing in hand and all transactions left.
You do not hold stock before the first day.
The day after the last is a base case.
questions.teaches: The answer is dp(0, false, k), the maximum profit starting on day 0 without stock and with k transactions remaining.
questions.rule: The state is the day, whether you hold stock, and how many transactions remain.

questions.q: On a day when you already hold the stock, which moves are possible?
questions.explain: You may sell or wait. The card next lists all the moves.
options: Buy or skip
Sell or skip
Buy, sell or skip
Skip only, until the transactions run out
optionExplain: Only one unit may be held, so a second purchase is not allowed.
Right: you cannot buy while holding one unit.
Buying is not allowed while holding.
You may sell on any day while holding.
questions.rule: dp(i, holding, remain) = max(skip, buy if not holding, sell if holding), and only a sale lowers remain.

questions.q: True or false: in the recurrence, the buy move adds -prices[i] and then moves to dp(i + 1, true, remain).
questions.explain: Buying spends prices[i], which is why it is added as a negative profit, and the holding flag becomes true.
questions.rule: dp(i, holding, remain) = max(skip, buy if not holding, sell if holding), and only a sale lowers remain.

questions.explain: The state is holding on the last day with 1 transaction left. Selling on day 5 gives 3 + dp(6, 0, 0) = 3, and skipping gives 0, so the larger value is 3.
questions.rule: dp(i, holding, remain) = max(skip, buy if not holding, sell if holding), and only a sale lowers remain.

questions.q: For prices = [2, 4, 1] and k = 2, what is the maximum profit?
questions.explain: The best plan is one profitable trade.
options: 3, from buying at 1 and selling at 4
5, from adding both gains 2 and 3
0, since the last price is lower than the first
2, from buying at 2 and selling at 4
optionExplain: The 1 comes after the 4, so that trade is not possible.
There is only one gain available.
The first trade already makes a profit of 2.
Right: the later fall to 1 offers no second profit.
questions.rule: dp(i, holding, remain) = max(skip, buy if not holding, sell if holding), and only a sale lowers remain.

questions.q: This sale step does not lower remain. For prices = [1, 2, 1, 2] and k = 1, what does the code return?
questions.explain: The limit must be enforced by lowering remain when a sale completes a transaction.
options: 2, from two trades though only one is allowed
1, which is correct for a single trade
0, since selling is not allowed without lowering remain
3, since both prices of 2 are added to the profit
optionExplain: Right: remain does not shrink, so the limit is not enforced.
With no decrease in remain, a second trade is allowed.
Selling is still allowed; it costs no transaction.
Each sale gains 1 net of the buy, so the total is 2.
questions.rule: dp(i, holding, remain) = max(skip, buy if not holding, sell if holding), and only a sale lowers remain.

questions.q: You start with remain = 2, buy on day 0 and sell on day 3. What is remain after the sale, and why?
questions.explain: A transaction is one buy and one sell, counted at the sale.
options: 0, because the buy and the sale each use up one transaction
2, because remain counts only transactions that lost money
1, because a trade is counted only when the stock is sold
1, because the buy used one and the sale gave one back
optionExplain: The buy does not use one up.
remain counts completed trades of any result.
Right: a buy leaves remain unchanged.
The sale does not give one back.
questions.teaches: When we buy we have not yet completed a transaction, so remain stays the same; when we sell, we use up one of our transactions, so remain - 1.
questions.rule: dp(i, holding, remain) = max(skip, buy if not holding, sell if holding), and only a sale lowers remain.

questions.q: In the stock recurrence, when does the profit from the remaining days become zero without more work?
questions.explain: Two things end the recursion. The card next states them.
options: When the price on the current day is lower than on the next day
When the stock is not held at the start of the day
When the profit so far is zero or negative
When the days run out or no transactions are left
optionExplain: Prices do not end the recursion.
Not holding does not end the choices; a buy may follow.
The profit so far is not part of the state.
Right: nothing more can be earned in either case.
questions.rule: Base cases: no days or no transactions left. Cost: O(n * k), because holding contributes a constant.

questions.q: When remain is 0, the profit that can still be made is ____.
questions.explain: With no transactions left, no more profit can be earned.
questions.rule: Base cases: no days or no transactions left. Cost: O(n * k), because holding contributes a constant.

questions.q: For 100 daily prices and k = 5, the product of the ranges n * 2 * k gives ____ states.
questions.explain: 100 * 2 * 5 = 1000 states, and the O(1) work per state keeps the time and space proportional to this.
questions.rule: Base cases: no days or no transactions left. Cost: O(n * k), because holding contributes a constant.

questions.q: In the bottom-up code, why does the loop over remain begin at 1 and not at 0?
questions.explain: Start the loops after the base cases that the array already holds.
options: remain = 0 would divide by zero in the recurrence
remain = 0 is a base case, and the array is already 0 there
Python arrays cannot use the index 0 for a third dimension
Transactions are counted from 1 as the first trade is trade 1
optionExplain: The recurrence has no division.
Right: those cells need no computation.
Index 0 is valid in any dimension.
The loop starts at 1 because index 0 is the base case.
questions.rule: Base cases: no days or no transactions left. Cost: O(n * k), because holding contributes a constant.

questions.q: True or false: a time of O(n * 2 * k) grows faster than O(n * k).
questions.explain: Constant factors such as the 2 from holding are dropped in big-O, so both describe the same growth.
questions.rule: Base cases: no days or no transactions left. Cost: O(n * k), because holding contributes a constant.

questions.q: A DP has state (i, remain) with base cases i = n and remain = 0. How should its bottom-up loops run?
questions.explain: Whatever the number of variables, begin at the base cases.
options: i from n - 1 down to 0, remain from 1 up to k
i from 0 up to n - 1, remain from k down to 1
i from 0 up, remain from 0 up, as in any nested loop
The loop order does not matter since the cache fills the cells
optionExplain: Right: start from the base cases and move toward the answer.
The loops would read cells that are not filled yet.
The base cases would be recomputed from empty cells.
A plain table has no cache; each cell must be filled in order.
questions.teaches: Configuring the for loops can be tricky; the important thing is to start iterating from the base cases, so i starts at n and remain starts at 1.
questions.rule: Base cases: no days or no transactions left. Cost: O(n * k), because holding contributes a constant.

questions.q: In the piles-of-coins problem, which state variables does the book use?
questions.explain: An index plus a count of coins left. The card next gives the recurrence.
options: The pile index and the number of coins still allowed to be taken
The pile index and the value of the top coin of that pile
The pile index and the total value collected so far
The pile index and the number of coins in that pile
optionExplain: Right: an index and a numerical constraint.
The top coin is read from the input and is not a variable.
The total is the return value, not part of the state.
The pile size is part of the input and does not describe the allowance that is left.
questions.rule: At each pile, skip it or try every number of top coins, then recurse with fewer coins allowed.

questions.q: After taking the first 2 coins of pile i, the next call is dp(i + 1, remain - ____).
questions.explain: Taking j + 1 = 2 coins uses 2 of the allowance, so the call is dp(i + 1, remain - 2).
questions.rule: At each pile, skip it or try every number of top coins, then recurse with fewer coins allowed.

questions.q: For piles = [[5, 1], [4, 4, 4], [10]], the value of dp(1, 2) (piles 1 and 2 with 2 coins) is ____.
questions.explain: Taking one 4 from pile 1 and the 10 from pile 2 gives 14; taking two 4s gives 8.
questions.rule: At each pile, skip it or try every number of top coins, then recurse with fewer coins allowed.

questions.q: For piles = [[5, 1], [4, 4, 4], [10]] and k = 3, what is the largest total?
questions.explain: Table check: dp(0, 3) = 19.
options: 12, from the three 4s
18, from the 10 and two 4s
19, from the 5, one 4 and the 10
16, from the 5, the 1 and the 10
optionExplain: That is smaller than taking one coin from each pile.
The 5 on top of pile 0 is worth more than a second 4.
Right: the top coins of the three piles.
