The 1 is below the 5, and a 4 is a better third coin.
questions.rule: At each pile, skip it or try every number of top coins, then recurse with fewer coins allowed.

questions.q: True or false: using dp(i + 1, remain - j) after taking j + 1 coins still respects the limit of k coins.
questions.explain: Taking j + 1 coins must lower the allowance by j + 1. With remain - j the first coin is free, and the code returns 27 instead of 19 on the example piles.
questions.rule: At each pile, skip it or try every number of top coins, then recurse with fewer coins allowed.

questions.q: A DP picks books from shelves and may take several from the top of one shelf. Which part of the recurrence chooses how many?
questions.explain: A choice among many amounts is a loop inside the state.
options: The base case, which fixes the count for each shelf
The memo, which stores the best count for each shelf
The state variable remain, which counts the shelves
A loop over the counts inside each state, trying every possibility
optionExplain: Base cases give known values; they do not choose counts.
The memo stores answers; it does not choose.
remain counts the allowance, not shelves.
Right: at every state try all the possibilities.
questions.teaches: At every state we need to try all possibilities, so we use a loop over the number of coins to take from the current pile.
questions.rule: At each pile, skip it or try every number of top coins, then recurse with fewer coins allowed.

questions.q: The coins DP has n * k states, and a loop of about x steps in each. What is its time complexity?
questions.explain: States times the loop length. The card next gives the cost.
options: O(n * k)
O(n + k + x)
O(n * k * x)
O(x)
optionExplain: That would hold if each state did O(1) work.
Work multiplies across states; it is not added.
Right: states times work per state.
The loop runs in every state, not once.
questions.rule: Time is O(n * k * x) and space is O(n * k).

questions.q: True or false: the space of the coins DP is O(n * k), the number of states.
questions.explain: The memo or table stores one value per state, and the loop adds no storage.
questions.rule: Time is O(n * k * x) and space is O(n * k).

questions.q: With n = 20 piles, k = 10 and an average pile length x = 5, the work is about ____ steps.
questions.rule: Time is O(n * k * x) and space is O(n * k).

questions.q: Every pile holds exactly one coin, so x = 1. What does the time become?
questions.explain: A loop of length 1 adds no factor.
options: O(n * k)
O(n * k * k)
O(n)
optionExplain: Right: each state does O(1) work.
The loop over j has length 1, not k.
The k values of remain still give n * k states.
There are still many states.
questions.rule: Time is O(n * k * x) and space is O(n * k).

questions.q: A learner says the time is O(n * k) because there are n * k states. What is missing?
questions.explain: Multiply by the work done at each state.
options: Nothing is missing, since the state count is the time
The space term, which should be added to the time
The base cases, which cost O(n * k) each
Each state runs a loop of about x steps: O(n * k * x)
optionExplain: The state count is the time only when each state does O(1) work.
Time and space are separate measures.
The base cases cost O(1).
Right: the work per state is not O(1).
questions.rule: Time is O(n * k * x) and space is O(n * k).

questions.q: Piles have different lengths. How does the book handle this in the time bound?
questions.explain: Name the quantity and say that it is an average.
options: It uses the length of the longest pile for every state
It uses x, the average number of coins per pile, in O(n * k * x)
It ignores the pile lengths, since they are constants
It uses the total number of coins instead of n
optionExplain: The book uses the average.
Right: x stands for the average pile length.
The loop length is part of the work per state.
n is the number of piles.
questions.teaches: The book writes the average number of coins per pile as x, which gives a time complexity of O(n * k * x) and a space complexity of O(n * k).
questions.rule: Time is O(n * k * x) and space is O(n * k).

questions.q: A DP walks over a grid of squares. Which state describes where it is?
questions.explain: Row and column name a square. The card next explains the graph view.
options: Only the number of squares visited so far
Only the row, since columns follow from the moves
The row and the column of the square
The value written in the square
optionExplain: Different squares can have the same count.
The column is needed to name the square.
Right: a position on a grid takes two coordinates.
Two squares can hold the same value.
questions.rule: Treat each square as a state (row, col), and write each square's answer from its neighbours.

questions.q: True or false: a matrix can be modelled as a graph in which each square is a node and adjacent squares are joined by edges.
questions.explain: This is the same model as in the trees and graphs chapter.
questions.rule: Treat each square as a state (row, col), and write each square's answer from its neighbours.

questions.q: A grid has 6 rows and 4 columns and the state is (row, col). The number of states is ____.
questions.explain: There is one state per square: 6 * 4 = 24.
questions.rule: Treat each square as a state (row, col), and write each square's answer from its neighbours.

questions.q: A grid DP has the state (row, col). What is its dimensionality?
questions.explain: Two coordinates, two dimensions.
options: Two, since it has two state variables
One, since a grid is one flat block of cells
Four, since each square has four neighbours
Three, since a move is down, right or stay
optionExplain: Right: dimensionality counts the state variables.
The state still has two variables.
The number of neighbours is not the number of state variables.
Moves are part of the recurrence, not state variables.
questions.rule: Treat each square as a state (row, col), and write each square's answer from its neighbours.

questions.q: A learner uses only the column as the state of a grid DP, saying the row follows from the moves. What is wrong?
questions.explain: A state must fully describe the scenario.
options: Nothing: the row follows from the number of moves, so one variable suffices
The column cannot be used as an index into a grid
The state is fine, but the table must then be three-dimensional
Different squares in the same column would share a state, but their answers differ
optionExplain: The number of moves is not in the state, so the row is unknown.
The column is a valid index.
The table follows from the state variables.
Right: the state must name the square.
questions.rule: Treat each square as a state (row, col), and write each square's answer from its neighbours.

questions.q: A drone crosses a city grid from the north-west to the south-east corner, moving east or south. What does the book say about this setup?
questions.explain: Recognise the common pattern: top-left start, bottom-right goal, down or right.
options: A start in the middle and moves in all four directions
Top-left start, bottom-right goal, moves down or right
A goal on the top row and moves up or left
A start on any square and unlimited jumps
optionExplain: The common scenario in the book has fixed corners and two directions.
Right: a very common scenario for matrix DP.
The usual direction is toward the bottom right.
Unlimited jumps are not the usual scenario.
questions.teaches: Starting in the top left, wanting to reach the bottom right, and moving only down or right is a very common scenario in matrix DP problems.
questions.rule: Treat each square as a state (row, col), and write each square's answer from its neighbours.

questions.q: A robot moves only down or right. From which squares can it enter square (row, col)?
questions.explain: Above and to the left. The card next gives the recurrence.
options: From the square below and the square on the right
From the square above and the square on the left
From all four neighbouring squares
From the squares on the same row or the same column
optionExplain: Those squares are further along the path.
Right: those are the only two moves that end there.
Moving up or left is not allowed.
Only the adjacent squares, one move away, are the sources.
questions.rule: Paths to a square = paths to the square above + paths to the square on the left, with dp(0, 0) = 1.

questions.q: The base case is dp(0, 0) = ____, since there is one way to be at the start: begin there.
questions.explain: There is a single way to be at the start, by starting there.
questions.rule: Paths to a square = paths to the square above + paths to the square on the left, with dp(0, 0) = 1.

questions.q: On a 4 by 4 grid, the number of paths from the top left to the bottom right is ____.
questions.explain: The grid values run 1 1 1 1 / 1 2 3 4 / 1 3 6 10 / 1 4 10 20, so the corner holds 20.
questions.rule: Paths to a square = paths to the square above + paths to the square on the left, with dp(0, 0) = 1.

questions.q: In the unique-paths table, what is dp(0, c) for any column c of the first row?
questions.explain: Squares on the edge have only one predecessor.
options: 0, since the first row has no square above it
c, since there are c squares to the left
2, since each square can be entered in two ways
1, as there is one way along the top edge
optionExplain: The left square still contributes.
Only one path runs along the top edge.
The first row has only one way in.
Right: nothing is above the square, so only the left term counts.
questions.rule: Paths to a square = paths to the square above + paths to the square on the left, with dp(0, 0) = 1.

questions.q: True or false: setting dp(0, 0) = 0 as the base case still gives the right number of paths.
questions.explain: Every count is built from the start square, so a seed of 0 gives 0 for every square.
questions.rule: Paths to a square = paths to the square above + paths to the square on the left, with dp(0, 0) = 1.

questions.q: A robot may now move down, right, or diagonally down-right. How does the recurrence for the number of paths change?
questions.explain: Add one term for each way a square can be entered. The extra term is still O(1) work per state, so time and space stay O(n * m).
options: It stays the same, since the diagonal is the sum of the other two
It becomes a maximum of the three terms
It gains a third term, dp(row - 1, col - 1), for the diagonal move
It uses only the diagonal term
optionExplain: The diagonal is a separate move and a separate predecessor.
The problem counts paths, so terms are added.
Right: each allowed move adds a predecessor.
All allowed moves count.
questions.teaches: Because the work at each state is O(1), the time and space of unique paths are both O(n * m).
questions.rule: Paths to a square = paths to the square above + paths to the square on the left, with dp(0, 0) = 1.

questions.q: In minimum path sum, how does the recurrence differ from unique paths?
questions.explain: A minimum plus the cell's own value. The card next gives it.
options: It adds the two neighbours and ignores the number in the square
It takes the larger of the two neighbours
It takes the smaller neighbour and ignores the square's own number
It takes the smaller of the two neighbours and adds the square's own number
optionExplain: That is unique paths, which counts paths instead of costs.
The goal is the smallest sum.
The square's number is part of the sum along the path.
Right: min replaces the sum, and the square's value is added.
questions.rule: dp(row, col) = grid[row][col] + min(above, left), with the start square's own value as the base case.

questions.q: True or false: the base case of minimum path sum is dp(0, 0) = grid[0][0], the value of the starting square.
questions.explain: The path starts at (0, 0), so its sum already includes that square.
questions.rule: dp(row, col) = grid[row][col] + min(above, left), with the start square's own value as the base case.
dp(row, col) = grid[row][col] + min(above, left), with the start square's own value as the base case.

questions.q: For grid = [[2, 4, 3], [6, 1, 5], [3, 2, 7]], what is the smallest path sum?
optionExplain: That leaves out the 2 in the start square, which is on every path.
Right: the table ends with 16 in the bottom right.
This is the sum along the top row and then down the right column.
This is the sum of the smallest numbers 2, 3, 1, 2 and 5, which is not a valid path.
questions.rule: dp(row, col) = grid[row][col] + min(above, left), with the start square's own value as the base case.

questions.q: Setting dp[0][0] = 0 instead of grid[0][0] gives 14 on [[2, 4, 3], [6, 1, 5], [3, 2, 7]]. What is wrong?
questions.explain: The base case must include the starting square.
options: Nothing: the true answer is 14
The recurrence should take the larger neighbour
The start square's value 2 is missing from every path sum
The bottom-right square is counted twice
optionExplain: The true answer is 16.
The goal is the smallest sum.
Right: the start square is part of the path.
It is counted once by the formula.
questions.rule: dp(row, col) = grid[row][col] + min(above, left), with the start square's own value as the base case.

questions.q: The task changes to find the largest path sum with the same moves. What changes in the recurrence?
questions.explain: Swap the choice operation and keep the rest. The work per state stays O(1), so the cost stays O(m * n), and bottom-up can again keep one row.
options: min becomes max; the base case and the answer stay the same
The base case becomes 0, since a largest sum starts empty
The moves must now include going up, to gain more
The recurrence must add the two neighbours
optionExplain: Right: the shape of the recurrence is unchanged.
The start square is still part of the path.
The moves are unchanged.
Adding the two would count squares twice.
questions.teaches: The time and space complexity of minimum path sum are the same as for unique paths, O(m * n), and the space can again be improved to O(n) with bottom-up.
questions.rule: dp(row, col) = grid[row][col] + min(above, left), with the start square's own value as the base case.

questions.q: To fill a row of the unique-paths table, what must be known about the earlier rows?
questions.explain: A square needs the square above and the square to the left. The card next uses this.
options: Only the row directly above
Every row above, since each square sums all the squares above
Only the first row, which holds the base cases
Nothing, since each square is computed on its own
optionExplain: Right: older rows are not read again.
A square reads only its two neighbours.
The row above changes with every row.
Each square needs the square above and the square to the left.
questions.rule: Keep only the previous row: O(n) space, same time, for a static recurrence that reads the row above.

questions.q: Keeping one row makes the space O(____), where n is the number of columns.
questions.explain: One row has n cells, so the space is O(n).
questions.rule: Keep only the previous row: O(n) space, same time, for a static recurrence that reads the row above.

questions.q: A grid has 1000 rows and 50 columns. A full table holds 50000 cells; the row-by-row version keeps ____ cells of the previous row.
questions.explain: Only the previous row of 50 cells is kept. The code builds the next row beside it, so at most two rows exist at once, which is still O(n) space.
questions.rule: Keep only the previous row: O(n) space, same time, for a static recurrence that reads the row above.

questions.q: For a 3 by 4 grid whose last row of counts is 1 3 6 10, what does the one-row code return?
questions.explain: The answer is the last cell after the last row.
options: 6, the middle cell of the last row
4, the last cell of the second row
10, the last cell of the last row
20, the sum of the last row
optionExplain: The answer is the last cell in the last row.
The answer needs all three rows.
Right: dp[n - 1] after the last row.
The answer is a single cell, not a sum of a row.
questions.rule: Keep only the previous row: O(n) space, same time, for a static recurrence that reads the row above.

questions.q: True or false: a memoized top-down solution can also be reduced to O(n) space by keeping one row.
questions.explain: The improvement is possible only in bottom-up; the top-down hash map and recursion stack keep their space.
questions.rule: Keep only the previous row: O(n) space, same time, for a static recurrence that reads the row above.

questions.q: In the one-row code, how is dp[row - 1][col] found for the row being built?
questions.explain: The stored row serves as the row above.
options: It is recomputed from the base cases at the start of each row
The stored previous row serves as the row above
It is read from a full table kept on the side
It is not needed, since a square depends only on the left square
optionExplain: That would repeat work the stored row already holds.
Right: both neighbours are available in two rows.
The point is that no full table is kept.
The row above is needed too.
questions.teaches: To find dp[row - 1][col] we reference the stored previous row, and to find dp[row][col - 1] we use the previous square in the current row.
questions.rule: Keep only the previous row: O(n) space, same time, for a static recurrence that reads the row above.

questions.q: Two sorted lists are merged with one index in each. The loop stops as soon as one list runs out. What must happen next?
options: The remaining items of the other list are still handled
The merge is finished, because the shorter list sets the length
Both indexes restart at zero for a second pass
The remaining items are dropped as duplicates
optionExplain: Right: the main loop only covers positions where both lists still have items.
It feels complete, but items of the longer list have not been placed.
Restarting would revisit items that are already merged.
Nothing marks them as duplicates; they are unvisited.
questions.explain: The main loop needs both lists to have items. The card next shows the extra loops that handle the rest.
questions.rule: A loop over two inputs ends when one is used up, not both.

questions.q: Match each part of the two-pointer templates to what it is for.
pairs: left at 0 and right at the last index
i and j both at 0 over two inputs
A loop after the main loop, one per input
Handles items left once the other input ran out
Moving one pointer in each pass
Shrinks the remaining work so the loop ends
questions.explain: The first two lines set up the two templates. The follow-up loops cover the leftovers, and one move per pass guarantees progress.
questions.rule: Set up, advance, then drain.

questions.q: Merging [1, 4, 9] with [2, 3, 10, 11, 12], which follow-up loop does real work after the main loop, and on how many items?
options: The first input's loop, on its last 3 items
The second input's loop, on its last 3 items
The second input's loop, on all 5 items
Neither loop, because the main loop places every item
optionExplain: The first list is the one that ends; nothing is left in it.
Right: the first input is used up after 9 is placed, and 10, 11, 12 are left.
Items 2 and 3 were placed by the main loop, so only the last three remain.
The main loop stops once 9 is placed, with three items still waiting.
questions.explain: Tracing the pointers: the main loop places 1, 2, 3, 4, 9 and stops with i at 3 (first list done) and j at 2. Items 10, 11, 12 remain in the second list.
questions.rule: After the main loop, exactly one input still has items, or none.

questions.q: True or false: With the loop test left < right, the two pointers can land on the same position and pair an element with itself.
questions.explain: The loop only runs while left is strictly below right, so each pass compares two different positions. The pointers meeting ends the loop.
questions.rule: Strict less-than keeps the two pointers on different elements.

questions.q: The first input of the two-input template is empty from the start. What does the merge do?
options: It raises an error, because the first pointer starts out of range and the loop reads it
It returns an empty result, because one input has no items
The main loop never runs and the second input's loop copies everything
The first input's loop runs once to set up the pointers
optionExplain: The loop tests range before it reads, so nothing is read.
The follow-up loops exist exactly for this case.
Right: the test fails at once, and the leftover loop handles all items of the other input.
Its loop has nothing to run on when the input is empty.
questions.explain: With i at 0 and an empty first list, i < len(a) is false, so the main loop is skipped and the leftover loop for the second list copies everything: merge([], [5, 6]) gives [5, 6].
questions.rule: An empty input turns the template into a plain copy of the other input.

questions.q: A tool scans n sorted ages from both ends, running an O(log n) lookup each pass. What total does the book's formula give?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n squared)
O(n log n)
optionExplain: That counts the passes but ignores the lookup inside each one.
That keeps only the lookup and forgets that the scan makes n passes.
That would need linear work inside each pass, not logarithmic.
Right: n passes, each costing O(log n).
questions.explain: Each pass moves a pointer, so there are at most n passes, and each pass costs the work inside it: n times log n.
questions.rule: Two-pointer cost is the number of passes times the work per pass.
questions.teaches: The book states the cost of two pointers (sliding window included) as O(n times k), where k is the work done at each iteration.

questions.q: To count the subarrays whose sum is exactly k, what do you keep while scanning the array once?
options: A window that grows until its sum passes k, then shrinks from the left
A map from running totals seen so far to how often they occurred
A sorted copy of the array, to find pairs that add up to k
Only the previous running total, compared with k at each step
optionExplain: A window works for sums that only grow, but it misses subarrays that reach k and then pass through other values.
Right: a subarray ends here with sum k exactly when an earlier total equals the current total minus k.
Sorting breaks the order, and subarrays must stay contiguous.
One earlier total cannot count all earlier matches.
questions.explain: A counting map lets one pass match every earlier start at once. The card next shows the template.
questions.rule: Count exact subarrays by remembering earlier running totals.

questions.q: The exact-count template starts its map with running total 0 mapped to a count of ____.
questions.explain: A subarray that starts at the very first element has an earlier total of 0, so the map begins with 0 seen once.
questions.rule: Seed the map with total 0 seen once.

questions.q: Sales are [3, 1, 2, 7, 4, 2, 1, 1, 5]. With the window template, how long is the longest stretch totalling at most 8?
optionExplain: One day too few: a stretch of that length exists, but a longer one fits within 8.
That stretch adds up to more than 8.
Right: the best stretch found by the window has this many days and a total within 8.
That would need a total that stays within 8, but the days are too large for it.
questions.explain: The window reaches 4 days at its best while its total stays at 8 or less; a longer stretch always exceeds 8 here.
questions.rule: Grow the right edge; shrink the left edge only when the condition breaks.

questions.q: Put the steps of one pass of the sliding window template in order.
items: Add the new right element to the running value
While the window condition is broken, remove the left element and move left
Update the answer using the current window
Move right on to the next element
questions.explain: The window first takes the new element, then repairs itself from the left, and only then records the answer.
questions.rule: Add, repair, record.

questions.q: An exact-count template records the running total before looking up total minus k. For arr [4, 2] and k = 0, what goes wrong?
options: It returns 0 as before, since k = 0 changes nothing
It crashes because the map has no entry for the lookup key at that point
It returns 1, counting only the whole array
It returns 2 instead of 0, because each total matches itself
optionExplain: k = 0 is the case where the order matters most.
The lookup uses a default of 0, so it never fails.
Each of the two totals matches itself, so the count is 2.
Right: after recording, total minus 0 finds the total just stored, so every element counts a subarray that does not exist.
questions.explain: With k = 0 the lookup key equals the new total. Recorded first, it always finds itself. Looked up first, [4, 2] has no subarray with sum 0, and the answer is 0.
questions.rule: Ask the map first, then record the new total.

questions.q: A store answers 20,000 questions about sales between two days of a 50,000-day log. About how many steps does a prefix sum take?
optionExplain: Right: 50,000 to build it once plus 20,000 constant-time answers.
That is the cost of re-adding the days for every question.
That counts only the questions and forgets the one-time build.
That counts only the build and forgets that each question still needs a step.
questions.explain: Building the prefix sum costs 50,000 steps, and each question is then a subtraction of two entries: 50,000 + 20,000 = 70,000. Re-adding days per question would cost about 1,000,000,000.
questions.rule: Pay O(n) once for the prefix sum, then each range sum costs O(1).
questions.teaches: Building a prefix sum is O(n), and finding the sum of a subarray from a prefix sum is O(1).

questions.q: You reverse a linked list by redirecting each node's next pointer to the node before it. What must be saved before you redirect?
options: The head of the list
The length of the list
The current node's old next node
The value stored in the current node
optionExplain: The head is worth keeping only if you need it afterwards, and it does not save the rest of the list.
The length does not help you reach the next node.
Right: once the pointer is redirected, that node is no longer reachable from the current one.
The value stays in the node; the link to the next node is what is lost.
questions.explain: The redirect overwrites the only link to the rest of the list. The card next shows the order of the four steps.
questions.rule: Save the next node first.

questions.q: Put the four steps for one node in the reversal template in order.
items: Save the current node's next node
Point the current node's next at prev
Move prev forward to the current node
Move the current node on to the saved node
questions.explain: Saving comes first so no link is lost; then the pointer is flipped; then both markers advance.
questions.rule: Save, flip, advance prev, advance curr.

questions.q: The fast-slow template runs on a list holding 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Which value does slow hold when the loop ends?
optionExplain: That would need five passes, but fast runs out after four.
That would be after three passes, but fast can still make a fourth.
Right: fast ends after four passes, so slow has moved four nodes.
Slow moves one node per pass, so it cannot reach the end when fast has made only four.
questions.explain: Fast moves two nodes per pass, so it runs out after four passes. Slow moves one node per pass, so it sits on the fifth node, 5.
questions.rule: When fast has gone twice as far as slow, slow is at the middle.

questions.q: A middle-finding loop tests only that fast's next node exists before moving fast two nodes. Which inputs break it?
options: Lists with an odd number of nodes, where fast lands on the last node
Even-length lists, where fast steps onto an empty position
Lists with exactly one node, where the head has no next node
Lists longer than four nodes, since fast then runs off the end
optionExplain: On odd lengths fast lands on the last node, whose next is empty, so the loop stops safely.
Right: with four nodes fast moves from the first node to the empty end, and the next test reads past it.
A single node has no next node, so the loop stops at once.
Length alone does not decide it; the parity of the length does.
questions.explain: On an even-length list fast steps onto the empty position past the last node. The next test then reads a next field of nothing and fails. Testing fast itself first avoids it.
questions.rule: Test fast, then fast's next, before moving two nodes.

questions.q: Sort each task into the template it calls for.

items.t: Return the middle node in a single pass
Find where the second half of the list starts
Flip the links so the tail becomes the head
Undo the order of the nodes between positions i and j
Split a list at its halfway point
Return the new head after the links are flipped

questions.explain: Finding a position that sits at a fixed fraction of the list is the job of two pointers at different speeds. Changing the order of the nodes is the job of the reversal.
questions.rule: Different speeds find positions; flipped links change order.

questions.q: A playlist's last track may link back to an earlier one. Which O(n) checks does the book's cheat sheet list for such a loop?
options: Reversing the list and comparing it with the original
Sorting the tracks and looking for neighbours that match
Binary search over track positions
Fast-slow pointers, or a hash map of nodes already seen
optionExplain: Reversal changes order; the cheat sheet does not use it for loops.
Sorting would cost more than O(n) and ignores the links.
A linked list has no direct access by position, so binary search does not fit.
Right: both are named for cycle detection.
questions.explain: The cheat sheet gives cycle detection as O(n) using fast-slow pointers or a hash map. Our reading: a hash map costs extra memory, while fast-slow uses only two pointers.
questions.rule: Cycle detection costs O(n) with fast-slow pointers or a hash map.
questions.teaches: Detecting a cycle in a linked list is O(n), using fast-slow pointers or a hash map.

questions.q: You must keep the 3 largest numbers from a long stream and can store very little. What do you hold?
options: A max-heap that contains every number seen so far in the stream
A queue holding only the last 3 numbers that arrived in the stream
A sorted copy of the full stream, from which the top 3 are read
A min-heap capped at 3, dropping its smallest item when it grows
optionExplain: That keeps everything, which is the memory cost you wanted to avoid.
A queue keeps the most recent items, not the largest.
Sorting stores all the numbers and costs more than needed.
Right: the smallest of the kept numbers is the first to leave.
questions.explain: A capped heap throws away the worst item as soon as there are too many. The card next shows the template.
questions.rule: A heap capped at k keeps the k best.

questions.q: A monotonic increasing stack pops while the top is ____ than the new number.
questions.explain: The template pops tops that are greater than the new number, so what remains stays in increasing order. Flipping the comparison gives a decreasing stack.
questions.rule: Increasing stack: pop the greater tops.

questions.q: A monotonic increasing stack processes 5, 3, 8, 1, 4 in that order. What does it hold at the end, bottom to top?
optionExplain: The 3 was popped when 1 arrived, because it was greater than 1.
Right: 1 removes 8 and 3 before it, and 4 then sits above 1.
The 3 was popped by the 1, and the 1 still sits below the 4.
Those are values popped earlier, not values that remain.
questions.explain: The pops are 5 (by 3), 8 (by 1) and 3 (by 1), in the order [5, 8, 3]. Only 1 and 4 remain.
questions.rule: Each new number pops every greater top before it is pushed.

questions.q: Put the steps for one number in the top-k heap template in order.
items: Add the number to the heap
Check whether the heap holds more than k items
If it does, remove the head of the heap
Move on to the next number
questions.explain: Adding first and trimming after keeps the rule simple: the heap never stays above k items after a pass.
questions.rule: Add, check the size, trim the head.

questions.q: True or false: To keep the 3 smallest numbers instead, the same template works if the heap puts the largest number at its head.
questions.explain: The template removes the head whenever the size exceeds k. If the head is the largest item, what stays are the smallest. Our reading of the template's CRITERIA placeholder.
questions.rule: Choose the heap ordering so the unwanted item is at the head.

questions.q: A teammate rewrites a JavaScript loop using += to use an array and join, expecting a speedup. What does the book's benchmark say?
options: join was faster, because it builds the string in one step
They run at the same speed, since both are O(n)
Concatenation with += was faster than join in JavaScript
join was faster only for short strings
optionExplain: That is the common belief, but the book reports the opposite for JavaScript.
Both are linear in size, but the book reports a measured difference.
Right: the template note says benchmarking found += faster than .join().
The book makes no such split by length.
questions.explain: Under the efficient string building template the book adds that, in JavaScript, benchmarking shows concatenation with += is faster than using .join(). Language and engine matter, so measure when it matters.
questions.rule: Do not assume the builder pattern is fastest in every language.
questions.teaches: In JavaScript, the book's benchmarking shows concatenation with += is faster than using .join().

questions.q: A graph has a cycle and you traverse it with a stack or a queue. What stops the traversal from running forever?
options: Switching between a stack and a queue at each step
Stopping at the first node that has no neighbours
Visiting each node's neighbours in sorted order
A set of nodes that have already been added
optionExplain: Both structures still revisit nodes around a cycle.
A cycle has no such node, so this never triggers.
The order of neighbours does not stop a node being reached again.
Right: a node is never added twice, so no cycle can feed the loop again.
questions.explain: Remembering what was already reached is what makes the loop finish. The card next shows when to mark a node.
questions.rule: Remember reached nodes so a cycle cannot repeat them.

questions.q: Match each traversal to the structure that drives it.
questions.explain: A stack goes deep first, a queue goes level by level, recursion uses the call stack as its stack, and graphs add a seen set because of cycles.
questions.rule: Stack for depth, queue for breadth, seen set for cycles.

questions.q: Put the nodes in the order the iterative graph DFS template visits them, starting at node 0.
questions.explain: From node 0 the stack gets 1 then 2, so 2 comes off first. Node 2 adds 3 and 4, so 4 comes off first; then 3; node 1 is last. Our trace of the template.
questions.rule: A stack takes the most recently added neighbour first.

questions.q: True or false: Reading the queue's size inside the for loop, after each removal, still processes a tree one level at a time.
questions.explain: The size shrinks as nodes are removed, and children grow it, so the loop would no longer match one level. The size is read once, before the loop.
questions.rule: Fix the level size before the inner loop starts.

questions.q: A problem gives a graph as a list of edge pairs. What does the book say to do before using the graph templates?
options: Run the template on the pairs, treating each pair as a node
Convert the input into an adjacency list
Sort the pairs so neighbouring nodes sit next to each other
Add a seen set, which handles any input format
optionExplain: A pair is an edge, not a node, so the neighbour loop would break.
Right: the templates assume nodes 0 to n - 1 and an adjacency list.
Sorting does not give direct access to a node's neighbours.
A seen set stops repeats but does not give the templates the adjacency list they read.
questions.explain: The graph templates read graph[node] to find neighbours. The book says that, depending on the problem, you may need to convert the input into an equivalent adjacency list first.
questions.rule: Match the template's input shape before you traverse.

questions.q: A social app has 100,000 users and 500,000 friendship links; BFS does constant work per user. About how many steps, by the book's formula?
options: About 600,000
About 100,000
About 500,000
optionExplain: Right: the users plus the links.
That counts the users but forgets that every link is looked at.
That counts the links but forgets the work per user.
That multiplies users by links, but each link is examined once, not once per user.
questions.explain: Time is n times k plus e: with n = 100,000, k = 1 and e = 500,000 that is 600,000 steps.
questions.rule: Graph traversal costs the node work plus the number of edges.
questions.teaches: DFS and BFS on a graph take O(n times k + e), where n is the number of nodes, e the number of edges and k the work done at each node.

questions.q: A sorted array holds several copies of the target. A plain binary search for it returns which position?
options: The first copy, since the search moves left
The last copy, since equal values go right
Whichever copy the midpoint reaches first
The number of copies
optionExplain: Nothing in the plain search pulls it toward the first copy.
An equal middle ends the search; it does not push right.
Right: the search stops at the first equal middle value it meets.
The search returns a position, not a count.
questions.explain: The plain search returns as soon as the middle equals the target. The card next shows templates that return the first or last copy.
questions.rule: A plain search finds a copy, not a chosen copy.

questions.q: Match each template to what it returns.
pairs: A matching index, or the insertion point if the target is absent
The first position the target could be inserted
The position just after the last copy
The smallest answer for which the check passes
questions.explain: Each template ends with a return that has a specific meaning. The duplicates templates differ only in the comparison.
questions.rule: Know what each template returns before you choose one.

questions.q: On [1, 2, 2, 2, 3], the right-most template searches for 2. What does it return?
optionExplain: That is what the plain template returns after landing on the middle.
That is the index of the last 2, not the position after it.
That is what the left-most template returns.
Right: index 4 is the position just after the last copy of 2.
questions.explain: The right-most search moves right past every value that equals the target and stops at 4. The left-most search stops at 1, and the plain one at 2.
questions.rule: Right-most returns the slot after the last copy.

questions.q: A check is true up to 7 and false above. Searching 1 to 50 for the largest passing number, what does the maximum template return?
optionExplain: That is the first failing number, which is where left ends.
Right: right ends on the last passing number.
That is the starting value of right, not where it finishes.
That is the starting value of left, and left moves up after each pass.
questions.explain: When the loop ends, left is the first failing value and right is the last passing one, so the maximum template returns right: 7.
questions.rule: Maximum returns right; minimum returns left.

questions.q: True or false: Changing the comparison from greater-or-equal to strictly greater in the left-most template turns it into the right-most template.
questions.explain: With strictly greater, equal values keep pushing left upward, so the search stops after the last copy. On [1, 2, 2, 2, 3] that gives 4 instead of 1.
questions.rule: One comparison separates left-most from right-most.

questions.q: A planner searches capacities from 1 to 1,000,000,000 for the smallest that works. About how many checks does it need at most?
optionExplain: That is the number of candidates, which is what the search avoids trying.
That is not a halving count of a billion candidates.
Nothing multiplies the 30 by a thousand.
Right: halving a range of a billion takes about 30 steps.
questions.explain: The range is the search space, and each check halves it. Counting the loop on 1 to 10^9 gives at most 30 passes.
questions.rule: Binary search takes about log2 of the search space.
questions.teaches: Binary search runs in O(log n) in the worst case, where n is the size of the initial search space, not necessarily the length of an array.

questions.q: In a backtracking loop over choices, what step follows the recursive call?
options: Saving the result in a memo table keyed by the current state
Undoing the change made to the state before the call
Resetting the answer to zero before the next choice
Sorting the remaining choices into a fixed order
optionExplain: That is for DP; backtracking does not reuse results by state.
Right: the next choice must start from the same state as this one.
That would erase answers recorded by earlier branches.
The order of choices is not what keeps branches independent.
questions.explain: Each branch changes the state, and the change must not leak into its siblings. The card next lists the steps.
questions.rule: Change, recurse, undo.

questions.q: Put the steps for turning a top-down solution into a bottom-up one in order.
items: Create an array sized by the state variables
Set the base cases in the array
Loop over the states from the base cases toward the answer
Replace each dp(...) call with a dp[...] read
Return the entry for the original question
questions.explain: The array and base cases come first, the loops visit states in dependency order, the calls turn into reads, and the answer is read at the end.
questions.rule: Array, base cases, loops, reads, answer.

questions.q: The backtracking subsets template runs on four distinct items. How many lists does it record, counting the empty one?
optionExplain: That is the count for three items.
Choosing 3 of 4 items, plus the others, does not give this total.
Right: each of the four items is either taken or left out, giving 2 to the power of 4.
That counts orderings of four items, but subsets ignore order.
questions.explain: The template records the current path at every call. For three items that is 8 lists, and each added item doubles it: 16 for four.
questions.rule: Each extra item doubles the subsets.

questions.q: Sort each step into the template it belongs to.

items.t: Undo the change after the recursive call
Return a stored answer when the state is in the memo
At the base case, modify the answer
Store the result for the state before returning
Loop over the choices, changing the state each time
Compute the answer with a recurrence relation

questions.explain: Backtracking explores choices and restores the state. Top-down DP caches an answer per state and computes it by a recurrence.
questions.rule: Undo marks backtracking; the memo marks DP.

questions.q: True or false: In a bottom-up conversion, the loops should start at the state that answers the original question and move toward the base cases.
questions.explain: The loops start at the base cases and end at the answer state, so each state reads entries that are already filled in.
questions.rule: Fill from the base cases up to the answer.

questions.q: A grid DP has 200 rows and 300 columns of states, each computed with constant work. By the book's formula, what is the time?
options: About 60,000 steps
About 500 steps
About 3,600,000,000 steps
About 200 steps
optionExplain: Right: one state per cell, constant work each.
That adds the sides instead of counting the cells.
That squares the number of states, but each state is computed once.
That counts the rows only.
questions.explain: DP time is the number of states times the work per state: 200 x 300 x 1 = 60,000. Space is O(n) for n states.
questions.rule: DP time is states times work per state.
questions.teaches: The book gives dynamic programming time as O(n times k), where n is the number of states and k the work done at each state, and space as O(n).

questions.q: According to the book, how long should your prepared self-introduction take?
options: 30 to 60 seconds
5 to 10 minutes
About 10 seconds, only your name and job title
As long as the interviewer keeps listening
optionExplain: Right: short enough to hold attention, long enough to cover three areas.
A long account feels thorough, but it uses time the problem will need.
Too short to cover your background and interests.
That leaves the length to chance instead of preparing it.
questions.explain: A prepared, rehearsed summary is brief by design. The card next lists what goes in it.
questions.rule: Keep the introduction brief and rehearsed.

questions.q: Which topics should the prepared introduction summarize? Select all that apply.
options: Your education
Your work experience
Your interests
The salary you expect
A solution to a practice problem
optionExplain: Right: education is one of the three areas.
Right: work experience is one of the three areas.
Right: interests are the third area.
Pay is not part of the introduction the book describes.
A practice solution belongs to later stages, not the opening.
questions.explain: The book names education, work experience and interests as the three areas for the 30 to 60 second summary.
questions.rule: Education, work experience, interests.

questions.q: The interviewer says she works on the checkout team and enjoys trail running, which you also do. What is the best use of this?
options: Say nothing about it, since personal topics are off limits in interviews
Remember her team, and mention that you also enjoy trail running
Spend your minute on running instead of your background
Ignore it, because only the technical rounds count
optionExplain: The book suggests mentioning a shared interest.
Right: you show attention and give them a way to connect.
The introduction still has to cover education, experience and interests.
Her work will help you ask questions later.
questions.explain: Paying attention to the interviewer's work gives you material later, and a shared interest is worth a short mention.
questions.rule: Listen for work you can ask about and interests you share.

questions.q: True or false: Because the interviewer introduces themselves first, you can skip rehearsing your own introduction.
questions.explain: The interviewer's introduction comes first, but you are then asked for yours. The book says to prepare and rehearse a brief one.
questions.rule: Prepare your introduction even though the interviewer speaks first.

questions.q: What if the interviewer mentions nothing you share an interest with?
options: Mention a hobby you do not have, to build rapport
Ask them to change the subject to something that you know about
Make your own introduction longer to fill the time
Skip the shared interest, but still listen to their work
optionExplain: An invented interest is not what the book advises, and it can be found out.
That interrupts the person who is introducing the team.
The introduction stays within 30 to 60 seconds.
Right: the shared-interest step is conditional; the listening is not.
questions.explain: The book says to mention an interest only if the interviewer mentioned one you share. The advice to listen applies in every case.
questions.rule: Share an interest only when there is one.

questions.q: Two panellists describe their teams, data and mobile. You get five minutes for questions at the end. What do you do?
options: Ask both the same prepared question about salary
Say you have no questions at all, to save the panel's valuable time
Ask each panellist about their own work, using what they said
Repeat your introduction in more detail
optionExplain: That ignores what each person told you about their work.
Having no questions can look like a lack of interest.
Right: what you heard at the start becomes your questions.
The closing minutes are for questions, not for another introduction.
questions.explain: The book says to pay attention when the interviewer talks about their work, since it helps you ask questions about it later.
questions.rule: What you hear at the start feeds the questions you ask at the end.
questions.teaches: Paying attention while the interviewer talks about their work helps you ask questions about that work later in the interview.

questions.q: The interviewer has finished reading you a problem. According to the book, what is the best first thing to say?
options: Name the algorithm you plan to use, so the interviewer sees your direction
Restate the problem in your own words and ask if that is right
Start writing code to save time
Ask what the optimal complexity is
optionExplain: Choosing a method before you are sure of the problem is premature.
Right: it confirms you heard the same problem they meant.
Time spent on the wrong problem costs more than a short check.
That is an answer you are expected to work toward, not to ask for.
questions.explain: A paraphrase catches misunderstandings before any design work. The card next lists what else to settle.
questions.rule: Confirm the problem first.

questions.q: Match each clarifying question to what it settles.
pairs: Will the input only have integers?
The types the input may hold
Will the input be sorted or unsorted?
Whether order can be relied on
Is the input guaranteed to have elements?
What should I do if an invalid input is given?
questions.explain: Each question closes one gap about the input before you design around it.
questions.rule: Ask about types, order, emptiness and invalid input.

questions.q: The interviewer reads a problem about delivery times without saying whether the list can be empty. What do you ask?
options: Whether you may use a library function for sorting the list
How the company ships its parcels
Whether the answer will be graded on speed
Whether the input is guaranteed to have elements
optionExplain: A sorting library is an implementation matter, not an input question.
That is background about the business, not about the input.
It does not settle what the input may contain.
Right: it settles the empty case before you design.
questions.explain: Asking about empty input shows attention to edge cases and tells you whether your code needs a guard.
questions.rule: Ask what the input guarantees.

questions.q: Sort each question by when it belongs in the interview.
groups: Ask while the problem is stated

items.t: Will the input be sorted?
How large can n be?
Why did you choose a hash map?
What does an average day look like?
Let me walk through the first example.
Is it ok if I import a library module?

questions.explain: Questions about the input and a walk through an example belong to the problem statement. Choice questions come in the follow-ups, questions about the job come at the end, and permission to import comes before coding.
questions.rule: Input questions come before design.

questions.q: You paraphrase the problem and the interviewer says that is not quite what they meant. What has the paraphrase done?
options: Shown that you cannot understand problems
Wasted time that the rest of the interview needed for the code
Found the misunderstanding before any design work
Replaced the need to ask about the input
optionExplain: Checking is a sign of care, not of weakness.
A correction here is far cheaper than one after the code is written.
Right: that is what it is for.
The paraphrase and the clarifying questions do different jobs.
questions.explain: Both sides now agree on what is asked, which is the reason for the step.
questions.rule: A paraphrase is a cheap test of understanding.

questions.q: The interviewer says the list holds at most 8 items. Which technique do the book's size clues point toward?
options: A hash map to avoid any search
A single pass that must finish in logarithmic time for huge input
A nested-loop solution only, since n is 100 to 1,000
Backtracking, since an exhaustive search is affordable here
optionExplain: A hash map can help, but the clue here points to backtracking.
Logarithmic time is for huge inputs.
At 8 items the input is far below that range.
Right: a very small n suggests backtracking.
questions.explain: A size this small leaves room for an exhaustive search such as backtracking.
questions.rule: The input size is a clue to the technique.
questions.teaches: The book says input size is a clue: a very small n suggests backtracking, n around 100 to 1,000 may make O(n squared) optimal, and a very large n may need better than O(n).

questions.q: You have picked an approach. According to the book, what should you do before you start coding?
options: Start coding right away and explain your plan once the code works
Explain the rough steps and check the interviewer agrees
Wait until the interviewer asks for your plan
Write out the full code in comments first
optionExplain: A flaw in the plan found late costs the most time.
Right: it surfaces problems with the plan while they are cheap to fix.
Waiting leaves them unable to hint early.
Comments are not what the interviewer needs; they need to understand your approach.
questions.explain: A short explanation of the steps lets both sides agree before time is spent on code. The card next lists the stage.
questions.rule: Agree on the plan before you code.

questions.q: Put the brainstorming steps in order.
items: Break the problem down and look for familiar patterns
Decide which structure or algorithm gives a good time complexity
Outline the rough steps of your algorithm
Explain the steps and check the interviewer agrees
questions.explain: You find patterns, choose a tool, outline the steps, get agreement, and only then code.
questions.rule: Pattern, tool, outline, agreement, code.

questions.q: While you outline a plan, the interviewer asks a leading question about a simpler structure. By the book's advice, how do you react?
options: Defend your plan firmly, since changing course in front of them looks weak
Switch at once without asking why
Say nothing and keep thinking silently
Explore the idea they raise, since it may lead to a better solution
optionExplain: Stubbornness is the behaviour the book warns about.
Exploring the idea means understanding it, not dropping your plan blindly.
Silence closes the door to further hints.
Right: they know the optimal solution and want you to succeed.
questions.explain: A hint is a sign the interviewer wants you to succeed. Exploring it keeps the conversation going.
questions.rule: Treat a hint as help.

questions.q: True or false: If you are not sure sliding window is the right idea, the safer move is to stay silent until you are certain.
questions.explain: Thinking out loud shows how you weigh trade-offs, and even a wrong idea lets the interviewer see your thinking and steer you.
questions.rule: Say the idea aloud even if you are unsure.

questions.q: The interviewer starts asking quiet questions that steer you away from your plan. What is the likely meaning?
options: It means the plan is correct and they are only checking the details
It may mean your plan is off track, so explore what they hint at
It means you should stop talking so they can think
It means the interview is over and you should wrap up
optionExplain: Hints are more often a nudge toward a better path.
Right: the book says they usually hint when you are on the wrong path.
Going silent removes the chance of more hints.
Hints are part of the conversation, not an ending.
questions.explain: Interviewers tend to hint subtly when you are on the wrong path. Treating it as a signal keeps you flexible.
questions.rule: A subtle hint often means: reconsider.

questions.q: A problem asks for the best stretch of consecutive days in a sales log. What should you say aloud while brainstorming?
options: That the problem looks like a graph search
Nothing yet, until you are sure of the final algorithm
That you will try every pair of days with two nested loops first, then improve it
That you are considering a sliding window, since each window is a stretch
optionExplain: Nothing in the problem suggests nodes and edges.
The book says that thinking aloud is the point.
That may be a starting brute force, but it is not the idea the book highlights here.
Right: this names the idea and its reason.
questions.explain: The book's example is a subarray problem, where you should be vocal about a sliding window because every window represents a subarray. It adds that even if you are wrong, the interviewer appreciates the thought process.
questions.rule: Name the idea and say why it fits.
questions.teaches: If a problem involves subarrays, say aloud that you are considering a sliding window, because every window represents a subarray; even a wrong idea shows your thought process.

questions.q: Halfway through coding you realize your plan may not work. According to the book, what do you do?
options: Tell the interviewer what worries you
Keep going quietly and hope it works out
Delete everything and begin again without a word
Ask the interviewer to give you the solution
optionExplain: Right: they can help, and silence cannot.
Hoping delays a problem that is cheaper to raise now.
Starting over silently loses the chance to discuss it.
The aim is to engage them in your thinking, not to hand off the task.
questions.explain: Interviewers want to help, but they can only help with what they hear. The card next shows the book's advice.
questions.rule: Voice your concern.

questions.q: Which habits does the book list for the implementation stage? Select all that apply.
options: Explain your decisions as you write
Ask the interviewer before importing a library
Repeat similar code instead of adding a helper
Say nothing until the code is finished
optionExplain: Right: for example, why you declare a set.
Right: make sure the interviewer is ok with it.
The book advises avoiding duplicated code and using helper functions.
The book tells you to stay in conversation, since silence makes it harder for the interviewer.
questions.explain: The book asks for spoken reasoning and a check on libraries, and against duplicated code and silence.
questions.rule: Talk, ask before importing, avoid duplication.

questions.q: You wrote three near-identical blocks that each check a different form field. What does the book suggest?
options: Leave them, because copies are quicker to read aloud
Fold them into a helper function or a loop
Comment each block so the repetition is explained
Wait for the interviewer to ask you to tidy them
optionExplain: Duplication makes the code longer and harder to change.
Right: similar code in several places should become one.
A comment does not remove the repetition.
The book asks you to avoid duplicated code yourself.
questions.explain: If you find yourself writing similar code in several places, the book says to create a function or simplify with a loop.
questions.rule: Similar code in three places wants one helper.

questions.q: Put the brute-force-first strategy in order.
items: Write a brute force solution and say it is suboptimal
Analyze each part to find the slow steps
Think about how to speed up those steps
Discuss the improvement with the interviewer
questions.explain: You get a working baseline first, then target its slow parts, and keep the interviewer in the conversation throughout.
questions.rule: Baseline first, then optimize the slow steps.

questions.q: A candidate is stuck and sits silent for four minutes before saying anything. What went wrong?
options: Nothing, because quiet thinking time is a sign of care and should not be interrupted by the interviewer
They should have switched languages
The interviewer could not tell where the candidate was stuck, so could not help
They should have asked for a harder problem
optionExplain: Thinking is fine, but silence leaves the interviewer in the dark.
Changing language does not address being stuck.
Right: communicating a concern is what lets them step in.
Being stuck is a reason to talk, not to change the task.
questions.explain: The book says it makes the interviewer's life a lot harder if you struggle in silence.
questions.rule: Say it when you are stuck.

questions.q: A knight on a board has 8 possible moves. How should the code handle them?
options: Handle the first move and add a comment for the rest
Write eight separate blocks, one for each of the possible knight moves
Loop over an array of the 8 offsets instead of writing 8 copies
Use recursion only for the two forward moves
optionExplain: A comment leaves seven moves unhandled.
Eight copies repeat the same logic.
Right: the same idea as looping over directions on a matrix.
That would skip moves the board allows.
questions.explain: The book's example is a DFS on a matrix, where you loop over a directions array of four pairs instead of writing the same logic four times.
questions.rule: Loop over a list of offsets instead of copying the logic.
questions.teaches: For a DFS on a matrix, the book loops over a directions array such as (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0) instead of writing the same logic four times.

questions.q: You are in a shared editor that cannot run code. How do you test your solution?
options: Print the result and read the console
Skip testing, because the code cannot be run in this environment
Walk through a test case by hand, tracking the variables
Ask the interviewer to run it on their machine
optionExplain: There is no console when code is not run.
The interviewer will still expect you to test it.
Right: you act as the computer.
That passes your job to them.
questions.explain: Without a runtime, you trace by hand. The card next lists the three environments.
questions.rule: No runtime means a hand trace.

questions.q: Match each environment to what you do.
pairs: Your own tests, code is run
Call the function in the outermost scope and print
Your own tests, code is not run
Walk through by hand, tracking variables
An error turns up in any environment
Stay calm and compare expected with actual values
questions.explain: Each environment has one main testing method, and the debugging advice is the same everywhere.
questions.rule: Method follows environment.

questions.q: You may run code and must write tests for a function summing a list's even numbers. Which set of tests shows the best variety?
options: Three lists of five even numbers
One long list of random numbers
Several lists that each hold exactly one even number among odd ones
An empty list, a list of only odd numbers, and a mixed list
optionExplain: These are the same kind of test, so they reveal little.
A single big case may hide the edge cases.
Repeating one test adds no variety.
Right: it covers edge cases and an ordinary input.
questions.explain: The book asks you to try a variety, including edge cases and intuitive inputs.
questions.rule: Mix edge cases and ordinary cases.

questions.q: Put the debugging steps in order for an environment that can run code.
items: Notice that the output is wrong
Add print statements in relevant places
Walk a small test case, stating the expected variable values
Compare expected and actual values aloud
questions.explain: You spot the issue, make the program show its state, trace a small case, and compare while talking.
questions.rule: Print, trace small, compare aloud.

questions.q: In a no-run editor, a candidate traces every iteration of a loop that builds a prefix sum over ten numbers. What is the improvement?
options: Skip the test entirely and trust the loop, since prefix sums are easy
Condense it: say what the prefix sum will look like afterwards
Trace it twice to be sure
Test only with an empty list
optionExplain: Trusting the loop gives no evidence it works.
Right: trivial parts should be condensed to save time.
A second full trace costs more time.
One edge case does not replace the walk-through.
questions.explain: The book says to condense trivial parts, such as a prefix sum, rather than walk through the for loop with every element.
questions.rule: Condense trivial steps; trace the interesting ones.

questions.q: An online assessment runs your code on hidden built-in tests. Where does the pressure land compared with a shared editor?
options: On writing tests, since none are given
On explaining the code aloud, since nothing else is checked by the platform
On your solution, since flaws are exposed and you write no tests
Equally on code and tests, since both matter
optionExplain: Built-in tests are given.
The platform checks results, not your explanation.
Right: most stress on the code, least on creating tests.
The two pressures move in opposite directions.
questions.explain: A built-in set includes small, huge and edge-case inputs, so a non-perfect solution is found out. Since the tests already exist, you write none.
questions.rule: Built-in tests stress the solution, not the tester.
questions.teaches: With built-in test cases, the environment puts the most stress on your code, because a non-perfect solution is exposed, but the least stress on creating your own tests.

questions.q: The interviewer asks for the time complexity of your solution. According to the book, which case do you state?
options: None, because complexity cannot be known without running the code
Only the best case, since it shows what your code can do at its peak
Only the average case, since it is the most likely
The worst case, plus the average if it is much faster
optionExplain: Complexity is reasoned about, not measured.
The best case is the least informative for planning.
The average hides the case that can break a system.
Right: worst-case terms, with the average as an addition.
questions.explain: Interview answers are given in worst-case terms. The card next adds the other questions to expect.
questions.rule: State the worst case.

questions.q: When you state the complexity of your algorithm, speak in terms of the ____ case.
questions.explain: The book says to speak in terms of the worst-case scenario, and to mention the average case too when it is much faster and the worst case is rare.
questions.rule: Speak in worst-case terms.

questions.q: Your structure is O(n squared) in the worst case but O(n log n) typically, and the worst case is rare. How do you answer?
options: Give only the typical case, since the worst case is rare
Give the worst case, and also mention the faster typical case
Give only the worst case, since the typical case is irrelevant
Say it depends and give no number
optionExplain: Leaving out the worst case hides a real risk.
Right: both facts, worst case first.
The book says to mention a much faster average case too.
A vague answer shows you cannot reason about cost.
questions.explain: State the worst case, and if it is rare and the average is significantly faster, mention that too.
questions.rule: Worst case first, then the average if it differs a lot.

questions.q: True or false: When asked whether your algorithm could be improved, the safest answer is to state firmly that it is already optimal.
questions.explain: The book warns against being confidently wrong. If the interviewer asks, the answer is usually yes.
questions.rule: Do not assert optimality you cannot back up.

questions.q: After your solution, the interviewer gives you an entirely new problem. Where do you restart?
options: At brainstorming, since the statement is clear
At implementation, since you already know the tools by now and can reuse them
At the problem statement: paraphrase, then ask about the input
At testing, since the earlier code is similar
optionExplain: The statement is not clear until you have checked it.
A new problem needs its own understanding first.
Right: a new problem begins from stage 2.
The new problem has no code to test yet.
questions.explain: The book says that for an entirely new question you restart from the problem statement.
questions.rule: A new problem restarts at stage 2.

questions.q: You find the largest value in an unsorted list. The interviewer asks if you can beat O(n). What do you say?
options: Probably not, since every element has to be looked at
Yes, with binary search, which takes only O(log n) comparisons on any list
Yes, by sorting first
No, because O(n) is the best any problem can do
optionExplain: Right: a problem that must look at every element cannot beat O(n).
Binary search needs sorted data, which you do not have.
Sorting costs O(n log n), which is worse.
Other problems allow better, such as O(log n).
questions.explain: The book says that if the problem must look at every element, you probably cannot do better than O(n); otherwise, probably not better than O(log n).
questions.rule: A problem that must read every element cannot beat O(n).
questions.teaches: If a problem must look at every element, you probably cannot do better than O(n); otherwise you probably cannot do better than O(log n).

questions.q: The interviewer asks if you have questions. According to the book, what is the best approach?
options: Repeat a joke from earlier to end on a light note
Say you have none, to avoid taking up more of their time
Ask how your coding answers were graded
Ask prepared questions about the work and the company
optionExplain: A joke does not use the time to learn or show interest.
No questions can read as a lack of interest.
That is not among the questions the book suggests, and it rarely helps.
Right: it shows interest and gives you information.
questions.explain: This time is for both sides. The card next lists questions worth preparing.
questions.rule: Come with questions.

questions.q: Which of these questions does the book suggest preparing? Select all that apply.
options: What does an average day look like?
Why did you decide to join this company instead of another one?
What is your favorite and least favorite thing about the job?
How much do you earn?
Did I pass the coding round?
Can I skip the rest of the interview?
optionExplain: Right: it is the first suggested question.
Right: it asks for the interviewer's own reasons.
Right: it asks for both sides of the job.
Pay is not on the book's list.
A request for a verdict is not on the list.
Nothing in the book supports leaving early.
questions.explain: The book's list includes the average day, why they joined, favourite and least favourite things, and the work to expect.
questions.rule: Ask about the work and the people.

questions.q: You have run out of prepared questions, and the interviewer is still describing their team's work. What do you do?
options: Listen and ask a follow-up about their last answer
Move on to the next topic on your prepared list of questions
Check the time and wrap up
Say you have everything you need
optionExplain: Right: follow-ups show you understood their answers.
Ignoring the answer shows you were not listening.
There is time left and you may still learn something.
That ends the conversation while they are still engaged.
questions.explain: The book asks you to be interested, keep smiling, listen and ask follow-up questions.
questions.rule: Follow up on what you hear.

questions.q: True or false: Once the technical part is over, your questions at the end cannot affect how the interviewer sees you.
questions.explain: The book says you will rarely improve the outcome at this point, but you can certainly make it worse.
questions.rule: At the end you can lose more than you can gain.

questions.q: What if the company's tech blog has a post about a decision you do not understand?
options: Use it to correct the post in front of the interviewer
Leave it out, as it may embarrass the interviewer who wrote the post
Mention that you read it but ask nothing
Turn it into a question about why they made that choice
optionExplain: That is contentious, not curious.
The book suggests asking, not avoiding.
Showing interest includes asking why.
Right: the book suggests compiling questions about the company's decisions.
questions.explain: Reading the blog and listing questions about the decisions behind it is how the book says to show interest.
questions.rule: Turn what you read into questions.

questions.q: You doubt you would enjoy the job after the interview. How does the outro help?
options: It lets you ask questions to learn if you want to work there
It does not help, since the company decides alone
It lets you hide your doubts so that the interviewer stays positive
It lets you restart the technical round
optionExplain: Right: an interview is a two-way street.
The book says you should also use the time to decide.
Hiding doubts does not help your decision.
Nothing allows a restart at this point.
questions.explain: The book says interviews are a two-way street, and the closing time is a chance to get to know the company.
questions.rule: Use the outro to decide, too.
questions.teaches: Interviews are a two-way street: use the closing time to get to know the company and see if you would like to work there.

questions.q: A loop checks whether each of n numbers has already been seen. Which collection keeps each check cheapest?
options: A hash set
An array
A linked list
A stack
optionExplain: Right: membership in a set does not scan the items.
Arrays are easy to build but need a scan to find a value.
Finding a value in a linked list means walking its nodes.
A stack only gives cheap access to its top.
questions.explain: Hashing finds an element without looking at the others. The card next lists the costs across structures.
questions.rule: Hashing makes membership cheap.

questions.q: Match each operation to its cost.
pairs: Append to the end of a dynamic array
Insert at an arbitrary array index
Check whether a key exists in a hash map
Add an element to a min-heap
questions.explain: End operations on a dynamic array are cheap on average, insertion in the middle shifts items, hashing finds keys directly, and a heap adds by moving up a tree.
questions.rule: Know which operations are cheap and which shift or scan.

questions.q: Sort each operation by its cost.

items.t: Read arr[i] in an array
Check whether a value exists in an array
Check whether a key exists in a hash map
Check whether a value exists in a hash map
Peek at the top of a stack
Reach a position in a linked list
Read the character at an index of a string
Check whether an element exists in a stack

questions.explain: Direct access by index, key or top is constant. Anything that has to look for a value, or walk a chain, scans.
questions.rule: Access by address is O(1); search by value is O(n).

questions.q: A loop runs 1,000 times, and each pass asks if a name is among 1,000 stored names. How do a set and a list compare?
options: A list takes about 1,000 steps and a set about 1,000,000
A set takes about 1,000 steps and a list about 1,000,000
Both take about 1,000 steps, since n is only 1,000
Both take about 1,000,000 steps, since each pass looks at every name
optionExplain: This reverses the two structures.
Right: a set check costs O(1), a list check O(n).
At n = 1,000 the scan per pass is still 1,000 steps.
A set does not look at every name.
questions.explain: Set: 1,000 passes times O(1) = 1,000. List: 1,000 passes times O(n) with n = 1,000 = 1,000,000.
questions.rule: Total cost is passes times cost per pass.

questions.q: True or false: Because search in a binary search tree is O(log n) on average, it is also O(log n) in the worst case.
questions.explain: The average case holds when the tree is well balanced. The worst case is a tree that is a straight line, where search is O(n).
questions.rule: A tree is only as fast as it is balanced.

questions.q: A program adds 100,000 file paths of about 200 characters each to a set. Which cost does the book's note on hashing suggest?
options: About 200 steps, since only one path is hashed
About 100,000 steps, since set operations are O(1)
About 20,000,000 steps, since each key costs its length to hash
About 100,000 times 100,000 steps, since each add scans the whole set
optionExplain: All 100,000 paths are added.
O(1) holds relative to the set's size and ignores the cost of hashing each long key.
Right: constant time is relative to the set's size, so long keys add a factor.
A set add does not scan the other items.
questions.explain: The book notes the O(1) operations are constant relative to n; with string keys, hashing costs O(m) for key length m. Here 100,000 x 200 = 20,000,000.
questions.rule: Hash costs are constant in n but not in key length.
questions.teaches: Hash map and set operations are O(1) relative to the size of the structure, but hashing a string key costs O(m) where m is the length of the key.

questions.q: A DFS visits all 50,000 nodes of a tree and does constant work at each. What is the time complexity?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n squared)
optionExplain: Right: n visits times constant work.
That would skip most nodes, but DFS visits every node.
Nothing here repeats the visit of every node for every other node.
A traversal of every node cannot be constant.
questions.explain: Visiting each node once with constant work is linear. The card next gives the general rule.
questions.rule: Visits times work per visit.

questions.q: A graph DFS or BFS takes O(n times k) plus a term for the number of ____.
questions.explain: The traversal also looks at every edge, so the number of edges is added to the node work.
questions.rule: Graph traversal adds the edges.

questions.q: A DP has 1,000 states, and each state does 20 steps of work. What is the time?
options: About 1,020 steps
About 20,000 steps
About 1 x 10^60 steps
About 1,000 steps
optionExplain: That adds the two numbers instead of multiplying them.
Right: states times work per state.
That raises 1,000 to the power of 20, which is not how DP cost works.
That ignores the 20 steps at each state.
questions.explain: DP time is the number of states times the work per state: 1,000 x 20 = 20,000.
questions.rule: States times work per state.

questions.q: A tree of 50,000 nodes now spends 26 steps at each node, looping over the alphabet. What is the total work?
options: About 50,000 steps, since the loop is constant
About 2,500,000,000 steps
About 1,300,000 steps, still linear in n
About 76 steps
optionExplain: The constant still multiplies the work, even if the class stays linear.
That squares n, but the loop runs over 26 letters, not over n.
Right: n times k with k = 26.
That adds 26 to 50 and ignores the scale.
questions.explain: Work per node is k = 26, so the total is 50,000 x 26 = 1,300,000. The class is still O(n), with a larger constant.
questions.rule: A constant k still multiplies the work.

questions.q: True or false: A BFS on a graph with 10,000 nodes and 1,000,000 edges takes about 10,000 steps, since each node is visited once.
questions.explain: Every edge is also examined, so the cost is about 10,000 plus 1,000,000 steps, which the edges dominate.
questions.rule: Edges can outnumber nodes: count them.

questions.q: A route planner runs DP over 60,000 states and stores one answer per state. How does its memory grow?
options: In proportion to the work per state
In proportion to the square of the number of states
Not at all, since DP only reuses answers
In proportion to the number of states
optionExplain: The work is time, not stored data.
One answer is stored per state, not per pair.
Reusing answers requires storing them.
Right: the book gives DP space as O(n) for n states.
questions.explain: DP space is O(n) in the number of states. The book also gives DFS and BFS space as typically O(n), or O(n + e) if the graph itself is stored.
questions.rule: DP memory follows the number of states.
