questions.teaches: DP space is O(n) for n states, and DFS or BFS space is typically O(n), but may be O(n + e) if the graph is stored.

questions.q: According to the book, a problem allows n up to 20. Which time complexity is the likely upper bound?
options: O(2 to the n)
O(log n)
O(n factorial)
O(n log n)
optionExplain: Right: about a million steps at n = 20.
That would be the target for huge inputs, not small ones.
n factorial at n = 20 is far too large.
This is possible but better than a limit this small requires.
questions.explain: Small limits allow exponential work. The card next gives the rough ladder of bounds.
questions.rule: Small n allows exponential time.

questions.q: Match each input limit to the complexity it suggests.
pairs: Factorial, or exponential with a base above 2
questions.explain: The larger the limit, the lower the power the intended solution can afford.
questions.rule: Limit up, allowed growth down.

questions.q: At n = 20, how does the step count of a 3 to the n solution compare with a 2 to the n solution?
options: About 1.5 times larger, the ratio of the two bases
About 3,325 times larger
About 20 times larger
About the same
optionExplain: That compares 3 with 2 and ignores the power of 20.
That confuses the exponent with the ratio.
A base of 3 grows much faster than a base of 2.
questions.rule: A larger base multiplies the step count enormously.

questions.q: Sort each limit by the technique it suggests.

items.t: n up to 8
n up to 18

questions.explain: Limits up to 20 suggest exhaustive recursion. Limits between about 20 and 1,000 allow nested loops.
questions.rule: Up to 20: recursion. 20 to 1,000: nested loops.

questions.q: True or false: With n up to 20, a factorial-time solution is as acceptable as one that takes 2 to the n steps.
questions.explain: 20! is about 2.4 quintillion, while 2^20 is 1,048,576. The factorial solution is far too slow at this limit.
questions.rule: At n up to 20, aim for about 2 to the n; factorial work fits only up to about n = 10.

questions.q: According to the book, an easy problem lists n up to 100 and a cubic brute force passes. What should you conclude?
options: No faster solution can exist, since the limit is small
The problem is mislabelled, since easy problems should be linear time
The limit must be wrong, since cubic is too slow at 100
A faster solution may exist; the small bound lets brute force pass
optionExplain: The small limit only means brute force is allowed.
Difficulty and complexity are separate things.
100^3 is a million steps, which is fast.
Right: easy problems often have this bound, which can mislead.
questions.explain: The book says easy problems usually have this bound, and that this can be deceiving: there may be solutions that run in O(n), but the small bound allows brute force to pass.
questions.rule: A small bound does not mean no faster solution.
questions.teaches: Problems marked easy often have n up to 100, which can be deceiving: faster solutions such as O(n) may exist, but the small bound lets brute force pass.

questions.q: A problem allows n up to 100,000. About how many steps does a nested loop over the input take?
options: About 100,000, which is fine
About 1,660,964, which is comfortably fast enough
About 10,000,000,000, which is too slow
About 100 million, which is borderline
optionExplain: That counts one pass, not two nested ones.
That is the n log n count, not a nested loop.
Right: 100,000 squared is 10 billion.
That is the count for n around 10,000.
questions.explain: Nested loops multiply n by n: 100,000 x 100,000 = 10,000,000,000. The card next lists the ways to avoid that.
questions.rule: Squaring 100,000 is too much.

questions.q: For limits up to 100,000, the slowest acceptable common time complexity is O(n times ____ n).
questions.explain: The slowest acceptable common cost is n log n, though O(n) is commonly the goal.
questions.rule: n log n is the ceiling; n is the goal.

questions.q: Which techniques can replace a nested loop when n is up to 100,000? Select all that apply.
options: Trying every subset by backtracking
A hash map
Recursion without storing answers
A monotonic stack
A second nested loop
Binary search
optionExplain: Subsets grow as 2 to the n, which is far too slow.
Right: a hash map answers lookups in O(1).
Repeating work without storing answers is slower, not faster.
Right: a monotonic stack handles comparisons with earlier items in one pass.
A further nested loop makes the cost worse.
Right: binary search cuts the range in half each step.
questions.explain: The book lists a hash map, two pointers such as sliding window, a monotonic stack, binary search and a heap as ways to simulate a nested loop quickly.
questions.rule: Replace the inner loop with a fast lookup.

questions.q: A problem asks about integers up to 1,000,000,000, so looping over them is out. What complexity does the book say is typical?
options: O(n log n), sorting all the numbers first
O(n), one pass over all the numbers
O(log n) or O(1)
O(n squared), comparing every pair of numbers
optionExplain: That is above a billion times the log.
A billion steps is too slow.
Right: halve the search space or compute the answer directly.
That is far beyond any budget at this size.
questions.explain: With huge inputs the usual acceptable cost is logarithmic or constant, using binary search or math and hash-map tricks.
questions.rule: Huge n needs log n or O(1).

questions.q: True or false: At n up to 100,000, an O(n squared) loop is acceptable if the code is well optimized.
questions.explain: The book calls nested loops that run in O(n squared) unacceptable in this range. You need a technique that simulates the inner loop in O(1) or O(log n).
questions.rule: Optimizing a quadratic loop does not rescue it at 100,000.

questions.q: A string problem has length up to 100,000, and the solution loops over the 26 letters at each position. Is that acceptable?
options: No, because any inner loop at all makes the whole cost O(n squared)
No, because the constant must be 1
Yes: about 2,600,000 steps, a constant factor that is fine
Yes, but only if the alphabet loop is replaced by a hash map
optionExplain: The inner loop runs 26 times, not n times.
The book allows a constant factor around 40.
Right: O(26n) is linear with a modest constant.
The book accepts looping over the alphabet; no replacement is needed.
questions.explain: The loop adds a factor of 26, giving 2,600,000 steps. The book says an O(n) algorithm can have a reasonably large constant factor, around 40, and names O(26n) as a common theme in string problems.
questions.rule: A constant like 26 is fine; a factor of n is not.
questions.teaches: For an O(n) algorithm the constant factor can be reasonably large, around 40, such as O(26n) from looping over the alphabet at each step.

questions.q: Your solution sorts an array of n numbers with the language's built-in sort. What cost do you state for that step?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(n squared)
O(log n)
optionExplain: Right: the usual assumption for built-in sorts.
A comparison sort cannot finish in linear time for general inputs.
Some simple sorts cost this much, but built-in sorts do not.
Sorting has to touch every element.
questions.explain: The safe assumption for a built-in sort is n log n. The card next adds what the book says about the algorithms behind it.
questions.rule: State sorting as O(n log n).

questions.q: A stable sort keeps records that have equal keys in their ____ relative order.
questions.explain: The book quotes the definition that a stable sort keeps R before S when both have the same key and R came first in the original list.
questions.rule: Stable means equal keys keep their order.

questions.q: A solution sorts 100,000 events and then makes one linear pass over them. What is the total time?
options: O(n log n), since the sort dominates
O(n), since the pass is linear
O(n squared), since both steps touch every event
O(log n), since sorting is the main step
optionExplain: Right: n log n plus n is still n log n.
The sort costs more than the pass.
Adding two costs does not multiply them.
Sorting touches every element, so it cannot be logarithmic.
questions.explain: The sort costs O(n log n) and the pass O(n). The larger term sets the total.
questions.rule: A dominant term sets the total.

questions.q: True or false: The general flowchart can tell you how to apply Dijkstra's algorithm to a shortest-path problem.
questions.explain: The flowchart covers only methods taught in the book's course, so more advanced algorithms such as Dijkstra's are excluded.
questions.rule: The flowchart is general, not complete.

questions.q: A team moves code from Python to C++ and relies on Python's sorting behaviour. What does the book say about C++?
options: It uses Timsort, as Python does, so the behaviour carries over
It always uses a stable sort
It has no built-in sort
The specific algorithm is not mandated and varies
optionExplain: The book names Timsort for Python, not for C++.
The book makes no such claim.
All major languages have a built-in method for sorting.
Right: you cannot count on Timsort's behaviour there.
questions.explain: The book says all major languages have a built-in sort, and the algorithm varies by language: Python uses Timsort, while in C++ the specific algorithm is not mandated and varies.
questions.rule: Assume the cost, not the algorithm, across languages.
questions.teaches: The sorting algorithm used varies by language: Python uses Timsort, but in C++ the specific algorithm is not mandated and varies.

questions.q: Which task is built from intervals of events on a number line?
options: Given a sorted list of prices, find the first price above a target amount
Given a text, decide whether its brackets are balanced from start to end
Given reservations as [arrive, leave, guests], find the busiest moment of a restaurant
Given a tree, find the length of the longest path from its root to a leaf
optionExplain: Nothing here is a stretch with a value; this is a search in sorted data.
Bracket checking walks one text and has no stretches carrying values.
Right: each reservation is a stretch of time with a number of guests, which is the pattern.
A tree path has no number line of events.
questions.explain: A reservation occupies a stretch of time and carries a number of guests, so the busiest moment asks about overlapping events. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: If a story says that between left and right there is value of something, think of events on a number line and reach for a difference array.

questions.q: In the usual input format [left, right, ____], the last number says how much of something the event carries.
questions.explain: Each inner array gives where the event starts, where it ends and the value it carries between those points.
questions.rule: If a story says that between left and right there is value of something, think of events on a number line and reach for a difference array.

questions.q: An irrigation plan lists watering jobs as [firstRow, lastRow, litres]. In the pattern's terms, what are the number line and the value?
options: The number line is the rows of the field and the value is the litres
The number line is the litres and the value is the last row
The number line is the list of jobs and the value is its length
The number line is the first row and the value is the last row
optionExplain: Right: positions run along the rows, and each job carries its litres between its two rows.
Litres are what each event carries, not the positions along the line.
The line is the thing the intervals sit on, not the list that holds them.
Both rows are endpoints; neither one is the value.
questions.explain: The two row numbers are left and right on the line of rows, and the litres are the value each job adds to every row it covers.
questions.rule: If a story says that between left and right there is value of something, think of events on a number line and reach for a difference array.

questions.q: Which problems fit the pattern of events on a number line, and which do not?

items.t: Bookings [arrive, depart, rooms]: find the most rooms in use at once
Roadworks [fromKm, toKm, delay]: find the slowest kilometre
Alerts [startSecond, endSecond, severity]: find when severity peaks
Find the longest increasing run in a list of daily temperatures
Count the words in a dictionary that start with a given prefix
Find the cheapest route between two cities

questions.explain: The first three each give a stretch with a value and ask about a point on the line. The others ask about runs, prefixes or routes, which are different patterns.
questions.rule: Look for stretches with values on a line.

questions.q: True or false: Any problem that gives an array of numbers can be solved with a difference array.
questions.explain: The method needs events with a start, an end and a value along a line. An array of numbers with no such stretches, such as a list to be searched, does not fit.
questions.rule: If a story says that between left and right there is value of something, think of events on a number line and reach for a difference array.

questions.q: Street lights come as [position, radius] with equal brightness. Which [left, right, value] describes a light at position 10 with radius 3?
optionExplain: That copies position and radius without turning them into endpoints.
The radius is a distance, not the brightness; brightness is the same for every light.
That swaps the sign: the light spreads out to both sides of 10, not between 3 and 10.
Right: left is 10 - 3 = 7, right is 10 + 3 = 13, and every light has the same brightness, 1.
questions.explain: An equivalent form: when brightness is not mentioned every light carries value 1, left is position - radius and right is position + radius.
questions.rule: If a story says that between left and right there is value of something, think of events on a number line and reach for a difference array.
questions.teaches: An equivalent input form can be computed: for lights given as [position, radius] with no stated brightness, value is 1, left is position - radius and right is position + radius.

questions.q: Two passengers ride from stop 3 to stop 7. Which pair of array updates lets a running total show who is aboard at each stop?
options: Add 2 at index 7 and subtract 2 at index 3
Add 2 at index 3 and subtract 2 at index 7
Add 2 at index 3 and add 2 at index 7
Add 2 at index 3 and make no other update
optionExplain: Reversed, the total would go negative before stop 7 and then rise.
Right: the total rises when they board and falls when they leave.
Adding at both ends would raise the total again at stop 7 instead of lowering it.
Without a decrease the two passengers would stay aboard for the rest of the road.
questions.explain: A running total rises at boarding and falls at drop-off, so the update at the end is a subtraction. The card next shows the whole method.
questions.rule: Add the value at left, subtract it at right, and a prefix sum over the array gives the amount at every point.

questions.q: The road array is created with length farthest + ____, so that index farthest exists.
questions.explain: Indexes run from 0 to farthest, which takes farthest + 1 cells.
questions.rule: Add the value at left, subtract it at right, and a prefix sum over the array gives the amount at every point.

questions.q: Trips [people, from, to] are [2, 1, 5] and [3, 3, 7]. The largest running total over the array is ____.
questions.explain: arr becomes [0, 2, 0, 3, 0, -2, 0, -3]. Its running totals are 0, 2, 2, 5, 5, 3, 3, 0, so the peak is 5. With capacity 4 the answer is False.
questions.rule: Add the value at left, subtract it at right, and a prefix sum over the array gives the amount at every point.

questions.q: A road has trips with the farthest drop-off at 50,000, and there are 1,000 trips. About how many steps does the build-and-walk method take?
options: About 50,000,000, which is n times m
About 51,001, which is n plus m
About 9,966, which is n log n
About 1,000, which is n
optionExplain: That would be the cost of adding every trip to every stop it covers, which the method avoids.
Right: 1,000 updates plus a walk over 50,001 cells is about 51,001 steps.
That is the cost of sorting the trips; this method does not sort.
The walk over the road array also counts, so the cost is not only the number of trips.
questions.explain: The updates cost O(n) and the walk over the array costs O(m), so the total is O(n + m).
questions.rule: Add the value at left, subtract it at right, and a prefix sum over the array gives the amount at every point.

questions.q: True or false: With subtraction at arr[to + 1], trips [2, 1, 5] and [3, 5, 7] show a load of 3 at stop 5.
questions.explain: Her version drops the first group one stop late, so stop 5 shows 2 + 3 = 5 instead of the correct 3. In car pooling the passengers get off at to, so the subtraction belongs at arr[to].
questions.rule: Add the value at left, subtract it at right, and a prefix sum over the array gives the amount at every point.

questions.q: A hotel logs 40 bookings as [checkIn, checkOut, rooms] over 365 days. Compared with sorting the bookings, what does the array method cost?
options: O(40 log 40), because the array must be sorted before the walk
O(40 x 365), because each booking is added to every night
O(365 log 365), because the nights are sorted into order
O(40 + 365) rather than O(40 log 40), and no sort is needed
optionExplain: That is the cost of the sorting approach, which the array replaces.
That is the cost of adding each booking to each night, which the subtraction trick avoids.
The nights are already in order as array indexes, so nothing sorts them.
Right: the array method has no sort; it does a pass over the bookings and a pass over the 365 nights.
questions.explain: Without the array method, the course says, the trips would have to be sorted, which costs O(n log n). The array trades that for O(n + m).
questions.rule: Add the value at left, subtract it at right, and a prefix sum over the array gives the amount at every point.
questions.teaches: Without the difference array the trips would have to be sorted, which gives a time complexity of O(n log n) instead of O(n + m).

questions.q: Street lights sit at positions up to 10^18. Which approach can still find the brightest spot?
options: Record only each light's start and end, sort them, and walk through with a running total
Make an array with one cell per position and add each light to its cells
Check every position from 0 up to 10^18 and count the lights there
Sort the lights by radius and report the position of the widest light
optionExplain: Right: only the endpoints matter, so the work depends on the number of lights.
That array would need 10^18 cells, far too large to store.
Counting at 10^18 positions would never finish.
The widest light is not necessarily where the most lights overlap.
questions.explain: Only the starts and ends of the lights change the brightness, so working with only those points avoids the huge line. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: When positions are too large to build, sort change records and walk them with a running total; the constraints decide which version to use.

questions.q: With equal brightness, each light's entry record carries the value ____.
questions.explain: The brightness goes up by 1 where a light starts shining and down by 1 after it stops.
questions.rule: When positions are too large to build, sort change records and walk them with a running total; the constraints decide which version to use.

questions.q: Lights are [5, 2] and [8, 1]. The records sort to (3, +1), (7, +1), (8, -1), (10, -1). Which position does the walk return?
options: 3, where the first light begins
8, where the first light's records end
7, where the running total first reaches 2
5, the position of the first light
optionExplain: At 3 the total is only 1.
At 8 the total has dropped back to 1.
Right: the totals are 1, 2, 1, 0 and the first time it reaches 2 is at position 7.
The position of a light is not necessarily the brightest point; the first light covers 3 to 7.
questions.explain: The running totals along the sorted records are 1 at 3, 2 at 7, 1 at 8 and 0 at 10. The best total is 2 and it is reached first at 7.
questions.rule: When positions are too large to build, sort change records and walk them with a running total; the constraints decide which version to use.

questions.q: Which workload calls for sorting change records rather than building an array of positions?
options: 12 events with positions up to 100
500 events with positions up to 2,000
5,000 events with positions up to 50,000
12 events with positions up to 10^15
optionExplain: A line of 100 cells is tiny, so the array version is fine.
An array of 2,000 cells is small, and the array version is cheaper than a sort.
50,000 cells fit easily in memory.
Right: an array of 10^15 cells cannot be built, but 24 records are easily sorted.
questions.explain: The choice depends on the constraints: the array version needs room for the whole line, the sorted version only for the events.
questions.rule: When positions are too large to build, sort change records and walk them with a running total; the constraints decide which version to use.

questions.q: True or false: With exit records at position + radius, not + 1, lights [5, 2] and [8, 1] still peak at 2.
questions.explain: Light 1 shines on 3 to 7, so its exit record belongs at 8. At 7 the tie sorts the exit before the new light's entry, the total never passes 1, and the walk reports 1. The course's code uses position + radius + 1.
questions.rule: When positions are too large to build, sort change records and walk them with a running total; the constraints decide which version to use.

questions.q: A log has records (50, +3) and (50, -2) at the same position. In the course's code, which is processed first when sorting?
options: (50, -2), because ties are broken by the smaller value
(50, +3), because larger changes are applied first
(50, +3), because entries are processed before exits
Either; the order of tied records never affects the result
optionExplain: Right: the comparator orders by position, then by value, so exits come before entries at a tie.
The comparator sorts by ascending value, not descending.
Entries have the larger value, so ascending order places them after exits.
Order among tied records can change the answer, as the previous question showed, so it is not arbitrary.
questions.explain: The code sorts by position and, on equal positions, by value, so a subtraction comes before an addition.
questions.rule: When positions are too large to build, sort change records and walk them with a running total; the constraints decide which version to use.
questions.teaches: When two change records share a position, the course's comparator orders them by value, so a decrease (exit) is processed before an increase (entry).

questions.q: Words car, cart and cat are stored in a tree with one letter per node, sharing beginnings. How many nodes, not counting the root?
optionExplain: 10 counts every letter of every word, with no sharing.
3 would be the letters of a single word.
Right: c, a and r form the path of car; cart adds a t below r; cat adds a t below a.
8 shares only the first letter c, but the three words share the a as well.
questions.explain: Sharing the beginning c-a gives 5 nodes: c, a, r, t below r, and t below a. The card next names this structure.
questions.rule: A trie is a tree in which each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that start alike share nodes.

questions.q: The root of a trie stands for the ____ string.
questions.explain: A path of zero characters spells the empty string, and every other node extends it by one character.
questions.rule: A trie is a tree in which each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that start alike share nodes.

questions.q: A trie stores the words tea, ten, to, inn and in, one character per node. How many nodes does it have, not counting the root?
optionExplain: Right: t, e, a, n (below te), o, i, n (below i), n (below in) gives 8 nodes.
13 is the number of letters in the words with no sharing.
6 counts the distinct letters t, e, a, n, o and i, but the letter n appears as separate nodes at three places.
10 gives in its own two nodes, although inn already passes through i and n.
questions.explain: Count a new node only where a word leaves the paths already present: tea gives 3, ten adds 1, to adds 1, inn adds 3 and in adds 0, which is 8.
questions.rule: A trie is a tree in which each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that start alike share nodes.

questions.q: A million words are stored in a trie. Which question is it best suited to answer?
options: Which two words are anagrams of each other?
Which word has the largest sum of its letter codes?
Which words end with the letters typed so far?
Which words begin with the letters typed so far?
optionExplain: Anagrams share letters, not beginnings, so the paths do not group them.
A sum of letter codes is not a prefix property.
Words with the same ending sit on different paths from the root.
Right: all those words lie below one node, reached by walking the typed letters.
questions.explain: A trie groups words by shared beginnings, so prefix questions are its strength.
questions.rule: A trie is a tree in which each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that start alike share nodes.

questions.q: True or false: A trie holding car and cat stores the letters c and a twice, once for each word.
questions.explain: The two words share the path c, a. Only the last letters, r and t, need separate nodes below the shared a.
questions.rule: A trie is a tree in which each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that start alike share nodes.

questions.q: A phone suggests contact names as the user types m, then a, then r. When the r arrives, what does a trie-based design do?
options: It starts again from the root and re-walks m, a and r
It moves one step from the node for ma to that node's child r
It adds the prefix mar to the trie as a new word
It scans the whole contact list for names containing mar
optionExplain: Restarting works but repeats steps that the tree already holds in place.
Right: the walk is kept, so each new character costs one step down the tree.
Typing is a query; it does not change the stored words.
Scanning the list is what the trie avoids.
questions.explain: Typed characters arrive as a stream, and the trie follows them one step at a time, so tracking the words that start with them costs one step per character.
questions.rule: A trie is a tree in which each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that start alike share nodes.
questions.teaches: A trie can follow a stream of typed characters: each new character is a single step from the current node to a child, which keeps track of the words that have the typed characters as a prefix.

questions.q: While inserting a word into a trie, the walk reaches a character that the current node has no child for. What should happen?
options: The word is rejected because the trie cannot grow
A new child node is created for it, and the walk steps into it
The walk returns to the root and the character is skipped
The walk stops and the rest of the word is stored as one string
optionExplain: A trie grows with every new word, so there is no rejection.
Right: missing children are created as the walk goes along.
Skipping the character would store a different word.
A trie holds one character per node, so the rest is not kept as one string.
questions.explain: Insertion creates the missing child and moves into it, so the path of the word always exists afterwards. The card next shows the loop.
questions.rule: To build a trie, walk each word from the root, creating a child only where one is missing.

questions.q: Building a trie costs O(n * k), where k is the ____ length of the words.
questions.explain: The course gives n as the number of words and k as the average length of a word; n * k is about the total number of characters.
questions.rule: To build a trie, walk each word from the root, creating a child only where one is missing.

questions.q: A trie already holds tea. Put the steps of inserting to into it in order.
items: See that t has no child o, so create one
Step into the new node o
questions.explain: t exists from tea, so the walk follows it. The child o is missing below t, so it is created and the walk steps into it.
questions.rule: To build a trie, walk each word from the root, creating a child only where one is missing.

questions.q: A trie holds tea and ten. How many new nodes does inserting team create?
optionExplain: Two would also create a node for a, which already exists below te.
Three would rebuild the whole path t, e, a.
Four would create a fresh node for every letter of team.
Right: t, e and a already exist, so only m is new.
questions.explain: Only the letters after the longest existing prefix tea create nodes, so team adds only m.
questions.rule: To build a trie, walk each word from the root, creating a child only where one is missing.

questions.q: A student's loop steps into a child only when it already existed, not after creating it. What does inserting ab into an empty trie produce?
options: The root gets two children, a and b, side by side
A path a then b below it, which is correct
Only the node a, because b is never reached
Nothing, because the loop throws an error
optionExplain: Right: after creating a, the walk stays at the root, so b is created as another child of the root.
That is the intended result, but this loop does not produce it.
The loop still looks at b; it checks the wrong node.
Nothing in the loop raises an error; it produces a wrong shape.
questions.explain: Stepping into the child must happen whether the child was found or newly created, or the walk never goes deeper than the root.
questions.rule: To build a trie, walk each word from the root, creating a child only where one is missing.

questions.q: A spell checker needs only the tree of prefixes and stores no data at nodes. Does it need a node class?
options: Yes: a trie cannot be built without a class for its nodes
No: arrays of 26 letters must replace hash maps instead
No: nested hash maps are enough, and a class is useful only to store data at each node
Yes: a class is the only way to record the children of a node
optionExplain: The tree is only children by character, which a hash map holds.
Arrays are another choice, but the course's template uses hash maps.
Right: a hash map from character to child map holds the tree on its own.
Hash maps hold children without a class.
questions.explain: The course notes that a class is only necessary if you want to store data at each node; otherwise a trie can be implemented using only hash maps.
questions.rule: To build a trie, walk each word from the root, creating a child only where one is missing.
questions.teaches: A class for trie nodes is only necessary to store data at each node; otherwise a trie can be implemented using only hash maps.

questions.q: A shop wants suggestions after every typed letter of a search word, from a list of 10,000 products. Which plan does the least repeated work?
options: Scan all 10,000 products again after every typed letter
Sort the product list again after every typed letter
Build a new tree from all products after every typed letter
Build a tree of prefixes once, then step down it as letters arrive
optionExplain: That repeats a full scan for each prefix.
Sorting does not give prefix matches and repeats work.
Rebuilding for each letter repeats the whole build.
Right: the products are processed once and each letter then costs one step.
questions.explain: A structure built once can serve every later prefix, which avoids repeated scans. The card next shows the costs.
questions.rule: A trie pays O(n * k) once and then answers each prefix in a step, which beats rescanning all products for each prefix.

questions.q: Once the trie is built, finding the matches for a whole search word of length m takes O(____) steps.
questions.explain: Each of the m characters is one step down the tree.
questions.rule: A trie pays O(n * k) once and then answers each prefix in a step, which beats rescanning all products for each prefix.

questions.q: A trie is built from 10,000 products of average length 10. The search word has 8 letters. About how many steps for n * k + m?
options: About 100,008
About 80,000
About 640,000
About 10,018
optionExplain: That is n * m, which mixes up the search word length with the product length.
That is n * m * m, the brute force cost, not the trie cost.
That adds n, k and m instead of multiplying n by k.
questions.explain: The build costs n * k and the walk costs m, which is 100,000 + 8 steps.
questions.rule: A trie pays O(n * k) once and then answers each prefix in a step, which beats rescanning all products for each prefix.

questions.q: A library catalogue with n titles checks every title against each of the m prefixes of a typed query. According to the course, what is that brute force time?
options: O(n + m)
O(n * m)
optionExplain: That is far smaller than checking every title for every prefix.
Right: n titles times m prefixes, each comparison up to m characters long, gives O(n * m^2).
That counts each title once per prefix but ignores the length of each comparison.
This leaves out n, the number of titles.
questions.explain: The course gives O(n * m^2) for the brute force, which the trie's O(n * k + m) beats because k is small.
questions.rule: A trie pays O(n * k) once and then answers each prefix in a step, which beats rescanning all products for each prefix.
questions.teaches: The brute force of comparing every product with every prefix has a time complexity of O(n * m^2), where n is the number of products and m is the length of the search word.

questions.q: The search word grows from 8 to 16 letters, with 10,000 products and average length 10. How do the two costs change?
options: Both grow about twice, to 1,280,000 and 200,016
Brute force stays at 640,000; the trie grows to 400,064
Brute force grows about four times, to 2,560,000; the trie to 100,016
Both stay the same, because the products have not changed
optionExplain: Doubling m doubles only a cost that is linear in m; n * m^2 is quadratic in m.
Brute force depends on m, and the trie's cost does not grow fourfold.
Right: n * m^2 grows with the square of m, while n * k + m changes only by the extra letters.
The search word is part of both costs, so changing it changes them.
questions.explain: Doubling m multiplies n * m^2 by 4, from 640,000 to 2,560,000, but adds only 8 to n * k + m.
questions.rule: A trie pays O(n * k) once and then answers each prefix in a step, which beats rescanning all products for each prefix.

questions.q: True or false: To get suggestions for each prefix of the search word, the trie must be rebuilt from the products once per prefix.
questions.explain: The trie is built once. The prefixes of the search word are then read by walking the existing tree.
questions.rule: A trie pays O(n * k) once and then answers each prefix in a step, which beats rescanning all products for each prefix.

questions.q: A search box must show the three alphabetically smallest products for the prefix typed so far. Where could those three be kept so each prefix is answered quickly?
options: In one sorted list of all products that is scanned for every prefix
In a hash set of all products, with the prefix as a key
In a short list stored at the tree node for that prefix
At the root only, in a list that is rebuilt for every prefix
optionExplain: Scanning the full list for each prefix is the slow brute force.
A set of products cannot answer which three come first for a prefix.
Right: the node for a prefix is reached in one step and can hold its answer ready.
Rebuilding at the root repeats the work for every prefix.
questions.explain: Every prefix has its own node, so each node can hold its own three answers. The card next shows how they are kept.
questions.rule: Keep a sorted list of at most three products at every trie node, and each prefix is answered by one step down the tree.

questions.q: Each trie node keeps at most ____ suggestions.
questions.explain: The problem asks for at most three products per prefix, so the lists never grow beyond three.
questions.rule: Keep a sorted list of at most three products at every trie node, and each prefix is answered by one step down the tree.

questions.q: Products are bag, baggage, banner, box and cat. What does the node for the prefix ba hold?
options: bag, baggage, banner
bag, baggage, banner, box
bag, baggage
banner, box, cat
optionExplain: Right: bag, baggage and banner start with ba, and all three fit under the cap.
box does not start with ba, so it is not on the path of ba.
banner starts with ba too; only the path bag has two products.
cat and box do not start with ba.
questions.explain: Three products begin with ba and they sort as bag, baggage, banner.
questions.rule: Keep a sorted list of at most three products at every trie node, and each prefix is answered by one step down the tree.

questions.q: A trie is built from 2,000 products of average length 6, with each node keeping at most three suggestions. About how much work is the build?
options: About 2,000 node updates, one per product
About 12,000 node updates, each sorting up to 2,000 strings
About 4,000,000 node updates, one per pair of products
About 12,000 node updates, each sorting at most four short strings
optionExplain: Each product touches a node for every one of its letters, not only one.
The cap keeps each list at about three or four strings.
The build visits each product's own path, not every pair of products.
Right: each product touches about 6 nodes, and each node's list is tiny.
questions.explain: 2,000 products times 6 letters is 12,000 updates, and sorting four strings at each is cheap.
questions.rule: Keep a sorted list of at most three products at every trie node, and each prefix is answered by one step down the tree.

questions.q: True or false: Sorting each node's suggestions costs O(p log p) for p matching products, so the build is much slower than O(n * k).
questions.explain: The list never holds more than three or four entries, so each sort takes constant time and the build stays close to O(n * k).
questions.rule: Keep a sorted list of at most three products at every trie node, and each prefix is answered by one step down the tree.

questions.q: With products as before, the search word is bagsx. The prefix bags has no matching node. What are the answers for bags and for bagsx?
options: An empty list for bags, then bag and baggage for bagsx
An empty list for each of the two prefixes
The suggestions of bag for both prefixes
An empty list for bags, then the three smallest products for bagsx
optionExplain: A longer prefix cannot match when a shorter prefix of it has no match.
Right: once a letter has no child, no longer prefix can match either.
Reusing the answer of bag would suggest products that do not start with bags.
The three smallest products do not start with bagsx.
questions.explain: After a dead end, every later prefix also gets an empty list: the course's code keeps returning empty lists from that point.
questions.rule: Keep a sorted list of at most three products at every trie node, and each prefix is answered by one step down the tree.
questions.teaches: After a letter with no child (a dead end), every later prefix of the search word also gets an empty list of suggestions.

questions.q: The binary numbers 1100 and 1010 are combined with AND. What is the result?
optionExplain: 1110 is the OR of the two numbers.
Right: only the leftmost place has a 1 in both numbers.
0110 is the XOR of the two numbers.
The numbers do share a 1 in the leftmost place, so the result is not all zeros.
questions.explain: AND is 1 only where both numbers have a 1, which is the leftmost place only. The card next states the rules for AND, OR and XOR.
questions.rule: OR keeps a 1 if any input is 1, AND needs all inputs to be 1, XOR needs an odd count of 1s, and a shift multiplies or floor-divides by 2.

questions.q: Match each operation to its rule for combining bits.
pairs: Result is 1 if any bit is 1
Result is 1 only if all bits are 1
Result is 1 if the number of 1 bits is odd
questions.explain: These are the course's three rules. They differ for inputs such as 1 and 1: OR gives 1, AND gives 1 and XOR gives 0.
questions.rule: OR keeps a 1 if any input is 1, AND needs all inputs to be 1, XOR needs an odd count of 1s, and a shift multiplies or floor-divides by 2.

questions.q: With x = 13 (1101) and y = 6 (0110), what is x ^ y?
optionExplain: 15 is x | y, where any 1 gives a 1.
4 is x & y, where both bits must be 1.
26 is x << 1, a shift of one place.
Right: 1101 XOR 0110 is 1011, which is 11.
questions.explain: Compare place by place: 1 and 0 give 1, 1 and 1 give 0, 0 and 1 give 1, 1 and 0 give 1, so 1011 = 11.
questions.rule: OR keeps a 1 if any input is 1, AND needs all inputs to be 1, XOR needs an odd count of 1s, and a shift multiplies or floor-divides by 2.

questions.q: A value n = 45 is shifted left by one place and also shifted right by one place. What are the two results?
options: 90 and 22
90 and 23
22 and 90
47 and 22
optionExplain: Right: left shift doubles to 90, and right shift floors 22.5 to 22.
A right shift floors; it does not round 22.5 up.
The two directions are swapped.
A left shift multiplies by 2; it does not add 2.
questions.explain: Left shift is multiplication by 2 and right shift is floor division by 2, so 45 gives 90 and 22.
questions.rule: OR keeps a 1 if any input is 1, AND needs all inputs to be 1, XOR needs an odd count of 1s, and a shift multiplies or floor-divides by 2.

questions.q: True or false: XOR of the three bits 1, 1 and 1 is 0, because equal bits cancel.
questions.explain: XOR gives 1 when the number of 1 bits is odd. Three 1s is an odd count, so the result is 1; only an even count gives 0.
questions.rule: OR keeps a 1 if any input is 1, AND needs all inputs to be 1, XOR needs an odd count of 1s, and a shift multiplies or floor-divides by 2.

questions.q: Panels A = 1010 and B = 0110 each mark which of four switches are on. Which result marks the switches that are on in exactly one panel?
options: 1110, which is A OR B
0010, which is A AND B
1100, which is A XOR B
1010, which is A alone
optionExplain: OR also marks the switch that is on in both panels.
AND marks only the switch that is on in both panels.
Right: XOR gives 1 where the two panels differ.
A alone ignores panel B.
questions.explain: The operation is applied to every bit position separately, so each switch is decided only by its own two bits: XOR is 1 exactly when they differ.
questions.rule: OR keeps a 1 if any input is 1, AND needs all inputs to be 1, XOR needs an odd count of 1s, and a shift multiplies or floor-divides by 2.
questions.teaches: A bit operation is applied on every bit separately: each result bit depends only on the two input bits in its own position.

questions.q: For x = 13 (1101), which operation with 0100 shows whether the bit worth 4 is set?
options: OR, then check whether the result is zero
XOR, then check whether the result equals x
Right shift by 4, then check whether the result is odd
AND, then check whether the result is non-zero
optionExplain: OR with a mask can only set bits, so the result is never zero here.
XOR changes the bit instead of reporting it.
Shifting right by 4 throws away that bit rather than testing it.
Right: AND keeps only that bit, so a non-zero result means it is set.
questions.explain: AND with 0100 keeps only the bit worth 4. The card next explains why and how to build the mask.
questions.rule: Build mask = 1 << i, then x & mask tells whether bit i is set and x ^ mask flips it.

questions.q: To reach bit i, the mask is 1 shifted left by ____ places.
questions.explain: Shifting 1 left i places puts the single 1 in position i, counted from 0 at the right.
questions.rule: Build mask = 1 << i, then x & mask tells whether bit i is set and x ^ mask flips it.

questions.q: x = 13 (1101) and mask = 1 << 2. What is x ^ mask?
optionExplain: Right: flipping the bit worth 4 turns 1101 into 1001, which is 9.
4 is x & mask, the test result.
17 would add 4 instead of flipping a bit that is already set.
13 would result if nothing had changed.
questions.explain: Bit 2 of 13 is set, so XOR clears it: 1101 becomes 1001 = 9, and the other bits stay the same.
questions.rule: Build mask = 1 << i, then x & mask tells whether bit i is set and x ^ mask flips it.

questions.q: A smart-home flag word keeps the porch light in bit 3. Which expression turns the light on if it is off and off if it is on?
options: flags & (1 << 3)
flags ^ (1 << 3)
flags >> 3
flags << 3
optionExplain: AND only reports the light's state and clears the other flags.
Right: XOR flips only bit 3.
A right shift moves all flags and discards some.
A left shift moves every flag to a different place.
questions.explain: The mask 1 << 3 has a single 1 in bit 3, and XOR with it flips that bit and nothing else.
questions.rule: Build mask = 1 << i, then x & mask tells whether bit i is set and x ^ mask flips it.

questions.q: True or false: For x = 13 and i = 2, the test (x & (1 << i)) == 1 correctly reports that bit 2 is set.
questions.explain: The AND gives 4, not 1, so the comparison with 1 fails although the bit is set. The test must compare with zero.
questions.rule: Build mask = 1 << i, then x & mask tells whether bit i is set and x ^ mask flips it.

questions.q: To flip bits 1 and 3 together, a mask of 1010 is used with XOR on x = 0101. What is the result?
optionExplain: 0000 would need every bit of x to flip.
1010 is the mask itself, not the combined result.
Right: every place where the mask has 1 is flipped, and the places with 0 are unchanged.
0101 is x unchanged, which is what the mask would do if all its bits were 0.
questions.explain: XOR with 0 leaves a bit unchanged and XOR with 1 flips it, so a mask with several 1s flips several bits at once.
questions.rule: Build mask = 1 << i, then x & mask tells whether bit i is set and x ^ mask flips it.
questions.teaches: Mask arithmetic: x XOR 0 leaves a bit unchanged and x XOR 1 flips it, so a mask with several 1s flips several chosen bits in one operation.

questions.q: What is 9 XOR 9?
optionExplain: Right: every bit of the two copies matches, so every result bit is 0.
9 would be the result of XOR with 0, not with itself.
18 is a sum, but XOR does not add.
1 is not the result because no bit position gives an odd count of 1s.
questions.explain: Two equal bits always give 0 under XOR (the count of 1s is 0 or 2, which is even). The card next states this property.
questions.rule: x XOR x is 0 and 0 XOR y is y, so equal numbers cancel out of an XOR.

questions.q: For any number x, x XOR x equals ____.
questions.explain: Each bit appears twice, so the count of 1s is even and the result is 0.
questions.rule: x XOR x is 0 and 0 XOR y is y, so equal numbers cancel out of an XOR.

questions.q: 6 XOR 3 XOR 6 equals ____.
questions.explain: The two 6s cancel to 0, and 0 XOR 3 is 3. In binary: 110 XOR 011 = 101, and 101 XOR 110 = 011.
questions.rule: x XOR x is 0 and 0 XOR y is y, so equal numbers cancel out of an XOR.

questions.q: The array [4, 7, 4, 9, 7] is XORed from left to right. What is the result?
optionExplain: 0 would need 9 to be paired as well.
31 is the sum of the numbers; XOR does not add.
Right: the 4s cancel, the 7s cancel, and only 9 remains.
4 is paired, so it cancels.
questions.explain: 4 XOR 4 = 0 and 7 XOR 7 = 0, whatever their positions, which leaves 0 XOR 9 = 9.
questions.rule: x XOR x is 0 and 0 XOR y is y, so equal numbers cancel out of an XOR.

questions.q: True or false: A number that appears three times in an array also vanishes when all numbers are XORed together.
questions.explain: Two of its three copies cancel, but the third remains. Only a number that appears an even number of times vanishes.
questions.rule: x XOR x is 0 and 0 XOR y is y, so equal numbers cancel out of an XOR.

questions.q: The array [2, 8, 2] is XORed as (2 XOR 8) XOR 2. Why is the result 8, when the two 2s are not adjacent?
options: XOR only compares neighbours, so 2 and 8 are cancelled first
The order of XORs is irrelevant, so the 2s can be paired anyway
XOR gives 8 because 8 is the largest number in the array
The result is not 8; the 2s must be adjacent to cancel
optionExplain: XOR does not work on neighbours only.
Right: the same answer comes out whatever the order, so equal numbers always cancel.
Size has nothing to do with it; the result is the leftover number.
Adjacency does not matter.
questions.explain: The course notes that the order in which you perform the XORs is irrelevant, which is why the pairs cancel wherever they sit.
questions.rule: x XOR x is 0 and 0 XOR y is y, so equal numbers cancel out of an XOR.
questions.teaches: The order in which XORs are performed is irrelevant, so equal numbers cancel even when they are not adjacent.

questions.q: In [4, 1, 2, 1, 2] every value appears twice except one. Which method finds the lone value using only a single extra variable?
options: Count each value in a hash map
Sort the array and compare neighbours
Add all the numbers and divide by two
XOR all the numbers into one variable
optionExplain: A hash map needs space for the counts.
Sorting works but takes more time, and the space depends on the language.
A sum does not separate the lone value from the pairs.
Right: pairs cancel under XOR, which needs only one variable.
questions.explain: XOR needs only one variable, which the card next explains.
questions.rule: XOR every number together: the pairs cancel and the one unpaired number is left.

questions.q: XORing all of [4, 1, 2, 1, 2] gives ____.
questions.explain: The two 1s cancel, the two 2s cancel, and 4 remains.
questions.rule: XOR every number together: the pairs cancel and the one unpaired number is left.

questions.q: Which method for Single Number takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
options: Count occurrences in a hash map
Sort first, then scan for the unpaired value
XOR every number into a variable
Keep a set and add or remove each number
optionExplain: A hash map needs O(n) space for its counts.
Sorting takes O(n log n) time.
Right: one pass and one variable.
The set can grow up to O(n) space.
questions.explain: XOR is the only method listed that uses a single variable and one pass.
questions.rule: XOR every number together: the pairs cancel and the one unpaired number is left.

questions.q: Each ticket is scanned in and out, except one scanned in only: [101, 205, 101, 330, 205]. What does the XOR method return?
optionExplain: Right: both 101s cancel and both 205s cancel, leaving 330.
0 is what would be left if 330 were paired too.
101 appears twice, so it cancels.
205 appears twice, so it cancels.
questions.explain: The ticket that appears once is the one that is left after the pairs cancel.
questions.rule: XOR every number together: the pairs cancel and the one unpaired number is left.

questions.q: True or false: The XOR method works only after the array has been sorted, so that equal numbers are next to each other.
questions.explain: The order of the XORs is irrelevant, so no sorting is needed. Sorting would only add O(n log n) time.
questions.rule: XOR every number together: the pairs cancel and the one unpaired number is left.

questions.q: In an array every value appears twice, except one that appears three times. What does XORing all the numbers return?
options: 0, since every value has a partner
The sum of the values that appear twice
The value that appears twice and is largest
The value that appears three times
optionExplain: There is no partner for the third copy.
XOR does not sum values.
Pairs always cancel regardless of size.
Right: two of its copies cancel and one remains.
questions.explain: The number the method finds is the one that appears an odd number of times. The course adds that this approach is faster in practice than the hash map, because integer and bit operations are extremely fast while a hash map has overhead.
questions.rule: XOR every number together: the pairs cancel and the one unpaired number is left.
questions.teaches: XOR leaves the value that appears an odd number of times; in practice this approach is even faster than a hash map, because bit operations are extremely fast and a hash map has overhead.

questions.q: A DP needs to memoize on the set of array items already used. Why can't a list of booleans be the memo key?
options: A list is too short to hold all the items
A list of booleans cannot be hashed
A list of booleans is slower to read than any other key
Memo keys must be numbers between 0 and 255
optionExplain: Length is not the problem.
Right: a hash table needs a hashable key, and mutable arrays are not hashable.
Reading speed is not the reason; hashing is.
Keys can be any hashable value.
questions.explain: Memoization stores answers in a hash table, so its keys must be hashable. The card next shows what is used instead.
questions.rule: Store used items as bits of an integer: XOR marks and unmarks, AND tests, and the integer can be a memo key.

questions.q: In a visited mask, bit i is 1 when item i has been ____.
questions.explain: The mask is a set of used items written as bits.
questions.rule: Store used items as bits of an integer: XOR marks and unmarks, AND tests, and the integer can be a memo key.

questions.q: Starting from mask 0, items 0, 3 and 5 are marked with XOR. What integer is the mask?
optionExplain: 8 adds the bit numbers 0, 3 and 5; the mask adds the values 1, 8 and 32 instead.
40 leaves out item 0, which adds 1.
9 stops after items 0 and 3.
questions.explain: Item 0 adds 1, item 3 adds 8 and item 5 adds 32, so the mask is 41.
questions.rule: Store used items as bits of an integer: XOR marks and unmarks, AND tests, and the integer can be a memo key.

questions.q: A DP picks from 12 tasks, each used at most once, with a mask as the state. How many different masks can occur?
optionExplain: 12 would count one mask per task, but any combination of tasks is a mask.
144 is 12 squared, which counts pairs, not subsets.
24 is twice the number of tasks.
Right: each of the 12 bits is 0 or 1, giving 2^12 = 4,096 masks.
questions.explain: Every subset of the 12 tasks has its own mask, and there are 2^12 subsets.
questions.rule: Store used items as bits of an integer: XOR marks and unmarks, AND tests, and the integer can be a memo key.

questions.q: True or false: Marking item 2 twice with XOR leaves item 2 marked.
questions.explain: The second XOR flips the bit back to 0, so item 2 is unmarked again. The same operation undoes itself.
questions.rule: Store used items as bits of an integer: XOR marks and unmarks, AND tests, and the integer can be a memo key.

questions.q: A tuple of booleans can be hashed too. Why does the course still prefer a mask for tracking used items in DP?
options: Changing a tuple at each state change is expensive and untidy, whereas an integer is cheap to update
Tuples cannot be hashed in any language, so they cannot serve as memo keys
A tuple needs more memory than the whole input, so it cannot be stored
A mask lets several items share one bit, which saves space in the state
optionExplain: Right: tuples can be hashed, but each change builds a new tuple and the code gets messy.
Tuples can be hashed; that is the point of the comparison.
The cost is in the modification, not in a fixed memory size.
Each item has its own bit.
questions.explain: The course says tuples can be hashed, but modifying a tuple on each state change is expensive and not clean, so a bitmask is the best option.
questions.rule: Store used items as bits of an integer: XOR marks and unmarks, AND tests, and the integer can be a memo key.
questions.teaches: Tuples are hashable too, but modifying a tuple on every state change is expensive and not clean, which is why a bitmask is the best option.

questions.q: N-Queens II used three sets before. How many integers replace them in the bitmask version?
options: One: a single integer holds every attacked square
Two: one for rows and one for columns
Three: one for columns, one for diagonals, one for anti-diagonals
Eight: one integer for each queen
optionExplain: One integer would have to mix the three kinds of line, which the course keeps separate.
Rows do not need tracking because the search places one queen per row.
Right: the same three kinds of line are tracked, but as bits.
The integers track lines, not queens.
questions.explain: The three sets become three integers. The card next shows the masks.
questions.rule: Track columns and both diagonals as bits of three integers, test with AND, and place or remove a queen with XOR.

questions.q: In the bitmask version, a square is attacked when any of the three AND tests is what?
options: Zero
Equal to 1
Equal to the queen count
Non-zero
optionExplain: Zero means the line is free.
The AND gives the mask's value, not necessarily 1.
Queen counts are not part of the test.
Right: a non-zero AND means the line's bit is already set.
questions.explain: A set bit in the same place as the mask makes the AND non-zero, so the square is attacked.
questions.rule: Track columns and both diagonals as bits of three integers, test with AND, and place or remove a queen with XOR.

questions.q: For n = 6, a queen at row 2, column 4 sets bit ____ in the diagonals integer, where the bit index is row - col + n.
questions.rule: Track columns and both diagonals as bits of three integers, test with AND, and place or remove a queen with XOR.

questions.q: Why does the diagonal mask use row - col + n and not row - col?
options: Shifts cannot be negative, and row - col can be negative
Adding n makes diagonals and anti-diagonals use different bits
The board has n + 1 columns
Adding n keeps the shift an even number
optionExplain: Right: a negative shift is not allowed, so the offset n keeps the index at 1 or more.
The two integers are separate already.
The board has n columns.
The offset does not affect parity in any useful way.
questions.explain: row - col ranges from -(n - 1) to n - 1, and a left shift needs a non-negative amount.
questions.rule: Track columns and both diagonals as bits of three integers, test with AND, and place or remove a queen with XOR.
questions.teaches: Bit shifts cannot be negative, and row - col can be negative, so a constant n is added to the diagonal's bit index.

questions.q: For n = 8, which bit indexes does row - col + n use over the whole board?
options: From 0 up to 7
From 1 up to 15
From 0 up to 14
From 8 up to 16
optionExplain: 0 to 7 are the column indexes.
Right: the smallest is 0 - 7 + 8 = 1 and the largest is 7 - 0 + 8 = 15.
0 to 14 are the anti-diagonal indexes row + col.
The offset starts at the bottom of the range, not at n.
questions.explain: The smallest value is at row 0, column 7 and the largest at row 7, column 0, so the index runs from 1 to 15.
questions.rule: Track columns and both diagonals as bits of three integers, test with AND, and place or remove a queen with XOR.

questions.q: True or false: In the in-place version, after the recursive call returns, the queen's three bits can stay set.
questions.explain: Stale bits would make later squares look attacked. In the course's in-place version the same XOR removes the queen; in the sketch above, passing new values down does the same job.
questions.rule: Track columns and both diagonals as bits of three integers, test with AND, and place or remove a queen with XOR.

questions.q: The course writes (cols & currCol) != 0 with parentheses. What is the reason for them?
options: Parentheses make the AND run faster than the unbracketed form would
Bit operations have the highest priority and need grouping to lower it
Bit operations have low priority, so parentheses make the grouping explicit
Without parentheses the code would not compile in any language at all
optionExplain: Parentheses change the grouping, not the speed.
The priority is low, not high.
Right: with low priority, a bit operation can be grouped wrongly without parentheses.
The code may compile in some languages and still compute the wrong thing.
questions.explain: The course warns that bit manipulation operations have low priority (like the order of operations in arithmetic), so use parentheses.
questions.rule: Track columns and both diagonals as bits of three integers, test with AND, and place or remove a queen with XOR.
questions.teaches: Bit operations have low priority, as with PEMDAS, so parentheses should be used to make each term's grouping explicit.

questions.q: A calendar holds 1,000 meetings and a program checks every pair for overlap. How many pairs does it examine?
optionExplain: 1,000 would be one check per meeting, not per pair.
10,000 is not the number of pairs of 1,000 items.
1,000,000 counts ordered pairs and self-pairs; unordered pairs of different meetings are half of 1,000 * 999.
questions.explain: The number of pairs grows with the square of the count. The card next shows how sorting avoids checking them all.
questions.rule: Sort intervals by start time and compare neighbours, because any conflict appears between adjacent intervals.

questions.q: Before comparing neighbours, the intervals are sorted by their ____ time.
questions.explain: Sorting by start puts the intervals in the order in which they would be attended.
questions.rule: Sort intervals by start time and compare neighbours, because any conflict appears between adjacent intervals.

questions.q: Intervals [15, 20], [0, 30] and [5, 10] are sorted by start. Put them in the sorted order.
questions.explain: The starts are 0, 5 and 15, so the order is [0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]. The neighbours [0, 30] and [5, 10] already overlap.
questions.rule: Sort intervals by start time and compare neighbours, because any conflict appears between adjacent intervals.

questions.q: A system holds 100,000 intervals. About how many pair checks does the brute force need, compared with the work of sorting?
options: About 5 billion pair checks, against about 1.7 million for sorting
About 100,000 pair checks, against about 100,000 for sorting
About 5 billion for both, since sorting compares pairs too
About 1.7 million pair checks, against about 5 billion for sorting
optionExplain: Right: n(n-1)/2 is about 4,999,950,000, and n log n is about 1,660,964.
The brute force looks at pairs, which is far more than the number of intervals.
Sorting does not compare every pair; it takes about n log n comparisons.
That swaps the two costs.
questions.explain: The brute force is O(n^2) and sorting is O(n log n), which is millions rather than billions at this size.
questions.rule: Sort intervals by start time and compare neighbours, because any conflict appears between adjacent intervals.

questions.q: True or false: After sorting by start, a conflict can still lie between two intervals that are far apart in the list, so every pair must be checked.
questions.explain: If an interval overlaps an earlier one, it also overlaps the interval right before it in the sorted order, so checking neighbours is enough.
questions.rule: Sort intervals by start time and compare neighbours, because any conflict appears between adjacent intervals.

questions.q: A scheduling app sorts its n intervals in a language whose sort is quicksort. What extra space does the sort-and-scan approach use?
options: O(1), because only neighbours are compared during the scan
O(n), because every interval is copied into a new array first
O(n^2), because one entry is kept for each pair of intervals
About O(log n), because the space depends on the sort used
optionExplain: The scan uses O(1) but the sort may not.
Some sorts, such as Python's timsort, use up to O(n), but not all do.
The approach never stores pairs.
Right: the course says the space depends on the language, for example O(log n) for quicksort.
questions.explain: The extra space depends on the sort implementation. Python implements timsort, which uses up to O(n) space, whereas a language that uses quicksort uses O(log n).
questions.rule: Sort intervals by start time and compare neighbours, because any conflict appears between adjacent intervals.
questions.teaches: The extra space of sort-and-scan depends on the language's sort: Python's timsort uses up to O(n) space, while a quicksort-based language uses O(log n).

questions.q: Meetings are [9, 12], [10, 11] and [13, 14]. Can one person attend all of them?
options: Yes: the three meetings have different start times
No: the meeting at 10 starts before the 9 to 12 meeting ends
Yes: the last meeting starts after the others end
No: the person cannot attend three meetings in a row
optionExplain: Different start times do not prevent an overlap.
Right: 10 is earlier than 12, so the first two meetings overlap.
The last meeting is fine, but the first two clash.
Back-to-back meetings are fine when they do not overlap.
questions.explain: A clash exists whenever a meeting starts before the previous one ends. The card next turns this into a scan.
questions.rule: After sorting by start, a meeting clashes only if it starts before the previous one ends.

questions.q: After sorting, meeting i clashes when its start is less than the ____ of meeting i - 1.
questions.explain: The person would still be in meeting i - 1, which has not ended.
questions.rule: After sorting by start, a meeting clashes only if it starts before the previous one ends.

questions.q: The meetings [13, 15], [1, 6] and [4, 5] go through the course's method. What is returned?
options: true, because no two meetings have the same start
false, because after sorting, [4, 5] starts before [1, 6] ends
false, because [13, 15] starts before [1, 6] ends
true, because every meeting has a start before its end
optionExplain: Equal starts are not the test; the test is the start against the previous end.
Right: sorted by start the order is [1, 6], [4, 5], [13, 15], and 4 is less than 6.
13 is later than 6, so those two do not clash.
A valid start before end does not rule out an overlap.
questions.explain: Sorting gives [1, 6], [4, 5], [13, 15]. The comparison 4 < 6 fails the test at once, so the answer is false.
questions.rule: After sorting by start, a meeting clashes only if it starts before the previous one ends.

questions.q: After sorting 50,000 meetings, how many comparisons does the scan make at most?
optionExplain: The first meeting has no predecessor.
That would be half of the meetings, not n - 1.
That is the number of pairs; the scan compares neighbours only.
Right: each meeting from the second onward is compared with its predecessor, which is n - 1 comparisons.
questions.explain: The scan makes n - 1 comparisons, and the total cost is dominated by the sort.
questions.rule: After sorting by start, a meeting clashes only if it starts before the previous one ends.

questions.q: True or false: A student changes the test to intervals[i][0] <= intervals[i - 1][1]. Meetings [1, 3] and [3, 8] then still count as attendable.
questions.explain: With less-or-equal, the start 3 equals the previous end 3 and the test reports a clash. The course's strict less-than treats the meetings as not clashing.
questions.rule: After sorting by start, a meeting clashes only if it starts before the previous one ends.

questions.q: Meetings [9, 10] and [10, 11] are checked by the course's code. Why is there no clash?
options: A meeting runs up to but not including its end, so the first is over when the second begins
The two meetings have the same length, so neither can overlap the other
The code only checks the first and last meeting after the sort is done
The code treats any two meetings that touch as attendable by two people
optionExplain: Right: the meetings are written as [start, end), so the end is excluded.
Length is not part of the test.
The code compares every neighbouring pair.
The code is about one person; it only allows touching because of the half-open times.
questions.explain: The problem writes each meeting as [start, end), which runs up to but does not include the end. A meeting that starts exactly when another ends does not clash.
questions.rule: After sorting by start, a meeting clashes only if it starts before the previous one ends.
questions.teaches: Meetings are written as [start, end): a meeting runs from its start up to but not including its end, so a meeting that starts exactly when another ends does not clash.

questions.q: The intervals [2, 5], [4, 9] and [12, 14] are merged. What is the result?
options: [2, 5], [4, 9] and [12, 14] unchanged
optionExplain: The first two intervals overlap, so they cannot stay separate.
12 is later than 9, so [12, 14] does not overlap the merged interval.
Right: the first two overlap on 4 to 5 and merge, while [12, 14] stays apart.
[4, 5] is the overlap, but merging keeps the full span, not only the overlap.
questions.explain: Overlapping intervals combine into their full span. The card next gives the method.
questions.rule: Sort by start; extend the last merged interval's end with a max when the next one starts at or before it, else start a new interval.

questions.q: When two intervals [a, b] and [c, d] overlap, the merged interval ends at the ____ of b and d.
questions.explain: The union stretches to whichever end is further along the line.
questions.rule: Sort by start; extend the last merged interval's end with a max when the next one starts at or before it, else start a new interval.

questions.q: The intervals [6, 8], [1, 5], [2, 3] and [5, 7] are merged. What is returned?
optionExplain: The interval [5, 7] starts at 5, the end of [1, 5], so they merge.
Taking the end of [2, 3] would shrink the end of [1, 5] wrongly.
[2, 3] lies inside [1, 5] and merges.
Right: sorted they are [1, 5], [2, 3], [5, 7], [6, 8]; [2, 3] lies inside, 5 touches the end 5, and 6 is within 7.
questions.explain: After sorting, [1, 5] absorbs [2, 3] (end stays 5), then [5, 7] (start 5 is at most 5, end becomes 7), then [6, 8] (end becomes 8).
questions.rule: Sort by start; extend the last merged interval's end with a max when the next one starts at or before it, else start a new interval.

questions.q: True or false: A student sets ans[-1][1] = end instead of using the maximum. For the intervals [1, 10] and [2, 3] the code still returns [[1, 10]].
questions.explain: [2, 3] lies inside [1, 10], and the unconditional assignment shrinks the end from 10 to 3, so the code returns [[1, 3]]. Only max(previous end, end) keeps the end at 10.
questions.rule: Sort by start; extend the last merged interval's end with a max when the next one starts at or before it, else start a new interval.

questions.q: Reservations [1, 4], [3, 6] and [8, 9] are merged. What is the total length covered by the merged intervals?
optionExplain: Right: the merge is [1, 6] and [8, 9], with lengths 5 and 1.
5 counts only the merged interval [1, 6] and forgets [8, 9].
8 is the span from 1 to 9, which includes the gap.
9 adds all three original lengths, counting the overlap twice.
questions.explain: The merged intervals are [1, 6] and [8, 9], so the covered length is 5 + 1 = 6.
questions.rule: Sort by start; extend the last merged interval's end with a max when the next one starts at or before it, else start a new interval.

questions.q: Intervals [9, 11] and [11, 12] are merged by the course's code. What happens?
options: They stay apart, because merging needs a real overlap
They merge into [9, 12], because the second start equals the first end
They merge into [11, 11], the point they share
The code reports an error for touching intervals
optionExplain: The test uses less-or-equal, so touching counts as overlapping.
Right: the test is start less than or equal to the previous end, so touching intervals merge.
A merge covers the whole span, not only the shared point.
Touching intervals are an ordinary case.
questions.explain: The course merges when the start is less than or equal to the previous end, so touching intervals count as overlapping here, unlike the strict test used for meetings.
questions.rule: Sort by start; extend the last merged interval's end with a max when the next one starts at or before it, else start a new interval.
questions.teaches: In merge intervals the overlap test is start <= previous end, so intervals that only touch are merged.

questions.q: A problem says: return the answer modulo 1,000,000,007. What is the usual reason?
options: The answer is always a prime number
The answer is negative and must be made positive
The real answer could be too large to store in a variable
The judge only accepts answers with nine digits
optionExplain: The modulus is prime, but the answer is not.
Modular arithmetic is not about signs here.
Right: the true answer can be enormous, so only its remainder is asked for.
The answer can have fewer digits; the modulus bounds its size.
questions.explain: A huge exact answer cannot be stored, so the problem asks for the remainder. The card next shows how to compute it cheaply.
questions.rule: When a problem asks for an answer modulo x, reduce modulo x at every step instead of only at the end.

questions.q: On LeetCode the modulus is usually 10^9 + 7, which is ____.
questions.rule: When a problem asks for an answer modulo x, reduce modulo x at every step instead of only at the end.

questions.q: A loop multiplies 100,000 integers together and the problem asks for the product mod 1,000,000,007. Which plan fits the course?
options: Take the remainder after every multiplication
Compute the full product and take one remainder at the end
Take the remainder only after every 1,000 multiplications
Round each factor down to the nearest million first
optionExplain: Right: the running value never gets large, and the final remainder is the same.
That is correct but slow, with huge numbers, and may overflow.
Skipping steps lets the number grow before it is cut down.
Rounding changes the factors and so the answer.
questions.explain: Reducing at every step keeps the numbers small without changing the answer.
questions.rule: When a problem asks for an answer modulo x, reduce modulo x at every step instead of only at the end.

questions.q: Which statement should make you think of modular arithmetic?
options: Return the index of the target in the sorted array
Return the shortest path between two nodes
Return the answer modulo 10^9 + 7
Return the list of words with a given prefix
optionExplain: An index in a sorted array has no huge numbers.
A shortest path is a sum of small weights.
Right: an explicit modulus in the statement is the signal.
A list of words has no arithmetic.
questions.explain: The course says to think about it every time you are given an explicit modulus in the problem description.
questions.rule: When a problem asks for an answer modulo x, reduce modulo x at every step instead of only at the end.

questions.q: True or false: Taking the modulo only once, at the very end of the calculation, gives a wrong answer.
questions.explain: The answer is still correct. The problem is cost: arithmetic on numbers with many digits is slow, and in some languages they overflow.
questions.rule: When a problem asks for an answer modulo x, reduce modulo x at every step instead of only at the end.

questions.q: In an interview follow-up, you are asked how to keep a running product of a billion numbers from overflowing. Which idea applies?
options: Sort the numbers before multiplying them
Modular arithmetic: keep the running value reduced
Store the product as a string of digits
Use a trie to hold the partial products
optionExplain: Sorting does not shrink the product.
Right: reduced values stay small, which is the idea behind modular arithmetic.
A string of digits makes arithmetic even slower.
A trie stores strings by prefix, not products.
questions.explain: The course says any scenario where you could have potentially massive numbers, even outside an algorithm problem such as a system design interview or a follow-up question, calls for modular arithmetic.
questions.rule: When a problem asks for an answer modulo x, reduce modulo x at every step instead of only at the end.
questions.teaches: Think of modular arithmetic in any scenario with potentially massive numbers, even outside an algorithm problem, such as a system design interview or a follow-up question.

questions.q: Is (8 * 9) mod 5 equal to ((8 mod 5) * (9 mod 5)) mod 5?
options: No: the left side is 2 and the right side is 3
No: the left side is 3 and the right side is 12
Only when the product is smaller than 5
Yes: both are 2
optionExplain: The right side is 12 mod 5 = 2, not 3.
12 is not yet reduced; its remainder is 2.
It holds for any product, whatever its size.
Right: 72 mod 5 = 2, and 3 * 4 = 12 which leaves 2.
questions.explain: Reducing the factors first gives the same remainder as reducing the product. The card next states why this helps.
questions.rule: Applying the modulus after every operation gives the same remainder as applying it once at the end.

questions.q: Adding 14, 23, 35 and 41 with a remainder mod 9 taken after every addition ends with ____.
questions.explain: The running remainders are 5, 1, 0 and 5; the exact sum 113 also leaves 5.
questions.rule: Applying the modulus after every operation gives the same remainder as applying it once at the end.

questions.q: Multiplying 14, 23, 35 and 41 with a remainder mod 9 taken after every multiplication ends with which value?
optionExplain: 5 is the remainder of the sum, not the product.
2 is the remainder after the third multiplication, not the last.
Right: the running remainders are 5, 7, 2, 1, and the exact product 462,070 also leaves 1.
0 would need a factor divisible by 9.
questions.explain: 14 mod 9 = 5, then 5 * 23 mod 9 = 7, then 7 * 35 mod 9 = 2, then 2 * 41 mod 9 = 1.
questions.rule: Applying the modulus after every operation gives the same remainder as applying it once at the end.

questions.q: A program computes 13! (13 factorial) mod 1,000,000,007, reducing after every multiplication. What does it return?
optionExplain: Right: the exact 13! is 6,227,020,800, and subtracting 6 * 1,000,000,007 leaves 227,020,758.
That is the exact value, which is larger than the modulus and not a remainder.
13 is the last factor, not the remainder.
0 would need 13! to be a multiple of the modulus.
questions.explain: The stepwise result equals the remainder of the exact value: 6,227,020,800 - 6,000,000,042 = 227,020,758.
questions.rule: Applying the modulus after every operation gives the same remainder as applying it once at the end.

questions.q: True or false: Taking the remainder after every step can give a different final answer from taking it once at the end.
questions.explain: The final remainder is the same either way, however early you stop reducing. The difference is only in the size of the numbers handled.
questions.rule: Applying the modulus after every operation gives the same remainder as applying it once at the end.

questions.q: In a language whose integers overflow, why reduce at every step even if speed did not matter?
options: Overflow cannot happen with integer operations
It makes addition faster than multiplication
It changes the answer to a smaller one that is easier to check
It keeps the numbers small enough to be stored without overflowing
optionExplain: Fixed-size integers do overflow.
Reduction does not change the relative speed of operations.
The answer is unchanged by the reduction.
Right: reduced values fit in the integer type.
