questions.explain: The course notes that in a language with overflow it is a good bet to keep the numbers you work with smaller, regardless of speed.
questions.rule: Applying the modulus after every operation gives the same remainder as applying it once at the end.
questions.teaches: In a language with overflow, keeping the numbers small with a modulus is a good bet regardless of speed.

questions.q: Two numbers have x = 9 and y = 4, and one of them may be increased by 1. Which choice gives the larger product?
options: Increase x, the larger, because a larger number gains more: 10 * 4 = 40
Increase y, the smaller: 9 * 5 = 45 beats 10 * 4 = 40
Both give the same product
Neither changes the product
optionExplain: Raising x gives 40, which is less than 45.
Right: raising y adds x to the product, and raising x adds only y.
The two products are 45 and 40.
Any increase changes a product of non-zero numbers.
questions.explain: Raising the smaller number adds the larger number to the product, which is the bigger gain. The card next uses this for k operations.
questions.rule: Raise the smallest element k times using a heap, then multiply with a remainder after every multiplication.

questions.q: Each of the k operations increments the ____ element.
questions.explain: The smallest element is the one whose increase adds the most to the product.
questions.rule: Raise the smallest element k times using a heap, then multiply with a remainder after every multiplication.

questions.q: The numbers are 3 and 5 and k = 3. What is the largest product?
optionExplain: 24 comes from raising 5 to 8.
Right: the increments go 3 to 4, 4 to 5, then 5 to 6 on one of the 5s, which gives 5 * 6 = 30.
18 comes from leaving 5 and raising 3 to 6 only.
20 stops after only one increment.
questions.explain: Raise the smallest each time: (3, 5) becomes (4, 5), then (5, 5), then (5, 6), and 5 * 6 = 30.
questions.rule: Raise the smallest element k times using a heap, then multiply with a remainder after every multiplication.

questions.q: The numbers are 2, 2 and 7 with k = 4. What is the largest product?
optionExplain: 84 puts all four increments on one 2: 6 * 2 * 7.
98 corresponds to 7 * 7 * 2 and ignores the greedy rule.
126 is not reachable with four increments.
Right: the increments give 4, 4 and 7, so 4 * 4 * 7 = 112.
questions.explain: Raising the smallest each time gives (3, 2, 7), (3, 3, 7), (4, 3, 7), (4, 4, 7), and the product is 112.
questions.rule: Raise the smallest element k times using a heap, then multiply with a remainder after every multiplication.

questions.q: True or false: To maximise the product, each increment should go to the largest element, since a bigger factor gains more.
questions.explain: Raising the largest adds only the smaller factor. Raising the smaller adds the larger factor, so the smaller element should be raised.
questions.rule: Raise the smallest element k times using a heap, then multiply with a remainder after every multiplication.

questions.q: The array has 100,000 large elements, and the product is computed without any remainder before the final one. What does the course say happens?
options: The product outgrows a long, risking a wrong answer or Time Limit Exceeded
Nothing: the final remainder fixes a product of any size, however large
The heap overflows before the multiplication stage has even started
The k increments become impossible to apply once the heap is built
optionExplain: Right: the huge product overflows, or is too slow to compute.
The final remainder only works if the product could be stored and computed.
The heap holds small numbers; the product is the problem.
The increments work as normal.
questions.explain: The course's first version, which multiplies everything and takes the remainder at the end, can give a wrong answer or Time Limit Exceeded; taking the remainder at every multiplication passes.
questions.rule: Raise the smallest element k times using a heap, then multiply with a remainder after every multiplication.
questions.teaches: Computing the whole product before taking the remainder can run into Time Limit Exceeded or give a wrong answer, because the product becomes too large even for a long.

questions.q: The number 12 is read and then the digit 7 is appended on the right. What is the new number?
optionExplain: 19 adds the digit instead of shifting the number.
84 multiplies 12 by 7.
1207 shifts by two places instead of one.
questions.explain: Appending a digit multiplies by 10 and adds the digit. The card next shows how to keep this small.
questions.rule: Append each digit with curr = (curr * 10 + digit) % m, and report 1 when curr is 0.

questions.q: Appending digit d to a number curr gives curr * 10 + ____.
questions.explain: The old digits move one place left and the new digit fills the last place.
questions.rule: Append each digit with curr = (curr * 10 + digit) % m, and report 1 when curr is 0.

questions.q: For word 7140 and m = 7, what are the values of curr after each digit, in the course's method?
optionExplain: Those are the exact prefix values, not the reduced ones.
The second prefix, 71, is not divisible by 7.
The first prefix is divisible by 7, so curr is 0 there.
Right: 7 leaves 0, then 71 leaves 1, then 714 leaves 0, then 7140 leaves 0.
questions.rule: Append each digit with curr = (curr * 10 + digit) % m, and report 1 when curr is 0.

questions.q: With word 7140 and m = 7, what is the returned divisibility array?
optionExplain: Right: curr is 0 after the first, third and fourth digits.
71 is not divisible by 7, so the second entry is 0.
That is the list of remainders, not the divisibility flags.
714 is divisible by 7 (it is 7 * 102).
questions.explain: A 1 is reported wherever curr is 0, which happens after the digits 7, 714 and 7140.
questions.rule: Append each digit with curr = (curr * 10 + digit) % m, and report 1 when curr is 0.

questions.q: True or false: The course reduces curr modulo m after every digit, and this can change which prefixes are reported as divisible.
questions.explain: Reducing keeps the numbers small without changing any remainder, so the reported prefixes are the same as with the exact values.
questions.rule: Append each digit with curr = (curr * 10 + digit) % m, and report 1 when curr is 0.

questions.q: A digit string has 100,000 digits. Why is converting each prefix to an integer and testing it too slow?
options: Converting a string to an integer takes constant time, but there are too many prefixes
Each conversion costs time proportional to the prefix length, and 1 + 2 + ... + n is O(n^2)
A digit string cannot be converted to an integer at all by any language
Divisibility cannot be tested on an integer that has many digits
optionExplain: The conversion takes time proportional to the length of the string.
Right: about 5 billion character steps for n = 100,000.
Conversion is possible; the cost of repeating it for every prefix is the problem.
Divisibility can be tested, but slowly on huge numbers.
questions.explain: Converting a string of length n costs O(n), so converting every prefix costs 1 + 2 + ... + n, which is O(n^2).
questions.rule: Append each digit with curr = (curr * 10 + digit) % m, and report 1 when curr is 0.
questions.teaches: Converting each prefix string to an integer costs O(length) each time, so over all prefixes the cost is 1 + 2 + ... + n, which is O(n^2).

questions.q: Routes from A to D: P1 has tolls 2, 3, 2; P2 has tolls 6, 5; P3 has toll 9. Which route is cheapest?
options: P3, with a total toll of 9, because it has the fewest edges
P2, with a total toll of 11, because it has a middle number of edges
P1, with a total toll of 7
All three are equally cheap, because they join the same two cities
optionExplain: The fewest edges is not the lowest total toll.
P2 has the highest total, 11.
Right: 2 + 3 + 2 = 7, which is lower than 11 and 9.
The totals are 7, 11 and 9, so they differ.
questions.explain: The route with the most edges has the lowest total here. The card next defines the weight of a path.
questions.rule: On a weighted graph the shortest path is the one with the lowest sum of edge weights, not the fewest edges.

questions.q: The weight of a path is the ____ of the weights of its edges.
questions.explain: Add the edge weights along the path.
questions.rule: On a weighted graph the shortest path is the one with the lowest sum of edge weights, not the fewest edges.

questions.q: Order these routes from lowest weight to highest: P1 has edge weights 2, 3, 2; P2 has 6, 5; P3 has 9.
questions.explain: The weights are 7, 11 and 9, so the order from lowest to highest is P1, P3, P2.
questions.rule: On a weighted graph the shortest path is the one with the lowest sum of edge weights, not the fewest edges.

questions.q: A flight from A to C costs 250. Going A to B costs 120 and B to C costs 80. Which route is the shortest path by price?
options: A to B to C, with a total of 200
A to C direct, with a total of 250, because it has fewer flights
A to B to C, with a total of 80, because the last leg decides
Both are equal, because they link the same two cities
optionExplain: Right: 120 + 80 = 200, which is less than 250.
Fewer flights is not the same as a lower price.
All the legs count, not only the last one.
200 and 250 are different totals.
questions.explain: Compare totals: the connection through B costs 200 and the direct flight 250.
questions.rule: On a weighted graph the shortest path is the one with the lowest sum of edge weights, not the fewest edges.

questions.q: True or false: On a weighted graph, the path with the fewest edges is the shortest path.
questions.explain: The shortest path has the lowest total weight. A path with more edges can be lighter, as with 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 against a single edge of 9.
questions.rule: On a weighted graph the shortest path is the one with the lowest sum of edge weights, not the fewest edges.

questions.q: A graph has uneven edge weights. Why can breadth-first search not be trusted to find its shortest path?
options: It visits some nodes twice, which adds extra weight to the result
It can only start from node 0, so the source is fixed in advance
It stores weights in a queue that overflows on large graphs
It finds the path with the fewest edges, which may weigh more
optionExplain: Visiting nodes twice is not the issue; the criterion is.
BFS can start at any node.
Overflow is not the problem; the objective is.
Right: BFS counts edges, and with uneven weights the count does not decide the total.
questions.explain: The course says BFS is great for shortest paths but only works on unweighted graphs, because on weighted graphs a path with fewer edges does not necessarily have lower weight.
questions.rule: On a weighted graph the shortest path is the one with the lowest sum of edge weights, not the fewest edges.
questions.teaches: BFS only works on unweighted graphs: on a weighted graph a path with fewer edges does not necessarily have a lower weight, so the BFS used so far cannot be applied.

questions.q: Which container lets an algorithm take the node with the smallest path weight so far?
options: A queue, first in first out
A min-heap keyed by path weight
A stack, last in first out
A hash set of visited nodes
optionExplain: A queue serves nodes in arrival order, which suits counting edges.
Right: a min-heap gives the minimum on every pop.
A stack serves the most recently added node.
A set records membership and has no order of weights.
questions.explain: A min-heap returns the smallest weight first. The card next shows how it drives the algorithm.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's repeatedly pops the node with the smallest known distance from a min-heap and improves its neighbours' distances.

questions.q: At the start, distances is set to a large value for every node except the source, which gets ____.
questions.explain: The source is at distance 0 from itself, and every other node is unreached.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's repeatedly pops the node with the smallest known distance from a min-heap and improves its neighbours' distances.

questions.q: The popped node is at distance 5. An edge of weight 3 leads to a neighbour whose recorded distance is 9. What happens?
options: Nothing happens, because 8 is not larger than 5
distances for the neighbour becomes 8 and (8, neighbour) is pushed
distances for the neighbour becomes 3 and (3, neighbour) is pushed
The neighbour stays at 9 and (8, neighbour) is pushed anyway
optionExplain: The comparison is with the neighbour's recorded distance, 9.
Right: 5 + 3 = 8 is smaller than 9, so the neighbour improves.
The new distance is the popped distance plus the weight, not the weight alone.
A push only follows an update.
questions.explain: The candidate distance is curr_dist + weight = 8. Since 8 < 9 it is recorded and pushed.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's repeatedly pops the node with the smallest known distance from a min-heap and improves its neighbours' distances.

questions.q: The current node is at distance 5. For each edge, decide if the neighbour's distance is updated and pushed, or ignored.

items.t: Edge weight 3, neighbour's best is 9
Edge weight 4, neighbour's best is 9
Edge weight 2, neighbour's best is 6
Edge weight 1, neighbour not reached yet (large value)
Edge weight 6, neighbour's best is 12

questions.explain: The new distance is 5 + weight. It is updated only when strictly smaller: 8 < 9, 6 < large and 11 < 12 update, but 9 is not < 9 and 7 is not < 6.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's repeatedly pops the node with the smallest known distance from a min-heap and improves its neighbours' distances.

questions.q: Match each traversal to the container it uses to hold nodes still to visit.
questions.explain: DFS takes the newest node, BFS the oldest, and Dijkstra's the one with the smallest path weight.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's repeatedly pops the node with the smallest known distance from a min-heap and improves its neighbours' distances.

questions.q: True or false: Dijkstra's can use an ordinary queue, as BFS does, and still pops the node with the smallest path weight first.
questions.explain: A queue pops nodes in arrival order. Only the min-heap pops by path weight, which is what the algorithm depends on.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's repeatedly pops the node with the smallest known distance from a min-heap and improves its neighbours' distances.

questions.q: An unweighted graph is given to Dijkstra's. What weight does each edge effectively carry?
options: 0, since an unweighted graph has no weight to add up
The number of edges in the whole graph, shared by every edge
The distance from the source node to the edge being used
1, since all weights in an unweighted graph are equal to 1
optionExplain: Zero weights would make every path cost nothing.
The count of edges is not a per-edge weight.
Distances are computed, not given.
Right: each edge adds one step to the path weight.
questions.explain: The course says unweighted graphs can be thought of as weighted graphs where all weights are 1; then path weight is the number of edges.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's repeatedly pops the node with the smallest known distance from a min-heap and improves its neighbours' distances.
questions.teaches: An unweighted graph can be thought of as a weighted graph in which every edge has weight 1, so path weight then equals the number of edges.

questions.q: A popped heap entry says node 5 is at distance 12, but distances[5] is already 9. What should happen?
options: The entry is skipped, because a better path to node 5 was found earlier
distances[5] is changed to 12
The algorithm stops, because the heap is out of order
Node 5's neighbours are processed with distance 12
optionExplain: Right: 12 is worse than 9, so this entry is out of date.
That would replace a better distance with a worse one.
Out-of-date entries are normal and do not break the heap.
Processing at distance 12 would give worse distances to its neighbours.
questions.explain: An entry can outlive an improvement, so popped entries are checked against distances. The card next gives the loop.
questions.rule: Pop the smallest entry, skip it if stale, and push a neighbour only when the new distance is strictly smaller.

questions.q: A popped entry whose distance is greater than distances[node] is called ____ and is skipped.
questions.explain: A better path to that node was found after the entry was pushed.
questions.rule: Pop the smallest entry, skip it if stale, and push a neighbour only when the new distance is strictly smaller.

questions.q: Edges 0->1 (4), 0->2 (1), 2->1 (2), 1->3 (1), 2->3 (5), source 0. In which order are nodes processed, ignoring stale entries?
questions.explain: Node 0 is at distance 0, then node 2 at 1, node 1 at 3 (via node 2, which beats the direct 4), then node 3 at 4. The final distances are 0, 3, 1 and 4.
questions.rule: Pop the smallest entry, skip it if stale, and push a neighbour only when the new distance is strictly smaller.

questions.q: In the same graph, how many popped entries are skipped as stale?
optionExplain: Node 1 was reached twice, so an old entry remains.
Node 3 was also improved after its first push.
Right: the entry (4, node 1) is stale after node 1 improves to 3, and (6, node 3) is stale after node 3 improves to 4.
Only the nodes that improved leave a stale entry.
questions.explain: Six entries are pushed in all, including the first, and four of them are fresh when popped.
questions.rule: Pop the smallest entry, skip it if stale, and push a neighbour only when the new distance is strictly smaller.

questions.q: True or false: A neighbour is updated and pushed whenever the new distance is less than or equal to its recorded distance.
questions.explain: The update needs a strictly smaller distance. When dist is greater than or equal to distances[nei], a path at least as short is already known, so the new one is pointless.
questions.rule: Pop the smallest entry, skip it if stale, and push a neighbour only when the new distance is strictly smaller.

questions.q: A student deletes the line that skips stale entries. What does the course's idea say about the results?
options: The distances become wrong, because stale entries overwrite better ones
The loop never ends, because stale entries are pushed again and again
The distances are correct only for the source node and its neighbours
The distances are still correct; the check only avoids wasted work
optionExplain: A stale entry's longer distance fails the strict less-than test and changes nothing.
A stale entry does not push more than before.
All nodes are still correct.
Right: processing a stale entry cannot improve anything, so it only wastes effort.
questions.explain: The course labels the skip an optimization step: ignore the current path if a better one was found.
questions.rule: Pop the smallest entry, skip it if stale, and push a neighbour only when the new distance is strictly smaller.
questions.teaches: The check that skips stale entries is an optimization step: ignoring a current path when a better one was already found saves work and is not needed for the distances to be right.

questions.q: A signal starts at one node of a network. Which value is the time until every node has received it?
options: The largest of the shortest travel times to each node
The sum of the shortest travel times to each node
The smallest of the shortest travel times to each node
The shortest travel time to the last node in the input
optionExplain: Right: the signal reaches nodes in parallel, so the slowest node decides.
The signal travels along many edges at once, so times do not add up across nodes.
The smallest time is when the first other node hears it.
The input order says nothing about which node is the slowest.
questions.explain: Nodes receive the signal in parallel, so the finish time is set by the slowest one. The card next shows how to compute it.
questions.rule: Run Dijkstra's from the start node and return the maximum distance, or -1 if any distance is still infinite.

questions.q: If some node cannot receive the signal, the answer is ____.
questions.explain: An unreachable node keeps its large starting distance, which the course turns into -1.
questions.rule: Run Dijkstra's from the start node and return the maximum distance, or -1 if any distance is still infinite.

questions.q: Edges 1->2 (3), 1->3 (10), 2->3 (4), 3->4 (2); the signal starts at node 1. What is the answer?
optionExplain: 10 is the direct edge to node 3, but a faster route through node 2 takes 7.
Right: the times are 0, 3, 7 and 9, so node 4 hears last at 9.
12 would add the direct edge 10 and the final edge 2.
7 is the time to node 3, but node 4 comes later.
questions.explain: Node 3 is reached at 3 + 4 = 7 via node 2, which is better than 10, and node 4 at 7 + 2 = 9.
questions.rule: Run Dijkstra's from the start node and return the maximum distance, or -1 if any distance is still infinite.

questions.q: A network has edges 2 to 1 (1) and 2 to 3 (1). What is the answer if the signal starts at node 1?
options: 1, because the edges all have weight 1
0, because the signal starts at the source
-1, because node 1 has no outgoing edge
2, because there are two edges to follow
optionExplain: That is the answer from node 2, not node 1.
0 is the time at the source only.
Right: nothing leaves node 1, so nodes 2 and 3 are never reached.
Edges are followed only in their direction.
questions.explain: From node 2 both nodes are reached at time 1, but from node 1 no edge can be used, so the answer is -1.
questions.rule: Run Dijkstra's from the start node and return the maximum distance, or -1 if any distance is still infinite.

questions.q: True or false: The answer is the sum of the shortest times to all nodes.
questions.explain: The signal travels along different routes at the same time, so the answer is the largest of the shortest times, not their sum.
questions.rule: Run Dijkstra's from the start node and return the maximum distance, or -1 if any distance is still infinite.

questions.q: Nodes are labelled 1 to n, but the arrays are 0-indexed. For the edge [3, 1, 5], which entry is added to the graph?
options: From node 2 to node 0 with weight 5
From node 3 to node 1 with weight 5
From node 4 to node 2 with weight 5
From node 0 to node 2 with weight 5
optionExplain: Right: both labels shrink by 1 and the weight stays 5.
That uses the labels as array indexes without shifting.
That adds 1 instead of subtracting.
That reverses the direction of the edge.
questions.explain: The course builds the graph with 0-indexed nodes by subtracting 1 from each node label, and the start node k becomes k - 1.
questions.rule: Run Dijkstra's from the start node and return the maximum distance, or -1 if any distance is still infinite.
questions.teaches: Because the nodes are labelled from 1, the graph is built with 0-indexed nodes by subtracting 1 from every label, including the start node.

questions.q: Dijkstra's runs on a graph with V nodes and E edges using a binary heap. Which time cost is the best guess?
options: O(V + E), the same as an unweighted traversal
O(V * E), one pass over the edges for each node
O((V + E) log V)
O(log V), a single walk through the heap
optionExplain: That would apply if no heap operations were needed.
That is far larger than the heap-based cost.
Right: every node and edge does heap work that costs a logarithm.
The whole graph still has to be examined.
questions.explain: Heap operations on the nodes and edges add a log V factor to a plain traversal. The card next explains the counts.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's runs in O((V + E) * log V) time and O(V) space, with the cost of building the graph not included.

questions.q: Match each part of Dijkstra's to its cost in the course.
questions.explain: Pops O(V), pushes O(E) and a logarithmic cost for each give O((V + E) log V).
questions.rule: Dijkstra's runs in O((V + E) * log V) time and O(V) space, with the cost of building the graph not included.

questions.q: A graph has 10,000 nodes and 50,000 edges. About how many steps does (V + E) * log2 V represent?
options: About 60,000
About 797,000
About 133,000
optionExplain: 60,000 is V + E without the logarithmic factor.
Right: 60,000 * log2(10,000) is about 60,000 * 13.3, which is about 797,000.
500,000,000 is V * E, a much larger and wrong cost.
133,000 is 10,000 * 13.3, which leaves out the edges.
questions.explain: V + E = 60,000 and log2 of 10,000 is about 13.3, which gives about 797,000.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's runs in O((V + E) * log V) time and O(V) space, with the cost of building the graph not included.

questions.q: A graph has 1,000 nodes. Which is closer to the work of (V + E) * log2 V: 5,000 edges, or 1,000,000 edges?
options: Both give about 10 million, because only V matters
5,000 edges give about 10 million; 1,000,000 edges give about 60 thousand
Both give about 60 thousand, because the logarithm hides the edges
5,000 edges give about 60 thousand; 1,000,000 edges give about 10 million
optionExplain: The number of edges is part of the formula.
That swaps the two results.
The logarithm multiplies the edge count; it does not hide it.
Right: 6,000 * 10 is about 60 thousand and 1,001,000 * 10 is about 10 million.
questions.explain: When E grows from 5,000 to 1,000,000 the factor V + E grows from 6,000 to 1,001,000, which is the dense case.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's runs in O((V + E) * log V) time and O(V) space, with the cost of building the graph not included.

questions.q: True or false: The O((V + E) log V) cost includes the time to build the graph from the list of edges.
questions.explain: The course says these complexities do not account for creating the graph; they are for running Dijkstra's only.
questions.rule: Dijkstra's runs in O((V + E) * log V) time and O(V) space, with the cost of building the graph not included.

questions.q: Two libraries offer heaps with different costs per operation. What does the course say about Dijkstra's time bound?
options: It is fixed at O((V + E) log V) for any heap that is used
It depends only on the number of nodes and not on the edges
It depends on the heap implementation; O((V + E) log V) is the general form
It is always O(V^2) because the distances array is scanned
optionExplain: The bound shifts if the heap's operation costs shift.
The edges matter too.
Right: the heap's cost per operation feeds into the total.
The array is read, not scanned, for each step.
questions.explain: The course states that the time complexity depends on how your heap is implemented, and gives the general form as O((V + E) log V).
questions.rule: Dijkstra's runs in O((V + E) * log V) time and O(V) space, with the cost of building the graph not included.
questions.teaches: The time complexity of Dijkstra's depends on how the heap is implemented; O((V + E) log V) is the general form.

questions.q: A cycle of three edges has weights 5, -8 and 1. What happens to the weight of a path each time it goes once around the cycle?
options: It drops by 2 each lap
It rises by 2 each lap
It stays the same each lap
It drops by 8 only the first lap
optionExplain: Right: 5 - 8 + 1 = -2, so each lap lowers the total by 2.
The sum is negative, so the total falls.
The lap sum is -2, not 0.
Every lap repeats the same sum.
questions.explain: A lap adds the cycle's total weight, here -2. The card next shows why that is a problem.
questions.rule: Do not run Dijkstra's on a graph with a negative weight cycle, since every lap lowers the distances and the loop does not stop.

questions.q: A cycle whose edge weights add up to a negative number is a negative weight ____.
questions.explain: It is a cycle (a loop back to the start) whose total weight is below zero.
questions.rule: Do not run Dijkstra's on a graph with a negative weight cycle, since every lap lowers the distances and the loop does not stop.

questions.q: A cycle A to B (5), B to C (-8), C to A (1) is entered from A at distance 0. What is distances[A] after three laps?
optionExplain: 0 would mean the laps change nothing.
-2 is the value after a single lap.
6 has the wrong sign.
Right: each lap adds 5 - 8 + 1 = -2, so after three laps A is at -6.
questions.explain: The values of A after each lap are -2, -4 and -6, and they keep falling.
questions.rule: Do not run Dijkstra's on a graph with a negative weight cycle, since every lap lowers the distances and the loop does not stop.

questions.q: Which of these cycles makes Dijkstra's unsafe?
options: Edge weights 3, -2 and 1
Edge weights 5, -9 and 2
Edge weights 4, 4 and -1
Edge weights 6, -2 and -4
optionExplain: 3 - 2 + 1 = 2, which is positive.
Right: 5 - 9 + 2 = -2, a negative total.
4 + 4 - 1 = 7, which is positive.
6 - 2 - 4 = 0, which never lowers a distance.
questions.explain: Add the weights around the cycle: only a negative total is dangerous.
questions.rule: Do not run Dijkstra's on a graph with a negative weight cycle, since every lap lowers the distances and the loop does not stop.

questions.q: True or false: A loop that does not end on a graph with a negative cycle can be fixed by skipping stale entries.
questions.explain: Each lap produces a better distance, so the new entries are not stale. The algorithm keeps finding improvements and never stops.
questions.rule: Do not run Dijkstra's on a graph with a negative weight cycle, since every lap lowers the distances and the loop does not stop.

questions.q: A currency graph has a loop of trades whose combined cost is negative. What does the course's Dijkstra's loop do on it?
options: It stops after one lap and returns a wrong distance for the cycle
It never terminates, because each lap lowers the distances again
It returns the distance of the first lap as the shortest one
It raises an error as soon as it meets a negative edge
optionExplain: It does not stop; it keeps improving.
Right: the failure is an endless loop, not a wrong finite answer.
The first lap is not the best, and the loop does not stop there.
The code has no check for negative weights.
questions.explain: In the course's example the cycle weighs -495, so each pass lowers the distance further and the code never stops running.
questions.rule: Do not run Dijkstra's on a graph with a negative weight cycle, since every lap lowers the distances and the loop does not stop.
questions.teaches: On a graph with a negative weight cycle the code does not return a wrong answer, it never terminates, because every lap through the cycle lowers the distances again.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Positive daily sales, and a request for the longest run of days totalling at most a budget. Which pattern fits?
options: A max heap that holds the day with the largest sales so far
A sliding window that grows on the right and shrinks on the left
A stack that pairs each day with the nearest earlier day of larger sales
Backtracking over every subset of the days, listing each one
optionExplain: A heap suits a repeated maximum from a changing collection, but this statement asks about a contiguous run, not one extreme day.
Right: the constraint on a contiguous piece and the request for its longest length are the window cues.
A stack suits next-greater questions. Nothing here asks which day is larger than which.
Listing all subsets is for find-all tasks on tiny inputs, and a run of consecutive days is a much smaller space than all subsets.
questions.explain: A contiguous piece with a limit on its total, and a request for its longest length, is the classic window statement. The card names this and the other cues.
questions.rule: A limit on a contiguous piece plus a best length suggests a sliding window.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each cue in a statement to the pattern it suggests.
pairs: The most recent unresolved element must be handled first
For each element, find the next greater one
The maximum of a changing collection is needed again and again
Fewest moves from one state to another
questions.explain: Each cue comes from the course's own guides: last in, first out for a stack, next-greater for a monotonic stack, a repeated extreme for a heap and fewest operations between states for breadth-first search.
questions.rule: Learn each pattern together with the wording that calls for it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A transit app must find the fewest line changes between two stations, and every change counts equally. Which pattern fits?
options: Breadth-first search, because fewest steps between equal-cost nodes is its job
Depth-first search, because it follows one route to its end and reports it
Backtracking, because a route is a sequence of choices and every sequence can be listed in full
A prefix sum over the stations, because changes can be counted by subtraction
optionExplain: Right: stations are nodes, changes are edges of equal cost, and BFS reaches nodes in order of distance.
DFS finds a route, but the first route it finds can be longer than another, so it does not guarantee the fewest changes.
Backtracking lists everything at exponential cost. The statement asks for one fewest count, not for all routes.
Prefix sums answer range-sum queries on an array. Stations joined by lines form a graph, not an array of numbers.
questions.explain: Fewest steps between states of equal cost is the breadth-first search cue, and the wording gives it away before any code is written.
questions.rule: Fewest steps with equal costs suggests breadth-first search.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each statement by the cue it shows.

items.t: Longest substring with at most two distinct characters
Many requests, each asking for the total between two dates
Shortest run of positive values with a sum of at least a target
Thousands of queries about the sum of a range of readings
Count runs of positive values whose product stays below k
Check each split point of a list by comparing its left and right sums

questions.explain: A window statement defines which contiguous pieces are valid and asks for the best one. A prefix-sum statement asks for many range sums or a sum on each side of a point, so one pass of precomputed totals answers them.
questions.rule: A defined validity plus a best piece suggests a window; many range totals suggest prefix sums.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The task changes to counting runs whose total equals the budget exactly, and refunds can make a day negative. Which pattern now fits?
options: The same window, shrinking while the total exceeds the budget
Two pointers moving inward from both ends of the sales list
A min heap of the smallest totals found so far
Prefix sums with a hash map counting each earlier prefix
optionExplain: This worked for at most the budget on positive values. With exact totals and negative days, dropping a left day can put a valid run out of reach.
Inward pointers need a sorted list to decide which end to move, and sales are not sorted.
A heap keeps an extreme of a changing collection. The statement asks for a count of exact matches, not an extreme.
Right: an exact total breaks the window, and a counts map of earlier prefixes finds every run ending at the current day.
questions.explain: Changing the constraint from at most to exactly changes the cue: a window needs a rule that stays true when a valid window shrinks, and an exact total does not give one.
questions.rule: If the constraint becomes exact, move from a window to prefix sums with a counts map.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A window fits the longest substring with at most two distinct characters. What tracks the distinct count in O(1) per step?
options: A hash map of character counts, deleting a key when its count reaches zero
One integer holding the sum of the character codes in the window
A set rebuilt from scratch at every step, which costs time in the window size
A stack of characters, popping whenever the window shrinks
optionExplain: Right: the map holds one key per character in the window, so its length is the distinct count.
A single integer worked for sums and counts of zeros, but a sum cannot tell how many different characters it contains.
This gives the right count, but rebuilding the set at every step costs time in the window size instead of O(1).
A stack remembers order, not how many of each character are inside the window.
questions.explain: Distinct counts need to know how many of each value are in the window, which is what a counts map stores.
questions.rule: A window over distinct values keeps a counts map.
questions.teaches: When a window's rule is about distinct values, one integer is not enough: keep a hash map of counts, decrement when the left element leaves, and delete the key at zero so the map's length is the distinct count.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A signup form checks 50,000 times whether a username is among 50,000 taken names. Which structure keeps the loop fast?
options: An unsorted array scanned from the start for each check
A queue holding the names in the order they were taken
A hash set of the taken names
A stack with the newest name on top
optionExplain: An array scan is simple, but each check can read all 50,000 names, which adds up to about 2.5 billion steps.
A queue gives cheap access to its ends, not to a name in the middle, so a lookup still scans.
Right: a set answers present or not in O(1), so 50,000 checks cost about 50,000 steps.
A stack hands back the newest item cheaply, but finding an arbitrary name means scanning it.
questions.explain: Repeated presence checks are the case a hash set is built for. The card next compares the common operations and structures.
questions.rule: Repeated membership checks call for a hash set or map.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each repeated operation to the structure that makes it cheap.
pairs: Check whether a value is present
Read the smallest element of a changing collection
Remove a node you already hold a reference to
questions.explain: Each pairing follows the cost sheet: O(1) presence in a set, O(1) access by index in an array, O(1) peek at the minimum of a heap and O(1) removal of a held node in a doubly linked list.
questions.rule: Pair each repeated operation with the structure where it is O(1).

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A fleet of 1,000,000 sensors sends readings all day. Later you need how many readings each sensor sent. Which structure fits?
options: A hash map from sensor id to a running count
A hash set of the sensor ids that have reported
A min heap ordered by sensor id
A queue holding each reading in arrival order
optionExplain: Right: each key carries a value, the count, and each update and lookup is O(1).
A set tells you which sensors reported, but it cannot attach a count to each id.
A heap keeps the minimum cheap to read, but looking up one sensor's count would mean scanning the heap.
A queue keeps arrival order, but counting one sensor's readings means scanning the whole queue.
questions.explain: The set-or-map question is whether each key must carry something. Here every sensor id needs a count, so a map is needed.
questions.rule: Presence only means a set; a value per key means a map.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Checking 20,000 names against a list of 20,000 names by scanning takes up to ____ comparisons.
questions.explain: Each of the 20,000 checks can read all 20,000 names: 20,000 times 20,000 is 400,000,000. A set would answer each check in O(1), about 20,000 steps in all.
questions.rule: Repeats multiply: a scan inside a loop costs n times n.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: since hash map lookups are O(1), a 5,000-character key costs the same to look up as a one-character key.
questions.explain: The O(1) is constant relative to the size of the map. Hashing a string key takes time in the length of that key, so the 5,000-character key costs more.
questions.rule: Hash map O(1) is relative to the map's size, not to the key's length.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A leaderboard stores 1,000,000 scores in a binary search tree that has become a straight line. How many steps can one lookup take?
options: About 20, because log base 2 of 1,000,000 is about 20 and each step halves the tree
One step, because the tree remembers where each score sits
About 20,000,000, because a lookup costs n log n
Up to about 1,000,000, one step per node, as in a linked list
optionExplain: That is the average cost for a well-balanced tree, where each step discards half. A straight line discards only one node per step.
A tree keeps no index of its nodes. A lookup still walks from the root.
n log n is the cost of sorting n items. One lookup walks one path, at most n nodes long.
Right: in a straight line every node has one child, so a lookup may walk past every node.
questions.explain: A binary search tree gives O(log n) lookups on average, because a well-balanced tree is close to full at each depth. A tree that is a straight line behaves like a linked list.
questions.rule: A binary search tree is O(log n) when balanced and O(n) when it is a straight line.
questions.teaches: A binary search tree is O(log n) on average only when it is well balanced; in the worst case, a tree that is a straight line, search, insert and delete are O(n).

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A support desk must hand each agent the open ticket with the highest priority while new tickets keep arriving. Which structure fits?
options: A queue, which serves the ticket that has waited longest
A heap ordered by priority
A stack, which serves the newest ticket first
A hash set of ticket ids, which holds ids without any order
optionExplain: A queue ignores priority. The oldest ticket may be the least urgent.
Right: a heap returns the extreme in O(1) and takes each new ticket in O(log n).
A stack ignores priority too. The newest ticket is not necessarily the most urgent.
A set answers presence quickly, but it cannot say which ticket has the highest priority.
questions.explain: When the next item is the best by a key, a heap is the structure built for it. The card next compares this rule with the newest-first and oldest-first rules.
questions.rule: The best item by a key first calls for a heap.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which waiting item comes next? Sort each situation.

items.t: Matching a closing bracket with the latest unmatched opener
Visiting tree nodes level by level in breadth-first search
Undoing a typed character when backspace is pressed
Serving print jobs in the order they were submitted
Finishing the most recent unfinished function call
Handling customers in the order they joined the line

questions.explain: A stack hands back the item added last, which suits matching, undoing and the call stack. A queue hands back the item added first, which suits level order and first come, first served.
questions.rule: Newest first is a stack; oldest first is a queue.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: For each day of a step-count log, report how many days pass until a day with more steps. Which structure fits?
options: A queue that compares each day with the day after it, oldest first
A max heap of all step counts, popped one at a time to find each day's larger successor
A stack of days still waiting, popped when a day with more steps arrives
A hash map from each step count to its day number
optionExplain: Comparing neighbours finds only the next day. A later day with more steps may be several days ahead.
A heap gives the largest count overall, but the question asks for the next larger day after each specific day.
Right: this is the next-greater pattern, and the waiting days are resolved newest first.
A map finds a day by its step count, but the question asks which later day has a larger count.
questions.explain: For each element, the next element that meets a criterion is the monotonic stack cue. Each day is pushed once and popped once.
questions.rule: A next-greater question suggests a monotonic stack.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Repeated max removal costs n squared by scanning, n log2 n with a heap. At n = 65,536, scanning costs about ____ times more.
questions.explain: The ratio is n squared divided by n log2 n, which is n divided by log2 n. For n = 65,536, log2 n is 16, so the ratio is 65,536 divided by 16, which is 4,096.
questions.rule: A heap turns repeated extreme scans from n squared into n log n.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A teammate counts calls from the last 3,000 ms with a stack, since recent calls matter. What is the flaw?
options: Expired calls are the oldest, so the item to drop sits at the wrong end of a stack
Stack operations cost O(n) because each push shifts the existing items, which is too slow for a counter
Expiry depends on time values, so only a heap can order the calls
The newest call must be dropped first, which a stack cannot do
optionExplain: Right: calls leave in arrival order, which is the queue pattern. A stack hides the oldest call under the newer ones.
Stack push and pop are O(1), so cost is not the flaw. The order of removal is.
The calls already arrive in time order, so no heap is needed to know which is oldest.
The newest call is the one that should stay. A stack could drop it, which is the wrong action here.
questions.explain: The rule for which item leaves next decides the structure. Here the oldest call leaves first, so a queue fits and a stack does not.
questions.rule: Check which end items leave from before choosing a stack.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A monotonic decreasing structure gives each window-of-3 maximum in O(n). Why a deque rather than a stack?
options: A stack cannot keep its values in decreasing order, so it cannot hold a maximum at all
A deque stores more values, so it can hold the whole window
A deque sorts its items as they arrive, which a stack does not
Smaller values leave from the back and expired maxima leave from the front: two ends
optionExplain: A stack can be kept decreasing; the monotonic stack of the daily temperature problem is one. The window is what needs a second end.
Size is not the reason. The deque holds at most the window, and what matters is which ends it can change.
A deque does not sort by itself. Order is kept by removing smaller items before each new one is added.
Right: a stack only has one working end, and this task needs removals at both.
questions.explain: The window adds values on the right and loses old ones on the left, while the monotonic rule removes smaller values from the right. The deque stores indices, so the front can be checked against the window's left edge.
questions.rule: Use a deque when items must be removed at both ends.
questions.teaches: The deque stores indices, not values, so the algorithm can tell when the maximum at the front has slid out of the window and remove it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Why can binary search discard half of a sorted array after one comparison?
options: Sorted order means the comparison also decides every element in the discarded half
The array is stored in memory as two separate halves
Comparing with the middle element also sorts the half that remains
Only a few elements near the middle can hold the target, so the rest can be ignored safely
optionExplain: Right: if the target is larger than the middle element, it is larger than everything before it too.
Memory layout is not the reason. The halves exist only as index ranges.
A comparison reads values; it does not rearrange them. The array has to be sorted before the search starts.
Elements far from the middle can hold the target. They are discarded because order rules them out.
questions.explain: One comparison can speak for a whole half only because order links every element to the middle one. The card next lists what else order unlocks.
questions.rule: Sorted order lets one comparison rule out a whole half.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The course says to assume that sorting n items with a built-in sort costs O(____).
questions.explain: The cost sheet says it is usually correct to assume that sorting costs O(n log n), where n is the number of elements sorted.
questions.rule: Count a built-in sort as O(n log n).

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A clinic has 3,000 appointments, each with a start and end time. Which plan uses order to find whether any two overlap?
options: Put every start time in a hash set and look for duplicate start times among the appointments
Sort by start time, then compare each appointment with the one before it
Binary search the unsorted list for the earliest end time
Compare each appointment with the one booked right after it
optionExplain: A set finds equal start times, but two appointments can overlap with different starts.
Right: after sorting by start, any overlap shows up between neighbours, so one pass of about 3,000 comparisons follows a sort of about 35,000 steps.
Binary search needs a sorted search space, and the list is sorted by nothing yet.
Booking order has no link to time, so a conflict can sit between appointments far apart in that order.
questions.explain: Sorting by start time moves every conflict next to the interval it clashes with, replacing about 4.5 million pair checks with a sort and one pass.
questions.rule: Sort intervals by start time, then compare neighbours.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Appointments: 9 to 11, 1 to 4, 5 to 8, 3 to 6. Order them as a pass over the start-sorted list visits them.
questions.explain: Sorting by start time gives 1, 3, 5, 9. The first neighbour comparison, 3 to 6 against 1 to 4, already finds the conflict because 3 is earlier than 4.
questions.rule: Sort by start, then each interval is compared with its predecessor.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: binary searching candidate answers needs the candidates stored as a sorted array in memory.
questions.explain: The candidates can be a plain range of numbers. What the search needs is a check function and a cutoff where the results change from impossible to possible.
questions.rule: A threshold can stand in for a sorted array.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Binary searching truck capacities from 1 to 10^9 for 50,000 parcels, with a check that reads every parcel. About how many steps in all?
options: About 50,000, since binary search reads each parcel once
About 10^9, since each capacity is tried in turn
About 50,000 times 10^9, since each capacity needs a full check
About 1,500,000, from about 30 checks of 50,000 steps each
optionExplain: The 50,000 steps are the cost of one check. Every round of the search runs a fresh check.
Trying each capacity in turn is a linear scan of the range, which binary search is meant to avoid.
That multiplies by the size of the range. Binary search runs only about log of that size.
Right: halving a range of 10^9 takes about 30 rounds, and each round runs one full check.
questions.explain: The number of rounds depends on the size of the answer range, not on the input. With a range of k values and a check costing n, the total is n times log k.
questions.rule: A search over answers costs n log k: log k rounds, each running a check.
questions.teaches: Searching a range of candidate answers costs O(n log k) when a check takes O(n), where k is the size of the answer range, so even a huge range adds only a logarithmic factor.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Count the subarrays that sum to exactly k in an array that may hold negative numbers. Which tool is the best first guess?
options: A sliding window that shrinks while the sum is above k
Two pointers moving inward from both ends
Prefix sums with a hash map counting earlier prefixes
A min heap of the subarray sums found so far
optionExplain: Shrinking is safe only when a valid window stays valid. With negatives and an exact sum, dropping an element can lose a run.
Inward pointers need sorted data to decide which end to move, and nothing here is sorted.
Right: an exact sum breaks the window, and the counts map finds every earlier prefix equal to curr minus k.
A heap keeps an extreme; this task counts exact matches of a sum.
questions.explain: An exact constraint is the case where the window stops working. The card next lines up the four sequence patterns.
questions.rule: An exact count of subarray sums calls for prefix sums with a counts map.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each problem to the tool it suggests.
pairs: A pair summing to a target in a sorted array
Longest run of positive values with a total of at most k
Thousands of queries for the sum of a range
Count subarrays that sum to exactly k
Prefix sums with a counts map
questions.explain: Order gives the pointers their rule, a shrink-safe limit gives the window, many range queries justify one prefix build, and an exact count needs the counts map.
questions.rule: Each pattern needs a different property of the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A warehouse has 100,000 daily readings and answers 5,000 queries, each asking for the total between two days. Which plan is cheapest?
options: Add up each range directly, about 500,000,000 steps in all
Build prefix sums once, then subtract per query: about 105,000 steps in all
Keep a hash map from each day to its reading, which still adds every day in the range
Sort the readings first, then binary search for each query
optionExplain: This is correct but slow: each query can read up to 100,000 readings, and 5,000 queries multiply that.
Right: the O(n) build is paid once and each of the 5,000 queries costs O(1).
A map makes one reading cheap to fetch, but a range total still needs one fetch per day.
Sorting destroys the order of the days, so a range of days no longer maps to a range of the array.
questions.explain: Many range-sum queries are the prefix-sum cue. The cost drops from n times m to n plus m: 100,000 plus 5,000 steps instead of 500,000,000.
questions.rule: Many range sums justify building prefix sums once.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: How many subarrays of [3, 4, -7, 1, 3, 3, 1, -4] have a sum of exactly 7? ____
questions.explain: Prefix sums with a counts map that starts with the empty prefix find four: [3, 4], [3, 4, -7, 1, 3, 3], [1, 3, 3] and [3, 3, 1]. Leaving out the empty prefix would miss the two that start at index 0.
questions.rule: Seed the counts map with the empty prefix.
questions.hint: Each run ends at some index; ask how many earlier prefixes equal the current prefix minus 7.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: This window code reports 0 for nums = [3, 5, -1] and k = 7, but the whole array sums to 7. What breaks?
options: Dropping the 3 at total 8 is final, yet the later -1 would have brought the whole run back to 7
The loop should use if instead of while, so that it drops at most one number before checking the total
The answer should start at 1, because the empty subarray also has a sum to compare with k
curr should reset to 0 whenever it exceeds k, to restart the window
optionExplain: Right: the window assumes a shrunk window stays useful, which exact totals with negatives do not guarantee.
Dropping fewer numbers would still discard the 3 once. The problem is that the dropped number is needed again.
Counting an empty subarray changes the answer by a fixed amount but does not find the missing run.
Resetting throws away the whole window, which loses even more runs.
questions.explain: A window may shrink only when a valid window stays valid or the dropped part cannot matter again. An exact sum with negatives gives neither guarantee.
questions.rule: Exact sums with negatives need prefix sums, not a shrinking window.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A hotel has 80,000 bookings, each with arrival night, departure night and rooms. Nights run 1 to 365. Which method finds the busiest night?
options: A sliding window of fixed width over the nights
Prefix sums of the booking lengths, queried once per booking to find the busiest night
Add rooms at the arrival night, subtract them at departure, then take running totals
A min heap of arrival nights, popped one by one
optionExplain: Bookings have different lengths, so no single window width describes them.
Lengths say how long each stay lasts but not which nights overlap, so they do not give a nightly total.
Right: the running total of those changes is the number of rooms in use on each night.
A heap returns arrivals in order, but a night's total also needs the departures, which the heap ignores.
questions.explain: Bookings are events on a number line with a start, an end and a value. A difference array records the changes and a prefix sum recovers the totals.
questions.rule: Events on a number line call for a difference array and a prefix sum.
questions.teaches: A difference array adds a value at an event's start and subtracts it at its end, and a prefix sum over that array gives the value at every position, in O(n + m) with m the largest position, instead of sorting the events in O(n log n).

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A building map shows doors between rooms, and every door counts equally. Which method finds the fewest doors from the entrance to the exit?
options: Depth-first search, reporting the first path it finds to the exit
Counting the connected components of the rooms
An inorder walk of the rooms, as if they were a search tree
Breadth-first search from the entrance, level by level
optionExplain: DFS follows one route to its end, and the first route it finds can be longer than another.
Components tell you which rooms are reachable from each other, not how many doors separate two rooms.
Inorder order is defined for binary search trees, and a building map is a graph with cycles and no left or right.
Right: BFS reaches rooms in order of the number of doors, so the first arrival at the exit uses the fewest.
questions.explain: Fewest steps with equal costs is the breadth-first search case. The card next separates it from DFS and Dijkstra's algorithm.
questions.rule: Fewest steps on equal-cost edges calls for BFS.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each question to the traversal that answers it.
pairs: Maximum depth of a binary tree
The rightmost node on each level of a tree
Cheapest total toll across roads with different tolls
Number of separate friend groups in a social graph
questions.explain: Depth comes from combining subtree answers, which DFS does. Levels come from a queue. Different tolls need weights, and groups come from visiting every node once per component.
questions.rule: The question tells you whether order of visits, distance or weight matters.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A delivery network has roads with different toll amounts. Which method finds the cheapest total toll from the depot to every town?
options: Dijkstra's algorithm, which pops the town with the smallest known toll
BFS, which reaches towns in order of the number of roads and so finds the cheapest route
DFS with a seen set, which tries each town once
A sliding window over the towns in id order
optionExplain: Right: it measures total weight, and the tolls here are non-negative.
BFS minimises roads, not tolls. A route with more roads can cost less.
DFS visits each town once but gives no ordering by total toll.
Town ids have no relation to distances, so a window over them says nothing about toll.
questions.explain: Different weights and a question about the lowest total are the cue for Dijkstra's algorithm.
questions.rule: Lowest total weight on weighted edges calls for Dijkstra's algorithm.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Roads A-B, B-C and C-D cost 1 each; road A-D costs 10. For A to D, what do BFS and the cheapest toll report?
options: BFS finds the 3-road route costing 3; the cheapest toll is the direct road at 10
BFS finds the 1-road route costing 10; the cheapest toll is 3 over 3 roads
Both find the 3-road route costing 3
Both find the direct road costing 10
optionExplain: This swaps the two measures. BFS prefers fewer roads, and 3 is the cheaper toll, not the dearer one.
Right: BFS counts roads, so the direct road wins with 1, but the three small roads add up to 3, which is cheaper.
BFS reaches D first along the direct road, which has one road, so it does not choose the three small roads.
The direct road has the fewest roads, but the three small roads have the lower total.
questions.explain: BFS minimises the number of edges and Dijkstra's algorithm the total weight, and the two disagree when one heavy edge outweighs several light ones.
questions.rule: Fewest edges and lowest weight can be different routes.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: a DFS with a seen set returns the path with the fewest edges, because the seen set stops it from wandering.
questions.explain: A seen set prevents repeats but does not order the search by distance. In a square of four nodes where node 0 is also joined to node 3, a DFS that tries node 1 first reaches node 3 in three steps, while BFS finds it in one.
questions.rule: Only BFS guarantees the fewest edges.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A robot on a 50 by 50 grid may break at most 2 walls. BFS for the fewest moves uses how many states?
options: 2,500, one per cell
5,000, one per cell and a break count of 2, which doubles the 2,500 cells
7,500, one per cell and number of breaks left: 0, 1 or 2
6,250,000, one per pair of cells
optionExplain: The cell alone is not enough: reaching a cell with two breaks left is a different situation from reaching it with none left.
The break count takes three values, 0, 1 and 2, not two.
Right: the state is the cell plus the breaks left, so there are 2,500 cells times 3 values.
The state does not need a second cell. It needs only the cell and the breaks left.
questions.explain: The checklist for BFS asks whether the node needs extra state. Here it does, and every distinct combination is a separate state that can be visited once.
questions.rule: Count states as the product of the ranges of the state variables.
questions.teaches: BFS time and space grow with the number of states, which is the product of the ranges of each state variable, so one extra variable with 3 values triples the work.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: With coins 1, 3 and 4, taking the largest coin that fits at each step, how many coins make 6, compared with the fewest possible?
options: 3 coins, while 2 coins is possible
2 coins, which is also the fewest possible
2 coins, but 1 coin is possible
3 coins, which is also the fewest possible
optionExplain: Right: largest-first takes 4, then 1 and 1, which is 3 coins, while 3 and 3 is 2 coins.
Two coins is the fewest, but largest-first does not reach it: after taking 4 only 2 cents remain, which needs two 1-cent coins.
No single coin is worth 6, so 1 coin is not possible.
Three coins is what largest-first uses, but two 3-cent coins give fewer.
questions.explain: A locally best choice, the biggest coin, closed off a better combination. The card next shows how to choose among greedy, DP, backtracking and binary search.
questions.rule: A locally best choice can lose when choices interact.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: For a find-all task on an input of about 15 items or fewer, the course suggests the approach called ____.
questions.explain: The course says backtracking suits tasks that ask for all of something, and that very small input limits, around n of 15 or less, are a strong hint because the cost is exponential.
questions.rule: Find-all tasks on tiny inputs suggest backtracking.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Pick study days for the most total points, but studying on a day forces a rest day after it. Which approach fits?
options: Greedy, studying first on the day with the most points
DP, comparing studying a day against resting, using the best results of later days
Binary search on the total points, checking each total for whether it can be reached
Backtracking over every subset of days, even for 100,000 days
optionExplain: The best single day may block a neighbour, and two smaller days together could be worth more.
Right: choosing a day changes which days remain, so each choice must be compared with its alternative.
Binary search needs a yes-or-no check whose answers split into two zones. Here the choices interact, and the check is the hard part.
Backtracking is exponential and suits tiny inputs. A long calendar needs a polynomial method.
questions.explain: Decisions that affect later decisions are the DP sign. The greedy rule fails because the best-looking day can cost more than it gains.
questions.rule: When one choice rules out later ones, compare branches with DP.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Daily points 4, 9, 6, 5, 8; studying a day rules out both neighbours. What do largest-first greedy and the best plan score?
options: Both score 18
Both score 17
Greedy scores 17 and the best plan scores 18
Greedy scores 17 and the best plan scores 19
optionExplain: Greedy takes 9 first and so loses the 6, which the best plan keeps.
The best plan is not 17. Days 1, 3 and 5, with points 4, 6 and 8, are not neighbours and give 18.
Right: greedy takes 9, which rules out 4 and 6, then 8, for 17. Taking 4, 6 and 8 gives 18.
No set of non-neighbouring days totals 19. The best possible is 18.
questions.explain: Greedy commits to the 9 and cannot take it back, while the best plan skips it. The two totals differ by 1.
questions.rule: Test a greedy rule on a small case where an early pick blocks others.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: a greedy rule that matches the expected output on three sample inputs is thereby shown to be correct.
questions.explain: Samples cannot show that no input beats the rule. Correctness needs an argument that no other choice at a step can do better.
questions.rule: Greedy needs a proof, not samples alone.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: To list all 6-digit PINs using only digits 0 to 4, backtracking skips bad digits at once. How many full PINs does it build?
options: 1,000,000, the same as generating every PIN and checking it
30, from 5 digits times 6 positions, since each position adds its own 5 choices
3,125, from 5 choices at each of 5 positions
15,625, which is 5 choices at each of the 6 positions multiplied together
optionExplain: That is the exhaustive search. Backtracking does not build a PIN with a digit above 4.
Choices at the positions multiply, they do not add.
A PIN has 6 positions, not 5, so the count is 5 to the 6th.
Right: 5 to the 6th is 15,625, and each built PIN is already valid.
questions.explain: Backtracking reaches the same answers as exhaustive search, but it builds only the paths that can still succeed, here those with every digit from 0 to 4.
questions.rule: Prune as soon as a partial answer breaks the constraint.
questions.teaches: An exhaustive search generates every candidate and then checks each one, whereas backtracking abandons a path as soon as it cannot lead to a solution, so it generates far fewer possibilities.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which input limit most strongly hints that about 2 to the n work is intended?
options: n of at most 10
n of at most 1,000
n between 11 and 20
n of at most 100,000
optionExplain: At 10 even factorial and higher-base exponential costs are fast enough, so the hint is broader than 2 to the n.
At 1,000, 2 to the n is astronomically large. The hint here is about n squared.
Right: at 20, 2 to the n is about a million steps, while higher bases are already too slow.
At 100,000 only about n log n or O(n) is acceptable.
questions.explain: Each range of n allows a different cost, and 11 to 20 is where 2 to the n is the likely target. The card next lists all the ranges.
questions.rule: Limits of 11 to 20 point to about 2 to the n.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each limit on n to the cost it suggests.
pairs: Factorial or high-base exponential, so backtracking
About 2 to the n, a take-or-skip choice per element
About n cubed, brute force with nested loops
About n squared, with nested loops
questions.explain: Each range of n marks the largest cost a computer still handles quickly, from factorial at the smallest limits to n squared at about 1,000.
questions.rule: The limit tells you the largest cost class that can be intended.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A problem allows n up to 100,000 and your idea checks every pair, about 5 billion checks. What does the course suggest?
options: Keep it, since quadratic cost is fine at this limit and a computer handles 5 billion checks quickly
Replace the inner loop with a hash map, pointers, a window, a stack, binary search or a heap
Switch to backtracking, which is meant for large inputs
Sort first and then still compare every pair
optionExplain: Quadratic cost is acceptable only up to about 1,000. At 100,000 it means about 5 billion pair checks.
Right: at this limit nested loops are too slow, and these techniques simulate the inner loop in O(1) or O(log n).
Backtracking is exponential and suits limits around 15, not 100,000.
Sorting costs n log n but does not remove the pair loop, which stays quadratic.
questions.explain: The count of pair checks is n times n minus 1, divided by 2, which is 4,999,950,000. The course says nested loops are unacceptable here.
questions.rule: At 100,000 an O(n squared) idea needs a technique that replaces the inner loop.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: with n up to 15, an idea that tries all 15! orderings fits, because 15 is a small limit.
questions.explain: 15! is 1,307,674,368,000, about 1.3 trillion. Factorial is acceptable only at about n = 10, and from 11 to 20 the target is about 2 to the n.
questions.rule: A small limit does not make every cost acceptable.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A string problem allows length up to 100,000. Your O(n) idea loops over the 26 letters at each position, about 2,600,000 steps. Acceptable?
options: No: any constant factor above 1 makes a linear idea too slow once n reaches 100,000
No: the 26 makes it quadratic, like a nested loop over n
Yes, but only if the string is sorted first
Yes: it is still linear, and a constant factor of about 40 is reasonable for O(n)
optionExplain: Constants do matter, but only when they are large. A factor of 26 gives 2.6 million steps.
The loop over 26 letters does not grow with n, so it multiplies n by a constant instead of by n.
Sorting is not needed. The cost is already 26 times n.
Right: 26 is a constant, so the cost is O(26n), which is common in string problems.
questions.explain: At this limit the course accepts O(n) with a constant factor up to about 40, so a loop over the alphabet at each position is within bounds.
questions.rule: A moderate constant factor inside an O(n) idea is acceptable.
questions.teaches: For an O(n) algorithm the constant factor can reasonably be as large as about 40, so looping over the 26 letters at each position, O(26n), is acceptable.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In an interview you can see only a brute-force idea at first. What does the course suggest?
options: Stay silent until you have found the optimal solution on your own, then code it in one go
Skip it, because slow ideas cannot pass in an interview
Replace it with a known solution recalled from memory
Implement it, say it is brute force, then find the slow steps and improve them
optionExplain: Silence hides your thinking. The course asks you to keep talking so the interviewer can give hints.
A slow idea that you improve is a normal route, and small limits can even make it acceptable.
The course says it is important to understand solutions, not to memorise them, because follow-ups test understanding.
Right: the course says not to be scared of starting with brute force, as long as you acknowledge it and then optimise the slow parts.
questions.explain: Brute force is a starting point to improve, not a failure. The card next shows how to find the step worth improving.
questions.rule: Start with brute force, name it, then optimise the slow parts.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each slow step to the tool that speeds it up.
pairs: Adding up a range again for each of many queries
Scanning for the largest remaining item every round
Scanning ahead for the next greater value from each position
Solving the same recursive case again and again
questions.explain: Each tool removes one kind of repeated work: shared range totals, a maintained maximum, a stack that remembers unresolved items, and a cache of answers.
questions.rule: Find the repeated work, then pick the tool that removes it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A shop checks each of 50,000 orders against all earlier orders for a duplicate id, about 1.25 billion comparisons. What fixes the slow step?
options: A hash set of ids seen so far, checked in O(1): about 50,000 steps in all
A prefix sum of the ids, subtracted per order
A min heap of the ids, which finds the smallest id quickly
Memoizing each pair's comparison, so no pair is compared more than once in the loop
optionExplain: Right: the repeated work is a membership scan, which a set answers in O(1).
Prefix sums answer range totals, and a duplicate check is not a sum.
A heap finds the smallest id, but duplicate checking asks about a given id, which a heap cannot check quickly.
No pair is compared twice already, so there are no repeated calls to cache.
questions.explain: The inner loop asks whether an id exists among earlier ones. That is a membership question, and a set turns n squared over 2 comparisons into n lookups.
questions.rule: A repeated membership scan is replaced by a hash set.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: with n up to 100, a cubic brute force cannot pass, so a linear-time solution is required.
questions.explain: Up to 100, the expected cost is about n cubed, and the course notes that easy problems often have this bound because brute force can pass even when a linear solution exists.
questions.rule: A small limit can make brute force the intended answer.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Each of 100,000 queries asks how many of 1,000,000 unsorted prices are at least x. Scanning costs about 10^11 steps. Better plan?
options: Build a prefix sum of the unsorted prices and subtract per query
Put the prices in a hash set and check whether x is present
Sort the prices once, then binary search each query: about 22 million steps
Keep a heap of the prices and, for each query, pop prices until one falls below x
optionExplain: Prefix sums give totals over index ranges, not counts of prices above a value.
A set tests for one exact price. The queries ask for a count at or above x.
Right: the sort costs about 20 million steps and each query about 20, so the total is roughly 22 million.
Popping changes the heap, and walking it for each query can again cost the whole collection.
questions.explain: The repeated work is scanning for a position among the prices. Sorting once makes that position findable by binary search, and the count follows from it.
questions.rule: Pay for a sort once, then answer every query by binary search.
questions.teaches: If the prices are sorted, the insertion point i of x gives the count directly as m minus i, and sorting once costs O(m log m) while each query costs O(log m), for O((m + n) log m) in all.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Return the k most frequent words in a list of n words. Which two structures work together?
options: A hash map for the counts and a min heap capped at k
A stack for the counts and a queue for the order of the words
A set of the words and a queue of the last k words seen
Two sorted arrays, one holding words and one holding counts
optionExplain: Right: the map counts each word, and the capped heap keeps the k highest counts.
A stack and a queue keep arrival order. Neither looks up a word's count or ranks counts.
A set records presence only, and the last k words seen are not the k most frequent.
Keeping two arrays sorted together costs more than counting in a map and ranking with a heap.
questions.explain: Counting words is one job and ranking the counts is another, and each has its own structure. The card next shows more pairs like this.
questions.rule: A counts map plus a capped heap gives the k most frequent items.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each problem to the pair of patterns that solves it.
pairs: Count subarrays with an exact sum
Running prefix sum plus a counts map
Maximum of every window of size k
Smallest capacity that passes a check
Binary search plus an O(n) check
Fewest moves with limited wall breaks
BFS over cell and breaks-left states
questions.explain: Each pair splits a job: one pattern drives the loop or search, and the other answers the question asked at every step.
questions.rule: Name which pattern frames the solution and which answers its inner question.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Find the 10 most frequent of 1,000,000 words with a counts map and a min heap capped at 10. What is the cost?
options: O(n log n), about 20 million steps, since the heap grows to hold and sort every word
O(n log k), a few million steps, since the heap holds at most k + 1 items
O(k), since only 10 words matter
O(n squared), since each word is compared with every other
optionExplain: A heap that grows to n items would cost log n per operation, but the cap keeps it near 10 items.
Right: each of the n words costs a heap operation of O(log k), and k is only 10.
Every word must be counted and offered to the heap, so the work grows with n, not with k.
The map counts each word in O(1), so no word is compared with all the others.
questions.explain: Counting is O(n) and the capped heap adds log k per item. The cap is what turns log n into log k.
questions.rule: A heap capped at k costs O(n log k).

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: the shrinking while loop inside the window loop makes a window with a counts map O(n squared).
questions.explain: Each element enters the window once and leaves it once, so the left pointer moves at most n times in total. The solution stays O(n).
questions.rule: Count total movements, not nested loop headers.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A truck takes up to 3 events, each with an entry cost and a payout. Which plan picks the best affordable event each time?
options: Sort events by payout and take the three largest, ignoring whether the entry cost is affordable yet
