Binary search the entry cost, with a check that sums the payouts of affordable events
Keep a counts map from entry cost to payout and take any three of the events in it
Sort events by entry cost, add newly affordable ones to a max heap of payouts, pop the largest
optionExplain: The top payouts may not be affordable yet. Cash grows only after taking events.
A threshold on entry cost does not say which events to take. Each pick changes what is affordable.
A map stores a payout per cost but chooses nothing, and any three may be unaffordable or low in value.
Right: sorting exposes events as the cash grows, and the heap hands over the best payout among those.
questions.explain: Two jobs combine here: finding what is affordable now, which a sorted pointer does, and finding the best of those, which a heap does. In Python the max heap of payouts is simulated by storing each payout as a negative number.
questions.rule: Sort for what is available, use a heap for the best of it.
questions.teaches: Python's heapq is a min heap, so to get a max heap of payouts you store each payout as a negative number and negate it again when you pop.

questions.section: 2. Arrays and strings | 2.1 Arrays and strings

media.alt: Table comparing time costs of seven operations on an array or list versus an immutable string. Appending to the end: amortized constant for the list, linear for the string. Popping from the end: constant versus linear. Inserting or deleting away from the end: linear for both. Modifying an element: constant for the list, linear for the string. Random access by index: constant for both. Checking whether an element exists: linear for both.

questions.q: In the table, sort each operation by how its cost on an immutable string compares with its cost on a list.

items.t: Appending to the end
Popping from the end
Modifying one element
Reading an element by index
Inserting away from the end
Checking whether a value exists

questions.explain: Appending, popping and modifying each force a string to be rebuilt, so they are linear there but constant (append amortized) on a list. Reading by index is constant for both, and insertion and existence checks are linear for both.
questions.rule: Immutability makes every change to a string cost O(n), while reading by index stays O(1).

media.alt: Top: a row of eight numbers 3, 6, 2, 8, 1, 4, 1, 5 with the boxes 8, 1, 4, 1 highlighted, sum 14. Bottom: the prefix sums 3, 9, 11, 19, 20, 24, 25, 30. A long green line reaches the prefix value 25 and a short red line the value 11; 25 minus 11 gives 14, found in constant time.

questions.q: Suppose the highlighted subarray also took in the 2 on its left. Its sum is then 25 minus ____.
questions.explain: The new subarray starts at index 2, so the part to subtract is everything before index 2: 3 + 6 = 9, the prefix value at index 1. The sum is 25 - 9 = 16, which matches 2 + 8 + 1 + 4 + 1.
questions.rule: The sum of a subarray is the prefix value at its end minus the prefix value just before its start.

questions.section: Count the number of subarrays with an "exact" constraint

media.alt: An array 6, 5, -3, 2, -4, 8, 10 with k = 3. Marker j sits on -3 and marker i on 8. The first two numbers form a red prefix with sum 11, the stretch from -3 to 8 is green with sum 3, and everything up to the 8 is blue with sum 14. It shows that curr minus k equals the prefix sum before j.

questions.q: Suppose k = 8 in the diagram's array. With curr = 14 at the 8, how many subarrays ending there sum to 8?
options: One, because the earlier prefix sum 6 is found in the map once
Two, because the earlier prefix sum 6 occurred twice, giving two starts
Zero, because the prefix sum 14 is not equal to k, so nothing ends there
Three, because the prefix sums 6, 8 and 6 all count toward the answer
optionExplain: Tempting if you only check that 6 exists, but the map counts how often it occurred: 6 was the prefix after the first number and again after the -4.
Right: curr - k = 6, and 6 occurred twice before the 8, so [5, -3, 2, -4, 8] and [8] both sum to 8.
The lookup uses curr - k = 6, not curr itself; curr only has to differ from k.
The prefix sum 8 equals k but is not curr - k, so it is not a start point for a subarray ending at the 8.
questions.explain: The value to look up is curr - k = 14 - 8 = 6. The prefix sums before the 8 are 6, 11, 8, 10, 6, so 6 occurred twice and two subarrays end at the 8 with sum 8.
questions.rule: Each earlier occurrence of curr - k gives one subarray ending here with sum k.

questions.section: 4. Linked Lists | 4.2 Fast and slow pointers

media.alt: Two small linked-list drawings. Left, labelled as having no cycle: nodes 0, 1, 2 in a row with arrows pointing right. Right, labelled as having a cycle: four nodes 0, 1, 2, 3 in a square, with arrows 0 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 3 and 3 back to 0, so following next never ends.

questions.q: In the diagram's four-node cycle, slow and fast both start at node 0. They meet after ____ loop iterations.
questions.explain: Slow moves one node and fast two per iteration. After 1: slow at 1, fast at 2. After 2: slow at 2, fast at 0. After 3: slow at 3, fast at 2. After 4: both are at 0.
questions.rule: Inside a cycle, fast gains one position per iteration, so the two pointers must meet.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.2 Binary trees - DFS

media.alt: A binary tree with arrows from parent to child. Root 0 has children 1 (left) and 2 (right). Node 1 has children 3 (left) and 4 (right). Node 4 has only a right child, 6. Node 2 has only a right child, 5. Nodes 3, 6 and 5 are leaves.

questions.q: In the diagram's tree, which list is the inorder traversal?
optionExplain: This is the preorder: it lists each node before its subtrees.
This is the postorder: it lists each node after both subtrees.
Right: left subtree of 0 gives 3, 1, 4, 6 (4 has no left child, so 4 comes before its right child 6), then 0, then 2 followed by its right child 5.
This puts 6 before 4 and 5 before 2, as if a lone right child were visited before its parent; inorder visits the parent first when the left side is empty.
questions.explain: Inorder visits left subtree, node, right subtree. Node 4 has no left child, so it comes right before 6, and node 2 has no left child, so it comes right before 5.
questions.rule: Inorder: left subtree, then the node, then right subtree; a missing left child means the node comes first.

questions.section: 6. Trees and graphs | 6.4 Binary search trees

media.alt: A binary search tree: root 23 with left child 8 and right child 37. Node 8 has children 6 and 17; node 17 has children 9 and 20. Node 37 has children 29 and 50. Every node's left subtree holds smaller values and its right subtree larger ones.

questions.q: Suppose we search the diagram's BST for 25. Put the nodes compared, in order, until an empty child ends the search.
questions.explain: 25 is larger than 23, so go right to 37. 25 is smaller than 37, so go left to 29. 25 is smaller than 29 and 29 has no left child, so 25 is absent.
questions.rule: At each node of a BST, compare with the target and discard the subtree on the wrong side.

questions.section: How are graphs given in algorithm problems?

media.alt: A directed graph with arrows 0 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 0 and 2 to 3, drawn beside its four-by-four adjacency matrix of 0s and 1s. Row 0 has a 1 only in column 1, row 1 only in column 2, row 2 in columns 0 and 3, and row 3 is all zeros.

questions.q: In the diagram, which statements about the adjacency matrix are true? Select all that apply.
options: Row 3 is all zeros, because node 3 has no edges leaving it
Column 3 holds a single 1, in row 2, for the edge from 2 to 3
Row 2 holds a single 1, because node 2 has one edge leaving it
graph[0][2] is 1, because node 2 has an edge pointing to node 0
optionExplain: Right: a row lists the edges leaving a node, and node 3 has none.
Right: the edge from 2 to 3 is graph[2][3], so column 3 has its only 1 in row 2.
Node 2 has two edges leaving it, to 0 and 3, so row 2 has two 1s.
The edge from 2 to 0 is graph[2][0], row 2 and column 0; graph[0][2] would mean an edge from 0 to 2.
questions.explain: graph[i][j] equal to 1 means an edge from node i to node j, so rows show outgoing edges and columns show incoming ones. Node 3 has one edge in and none out; node 2 has two edges out.
questions.rule: graph[i][j] == 1 means an edge from i to j: read rows for edges out, columns for edges in.

media.alt: A directed graph of six cities numbered 0 to 5 with one route between any two. Arrows run from 0 to 1, from 3 to 1, from 2 to 3, from 4 to 0 and from 5 to 4. City 0 is at the left, and the other cities hang off it like a tree.

questions.q: In the diagram, which single road must be reversed so every city can reach city 0?
options: The road from 3 to 1, since the road leaving a middle city must be flipped
The road from 5 to 4, because it starts at the city farthest from 0
The road from 4 to 0, because it ends at city 0 itself and so blocks it
The road from 0 to 1, because it is the only one pointing away from 0
optionExplain: From 0 the cities are met in the order 1 then 3; the road 3 to 1 runs from farther to nearer, so it already points toward 0.
5 to 4 runs from a farther city to a nearer one, so it already leads toward 0.
A road ending at 0 is exactly what every city needs; 4 to 0 already points toward 0.
Right: moving away from 0 along 0 to 1, the original road points the wrong way. The others (3 to 1, 2 to 3, 4 to 0, 5 to 4) already point toward 0.
questions.explain: With one route between any two cities, every road must point toward 0. Four of the five roads do; only 0 to 1 points away, so exactly one reversal is needed.
questions.rule: A road met while moving away from city 0 is wrong exactly when it exists as given.

media.alt: Final eight-by-eight grid headed Done: every cell shows its steps to the nearest of four zeros, which sit at row 3 column 4, row 5 column 6, row 7 column 2 and row 8 column 8, counting from 1. Numbers grow by one per step away from a zero; the top-left corner shows 5 and the top-right corner 6, the largest.

questions.q: Suppose the zero at row 3, column 4 (counting from 1) were absent from the input. What would the top-left cell then show?
options: 7, the distance to the zero at row 7, column 2
5, unchanged, since the removed zero still counts
9, the distance to the zero at row 5, column 6
14, the distance to the zero at row 8, column 8
optionExplain: Right: the nearest remaining zero is at row 7, column 2, six rows and one column away, so 6 + 1 = 7.
The 5 came from the removed zero; without it that distance no longer exists.
The zero at row 5, column 6 is four rows and five columns away, which is farther than another zero.
That corner zero is the farthest of the three remaining zeros, so it is not the nearest.
questions.explain: Each cell shows the distance to its nearest zero. Without the zero at row 3, column 4, the remaining distances from the top-left corner are 7, 9 and 14, so the cell shows 7.
questions.rule: A cell's value is the distance to its nearest zero, so removing that zero raises it to the next nearest.

questions.q: In the diagram, the median arrow points at 26. Which statements about the two heaps are true?
options: The median is 26, the top of the max heap that holds the extra element.
Every hidden value in the min heap is at least 32.
The median is 29, the average of the two tops 26 and 32.
A hidden value in the max heap may be larger than 26.
Every hidden value in the max heap is at most 26.
optionExplain: Right: the heaps hold six and five values, an odd total, so the median is the extra top of the max heap.
Right: the whole min heap holds the upper half, so nothing in it is below its top, 32.
Averaging the tops is for an even count; here the sizes differ by one, so the extra top alone is the median.
A hidden max heap value above 26 would sit above the median, which breaks the lower half rule.
Right: the max heap holds the lower half, so no value in it exceeds its top, 26.
questions.explain: With an odd total the max heap holds one extra, and its top, 26, is the median. The halves are ordered: nothing in the max heap exceeds 26 and nothing in the min heap is below 32.
questions.rule: With an odd count, the median is the top of the larger heap, not an average.

media.alt: A row of eleven boxes split into two groups. Six green boxes under the label max heap end with the value 26 beside the middle; five blue boxes under min heap begin with 32. Other boxes show question marks for hidden values. An arrow under 26 marks the median. A note says hidden min heap values are at least 32 and hidden max heap values at most 26.

questions.q: In the diagram, a maximum is wanted and a check at 100,000 reports impossible. What can the search discard?
options: Only 100,000 itself, since the values next to it may still be possible
100,000 and every value above it, since the impossible zone has no breaks
Every value below 100,000, since smaller candidates must be impossible too
Nothing yet, since a maximum search has to test the larger values as well
optionExplain: The zones have no breaks, so no possible value can sit above an impossible one.
Right: the possible zone is on the left and the impossible zone is one unbroken block on the right.
Smaller values lie in or before the possible zone, so this discards the wrong side.
A maximum is the threshold between the zones, so the larger values add nothing once one check is impossible.
questions.explain: Impossible values form one unbroken zone to the right of the threshold. A failing check at 100,000 means everything from there upward fails too, so the range shrinks to the values below it.
questions.rule: One check says which side of the threshold you are on, so half the range goes.

media.alt: A number line from 0 through ten, hundred and thousand toward infinity, split into two colored blocks. The left block, labelled possible, covers the smaller values; the right block, labelled impossible, covers all larger ones. An arrow marks the boundary above one thousand, called the threshold, which is the answer to a maximum question and can be found by binary search.

questions.q: In the diagram, one level has 676 nodes and each node has 26 children. How many nodes are on the level below?
options: 702 nodes, from adding 26 to 676
456,976 nodes, from squaring 676
17,576 nodes, from 676 times 26
1,352 nodes, from doubling 676
optionExplain: Each of the 676 nodes gets its own 26 children, so the count is multiplied, not added to.
Squaring would give each node 676 children; here each node has only 26.
Right: every one of the 676 nodes has 26 children, and 676 times 26 is 17,576, which is 26 cubed.
Doubling would mean two children per node, but every node has 26.
questions.explain: Each level multiplies the node count by 26: 26, then 676, then 17,576. That is why exhaustive search over strings of length n grows as 26 to the power n.
questions.rule: With c choices per piece, level d of the tree holds c to the power d nodes.

media.alt: A tree for strings built from the letters a to z. The root is the empty string and has 26 children, one arrow to each letter, laid out in a row with a bracket beneath them. A caption says the level below holds 676 nodes and that every node has 26 children.

questions.q: Suppose the tree in the diagram were drawn for four distinct numbers: ____ nodes would stand after two numbers are chosen.
questions.explain: The first choice has 4 options. The second must skip the number already used, leaving 3. So 4 times 3 is 12; the diagram's three numbers give 3 times 2, which is 6.
questions.rule: Each level has one fewer child per node, because used numbers are skipped.

media.alt: A tree of orderings of the numbers 1, 2 and 3. The root is empty and has three children, one per number. Under each child hang the two numbers not yet used, and under each of those the one number left, so every path has three steps. The six leaves are labelled with the six orderings.

questions.q: Using the flowchart, which traversal does each problem lead to?

items.t: Graph: fewest moves between two cells of a maze
Tree: add up the values on one chosen level
Tree: check whether a root-to-leaf path adds up to 20
Graph: count the separate islands on a map
Tree: check whether two trees are identical

questions.explain: Shortest-path and level questions lead to breadth-first search. A graph question that is not about the shortest path, and a tree question that is not about levels, lead to depth-first search.
questions.rule: Shortest path or specific levels point to BFS; otherwise the chart points to DFS.

media.alt: A flowchart headed by the kind of input, with three starting boxes. For a graph, a question about the shortest path or fewest steps leads to breadth-first search, otherwise depth-first search. For a tree, a question about specific depths or levels leads to breadth-first search, otherwise depth-first search. For a linked list, finding a position or detecting cycles leads to fast and slow pointers, reversing to a prev pointer, and returning the original head to a dummy pointer.

questions.q: In the array and string flowchart, match each need to the technique it points to.
pairs: List every arrangement of a set of items
Find words that share a typed prefix
Repeatedly remove the largest remaining value
Check whether a given item has been seen
questions.explain: Asking for all of something points to backtracking, prefix matching to a trie, continuously removing the max or min to a heap, and finding a specific element to a hash map or set.
questions.rule: Read the wording of the question to find the branch of the flowchart.

media.alt: A flowchart for array or string input, starting at a Start box. A sorted array points to binary search and two pointers. Otherwise it asks what is wanted: all of something leads to backtracking; ways, best value or possibility lead to dynamic programming if choices affect later choices, else greedy; prefix matching leads to a trie; a specific element leads to a hash map or set; subarrays lead to sliding window; continuously removing the max or min leads to a heap.

questions.q: In the diagram, order the three routes from node 0 to node 4 by total weight, lowest first.
questions.explain: Going through 1 and 2 costs 2 + 1 + 3 = 6. The direct edge costs 10. Going through 3 costs 4 + 15 = 19. The route with the most edges is the cheapest.
questions.rule: Compare sums of edge weights, not numbers of edges.

media.alt: A directed weighted graph of five numbered nodes. Edges: 0 to 1 weight 2, 1 to 2 weight 1, 2 to 4 weight 3, 0 to 4 weight 10, 0 to 3 weight 4, and 3 to 4 weight 15. Three different routes lead from node 0 to node 4, with different numbers of edges and different total weights.
